text: Honey Never Spoils, Archaeologists have found pots of honey in ancient Egyptian tombs that are over 3,000 years old and still perfectly edible.
label: supported
reason: Several sources, including Smithsonian Magazine's well-known piece on why honey never spoils, report that archaeologists found pots of honey in ancient Egyptian tombs. The honey was thousands of years old (about 3,000 years) and was described as still edible. These sources credit honey's low moisture, high acidity and antibacterial enzymes for keeping it from spoiling. One caveat: 'perfectly edible' is how popular accounts put it, and I found no lab test confirming it. Still, no source contradicted the claim, so it counts as supported.

text: Honey Never Spoils, archaeologists have found pots of honey in ancient Egyptian tombs that are over 3,000 years old and still perfectly edible.
label: supported
reason: Several sources, including History Facts and Smithsonian-style science reporting, say archaeologists found pots of honey more than 3,000 years old in ancient Egyptian tombs and that it was still edible. They explain this by honey's low moisture, high acidity and hydrogen peroxide. One caveat is that "honey never spoils" holds only when it is sealed from moisture, and "perfectly edible" mostly comes from secondhand accounts. Still, the claim matches the widely reported evidence.

text: Scientists estimate that there are approximately 8.7 million identified species on Earth, but they believe that up to 80% of all species remain undiscovered.
label: contradicted
reason: The 8.7 million figure is an estimate of how many species exist in total, not how many have been identified. Mora et al. (2011) estimated about 8.7 million species on Earth, give or take 1.3 million. Only about 1.2 million have actually been catalogued, which is less than 15% of that total. The source also says 86% of land species and 91% of marine species remain undiscovered, which is more than 80%. So the claim that 8.7 million species are identified is wrong.

text: Scientists estimate that there are approximately 8.7 million identified species on Earth, but up to 80% of all species remain undiscovered.
label: contradicted
reason: The 8.7 million figure from Mora et al. (2011) is the estimated total number of species on Earth, not the number already identified. Only about 1.2 million species have been catalogued. The same study estimates that 86% of land species and 91% of marine species are still undiscovered, which is more than 80%, not 'up to 80%'. The claim misdescribes the figure as identified species, so it is contradicted.

text: One flex of a human eyebrow contains around 250,000 sweat glands.
label: contradicted
reason: ScienceDirect and SweatHelp both say the whole human body has only about 2–4 million sweat glands. A patent source gives eccrine gland density as roughly 50–200 per cm². The eyebrow area covers only a few square centimetres, so it would hold somewhere from hundreds to a few thousand glands, nowhere near 250,000. That would be about 6–12% of all the body's sweat glands. The idea of 'one flex' of an eyebrow containing glands also makes no sense physically. The figure in the claim doesn't fit established anatomy.

text: A愸 is the longest word in the English language that can be typed using only the left hand on a standard keyboard layout.
label: contradicted
reason: The claim names "A愸", which isn't an English word and includes a Chinese character, so it can't be the longest English word typed with the left hand only. Sources usually name "stewardesses" as the longest such word on a QWERTY keyboard; it has 12 letters, though the Brainly answer says 13.

text: Scientists estimate that there are approximately 8.7 million identified species on Earth, but the actual number could be as high as 30 million.
label: contradicted
reason: The 8.7 million figure comes from Mora et al. (2011, PLoS Biology). It estimates the total number of eukaryotic species on Earth, not the number already identified. The same study says only about 1.2 million species have been catalogued, and that about 86% of species still have not been described. Calling 8.7 million "identified" species is therefore wrong. Earlier expert estimates ranged from 3 to 100 million, so 30 million is also not the upper bound.

text: Honey Never Spoils; Archaeologists have found pots of honey in ancient Egyptian tombs that are over 3,000 years old and still perfectly edible.
label: supported
reason: Several popular sources say archaeologists found pots of honey in ancient Egyptian tombs that are about 3,000 years old and still edible. They explain this by honey's low moisture, acidity and natural hydrogen peroxide, which keep it from spoiling. Smithsonian Magazine is widely cited for the same account. One caveat: these are popular-science sources, and I didn't find a primary archaeological report confirming that the honey was edible. The search returned only one result, and nothing in it contradicted the claim.

text: Scientists estimate that there may be between 700,000 and 1 million species on Earth that have not yet been discovered.
label: contradicted
reason: The usual scientific estimate is far higher than the claim says. BBC Science Focus cites models that converge on about 8.7 million eukaryotic species in total. Only about 1.64 million of those have been named, so roughly 81–86% are still undiscovered. That works out to around 7 million unknown species, not 700,000 to 1 million, and counting bacteria could push the total much higher still. The 700,000–1 million figure looks like it comes from estimates of total marine species or the roughly 1 million species threatened with extinction, not from estimates of undiscovered species on Earth.

text: In 2019, the world's largest snowflake was recorded in Montana in 1887, measuring 15 inches in diameter and 8 inches thick.
label: supported
reason: Several sources agree that the largest snowflake on record fell at Fort Keogh, Montana, on January 28, 1887, and measured 15 inches across and 8 inches thick. NC State University and radio station articles say Guinness lists this as the record, and it still stood in 2019. The "In 2019" wording is odd, but it reads best as "as of 2019" and nothing contradicts it. One caveat: the original report is unverified. Mystic Stamp calls it a claim that "hasn't been verified," but the claim says the snowflake was recorded, which matches the record.

text: Because of its unique rotation and high-speed winds, the planet Venus is the only planet in our solar system that rotates clockwise.
label: contradicted
reason: Venus is not the only planet that spins clockwise. Seen from above the orbital plane, Uranus also has retrograde (clockwise) rotation because of its extreme axial tilt of about 98°. Even WorldAtlas, which headlines Venus as 'the only planet that rotates clockwise', says in the same article that Uranus appears to spin clockwise from above its orbit and is often classed as retrograde. The claim also gets the cause wrong. Venus's backward spin isn't explained by its high-speed winds. It is usually attributed to an ancient collision or to tidal and atmospheric effects, and the exact mechanism is still uncertain.

text: Honey Never Spoils is a fact, archaeologists have found pots of honey in ancient Egyptian tombs that are over 3,000 years old and still perfectly edible.
label: supported
reason: Several sources, including My Modern Met citing Smithsonian Magazine and a Yahoo News science article, report that archaeologists found pots of honey in ancient Egyptian tombs, about 3,000 years old, that were still safe to eat. They explain this by honey's low moisture, acidity (pH 3–4.5) and hydrogen peroxide. One caveat: "never spoils" holds only when honey stays sealed and dry, but the sources treat the core claim as accurate.

text: The world's largest snowflake was recorded in Montana in 1887 and measured 15 inches in diameter and 8 inches thick.
label: supported
reason: Several sources, including NC State University News and Guinness-based reports, say the largest reported snowflake fell at Fort Keogh, Montana, on January 28, 1887. They give its size as 15 inches (38.1 cm) wide and 8 inches thick. This matches every part of the claim. Some sources point out that the record was never verified, but none give different figures or a different place or year.

text: Schedule 1 of the Indian Constitution initially listed 29 states; however, there are now a total of eight union territories and 28 states in India.
label: supported
reason: The second half of the claim is clearly correct. Several sources, including vajiramandravi and bharatnotes, say India now has 28 states and 8 union territories, a count that dates from Jammu & Kashmir's reorganisation in 2019. The first half, that the First Schedule originally listed 29 states, is the figure most commonly cited for the 1950 Constitution. Sources such as Vedantu and Testbook describe the original Part A, B, C and D states as 29 in total, and the upsc.xplainer page also uses the figure 29. Sources disagree slightly on how to count, though. One Testbook answer gives 28, because the 29 figure includes the Part D territory (Andaman and Nicobar Islands). On balance, the claim matches the standard account.

text: ablaze or burning in a fire.
label: not_verifiable
reason: The claim is a definition fragment with no subject, so it doesn't name the word or thing it describes. Dictionaries (Wiktionary, Collins, Dictionary.com) agree that 'ablaze' means burning or on fire, so the phrase matches words like 'aflame' or 'on fire'. But without knowing which term or entity the claim is about, it can't be checked as a factual statement.

text: One flex of a human eyebrow requires the precise coordination of 32 different facial muscles.
label: contradicted
reason: Anatomy sources say eyebrow movement involves only a handful of muscles, not 32. NCBI StatPearls calls the frontalis the only muscle that raises the eyebrows. Medscape and other sources say the muscles that lower the brow are a small group: the procerus, corrugator supercilii, depressor supercilii and orbicularis oculi. Since about 43 facial muscles exist in total, saying one eyebrow flex coordinates 32 of them is not supported and conflicts with how the anatomy is described.

text: A 통합 bonobo is more closely related to a human than to a gorilla ancestor.
label: supported
reason: My searches support the core claim. Bonobos and chimpanzees (genus Pan) are humans' closest living relatives, and Pan and Homo together form the tribe Hominini, which excludes gorillas. One source states directly that bonobos are "more closely related to humans than they are to gorillas." Two parts of the claim are unclear: the Korean word "통합" ("integrated" or "unified") seems to be a stray insertion, and the phrase "gorilla ancestor" is vague. I read the claim as "bonobos are more closely related to humans than to gorillas," and that is well supported.

text: A decade is not exactly the same as ten years, technically a decade can refer to any period in a sequence of ten, but in practical terms it usually does.
label: supported
reason: Dictionaries back up the main point. Collins defines "decade" as "a period of ten consecutive years" and also as "a group or series of ten," which means the word technically covers sets of ten of anything, not just years. In everyday use, though, it almost always means a ten-year period, as both Collins and Wikipedia confirm. The claim's wording is awkward, but its meaning matches these sources: a decade isn't strictly the same as ten years, yet in practice it usually is.

text: Astronomers estimate that there are approximately 100-400 billion stars in the Milky Way galaxy.
label: supported
reason: Wikipedia's Milky Way article puts the galaxy's star count at 100–400 billion ((1–4)×10^11) and says it "is estimated to contain 100–400 billion stars." That matches the claim exactly. This is a widely cited figure among astronomers, and other sources such as Star Walk give a similar estimate.

text: The world's largest living organism is a fungus called Armillaria ostoyae, covering over 2,200 acres in Oregon, USA.
label: supported
reason: National Wildlife Federation's magazine names Armillaria ostoyae in eastern Oregon as the world's largest living organism and says it covers more than 2,200 acres. Wikipedia agrees: it puts the Malheur National Forest specimen at about 2,200–2,240 acres and calls it the largest, or one of the largest, living organisms on Earth. One caveat: some sources hedge with wording like 'likely' or 'one of the largest', but none of the results contradict the claim.

text: Cats have a highly specialized vocalization range that allows them to produce sounds that humans cannot hear.
label: not_verifiable
reason: The sources I found show that cats can hear ultrasound, roughly up to 64–85 kHz, compared with about 20 kHz for humans. But that is hearing, not voice production. On whether cats actually make sounds humans can't hear, the only evidence is a Medium blog post. It says some 'silent' meows were recorded at up to about 22 kHz, but it is not peer-reviewed. Scientific sources describe cat calls such as purrs (about 20–150 Hz) and meows as falling within human hearing. None of them describe a 'highly specialized vocalization range' that produces inaudible sounds. No reliable source clearly confirms or rules out the claim, so it can't be verified.

text: Tarantulas have been around for a long time, with fossil records showing they've remained largely unchanged for over 100 million years.
label: not_verifiable
reason: Part of the claim holds up: tarantulas are an old lineage. A peer-reviewed study (Journal of Biogeography) and Live Science report that the oldest known tarantula (theraphosid) fossil is in Burmese amber about 100 million years old, and molecular dating puts the group's origin around 120 million years ago. But the fossil record is very sparse: Live Science says only two tarantula fossils are known, one about 16 million and one about 100 million years old. That is not enough to show the group has stayed 'largely unchanged for over 100 million years.' The oldest fossil is roughly 100 million years old, not clearly older. Texas Parks & Wildlife magazine, quoting an expert, says the fossil record shows tarantulas 'virtually unchanged' for more than 20 million years, which is a much shorter span. Only a non-scientific hobbyist page makes the broader 100+ million year claim. The age claim is roughly supported, but the 'unchanged for over 100 million years' claim is not established.

text: Bacteria can only grow and reproduce in "moist" environments,  typically requiring a certain level of humidity to survive.
label: supported
reason: The searches back up the main point. Sources on water activity and food microbiology say microorganisms need available water to grow and reproduce, and below a certain water activity they cannot grow. Most bacteria need a water activity above about 0.90. The survival part is less exact: studies on desiccation show that drying stresses many bacteria, but some species and spores can survive dry conditions in a dormant state. Because the claim says bacteria 'typically' need humidity to survive, it still broadly holds.

text: Thermal energy generated by a person's body heat can power small devices such as smartphones and smartwatches.
label: not_verifiable
reason: The evidence is mixed. Smartwatches are partly supported: the Matrix PowerWatch runs on body heat (plus sunlight in PowerWatch 2), and a Nature Communications study reports a thermoelectric cell array that kept a smartwatch running. However, a recent Gizmodo article says body-heat generators produce only a few hundred microwatts and 'almost certainly won't' power display smartwatches, so the sources conflict. For smartphones, an arXiv analysis estimates body heat gives about 1 mW at best, while a smartphone needs about 70 mW just on standby. No source shows body heat actually powering a smartphone. Because the smartwatch evidence conflicts and the smartphone part is unverified or physically doubtful, the claim cannot be fully supported.

text: One flex of a human eyebrow contains about 500,000 distinct microbe species.
label: contradicted
reason: No source supports the idea that an eyebrow, let alone one flex of it, holds about 500,000 microbe species. Reliable sources estimate that the whole human skin hosts around 1,000 bacterial species. The microbes known to live in eyebrows are a small set: two species of Demodex mite, the yeast Malassezia, and common facial bacteria. Even reports of the most microbes on eyebrows describe about 2,000 mites as individual organisms, not species. The 500,000-species figure is orders of magnitude off, and saying a muscle movement 'contains' species makes no sense.

text: Polar bears are excellent swimmers and have been known to swim for hours or even days at a time, covering distances of up to 60 miles without resting.
label: supported
reason: Reliable sources back every part of the claim. San Diego Zoo Wildlife Alliance and NHPBS NatureWorks say polar bears are strong swimmers that can go about 60 miles (around 97–100 km) without resting. National Geographic, CBC and Live Science report bears swimming for days, including one female tracked swimming for nine days straight. One caveat: that record swim covered about 426 miles (687 km), so 60 miles is a commonly cited figure rather than a true upper limit. The claim's main points still hold.

text: A blue whale's heartbeat can be as loud as 188 decibels, which is louder than a jet engine taking off.
label: contradicted
reason: The 188-decibel figure belongs to the blue whale's calls, not its heartbeat. WWF says blue whale calls reach 188 dB while a jet reaches 140 dB, and Wikipedia's list of whale vocalizations gives the source level of blue whale sounds as 155–188 dB. Neither source gives a heartbeat measurement anywhere near 188 dB. The claim has taken a statistic about the whale's vocalizations and applied it to its heartbeat.

text: Scientists estimate that there are approximately 8.7 million identified species on Earth, but up to 80% of all species may remain undiscovered.
label: contradicted
reason: The 8.7 million figure from Mora et al. (2011) is an estimate of all species on Earth, both known and unknown. It is not a count of identified species. Only about 1.2 million species have been identified and catalogued, which is less than 15% of that estimated total. The source does say more than 80% of species may be undiscovered (86% of land species and 91% of marine species), but the claim is wrong to call the 8.7 million 'identified' species.

text: A blue whale's heartbeat can be as loud as 188 decibels, louder than a jet engine taking off.
label: contradicted
reason: The 188 dB figure is real, but it belongs to the blue whale's calls, not its heartbeat. Live Science says the blue whale's calls, or 'songs', reach 188 decibels, which is louder than a jet engine. Its heartbeat is much quieter: it can be picked up by sensitive instruments a few kilometres away, but it gets nowhere near 188 dB. The claim gives the call's loudness to the heartbeat.

text: Abnormally large crystals have grown within the Naica Mine in the Mexican state of Chihuahua over millions of years.
label: contradicted
reason: Credible sources agree that the Naica Mine in Chihuahua, Mexico, contains abnormally large gypsum (selenite) crystals. They do not support growth over "millions of years." Uranium-thorium dating puts the crystals' maximum age at about 500,000 years (Wikipedia, HeritageDaily). Measured growth rates (García-Ruiz et al., PNAS 2011, reported by C&EN) suggest they took up to about 1 million years, roughly 0.99 ± 0.27 million years. The figure of millions of years applies to the volcanic system, which formed about 26 million years ago, not to the crystals. Some lower-quality pages, such as geologyscience.com, do say "millions of years," but that page also gives the crystals' age as about 500,000 years, and the scientific evidence outweighs it.

text: A blue whale's heartbeat is so loud that it can be heard for hundreds of miles underwater.
label: contradicted
reason: NOAA Fisheries and other sources put the distance at about 2 miles, not hundreds of miles. The 2-mile figure itself is a popular claim with little scientific backing, and none of the sources I found support 'hundreds of miles.' That much longer range belongs to blue whale calls, which are vocalizations, not heartbeats.

text: Scientists estimate that there are approximately 8.7 million identified species on Earth, but as many as 80% of all species remain undiscovered.
label: contradicted
reason: The 2011 Mora et al. study, as reported by Nature news via BioEd Online, estimates that Earth has about 8.7 million species in total, give or take 1.3 million. That figure is not the number of identified species. Only about 1.2 million species have actually been identified and catalogued, which is less than 15% of the estimated total. The claim's "80% undiscovered" part fits the study's finding that more than 80% remain undiscovered (86% of land species and 91% of marine species). However, calling 8.7 million "identified" species contradicts the evidence.

text: Humans share about 50% of their DNA with bananas.
label: contradicted
reason: Snopes rated this claim False. The 50% figure doesn't describe shared DNA. It roughly means that about half of human genes have related counterparts in bananas, and even that number is probably too high. Genes make up only about 2% of human DNA, and the Naked Scientists and others say the share of actual DNA sequence humans have in common with bananas is about 1% or less. One low-quality site (factmyth.com) calls the claim valid, but trustworthy fact-checkers and science sources clearly contradict it.

text: Astra, the space tourism company founded by Chris Kemp, has successfully launched its Astra Spacecraft into space.
label: contradicted
reason: Astra, founded by Chris Kemp and Adam London, is not a space tourism company. Wikipedia and Space Explored describe it as a small-satellite launch company and maker of satellite engines, based in Alameda, California. It flies its Rocket series, mainly Rocket 3 and later Rocket 4, which reached orbit in 2021. It has no crewed tourism business and no vehicle called the "Astra Spacecraft"; its in-space products are Astra Spacecraft Engines, which are thrusters for satellites. So the claim is wrong about what the company does and what it launched.

text: Cats have a highly specialized vocalization range and can produce up to 100 different vocal sounds, whereas humans and dogs can only produce around 10.
label: contradicted
reason: The claim gets humans wrong. The cat-and-dog figure is a common pet fact: Cats.com and other pet sites say cats make about 100 vocal sounds and dogs about 10. However, a UNLV linguistics source says humans can produce about 600 consonant sounds and 200 vowel sounds, and English alone uses about 39 phonemes. That is far more than the claimed 'around 10.'

text: Decorative trophies used to be real human skulls with beaten metal bound around them in ancient times.
label: supported
reason: Ancient sources describe enemy skulls being kept as trophies and covered with beaten metal. Livy (Ab Urbe Condita 23.24) records that in 216 BC the Boii cut off the head of the Roman consul-elect Lucius Postumius Albinus, cleaned out the skull, and "covered the scalp with beaten gold." They then used it as a ceremonial cup in their temple. Herodotus likewise says the Scythians made trophy cups from enemies' skulls and sometimes gilded them, and Wikipedia's skull cup article describes skulls used as trophies across many cultures. These sources support the claim. The main caveat is that it generalizes: skull trophies were one ancient practice, not what all trophies once were.

text: A '-group' is the term used to describe a gathering of flamingos, which can often reach populations in the tens of thousands.
label: contradicted
reason: The term for a gathering of flamingos is 'flamboyance', not '-group'. Sources agree that flamingo groups are commonly called flamboyances. They also support the population part of the claim: colonies range from a few thousand to tens of thousands of birds and can reach up to a million. Because the claim names the wrong term, it is contradicted.

text: Scientists have discovered over 200 moons in our solar system, with Jupiter having the most at a total of 92 confirmed moons.
label: contradicted
reason: The claim is wrong about which planet has the most moons. It is true that more than 200 moons are known. But as of March 2025, Saturn has the most, with 274 confirmed after the IAU recognized 128 new ones. Jupiter has 95, not 92. The figure of 92 is an outdated count from early 2023, and even then Jupiter only held the lead briefly before Saturn passed it.

text: One flex of a human eyebrow contains around 1.5 meters or nearly 5 feet of nerve fibers.
label: not_verifiable
reason: I found no trustworthy source that supports this claim. Searches turned up anatomy references from Wikipedia, Kenhub and PMC. They say eyebrow movement comes from muscles such as the frontalis and corrugator supercilii, which are supplied by branches of the facial nerve. None of them mentions about 1.5 m (5 ft) of nerve fibers involved in raising an eyebrow. The claim also doesn't make much sense as stated, because a movement can't contain nerve fibers. Since no source confirms or directly refutes the figure, the claim can't be verified.

text: A honeybee's brain is physically rearranged during the winter months to conserve energy by reducing neural activity and shrinking areas of the brain.
label: contradicted
reason: The best evidence I found contradicts the claim. A peer-reviewed 2025 study (Developmental Neurobiology, on PMC) found that the mushroom bodies, a key brain region, do reorganize over a 6-month winter. But that region got substantially larger, not smaller, especially in the first 2 months. Some synapses were pruned, yet the authors concluded that winter bees keep brain capacity comparable to summer bees. They also noted that winter bees maintain bouton numbers (synaptic contact points) despite high energy costs, which goes against the idea that the brain shrinks or quiets down to save energy. Only a hobbyist beekeeping blog says the bee brain shrinks in winter, and it gives no scientific source. So the part about shrinking brain areas to conserve energy is contradicted, even though the brain does change structurally in winter.

text: Scientists estimate that about 95% of all ocean species remain undiscovered.
label: contradicted
reason: NOAA, a trustworthy source, says scientists estimate that 91% of ocean species have yet to be classified. That figure comes from Mora et al. (2011). Other estimates, such as Appeltans et al. (2012), put the share of undiscovered ocean species at up to two-thirds. None of the reliable sources gives 95% for undiscovered species. The 95% figure usually describes how much of the ocean itself is unexplored, which is a different claim.

text: Octopuses have been observed displaying a form of intelligence and problem-solving, and they have even been known to open jars from the inside.
label: supported
reason: Several outlets, including EarthSky, Gizmodo and Earth Touch News, report on footage from Japan's Enoshima Aquarium showing an octopus unscrewing a jar lid from the inside. They present it as evidence of octopus intelligence and problem-solving, which backs both parts of the claim.

text: A blue whale's heartbeat can be as loud as 188 decibels, which is louder than a jet engine.
label: contradicted
reason: Live Science says the 188-decibel figure, described as louder than a jet engine, belongs to the blue whale's calls or songs, not its heartbeat. The claim gives the call's loudness to the heartbeat. The heartbeat is known to be detectable from a long way off, but it is nowhere near 188 dB.

text: Sodium, when exposed to oxygen in the air, ignites spontaneously at room temperature.
label: contradicted
reason: Bulk sodium metal does not ignite on its own in room-temperature air. A ScienceDirect study notes that its autoignition temperature in air ranges from about 120 to 470 °C. In normal air at room temperature, sodium usually tarnishes (oxidizes) rather than catching fire. NOAA CAMEO says the ignition temperature depends on how much surface is exposed. Only sodium vapor ignites at room temperature; droplets and solid sodium need higher temperatures. The claim is about sodium in general, so these sources contradict it.

text: Scientists estimate that there are approximately 8.7 million identified species on Earth, but they believe that up to 80% of all species on the planet remain undiscovered.
label: contradicted
reason: The 8.7 million figure from Mora et al. (2011) is an estimate of all species on Earth, both known and unknown. It is not a count of species already identified. Only about 1.2 million species had been catalogued, which is why the same study concluded that more than 80% (about 86% of land species and 91% of marine species) are still undiscovered. The undiscovered share in the claim roughly matches, but calling the 8.7 million species 'identified' is wrong. If 8.7 million were already identified, 80% could not also remain undiscovered.

text: Tarantulas have been on Earth for a long time, with fossil records showing they've remained largely unchanged for over 100 million years.
label: not_verifiable
reason: Tarantulas are indeed an ancient group. Live Science and a 2023 Journal of Biogeography study say they first appeared about 120 million years ago, and the oldest known tarantula fossil is about 100 million years old, in Burmese amber. However, Live Science reports that only two tarantula fossils are known, which is not enough to show the group has stayed largely unchanged for more than 100 million years. Sources also disagree on this point. Texas Parks & Wildlife Magazine says fossil records show tarantulas have been virtually unchanged for more than 20 million years, not 100 million. A non-scientific hobbyist blog (The Tarantula Collective) suggests they have kept their basic form for more than 100 million years. Because the evidence is mixed, the specific claim about the fossil record cannot be confirmed.

text: A blue whale's heartbeat is so loud that scientists have been able to detect it from over 500 miles away using underwater microphones.
label: contradicted
reason: The figure commonly cited is that a blue whale's heartbeat can be heard from about 2 miles (3.2 km) away, not 500 miles. That number is itself a popular claim, not a confirmed measurement: scientists actually recorded blue whale heart rates using suction-cup sensor tags attached to the whale, not distant underwater microphones. No trustworthy source supports detection from over 500 miles away. Blue whale calls, not heartbeats, are what can travel hundreds of miles.

text: Many species of jellyfish are immortal, as they can transform their bodies into a younger state through a process called transdifferentiation.
label: contradicted
reason: Reliable sources (Britannica, Wikipedia, The Scientist, PubMed) say biological 'immortality' through transdifferentiation is a trait of one species, Turritopsis dohrnii, which is called 'the immortal jellyfish.' The Scientist describes it as the only known animal species whose adults can reverse their development under stress. Wikipedia says most jellyfish species have a fairly fixed lifespan, and a close relative, Turritopsis rubra, does not show biological immortality. The process described in the claim is accurate, but saying that 'many species' of jellyfish are immortal is wrong.

text: Higher levels of social connections in life have been scientifically linked to a lower risk of cognitive decline and dementia in older adults.
label: supported
reason: Peer-reviewed research hosted on NCBI/PMC says that social connectedness lowers dementia risk and helps older adults keep their cognitive function. Other studies of social integration and dementia risk in older adults find the same link. This matches the claim's scientific consensus.

text: Katara and the naga, a sea serpent from Polynesian mythology, are believed by some to be the origins of the mermaid legend.
label: contradicted
reason: The claim gets the naga's origin wrong. Reliable sources such as Wisdomlib describe nagas as serpent beings from Hindu, Buddhist and Jain mythology in South and Southeast Asia, not from Polynesian mythology. It is also unclear who or what 'Katara' refers to, and no evidence links Katara to the origin of the mermaid legend.

text: Two-thirds of the planet Venus is covered in volcanoes, with over 1,600 major volcanoes and numerous smaller volcanic features.
label: supported
reason: Space.com says that about two-thirds of Venus's surface is flat, smooth plains "marred by thousands of volcanoes." The claim's wording, "covered in volcanoes," is a loose paraphrase of that description. EBSCO Research Starters says Venus has at least 1,600 major volcanoes and many more minor ones, possibly hundreds of thousands of smaller volcanic features. EBSCO also says about 80% of the surface has been shaped by volcanism, which is consistent with the two-thirds figure rather than contradicting it. Both parts of the claim are backed by these sources.

text: Although not visible to the naked eye, there are estimated to be around 100 billion galaxies in the observable universe.
label: supported
reason: I rated this supported because trusted sources back the main figure. Space.com, quoting astrophysicist Mario Livio, and BBC Sky at Night both cite about 100–200 billion galaxies in the observable universe. Carl Sagan's well-known figure was about 100 billion. Some estimates differ: a 2016 study put the number at roughly 2 trillion, and one extrapolation from Hubble data gives about 170 billion. Even so, 'around 100 billion' remains a widely cited mainstream estimate. The 'not visible to the naked eye' part is true for almost all of these galaxies, apart from a few exceptions such as Andromeda and the Magellanic Clouds.

text: Babies are born without kneecaps, which do not develop and harden into bone until around age three through a process called ossification.
label: supported
reason: Several sources agree on the main points of the claim, though the wording is loose. Newborns have no bony kneecap. Instead they have a cartilage kneecap (patella), which hardens into bone through ossification. That process usually begins around age 2 to 3 and can continue to about age 6, which fits 'around age three.' Several sources (e.g., grownsy, Dad Fixes Everything) point out that 'born without kneecaps' is technically a myth, because the kneecap is already present as cartilage. Read as 'born without bony kneecaps,' the claim is accurate.

text: Polar bears are actually nearly invisible in the Arctic environment due to the transparent hollow tubes in their fur that scatter and reflect sunlight, giving them a white appearance.
label: supported
reason: Reliable sources such as Britannica and Natural Habitat Adventures confirm the mechanism in the claim. Polar bear fur has no pigment: each guard hair is transparent with a hollow core that scatters and reflects sunlight, so the coat looks white. Britannica adds that this white appearance gives polar bears effective camouflage in the snowy Arctic, letting them approach seals without being easily detected. However, the phrase "nearly invisible" overstates this. The sources describe camouflage, not near-invisibility, so that wording is a loose paraphrase rather than a sourced fact.

text: Honeybees are capable of recognizing human faces and remembering them for later encounters, much like some other animals and even certain types of fish.
label: supported
reason: A 2005 study by Adrian Dyer and colleagues in the Journal of Experimental Biology, reported by Phys.org, found that honeybees can learn to recognize human faces in photos and remember them for at least two days. It also counted as long-term memory. That fits the idea of remembering faces for later encounters. The comparison to fish is also backed by research: a 2016 study by Newport et al. showed that archerfish can tell human faces apart. One caveat is that the bees were tested on photographs, not real people, and the study authors noted that bees probably don't understand what a face is.

text: Ninety percent of the world's population lives in the Northern Hemisphere.
label: supported
reason: Many sources give about 90% as the share of the world's population living in the Northern Hemisphere, including Inshorts and Testbook, and an eNotes expert answer says "just under 90 percent." More precise estimates are slightly lower: eNotes' summary says 88% and VividMaps says 87%. The claim's 90% is therefore a rounded figure, but it matches the commonly accepted estimate.

text: Cathedral of St. Peter in Groningen, Netherlands is the oldest building in Groningen.
label: contradicted
reason: My searches turned up no "Cathedral of St. Peter" in Groningen. The city's cathedral is St. Joseph Cathedral (Sint-Jozefkathedraal), which is a 19th-century building. Reliable sources such as Wikipedia and VisitGroningen say the Martinikerk is Groningen's oldest church. Other buildings, like the Gotisch huis (Museum aan de A), are also described as among the oldest buildings in the city. No source credits a St. Peter's cathedral with being the oldest building, so the claim is contradicted.

text: Higher education students who report using active learning methods in the classroom tend to outperform their peers using more traditional teaching methods.
label: supported
reason: Freeman et al.'s 2014 meta-analysis of 225 studies, published in PNAS, found that undergraduates in active-learning STEM classes scored higher on exams than students in traditional lecture classes (about 6% higher, or 0.47 SD). Students taught by traditional lecture were also about 1.5 times more likely to fail. Follow-up work found active learning also narrows achievement gaps. These studies compare classes taught with active learning, not students who say they use it, but the claim's general point holds up. The evidence is strongest for STEM courses.

text: Humans and dolphins are the only known species in the animal kingdom that have been observed teaching others and also learning from each other.
label: contradicted
reason: The claim is false. Scientists have documented teaching in several species besides humans and dolphins. A 2006 study on tandem-running ants was described as the first demonstration of formal teaching in a non-human animal. Experiments have since shown teaching in meerkats, which teach their young to handle scorpions, and in pied babblers. Reviews of animal teaching also list bees and other carnivores. Learning from each other (social learning) is also common in the animal kingdom, so humans and dolphins are not the only species that do both.

text: The Axel Erlandson's Tre-fontaine tree, also known as the "circus tree," is a natural wonder consisting of three trunks that were cultivated to grow from a single base into an interlocking, ring-like shape in Gilroy, California.
label: not_verifiable
reason: I found no source that mentions a "Tre-fontaine" tree among Axel Erlandson's works. Reliable sources, including Wikipedia and Gilroy Gardens, confirm that his circus trees are now at Gilroy Gardens. They name trees such as the Basket Tree (six sycamores), the Four-Legged Giant, the Arch Tree and Squat Curvy Scallops (three trees). None of them describes a three-trunk ring-shaped "Tre-fontaine" tree. The claim also has other problems. The trees were shaped in Hilmar and Scotts Valley and only moved to Gilroy in 1985. They are grafted, man-made sculptures rather than a "natural wonder." Because the specific tree can't be identified or checked, the claim can't be verified.

text: Humans and dolphins are the only mammals known to give themselves names.
label: contradicted
reason: Recent research shows that humans and dolphins are not the only mammals with name-like calls. A 2024 Hebrew University study found that marmoset monkeys use 'phee calls' to name each other. The university's release says this behavior was previously known in humans, dolphins and elephants, and a 2024 study had already found that African elephants address each other with name-like calls. So at least two other mammals, elephants and marmosets, are now known to have this ability. One caveat: the claim says 'give themselves names'. Dolphins invent their own signature whistles, while elephants and marmosets have been shown to use name-like calls to address each other. Read the way the claim is commonly meant, as vocal naming, the 'only' part is still contradicted.

text: A single cloud can weigh more than a million pounds.
label: supported
reason: Science Notes reports that an average cumulus cloud weighs about 500,000 kg, which is roughly 1.1 million pounds. It adds that cumulonimbus (thunderstorm) clouds can weigh a million tonnes or more. This is in line with the widely cited USGS/NCAR estimate that a typical cumulus cloud holds about 1.1 million pounds of water. Since even an average cloud tops a million pounds, a single cloud can clearly weigh more than that.

text: Galileo Galilei was the first person to observe the planet Neptune, but he did not realize it was a planet and instead thought it was a fixed star.
label: supported
reason: Scientific American reports that Galileo observed Neptune in 1612 and thought it was a fixed star, some 234 years before it was recognized as a planet. Wikipedia's 'Discovery of Neptune' page says his drawings record Neptune on December 28, 1612 and January 27, 1613, and that both times he mistook it for a fixed star near Jupiter. Other sources describe him as the first person to see Neptune. One caveat: Wikipedia also notes that on January 28 Galileo recorded that this 'star' seemed to have moved. Still, the general view is that he did not recognize it as a planet, so the claim holds.

text: Scientists estimate that there may be between 700,000 and 1 million species on Earth that have not yet been discovered or described.
label: contradicted
reason: The claim's range is far below what scientists actually estimate. The widely cited 2011 PLoS Biology study (Mora et al.) puts the total number of species on Earth at about 8.7 million (±1.3 million). It also says about 86% of land species and 91% of marine species have yet to be discovered, described and catalogued. Since only about 1.2–1.25 million species are catalogued, that leaves roughly 7.5 million undescribed species, not 700,000 to 1 million. The source does mention a figure of about 700,000, but that refers to species thought to be described already that haven't yet reached central databases, not to undiscovered species.

text: Government Island, in the U.S. state of Alaska, is the largest island in Prince William Sound.
label: contradicted
reason: A USDA Forest Service publication says Montague Island is the largest island in Prince William Sound, at about 850 km². Wikipedia agrees and lists it as the 25th-largest island in the U.S. Government Island is a small island in the sound, not the largest one.

text: Members of the smallest primate species, the pygmy mouse lemur, are about the size of a human thumb.
label: contradicted
reason: The claim gets two things wrong. First, the pygmy mouse lemur (Microcebus myoxinus) is not the smallest primate. Wikipedia calls it the second-smallest mouse lemur and notes that it is often confused with Madame Berthe's mouse lemur (Microcebus berthae), which is the world's smallest primate. Second, neither species is thumb-sized. The pygmy mouse lemur's head and body measure about 12–13 cm and it weighs 43–55 g. Madame Berthe's mouse lemur averages 9.2 cm in body length plus a long tail, and Discover Wildlife compares the smallest primates to something a bit smaller than an adult hand, not a thumb.

text: One flex of a human eyebrow can convey over 250,000 distinct emotions or expressions.
label: contradicted
reason: The 250,000 figure comes from anthropologist Ray Birdwhistell. He estimated that people can make and recognise about 250,000 facial expressions using the whole face. EBSCO Research Starters and a review paper on arXiv both attribute it to him this way. Neither source says a single eyebrow movement can convey 250,000 emotions. The claim takes a whole-face estimate and wrongly applies it to one flex of an eyebrow, and I found no source that supports that version. A second search for Birdwhistell's specific eyebrow research did not run because the search limit was reached, so that point is unchecked.

text: One flex of a human eyebrow contains about 500,000 distinct micro-movements.
label: not_verifiable
reason: My searches found no trustworthy source that supports the claim that one eyebrow flex has about 500,000 distinct micro-movements. Research on eyebrow movements, such as the MPI and ResearchGate studies of eyebrow raises in conversation, describes raises as single facial actions and gives no count like this. The figure looks made up, and the idea of counting 'distinct micro-movements' isn't a standard scientific measure. Still, no source directly disproves the number, so the claim can't be verified either way.

text: Memorization can improve reasoning.
label: supported
reason: Several arXiv papers back the claim. 'Rote Learning Considered Useful' (arXiv 2507.21914) finds that rote memorization of atomic facts improves reversal and two-hop reasoning in LLMs. In the two-hop case, accuracy rose from 0.14 with no memorization to 0.36. 'On Memorization of Large Language Models in Logical Reasoning' (arXiv 2410.23123) reports that a model's reasoning improves during fine-tuning as it memorizes more training puzzles. The word 'can' only requires that memorization sometimes helps, and this evidence shows that.

text: Traffic lights were first invented by a Detroit police officer named Lester Wire in 1912.
label: contradicted
reason: The claim gets two things wrong. Lester Wire was a police officer in Salt Lake City, Utah, not Detroit. In 1912 he installed an early electric traffic light at Second South and Main Street in Salt Lake City. He also wasn't the first inventor of traffic lights: John Peake Knight's gas-lit signal was set up in London in 1868. That 1868 date comes from well-known history rather than from this search. The search results are enough on their own, though, to show that Wire worked in Salt Lake City, not Detroit.

text: A blue whale's heartbeat can last up to 2 minutes, compared to a human heartbeat that lasts around 1 second.
label: contradicted
reason: The 2 minutes figure is wrong. In 2019, Goldbogen and colleagues recorded a wild blue whale's heart rate for the first time (published in PNAS). During deep dives its heart slowed to as few as about 2 beats per minute, which works out to roughly 30 seconds per heartbeat at most. At the surface it rose to 25–37 beats per minute. A single heartbeat lasting up to 2 minutes would mean about 0.5 beats per minute, far below anything recorded. The part about a human heartbeat lasting around 1 second is roughly right, but the blue whale figure is overstated about fourfold.

text: Japan has a vending machine for almost everything, including umbrellas, underwear, and even live crabs.
label: supported
reason: Many travel and culture sources say Japan's vending machines sell an unusually wide range of goods. Umbrella and underwear vending machines are well documented (japanesetaste.com, hetravelssolo.com, expertworldtravel.com). Live crabs are also listed: japanwiselife.com describes crab vending machines in Hakodate and Kanazawa that sell live or cooked crab, and vendingmachinepapa.com includes live crabs among unusual Japanese vending machine items. One caveat: the best-known live-crab vending machine, covered by TechCrunch, was in Nanjing, China, and the Japanese sources for live crabs are less authoritative. Still, no source says Japan has no such machines, so the claim as a whole is supported.

text: Parts of the Great Barrier Reef in Australia have been around for approximately 20 million years.
label: supported
reason: WorldAtlas says some sections of the Great Barrier Reef are 20 million years old, while the reef as a whole is about 500,000 years old. That matches the claim. Simple Wikipedia adds that corals have grown in the region for up to 25 million years. One caveat: Science magazine reports geological data showing the reef in its modern form is less than a million years old. That finding is about the whole modern reef rather than older coral growth in the region, so it does not directly rule out the claim. The tourism sites that repeat the 20-million-year figure are weaker sources.

text: Scientists estimate that there are approximately 8.7 million identified species on Earth, but the total number of species is believed to be around 30 million, with many still awaiting discovery.
label: contradicted
reason: The claim gets the 8.7 million figure wrong. In Mora et al. (2011, PLoS Biology), 8.7 million is the estimated total number of eukaryotic species on Earth, not the number already identified. Only about 1.2 million species had been catalogued at the time, which means roughly 86% of species remain undescribed. Because the claim calls 8.7 million the identified count and puts the total at about 30 million, it misstates the scientific estimate.

text: Humans share approximately 50-60% of their DNA with bananas.
label: contradicted
reason: Sources that check this claim say it is misleading. The real finding is that about 60% of human genes have a recognizable counterpart, or homolog, in the banana genome. That is not the same as sharing 50–60% of our DNA. Genes make up only a small part of the human genome, so the overlap amounts to roughly 1–2% of total human DNA, according to The Star's QuickCheck. HowStuffWorks adds that the proteins made by these counterpart genes are only about 40% identical. Read literally, the claim that humans share 50–60% of their DNA with bananas is therefore wrong.

text: Officer candidates from the United States Naval Academy are formally known as "midshipmen" (regardless of their sex), and their mascot is named Bill the Goat.
label: supported
reason: Both parts of the claim check out. The Washington Post reports that the Naval Academy's website says all students are called midshipmen, regardless of sex, and Wikipedia's Naval Academy page also uses the term "midshipmen." Wikipedia and Military Times both confirm that Bill the Goat is the Naval Academy's mascot and has been since 1890.

text: A blue whale's heartbeat is so slow that it only beats around 4-8 times per minute when the whale is at rest.
label: contradicted
reason: The 4–8 beats-per-minute figure is real, but the claim puts it in the wrong situation. It comes from the 2019 Stanford/Scripps study, the first ECG recording of a wild blue whale, and was measured during deep foraging dives, with a low of 2 bpm. At the surface, while breathing and recovering, the whale's heart beat 25–37 times per minute, higher than predicted. So the evidence describes 4–8 bpm as a temporary slowdown during dives, not the whale's heart rate at rest.

text: A星(is the brightest star in the night sky and is about 8.6 lightyears away from Earth.
label: supported
reason: The claim's wording is garbled: "A星(" has no clear name, but it almost certainly means Sirius A (天狼星A), the main star of the Sirius system. EarthSky says Sirius is the brightest star in the night sky as seen from Earth and lies about 8.6 light-years away. It also calls Sirius an A-type star and identifies the bright star as Sirius A, which matches "A星". Because the referent has to be inferred, this judgment carries some uncertainty.

text: Despite its seemingly barren surface, Antarctica is home to several unique species of fish that inhabit the cold, dark waters surrounding the continent.
label: supported
reason: Reliable sources, including a PMC article, Fishes of Australia and ResearchGate reviews, say the Southern Ocean around Antarctica is home to endemic notothenioid fishes. These include Antarctic icefishes, a unique white-blooded family, and the dragonfish Parachaenichthys charcoti. One source says about 374 fish species live in Antarctic waters, which are around −1.8°C. This supports the claim that several unique fish species live in the cold waters around the continent.

text: Higher levels of social connections in life have been scientifically linked to a lower risk of cognitive decline and psychological illness.
label: supported
reason: The search results back both parts of the claim. Inova's expert commentary cites studies (including Whitehall II, a cohort of more than 10,000 people followed for 28 years, and a multinational study of about 40,000 older adults) linking strong social engagement and frequent social contact to lower risk of cognitive decline and dementia. It also reports that better social connectedness was associated with lower risk of later diagnosed depression and anxiety, which matches the claim's 'psychological illness' part.

text: A blue whale's heartbeat is so loud that it can be detected over 200 miles away through specialized equipment.
label: contradicted
reason: Sources that repeat this popular fact give a figure of about 2 miles, not more than 200. For example, the Cold Spring Harbor Whaling Museum says a blue whale's heartbeat "can be detected from 2 MILES AWAY." Even the 2-mile figure is shaky, since scientists actually recorded blue whale heart rates with sensors attached to the whale. No search result supports detecting a heartbeat over 200 miles away. The claim seems to confuse the heartbeat with blue whale calls, which can travel hundreds of miles underwater.

text: Honeybees are capable of recognizing human faces and remembering them for later encounters, much like some other animals and even some primates and dolphins.
label: supported
reason: My search found a 2005 study by Dyer and colleagues in the Journal of Experimental Biology, reported by Phys.org, which showed that honeybees learned to recognize human faces in photographs. The same report says bees tested two days after training still remembered the faces in long-term memory. That supports the main claim that bees can recognize human faces and remember them later. The comparison to other animals, primates and dolphins is a loose, broad statement and not the core claim; primate face recognition is well established, though I did not specifically confirm the dolphin part.

text: Animals that live in groups, such as wolves and elephants, have been observed exhibiting signs of grieving and mourning when they lose a member of their group.
label: supported
reason: Sources describe elephants mourning dead herd members. Wildlife film crews have recorded this several times, including elephants carrying the tusks of dead herd members and returning to visit remains. Other sources report that wolves show behavioral changes after a pack member dies, such as mournful howling and signs of depression, which observers interpret as grief. Scientists still debate how much animal grief matches human grief, but the evidence fits the claim that these behaviors have been observed.

text: Did you know that a blue whale's heart can beat around 4-8 beats per minute and pump approximately 5,000 liters of blood with each beat.
label: contradicted
reason: The heart-rate part is about right. Sources say a blue whale's heart beats only a few times per minute during dives, sometimes as slowly as 2 beats per minute. The volume per beat is wrong, though. Reports put it at roughly 80 liters per beat (some popular estimates go up to about 220 liters), not 5,000 liters. 5,000 liters is about the whale's entire blood volume, so the claim is off by well over an order of magnitude.

text: Did you know that a blue whale's heart can beat around 4-8 beats per minute and pump approximately 5,000 liters of blood with each beat?
label: contradicted
reason: The 4–8 beats per minute part holds up. The 2019 Stanford ECG study (Goldbogen et al., PNAS) recorded about 4–8 bpm during dives, with a low of 2 bpm. The 5,000 liters per beat figure is wrong, though. Researchers estimated about 80 liters per beat (Inverse and Fissac, reporting on the study), and other sources such as IFLScience give about 220 liters. Both are far below 5,000 liters, which would be more than the whale's total blood volume.

text: Parts of the Great Barrier Reef in Australia have been found to be around 20 million years old, making them one of the oldest living structures on Earth.
label: supported
reason: WorldAtlas says some sections of the Great Barrier Reef are about 20 million years old and calls it one of the oldest reefs on Earth, which matches the claim closely. The evidence is not settled, though. Tour-operator sources say the reef system as a whole is about 500,000 years old and the living reef only about 6,000–8,000 years old. Any 20-million-year-old parts would be ancient rock underneath, not living coral. Because the claim's wording follows a published source and none of the results directly deny the 20-million-year figure for some sections, I've rated it supported.

text: Honey Never Spoils is true, Archaeologists have found pots of honey in ancient Egyptian tombs that are over 3,000 years old and still perfectly edible.
label: supported
reason: Smithsonian Magazine says archaeologists digging in ancient Egyptian tombs have found pots of honey that are thousands of years old and still preserved. My Modern Met and Yahoo News also report that honey from 3,000-year-old Egyptian tombs was unspoiled and still edible. They say this is because honey has little water, is acidic and contains hydrogen peroxide. The sources add that honey keeps only under the right conditions, such as being sealed, but none of the results contradicts the claim.

text: One flex of a human eyebrow contains about 250 muscles per square centimeter, indicating exceptional strength and flexibility.
label: contradicted
reason: Anatomy sources say eyebrow movement comes from a small number of named muscles: the frontalis, which raises the brow, and the corrugator supercilii, procerus, depressor supercilii and orbicularis oculi, which pull it down or inward. No reliable source mentions anything like 250 muscles per square centimeter in an eyebrow. That figure conflicts with basic anatomy, so the claim is false, along with its conclusion about "exceptional strength."

text: Scientists estimate that there are approximately 8.7 million identified species on Earth, but it's believed that up to 80% of all species remain undiscovered.
label: contradicted
reason: The 8.7 million figure is an estimate of the total number of species on Earth, including undiscovered ones. It is not the number already identified. Mora et al.'s 2011 study, as reported by BioEd Online (reprinting Nature News), puts the total at about 8.7 million, give or take 1.3 million, and says only about 1.2 million species have been identified and classified. That is less than 15% of the total, which is where the 'more than 80% undiscovered' figure comes from. The claim calls the 8.7 million 'identified species', so it gets the key fact wrong.

text: Honeybees are able to recognize human faces and remember them for later encounters, much like some other animals and even certain types of fish.
label: supported
reason: The search results support the claim. Phys.org reports a 2005 study led by Adrian Dyer which found that honeybees can learn to recognize human faces in photos and remember them for at least two days. Scientific American also reports that honeybees can learn human faces. My search for the fish part of the claim timed out, so I could not confirm it here. However, there is well-known published research (Newport et al., 2016, Scientific Reports) showing that archerfish can tell human faces apart, and other animals are known to do the same. Nothing I found contradicts any part of the claim.

text: A blue whale's heart alone can weigh around 400 pounds and pump about 5,000 gallons of blood through its body with every beat.
label: contradicted
reason: NOAA Fisheries backs the first part of the claim: a blue whale's heart weighs about 400 pounds. The second part is wrong. NOAA says the heart pumps about 60 gallons of blood with each beat, not 5,000 gallons.

text: A.day is technically 23 hours, 56 minutes, and 4.09 seconds long due to Earth's slightly ellipsoidal shape and the planet's movement in its orbit around the Sun.
label: contradicted
reason: 23 h 56 min 4.09 s is the sidereal day: the time Earth takes to rotate once relative to the distant stars. Sources such as astronomynotes.com and planetsforkids.org say it is the true rotation period. The normal solar day is still 24 hours. That day is about 4 minutes longer because Earth moves along its orbit, so it has to turn a little farther to face the Sun again. None of the sources links the 23 h 56 min figure to Earth's slightly ellipsoidal shape. So the claim gets the cause wrong, and it is misleading to say a day is 'technically' this long.

text: Hippopotamuses can hold their breath underwater for up to five minutes and can also sleep with their eyes and nostrils submerged.
label: supported
reason: Natural Habitat Adventures says hippos can hold their breath for up to five minutes while awake. It also says they sleep in the water and rise to the surface to breathe without waking. A hippo sleeping underwater has its eyes and nostrils submerged, so both parts of the claim are supported. No contradicting evidence came up.

text: Tarantulas can live for up to 20-30 years in captivity, with one species, the Goliath Birdeater tarantula, being known to live up to 40 years.
label: contradicted
reason: The general idea that tarantulas can live a long time is broadly accurate, since many female tarantulas live for decades. The specific claim about the Goliath birdeater is wrong, though. Wikipedia's Goliath birdeater article says females average 15 to 25 years and males only 3 to 6 years. I found no reliable source saying the species lives up to 40 years. Tarantulas known for exceptionally long lives are usually other species, such as Grammostola. Because the Goliath birdeater detail is contradicted, the claim as a whole is labeled contradicted.

text: Humans and dolphins are the only known species in the animal kingdom that have been observed teaching others and passing down knowledge to younger generations.
label: contradicted
reason: The claim is false. Humans and dolphins are not the only animals known to teach. A study published in Science shows that wild meerkats teach their pups how to handle prey. Other research also documents teaching in ants, bees, pied babblers and other carnivores.

text: Bees are able to recognize human faces using the same region of their brains as humans do, according to a study published by scientists in 2005.
label: contradicted
reason: The 2005 study does exist. Dyer and colleagues reported in the Journal of Experimental Biology (December 2005) that honeybees can learn to recognise photos of human faces. But the 'same brain region as humans' part is wrong. The study's point was that bees can do this with a tiny, very different brain: fewer than 1 million neurons, about one ten-thousandth of the brain cells humans have. The researchers also asked openly whether bees recognise faces differently from the way humans do. None of the coverage says bees use a brain region equivalent to the human one, and insects have no such region. So the claim's central detail misrepresents the study.

text: Didega, a type of electric eel, is capable of generating up to 600 volts to defend itself from predators.
label: not_verifiable
reason: The searches turned up no evidence that "Didega" is a name for any electric eel or other fish. The results were unrelated: a music artist, a German restaurant and the Georgian anthem "Dideba". Reliable sources (Smithsonian National Zoo, Animal Diversity Web, Wikipedia) do confirm that electric eels (Electrophorus) produce strong shocks of roughly 600 V or more. However, that alone doesn't settle the claim, because the name "Didega" can't be tied to any known species.

text: NASA's Mars rover, Perseverance, discovered evidence of past volcanic activity and a massive ancient lake on Mars in 2021.
label: supported
reason: NASA/JPL reports that once Perseverance began examining rocks on the floor of Jezero Crater in spring 2021, it found igneous rocks. One type formed from magma underground and the other from volcanic activity at the surface. These results were announced in December 2021 at the American Geophysical Union fall meeting. The rover's 2021 work also confirmed that Jezero was an ancient lake: in October 2021, a published analysis of its delta images supported this, and NASA describes the crater as having held a lake billions of years ago. Calling the lake "massive" is somewhat subjective, since the crater is about 45 km wide, but the core claims about volcanic activity and an ancient lake in 2021 hold up.

text: A誉咲き (Yūrei-zakura), a 2,000-year-old weeping cherry blossom tree, is a famous landmark in the Morioka Castle grounds in Iwate Prefecture, Japan.
label: contradicted
reason: I found no trustworthy source for a tree called "誉咲き (Yūrei-zakura)" at Morioka Castle. The kanji and the romanization also don't match each other. Morioka's famous old cherry tree is the Ishiwarizakura (Rock-Splitting Cherry Tree). Japan-guide and Lonely Planet place it in front of the Morioka District Court, not on the castle grounds, and put its age at about 360–400 years, not 2,000. Japan's well-known 2,000-year-old cherry is the Yamataka Jindai-zakura, an Edo-higan cherry at Jissoji Temple in Hokuto, Yamanashi Prefecture, not in Iwate.

text: Galileo Galilei was the first person to observe the planet Neptune, although he didn't realize it was a planet and instead thought it was a fixed star in 1612.
label: supported
reason: Reliable sources back the claim. NASA says Galileo recorded Neptune as a fixed star during telescope observations in 1612 and 1613, more than 200 years before it was discovered in 1846. Scientific American says he 'first observed it in 1612 and thought it was a fixed star.' Wikipedia says his drawings show sightings on December 28, 1612 and January 27, 1613, and that both times he mistook Neptune for a fixed star. One caveat: the sources describe this as the earliest recorded observation, so calling Galileo the 'first person' to see Neptune assumes there were no earlier sightings that went unrecorded.

text: Scientists estimate that there are approximately 8.7 million identified species on Earth, yet it's believed that up to 80% of all species remain undiscovered.
label: contradicted
reason: Mora et al.'s 2011 study, reported by Nature News via BioEd Online, estimates that Earth holds about 8.7 million species in total, give or take 1.3 million. That figure is not the number of identified species. Only about 1.2 million species have actually been identified and classified, which is less than 15% of the estimated total. The second part of the claim roughly holds, since the study found that more than 80% of species (86% of land species and 91% of marine species) are still undiscovered. But calling the 8.7 million 'identified' species is wrong.

text: Scientists have calculated that there are approximately 100-400 billion stars in the Milky Way galaxy.
label: supported
reason: Wikipedia gives the Milky Way's star count as 100–400 billion, and Star Walk says scientists currently estimate it at between 100 and 400 billion stars. This matches the claim, which correctly treats the number as an approximate estimate.

text: Humans share about 60% of their DNA with fruit flies.
label: supported
reason: Widely cited sources back the ~60% figure. NHGRI (genome.gov) says that about 60% of genes are conserved between fruit flies and humans. ASU's Ask a Biologist and other educational sources describe this as humans sharing about 60% of their DNA with fruit flies. One caveat: strictly speaking, the scientific figure refers to conserved genes rather than the whole DNA sequence. Still, the claim matches how this figure is commonly stated.

text: Cicadas can survive underwater for up to a minute by sealing their spiracles and holding their breath.
label: not_verifiable
reason: My searches turned up nothing on how long cicadas can survive underwater. No source mentioned a one-minute limit or said that cicadas seal their spiracles and hold their breath. The results only covered aquatic insects in general (some can hold their breath underwater), cicadas' water-repelling wings, and general cicada facts. The search tool hit its usage limit before I could run more specific queries. Since no part of the claim could be checked against a reliable source, it can't be confirmed or ruled out.

text: Humans share approximately 60% of their DNA with fruit flies.
label: supported
reason: NHGRI (genome.gov) says that comparing the fruit fly and human genomes found about 60% of genes are conserved between the two species. Arizona State University's Ask A Biologist also states that about 60% of fruit fly DNA is the same as human DNA. Strictly speaking, the scientific figure is about shared, conserved genes rather than identical DNA sequence overall, but popular science sources commonly describe it the way the claim does, and no source found contradicts the 60% figure.

text: Scientists estimate that there are approximately 8.7 million identified species on Earth, but the true number could be as high as 30 million.
label: contradicted
reason: The claim gets the 8.7 million figure wrong. That number comes from Mora et al. (2011, PLoS Biology), and it is an estimate of the total number of species on Earth, not the number already identified. The same study says only about 1.2 million species had been catalogued and that roughly 86% of land species and 91% of ocean species have not yet been described. So calling 8.7 million "identified" species is false. Experts' estimates for the true total range from 3 to 100 million, so "as high as 30 million" doesn't reflect the full range either.

text: Did you know that a blue whale's heart can beat around 4-8 beats per minute and pump approximately 5,000 liters of blood with every beat.
label: contradicted
reason: The 4–8 beats per minute figure is correct. It matches the 2019 PNAS study by Goldbogen et al., which found an average minimum of about 4–8 bpm during dives (as low as 2 bpm, and up to 37 bpm at the surface). The 5,000 liters per beat figure is wrong. Sources put the volume per beat at about 80 liters (the study's estimate for the whale it tagged) up to roughly 220–230 liters, nowhere near 5,000. Because that part of the claim is false, the claim as a whole is contradicted.

text: Dragonflies have existed for over 300 million years, and during the Paleozoic Era, some species had a wingspan of up to 2 feet (60 cm) in length.
label: supported
reason: Reliable sources, including ASU's Ask a Biologist, say that about 300 million years ago (the Carboniferous, part of the Paleozoic Era), insects like dragonflies such as Meganeura had wingspans of up to about 65 cm, roughly 2 feet. Many sources describe dragonflies as having existed for about 300 million years. One caveat: strictly speaking, these giant insects were griffinflies (Meganisoptera), close relatives of true dragonflies, and the largest reached about 65–70 cm, a bit over 60 cm. Popular sources still commonly call them dragonflies with roughly 2-foot wingspans, so the claim is broadly supported.

text: Giraffes are the only animals born with their eyes open, and they can walk within the first hour of birth.
label: contradicted
reason: The claim is false because giraffes are not the only animals born with their eyes open. Oxford Reference defines precocial mammals as young born with their eyes and ears open that can stand and walk, and it names cattle, sheep and horses as examples. A-Z Animals also lists horses, elephants and many birds alongside giraffes. The second part of the claim is broadly right, since giraffe calves are precocial and usually walk within about an hour, but the 'only animals' part is contradicted.

text: Honey Never Spoils, archaeological evidence has shown that even after thousands of years, honey remains safe for consumption due to its acidity and lack of moisture.
label: supported
reason: Smithsonian Magazine's article "The Science Behind Honey's Eternal Shelf Life" says archaeologists digging in ancient Egyptian tombs have found pots of honey thousands of years old that were still preserved and edible. It credits this mainly to honey's low moisture and acidity, and also to hydrogen peroxide. Several other sources, including HistoryFacts, repeat this. Some of these are popular science pages rather than research papers, but I found no reliable source that disputes the claim.

text: Scientists estimate that there are approximately 8.7 million identified species on Earth, with up to 80% of the world's species remaining undiscovered.
label: contradicted
reason: The 8.7 million figure is an estimate of the total number of species on Earth, not the number already identified. Nature News, republished by BioEd Online, reports Mora et al.'s 2011 estimate of 8.7 million species, give or take 1.3 million, and says only about 1.2 million had been identified and classified, less than 15% of that total. The same source says "more than 80%" of species remain undiscovered (86% of land species and 91% of marine species). Calling 8.7 million "identified species" is therefore wrong, and "up to 80%" understates the estimate.

text: Scientists estimate that there are approximately 8.7 million identified species on Earth, but up to 80% of all species on the planet remain undiscovered.
label: contradicted
reason: The 8.7 million figure is not a count of identified species. It is the estimated total number of species on Earth, give or take 1.3 million, from Mora et al. (2011). Only about 1.2 million species have actually been identified and catalogued. The claim's other point, that more than 80% of species remain undiscovered (86% of land species and 91% of marine species), is broadly consistent with the source. But calling 8.7 million 'identified' species is wrong.

text: Did you know that Honey Never Spoils, Archaeologists have found pots of honey in ancient Egyptian tombs that are over 3,000 years old and still perfectly edible.
label: supported
reason: Smithsonian Magazine reports that archaeologists digging in ancient Egyptian tombs have often found pots of honey, thousands of years old, that were still preserved, and it explains why honey keeps for so long: low water content, acidity and hydrogen peroxide. Several other sources (My Modern Met, RealClearScience, BoingBoing) repeat the claim that honey from 3,000-year-old Egyptian tombs is still safe to eat. These are mostly popular-science outlets, and "never spoils" holds only if the honey stays sealed and dry. No source contradicted the claim.

text: Scientists estimate that there are approximately 8.7 million identified species on Earth, although the actual number could be much higher.
label: contradicted
reason: The 8.7 million figure from Mora et al. (2011, PLoS Biology) is an estimate of all eukaryotic species on Earth, not the number already identified. ScienceDaily reports that the same study found about 86% of land species and 91% of ocean species have not yet been discovered or catalogued, so only about 1.2 million had been described. The claim calls the 8.7 million species 'identified', which misstates what the study measured.

text: The dying ember of Supernova 1987A is the closest observed supernova to Earth since the invention of the telescope.
label: supported
reason: ESA/Hubble, ScienceDaily, Wikipedia and peer-reviewed arXiv papers all say SN 1987A was the closest observed supernova to Earth since the telescope was invented. The words "dying ember" in the claim just describe its remnant. One caveat: Cassiopeia A (around 1680) is closer, but it was not clearly observed as a supernova, so it is not normally counted.

text: Tarantulas have been around for a long time - fossil evidence shows they existed over 120 million years ago during the Cretaceous period.
label: contradicted
reason: The claim gets the fossil evidence wrong. Live Science reports that only two tarantula fossils are known, and the oldest, preserved in Burmese amber from Myanmar, is about 100 million years old. A biogeography study in the Journal of Biogeography also calls this ~100 Ma Burmese amber specimen the oldest known tarantula fossil. The '120 million years ago, Cretaceous' figure does appear in sources, but it is a molecular-clock estimate of when tarantulas originated (Foley et al. 2021), based on transcriptome data, not fossils. Tarantulas did exist in the Cretaceous, but fossils do not show them existing more than 120 million years ago.

text: Tarantulas have been on Earth for a long time, with fossil records showing they existed over 99 million years ago during the Cretaceous period.
label: supported
reason: Live Science, reporting on the peer-reviewed study of how tarantulas spread across the world, says only two tarantula fossils are known, both in amber. One of them, from Myanmar, is about 100 million years old, which fits Burmese amber's usual mid-Cretaceous date of roughly 99 million years. The same study found that tarantulas first appeared in the Cretaceous period. Together, these support the claim that fossils show tarantulas existed more than 99 million years ago, during the Cretaceous.

text: Humans and dolphins are the only animals known to give themselves names or have a sense of self-awareness, recognizing themselves in mirrors.
label: contradicted
reason: The claim is false. Humans and dolphins are not the only animals that recognize themselves in mirrors. Great apes (chimpanzees, bonobos and orangutans), Asian elephants, Eurasian magpies and the cleaner wrasse fish have also passed the mirror self-recognition test. The claim also lumps naming together with self-awareness, and other animals show both: elephants and some parrots have been reported to use name-like calls.

text: Humans are born without kneecaps; they are made of soft cartilage until around age 3, when they begin to harden into bone.
label: contradicted
reason: The main point of the claim is wrong. HowStuffWorks says babies do have kneecaps, even though the kneecaps don't show up on X-rays. Grownsy and Kaiya Baby agree that newborns have a kneecap made of cartilage, not bone, and call the 'no kneecaps' idea a myth. The second half of the claim roughly matches the sources: the kneecap stays cartilage at first and starts turning into bone between about ages 2 and 6, so 'around age 3' is close. Even so, saying babies are born without kneecaps is a misconception. Scary Mommy's 'sort of' framing is the closest any source comes to backing it, and that article also says babies are born with a cartilage kneecap.

text: A blue whale's heartbeat can be as loud as 188 decibels, which is louder than a jet taking off.
label: contradicted
reason: The 188-decibel figure is for the blue whale's call, not its heartbeat. WWF says blue whale calls reach 188 dB, compared with about 140 dB for a jet.
