Wikipedia's list of whale vocalizations gives blue whale sound source levels of 155–188 dB. No reliable source says the heartbeat reaches anything close to 188 dB. Sources such as NOAA only say the heartbeat can be heard or detected up to about 2 miles away, and even that claim is disputed. The claim takes a fact about the whale's call and wrongly applies it to the heartbeat.

text: A blue whale's heartbeat is so powerful it can be detected from over two miles away.
label: supported
reason: NOAA Fisheries, a reliable government source, says a blue whale's heartbeat "can be heard 2 miles away," and the Cold Spring Harbor Whaling Museum says it can be detected from 2 miles away underwater. The only sources that disagree are Brainly community answers, which are not reliable. One small mismatch remains: the reliable sources say "2 miles," while the claim says "over two miles." That wording difference is minor, so the claim is supported overall.

text: Biologically speaking, there is no such thing as a truly 'blue' eye - all blue eyes are actually a result of the way light interacts with the structure of the iris itself.
label: supported
reason: The American Academy of Ophthalmology says blue eyes contain no blue pigment. Their colour comes from the way the iris stroma, which has no pigment in that front layer, scatters light so that more blue light is reflected back out. This is the same reason the sky and water look blue. A USPTO patent document adds that the stroma has no blue pigment and that the blue appearance comes from light passing through its collagen fibres. Together, these sources back the claim that blue eye colour is structural rather than pigment-based.

text: Giraffes are the only animals born with their eyes open.
label: contradicted
reason: The Oxford Reference entry on 'precocial' says many young mammals are born with their eyes and ears open, including grazing animals such as cattle, sheep and horses. Guinea pigs are also born with their eyes open. Because many species besides giraffes are born this way, giraffes are not the only ones, so the claim is false.

text: Scientists estimate that there are approximately 8.7 million identified species on Earth, but it is believed that up to 80% of all species remain undiscovered.
label: contradicted
reason: The 8.7 million figure is an estimate of all species on Earth, both known and unknown. It is not a count of identified species. Mora et al.'s 2011 estimate, as reported by Nature News, gives about 8.7 million species in total, with only about 1.2 million identified and catalogued, which is less than 15%. The '80% undiscovered' part fits the finding that more than 80% of species (86% of land species, 91% of marine species) are still undiscovered. Calling 8.7 million 'identified species' contradicts the source.

text: A giant squid's eyes are said to be the largest of any animal, with some specimens having eyes that are up to 10 inches in diameter.
label: supported
reason: The Smithsonian, a reliable source, says giant squid have the largest eyes in the animal kingdom, at up to 10 inches in diameter (si.edu, ocean.si.edu). National Geographic Kids and NBC News say the same. Some sources, such as Britannica Kids, say the colossal squid's eyes may be slightly larger. Because the claim only says the giant squid's eyes are 'said to be' the largest, and the Smithsonian says exactly that, both parts of the claim are supported.

text: A blue whale can hold its breath underwater for approximately 20 minutes.
label: supported
reason: Britannica says blue whales usually dive for about 10 to 20 minutes and can stay under for up to roughly half an hour when needed. A breath-hold of about 20 minutes fits that typical range. Some sources give longer maximums, but that doesn't contradict an 'approximately 20 minutes' figure.

text: Caterpillars can eat up to 27,000 times their body weight in a single day, which is equivalent to a human eating around 45,000 pizzas.
label: contradicted
reason: Several reliable sources (The Naked Scientists, 13abc, Twinkl, KidsKonnect) say caterpillars eat about 27,000 times their body weight across their whole larval stage, which lasts about 3–4 weeks. They do not say this happens in a single day. Only one low-quality page (an Amherst 'statustest' subdomain) repeats the 'single day' version. The pizza comparison was not checked, but the time-frame error is enough to contradict the claim.

text: Scientists estimate that there are approximately 100-400 billion stars in the Milky Way galaxy.
label: supported
reason: Wikipedia's Milky Way article says the galaxy is estimated to contain 100–400 billion stars, which matches the claim. Other sources, such as Universe Today, give similar estimates.

text: Blue crystals of lapis lazuli have been found buried with the dead in ancient Egyptians' elaborate tombs, and were believed to hold spiritual and magical powers.
label: supported
reason: Several sources say lapis lazuli was placed in ancient Egyptian tombs, including Tutankhamun's, and was believed to have spiritual, protective and magical significance. They link it to resurrection, the Book of the Dead's burial rites, and amulets meant to protect the dead. One small wording issue: lapis lazuli is a rock rather than a crystal, but this doesn't change the main point of the claim.

text: Galaxies in the observable universe are moving away from each other at speeds of up to 3 million kilometers per hour due to the expansion of the universe.
label: contradicted
reason: The claim puts the top recession speed at 3 million km/h, which badly understates it. Trustworthy sources (Scientific American, Kavli Foundation, Phys.org, and peer-reviewed papers on arXiv) say the most distant galaxies recede from us faster than the speed of light because of cosmic expansion. That is more than about 1.08 billion km/h. Even nearby galaxies recede at over 240,000 km/h, and recession speed keeps rising with distance, so it has no upper limit of 3 million km/h.

text: Scientists estimate that there are approximately 8.7 million identified species on Earth, but the exact number is believed to be much higher as many remain undiscovered.
label: contradicted
reason: The 8.7 million figure is wrong in the way the claim uses it. It comes from Mora et al. (2011, PLoS Biology), and it estimates the total number of species on Earth, including the ones nobody has found yet. It is not a count of identified species. The same study says only about 1.2 million species had been catalogued, which means roughly 86% of species are still undescribed. Other sources put described species at around 2 million. So 8.7 million is the estimated total, not the number identified.

text: A giant squid's eyes are enormous, with some specimens having eyes that are up to 10 inches in diameter, which is the largest of any known animal.
label: supported
reason: The Smithsonian says giant squid have the largest eyes in the animal kingdom, measuring up to 10 inches across. National Geographic Kids gives the same figure, about 10 inches (25 cm), and calls them the largest eyes in the animal kingdom. One caveat: National Geographic Kids and some other sources say the colossal squid's eyes match or beat the giant squid's. Still, trustworthy sources back the claim as worded.

text: Honeybees are able to recognize and remember human faces, and are even capable of distinguishing between them, similar to some primates.
label: supported
reason: Dyer et al.'s 2005 study in the Journal of Experimental Biology found that honeybees could learn to tell apart photos of similar human faces, recognize them, and remember them for at least two days. The research and news coverage compare this ability to face processing in humans and other primates, which supports the claim. One caveat: the bees were tested on photographs, not real faces.

text: Many species of jellyfish are immortal, as they are biologically capable of reversing their aging process through transdifferentiation.
label: contradicted
reason: The claim says "many species" of jellyfish are immortal, and that's wrong. Trustworthy sources describe the ability as belonging to one species, Turritopsis dohrnii. The Scientist calls it "the only known animal species" whose adults can reverse their development under stress, and it notes that a closely related species, Turritopsis rubra, does not show this biological immortality. EBSCO also describes T. dohrnii as unique. The transdifferentiation part is accurate for T. dohrnii, but it does not apply to many jellyfish species.

text: Tarantulas have been on Earth for a long time, with fossil evidence showing they existed around 120 million years ago during the Cretaceous period.
label: supported
reason: Reliable reports on the 2021 Carnegie Mellon study by Foley et al. say tarantulas first appeared about 120 million years ago, in the Cretaceous (Phys.org, Live Science, Smithsonian, SciTechDaily). That backs up the claim's main point that tarantulas are ancient and date to about 120 million years ago. One detail is less exact: the 120-million-year date comes from a genetic family tree whose timing was calibrated with fossil data, not from a fossil that old. The oldest known tarantula fossil, preserved in Burmese amber, is about 100 million years old, which is still in the Cretaceous. Because fossil data helped set the date and the actual fossils confirm tarantulas lived in the Cretaceous, the claim is broadly supported.

text: A blue whale's heartbeat can last up to 2 minutes and is the slowest heartbeat of any animal on record.
label: contradicted
reason: Reliable reports on the 2019 Stanford study (Goldbogen et al.) say a diving blue whale's heart slows to as few as 2 beats per minute. That puts roughly 30 seconds between beats, not a single heartbeat lasting up to 2 minutes, so the claim confuses the rate with the length of a beat. ABC News also describes it only as 'one of the slowest' heart rates, which does not back the claim that it is the slowest of any animal on record.

text: Galileo Galilei was the first person to observe the planet Neptune using a telescope, but he didn't officially discover it due to limited information from his observation, as Pluto was officially discovered by Clyde Tombaugh in 1930 and Neptune was officially discovered by Johann Galle and Heinrich d'Arrest in
label: supported
reason: The individual facts in the claim check out. Galileo sketched Neptune on Dec 27/28, 1612 and again in January 1613 while observing Jupiter's moons. He took it for a fixed star, so he never recognized it as a planet. Johann Galle, working with Heinrich d'Arrest, made the official telescopic discovery in September 1846, based on Le Verrier's prediction. Clyde Tombaugh discovering Pluto in 1930 is well established. Two caveats: the claim is cut off before the year (1846), and the 'as Pluto was discovered...' wording links facts that have nothing to do with each other. Neither of these makes any stated fact false.

text: One flex of a human eyebrow contains from around 110,000 to 210,000 hair follicles and other types of hairs.
label: contradicted
reason: The claim overstates the number by roughly a thousand times. Reliable sources say a human eyebrow has a few hundred hairs, not 110,000 to 210,000. The Donovan Hair Clinic says most people have 200–400 eyebrow hairs, usually about 225–265. Other sources give about 250 per eyebrow, and Harvard's BioNumbers lists 600 hairs for both eyebrows combined. Numbers around 100,000–150,000 describe the hair on the scalp, not an eyebrow.

text: One flex of a human eyebrow is made up of around 990 muscles with the rest of 75 different muscles to make a total.
label: contradicted
reason: Anatomy sources say eyebrow movement comes from just a few forehead muscles: the frontalis, procerus, corrugator supercilii and orbicularis oculi (sometimes also the depressor supercilii). Nothing close to 990 muscles is involved. The whole human face has only about 43 muscles, so the claim's figures of 990 muscles in an eyebrow flex plus 75 others are wrong.

text: One flex of a human eyebrow muscle requires the simultaneous coordination of at least seven underlying muscles.
label: contradicted
reason: Anatomical sources such as NCBI StatPearls, Medscape and ScienceDirect say the eyebrow is moved by a small group of muscles. The frontalis is the only muscle that raises it. The procerus, corrugator supercilii, depressor supercilii and orbital orbicularis oculi pull it down. Raising the eyebrows is described as mainly the frontalis contracting, and the full brow muscle group is only about four or five muscles. No reliable source says one eyebrow movement requires seven or more muscles working together, and the anatomy described in these sources conflicts with that number.

text: One flex of a human eyebrow requires the simultaneous movement and coordination of approximately eight separate muscle groups.
label: contradicted
reason: Trusted anatomy sources say only four or five muscles control the eyebrow. The frontalis is the only muscle that raises it. The procerus, corrugator supercilii, depressor supercilii and the orbital part of the orbicularis oculi pull it down (StatPearls/NCBI, Medscape, ScienceDirect). Raising an eyebrow mainly takes one muscle on each side, and even all the eyebrow muscles together come to about five. None of the sources support the claim that one eyebrow movement coordinates about eight separate muscle groups.

text: A large percentage of humans are born with a slight imbalance in hand strength, with the majority favoring their right hand regardless if they recognize they have a preferred hand.
label: supported
reason: The sources back each part of the claim. Tan's studies of human newborns, published on PubMed (about 103–121 babies tested within two days of birth), found that the grasp reflex was on average stronger in the right hand than the left. That supports an imbalance in hand strength present at birth, mostly favoring the right hand. Ultrasound studies (Hepper; Parma/SISSA) show a right-hand bias before birth, at a stage when there is no conscious recognition of a preferred hand. Grip-strength research in adults (Petersen et al., PubMed 2750859; Scientific Reports 2025) finds the dominant hand is roughly 10% stronger in right-handers, which fits the idea of a slight imbalance. The claim's vague wording ('large percentage', 'regardless if they recognize') can't be checked exactly, but nothing in the evidence contradicts it.

text: A oku, or hundred trillion, is the Japanese term for 10^22, or a 1 followed by 22 zeros.
label: contradicted
reason: In Japanese numbering, oku (億) means 10^8, which is one hundred million. It does not mean 10^22 or a hundred trillion. The large-number units go man 10^4, oku 10^8, chō 10^12, kei 10^16, gai 10^20 and jo 10^24. No single basic unit stands for 10^22, and in any case 10^22 is ten sextillion, not a hundred trillion (10^14). Every numeric part of the claim is wrong.

text: Child prodigy Ruth Lawrence earned a PhD in mathematics from Harvard University at the age of 18 in 1988.
label: contradicted
reason: The claim gets the university, her age and the year wrong. Ruth Lawrence earned her doctorate in mathematics (a DPhil) at Oxford in June 1989, when she was 17, not at Harvard in 1988 at 18. She went to Harvard later, becoming a junior fellow there at 19. Wikipedia also lists her education as Oxford (MA, DPhil).

text: Humans share about 50% of their DNA with bananas, indicating a common ancestor in the distant past.
label: contradicted
reason: Snopes, a reliable fact-checking site, rates the claim that humans share 50% of their DNA with bananas as false. It says there is no reading of that statement that makes it factual. The figure that gets passed around really means that about half of human genes have a counterpart gene in bananas, which is not the same as sharing half our DNA. Snopes also cites an expert who points out that humans share well under 1% of whole-genome DNA with zebrafish, which are far closer relatives than bananas, so the true figure for bananas would be much lower. Humans and bananas do share a very distant common ancestor, but the 50% DNA part of the claim is wrong.

text: Elara, the moon of Neptune, is the first natural satellite discovered to orbit in a retrograde (backward) direction around its parent planet.
label: contradicted
reason: The claim is wrong on two counts. Elara is a moon of Jupiter, not Neptune; Charles Dillon Perrine discovered it at Lick Observatory in 1905. It also orbits in a prograde direction, not a retrograde one. The NASA Planetary Data System and other sources describe it as a prograde irregular satellite of Jupiter. From general astronomical knowledge rather than the search results: the first retrograde satellite discovered was Saturn's moon Phoebe, in 1899.

text: A blue whale's heartbeat is so loud, it can be heard for hundreds of miles underwater, making it the loudest animal on Earth.
label: contradicted
reason: NOAA Fisheries says a blue whale's heartbeat can be heard about 2 miles away, not hundreds of miles. Some sources question even the 2-mile figure. The blue whale's reputation as one of the loudest animals comes from its vocal calls, which can travel very long distances underwater, not from its heartbeat. The claim gets the heartbeat's range wrong and wrongly credits its loudness to the heartbeat.

text: Humans are born without kneecaps; they do not appear until around 3-5 years of age.
label: contradicted
reason: Babies are not born without kneecaps. HowStuffWorks says the idea that newborns lack kneecaps is a myth. At birth the kneecap is already there, but it is made of cartilage. That cartilage hardens into bone (ossifies) between about 3 and 5 years of age. The 3–5 year timeframe in the claim refers to when the kneecap becomes bone, not when it first appears. So the claim that kneecaps are absent at birth is wrong.

text: Turtles have a unique respiratory system that allows them to hold their breath underwater for extended periods, with some species able to stay submerged for up to five months.
label: supported
reason: I found support for both parts of the claim. The Spokesman-Review says western painted turtles can get through cold weather for up to five months without surfacing for air while brumating. The Nature Conservancy and Cambridge Day describe the adaptations involved: absorbing oxygen through the skin and other surfaces, tolerating very low or no oxygen, storing lactic acid in the shell, and slowing their metabolism. Lab tests show adults surviving more than 100 days in 3°C water without oxygen. Other sources cite 3–4 months, but that fits with 'up to five months' and doesn't contradict it. The Conversation questions whether turtles really breathe through the cloaca, but it still confirms they can survive months underwater. Calling the system 'unique' is loose wording, but the main point is well supported.

text: Although not visible to the naked eye, there are estimated to be approximately 40 billion billion, or 4 x 10^22, stars in the observable universe.
label: contradicted
reason: The claim contradicts itself, and its worded figure is far below the accepted estimates. '40 billion billion' equals 4 × 10^19, not 4 × 10^22, so the two numbers are 1,000 times apart. Reliable sources estimate roughly 10^22 to 10^24 stars in the observable universe, with commonly cited figures of about 6–7 × 10^22 or 2 × 10^23 (about 200 sextillion). That puts '40 billion billion' (4 × 10^19) well below the scientific range. 4 × 10^22 is close to the low end of the range, but it does not rescue the statement because the claim equates it with an incorrect figure.

text: Japan has a vending machine for almost everything, including live crabs, which can be found in some cities.
label: contradicted
reason: The well-documented live-crab vending machines are in China, not Japan. NPR, Japanese Wikipedia, Record China and Livedoor all report that they were installed at a Nanjing subway station in 2010, with others later in Hangzhou. Japanese Wikipedia lists the live Shanghai-crab machine as being in Nanjing, China. Japanese outlets such as Gizmodo Japan describe it as a Chinese novelty. The crab vending machines found in Japan, such as the ones in Fukui and Kasumi/Takarazuka, sell cooked or processed crab products. Only one low-reliability travel-guide page vaguely says machines in Hakodate and Kanazawa sell 'live crabs or packaged cooked crab,' and it gives no specific details. The claim that live crabs are sold from vending machines in Japanese cities appears to come from mixing up the Nanjing machine with Japan.

text: A "jiffy" is an official unit of time that equals about 1/100th of a second.
label: contradicted
reason: There is no single official jiffy. Wikipedia describes it as an informal term for a short period of time, and it has several unrelated technical meanings. Gilbert N. Lewis proposed it as the time light takes to travel 1 cm, about 33 picoseconds. Other fields use 1/60 or 1/50 of a second for AC power cycles, or values like 0.01 s in computing. The 1/100-second meaning is just one convention, which TodayIFoundOut links to common stopwatch resolution. Calling it an official unit equal to about 1/100 of a second is therefore inaccurate.

text: Tarantulas have been on Earth for a long time, with fossil records showing that they've remained largely unchanged for over 100 million years.
label: not_verifiable
reason: The first part of the claim holds up: tarantulas are an old group. Researchers estimate they appeared about 120 million years ago, and the oldest theraphosid fossil, in Burmese amber, is dated to around 100 million years ago. The fossil detail does not hold up as well. LiveScience reports that only two tarantula fossils are known, one about 16 million years old and one about 100 million years old. Two fossils are too few to show the group stayed 'largely unchanged for over 100 million years.' Texas Parks & Wildlife Magazine says the fossil record shows tarantulas 'virtually unchanged' for more than 20 million years, not 100 million. A tarantula-hobby site does say they have survived about 120 million years while staying recognizably tarantulas, but that site is less trustworthy. Because the evidence for the 'unchanged for over 100 million years' part is mixed and weak, the claim cannot be confirmed or ruled out.

text: Octopuses have nine brains, with a large central brain and eight smaller mini-brains located in each of their arms, allowing them to think and problem-solve independently.
label: supported
reason: Many popular sources back the claim. A-Z Animals, Discovery and SpaceDaily describe octopuses as having nine brains: one central brain plus neuron clusters in each of the eight arms. ScienceDaily and OIST report that about two-thirds of an octopus's neurons are in its arms and body, and that the arms can act somewhat on their own. Discovery says the arms 'have minds of their own' and can make decisions. One caveat: some sources, such as Biology Insights, call 'nine brains' a simplification and say the arms have ganglia, not true brains. Saying the arms can 'problem-solve' on their own also overstates what the research shows. Still, most sources agree with the main idea.

text: Seals are able to slow down their heart rate dramatically to conserve energy, with some species' hearts beating as slowly as four to eight beats per minute while they sleep underwater.
label: not_verifiable
reason: I found strong support for the general idea, but not for the sleep detail. An A-Z Animals article says a seal's heart rate can fall from about 100 to as low as 4–10 beats per minute during a dive, which saves oxygen. That fits the claim's description of dramatic slowing and a very low rate. However, the evidence ties that rate to diving, not to sleeping underwater. A Science paper confirms that elephant seals sleep during dives, but nothing I found reports heart rates of 4–8 beats per minute while seals sleep underwater. My searches were cut off by a tool limit before I could check this further, so the sleep-specific part of the claim remains unverified.

text: A chunk of the Dead Sea has been found to be so dense with salt that objects can actually float on its surface.
label: supported
reason: Reliable sources, including NOAA and educational pages about the Dead Sea, say its water is extremely salty and dense. Below about 100 m it reaches 332 ppt and is saturated. Because of that density, people and objects float easily on the surface. The phrase "a chunk of the Dead Sea" is strange wording, but the main point of the claim matches well-established fact.

text: A rolling ball of glass can melt in extreme heat without shattering due to itsirse uniformly distributed thermal stress.
label: not_verifiable
reason: I couldn't find a trustworthy source that discusses a rolling glass ball melting in extreme heat without shattering. The claim is also partly garbled ("itsirse"), and its causal explanation is vague. What sources do say is that glass shatters from uneven temperatures and thermal stress, for example when it is poorly annealed or suffers thermal shock. That means heating glass slowly and evenly can lower the chance of cracking. But nothing I found says that rolling a glass ball spreads thermal stress evenly enough to stop it from shattering as it melts. So the specific claim can't be confirmed or ruled out.

text: Bacteria can only grow and reproduce in "moist" environments,  typically requiring a certain level of humidity or water to survive.
label: supported
reason: I found reliable sources that back the main point. An eLife study, also on PMC, says that "like all other organisms, bacteria need water to survive." Sources on water activity say moisture levels decide whether microbes can grow and multiply. Bacteria do not grow when water availability is below certain thresholds, and they can become dormant instead. The claim's wording about survival is a bit broad, because some bacteria can endure dry periods without growing. Still, that does not contradict its main point that growth and reproduction need moisture.

text: Level 1 is the highest international classification level of wheelchair basketball, for which athletes have the physical ability to propel themselves at a rapid speed and quick reaction time.
label: contradicted
reason: In wheelchair basketball, players are classified from 1.0 to 4.5 points. A 1.0-point player is in the lowest functional category, with little or no trunk control, while 4.5 is the highest. Calling Level 1 the highest classification, with the greatest physical ability, gets the scale backwards.

text: Galileo Galilei was the first person to observe the planet Neptune, but he didn't recognize it as a planet due to poor telescope quality and the fact that it was near conjunction with Jupiter.
label: supported
reason: Wikipedia's 'Discovery of Neptune' article and a 2022 paper in the Journal of Astronomical History and Heritage (arXiv) both say Galileo observed Neptune on December 28, 1612 and January 27, 1613. These are the earliest recorded observations of the planet. Both times he took it for a fixed star while it sat in close conjunction with Jupiter, and Wikipedia adds that it was too small and moved too little to show up clearly as a planet in his small telescope. One caveat: the sources say his records are the earliest known, not that nobody could have seen it before him. Also, 'poor telescope quality' is a simplification, since the sources mainly point to the telescope being small and to Neptune's very slow apparent motion at the time. The claim's main points match the sources.

text: Plants can produce sounds when they are injured, stressed, or diseased through ultrasonic clicks that are too faint to be audible to humans.
label: supported
reason: The 2023 Cell study by Khait et al. found that stressed plants give off airborne ultrasonic clicks. It recorded these clicks from tomato and tobacco plants that were dried out (stressed) or had their stems cut (injured), and it also recorded sounds from tomato plants infected with tobacco mosaic virus (diseased). Science News reported the same findings. One detail is slightly off: people can't hear these clicks mainly because their frequency is too high (ultrasonic), not because they are too quiet. The rest of the claim matches the research.

text: publik Library' was first used in 1852 by Peterborough Town Library in England
label: contradicted
reason: The Peterborough Town Library is in Peterborough, New Hampshire, USA, not England. It was founded in 1833, not 1852, and is known as the first free public library supported by taxes. The year 1852 belongs to other libraries, such as the Manchester Free Library in England and the Boston Public Library's opening.

text: Tarantulas have been on Earth for approximately 120 million years, with fossil records showing they've remained largely unchanged since the Cretaceous period.
label: not_verifiable
reason: The age is supported, but the fossil part of the claim is not. A Carnegie Mellon study reported by Live Science, Smithsonian and Big Think dates tarantulas' origin to about 120 million years ago, in the Cretaceous. That estimate came from a molecular family tree built from transcriptome data, though, not from fossils showing the spiders stayed the same. Sources describe the tarantula fossil record as very sparse. Only a few specimens can be convincingly assigned to Theraphosidae, most in Miocene amber about 16–23 million years old. The oldest proposed specimen is in Burmese amber from about 100 million years ago. No source found says fossils show tarantulas have 'remained largely unchanged since the Cretaceous,' so that part can't be verified and appears to overstate the evidence.

text: The Axel Erlandson's Tree Circus, located in California, features a collection of intricately grafted trees, resulting from decades of careful cultivation and training.
label: supported
reason: Gilroy Gardens and Roadside America say Swedish immigrant Axel Erlandson began shaping and grafting living trees in the 1920s. In 1946–47 he opened the 'Tree Circus' in Scotts Valley, California, to show them. That matches the claim's California location, intricately grafted trees and decades of cultivation and training. One detail: the original attraction has since closed. Many of its trees were moved and are now shown as the 'Circus Trees' at Gilroy Gardens, which is also in California. A few remain at the old Scotts Valley site. So the claim's present-tense wording is a little dated, but its substance holds.

text: Scientists estimate that there are approximately 8.7 million identified species on Earth, but the total number of species, including those that have not been discovered, is thought to be around 30 million.
label: contradicted
reason: The claim gets the key figure wrong. The 8.7 million number from Mora et al. (2011, PLoS Biology) is an estimate of all species on Earth, both known and undiscovered. It is not a count of species already identified. Only about 1.2 to 2 million species have actually been described. The claim also gives about 30 million as the scientific estimate for the total, but this study puts the total at 8.7 million, give or take 1.3 million.

text: Galileo Galilei was the first person to observe the planet Neptune, although his notes did not recognize it as a planet and he observed it as a fixed, albeit dim, star.
label: supported
reason: Wikipedia's 'Discovery of Neptune' article says Galileo's drawings record Neptune on December 28, 1612, and January 27, 1613. Both times he mistook it for a fixed star, did not recognise it as a planet, and is not credited with its discovery. Scientific American likewise says he observed it in 1612 and thought it was a fixed star, 234 years before it was identified as a planet. Other sources describe his sighting as the first observation of Neptune. Neptune is too faint to see with the naked eye, which fits the claim's 'dim star' description. One nuance: Wikipedia notes that in January 1613 Galileo wrote that this background star seemed to have moved, but he still never identified it as a planet.

text: Polar bears are excellent swimmers and have been known to swim for hours or even days at a time while searching for food or shelter.
label: supported
reason: Reliable sources (CBC, reporting on a USGS study in Polar Biology) say polar bears are strong swimmers. One tracked female swam about 687 km nonstop over nine days in the Beaufort Sea, moving between ice floes and between ice and land. Swims lasting hours or days while looking for food or suitable habitat are well documented.

text: A blue whale's heartbeat can be as slow as two beats per minute when it is at rest.
label: contradicted
reason: The 2 beats-per-minute figure is real, but the claim gives the wrong context. It comes from the first ECG recording of a blue whale, made by Stanford's Goldbogen Lab in 2019. CBC and CNN both report that the whale's heart rate fell as low as 2 bpm during feeding dives. They describe this happening as the whale dove and lunged for food, not while it was resting. During those dives the rate was usually 4–8 bpm, and it rose to 25–37 bpm after the whale surfaced to breathe. The low rate is linked to breath-hold diving, so the claim's 'when it is at rest' does not match the evidence.

text: Higher levels of social connections in life have been scientifically linked to a lower risk of cognitive decline and dementia in older age.
label: supported
reason: A meta-analysis from UNSW's Centre for Healthy Brain Ageing, published in Alzheimer's & Dementia, pooled 13 international studies of people aged 65 and over. It found that social connections, such as living with others, interacting with friends and family, and community engagement, are linked to a lower risk of mild cognitive impairment, dementia and death. Broader research also identifies social isolation as a dementia risk factor. Together, this backs the claim that more social connection is scientifically linked to a lower risk of cognitive decline and dementia in later life.

text: Higher levels of social connections in life have been scientifically linked to a lower risk of cognitive decline and psychological disorders.
label: supported
reason: Several sources back both parts of the claim. A pooled analysis of 13 longitudinal cohort studies, published in Alzheimer's & Dementia, found that good social connections were linked to a lower risk of mild cognitive impairment, dementia and death. A long-running British study likewise found that more social contact at age 60 was tied to lower dementia risk. The CDC and health-system sources (BJC, Healthline) say social connection lowers the risk of depression and helps people manage stress and anxiety, which supports the psychological-disorder part.

text: Large corporations like IBM, Microsoft, and Google have been using artificial intelligence (AI) for decades in products such as chatbots and voice assistants.
label: supported
reason: Histories of conversational AI back up the general claim. IBM's work goes back to the Shoebox speech-recognition machine in the early 1960s. Microsoft shipped AI-based assistants such as Office's Clippy in the 1990s and Cortana in 2014. Google brought in voice search in the late 2000s, followed by Google Now and Google Assistant. 'For decades' fits IBM and Microsoft easily. It is a looser fit for Google, which was founded in 1998, and for voice assistants as a product category, since Cortana and Google Assistant only date from the 2010s. Even so, the broad claim matches the documented history.

text: A якості fact is that humans share about 50-60% of their DNA with bananas.
label: contradicted
reason: The claim mixes up genes and DNA. The 50–60% figure comes from NHGRI work showing that roughly 60% of human genes have a recognizable counterpart in bananas. That is not 60% of our DNA. IFLScience says the popular statement is technically wrong "because it's not 60 percent, and it's not DNA." HowStuffWorks says there is some truth to the figure, "but it's not the whole truth." The Star's fact-check points out that genes make up only a small part of the genome, so the overlap is about 1–2% of the whole human genome. ProteinIQ's orthology analysis estimates the shared portion at less than 0.1%. Some casual trivia sites repeat the 60% DNA figure, but the more reliable sources reject the claim as worded.

text: Near the surface of Greenland and Antarctica, scientists have discovered remnants of ancient forests preserved beneath the ice sheets for millions of years.
label: contradicted
reason: Scientists have found ancient plant and forest remnants beneath both ice sheets. Examples include plant fossils and forest DNA from Greenland ice cores, and a 90-million-year-old rainforest in Antarctic sediments. The claim gets the location wrong, though. These finds were not near the surface. In Greenland they came from the bottom of ice cores, about 1.4 km (roughly a mile) down. In Antarctica they came from deep sediment beneath the ice and seafloor. Also, the Greenland material is mostly under about 1 million years old. Because the 'near the surface' part is contradicted, the claim as stated does not hold.

text: Honeybees are capable of recognizing human faces and remembering them for later encounters, much like some other animals and even certain primates.
label: supported
reason: A 2005 study by Dyer and colleagues in the Journal of Experimental Biology found that honeybees could learn to recognize human faces in photographs and still remember them at least two days later, which shows long-term memory. Phys.org reported the result and noted that face recognition is also known in other animals, including primates. One caveat: the bees were tested on photos, not real people.

text: Tarzon, or giant water lilies, are capable of supporting up to 70 pounds due to their large leaves and unique structure.
label: not_verifiable
reason: The weight figure checks out, but the name doesn't. Trustworthy sources, including Bok Tower Gardens, say giant Victoria water lily leaves can hold about 70 pounds, and other accounts give figures around 65 to 100 pounds. Leaf structure is the usual explanation for this. However, no source calls giant water lilies "Tarzon." They are known as Victoria amazonica, the Amazon water lily, the royal water lily, or vitória-régia. Because the main subject of the claim can't be identified or verified, the claim as a whole is inconclusive.

text: A blue whale's heartbeat is so loud that it can be detected from over 500 miles away underwater.
label: contradicted
reason: Sources commonly put the distance at about 2 miles, not more than 500 miles. The Whaling Museum says a blue whale's heartbeat "can be detected from 2 MILES AWAY." The 500+ mile figure seems to come from the range of blue whale calls, not their heartbeats. Even the 2-mile figure is a popular claim and hasn't been well established by science.

text: Ahead of the development of modern antibiotics, Penicillium mould was first used by Scottish scientist Alexander Fleming in 1928 to cure bacterial infections.
label: contradicted
reason: Fleming did discover penicillin's antibacterial effect from Penicillium mould in 1928. He did not use it to cure bacterial infections that year, though. Wikipedia and The Conversation both say the first successful treatment came in 1930, when Fleming's student Cecil George Paine used it on eye infections. Fleming himself first treated a patient with purified penicillin in 1942. Penicillium moulds had also been used against infections before 1928, so it is wrong to say Fleming was the first to use them for this.

text: Electric bees (also known as Wallace's giant bee) have the largest bee body size in the world.
label: not_verifiable
reason: The size part checks out. Wikipedia, Guinness World Records and the University of Sydney all say Wallace's giant bee (Megachile pluto) is the largest known living bee, with females up to about 4.5 cm long and a wingspan of about 63.5 mm. The other part doesn't. These sources give its other names as 'Wallace's giant bee' and 'raja ofu' ('king of the bees'), and none calls it the 'electric bee.' The searches found nothing linking that name to this species. No source directly says the name is wrong, so the alias can't be confirmed or ruled out, which makes the claim as a whole inconclusive.

text: A\model of a human nose can detect odors even after being removed from the body.
label: not_verifiable
reason: I only found results about electronic noses that detect human body odour, and studies of what the human nose can smell. None of them describe a model of a human nose that still detects odours after being removed from a body. The claim is also unclear: it doesn't say which model it means, and a model was never part of a body, so 'removed from the body' doesn't make sense as written. The search tool hit its usage limit before I could look into other readings, such as lab-grown smell tissue or sensors built with human smell receptors. That leaves the claim unconfirmed and not disproved.

text: Cats have a highly specialized vocalization range that allows them to vocalize at frequencies that humans can't hear.
label: not_verifiable
reason: My searches only turned up evidence about what cats can hear, not what sounds they make. Trustworthy sources, including an Acoustics Today review and an ASA abstract on cat ABR audiometry, confirm that cats hear well into the ultrasonic range, well above the roughly 20 kHz limit of human hearing. The claim, however, is about cat vocalizations. No source I found shows that cats produce calls at frequencies humans can't hear. The ultrasonic-vocalization literature I found covers rodents such as mice and rats, not cats. As far as I know, typical cat sounds like meows and purrs fall within the range humans can hear, but none of the results confirmed this either. My search budget ran out before I could look for direct evidence on cat vocal frequencies or the popular 'silent meow' idea, so the claim can't be confirmed or ruled out.

text: Polar bears can swim for hours or even days at a time, covering distances of up to 60 miles without resting.
label: supported
reason: The search results back up both parts of the claim. Polar bears can swim for days without stopping: CBC and Live Science report GPS tracking studies of multi-day swims. Polar Bears International's polarbears.com and Swan Expeditions both say polar bears can swim about 60 miles (96–100 km) without resting. One caveat is that 60 miles is not actually the upper limit. Studies have recorded swims of hundreds of miles, including one female bear that swam for nine days. That means the bears can do at least what the claim describes, so the record does not contradict it, but the phrase "up to" understates the maximum.

text: vgStructures exist within living organisms and some astronauts have walked on the Moon
label: supported
reason: Both parts of the claim check out, though "vgStructures" looks like a typo for "structures". I'm treating it that way. Twelve Apollo astronauts walked on the Moon between 1969 and 1972, starting with Neil Armstrong and ending with Gene Cernan (Wikipedia's list of Apollo astronauts, ABC7). It is also basic, well-established biology that structures such as cells, organelles and organs exist within living organisms. Nothing I found contradicts either part.

text: Scientists estimate that there are approximately 8.7 million identified species on Earth, but up to 80% of all species remain undiscovered and unclassified.
label: contradicted
reason: The 8.7 million figure is wrong for this claim. Mora et al. (PLoS Biology, 2011) give it as an estimate of the total number of eukaryotic species on Earth, both known and unknown. It is not a count of identified species. Only about 1.2 million species had been described, and the study found that about 86% of existing species have not yet been described. Calling 8.7 million 'identified' species gets the study backwards.

text: The Axel Erlandson Tree Circus, located in Felton, California, features a collection of trees that have been grafted and pruned into unique shapes, including spirals and rings.
label: contradicted
reason: Axel Erlandson's Tree Circus was not in Felton. It opened in 1947 in Scotts Valley, California. In 1985 the surviving trees were moved to Gilroy, where they are now shown at Gilroy Gardens. The part about grafted and shaped trees in spirals, rings and other forms is accurate, but the location in the claim is wrong.

text: Aola Island in the Solomon Islands is home to the world's largest saltwater lagoon, Marovo Lagoon, which covers an area of approximately 700 square kilometers.
label: contradicted
reason: Marovo Lagoon is often described as the world's largest saltwater lagoon and covers more than 700 km², but it is not on Aola Island. It sits in Western Province and wraps around the New Georgia, Vangunu and Gatokae islands. Aola is a bay and village on the northeast coast of Guadalcanal. The claim puts the lagoon in the wrong place, so it is contradicted.

text: Humans and dolphins are the only animals known to give names to themselves and also to identify themselves by name.
label: contradicted
reason: The claim is contradicted. A 2024 study reported by AFP via France24 found that elephants use their own individual name-like calls for each other, and that each elephant recognizes and reacts to calls addressed to it. The same report says parrots, as well as dolphins, address each other by imitating each other's sounds. Separate research reports that marmosets do something similar. So humans and dolphins are not the only animals known to use names and respond to their own.

text: M dla Mountains is the highest peak in the Solar System, with a height of approximately 27 km, located on Mars.
label: contradicted
reason: No mountain called "M dla Mountains" exists. The Wikipedia list of named Martian mountains does not include it, and a search turns up nothing. Reliable sources (EBSCO, BBC Science Focus) name a different mountain on Mars, Olympus Mons, as the tallest in the Solar System. Its height is usually given as about 21.9–22 km, though some figures go up to about 25–27 km. The BBC also notes the central peak of Vesta's Rheasilvia crater as a rival candidate. Because the claim gives the wrong name for the Solar System's highest peak, it is contradicted.

text: Scientists have discovered that octopuses have a highly developed nervous system with nine brains, eight of which are in their arms.
label: supported
reason: Trustworthy popular-science sources back the claim. A PBS Nature episode features a Monterey Bay Aquarium marine biologist explaining that octopuses have one main brain in the head and a 'brain' in each of their eight arms, nine in all, which lets each arm act fairly independently. Other sources describe the same complex nervous system. One caveat: scientists usually call the arm structures nerve cords or ganglia rather than true brains. Still, the 'nine brains' description is widely used by experts, so the claim stands.

text: France and the United States share the only international border that is to the north and south poles, due to their claims to the region surrounding the geographic poles.
label: contradicted
reason: The claim is false. Only seven countries have formal territorial claims in Antarctica: Argentina, Australia, Chile, France, New Zealand, Norway and the United Kingdom. The United States is not one of them. France's claim, Adélie Land, is a wedge-shaped sector that runs to the South Pole. Under the Antarctic Treaty, these claims are frozen and not recognized. No country owns the North Pole, which sits in international waters in the Arctic Ocean. So France and the US do not share a polar border, and no 'international border at the north and south poles' exists for them to share.

text: Schedule 1 of the Indian Constitution initially listed 29 states, but that number has since increased to 28, then to 29 and set back to 28, but then after the removal of Jammu and Kashmir now it is 28, but now it is a Union Territory and Ladakh is, then recently
label: not_verifiable
reason: The claim is garbled and cuts off mid-sentence ("then recently"), so it can't be checked as a whole. Its last fully stated parts do match the sources: India now has 28 states (vajiramandravi.com, 2025), Telangana's creation in 2014 brought the count to 29, and in 2019 Jammu and Kashmir became a Union Territory along with Ladakh, bringing it back to 28. But the opening is shaky. The 1950 First Schedule listed 28 states (9 Part A, 9 Part B and 10 Part C), plus one Part D territory. That only makes 29 if the territory is counted. The claim also says the number "increased to 28", which can't follow from 29. It leaves out the 1956 reorganisation that cut the states to 14 before they grew again. With a contradictory starting count and an unfinished ending, the claim can't be clearly confirmed or refuted.

text: A blueprint is typically a large-scale detailed drawing or diagram that is often used in planning, construction, and architecture projects.
label: supported
reason: Reliable references back up the claim. Wikipedia and EBSCO describe a blueprint as a reproduction of a technical, engineering or architectural design drawing. Wiktionary defines it, in architecture and engineering, as 'a detailed technical drawing'. Other sources say these drawings are used by architects, engineers, builders and planners on construction projects. The sources I found don't mention size, so 'large-scale' isn't directly confirmed, but it is a loose, typical description and nothing contradicts it.

text: Female mangrove crabs can change sex from female to male naturally as part of their growth and lifecycle.
label: contradicted
reason: The search results show that mangrove/mud crabs (Scylla spp.) are gonochoristic. That means each crab develops as either a male or a female from the juvenile stage and stays that sex. A ScienceDirect overview of sexual systems uses Scylla serrata as its example of gonochorism, with juveniles becoming primary males or primary females. Sex-determination research on Scylla also notes that most malacostracan crustaceans are gonochoristic. The only female-to-male change found in mud crabs was artificial: in experiments, crabs were masculinized by giving them 17α-methyltestosterone, and the authors noted that sex reversal is not yet common in crustaceans, especially mud crabs. Other sex changes in crabs come from parasites such as Sacculina, not from normal growth. No source supports a natural female-to-male change as part of the mangrove crab lifecycle.

text: Humans and dolphins are the only known species in the animal kingdom that have their own unique signature whistles, similar to human names, to identify themselves.
label: contradicted
reason: The claim says humans and dolphins are the only species with name-like identifiers, but that isn't true. A 2024 study reported by AFP/France24 found that elephants call each other by individual names. The same report notes that parrots, like dolphins, address each other by imitating others' calls. So dolphins are not the only non-human animals known to use name-like vocal labels.

text: A blue whale's heartbeat can be as slow as two beats per minute when the whale is at rest.
label: contradicted
reason: The 2019 Stanford study led by Goldbogen recorded a minimum heart rate of about 2 beats per minute, but this happened during deep foraging dives, not while the whale was at rest. Newsweek, Futurity and The Scientist all tie the 2 bpm low to diving, with typical diving rates of 4–8 bpm. At the surface, when the whale was not diving, its heart rate rose as high as 37 bpm. The number in the claim is right, but the condition attached to it, 'at rest,' does not match the evidence.

text: Bernard Bartalan, a Brazilian, holds the Guinness World Record for being the largest popcorn consumer, having eaten 237 buckets of popcorn at the cinema.
label: not_verifiable
reason: I found nothing to back up this claim. Searching for 'Bernard Bartalan' with popcorn or Guinness only turned up pages about the meaning of the name and unrelated sites. Searches for popcorn world records found other Guinness titles, such as the largest popcorn sculpture and the Galactus popcorn container from Fantastic Four, the largest sold in cinemas. None of them mention a 'largest popcorn consumer' record, a Brazilian record holder or 237 buckets. My Portuguese-language search didn't run because I hit the search limit. With no evidence for or against it, I can't verify the claim either way, though it looks likely to be made up.

text: Gravity is approximately 30% weaker at the summit of Mount Everest, the world's highest mountain, due to the mountain's extreme altitude.
label: contradicted
reason: Several sources agree that gravity at the summit of Everest is only about 0.28–0.3% weaker than at sea level (about 9.776 m/s² compared with 9.807 m/s²), not about 30%. Basic physics gives the same result: Everest is roughly 8.8 km high and Earth's radius is about 6,371 km, which works out to a drop of about 0.28%. The claim overstates the effect by about 100 times. It looks like someone mixed up 0.3% with 30%, or confused gravity with air pressure, which really is about a third of the sea-level value at the summit.

text: Honey NeverSpoils, an archaeological team found pots of honey in an ancient Egyptian tomb that were over 3,000 years old and still perfectly edible.
label: supported
reason: Reputable sources such as The Conversation and Smithsonian Magazine report the widely cited account that archaeologists digging in Egyptian tombs found pots of honey about 3,000 years old that were still edible. They tie this to honey's low water content, high sugar content and hydrogen peroxide, which together keep it from spoiling. The original archaeological source is poorly documented, but no search result contradicts the claim.

text: Tarantulas have been around for a long time, with fossil records showing they existed over 100 million years ago during the Cretaceous period.
label: supported
reason: A peer-reviewed study in the Journal of Biogeography (Wiley) says the oldest known tarantula fossil (Theraphosidae, Protertheraphosinae) comes from Burmese amber dated to about 100 million years ago, which falls in the mid-Cretaceous. The same study estimates that the tarantula lineage split from its closest relatives in the early Cretaceous, around 120 million years ago. One caveat: Burmese amber is usually dated to about 99 million years ago, so 'over 100 million years ago' is slightly generous for the fossil itself. Still, the core claim holds: there is a Cretaceous fossil record and the age is roughly 100 million years or more.

text: The Axel Erlandson's Tree Circus in California is a collection of tree sculptures with better-known examples including a basket-weave tree and a seven-trunked sycamore.
label: not_verifiable
reason: I could confirm only part of the claim. Erlandson's Tree Circus was a roadside attraction of grafted, shaped trees in Scotts Valley, California. Many of the trees now stand at Gilroy Gardens. Its iconic Basket Tree was made from six sycamores grafted into a woven, diamond pattern, which matches the 'basket-weave tree.' I found no source mentioning a 'seven-trunked sycamore' among his well-known trees. Wikipedia names the Basket Tree and the Needle and Thread Tree as his most famous, and the only sycamore counts I found were six for the Basket Tree and four for the Four-Legged Giant. My search limit ran out before I could check the full tree list, so I can't confirm or rule out the seven-trunked sycamore.

text: A blue whale's heartbeat can be as loud as 188 decibels, which is louder than a jet engine during takeoff.
label: contradicted
reason: The 188-decibel figure applies to blue whale calls (vocalizations), not their heartbeat. WWF says blue whale "calls reach 188 decibels, while a jet reaches 140 decibels," and Wikipedia gives blue whale vocalization source levels of 155–188 dB. No reliable source says the heartbeat reaches 188 dB. Sources about the heartbeat only claim it can be heard about 2 miles away, and even that claim is disputed. The claim takes a real statistic about calls and wrongly applies it to the heartbeat.

text: Humans and dolphins are the only mammals known to give themselves names, a trait demonstrated by the unique signature whistles used by dolphins to identify and address one another.
label: contradicted
reason: The claim that humans and dolphins are the only mammals known to use names doesn't hold up. A 2024 study in Nature Ecology and Evolution, run by Colorado State University and covered by ScienceDaily, AFP/France24, RTE and Al Jazeera, found that wild African elephants call each other with individual name-like calls. Unlike dolphins, they do this without imitating the other animal's sound. Separate 2024 research reported the same kind of behaviour in marmosets. Dolphins do use signature whistles, but they are not the only mammals besides humans known to do this.

text: Plants can make sounds when they are under stress, including clicking, hissing, and even sounds in the ultrasonic range that are inaudible to humans.
label: not_verifiable
reason: Most of the claim holds up, but one detail could not be confirmed. Reliable sources on the 2023 Tel Aviv University study (Khait et al., Cell) say that tomato and tobacco plants under drought stress or with cut stems emit airborne ultrasonic clicks or pops that humans cannot hear. Unstressed plants stayed mostly quiet. Science News, CNN, Nature, Phys.org and the NHM all describe these sounds as clicks or pops, likened to popping popcorn or bubble wrap. None of the sources found describes the sounds as 'hissing,' and targeted searches for hissing turned up nothing. Also, the clicks themselves are the ultrasonic sounds, not a separate audible category. Because the 'hissing' part cannot be verified, the claim as a whole is inconclusive.

text: εριodicals were first developed in France in 1665.
label: contradicted
reason: Printed periodicals were around well before 1665. Historians generally treat Mercurius Gallobelgicus, published in Cologne from 1594, as the first printed news periodical. In 1665 France produced the Journal des sçavans, usually called the first scholarly or scientific journal, but that was not the first periodical of any kind. So the claim's general statement about periodicals is wrong on both place and date.

text: France and the United States are the two countries with the most UNESCO World Heritage sites, but Italy has the most with 58 recognized sites.
label: contradicted
reason: Recent rankings show Italy in first place with 62 UNESCO World Heritage sites, followed by China with 61, France with 56 and Germany with 55. That means France and the United States are not the top two countries; China is second and the US is not in the top five. The claim also contradicts itself by naming France and the US as the top two and then saying Italy has the most. Italy's figure of 58 is also out of date.

text: A blue whale's heart alone can weigh up to 400 pounds and pump over 5,000 gallons of blood through its body with every beat.
label: contradicted
reason: NOAA Fisheries says a blue whale's heart weighs about 400 pounds, which matches the first part of the claim. But NOAA also says the heart pumps about 60 gallons of blood with each beat, not more than 5,000 gallons. The claim overstates the volume per beat by roughly 80 times, so it is contradicted.

text: Arectangle divided into a square and two equal rectangles, each of which is also divided into a square and two equal rectangles, is called a "golden rectangle".
label: contradicted
reason: A golden rectangle is a rectangle whose sides are in the golden ratio (about 1.618:1). Its defining property is that cutting off one square leaves a single smaller rectangle that is also golden. The claim says the cut leaves a square and two equal rectangles, which doesn't match this definition. A quick check of the math backs this up: when a square plus two equal rectangles similar to the original fill a rectangle, the side ratio comes out to 2, not φ.

text: Geokinetics refers to the study of the flow and movement of tectonic plates, and other processes that shape the Earth's crust.
label: supported
reason: "Geokinetics" is not a common dictionary term. Most search hits use it for other things: an oil-services company, a geotechnical firm, a philosophical theory of Earth as material flow, or the fantasy power "geokinesis." However, the U.S. Air Force Handbook of Geophysics and the Space Environment (1985), a credible scientific source, has a chapter titled "Geokinetics." That chapter covers "the general characteristics, magnitude, and measurement of crustal motions" and includes sections on Earth's structure, plate tectonics and plate motions, seismic waves, and tectonic horizontal and vertical displacements. This scientific use matches the claim: the study of how tectonic plates move and of other processes that shape the crust. Nothing found contradicts that meaning, though the term is rare and has some non-geological uses.

text: Scans of the Egyptian Great Pyramid's internal chamber, created in 2017, revealed a substantial void above the Queen's Chamber that has yet to be fully explained.
label: contradicted
reason: The 2017 ScanPyramids muon imaging study, published in Nature on 2 November 2017, found a large void, the 'Big Void', above the Grand Gallery. It did not find one above the Queen's Chamber. The year and the size of the void match, and it is still unexplained, but the claim puts it in the wrong place. Also, the void was found by scanning the pyramid with cosmic-ray muons, not by scans of a single internal chamber.

text: In 2019, the world's largest living organism was discovered in a forest in Oregon, covering over 2,200 acres, and is estimated to be around 2,400 years old.
label: contradicted
reason: The organism in the claim is the "Humongous Fungus" (Armillaria ostoyae) in Oregon's Malheur National Forest. Its size (about 2,385 acres) and age estimate (2,400 to 8,650 years) roughly match the claim. However, the date is wrong: sources say it was discovered in 1998, not 2019.

text: Scientists estimate that there may be between 700,000 to 1 million species of insects on Earth, but only about 1 millionth of them have been formally described and named.
label: contradicted
reason: The claim gets both numbers wrong. Science reports that scientists have already described about 1 million insect species. Estimates of the total number of insect species on Earth are around 6 million (the earlier consensus) or as high as about 20 million (a newer study). So the true total is far above 700,000 to 1 million, and the share that has been described is roughly 5–15%, not one millionth.

text: Biscayne National Park in Florida is the only national park in the United States that consists of 95% water.
label: contradicted
reason: Biscayne National Park is about 95% water, but it isn't the only U.S. national park that is overwhelmingly water. The NPS and other sources say Dry Tortugas National Park, also in Florida, is 99% water. That means the claim that Biscayne is the only national park with this makeup is false.

text: Research has shown there are more possible iterations of a game of chess than there are atoms in the known universe.
label: supported
reason: Several sources, including the Museum of Science and Fermat's Library, cite Claude Shannon's estimate (the "Shannon number") of about 10^120 possible chess games. That is far more than the roughly 10^80 atoms estimated to exist in the observable universe. The research behind the claim is Shannon's widely cited estimate, so the claim is supported.

text: Plants can make sounds, but humans can't hear them as they are typically produced at frequencies that are too low to be detected by the human ear.
label: contradicted
reason: Plants can make sounds, but the reason given in the claim is wrong. In a 2023 study published in Cell (Khait et al.), researchers recorded stressed tomato and tobacco plants making airborne clicks. These clicks are ultrasonic, meaning their frequency is too high for people to hear, not too low. The scientists had to shift the recordings down into the human hearing range before anyone could listen to them.

text: A chunk of the Dead Sea has been found to be so dense with salt that objects with lower densities than it will actually float.
label: supported
reason: The American Museum of Natural History says the Dead Sea's water is almost six times as salty as the ocean. It also says human bodies are less dense than that water, so people float in it effortlessly. That supports the main point of the claim: the Dead Sea is dense enough with salt that less-dense objects float. The claim's wording, "a chunk of the Dead Sea has been found," is odd, but the physical fact behind it matches the source.

text: Tarantulas have been around for a long time, with fossil records showing that they have remained largely unchanged for over 100 million years.
label: not_verifiable
reason: The first part of the claim holds up: tarantulas are an ancient group. A 2023 Journal of Biogeography paper and Live Science both say the oldest known tarantula fossil, from Burmese amber, is about 100 million years old, and genetic estimates put the group's origin at about 101–120 million years ago. The specific claim that fossils show tarantulas staying largely unchanged for over 100 million years is not supported. Live Science reports that only two tarantula fossils are known, one about 16 million years old and one about 100 million years old. That is about 100 million years, not clearly more, and two fossils are too few to show long-term stability. Texas Parks & Wildlife magazine quotes an expert who says the fossil record shows tarantulas 'virtually unchanged' for more than 20 million years, a much shorter span. Tarantula-like ancestors go back about 240 million years, but those are earlier mygalomorph spiders, not tarantulas. Some hobbyist sites repeat the over-100-million-years idea, but reliable sources don't back up the 'unchanged' part, so the evidence is mixed and incomplete.

text: Tarantulas have been around for a long time, with fossil records showing that they've remained largely unchanged for over 100 million years.
label: contradicted
reason: Tarantulas are old, but the evidence does not support the claim's specific fossil statement. Texas Parks & Wildlife Magazine says fossil records show tarantulas 'virtually unchanged, for more than 20 million years,' not over 100 million. Live Science reports that only two tarantula fossils are known, both preserved in amber: one is about 16 million years old and the other about 100 million. That is too few fossils to show more than 100 million years without much change. The roughly 120-million-year origin date comes from a molecular family-tree study calibrated with fossils, not from fossils showing the spiders stayed the same. Another source says tarantulas are not 'living fossils' and changed considerably over time. The 'unchanged for over 100 million years' part is therefore an exaggeration that these sources contradict.

text: Scientists estimate that there are approximately 8.7 million identified species on Earth, but the total number of species, including those that have not been discovered, is estimated to be around 30 million.
label: contradicted
reason: The 8.7 million figure is wrong for identified species. It comes from the Mora et al. 2011 PLoS Biology study, which gives it as the estimated total number of species on Earth (give or take 1.3 million), including those not yet discovered. Only about 1.2–2 million species have actually been identified and described. So the claim's split between 8.7 million identified species and about 30 million in total misstates the scientific estimate.

text: France and the United States share the only international border that is to the north and south poles, due to their claims to the region surrounding the geographic North Pole and their joint claims of Adélie Land in Antarctica.
label: contradicted
reason: The claim is false. Wikipedia and other sources say Adélie Land is claimed by France alone, as part of the French Southern and Antarctic Lands. The United States has never made a territorial claim in Antarctica, so there is no joint French–US claim to Adélie Land. Neither country claims the area around the geographic North Pole either, since it is international waters. That means there is no French–US border reaching either pole.

text: A ball of glass will float in the dead sea, due to its unusually high salt content which increases the water's density.
label: contradicted
reason: The claim is false for a solid glass ball. Dead Sea water is very dense, at about 1.235 g/cm³, but ordinary glass is about 2.2–2.5 g/cm³, roughly twice as dense. Because the glass is denser than the water, a solid glass ball would sink even in the Dead Sea. The high salt content does raise the water's density, but not enough to make glass float. Only a hollow glass ball with trapped air could float, and the claim doesn't say the ball is hollow.

text: A partitions of the Mandelbrot set can form the swirling patterns which in turn appear similar to Romanesco broccoli.
label: supported
reason: Search results put the Mandelbrot set and Romanesco broccoli side by side as examples of fractals. Real Python uses the self-similar Romanesco to explain the Mandelbrot set's repeating structure, and notes that the Mandelbrot set contains slightly different smaller copies of itself. Pardesco names the Mandelbrot set's boundary and Romanesco's 'spiral florets' as the same kind of fractal pattern. No result contradicts the claim. However, no result I found says directly that particular swirling regions of the Mandelbrot set look like Romanesco, so this support is moderate and partly inferred. My search tool also hit its usage limit before I could look for a more direct source.

text: A partitions of the Mandelbrot set can form the swirling patterns which in turn appear similar to miniature versions of the Mandelbrot set itself.
label: supported
reason: Several sources describe zooming into regions of the Mandelbrot set, such as Seahorse Valley. Branches give way to spirals that look like seahorse tails, and around and within those spirals sit small copies of the whole set, called 'minibrots'. These copies keep the same cardioid-and-circles shape, so the set is roughly self-similar. That matches what the claim seems to mean: parts of the set form swirls that lead to miniature versions of the set. The claim is loosely worded, but its basic idea is consistent with the sources.

label: not_verifiable

text: Penguins are highly social animals and often live in large colonies, with some species forming colonies that can number in the hundreds of thousands.
label: supported
reason: SeaWorld's penguin behaviour page backs every part of the claim. It calls penguins "among the most social of all birds" and says all species are colonial. It also says they nest in huge colonies called rookeries, some of which hold hundreds of thousands of penguins. A second source says the same thing about colony sizes. I found nothing that contradicts the claim.

text: Scans of the Egyptian Great Pyramid's internal chamber, created in 2017, revealed a large, previously unknown cavity inside the structure.
label: supported
reason: A 2017 paper in Nature from the ScanPyramids project reported that cosmic-ray muon scans of Khufu's Great Pyramid found a large void that had not been known before, sitting above the Grand Gallery. The void was first detected by films placed in the Queen's chamber, and news outlets such as Science News and ABC covered the finding in November 2017. The claim's wording is a little loose: the scans imaged the pyramid from inside chambers rather than scanning a single chamber, and the data were collected over several years before being published in 2017. These differences don't undercut the main point that 2017 scans revealed a large, previously unknown cavity.

text: Scans of the Egyptian Great Pyramid's internal chamber, created in 2017, revealed a large, previously unknown void or cavity above its King's Chamber.
label: contradicted
reason: The 2017 ScanPyramids muon-imaging study, published in Nature, did find a large, previously unknown void in the Great Pyramid. But it located this "Big Void" above the Grand Gallery, not above the King's Chamber. The scans were also made with muon detectors placed in and around the pyramid, not as scans of a single internal chamber. Because the claim puts the void in the wrong place, it is contradicted.

text: Trapiche rubies, a rare type of star ruby with a six-pointed star in a six-rayed pattern, can only be found in Myanmar.
label: contradicted
reason: GIA says trapiche rubies were first documented from Mong Hsu, Myanmar, in 1995 and have since turned up in other countries, including Guinea, Kashmir, Pakistan, Nepal, Sierra Leone and Tajikistan. Mindat also lists localities in Tajikistan and Vietnam. That means they are not found only in Myanmar. The claim also gets the stone wrong: trapiche rubies are not star rubies. Their six-spoke pattern comes from dark inclusions, while a star ruby's star comes from asterism.

text: Black bears are excellent climbers and have been known to climb trees to escape danger, protect themselves from extreme weather conditions, or even to hibernate during winter months.
label: supported
reason: Reliable sources back every part of the claim. The National Park Service says black bears' curved claws let them climb trees. It also says Great Smoky Mountains black bears often den high above the ground in standing hollow trees during winter to escape the cold, which covers both hibernating in trees and shelter from harsh weather. Vermont Fish & Wildlife says black bears climb trees to escape danger and that trees protect them from severe weather. Other sources describe black bears as renowned climbers that climb to escape predators and hibernate in tree cavities. One caveat: some sources note that tree denning is less common than ground denning. That doesn't contradict the claim, which only says bears 'have been known' to do this.

text: Cinderella is the most translated fairy tale in the world, with translations in over 1,500 languages.
label: contradicted
reason: The claim is contradicted. No source I found says Cinderella is the most translated fairy tale, and the figure of more than 1,500 languages is far off. Pook Press says the Grimm version of Cinderella (Aschenputtel) has been translated into about fifty languages. Wikipedia's list of works by number of translations, along with several translation-industry articles, puts books like The Little Prince at the top with a few hundred languages, roughly 300 to 500 or more. Anthologies of Andersen and Grimm tales are also in the low hundreds. No fairy tale comes close to 1,500 languages, so both the 'most translated' title and the language count are unsupported, and the number is contradicted by the evidence.

text: France and the United States are connected by a 2,000-year-old underwater cave and tunnel system.
label: contradicted
reason: No real tunnel or cave system links France and the United States. Wikipedia describes a transatlantic tunnel as only a theoretical idea, and Live Science says one is probably not possible with current technology. Live Science also notes that the longest undersea tunnel section in the world is the Channel Tunnel's 37.9 km stretch between England and France, which opened in 1994. A 2,000-year-old underwater cave and tunnel system crossing the Atlantic does not exist.

text: Humans are born without kneecaps, and they typically develop and harden between the ages of 3 and 5 years old.
label: contradicted
reason: The claim gets the timing roughly right but its main premise is wrong. Babies are not born without kneecaps. Wikipedia and several pediatric and health sources say infants are born with kneecaps (patellae) made of soft cartilage. These form before birth, around 4 months into pregnancy. The idea that babies have no kneecaps is a myth that exists because cartilage doesn't show clearly on X-rays. The kneecap does start hardening into bone in early childhood, around age 3 (with sources giving ranges of 2–6 or 3–5), and the process finishes around puberty. Because the claim says humans are born without kneecaps and that the kneecaps 'develop' between ages 3 and 5, it is contradicted.

text: Securitas Express is a unique form of robust and tamper-proof overnight postal service that originated in ancient Rome.
label: contradicted
reason: According to Wikipedia's Securitas AG article, Securitas Express AG was founded in 1963 as part of the Swiss Securitas Group. It is a modern Swiss company that specialized in transporting money and valuables. It is not a postal service from ancient Rome, so the claim about where it came from is contradicted. The name 'Securitas' is Latin, but that doesn't link the company to Roman postal history.

text: Clouds can weigh more than a million pounds, as a single cumulus cloud can contain up to 1.1 million pounds of water.
label: supported
reason: Several sources, citing an estimate from the U.S. National Center for Atmospheric Research (NCAR), say an average cumulus cloud of about 1 cubic km weighs roughly 1.1 million pounds (500,000 kg) of water. Some note that denser clouds such as cumulonimbus weigh even more. This supports the main point that clouds can weigh more than a million pounds and that a cumulus cloud can hold about 1.1 million pounds of water. One caveat: the sources give 1.1 million pounds as an average or typical figure, not a maximum, so the claim's 'up to' wording is imprecise but does not change its main point.

text: Content navigation platform, Pinterest, was initially named Tote.
label: supported
reason: Sources agree that Pinterest grew out of Tote, a mobile shopping app made by co-founders Ben Silbermann and Paul Sciarra. Wikipedia says Pinterest "emerged from an earlier app" called Tote, and the Timeline of Pinterest says Cold Brew Labs dropped Tote to build Pinterest. Another source says Pinterest "began as a mobile shopping app called Tote." One caveat: strictly speaking, Tote was an earlier product that Pinterest pivoted from, not just an older name for the same platform. Still, the claim's main point, that Pinterest started out as Tote, matches the sources.

text: Honey Never Spoils, and archaeologists have found pots of honey in ancient Egyptian tombs that are over 3,000 years old and still perfectly edible.
label: supported
reason: Several sources, including Smithsonian Magazine and a Boing Boing piece that cites it, report that archaeologists have found pots of honey in ancient Egyptian tombs that were still safe to eat after about 3,000 years. They explain that honey keeps so long because it holds very little water, is acidic, and releases small amounts of hydrogen peroxide. One caveat: honey can still ferment if it soaks up moisture, so "never spoils" is a popular simplification, but sealed honey does keep almost indefinitely.

text: S urgery was first performed using anesthesia on March 30, 1842, by Dr. Crawford Long.
label: supported
