reason: The Georgia Historical Society's marker text says that on March 30, 1842, Dr. Crawford W. Long performed "what is considered the first surgery using anesthesia." He used sulfuric ether to remove a cyst from James Venable's neck. National Doctors' Day falls on March 30 to mark this event. One caveat: earlier anesthesia, such as Hanaoka Seishū's in Japan in 1804, means this is the conventional claim to "first" rather than an undisputed one.

text: Scientists estimate that there are approximately 8.7 million identified species on Earth, but the actual total number could be as high as 30 million.
label: contradicted
reason: The claim treats 8.7 million as the number of identified species, but that's wrong. 8.7 million (give or take 1.3 million) is Mora et al.'s 2011 estimate of all eukaryotic species on Earth, both known and unknown. Only about 1.2 to 2 million species have actually been described. Earlier estimates also ran from 3 million to 100 million, not a 30 million maximum.

text: Honey Never Spoils, as archaeologists have found pots of honey in ancient Egyptian tombs that are over 3,000 years old and still perfectly edible.
label: supported
reason: Smithsonian Magazine reports that archaeologists excavating ancient Egyptian tombs have found pots of honey that are thousands of years old and still preserved. It explains why: honey has very little moisture and is acidic. Several other sources, including My Modern Met, Boing Boing and RealClearScience (which republished the Smithsonian piece), describe the honey as 3,000 years old and still safe to eat. One limit: the Smithsonian text I checked says 'still preserved' rather than 'edible.' The specific 'edible after 3,000 years' wording comes from those less authoritative secondary sources. No result I found contradicts the claim.

text: Scientists estimate that there are approximately 8.7 million identified species on Earth, but the actual number could be significantly higher.
label: contradicted
reason: The 8.7 million figure from Mora et al. (2011) is an estimate of the total number of eukaryotic species on Earth, mostly unidentified. It is not a count of identified species. According to the source, only about 1.25 million species had been described and catalogued, so calling 8.7 million 'identified species' is wrong.

text: Scientists estimate that there are approximately 8.7 million identified species on Earth, but the total number of existing species, including those not yet discovered, is believed to be around 30 million.
label: contradicted
reason: The 8.7 million figure (Mora et al., 2011, PLoS Biology) is an estimate of all species on Earth, including those not yet discovered. It does not count species already identified. Only about 1.2 to 2 million species have been described. The claim treats 8.7 million as the number of identified species and gives 30 million as the total, which misstates what the study found.

text: Tarantulas have been around for a long time, with fossil records showing that they existed during the Cretaceous period, more than 100 million years ago, at the same time as dinosaurs.
label: supported
reason: Live Science, writing up the 2021 Foley et al. study, says one of the only two known tarantula fossils is in amber from Myanmar and is about 100 million years old. That puts it in the Cretaceous, when dinosaurs were alive. Molecular dating in the same study, reported by Phys.org, Smithsonian and SciTechDaily, places the origin of tarantulas about 120 million years ago, also in the Cretaceous. One caveat: the fossil itself is dated to about 100 million years, not clearly more. The tarantula fossil record is also very sparse, so the 'more than 100 million years' figure leans partly on the molecular estimate.

text: Chocolate syrup was originally invented by Milton Hershey in 1894 as a topping for ice cream, but it eventually became popular as a topping for pancakes and other desserts.
label: contradicted
reason: The Hershey Community Archives says the Hershey Chocolate Company did not start making and selling chocolate syrup until 1926. That followed formula work in an experimental kitchen around 1922–23. At first the syrup was sold to commercial users, mainly for soda fountain drinks. The claim says Milton Hershey invented it in 1894 as an ice cream topping, which conflicts with both the date and the original purpose. The year 1894 is when he founded the Hershey Chocolate Company, not when the syrup was created.

text: A blue whale's heart alone can weigh as much as 400 pounds and pump nearly 5,000 gallons of blood through its body with every beat.
label: contradicted
reason: NOAA Fisheries says a blue whale's heart weighs about 400 pounds, so that part of the claim holds up. But NOAA also says the heart pumps about 60 gallons of blood with each beat, not nearly 5,000 gallons. The volume figure is wrong by roughly 80 times.

text: Rome is considered to be the second most populous city in the world with over 3,700,000 inhabitants.
label: contradicted
reason: Rome is not the world's second most populous city. Wikipedia lists it as Italy's largest city and only the fourth most populous city in the EU by population within city limits, with about 2.8 million residents there (4.2–4.3 million in the wider metropolitan city). Cities like Tokyo, Delhi and Shanghai are far larger, so the claim that Rome ranks second in the world is false.

text: A blue whale can hold up to 2,000 gallons of water in its mouth, but it only swallows a small amount of that water, as the baleen filters it.
label: contradicted
reason: Reliable sources put a blue whale's mouth capacity far above 2,000 gallons, so the claim's 'up to 2,000 gallons' limit is wrong. Wikipedia says the mouth can hold up to 90 tonnes of food and water, which is roughly 24,000 gallons. Other sources give figures of 10,000 to 15,000 gallons or more per gulp. The point about baleen filtering out most of the water before the whale swallows is accurate, but the stated capacity is contradicted.

text: A giant squid's eyes are enormous, with some specimens having eyes that are up to 10 inches in diameter, which is thought to be the largest of any animal.
label: supported
reason: The Smithsonian's page on a giant squid eye says giant squid have the largest eyes in the animal kingdom, measuring up to 10 inches across, which matches the claim. Some sources, such as LiveScience, give the title to the colossal squid instead. Even so, a trustworthy source directly backs every part of the claim, and the claim's wording ('thought to be') leaves room for that disagreement.

text: A blueprint is typically a large-scale detailed drawing or diagram that is often used in planning, construction, and architecture, typically printed in white lines on a blue background.
label: supported
reason: Wikipedia describes a blueprint as a reproduction of a technical or engineering drawing. It says blueprints are characterized by white lines on a blue background and notes their use in architectural offices. Collins Dictionary also defines a blueprint as a print of plans and technical drawings made of white lines on a blue background. These sources support the claim's main points: a detailed drawing or plan used in planning, construction and architecture, traditionally printed in white on blue. The "large-scale" wording was not stated directly, but it fits the standard description and nothing contradicts it.

text: One flex of a human eyebrow requires approximately 137 muscles.
label: contradicted
reason: The claim is false. Anatomy sources say only a small group of facial muscles moves the eyebrows: the frontalis raises them, and the corrugator supercilii, depressor supercilii and procerus pull them inward and down, together with the orbicularis oculi. That is about five muscles, nowhere near 137. The whole human face has only about 40 muscles, so 137 muscles for one eyebrow movement is not possible.

text: Scientists estimate that there are approximately 8.7 million Identified species on Earth, but the actual number could be as high as 30 million when including undiscovered species.
label: contradicted
reason: The claim gets the 8.7 million figure wrong. In the 2011 study by Mora et al. (PLoS Biology), 8.7 million (give or take 1.3 million) is the estimated total number of species on Earth, counting those not yet discovered. It is not the number already identified. Only about 1.2 million species had been catalogued at the time, and roughly 2 million have been described now. The study concluded that about 86% of land species and 91% of ocean species are still undescribed. Higher totals, such as 30 million or the 3–100 million range given by experts, are separate estimates of all species. They are not a step up from an 8.7 million count of known species.

text: Tarantulas have been around for a long time, with the earliest known tarantula fossils dating back to the Cretaceous period, over 100 million years ago.
label: supported
reason: A peer-reviewed paper in the Journal of Biogeography (Wiley) says the oldest known tarantula fossil (Protertheraphosinae, Wunderlich & Müller 2020) comes from Burmese amber dated to about 100 million years ago. That puts it in the Cretaceous. The same study dates the split of tarantulas from their closest relatives to the early Cretaceous, about 120 million years ago. One caveat: Burmese amber is usually dated to about 99 million years ago, so "over 100 million years ago" is slightly generous. Still, sources commonly round the age to about 100 million years, so the claim holds overall.

text: Abnormally large crystals have grown within the Naica Mine in Mexico's Chihuahuan Desert due to mining of lead and zinc deposits there over millions of years.
label: contradicted
reason: Reliable sources say the giant selenite (gypsum) crystals at Naica formed naturally. Hot, mineral-rich water filled the caves, and when its temperature fell just below about 56–58 °C, anhydrite dissolved and gypsum crystals grew slowly for roughly 500,000 years. Mining for lead, zinc and silver did not cause this growth. Miners only found the caves, in 1910 and 2000, and pumping out the water actually stopped the crystals from growing. The claim is therefore wrong to say mining caused the crystals, and also wrong to say they took 'millions of years' to grow.

text: Bacteria can exist in almost every environment on Earth, including extreme conditions like the freezing temperatures of Antarctica and the intense heat of deep-sea vents.
label: supported
reason: NASA Astrobiology material says bacteria have been found in liquid water pockets inside lake ice in Antarctica's McMurdo Dry Valleys. It also says bacteria live around deep-sea hydrothermal vents, where the water can reach 248°F. Bacteria being found in almost every environment on Earth is a widely accepted fact in microbiology, and the extremophile examples in the source back up the claim.

text: Deep-sea vent organisms have been discovered that can survive in extremely hot environments with temperatures exceeding 400 degrees Celsius.
label: contradicted
reason: The record for heat tolerance in vent organisms is about 122°C, set by Methanopyrus kandleri strain 116, which can grow at that temperature only under high pressure (PNAS). Vent fluids can be hotter than 400°C, but no organism has been found that survives temperatures anywhere near that, so the claim greatly overstates what is known.

text: M dla Mountains is the highest peak in the Solar System, with a height of approximately 27 km, located on the planet Mars.
label: contradicted
reason: No mountain called "M dla Mountains" shows up anywhere in the results, including Wikipedia's list of named mountains on Mars. The tallest mountain on Mars, and the one usually called the tallest in the Solar System, is Olympus Mons. Its height is given as about 21.9 km, or roughly 22–26 km of local relief above the surrounding plains, not around 27 km. It is roughly tied with Rheasilvia's central peak on the asteroid Vesta. The claim gives the wrong name for the mountain, and its height is also off.

text: A blue whale's heart alone can weigh around 400 pounds and pump over 5,000 gallons of blood through its body with each beat.
label: contradicted
reason: NOAA Fisheries confirms that a blue whale's heart weighs about 400 pounds, so that part of the claim is right. The same source says the heart pumps about 60 gallons of blood per beat, not over 5,000 gallons. Other sources give similar figures of 58 to 60 gallons (about 220 liters) per beat, so the per-beat volume in the claim is wrong by a wide margin.

text: In New York City, there is a secretly located apartment in the New York Public Library,dımatically decreasing the maintenance  and upkeep cost for the superintendant that is hidden from the general public.
label: not_verifiable
reason: Reliable sources (Atlas Obscura, Untapped Cities, 6sqft) confirm that the NYPL's main Fifth Avenue building once had a hidden eight-room apartment where the superintendent lived. It was built so someone would be on site to deal with things like the boilers. I found no source saying the apartment greatly reduced maintenance or upkeep costs, so that part can't be checked. The claim also describes the apartment as if it is still in use, but it has been empty for decades. Because the cost part is unverified, the claim as a whole is inconclusive.

text: Beehive-shaped structures in Antarctica, known as "blood falls", seep a deep red liquid, which is actually ancient saltwater rich in iron that flows from beneath Taylor Glacier.
label: contradicted
reason: The claim gets the source of the liquid right. Scientific American, Science News Explores and Wikipedia all describe Blood Falls as iron-rich, salty subglacial water, possibly from ancient seawater, that flows from beneath Taylor Glacier and stains red as the iron oxidizes. However, the claim misdescribes what Blood Falls is. It is not a set of 'beehive-shaped structures.' Reliable sources describe it as a single blood-red waterfall, plume or outflow at the end of Taylor Glacier. Science News Explores, for example, calls it a five-story waterfall coming out of the glacier. Because the feature's form is wrong, the claim as a whole is contradicted.

text: Honeybees are able to recognize and remember human faces, and are even capable of distinguishing between them, much like primates and dolphins.
label: supported
reason: Dyer et al.'s 2005 study in the Journal of Experimental Biology, reported by phys.org and JEB, found that honeybees could learn to tell apart and recognize photos of human faces from a standard psychology test, and that they remembered them for at least two days. Scientific American and The Conversation report the same result and note that face recognition was long thought to be limited to large-brained mammals such as primates. The search results did not directly confirm the comparison with dolphins, but that is a minor framing detail and nothing contradicted it.

text: Tibet is home to the world's highest saltwater lake, Namtso Lake, with an elevation of over 15,479 feet above sea level.
label: supported
reason: I found many sources calling Namtso in Tibet the world's highest saltwater lake. These include the Chinese Academy of Sciences' Institute of Geographic Sciences (IGSNRR), chinaculture.org, Baidu Baike and several travel sites. Wikipedia gives its elevation as 4,718 m (15,479 ft). Two caveats: the elevation is about 15,479 ft, not 'over' it, which is a small imprecision. Some sources also qualify the title, for example 'one of the world's highest large saltwater lakes', or dispute it, but these are less authoritative. Overall, the evidence supports the claim.

text: Snails are able to sleep for up to 3 years in a state of dormancy called estivation, which helps them conserve energy during periods of extreme heat or drought.
label: supported
reason: Several sources say some snails can stay dormant for up to about three years. During this estivation they seal themselves into their shells to survive heat and drought. The best-known case is the Egyptian desert snail at the British Museum, which revived after roughly four years glued to a display card. Some fact-check posts call the 'sleeps three years' line a myth, but their point is that this is dormancy rather than ordinary sleep. They still accept that dormancy can last for years, and the claim already describes it as estivation. Most sources here are popular-science sites, not peer-reviewed research.

text: Seals use a series of short dives to hunt underwater, with the Weddell seal able to stay submerged for up to 80 minutes at a time.
label: supported
reason: Oceanwide Expeditions says Weddell seals can stay underwater for up to 80 minutes at a time, and that these long dives are used both for feeding and for finding new breathing holes. That matches the claim's key detail. The general point that seals hunt with repeated, mostly short dives fits what is known about their foraging, and no source contradicted it. The two parts of the claim sit a little awkwardly together, since 80 minutes is the maximum and most dives are much shorter.

text: A\model of a human nose can detect odors even if the person has lost their sense of smell.
label: supported
reason: A Science news report from Nov. 2025, covering a study in Science Advances, describes an artificial 'nose', a device that mimics the nose's job of detecting odors. In a proof-of-concept test, it let people who had lost their normal sense of smell detect when certain odors were present. The device works through trigeminal nerve stimulation, not real olfaction. That backs the claim that a model of the nose can detect odors for people with smell loss, though 'model of a human nose' is loose wording.

text: Cats have a highly specialized vocalization range, with some species able to produce over 100 different sounds.
label: supported
reason: Several popular sources repeat the claim that cats can make over 100 different vocalizations. One example is Spectrum News' Pet Pointers segment, which says cats can produce more than 100 sounds while dogs have about 10. That backs up the claim. However, this figure is a popular factoid and not a well-established scientific finding. Formal studies usually describe a much smaller number of distinct call types, and the claim's wording about 'some species' is vague.

text: Honeybees are able to fly by using electricity generated by the movement of their wings to attract pollen.
label: contradicted
reason: Honeybees fly using aerodynamics, not electricity. Altshuler et al. (PNAS 2005, Caltech) showed that their lift comes from short, high-frequency wing strokes, leading-edge vortices and related unsteady aerodynamic effects. It is true that bees pick up a positive static charge from friction with the air while flying, and that this charge helps attract pollen (AskNature, Science Friday). But that charge is a side effect of flight, not what lets them fly. So the claim wrongly connects flight to electricity, and the reason it gives for flying (to attract pollen) doesn't hold up.

text: One in every five countries in the world uses a storm-prevention system known as cloud seeding.
label: not_verifiable
reason: The share of countries is roughly right, but the description of cloud seeding is not. A 2025 GAO report says the WMO found at least 50 countries running weather-modification programs in 2015. GAO itself listed 39 countries doing cloud seeding in 2020–2024, and said that list was incomplete. Out of about 195 countries, that works out to roughly one in five to one in four, so the number is plausible but not exact. Calling cloud seeding a 'storm-prevention system' is misleading. The sources describe it mainly as a way to increase rain or snow, for example to fight drought, raise hydropower output or add snow for ski resorts. Hail suppression is only one use. I found no source stating 'one in five countries' or describing cloud seeding mainly as storm prevention, so the claim as worded can't be fully verified.

text: wallets made of metal were first introduced in ancient Greece around 600 BC
label: contradicted
reason: The sources I found contradict the claim. Wallet histories trace the word and earliest wallets to ancient Greece, roughly 700–480 BC, but they describe the Greek "kibisis" as a sack or leather pouch for carrying coins, not a metal wallet. The "metal" and "around 600 BC" details seem to come from a mix-up with the history of coins: Greek city-states began using metal coinage around 600 BC. None of the sources says metal wallets started in ancient Greece; they are treated as a much later material option.

text: Caterpillars can eat up to 27,000 times their body weight in a single day, which is equivalent to a human eating around 46,000 pizzas.
label: contradicted
reason: Sources that cite the 27,000× number say it covers the caterpillar's whole feeding stage, not one day. The Naked Scientists says caterpillars eat 27,000 times their body weight in leaves "in the 4 weeks that they're caterpillars." The well-known record, for the Polyphemus moth caterpillar, is about 86,000 times its birth weight over roughly 56 days, not in 24 hours. The claim that this happens in a single day is therefore wrong. No source I found supported the 46,000-pizza comparison.

text: Scientists estimate that there are approximately 8.7 million identified species on Earth, but the total number of species is believed to be around 30 million.
label: contradicted
reason: The 8.7 million figure from Mora et al. (2011, PLoS Biology) is an estimate of the total number of eukaryotic species on Earth, not the number already identified. According to ScienceDaily, about 8.7 million (±1.3 million) is the estimated total, and only a fraction of these, roughly 1.2 million, have been described. So the claim gets wrong both the number of identified species and the 8.7 million figure's meaning. The 30 million total also does not match this widely cited estimate.

text: Schedule 1 of the Indian Constitution initially listed 29 states, but as of 2023, the number of officially recognized states in India is 28, with the change following the creation of the union territories of Jammu and Kashmir and Ladakh in 2019, and the abolishment of the state Jammu
label: supported
reason: The sources back each part of the claim. Several Indian civil-services study sites (Vajiram & Ravi, Vedantu, UPSC prep material) say the 1950 Constitution grouped the states into Parts A, B, C and D, '29' in total. Strictly, that count of 29 includes the Part D territory (Andaman and Nicobar), and the original Schedule is the full list of these entries. Before 2019 there were also 29 states, with Telangana becoming the 29th in 2014. iPleaders says India now has 28 states and 8 union territories, a count that reflects the 2019 reorganisation, when the state of Jammu and Kashmir was abolished and replaced by the union territories of Jammu and Kashmir and Ladakh. The claim's last sentence is cut off, but its meaning is clear.

text: Scientists estimate that there are approximately 8.7 million identified species on Earth, but some estimates suggest that the total number of existing species could be as high as 30 million.
label: contradicted
reason: The 8.7 million figure (Mora et al., PLoS Biology, 2011) estimates the total number of species on Earth, both known and unknown. It is not the number of identified species. Only about 1.2 to 2 million species have been formally described. The claim calls 8.7 million the identified count, which is wrong.

text: A large percentage of human brains are actually more active and efficient at night, which is why many people report doing their best thinking and being most creative later in the evening.
label: contradicted
reason: The evidence contradicts this claim. Only about 15–20% of people are true night owls whose brains peak in the evening. That is a minority, not the 'large percentage' the claim describes. Research also gives a different reason for nighttime creativity. Wieth & Zacks (2011, Thinking & Reasoning) found that insight and creative problem-solving improve at a person's non-optimal time of day, because inhibitory control is weaker then, not because the brain is more active or efficient. So the claimed cause (brains being more efficient at night) does not hold, and the claimed share of people is overstated.

text: A blue whale's heartbeat is so loud it can be detected over 500 miles away with some specialized equipment.
label: contradicted
reason: The claim is false because of the distance. Sources that repeat this popular fact say a blue whale's heartbeat can be detected from about 2 miles away, not more than 500 miles. Even the 2-mile figure is a widely repeated claim rather than a well-established measurement. The 500-plus-mile figure usually refers to how far blue whale calls travel, not their heartbeat. Real heart-rate readings (for example, the 2019 study of 2 to 37 beats per minute) came from a sensor attached to the whale, not from listening at a distance.

text: Beneath the ice of Antarctica lies a network of hundreds of subglacial lakes, with the largest being Lake Vostok, which is roughly the size of Lake Ontario.
label: supported
reason: Several sources agree with the claim. HowStuffWorks says Lake Vostok is the largest of Antarctica's 379+ subglacial lakes, which are often interconnected, and that it is "roughly the size of Lake Ontario." Study.com likewise says Antarctica has hundreds of subglacial lakes and that Vostok, the largest, is about the size of Lake Ontario. By surface area, Vostok (about 12,500 km²) is smaller than Lake Ontario (about 19,000 km²), but the comparison is widely used and the word "roughly" covers the difference.

text: Burning entirely in space, without any visible evidence, there is a gigantic cannonball-shaped star called VY Canis Majoris located in the constellation Canis Major.
label: contradicted
reason: It is true that VY Canis Majoris is a huge red hypergiant in the constellation Canis Major, about 3,800 light years away and roughly 1,420 times the Sun's radius. The claim's description of it as burning "without any visible evidence" is wrong. VY CMa is a variable star with an apparent visual magnitude between about 6.5 and 9.6, so it can be seen with binoculars or a small telescope, and it is one of the brightest infrared objects in our part of the galaxy. Nothing supports calling it "cannonball-shaped" either; it is studied for its asymmetric outflows. Because part of the claim is directly contradicted, I've labelled it contradicted.

text: Honeybees are able to fly by using their wings to generate an electric charge, which helps them attract the pollen they need to survive.
label: contradicted
reason: Part of the claim is right: as bees flap their wings in flight, friction with the air builds up a positive static charge, and that charge helps pollen jump onto the bee (Science Friday, UMass Boston). But the claim gets the cause backwards. It says bees fly by generating this charge. In fact, bees fly using aerodynamic lift from their flapping wings, and the charge is only a side effect of flight. None of the sources found say the charge makes flight possible, so the main point of the claim is wrong.

text: Rubber ducks were originally made from rubber, but most modern rubber ducks are now made from vinyl, a more durable and easier to clean material.
label: supported
reason: Reliable sources, including Compound Interest's chemistry infographic and the St Neots Museum, say the first rubber ducks were made in the 1800s from real vulcanised rubber. They also say modern ducks, starting with Peter Ganine's 1947 design, are made from plasticised PVC (vinyl), and that the 'rubber' name stuck anyway. The sources don't directly confirm that vinyl is more durable and easier to clean, but they don't contradict it, and it's a commonly stated reason for the switch. That makes it a minor detail, so I judged the claim supported overall.

text: A誉咲き (Yūrei-zakura), a 2,000-year-old weeping cherry blossom tree in Japan, is a popular tourist destination and national treasure.
label: contradicted
reason: My searches found no 2,000-year-old weeping cherry tree called "Yūrei-zakura" (the Japanese text in the claim also looks garbled). Japan's well-known roughly 2,000-year-old cherry tree is the Yamataka Jindai-zakura at Jissō-ji Temple in Hokuto, Yamanashi. It is an Edo-higan cherry, and none of the sources describe it as a weeping cherry. It is also listed as a national natural monument, not a "national treasure." It is a famous spot that people visit, but the claim gets the tree's name, type and official status wrong.

text: A blue whale's heartbeat is visible to the human eye, but can be slow as 4-8 beats per minute when the whale is at rest.
label: contradicted
reason: The 4–8 bpm figure comes from the 2019 Stanford/Goldbogen study, and it was measured during deep foraging dives, not at rest. At the bottom of a dive the heart averaged 4–8 bpm, with a low of 2 bpm, and it rose to 25–37 bpm at the surface. One source gives a resting rate of about 16–24 bpm and lists 4–8 bpm as the diving rate, which conflicts with the 'at rest' framing. That source is a Southwestern University event page, so it carries less weight than the study coverage. No source I found supports the claim that the heartbeat is visible to the human eye. Because the claim misstates the context of the 4–8 bpm figure, it is contradicted.

text: Geokinetics refers to the study of the flow and movement of tectonic plates, within the field of geology.
label: not_verifiable
reason: I could only run one search before hitting the tool limit, so I couldn't check this properly. The one result I found (P2P Foundation Wiki) describes geokinetics as a theory of the Earth as a material flow. That is Thomas Nail's philosophical framework, not a branch of geology about the flow and movement of tectonic plates. I found no dictionary or geology source that defines geokinetics as the study of tectonic plate movement, and none that contradicts it either. The word is sometimes used loosely for movements of the Earth's crust, but the claim's narrow wording (tectonic plates, within geology) remains unconfirmed.

text: Scientists estimate that there are approximately 8.7 million identified species on Earth, but this number is constantly being updated as new discoveries are made.
label: contradicted
reason: The 8.7 million figure from Mora et al. (2011) estimates the total number of species on Earth, including ones nobody has found yet. It is not a count of identified species. The study says about 86% of land species and 91% of marine species have not yet been discovered or described. Only about 1.2 million species had been described and catalogued, so calling 8.7 million 'identified species' is wrong.

text: العظيم Clearance Library has collected more than 100000 books.
label: not_verifiable
reason: I couldn't identify what "العظيم Clearance Library" refers to. It mixes an Arabic word, al-Azim ("the Great"), with the English word "Clearance", and may be a garbled translation. My searches found only unrelated results: retail "clearance books" pages, other libraries with 100,000+ items, and general Arabic articles about large libraries. Since the library has no clear referent and nothing I found confirms or contradicts the claim of more than 100,000 books, the claim can't be verified.

text: Polar bears are excellent swimmers and have been known to swim for hours or even days at a time, covering distances of up to 60 miles (97 kilometers) without resting.
label: supported
reason: Reputable sources back the main parts of the claim. NH PBS NatureWorks says polar bears can swim as far as 60 miles (96.6 km) without resting, and the San Diego Zoo Wildlife Alliance says they have been known to swim more than 60 miles (100 km) without rest. Ocean Conservancy describes them as strong swimmers. GPS tracking reported by Live Science, National Geographic, CBC and Guinness confirms swims lasting days, including a record 9-day, 687 km (426 mile) swim. The one weak point is the phrase 'up to 60 miles': it understates the documented maximum, since bears have swum much farther. The commonly cited 60-mile figure and the hours-to-days claim are still well supported.

text: A baby octopus is about the size of a grain of rice when it is born.
label: supported
reason: Several sources say newly hatched octopuses are roughly the size of a grain of rice. Monterey Bay Aquarium reports that even the giant Pacific octopus hatches from a rice-grain-sized egg, as a hatchling just over a quarter-inch long. ZooBorns also describes hatchlings as about rice-grain size. Scitechdaily reports that pygmy zebra octopus hatchlings are about the size of a grain of rice, and other sources put most species at birth at about 3–7 mm. Hatchling size varies somewhat between species, but no source contradicts the claim as a general statement.

text: A fetus can develop its unique fingerprints as early as 3 months in the womb, and these prints remain unchanged for the rest of a person's life.
label: supported
reason: My sources agree with the main points of the claim. The Conversation and several other sources say fingerprint ridges start forming in the womb at about 10 weeks. Other sources put the start at 10–13 weeks, near the end of the first trimester. That is roughly 3 months, which matches "as early as 3 months." Sources also say the patterns become set and fully formed by about weeks 16–17. The NIJ/OJP forensic reference says the unique features of friction ridge skin persist from before birth until decomposition after death. ScienceABC and Wikipedia likewise say fingerprints stay the same throughout life. One caveat is that the claim is a little loose on timing: formation starts around 10 weeks, but the unique details are not complete until about 15–17 weeks. Even so, the timeline broadly fits the claim, and nothing I found contradicts it.

text: Humans and dolphins are the only known animals that give themselves names, apart from some bird species and primates that have been observed to use identifier vocalizations.
label: contradicted
reason: The claim says humans and dolphins are the only known name-users, with exceptions only for some birds and primates. Current evidence does not support that limit. Research reported in 2024 suggests African elephants address each other with distinct, arbitrary 'name' rumbles and react most to their own. Egyptian bats are also put forward as possible name-users. Neither elephants nor bats are birds or primates. One caveat: a recent opinion piece in Trends in Cognitive Sciences questions how strong the evidence is for elephants and marmosets, so whether other animals truly use names is still debated. Even so, the evidence about elephants contradicts the claim's exclusive list.

text: Humans and dolphins are the only mammals known to give themselves names, or more specifically, unique identifiers that serve as names.
label: contradicted
reason: The claim is out of date. Humans and dolphins are no longer the only mammals known to use name-like identifiers. A 2024 study found that African elephants call each other by individual names. A Hebrew University study, reported by EurekAlert and CNN in August 2024, found that marmoset monkeys use specific 'phee-calls' to name each other, a behaviour previously known only in humans, dolphins and elephants. Dolphins do have signature whistles, but the word 'only' makes the claim false.

text: Japan has a vending machine for almost everything, including live crabs, fresh eggs, and underwear.
label: not_verifiable
reason: Two parts of the claim check out, but the live crab part doesn't. Several sources confirm that Japan has vending machines for fresh eggs (for example, one in Nagoya that is restocked every morning) and machines selling new underwear and pantyhose. The best-known live crab vending machine, which most 'weird vending machine' lists cite, is in Nanjing, China, not Japan. TechCrunch, Gizmodo Japan and Livedoor News all report this, and Complex says outright that the crab machine was in China rather than Japan. A few lower-quality travel and blog sites (Japan Wise Life, euro-japan.de, vendingmachinepapa) say Japan also has live crab machines, such as in Hakodate. However, I found no trustworthy source to confirm this. Some of these sources may be confusing the Chinese machine with Japan, or mixing up live crabs with packaged or cooked crab products. Because the evidence for the live crab part is weak and mixed, the claim can't be fully verified.

text: Mathematicians used a combination of over 13 billion digits in calculations to find solutions for the mathematical constant Pi in 2019.
label: contradicted
reason: The record pi calculation in 2019 was done by Google's Emma Haruka Iwao, a software engineer, not by mathematicians. Using Google Cloud, she computed pi to 31.4 trillion digits (31,415,926,535,897), which is about 3.14 × 10^13. The claim's figure of 'over 13 billion digits' seems to come from misreading that '10 to the 13th' and gets the scale badly wrong. Strictly speaking, 31.4 trillion is 'over' 13 billion, but the specific figure and the description don't match the documented event.

text: Plants are capable of producing flowers in response to the direction of sunlight, a phenomenon known as heliotropism.
label: contradicted
reason: Heliotropism isn't about plants producing flowers. Wikipedia and dictionaries define it as the daily or seasonal movement of plant parts (flowers or leaves) in response to the Sun's direction, or growth toward the sun, as with sunflowers tracking it across the sky. The claim mixes up moving toward sunlight with flowering. Light-triggered flowering is controlled by photoperiodism (day length), not by the direction of sunlight.

text: A photographer's camera and a painter's canvas have one functional similarity: the approach to composition.
label: supported
reason: My search supports this claim, as long as "one functional similarity" is read as "one similarity among others" and not "the only similarity." Several sources say composition is a shared principle of photography and painting. LearningWithExperts says the technical sides of the two media don't overlap, but the visual sides do, "particularly the way in which it is composed." A ResearchGate paper says photographic composition is "essentially the same as painting," and photographer Ed Kashi says both use composition. The same sources also name other shared traits, such as light, colour and form. So if the claim meant composition is the only similarity, the evidence would not back that stronger reading.

text: Galileo Galilei was the first person to observe the planet Neptune, although he did not realize it was a planet, in 1613.
label: supported
reason: Reliable sources, including Wikipedia, Astronomy.com and Space.com, say Galileo's drawings show Neptune on December 28, 1612 and again on January 27, 1613. Both times he mistook it for a fixed star near Jupiter. Astronomy.com says he may have been the first to see the planet. His first sighting was actually in late December 1612, not 1613. Still, he did observe Neptune in January 1613 and did not realize it was a planet, so the core claim holds.

text: Honeybees are able to fly by using their wings to generate electricity through a process called triboelectrification.
label: contradicted
reason: The claim gets cause and effect backwards. Studies do show that bees build up a positive electrostatic charge through triboelectric friction as their wings beat against the air. Scientific sources describe this charge as a byproduct of flight that matters for pollination and sensing flowers' electric fields. They do not describe it as what keeps the bee in the air. Honeybees fly because their flapping wings create aerodynamic lift, not because they generate electricity.

text: Some mushrooms, specifically the Armillaria ostoyae fungus, can grow to be over 2,200 acres in size, making them among the largest living organisms in the world.
label: supported
reason: The Oregon Encyclopedia and Discover Magazine both say the Armillaria ostoyae "Humongous Fungus" in Oregon's Malheur National Forest covers about 2,385 acres, which is more than 2,200 acres. Wikipedia gives a figure of about 2,200 acres. These sources and OPB describe it as among the largest, or the largest, living organisms on Earth.

text: Spiders have been present on Earth for at least 318 million years, with ancient fossils of spider-like creatures found dating back to the Devonian Period.
label: supported
reason: Reliable sources back both parts of the claim. Wikipedia's Evolution of Spiders article and the Australian Museum both say that Attercopus, an arachnid that resembled a spider, lived about 380 million years ago in the Devonian. A PMC paper says spider-related uraraneids are known from about 385 million years ago. The oldest unequivocal true spiders come from the Carboniferous. One source dates them to about 315 million years ago (Arthrolycosa and the mesotheles), and the Wikipedia article on spiders gives 319 to 299 million years ago. The Devonian spider-like fossils on their own show that this lineage goes back well over 318 million years, so 'at least 318 million years' fits the evidence. Attercopus is no longer considered a true spider, but the claim only calls the Devonian fossils 'spider-like,' which matches the current view.

text: A blue whale's heartbeat is so loud it can be detected over 500 miles away underwater.
label: contradicted
reason: The usual popular claim is that a blue whale's heartbeat can be detected about 2 miles (roughly 3 km) away, not over 500 miles. The Whaling Museum blog repeats that 2-mile figure, and even that figure is a loosely sourced popular claim. Distances of hundreds of miles apply to blue whale calls, not heartbeats. Scientists measured a blue whale's heart rate in 2019 with a tag attached by suction cups, not by hearing it from far away. Since even the popular version says about 2 miles, the 500-mile claim is contradicted.

text: Tarantulas have existed on Earth for at least 100 million years, with fossil evidence showing they crawled in what is now Europe and North America during the Cretaceous period.
label: contradicted
reason: The 100-million-year figure holds up, but the location doesn't. Peer-reviewed studies (J. Biogeography 2023, PeerJ 2021) and Live Science say the oldest tarantula (theraphosid) fossil comes from Burmese amber in Myanmar and is about 100 million years old. They report only two known tarantula fossils: that one, and a Miocene fossil about 16 million years old from Chiapas amber in Mexico. No source found reports a Cretaceous tarantula fossil from Europe or North America. Studies that date the group's origin to the Cretaceous rely on time-calibrated family trees, not on fossils found there.

text: Plants can make sounds, too, such as the noise some plants make when they lose water, though the frequency is usually beyond the range of human hearing, and vegetables and fruits can also make various sounds as they grow.
label: supported
reason: Tel Aviv University research (Khait et al., 2023, in Cell), reported by Washington Post, AFTAU and Sci.News, found that stressed plants, including tomato and tobacco plants short of water, give off ultrasonic clicks. These sounds are above the range of human hearing. Other reports show that crops can also make noise while growing: fast-growing forced rhubarb creaks and pops loudly enough to hear. The evidence points the same way for both parts of the claim. The only gap is that I found no specific example of a fruit making sounds as it grows; the growing-sound evidence centres on rhubarb.

text: Ocean waves can travel at speeds of up to 35 miles per hour, with the longest waves recorded being over 1,700 feet long and occurring in the North Atlantic Ocean.
label: contradicted
reason: I found three problems with the claim. First, the speed cap is wrong: tsunamis cross deep ocean at about 500 mph (Smithsonian, 13News), much faster than 35 mph. Second, the length figure is wrong: Guinness World Records lists the longest ocean wavelength as about 12,000 km for tides, with tsunamis around 200 km. Both far exceed 1,700 feet. Third, the ~1,700-foot figure appears to come from the 1958 Lituya Bay megatsunami in Alaska, which is not in the North Atlantic. That number was a run-up height of about 1,720 to 1,740 feet, not a wave length. The North Atlantic record is a 62.3-foot significant wave height measured by a buoy, which is a height, not a length.

text: In the heart of the Amazon rainforest, there's a unique species of jellyfish called the Turritopsis dohrnii, also known as the "immortal jellyfish," that's scientifically proven to be biologically immortal.
label: contradicted
reason: Turritopsis dohrnii, the 'immortal jellyfish', is a real species, and it can revert to an earlier life stage. However, it is a small marine hydrozoan that lives in the Mediterranean Sea and in waters off Japan, not in the Amazon rainforest. Wikipedia, iNaturalist and a PubMed review all describe it as an ocean species. Because the location in the claim is wrong, the claim is contradicted.

text: Aola Island in the Solomon Islands is home to the world's largest saltwater lagoon, Marovo Lagoon, which covers an area of approximately 700 square kilometers (270 square miles).
label: contradicted
reason: Marovo Lagoon is in the New Georgia Islands of Western Province. It surrounds New Georgia, Vangunu and Gatokae, not "Aola Island." Aola is a place on Guadalcanal. The sources do back the rest of the claim: the lagoon covers about 700 km² and is often called the world's largest saltwater lagoon. But the claim's location is wrong.

text: A blue whale's heartbeat can be as slow as about two beats per minute when the whale is resting or sleeping.
label: contradicted
reason: The ~2 beats per minute figure is real, but it comes from the first ECG recording of a blue whale (Goldbogen et al., 2019). That low was measured during deep foraging dives, not while the whale was resting or sleeping. Coverage of the study says the heart rate fell to about 4–8 bpm on dives, hit a low of 2 bpm, and climbed to as much as 37 bpm at the surface. So the claim pins the number on the wrong situation. The study did not measure heart rate during rest or sleep, and the whale's heart beat much faster at the surface than during dives.

text: Freshwater jellyfish are found in rivers, lakes, and wetlands worldwide, and their existence is still a mystery to scientists.
label: supported
reason: Reliable sources broadly back the claim. A PMC review, Wikipedia and Love Your Lake say freshwater jellyfish (mainly Craspedacusta sowerbii) live on every continent except Antarctica. Science Friday and FVISS place them in lakes, reservoirs, ponds, rivers and streams. Science Friday, in a piece titled "The Mysteries Of Freshwater Jellyfish," and Great Lakes Now say scientists "still don't know much" about them, and the PMC review describes knowledge gaps. Two caveats: no source names wetlands specifically, and Wikipedia says they are generally not seen in fast-flowing rivers. Saying their "existence" is a mystery overstates the sources, which describe gaps in knowledge about the species. Overall, the evidence supports the claim's main point.

text: Honeybees are able to recognize human faces and remember them for later encounters, much like some other animals and even some types of fish.
label: supported
reason: Reputable outlets (Science, and Phys.org reporting on a 2005 study in the Journal of Experimental Biology by Dyer and colleagues) say honeybees can learn to recognize human faces in photos and remember them for at least two days, even after the reward is removed. Other research has found that some animals can also recognize human faces, including a fish, the archerfish (a 2016 Oxford study). I didn't check that study in this search, though. Nothing I found contradicts the claim.

text: Humans are the only species known to have a unique nose print, just like fingerprints, which can be used for identification purposes.
label: contradicted
reason: The claim is false. Humans are not the only species with unique nose prints. Dogs are well known to have nose prints unique to each individual, much like fingerprints, and these prints are used to identify them. US patents describe biometric ID systems based on canine and feline noseprints (cattle muzzle prints are also used for ID). Human noses are also not normally used for print-based identification at all; that role belongs to fingerprints.

text: Japan has a vending machine for almost everything, including umbrellas, underwear, and live crabs.
label: contradicted
reason: Two of the three examples check out, but the live-crab one does not. Several sources describe umbrella vending machines in Japan, and Kotaku reports that machines selling new underwear are legal there. The widely reported live-crab vending machine, however, was in China, not Japan. Gizmodo Japan, Record China and Livedoor News say it appeared in 2010 in a Nanjing subway station, selling live Shanghai hairy crabs, and Gizmodo describes China as Japan's neighbor. Record China also reports a live-crab machine in Hangzhou. The crab machines found in Japan sell frozen crab (for example, one in Hakodate stocked with crab from the waters off Nemuro) or crab paste (at the Fukui Shinkansen station). A few low-credibility listicle and blog sites do say Japan has live-crab machines. They appear to be repeating the Chinese story, so I gave more weight to the news reports and judged the claim contradicted.

text: Scientists have discovered approximately 8.7 million identified species on Earth to date, but it's estimated that up to 80% of all species remain undiscovered.
label: contradicted
reason: The 8.7 million figure is wrong for what the claim says. It comes from Mora et al.'s 2011 estimate of the total number of species on Earth, not the number already identified. Only about 1.2 million species had been identified and catalogued, which is less than 15% of that total. The estimate also implies that 86% of land species and 91% of marine species remain undiscovered, more than 80%, not "up to 80%".

text: A blue whale's heartbeat can be as loud as 188 decibels, louder than a jet engine and almost as loud as a Saturn V rocket during launch.
label: contradicted
reason: Reliable sources, including WWF and Wikipedia's list of whale vocalizations, give 188 decibels as the loudness of a blue whale's calls, not its heartbeat. WWF compares that 188 dB to a jet's 140 dB. No source attributes 188 dB to the heartbeat, which is far quieter. The claim confuses the whale's vocalizations with its heartbeat.

text: A blue whale's heartbeat can be as loud as 188 decibels, louder than a jet taking off, which can be heard for hundreds of miles underwater.
label: contradicted
reason: The 188-decibel figure and the 'heard for hundreds of miles underwater' detail describe the blue whale's call, not its heartbeat. Enchanted Learning says the blue whale's call can reach up to 188 dB and its loud whistle can be heard for hundreds of miles underwater. The claim gives those numbers to the heartbeat instead. A blue whale's heartbeat is far quieter: popular accounts say it might be detectable from about 2 miles away, and even that is often called an exaggeration.

text: Beehive-shaped structures in Mexico, known as "sweat houses," have been discovered to be around 1,000 years older than initially believed.
label: not_verifiable
reason: I couldn't verify this claim before my search limit ran out. The results I got were general background only: a Wikipedia page on beehive houses around the world and a Penn Museum article about Mexican and Mayan sweat baths. Neither mentions a discovery that beehive-shaped sweat houses in Mexico are about 1,000 years older than thought. Nothing I found supports or contradicts the claim.

text: Dragonflies have been around for over 300 million years, with the oldest known fossil dating back to the Paleozoic Era.
label: supported
reason: Several sources (for example NatureNorth and Better Planet Education) say that dragonflies and their ancestors were around more than 300 million years ago. They cite fossils from about 325 million years ago in Upper Carboniferous rocks. The Carboniferous is part of the Paleozoic Era. One caveat: some sources say the earliest true dragonflies date to about 250 million years ago, but the ancestral forms are widely described as dragonflies over 300 million years old.

text: Honeybees are able to fly by using their wings to generate electricity and create a difference in air pressure above and below their wings.
label: contradicted
reason: Honeybees fly using aerodynamics. They flap their wings in short, very fast strokes (about 230 times per second), which creates a leading-edge vortex and other unsteady airflow effects that produce lift. A PNAS study (Altshuler et al., 2005) found this. The claim's point about a pressure difference above and below the wings fits this mechanism. But the claim also says bees use their wings to generate electricity to fly, and that is false. Bees do pick up an electrostatic charge as they fly, but flight researchers credit the lift to wing movement, not electricity.

text: Humans share about 50% of their DNA with bananas, highlighting the genetic similarities between different species through evolution.
label: contradicted
reason: Snopes, syndicated on Yahoo News, fact-checked the idea that humans share 50% of their DNA with bananas and rated it False. It says the statement cannot be read as factual in any scenario. The popular figure comes from a mix-up between genes that have counterparts in both species and actual DNA. Orthology analyses find that at most about 25% of human genes have banana orthologs, and because protein-coding DNA is only about 2% of the genome, the real shared DNA is far below 50%. Factmyth.com repeats the 50% figure, but it is not a reliable source and itself notes the coding-DNA objection.

text: A chunk of the Dead Sea has been found to be so dense with salt that objects with lower densities, like humans, naturally float when submerged in it.
label: supported
reason: The American Museum of Natural History (AMNH) says the Dead Sea is so salty that its water is denser than the human body, so people float in it easily. That covers the main point of the claim: the high salt content makes the water dense, and less dense objects like humans float. The wording "a chunk of the Dead Sea has been found" is odd, but the basic fact is well established.

text: Ahead of the development of modern antibiotics, Penicillium mould was first used by Scottish scientist Alexander Fleming in 1928 to treat bacterial infections.
label: contradicted
reason: Reliable sources (ACS, Britannica, Wikipedia) say Fleming discovered, or first observed, penicillin's antibacterial effect from Penicillium mould in 1928, but he did not use it to treat bacterial infections that year. Wikipedia says his student Cecil Paine first treated an eye infection with it in 1930, and Fleming himself first treated a patient with purified penicillin in 1942. Florey and Chain's team made it usable as a treatment around 1941. Moulds were also used as folk remedies long before Fleming. The 1928 date and Fleming's role as discoverer are right, but the claim that he 'first used' it in 1928 to treat infections is false.

text: Honeybees are able to fly by using electricity generated from the friction of their wings beating to attract and trap pollen particles.
label: contradicted
reason: The claim mixes up two things. Bees do build up a positive static charge while flying, mostly from air friction on their body hairs as they flap their wings, and that charge helps pull pollen onto them. But the charge is a side effect of flying. It isn't what lets them fly. Bees stay in the air because their beating wings produce aerodynamic lift. AskNature and Science Friday both say the charge comes from flight and is used to collect pollen. Neither says electricity powers flight, so the claim that bees are able to fly by using electricity is wrong.

text: Humans and dolphins are the only mammals known to give themselves names based on unique signature whistles.
label: contradicted
reason: The claim says humans and dolphins are the only mammals known to have names. That is wrong. A 2024 study in Nature Ecology & Evolution, reported by AFP via France24 and RTE, found that African elephants call each other by individual names they invent. These names are not imitations of the recipient's own call. Marmosets have also been reported to use name-like calls. So dolphins are not the only non-human mammals with name-like vocal labels. The claim's wording is also odd: dolphin signature whistles are dolphin names, and humans do not name themselves with whistles.

text: Humans are born without kneecaps; they do not develop until around 3-5 years of age, and are made entirely of cartilage until then.
label: contradicted
reason: The claim gets the 3–5 year timing right but is wrong on the main point. HowStuffWorks says the cartilage hardens into bone somewhere between ages 3 and 5. However, HowStuffWorks, Grownsy (citing NIH research) and a health professional on JustAnswer all say babies are born with kneecaps. At birth the kneecaps are made of cartilage rather than bone. So the kneecap is there from birth; only the bone forms later. The claim even undercuts itself by saying the kneecaps are absent and also made of cartilage. Some trivia sites repeat the 'born without kneecaps' line, but they explain that they mean babies lack a bony kneecap, not that there is no kneecap at all.

text: Our solar system is not perfectly aligned with the Milky Way galaxy, with Earth tilted at about 63 degrees to the galactic plane.
label: supported
reason: I found support for both parts of the claim. Swinburne University's astronomy encyclopedia says the galactic plane is tilted 63 degrees to the celestial equator, which is the projection of Earth's equator. Britannica gives about 62°36′. The same Swinburne source and other sources say the plane of the solar system (the ecliptic) is tilted about 60 degrees to the galactic plane, so the solar system is not aligned with the Milky Way. The 63-degree figure describes Earth's equator rather than the solar system's orbital plane, but that matches the claim's wording that Earth is tilted at about 63 degrees.

text: Tarantulas have been on Earth for around 120 million years, having outlived the dinosaurs.
label: supported
reason: Reliable science news outlets (Phys.org, Live Science, Smithsonian, IFLScience), all covering a 2021 PeerJ study by Foley et al., report that tarantulas first appeared about 120 million years ago in the Cretaceous period, when dinosaurs were still alive. Tarantulas are still around today, while the non-avian dinosaurs died out about 66 million years ago, so tarantulas did outlive them. One caveat: the 120-million-year figure is a molecular-clock estimate, and earlier studies gave a range of about 150 to 71 million years ago. The claim says 'around' 120 million years, so it fits the evidence.

text: Tarantulas have been on Earth for over 100 million years, predating the dinosaurs that roamed during the Cretaceous period.
label: contradicted
reason: The first part of the claim is right: reputable sources (Foley et al. 2019/2021 phylogenomics, reported by Phys.org, Live Science and Smithsonian) say tarantulas (Theraphosidae) first appeared about 120 million years ago, which is more than 100 million years. The second part is wrong. That date falls inside the Cretaceous (about 145–66 million years ago), so tarantulas arose during the Cretaceous and lived alongside its dinosaurs. They did not come before them. Dinosaurs had already existed since the Triassic, so tarantulas did not predate dinosaurs at all.

text: A blue whale's heart alone can weigh around 400 pounds and pump over 5,000 gallons of blood through its body with every beat.
label: contradicted
reason: NOAA Fisheries backs up the weight: it says a blue whale's heart weighs about 400 pounds. But NOAA also says the heart pumps about 60 gallons (around 220 liters) of blood with each beat, not more than 5,000 gallons. The Royal Ontario Museum figures, as reported in other coverage, give the same ~60 gallons per beat. Because the per-beat volume in the claim is far too high, the claim is contradicted.

text: Scientists have confirmed the existence of a fifth ocean, known as the Southern Ocean, which surrounds Antarctica and extends north to the coast of South America, Africa, and Australia.
label: contradicted
reason: The Southern Ocean does surround Antarctica, and National Geographic formally recognized it as the fifth ocean in 2021. But that recognition came from a mapmaking organization, so "scientists have confirmed its existence" overstates it. The bigger problem is the extent. National Geographic, the Washington Post and CNN all say the Southern Ocean's northern boundary is about 60°S latitude, roughly where the Antarctic Circumpolar Current flows. It does not reach the coasts of South America, Africa or Australia, all of which lie well north of 60°S. That part of the claim is wrong.

text: Astronomers estimate there are between 200 and 400 billion stars in the Milky Way galaxy.
label: supported
reason: Big Think's "Starts With a Bang" column by astrophysicist Ethan Siegel says current estimates put the most likely number of stars in the Milky Way between 200 billion and 400 billion. That matches the claim. Some sources still give a wider range of 100 to 400 billion, but the article says newer data rule out the old figure of about 100 billion and leave about 200 billion as a reasonable lower bound.

text: Scientists have trained honeybees to detect cancer through scent, as some cancers emit unique odors that the bees can recognize.
label: supported
reason: The claim holds up. Michigan State University researchers found that honeybees can use their sense of smell to pick out the chemical signatures of lung cancer, both in synthetic breath mixtures and in cancer cell lines. Smithsonian Magazine and VOA News reported the work, and it involved recording the bees' brain activity as they responded to these odors. Other sources describe bees being trained by classical conditioning to tell healthy cells from cancer cells, and to recognize odors linked to illnesses such as lung cancer. This matches the claim that some cancers give off distinctive scents that bees can learn to detect. Note that this is still lab research: the bees were tested on synthetic breath and cell lines, not real patients' breath, and the method is not used clinically yet.

text: Arectangle divided into a square and two equal rectangles, each of which is also divided into a square and two equal rectangles has a total area that follows the Fibonacci sequence.
label: not_verifiable
reason: I found no source that describes this construction or links it to the Fibonacci sequence. The search results only cover the usual Fibonacci-rectangle facts: squares with Fibonacci side lengths fit into Fn×Fn+1 rectangles, and dissection fallacies are built on Cassini's identity. Neither describes a square plus two equal rectangles. A rough check of my own (not from a source) also argues against the claim. If the two equal rectangles have the same shape as the original, the rectangle must be 1×2, and the areas then shrink by a fixed factor at each step. That is a geometric pattern, not a Fibonacci one. The claim is also vague about which areas are supposed to follow the sequence. Since no reliable source confirms or directly refutes it, the claim can't be verified.

text: A blue whale's heartbeat is so loud, it can be heard for hundreds of miles underwater.
label: contradicted
reason: NOAA Fisheries says a blue whale's heartbeat can be heard about 2 miles away, not hundreds of miles. Other popular sources give the same figure. The 'hundreds of miles' distance actually describes how far blue whale calls and songs travel, not their heartbeats.

text: Areatment-free glass, known as 'Prince Rupert's Drops', can withstand extreme pressure on its body but will explode if its tail is even lightly scratched.
label: supported
reason: Purdue University and New Atlas both describe Prince Rupert's drops as glass 'tadpoles' whose heads survive hammer blows, but the whole drop bursts into powder when the tail is snipped or broken with very slight finger pressure. That matches the main claim. Two parts are worded loosely. Sources talk about breaking the tail, not just scratching it, though any damage to the tail sets off the explosion. And the drops are made by dripping molten glass into cold water, so 'treatment-free' (garbled as 'Areatment-free' in the claim) only holds if it means no extra treatment beyond that.

text: Areatment-free glass, known as 'Prince Rupert's Drops', can withstand extreme pressure on its body, but shatters instantly when its tail is damaged.
label: supported
reason: Reliable sources (Amusing Planet, Purdue University research news) describe Prince Rupert's drops as tadpole-shaped pieces of glass. Their bulbous head can take hammer blows, bullets and compressive stress of up to about 100,000 psi. Snapping or cracking the thin tail makes the whole drop explode into powder instantly. That matches the main point of the claim. One caveat: "Areatment-free" looks like a typo for "treatment-free", and that wording is debatable, because the drops get their strength from being quenched in cold water, which is a form of thermal tempering. Since the claim's core facts are confirmed, I rated it supported.

text: Higher levels of social connections in life have been scientifically linked to a lower risk of cognitive decline and dementia.
label: supported
reason: Scientific research backs this claim. A UNSW Sydney meta-analysis pooled 13 international studies of people aged 65 and over. It was published in Alzheimer's & Dementia, the journal of the Alzheimer's Association, and found that good social connections were linked to a lower risk of mild cognitive impairment, dementia and death. The researchers also recommended prioritising social connection to reduce the risk of cognitive decline. This fits with wider research showing that social isolation raises dementia risk.

text: Higher levels of social connections in life have been scientifically linked to a lower risk of cognitive decline and psychological disorders, including dementia and depression.
label: supported
reason: Reliable sources back the claim. A UNSW meta-analysis of 13 studies, published in Alzheimer's & Dementia, found that good social connections were linked to a lower risk of mild cognitive impairment, dementia and death. A CDC MMWR report and a review of the National Academies report state that social disconnection (isolation and loneliness) raises the risk of dementia, depression and anxiety, including about a 50% higher dementia risk. That is the reverse side of the claim's statement that more social connection goes with lower risk of these conditions.

text: Higher levels of social connections in life have been scientifically linked to a lower risk of dying from all causes.
label: supported
reason: A peer-reviewed meta-analysis by Holt-Lunstad et al. (PLoS Medicine, 2010; 148 studies, about 308,000 participants) found that people with stronger social relationships had about 50% better odds of survival, a lower risk of dying from any cause. It also found that social relationships affect mortality risk about as much as established risk factors such as smoking. This scientific evidence supports the claim.

text: Polar bears are excellent swimmers, and they have been known to swim distances of up to 60 miles (97 kilometers) or more without resting.
label: supported
reason: NH PBS NatureWorks says polar bears are very good swimmers that can swim as far as 60 miles (96.6 km) without resting. This matches the claim. Other well-known reports go further, including a tracked swim of hundreds of kilometers over several days, which fits the claim's "or more."

text: Scans of the Egyptian Great Pyramid's internal chamber, created in 2017, revealed a substantial previously undiscovered void above the Queen's Chamber.
label: contradicted
reason: The 2017 muon scans did find a large hidden void, the ScanPyramids Big Void, which is at least 30 m long. But the Nature paper reporting it places the void above the Grand Gallery, not above the Queen's Chamber. The Queen's Chamber is only where some of the detectors were set up to make the first observations. The claim also says the scans were "of the internal chamber", which doesn't fit: the scans imaged the pyramid's interior using detectors placed in the chamber and outside the pyramid.

text: Seven percent of all the English words in the Oxford English Dictionary have been borrowed from Arabic.
label: contradicted
reason: The claim is false. Arabic's share of the OED is a small fraction of 1%, not 7%. A EURALEX 2020–2021 study searched the OED's etymology data and found 409 Arabic loanwords. A ResearchGate paper, citing Durkin (2014), notes that the OED records relatively few direct Arabic loans, though many Arabic words reached English through other languages. The OED has hundreds of thousands of entries, so 409 words is far below 7%. Even generous counts that include indirect borrowings (roughly a few thousand) would not reach 7%.

text: Seven percent of all the English words in the Oxford English Dictionary have been used in the lyrics of the Beatles's songs.
label: contradicted
reason: I found no source for the 7% figure, and the numbers I could find point to a share far below 7%. A lyric analysis on a personal blog (the source linked here) found that the Beatles' lyrics use about 3,326 unique words. The OED's own count, which I know from background knowledge because my searches didn't confirm it, is about 171,000 words in current use and more than 600,000 word forms overall. That would put the Beatles' share at roughly 2% of current-use words, or about 0.5% of all forms. Reaching 7% would take a vocabulary of at least about 12,000 words. That is more than Eminem's reported record of about 8,800 unique words, according to a Musixmatch figure cited on an editor's blog. Because the main figure comes from blogs, the evidence is only moderately strong, but it consistently points against the claim.

text: Tibet has a railway line with a station at Doctime which is at an altitude of more than five kilometers, making it the world's highest railway station.
label: contradicted
reason: The world's highest railway station is Tanggula station, not a place called "Doctime". Guinness World Records and Wikipedia both say Tanggula is on the Qinghai–Tibet (Qingzang) railway in Tibet, at 5,068 m above sea level. So the claim is right that Tibet's railway has a station above 5 km that is the highest in the world, but it names the wrong station. My searches turned up no station called Doctime.

text: Plants can make sounds, too, as researchers have discovered that when a plant is cut or injured, it releases ultrasonic sounds that are beyond human hearing range.
label: supported
reason: A peer-reviewed study by Khait et al. (Cell, 2023) found that tomato and tobacco plants give off airborne ultrasonic sounds when stressed. This happened both when their stems were cut and when they were dehydrated, and stressed plants made far more sounds than unstressed ones. Coverage of the study reports frequencies of about 20–100 kHz, which is above what humans can hear. That matches what the claim says.

text: A blue whale's heartbeat can be as slow as one to four beats per minute when the animal is fully submerged and not exerting itself.
label: contradicted
reason: The claim's figures don't match the only direct measurement. In the first recorded blue whale heartbeat (Goldbogen lab, Stanford, 2019), the diving whale's heart rate fell to an average minimum of about 4–8 beats per minute, with a single low of 2 bpm, reported by Futurity and CNN. No rate of 1 bpm was recorded, and 1–4 bpm was not the typical minimum. The slowest rates also came during foraging dives, when the whale was lunging for food, not while it was resting.

text: A large percentage of humans are born with a unique birthmark on their body; however, only about 1 in 100 people naturally have freckles.
label: contradicted
reason: Freckles are far more common than 1 in 100 people. Simple English Wikipedia estimates that about 1.5 billion people worldwide have freckles, roughly 20% of the global population. KnowYourDNA puts the figure at about 10–15%. Both estimates contradict the claim's "about 1 in 100" figure. The search did not check the first part of the claim, about birthmarks, but the freckle figure alone makes the claim false.

text: Astronauts in space cannot cry in the usual way because tears do not flow downwards due to the microgravity environment.
label: supported
reason: Space.com reports Chris Hadfield's demonstration from the ISS: in microgravity, tears don't fall but collect in a ball around the eye. On Earth, tears run down the face only because of gravity. Futurism and ScienceABC say the same thing. Astronauts still produce tears, but the usual flow down the cheeks doesn't happen, which matches the claim.

text: Honeybees are able to fly by using electricity generated by the movement of their wings, which helps to attract pollen from flowers.
label: contradicted
reason: The claim gets the mechanism of flight wrong. Bees fly because their wings produce aerodynamic lift, not because they use electricity. It is true that bees pick up a static (electrostatic) charge while flying, mostly from friction with charged particles in the air, and that this charge can help pollen jump to them and lets them sense whether a flower has already been visited. That charge is a side effect of flying, though, not what lets bees fly. Credible sources such as National Geographic and Science Friday describe this static charge and its role in pollination, and none of them say electricity powers bee flight. The central part of the claim is therefore false.

text: Humans are the only known species capable of crying emotional tears, with research suggesting this ability is unique to humans.
label: supported
reason: Trustworthy sources back the claim. Scientific American says that "Scientists generally agree that tears of sadness are uniquely human." Discover Magazine's headline is "Humans Are the Only Animals That Cry", and Sciencing calls it the general scientific consensus that humans are the only species known to shed tears for emotional reasons. No source I found contradicts this, and the claim's wording ('only known species', 'research suggesting') matches the hedged way these sources state the consensus.

text: Humans share about 50-60% of their DNA with fruit flies, indicating a shared genetic ancestry.
label: supported
reason: Reputable sources back the figure: the Max Planck Society says about 60% of fruit fly genes have a similar counterpart in humans, and another source says 60% of the human genome overlaps with the fruit fly genome. These shared genes include about 75% of known human disease genes, which points to common ancestry. Strictly speaking, the 60% refers to similar genes rather than identical DNA, but this matches the common wording of the claim and the claim's 50–60% range.

text: Octopuses have nine brains, with a large central brain and eight smaller mini-brains located in each of their eight arms.
label: supported
reason: Trusted sources, including PBS Nature with a Monterey Bay Aquarium marine biologist, describe octopuses as having nine brains: one main brain in the head and one in each of the eight arms. Biologically, the 'mini-brains' are clusters of nerve cells (ganglia) in the arms that hold a large share of the octopus's neurons. 'Nine brains' is a common simplification of this, but it fits the claim as worded.

text: Sweden has a "Freedom to Roam" law that allows anyone to camp or forage in public or private wilderness areas.
label: supported
reason: Reliable sources, including Visit Sweden, the Swedish Tourist Association and West Sweden tourism, describe Allemansrätten (the Right of Public Access), often translated as the 'freedom to roam'. It lets anyone, tourists included, camp and pick wild berries, mushrooms and flowers on most land, including privately owned land. Some limits apply: you must stay away from homes and cultivated fields, you can't pick protected species, and you need permission for long stays or large groups. Two caveats don't change the verdict. First, it's a customary right recognised in the constitution rather than a single statute. Second, Visit Sweden says picking isn't technically part of the right, but landowners can't stop people from picking where the right applies. The claim's core matches the evidence.

text: Scientists estimate that there are approximately 8.7 million identified species on Earth, but the total number, including unidentified species, is believed to be around 30 million.
label: contradicted
reason: The 2011 study by Mora et al. (PLoS Biology), as reported by ScienceDaily, gives about 8.7 million (±1.3 million) as the estimated total number of eukaryote species on Earth, including undiscovered ones. That figure is not the number of identified species. Only about 1.2 million species have been described. So the claim gets wrong what the 8.7 million figure means, and its 30 million total does not match this estimate.

text: Scientists estimate that there may be between 700,000 and 1 million species on Earth that have not yet been formally described or discovered.
label: contradicted
reason: Scientists' estimates of undescribed species are far higher than the claim. The widely cited 2011 PLoS Biology study (Mora et al.), reported by National Geographic, The Scientist and the California Academy of Sciences, puts the total number of eukaryotic species at about 8.7 million (±1.3 million). Only about 1.2 million of these have been described, so roughly 86% (around 7.5 million species) are still unknown. That is several million undescribed species, not 700,000 to 1 million. The claim's range is much closer to unrelated figures, such as the roughly 1 million species threatened with extinction or the number of species already described.

text: A blue whale's heartbeat can be as loud as a jet engine, reaching levels of up to 188 decibels.
label: contradicted
reason: The 188-decibel, louder-than-a-jet-engine figure is real, but it describes blue whale calls, not their heartbeat. Live Science and Enchanted Learning both say blue whale calls or songs reach up to 188 dB and can be louder than a jet engine. The claim wrongly attributes that loudness to the heartbeat, and no source says a blue whale's heartbeat gets anywhere near that level.

text: A set of human lungs, after being removed from the body and inflated, can float on water due to the air filling the alveoli.
label: supported
reason: The lung float (hydrostatic) test depends on this exact principle: lungs that contain air float in water, and lungs with no air sink. Wikipedia's article on the test says that lungs that float are taken to have been aerated. A removed, inflated lung has air-filled alveoli, which make it less dense than water, so it floats.
