The test's known caveats, such as gas from decomposition, are about using it to judge whether an infant breathed. They don't change the basic physics in the claim.

text: Bees are capable of recognizing human faces and remembering them for later encounters, a unique ability shared by only a few insects.
label: supported
reason: Phys.org reports on a study by Adrian Dyer in the Journal of Experimental Biology. Honeybees learned to recognize human faces in photos and remembered them for at least two days. Dyer said this was, as far as he knew, the first time an invertebrate had been shown to recognize the faces of another species. That fits the claim that only a few insects have this ability. The source doesn't list which other insects can do it, so that part is only indirectly supported.

text: Polar bears are excellent swimmers, with some individuals known to swim for hours or even days at a time, covering distances of up to 60 miles without resting.
label: supported
reason: Several sources support the claim. The New Hampshire PBS NatureWorks page, the San Diego Zoo Wildlife Alliance, Ocean Conservancy and Swan Expeditions all describe polar bears as strong swimmers that can swim about 60 miles (roughly 100 km) without resting. Live Science and Ocean Conservancy report GPS tracking showing swims lasting days, including one female's nonstop 9-day, 426-mile swim. One caveat: that record shows 60 miles is not a true maximum, so 'up to 60 miles' understates the longest recorded swims. Still, 60 miles without rest is the figure most sources give, and no source contradicts the core claim.

text: vite is a Japanese island in the East China Sea.
label: contradicted
reason: In reliable sources, "Vite" refers to a frontend build tool for web development. Its name is the French word for "fast," and it is not a Japanese island. A search for Japanese islands in the East China Sea, such as Nakaenoshima, Kamikoshiki-shima and the Senkaku Islands, turned up no island called Vite. The claim mistakes a software tool for a geographic place.

text: A fungus called Armillaria ostoyae is considered the world's largest living organism, spanning over 2,200 acres and estimated to be around 2,400 years old.
label: supported
reason: Guinness World Records says the Armillaria ostoyae fungus in Oregon's Malheur National Forest covers 965 hectares (2,385 acres), which is more than 2,200 acres. It gives the fungus's age as at least 2,400 years, and possibly as much as 8,650. Discover Magazine also calls it the world's largest organism at 2,385 acres. One small caveat: Discover gives the age as 8,650 years, but that is the upper end of the same Guinness estimate. It is not a separate figure that contradicts the claim.

text: A chunk of the Dead Sea has been found to be so dense with salt that objects can actually float on its surface with great ease.
label: supported
reason: The American Museum of Natural History says the Dead Sea is almost six times as salty as the ocean. Because its water is denser than the human body, people float in it effortlessly. That backs up the main point of the claim: the Dead Sea is so salty that things float on it easily. The phrase "a chunk of" is odd wording, but it doesn't contradict this well-known fact.

text: A chunk of the Dead Sea has been found to be so dense with salt that objects can be suspended in it without actually sinking.
label: supported
reason: Several sources, including the American Museum of Natural History, say the Dead Sea's brine is so salty (about 34% dissolved salts, roughly ten times saltier than the ocean) that the water is denser than the human body. Because of this, people and objects float on it easily and it is extremely hard to sink. That matches the core of the claim. The wording "a chunk... has been found" is odd, but this buoyancy is a well-documented property of the Dead Sea as a whole.

text: A chunk of the Dead Sea has been found to be so dense with salt that objects can be suspended in it without sinking.
label: supported
reason: Several sources, including IFLScience and Science Times, say the Dead Sea is a hypersaline lake. Its salinity is about 34%, roughly ten times that of the ocean, and its density is about 1.24 kg/L, compared with roughly 1.0 kg/L for the human body. That makes it so buoyant that people and objects float rather than sink. The sources describe the lake's water in general, not one particular newly discovered area. Still, the main point of the claim matches well-documented facts: the water is dense enough with salt that things stay up without sinking.

text: Bacteria can only grow and reproduce in "moist" environments,  typically requiring a certain level of humidity to thrive
label: supported
reason: The sources agree that bacteria need water to grow and reproduce. A PMC (NCBI) review calls the presence of water a necessary condition for bacterial reproduction. Food-science and patent sources add that most bacteria stop growing once water activity falls below about 0.91, so they need a minimum level of available moisture. Bacteria can survive drying, but they cannot grow or reproduce without water. That matches what the claim says.

text: Bacteria can only grow and reproduce in "moist" environments,  typically requiring a certain level of humidity.
label: supported
reason: Sources on water activity say microorganisms, including bacteria, need water to grow and reproduce. Each one has a minimum water activity below which it cannot grow, and most bacteria need a water activity above about 0.90. Bacteria may survive dry conditions, for example as spores, but they do not grow or reproduce without enough available moisture. This supports the claim.

text: Honeybees are able to fly by using their wings to generate electricity and create an electric charge that helps reduce air resistance.
label: contradicted
reason: Honeybees fly using aerodynamic forces made by their flapping wings. Caltech research (PNAS 2005) found that their lift comes from short-amplitude, high-frequency wing strokes (about 230 Hz) and unsteady aerodynamic forces when the stroke reverses direction. Bees do build up static charge as they fly, but sources describe this charge as useful for picking up pollen and sensing flowers. They don't say it reduces air resistance or makes flight possible, so the claimed way bees fly is wrong.

text: Honeybees are able to fly by using their wings to generate electricity and create an electric charge which aids in lift.
label: contradicted
reason: The claim is false. Reliable sources, including Nature and beekeeping suppliers such as Dadant and Mann Lake, explain that honeybees fly by aerodynamics. Their rapid wingbeats, short stroke amplitude and wing rotation create leading-edge vortices, sometimes called 'tiny tornadoes', that generate lift. Bees do pick up a static electric charge as they fly, but that charge helps with things like pollen transfer, not lift. No source says bees generate electricity with their wings to help them fly.

text: Galileo Galilei was the first person to observe the planet Neptune using a telescope, but he didn't recognize it as a planet and documented it as a fixed star in 1613.
label: supported
reason: NASA says Galileo recorded Neptune as a fixed star when he observed it through his small telescope in 1612 and 1613, more than 200 years before it was discovered in 1846. A ResearchGate paper reports that his notebooks include drawings from December 1612 and January 1613, and that he took Neptune for a fixed star. His observations are the earliest known telescopic sightings of Neptune, which supports the 'first person' part. The year 1613 matches his January 1613 records, though his sightings started in late December 1612.

text: One flex of a human eyebrow contains about 250,000 bits of information.
label: not_verifiable
reason: I couldn't find any reliable source for the claim that one eyebrow flex carries about 250,000 bits of information. My searches turned up only research on what eyebrow movements signal in conversation, such as pitch accents, turn-taking and emphasis, and general eyebrow trivia. None of it puts a number on the information in an eyebrow movement. I also found nothing that directly disproves the figure, so the claim can't be verified either way. It looks like an unsourced factoid.

text: One flex of a human eyebrow contains around 110 muscles and utilizes one-tenth of the brain's total processing power when used in facial expressions.
label: contradicted
reason: Anatomy sources show that only a handful of muscles move the eyebrow: the frontalis, corrugator supercilii, depressor supercilii, procerus and orbicularis oculi. The whole human face has only about 40 muscles, so a single eyebrow flex cannot involve around 110. No credible source supports the idea that an eyebrow movement uses one-tenth of the brain's processing power, and the claim looks made up.

text: One flex of a human eyebrow contains around 110 muscles and utilizes one-tenth of the brain's total processing power when used in social interactions.
label: contradicted
reason: Anatomy sources such as ScienceDirect say only a few muscles move the eyebrows: the frontalis, corrugator supercilii, depressor supercilii, procerus and orbicularis oculi. That is nowhere near 110. The whole face has only about 40 muscles. I found nothing to support the idea that moving an eyebrow uses one-tenth of the brain's processing power, and the figure appears to be made up.

text: One flex of a human eyebrow contains from around 110,000 to 210,000 hair follicles and other types of hairs embedded along the bone structure beneath.
label: contradicted
reason: Several sources say an average eyebrow has about 250 hairs. Even eyebrows that have never been plucked are reported to reach only about 1,100 hairs. The claim's figure of 110,000 to 210,000 follicles is in line with estimates for the whole scalp, not one eyebrow, so it is off by several orders of magnitude.

text: Scientists estimate that there are approximately 8.7 million Identified species on Earth, but the total number, including unidentified species, could be as high as 30 million.
label: contradicted
reason: The 8.7 million figure from Mora et al. (2011) is an estimate of the total number of species on Earth, including the ones nobody has identified yet. It is not a count of identified species. The same study says only about 1.2 million species have been catalogued, and roughly 86% of species have not yet been described. That means the claim's statement that about 8.7 million species have been identified is wrong.

text: Scientists estimate that there are approximately 8.7 million identified species on Earth, but only about 1.3 million of those have been formally described and named.
label: contradicted
reason: The 8.7 million figure (Mora et al., 2011, PLoS Biology) is an estimate of the total number of species thought to exist on Earth. It is not a count of identified species. Most of those species have never been discovered or identified. The study put the number of described and catalogued species at about 1.2–1.25 million. The 1.3 million figure the claim uses is actually the study's margin of error ('give or take 1.3 million'), not the number of described species. So the claim gets the basic framing wrong by calling 8.7 million 'identified species,' and it also blurs the numbers.

text: Japan has the world's oldest known living tree, a white pine tree called "Jōmon Sugi," which is estimated to be around 2,000 to 7,200 years old.
label: contradicted
reason: The age estimate of 2,000 to 7,200 years is right, but the claim gets two other things wrong. Wikipedia and the Japan National Tourism Organization both describe Jōmon Sugi as a Japanese cedar (Cryptomeria japonica, or 'sugi') on Yakushima, not a white pine. It is the oldest and largest of the Yakushima cedars, not the world's oldest known living tree. Trees such as the Great Basin bristlecone pine 'Methuselah' are more reliably dated as older. The misidentified species alone contradicts the claim.

text: Black holes are among the densest objects in the universe, with some having a density that is equivalent to the mass of approximately one billion tons packed into a sugar-cube-sized space.
label: not_verifiable
reason: I found plenty of support for black holes being among the densest objects, but no source that applies the sugar-cube figure to black holes. NASA and Space.com give 'about 1 billion tons per sugar cube' as the density of neutron star material, not black holes. Wikipedia notes that a supermassive black hole's average density, measured within its event horizon, can be very low. By my own rough calculation, a black hole of a few solar masses would have an average density in that range, but no source I found says so. The claim seems to borrow a neutron-star figure, and the black-hole version isn't confirmed or clearly refuted.

text: Sharks have been on the planet longer than trees, with the earliest known shark-like species dating back to around 440 million years ago.
label: supported
reason: Sources say sharks are older than trees. EarthDate says the oldest shark-like scales are up to about 455 million years old, Ordovician in age, and the oldest known tree, Archaeopteris, dates to about 385 million years ago. Another source says shark ancestors appeared around 450 million years ago and describes sharks as existing since about 440 million years ago. Exact estimates vary between roughly 440 and 455 million years ago, but that fits the claim's approximate date of around 440 million years ago.

text: A giant squid's eyes are said to be the largest of any animal, with some specimens having eyes that are up to 27 centimeters, or roughly 11 inches, in diameter.
label: supported
reason: The 27 cm (11 in) figure is supported. Wikipedia-derived sources, such as Animalia and the Architeuthis entry, say the giant squid has eyes up to at least 27 cm (11 in) across. They describe these as the largest eyes of any living creature except perhaps the colossal squid. Other sources simply say the giant squid has the largest eyes of any animal, so the claim's hedged wording, 'are said to be,' holds up. One caveat: several sources (IFAW, Mission Blue, Wikipedia's colossal squid article) give the record for largest eyes to the colossal squid, also at about 27 cm. That makes 'largest' a softer point, but the claim only says the giant squid's eyes are 'said to be' the largest.

text: Tarantulas can live up to 20-30 years in captivity, with some species reportedly living into their 40s.
label: supported
reason: Several sources agree that female tarantulas often live 20–30 years in captivity. The Tarantula Collective says lifespans of 20–30 years refer almost always to females, and it gives 25–30 years in captivity for species such as the Mexican red knee. A-Z Animals puts the typical range at 10–30 years. It adds that some females have been reported living almost 40 years and in exceptional cases more than 40, and it cites claims of Brachypelma hamorii females living up to 40 years. The claim says the 40s are only 'reportedly' reached, which matches the evidence. Still, those 40-plus figures come from popular sources, not documented records. The famous 43-year-old spider, 'Number 16', was a wild trapdoor spider, not a tarantula, and Wikipedia says the earlier record holder was a 28-year-old tarantula.

text: Tarantulas have been around for a long time, with fossil records showing they've remained largely unchanged for over 120 million years.
label: contradicted
reason: The fossil part of the claim doesn't hold up. Molecular dating studies (reported by Phys.org, Live Science and Smithsonian) estimate that tarantulas first appeared about 120 million years ago. That figure comes from phylogenetic modeling, not from fossils. The oldest known theraphosid (tarantula) fossil is in Burmese amber dated to about 100 million years ago, according to the Journal of Biogeography and Live Science. Texas Parks & Wildlife Magazine says fossil records show tarantulas have been 'virtually unchanged' for more than 20 million years, not 120 million. Tarantulas are ancient, but the fossil record does not show them largely unchanged for over 120 million years.

text: A newborn giraffe is about 6 feet tall and can walk within the first hour of its birth.
label: supported
reason: Several sources agree that a newborn giraffe calf is about 6 feet (1.8 m) tall and can stand and walk within about an hour of being born. Some say it can walk within 30 minutes. None of the results contradict the claim. The sources are savegiraffesnow.org, africafreak.com, animalfactsencyclopedia.com and storyteller.travel.

text: Honeybees are able to fly by using their wings to generate electricity, known as triboelectrification, and then use that electricity to attract pollen and other particles to themselves.
label: contradicted
reason: Bees do pick up static charge while flying (triboelectric charging from friction with the air), and that charge helps pollen stick to their bodies. Science Friday describes a bee's hairs becoming positively charged as it flaps its wings, which attracts pollen. But the claim gets the cause backwards: bees do not fly by generating electricity. Flight comes from the aerodynamic lift and thrust of flapping wings, and the charge is only a side effect of flying. Since the core claim about how bees fly is false, the statement is contradicted.

text: Plants are capable of producing sounds when they experience stress or injury, which researchers have found can range in frequency from 10-240 Hz.
label: contradicted
reason: Research does show that stressed plants make sounds, but the frequency range in the claim is wrong. The main study (Khait et al., 2023, published in Cell) recorded drought-stressed and cut tomato and tobacco plants. Their sounds were ultrasonic clicks, mostly between about 40 and 80 kHz, with a measured range of roughly 20–100 kHz. That is far above 10–240 Hz and beyond what humans can hear. Reports from Smithsonian, Scientific American and Sci.News give the same figures. I found no source saying stress-induced plant sounds fall in the 10–240 Hz range.

text: Honey Never Spoils, as Archaeologists have found pots of honey in ancient Egyptian tombs that are over 3,000 years old and still perfectly edible.
label: supported
reason: Many sources, including History Facts and coverage that draws on Smithsonian Magazine, report that archaeologists found pots of honey in ancient Egyptian tombs that were more than 3,000 years old and still edible. The same sources say honey resists spoiling because it has little water, is highly acidic and contains natural hydrogen peroxide. A caveat applies: the edibility reports are mostly popular retellings rather than lab tests, and honey can ferment if it absorbs moisture, so 'never spoils' really means 'when properly sealed.' None of the sources I found contradicted the claim.

text: A surge of water treetops high would in one minute consume all oxygen from air for two human lives' requirements for over 30 years.
label: not_verifiable
reason: I couldn't find any source that makes or supports this claim. My searches only returned general facts about how much oxygen trees produce and how much fires use. None of them said that a treetop-high surge of water uses up oxygen. Floodwater doesn't burn oxygen from the air the way fire does, so the claim may be a garbled version of a statistic about a wildfire or a 'wall of flame.' I couldn't confirm that either, because the search tool hit its usage limit before I could check the fire version. With no direct evidence for or against the exact claim, the verdict is inconclusive.

text: It is estimated that about 75% of a Sahara Desert storm's particles are transported across the Atlantic Ocean and reach Central and South America.
label: contradicted
reason: NASA's Goddard Scientific Visualization Studio, backed up by Wikipedia's Saharan Air Layer article, says winds carry only about 20% of a Saharan storm's dust out over the Atlantic. Of that, about 20%, or roughly 4% of a single storm's dust, makes it all the way to the western Atlantic. The rest settles into the ocean or is washed out by rain. That is far below the claimed 75%.

text: New York City's famous Grand Central Terminal has a secret train platform, known as Track 61, hidden beneath the Waldorf Astoria Hotel.
label: supported
reason: Wikipedia's Track 61 article says the platform is beneath the Waldorf Astoria New York, in an underground storage yard northeast of Grand Central Terminal, and that it is part of the Grand Central Terminal complex. Other sources, such as Gothamist and CNN, also call it a secret platform under the Waldorf-Astoria. The only nuance is that the track is in an adjacent storage yard rather than the main terminal, but it is still part of the Grand Central complex, so the claim holds.

text: Scientists estimate that there may be between 700,000 and 1 million species on Earth that have not yet been discovered or classified.
label: contradicted
reason: The best-known scientific estimate (Mora et al. 2011, PLoS Biology) puts the total number of eukaryotic species at about 8.7 million (range 7.4–10 million). Only about 1.2 million of these have been described, so roughly 86% of land species and 91% of marine species are still unidentified. That leaves around 7.5 million species undiscovered, far more than the claim's 700,000 to 1 million. The 700,000–1 million figure does not match mainstream estimates of undiscovered species on Earth.

text: Walking on water is possible for certain animals like the Basilisk lizard and some insects due to the surface tension of the water and their unique physical characteristics.
label: contradicted
reason: Some animals can indeed walk on water. Small insects such as water striders do it because of surface tension. But the claim also says surface tension explains the basilisk lizard, and that part is wrong. Physics World says basilisks are 'much too heavy to be supported by surface tension.' A PNAS study shows they stay up by quickly slapping and stroking the water with their large feet, which produces enough force to hold them up.

text: Water can boil without bubbling if boiled in a vacuum or when extremely pure, a process known as "silent boiling."
label: contradicted
reason: Reliable sources contradict the claim. Wikipedia's Superheating article says very pure water heated past its boiling point in a smooth container does not boil. This is called superheating, also known as "boiling delay" or "boiling retardation." The water simply sits there without bubbling and may later erupt violently. That is a failure to boil, not a quiet form of boiling. Wikipedia's Boiling article defines boiling as vapour bubbles forming inside the liquid. Water in a vacuum boils at a lower temperature and still produces vigorous bubbles. No authoritative source recognizes "silent boiling" as the name for this. The term only shows up on a low-quality food blog, which treats it as the same thing as film boiling, an unrelated phenomenon.

text: Plants can make sounds, such as hissing and squeaking, when their stems and leaves experience stress or damage.
label: supported
reason: Reputable sources confirm the main point of the claim. Reporting from London's Natural History Museum and Science News Explores on a 2023 study in the journal Cell says tomato and tobacco plants made airborne sounds when they were dehydrated or had their stems cut. The study also recorded sounds from other plants, including corn, wheat, grape and cactus. The descriptions are not an exact match, though. The study and most coverage call the sounds ultrasonic 'pops' or 'clicks', too high-pitched for people to hear. Some outlets, such as Live Science, describe stressed plants as 'squealing', but no source I found uses the word 'hissing'. Also, the study tested stem cutting and drought, not leaf damage. Because plants do make sounds under stress and damage, I rated the claim supported, but the specific sound words are loose.

text: Caterpillars can eat up to 27,000 times their body weight in a single day, which is equivalent to a human eating around 44,000 pizzas.
label: contradicted
reason: Several sources give the 27,000-times-body-weight figure, but they say it applies to the caterpillar's whole larval stage, not to a single day. The Naked Scientists says caterpillars eat this much over the roughly 4 weeks they spend as caterpillars. 13abc says some eat this much before they pupate three to four weeks after hatching, and KidsKonnect calls it a lifetime total. Only one low-quality page (statustest.amherst.edu) says 'in a single day', which conflicts with the more reliable sources. I found nothing to back up the comparison to a human eating 44,000 pizzas. Because the time frame is wrong, the claim is contradicted.

text: Tarantulas have been on Earth for a long time, with fossil evidence showing that they existed over 100 million years ago during the Cretaceous period.
label: supported
reason: A 2023 paper in the Journal of Biogeography (Wiley) includes the oldest known theraphosid (tarantula) fossil, preserved in Burmese amber and dated to about 100 million years ago (Wunderlich & Müller, 2020). Live Science also reports a Myanmar amber tarantula fossil of about 100 million years old, which falls in the Cretaceous. Molecular dating puts the group's origin at about 120 million years ago, in the mid-Cretaceous. One caveat: the fossil is dated to roughly 100 million years, so 'over' 100 million is a slight stretch, but the core claim of Cretaceous-age fossil tarantulas holds up.

text: A new discovery in a network of underwater caves in Mexico revealed the bones of an enormous Ice Age creature known as the Short-Faced Bear whose species became extinct about 11,000 years ago.
label: supported
reason: Several outlets, including Live Science, Smithsonian, ScienceAlert, Gizmodo and ABC News, reported in 2019 that divers found bones of the short-faced bear Arctotherium wingei in Hoyo Negro. Hoyo Negro is a flooded pit in the Sac Actun underwater cave system on Mexico's Yucatán Peninsula. The coverage calls the bears Ice Age 'giant meat eaters' and dates the bones to the Late Pleistocene, about 11,300 years ago. That fits a species that died out roughly 11,000 years ago, though none of the sources I found gives an extinction date directly. 'Enormous' is a stretch for a bear of about 150 kg, but the reporting itself describes it as 'giant.' Nothing I found contradicts the claim.

text: Honey Never Spoils, Archaeologists have found pots of honey in ancient Egyptian tombs that are over 3,000 years old and still perfectly edible
label: supported
reason: I found several sources saying archaeologists discovered pots of honey in ancient Egyptian tombs that were about 3,000 years old and still safe to eat. They include History Facts, My Modern Met and Dallas Express, along with other outlets. They also explain that honey's low moisture and high acidity keep it from spoiling. These are mostly popular-science sites rather than primary archaeological reports, and some say the honey must be well sealed to last that long. Even so, no reliable source I found contradicts the claim.

text: Scientists believe that there are approximately 8.7 million identified species on Earth, but the estimated total number, including those that have not been discovered, is thought to be around 30 million.
label: contradicted
reason: The claim gets the numbers wrong. The 8.7 million figure from Mora et al. (2011, PLoS Biology) is the estimated total number of species on Earth, including ones not yet discovered. It is not the number already identified. Only about 1.2 to 2 million species have been described; the study itself notes that only about 953,000 of an estimated 7.77 million animal species have been catalogued. The study does not support a total of around 30 million either, and earlier estimates ranged from 3 million to 100 million.

text: A lump of pure gold the size of a matchbox can be flattened into a sheet the size of a tennis court.
label: supported
reason: Several sources describe this exact fact, and a quick calculation backs it up. A fact-check post rates it "True" because gold is malleable enough to be beaten into translucent sheets, and trivia sites such as thefactbase and funfactz repeat it. These are not highly authoritative sources, but more reputable gold references give the underlying figure: about 1 gram of gold can be beaten into roughly 1 m², or an ounce into about 300 sq ft (hypertextbook, a gold dealer's fact list). A matchbox holds about 20–30 cm³, which is roughly 400–600 g of gold. At that rate it would cover about 400 m² or more, larger than a doubles tennis court (about 261 m²). The resulting sheet would be about 0.1 µm thick, which is within what gold leaf can reach.

text: High-speed camera footage revealed that a mantis shrimp can accelerate its claws at the speed of a .22 caliber bullet when attacking prey.
label: supported
reason: Several sources say Sheila Patek's group recorded the mantis shrimp's strike with high-speed cameras and found it reaches the acceleration of a .22 caliber bullet. ScienceBlog says Patek's group published the first proper high-speed footage of the strike in 2004, and other sources say the same. The research compares the acceleration, not the speed: a .22 bullet travels much faster than the shrimp's appendage. The claim's wording, 'accelerate its claws at the speed of', is loose but conveys the acceleration comparison. Strictly, the appendage is a raptorial club rather than a claw, but the claim's main point holds.

text: Honeybees are able to fly by using electricity generated from the movement of their wings and bodies.
label: contradicted
reason: Scientific sources say honeybees fly using their flight muscles and wing aerodynamics, not electricity. A PNAS study found that bees stay aloft with short-amplitude, high-frequency wing strokes that create lift, and their thorax muscles drive the wings. Bees do pick up an electrostatic charge as they fly, but that charge is a side effect (it helps with things like pollen sticking to them). It doesn't power or enable flight.

text: Honeybees are able to fly by using electrostatic charges to help lift and propel themselves through the air.
label: contradicted
reason: A peer-reviewed PNAS study (Altshuler et al., 2005) shows that honeybees fly using aerodynamic forces. Their wings make short, very fast strokes (about 90° at roughly 230 Hz), producing lift through mechanisms such as leading-edge vortices. Bees do pick up a slight positive static charge as they fly, but that charge helps pollen stick to their bodies and lets them sense electric fields around flowers. It does not lift or push them through the air. The claim confuses a side effect of flight with how bees actually fly.

text: Humans and dolphins are the only mammals known to give names to themselves and each other.
label: contradicted
reason: A 2024 study in Nature Ecology & Evolution found that African elephants call each other by individual, name-like calls and respond to their own. That means humans and dolphins are not the only mammals known to use names for one another. Elephants are reportedly the first non-human animals found to use names that are not imitations of the recipient's own call, which dolphins do. Marmosets have also been reported to use name-like calls.

text: Members of the smallest primate species, the pygmy mouse lemur, are about the size of a human thumb and weigh approximately 30 grams.
label: contradicted
reason: The claim doesn't hold up for the species it names. The pygmy mouse lemur is Microcebus myoxinus, also called Peters' mouse lemur. Sources describe it as weighing 43–55 g and as the second-smallest mouse lemur, not the smallest primate. The smallest primate is generally given as Madame Berthe's mouse lemur (Microcebus berthae), which weighs about 30 g. The claim appears to apply that species' title and weight to the wrong animal. Some informal sources do use the two names loosely.

text: Owens Falls in Idaho, USA holds the Guinness World Record for the world's shortest known waterfall with a total height of just 10 feet.
label: not_verifiable
reason: I found no trustworthy source that mentions a waterfall called "Owens Falls" in Idaho. Searches for that name in Idaho only returned unrelated results, such as businesses and the Owens Lights holiday display in Idaho Falls. I also found no Guinness World Records listing for a "shortest waterfall" category. Guinness has records for the widest waterfall (Khône Falls) and the tallest single drop (Angel Falls), and the Roe River's "shortest river" record was dropped in 2006, but none of these involve Owens Falls. A few low-quality sites make different "shortest waterfall" claims that don't hold up, including one calling Italy's Cascata delle Marmore about 2 feet tall, when it is actually about 165 m. Since there is no reliable evidence either confirming or directly refuting the claim, it can't be verified.

text: Turtles have an innate navigational ability that allows them to migrate thousands of miles each year and still return to their birthplace to lay eggs.
label: supported
reason: Wikipedia's article on sea turtle migration supports the main points of the claim. It says sea turtles can travel up to 10,000 miles or more per year, often covering thousands of kilometres between feeding and nesting sites. It says females return to the beach where they hatched to lay eggs. It also says hatchlings have an innate navigational behaviour, while adults may also navigate using learned features of the magnetic field. Two caveats: the claim says 'turtles' in general, but this evidence is about sea turtles, and individual females usually nest every few years rather than every year. Even so, the overall claim matches the evidence.

text: A blue whale's heartbeat can be as loud as 188 decibels, louder than a jet taking off.
label: contradicted
reason: The 188 dB figure belongs to the blue whale's call, not its heartbeat. Enchanted Learning and Wikipedia's list of whale vocalizations both give 188 decibels (re 1 µPa at 1 m) as the upper source level of blue whale vocalizations, the low-frequency calls that can travel hundreds of miles underwater. Enchanted Learning compares that call with a jet at about 140 dB. Neither source says a heartbeat reaches that loudness. The claim takes a real figure about the whale's call and wrongly applies it to the heartbeat.

text: Astronauts cannot cry in the classical sense while in space because their tears do not fall downwards due to the lack of gravity.
label: supported
reason: Several sources, including Space.com coverage of Chris Hadfield's video and a Futurism article, describe the same thing: in microgravity, the eyes still make tears, but the tears don't fall. Instead they collect as a liquid ball on the eye. Futurism concludes that astronauts 'technically can't cry' in the usual sense. Other sources say astronauts 'can cry, but the tears don't fall,' which is the same idea and matches the claim's 'in the classical sense' wording. Strictly, the tears don't fall because of microgravity (free fall) rather than an absence of gravity, but sources commonly describe it as weightlessness, so this doesn't change the verdict.

text: Astronauts cannot cry in the same way as people on Earth because the absence of gravity in space affects the flow of tears.
label: supported
reason: Space.com describes Canadian astronaut Chris Hadfield's video showing that astronauts' eyes still produce tears in space but that "tears don't fall." Instead, the water collects as a ball on the eye, because tears only run down the face on Earth due to gravity. ScienceABC agrees that astronauts can cry but the tears don't fall. So crying in space works differently from crying on Earth because of microgravity, which matches the claim.

text: Butterfly species have been around for over 200 million years, long before dinosaurs existed on Earth.
label: contradicted
reason: Butterflies are not more than 200 million years old, and they did not exist before dinosaurs. A 2023 study in Nature Ecology & Evolution found that butterflies first appeared about 100–101 million years ago, in the mid-Cretaceous, when dinosaurs were already alive. Dinosaurs date back roughly 230 million years. The oldest known Lepidoptera fossils, from the wider moth lineage, are about 200 million years old, but true butterflies appeared much later.

text: Firefighters used a technique called a "firebreak" to contain and extinguish the Great Fire of London in 1666.
label: supported
reason: Reliable sources say firebreaks were used against the Great Fire of London. Wikipedia describes making firebreaks by removing buildings in the fire's path as the main firefighting technique of the time. It also credits the Tower of London garrison's use of gunpowder to create effective firebreaks, together with the dropping east wind, with halting the fire. The London Gazette likewise says houses were pulled down with firehooks or blown up with explosives to create firebreaks. One caveat: the people doing this were soldiers, officials and citizens, not a modern fire service, and the falling wind was also a key factor.

text: France and the United States are the two countries with the most time zones, with a total of 12 time zones each.
label: contradicted
reason: The claim is wrong about the United States. France does lead with 12 time zones (13 if you count its Antarctic claim), but the United States has 11, not 12. That puts the US in a tie with Russia for second place, so France and the US are not tied at 12 each.

text: Honeybees are able to fly by using their wings to generate electricity through a process known as "triboelectric charging."
label: contradicted
reason: Honeybees fly by aerodynamics. Rapid wingbeats, how the wings move, and strong thorax muscles produce lift. Electricity is not what keeps them in the air. Bees do pick up an electrostatic charge through triboelectric (friction) charging as they fly, but that charge is a side effect, and research links it to things like pollination. No source found says bees use their wings to make electricity in order to fly, so the claim gets the mechanism wrong.

text: Owens Falls Dam, located in Uganda, is considered the original source of the Nile River.
label: contradicted
reason: The sources contradict this claim. Ripon Falls, not Owen Falls Dam, was traditionally considered the source of the Nile. Speke identified Ripon Falls, the outlet of Lake Victoria, as the river's source. Owen Falls Dam (now Nalubaale) was built near Jinja, Uganda, between the early 1950s and 1954. It is not the original source. Its construction submerged Ripon Falls. The dam's location in Uganda is correct, and it sits near the Nile's outlet from Lake Victoria.

text: Seals and sea lions can slow down their heart rate dramatically to help conserve energy and oxygen while they are underwater.
label: supported
reason: Research in the Journal of Experimental Biology shows that diving mammals, sea lions included, lower their heart rate underwater (bradycardia) to save the oxygen stored in their blood. On long dives, sea lion heart rates fell as low as 6 beats per minute, which counts as a dramatic slowdown. This dive response is also well documented in seals, so the claim holds for both animals.

text: An iceberg contains approximately 7-10% of its mass above the water's surface, while the remaining 90-93% is submerged.
label: supported
reason: The sources I found give the standard figure of about one-tenth of an iceberg above water and about 90% below. Wikipedia says "typically about one-tenth of the volume of an iceberg is above water," and several educational sites describe the same 10/90 split. The claim's ranges (7–10% above, 90–93% below) match this approximate figure. The sources don't state a 7% figure directly, and they describe the split by volume rather than mass. For an object that floats, though, the fraction below water by volume equals the ratio of its density to the water's density (roughly 917/1025, or about 89–90%). On that basis the claim fits the evidence.

text: A blue whale's heartbeat can be heard for hundreds of miles underwater, and a single beat can be as long as two minutes.
label: contradicted
reason: Both parts of the claim are wrong. NOAA Fisheries says a blue whale's heartbeat can be heard about 2 miles away, not hundreds of miles. The second part is also false. Research by Goldbogen et al. (2019) found that during dives a blue whale's heart rate drops to about 2 beats per minute at its lowest. That means beats come about 30 seconds apart. A single beat does not last two minutes.

text: Harnessing the geothermal energy from beneath Yellowstone National Park could provide enough power to meet the electricity needs of the entire United States.
label: supported
reason: Several sources back the claim. National Geographic reports that experts agree Yellowstone holds enough geothermal energy to power the entire country, and its headline says it could power the entire continental U.S. An American Bar Association article cites peer-reviewed research (Renewable Energy, 2022) suggesting Yellowstone's geothermal energy alone could power the whole nation for centuries. Construction Physics, discussing NASA JPL's thought experiment, also says the electricity could be enough for the entire US. Development is legally barred and technically speculative, but those limits don't conflict with the claim that it 'could' meet national needs.

text: Humans share about 60% of DNA with fruit flies, highlighting the shared genetic ancestry among different species.
label: supported
reason: NHGRI (genome.gov) reports that comparing the fruit fly and human genomes found about 60% of genes are conserved between the two, which it describes as a shared core set of genes. ASU's Ask A Biologist and other sources also give the figure as about 60% of DNA. Strictly speaking, the scientific measure is about 60% of genes being conserved, not 60% of all DNA. Still, the claim matches widely reported figures and the idea of shared ancestry it describes.

text: Plants can grow in mid-air, without soil, using a process known as hydroponic growth or aeroponic growth.
label: supported
reason: Reliable sources, including a US patent document on aeroponic systems, describe aeroponics as growing plants "in an air or mist environment without the use of soil." They describe hydroponics as soilless growing that uses water as the medium. Together this backs the claim that plants can be grown without soil, and with roots suspended in air in the aeroponic case. The phrase "mid-air" fits aeroponics more than hydroponics, but the claim lists the two as alternatives, so this doesn't make it wrong.

text: Spiders have been around for a long time, with fossil evidence showing they existed at least 318 million years ago.
label: not_verifiable
reason: Reliable sources agree that spiders are ancient and that the oldest true spider fossils come from the Carboniferous. However, I couldn't find a source that gives the specific figure of at least 318 million years. The dates I found are lower or less specific: Guinness and Wikipedia put the earliest fossil spiders at about 300 million years ago, Scientific American and the Royal Society paper cite fossils about 305 million years old, and Germany's oldest spider fossil, Arthrolycosa wolterbeeki, is dated to 310–315 million years ago. Wikipedia also mentions an older claimed spider, Attercopus, at 380 million years, and a molecular-clock estimate that spiders split from other chelicerates 375–328 million years ago, but these are a disputed claim and a genetic estimate, not confirmed fossils. Because no source confirms or clearly rules out the 318-million-year figure, the claim is inconclusive.

text: Tarantulas have been on Earth for a long time, with fossil evidence showing they existed over 100 million years ago during the Cretaceous period.
label: supported
reason: The Journal of Biogeography (Wiley) study calls a Burmese amber specimen 'the oldest theraphosid fossil,' dated to about 100 million years ago in the Cretaceous (Wunderlich & Müller, 2020). Live Science also reports a Myanmar amber tarantula fossil about 100 million years old. Molecular dating studies (PeerJ, as covered by SciTechDaily and Big Think) put the origin of tarantulas at about 120 million years ago, also in the Cretaceous. One caveat: the fossil is dated to roughly 100 million years, so the word 'over' is loose. The 120-million-year figure comes from genetic dating, not from a fossil. A hobbyist site (birdspiders.ch) says there is no evidence of tarantulas before 65 million years ago, but it is less authoritative and appears outdated. Overall, the claim is substantially supported.

text: Tarantulas have been on Earth for a long time, with fossil evidence showing they existed over 100 million years ago, during the Cretaceous period.
label: supported
reason: Live Science, reporting on a phylogenetic study, says one of the two known tarantula fossils is preserved in amber from Myanmar and is about 100 million years old. The same study dates the origin of tarantulas to the Cretaceous period, around 120 million years ago. This backs the claim that tarantulas have existed for a very long time, going back to the Cretaceous. One caveat: Burmese amber is usually dated to about 99 million years, so 'over 100 million years' is a slight rounding of the fossil's age.

text: Humans share about 50-60% of their DNA with bananas.
label: contradicted
reason: The figure is real but the claim misreads it. Expert-sourced explainers from IFLScience and HowStuffWorks say the 50–60% number comes from a 2013 NHGRI comparison. It means about 60% of human genes have a recognizable counterpart in the banana genome. It does not mean that 50–60% of human DNA is shared. Genes make up only a small part of the genome, so the overlap is about 1–2% of human DNA. Even those matching genes encode proteins that are only about 40% identical. A geneticist quoted by HowStuffWorks says we share about 50% of our genes with bananas, 'which turns out to be only about 1 percent of our DNA'. IFLScience says nearly every part of the 60%-of-DNA claim is 'technically incorrect'. A Malaysian fact-check site (The Star) rates the claim TRUE, but its own explanation agrees that it's about 60% of genes, or roughly 1–2% of the genome. So the claim as worded, about DNA, is contradicted.

text: Humans and elephants share a similar rate of gestation, with human pregnancies lasting approximately 280 days and elephant pregnancies lasting almost two years, around 640-660 days.
label: contradicted
reason: The figures in the claim are right, but they disprove its main point. Live Science gives elephant gestation as about 640–660 days (roughly 95 weeks) and human pregnancy as about 280 days (40 weeks). It contrasts the two and notes that elephants have the longest gestation of any mammal. Since elephant pregnancies last more than twice as long as human ones, saying the two species 'share a similar rate of gestation' is false.

text: Honeybees are able to fly by using their wings to create a whirlpool of air above and below them, which generates lift and allows them to hover and maneuver.
label: supported
reason: Scientific American's article on the research into honeybee flight says honeybees flap and rotate their wings about 240 times a second. Together with the flexible wings, this lets them create a vortex (a whirlpool of air) that lifts them into the air, and it allows them to stay aloft and produce extra lift when needed. That matches the claim's main point that bees generate lift by creating swirling air. The detail 'above and below them' is loose popular wording rather than an exact description, since the lift-producing vortex forms along the wing's leading edge, but it does not contradict the claim.

text: France and the United States share the only international border that is to the north and south poles, due to their claims to the region surrounding the geographic North Pole and South Pole.
label: contradicted
reason: The claim is false. Seven countries claim territory in Antarctica: Chile, Argentina, the UK, Norway, Australia, New Zealand and France. The United States is not one of them; it has made no claim and has only reserved the right to make one. So the US has no claim near the South Pole, and France and the US cannot share a border there. Neither country claims the area around the geographic North Pole either, which sits on international Arctic Ocean waters. No 'polar' border between France and the US exists.

text: Bernard Bartalan, an Austrian-language teacher, holds the Guinness World Record for the longest duration without sleep, staying awake for 264.4 hours (11 days) in 1964.
label: contradicted
reason: The 264.4-hour (about 11-day) record from 1963–64 was set by Randy Gardner, a 17-year-old high school student from San Diego, California. It was not set by an Austrian-language teacher called Bernard Bartalan. Wikipedia also describes Gardner as having "once held" the record, which suggests it is no longer a current Guinness-recognised record.

text: A blue whale can hold its breath for approximately 20 minutes while underwater.
label: supported
reason: Several sources say blue whales usually hold their breath for about 20 minutes. A scientist answering on I'm a Scientist wrote that blue whales "usually hold their breath for about 20 minutes," and a whale-watching operator gives a typical range of 15–20 minutes, with occasional dives of up to 35. Britannica says blue whales dive for up to 30 minutes, which still fits a typical breath-hold of about 20 minutes. No source contradicts the claim.

text: A blue whale's heartbeat is so loud that it can be detected from over 500 miles away, and is louder than any other animal's or most natural events.
label: contradicted
reason: NOAA Fisheries and other sources say a blue whale's heartbeat can be heard or detected about 2 miles away, not more than 500 miles. The 500+ mile figure seems to come from blue whale calls, not heartbeats. Since the main distance claim is wrong, the claim is contradicted, and nothing found supports the part saying it is louder than any other animal or most natural events.

text: Astronauts cannot cry in the classical sense in space due to the lack of gravity, which prevents tears from rolling down their faces.
label: supported
reason: Several sources, including Space.com, ScienceABC and Futurism, describe Chris Hadfield's demonstration on the ISS. In microgravity, tears still form, but they don't run down the face. Instead they collect in a liquid ball on the eye. Futurism concludes that astronauts 'technically can't cry' in the usual sense. This matches the claim's point that weightlessness keeps tears from rolling down the face. Other sources make clear that crying itself still happens, which fits the claim's 'in the classical sense' wording.

text: Black bears are excellent climbers and have been known to climb trees to escape danger, protect themselves from extreme weather conditions, or even to hibernate during the winter months.
label: supported
reason: Every part of the claim is backed by reliable sources. Vermont Fish & Wildlife says black bears climb trees to escape danger, and the University of Arkansas Extension calls tree climbing "second nature" to them. On weather, the North American Bear Center (bear.org) says black bears often climb trees during thunderstorms, and the Arkansas publication notes that bears in bottomland hardwood areas den in raised tree cavities to escape seasonal flooding. On hibernation, the National Park Service says many Great Smoky Mountains bears den high up in standing hollow trees, and NC State Extension and Alaska Fish & Game also report dens in tree cavities or hollow trees. No source contradicts the claim.

text: Black bears are excellent climbers and have been known to climb trees to escape danger, protect themselves from extreme weather, and even hibernate.
label: supported
reason: Reliable wildlife-agency sources back each part of the claim. Vermont Fish & Wildlife says black bears climb trees to feed and to escape danger, and the American Bear Association says mother bears teach their cubs to climb trees for safety. The National Park Service says black bears den in the winter to get away from the cold, using hollow trees or spots high in trees. It also notes that bears in the Great Smoky Mountains often den high above the ground in standing hollow trees. Research on southern Appalachian dens found that most were in tree cavities high above the ground. Alaska and Maine have also documented black bear dens in trees. The weather part is supported through tree denning to escape the cold, not as a general habit of climbing to shelter from weather. Technically, black bears enter torpor rather than true hibernation, but that is common wording and does not contradict the claim.

text: Securitas Express is a unique form of robust and tamper-proof overnight postal service that originated in medieval Sweden in 1636.
label: contradicted
reason: I found no evidence of a 1636 Swedish postal service called "Securitas Express". Sweden's 1636 postal service was Kungliga Postverket (the Royal Postal Agency), set up by Axel Oxenstierna, which later became Posten / PostNord Sverige. Securitas AB is a modern Swedish security company, not a 17th-century postal service. Also, 1636 falls in Sweden's Great Power era, not the medieval period. My last search on "Securitas Express" itself didn't run because the search limit was reached. Still, the sources found attribute the 1636 founding to a different organization, so the claim looks like a mix-up of unrelated facts.

text: Galileo Galilei was the first person to observe the planet Neptune using a telescope, but he didn't recognize it as a planet and thought it was a star, in 1612.
label: supported
reason: Reliable sources back the claim. Scientific American says Galileo first saw Neptune in 1612 and thought it was a fixed star, 234 years before it was identified as a planet. Astronomy.com says his telescope sketches from December 1612 to January 1613 show Neptune, that he seems to have mistaken it for a star, and that he may have been the first to spot it. A 2009 hypothesis by David Jamieson suggests Galileo may have noticed that it moved. However, Astronomy.com says the available evidence indicates he probably did not realise it was a planet, so this does not undercut the claim.

text: Content navigation platform, Pinterest, was initially named "Tote."
label: supported
reason: The sources back the claim, though "initially named" is a loose way to put it. Wikipedia says Pinterest grew out of an earlier app called Tote, made by Ben Silbermann and Paul Sciarra. Startup Grind and Fast Company say the same, describing Tote as their first product, a mobile shopping app. Other sources say outright that "Pinterest began as a mobile shopping app called Tote." Strictly speaking, Tote was a separate earlier product that the company moved away from, not just Pinterest under an older name. Still, the origin story is well documented and no source contradicts it.

text: Denmark is home to the oldest amusement park in the world, Bakken, which has been in operation since 1583.
label: supported
reason: Several sources describe Bakken (Dyrehavsbakken), just north of Copenhagen, as the world's oldest operating amusement park, dating back to 1583. That year a natural spring was found in Dyrehaven, and the site grew into a fairground from there. This matches the claim.

text: Giraffes are the only animals born with their eyes open, this helps them to quickly adapt and defend themselves from predators in their surroundings.
label: contradicted
reason: The claim says giraffes are the only animals born with their eyes open, and that is false. Oxford Reference defines precocial mammals as young born with their eyes and ears open, and gives cattle, sheep and horses as examples. Merriam-Webster also says hares are born with their eyes open. Giraffe calves are precocial, but many other animals are too, so the 'only animals' part is wrong.

text: Tweeting birds and specifically, the Northern Cardinal, are known for complex songs with up to 200 different melodies.
label: contradicted
reason: Ornithology sources describe the Northern Cardinal as having a small song repertoire, nowhere near 200 melodies. Birds of the World (Cornell Lab) reports that males use 9–14 syllable types and 8–10 commonly used song types. A University of Cincinnati study recorded individual repertoires of only about 7–9 song types. The ScienceDirect topic page calls cardinal song 'relatively simple', made from 8–21 syllables. The 'up to 200 different melodies' figure is therefore contradicted.

text: tasar Himb Again is the highest peak in the solar system, standing at a height of approximately 27 km, and it is located on Mars.
label: not_verifiable
reason: I couldn't find any feature called "tasar Himb Again" on Mars or anywhere else in the solar system. A search for the name only turned up the Tarsar Marsar trek in Kashmir, so the name has no clear referent. The tallest peak in the solar system is generally said to be Olympus Mons on Mars, at about 22 km above datum (some figures, measured from the surrounding plains, are closer to 26–27 km). Because the claim gives a garbled or nonexistent name, it can't be matched to Olympus Mons with confidence, and its main subject can't be verified.

text: In New York City, there is a secretly located apartment in the New York Public Library,dımatically decreasing the maintenance  and upkeep cost for the superintendant that is hidden from the public.

reason: There really was a hidden apartment. But the claim speaks in the present tense, and the same source says the last resident custodian retired in 2006 and all the apartments have since been turned to other library uses. I also found nothing showing that the apartment 'dramatically decreased' maintenance and upkeep costs. text: Owens Falls Dam, located on the Niagara River, was the first hydroelectric power plant in the world and was operational in 1895.
label: contradicted
reason: The claim is wrong on location and date. Owen Falls Dam, now called Nalubaale Power Station, sits on the White Nile near Lake Victoria in Uganda, not on the Niagara River. It was finished in 1954, not 1895. That also rules out its being the world's first hydroelectric power plant.

text: A blue whale can drink up to 50 gallons of its mother's milk per day when it's a calf.
label: supported
reason: National Geographic reports that blue whale calves drink 50 gallons (190 liters) of milk a day, and Vice gives the same figure. That matches the claim's 50 gallons per day. One caveat: other sources give higher estimates, including Monterey Bay Aquarium at 100 gallons and some secondary sites at 100–150 gallons. Those figures make the 'up to' upper limit uncertain, but they don't contradict the 50-gallon amount that reputable sources cite.

text: A large percentage of human brains are actually more active and 'right-brained' in both creative, or 'left brained' operations of the brain.
label: contradicted
reason: The claim says a large share of human brains are more active on one side, "right-brained" or "left-brained." A 2013 University of Utah study scanned more than 1,000 brains and found no evidence that people are right-brained or left-brained. Individual networks are lateralized, but people use both hemispheres about equally overall. Science news coverage of the study calls the left/right-brain idea a myth.

text: Aolphin's are known to often carry seaweed in their mouths and rely on it as a form of medical treatment.
label: not_verifiable
reason: "Aolphin's" is most likely a typo for dolphins. The first part of the claim checks out: dolphins have been widely seen carrying and playing with seaweed, including in more than 100 documented events across different populations. The medical part does not. The strongest self-medication evidence (Ziltener et al., reported in Scientific American) involves bottlenose dolphins rubbing against corals and sponges, not seaweed. Researchers only suggest the seaweed behaviour may be playful and could possibly help with skin treatment or parasite removal. Nothing shows that dolphins rely on seaweed as a form of medical treatment, so that part of the claim can't be verified.

text: Honeybees are able to recognize human faces, using the same areas of their brains that humans use for this purpose.
label: contradicted
reason: The research supports the first part: honeybees can learn to recognize human face images. The second part is wrong. Studies such as Avarguès-Weber et al. in the Journal of Experimental Biology found that bees use a similar strategy, configural processing, but they do it with a 'non-specialized brain' that lacks the brain regions humans use for faces, like the fusiform face area. So bees do not use the same brain areas as humans; they reach a similar result with a different brain structure.

text: Tigers have striped skin, not just striped fur, meaning their stripes are also visible when they are shaved.
label: supported
reason: Several sources say tigers' skin has the same stripe pattern as their fur, so a shaved tiger would still show stripes. Most say this happens because pigment in the skin and the dark hair follicles sitting in it show through, a bit like beard stubble. The sources (Biology Insights, QuizzClub, FunFactz and Medium) are popular-science and trivia sites, not peer-reviewed research. Still, they agree with each other and with the widely known fact, and none of the results contradicted the claim.

text: _runner's_ Livermore California has the longest name of any three-syllable city.
label: contradicted
reason: Livermore has three syllables, and its name is 9 letters long. But other three-syllable city names are clearly longer. Syllablecount.com confirms that Charlottesville, Virginia has 3 syllables, and its name is 15 letters long. So Livermore does not have the longest name of any three-syllable city. I found no source that supports the claim.

text: Astronauts cannot cry in space because the microgravity environment prevents tears from flowing downward and out of the eyes.
label: contradicted
reason: The claim is wrong. Astronauts can cry in space. Their eyes still make tears, but in microgravity the tears don't run down the face. Instead they collect as a ball of liquid on the eye. In a video from the ISS, Canadian astronaut Chris Hadfield said "Your eyes will definitely cry in space" and explained that the tears just don't fall. So microgravity changes how tears behave, but it doesn't stop astronauts from crying.

label: not_verifiable

text: Bionic limbs can be controlled directly by the user's thoughts, using electroencephalography (EEG) sensors that read brain signals.
label: supported
reason: Research supports the claim. A peer-reviewed paper in ASTESJ describes a prototype prosthetic arm that is "controlled by the brain commands, obtained from an electroencephalography (EEG) headset". In that design, EEG sensors pick up brain signals, which are processed and turned into arm movements. This shows bionic limbs can be controlled by thought through EEG. One caveat: EEG control is mostly found in research prototypes. Most commercial bionic limbs read muscle signals (EMG) instead.

text: Cheryl Henry, the first captain of the female Marines, later changed her name to Sue Phelan.
label: not_verifiable
reason: I found nothing linking 'Cheryl Henry' to being the first captain of female Marines, or to the name 'Sue Phelan'. Searches for 'Cheryl Henry' turned up unrelated people: an NSWC Dahlgren employee, an actress, and a 1990 Houston homicide victim. Searches for 'Sue Phelan' turned up a ceramic artist and other unrelated people. The Wikipedia pages on women in the US Marine Corps don't mention either name. The search limit was reached before I could try more queries. Because nothing confirms or rules out either part of the claim, it can't be verified.

text: Didaskaleinophobia is a term used to describe a fear of going to school.
label: supported
reason: Several sources, including a hypnotherapy clinic's page and general phobia references, define didaskaleinophobia (also called scolionophobia) as the fear of going to school. This is a widely accepted definition of the term.

text: Dragonflies have existed for over 300 million years, and during the Paleozoic Era, some species had a wingspan of up to two feet.
label: supported
reason: Several sources describe dragonfly-like insects living about 300 million years ago, in the late Paleozoic (Carboniferous–Permian), with very large wings. Arizona State's Ask A Biologist gives wingspans of up to 65 cm, which is a little over two feet. ABC News describes Paleozoic dragonflies with wingspans of about two and a half feet 300 million years ago. So the claim's main points hold: the lineage is about 300 million years old, and some Paleozoic species had wingspans of roughly two feet. One caveat: these giants (Meganeura and its relatives, order Meganisoptera, sometimes called griffinflies) were not true modern dragonflies (order Odonata). They are popularly called giant dragonflies, and some sources put their wingspans a bit above two feet.

text: Giraffes are the only animals born with their eyes open, and they are also able to walk within their first hour of life.
label: contradicted
reason: The claim is false because giraffes are not the only animals born with their eyes open. Oxford Reference defines precocial mammals as young born with their eyes and ears open and able to stand and walk. It names the young of cattle, sheep and horses as examples. A pet site also lists guinea pigs and other animals born with their eyes open. It is true that giraffe calves can walk soon after birth, but the claim's main 'only animals' statement is wrong, so the claim as a whole is contradicted.

text: Honeybees are able to fly by using electricity generated from the friction of their moving wings to attract and propel pollen particles.
label: contradicted
reason: The sources say bees build up a positive electrostatic charge while flying, and that this charge helps pull pollen onto their bodies. They do not say bees use that electricity to fly. Bee flight comes from flapping their wings. The claim reverses cause and effect: the charge is a side effect of flight that helps with pollen collection, not the way bees stay in the air. The charge is also usually said to build up from friction with the air on the bee's body hairs and cuticle, not just from the wings.

text: Jurassic Park novelist Michael Crichton was not only a talented author, but he also held a medical degree from Harvard Medical School.
label: supported
reason: Crichton's official website says he graduated summa cum laude from Harvard College in 1964 and earned his MD from Harvard Medical School in 1969. He wrote novels while he was a medical student, and he went on to write Jurassic Park. The claim that he held a Harvard medical degree is therefore correct, even though he never practised medicine.

text: Roses arranged in a specific pattern in the shape of " corpuscular roses" by Robert Hooke in 1661, were the first object viewed under an improved compound microscope.
label: contradicted
reason: I found no evidence for 'corpuscular roses' or for Hooke arranging roses in 1661. Trusted histories describe Hooke's improved compound microscope work through Micrographia (1665), which covers objects like cork cells and a feather shaft. Its first observation is the point of a needle, not roses. Compound microscopes were also in use decades before Hooke, so roses were not the first object viewed under one. The claim looks made up and conflicts with the documented history.

text: Scientists estimate that there are approximately 8.7 million identified species on Earth, with up to 80% of all species still remaining undiscovered.
label: contradicted
reason: The 8.7 million figure from Mora et al. (2011) is an estimate of all species on Earth, not of identified species. Only about 1.2 million species have been identified and catalogued, which is less than 15% of that estimate. The same study found that more than 80% of species (86% on land, 91% in the ocean) are still undiscovered, so the claim's 'up to 80%' figure is also too low, and calling the 8.7 million 'identified' is wrong.

text: Scientists estimate that there are around 8.7 million identified species on Earth, but the actual number could be as high as 30 million.
label: contradicted
reason: The 8.7 million figure from Mora et al. (2011) is an estimate of all species on Earth, including the ones nobody has found yet. It is not a count of identified species. The study's own breakdown says only about 1.2 million species (for example, about 953,000 animals) have been described and catalogued, and that roughly 86% of land species and 91% of marine species are still undiscovered. Calling 8.7 million 'identified species' gets the study wrong, so the claim is contradicted no matter what upper estimates exist.

text: Scientists estimate that there are around 8.7 million identified species on Earth, but up to 80% of all species remain undiscovered.
label: contradicted
reason: The claim gets the 8.7 million figure wrong. In the 2011 study by Mora and colleagues, 8.7 million (give or take 1.3 million) is the estimated total number of species on Earth, not the number already identified. Only about 1.2 million species have been formally described. The same study found that more than 80% of species are still undiscovered (86% on land and 91% in the oceans), so calling that share 'up to 80%' also understates it.

text: Sweden has the highest number of McDonald's restaurants per capita in Europe, with around 258 locations spread throughout the country.
label: contradicted
reason: Both parts of the claim are wrong. McDonald's own 2023 restaurant count lists 196 locations in Sweden (195 the year before), not 258. Swedish news reports from 2024–25 put the chain's 200th Swedish restaurant at Mall of Scandinavia, so the total is about 200. Sweden also doesn't have the most McDonald's per person in Europe. Visual Capitalist, using McDonald's 2024 restaurant counts, puts France (23.2 per million people), Austria (22.4) and the UK (21.2) ahead of Sweden, which comes out at roughly 19 per million. A few travel blogs repeat the 'most per capita in Europe' line, but the official figures don't back it up.

text: Tarantulas have been on Earth for over 100 million years, with fossil records showing they existed even in the time of the dinosaurs.
label: supported
reason: The search results back the claim. Live Science reports on a PeerJ study that traced tarantula origins to more than 100 million years ago. The same study notes a tarantula fossil preserved in Myanmar amber that is about 100 million years old, which dates to the Cretaceous, when dinosaurs were alive. IFLScience and Big Think report that the dated family tree goes back about 120 million years, to when tarantulas lived alongside dinosaurs. One caveat: the fossil record is sparse (only two known tarantula amber fossils), and the 120-million-year figure comes from molecular dating calibrated with fossils. Still, the claim as stated holds up.

text: giànhamas are a type of Spanish doll; the name 'gingerbread,' referring to some edible mammals, is unknown in that language though.
label: not_verifiable
reason: I couldn't find "giànhamas" as a Spanish doll or as any known term. Searches only turned up generic Spanish doll listings and unrelated "Hama"/Hamas pages, so the main subject has no clear referent. The second part is also muddled: gingerbread is a ginger-flavored cake or cookie, not "edible mammals". Spanish dictionaries (Cambridge, SpanishDict) translate it as "pan de jengibre", so the idea is familiar in Spanish even though the English word isn't used. With no identifiable subject and a garbled premise, I can't support or contradict the claim.

text: oplAnimationFrame is an online database which contains details of numerous animated films and television shows.
label: not_verifiable
reason: I found no source showing that an online database called "oplAnimationFrame" exists. Searches for the name returned only programming material about animation-frame callbacks, such as JavaScript's requestAnimationFrame and onAnimationFrame methods. Real animation databases like The Big Cartoon DataBase and TMDB came up, but none of them is called oplAnimationFrame. Since the name has no clear match, the claim can't be confirmed or disproven.

text: Bernard Bartalan, an Austrian-language teacher, holds the Guinness World Record for the longest duration without sleep, staying awake for a total of 264.4 hours (or 11 days).
label: contradicted
reason: The 264.4-hour (about 11 days and 25 minutes) record belongs to Randy Gardner, a 17-year-old American high school student from San Diego who set it in 1963–64. It was not set by anyone called "Bernard Bartalan," and I found no source that mentions such a person in connection with this record. Wikipedia also notes that Guinness's own record was 276 hours, set by Toimi Silvo in Finland. Several sources add that Guinness no longer accepts or tracks sleep-deprivation records, so the claim that someone currently holds this Guinness record is also wrong.

text: A chunk of the Dead Sea has been found to be so dense with salt that objects with a density lower than it will float on the surface.
label: supported
reason: Reliable sources, including NOAA's JetStream page on the Dead Sea, say its water is extremely salty. Below about 100 m it holds about 332 ppt of salt and is fully saturated, which makes it very dense. Basic buoyancy means anything less dense than this water floats, and sources note that people float on it easily. The claim's odd wording ('a chunk of the Dead Sea') does not change the main point, which the evidence backs.

text: Migrating animals that travel alone can be referred to as 'solitary migrants', often excluding species, like some birds that follow each other in loose groups but not considered part of a specific flock.
label: not_verifiable
reason: The first part holds up. Sources use 'solitary migrants' for animals that migrate alone: Birds & Blooms says hummingbirds are solitary migrants, and a Trends in Ecology & Evolution review uses the term for species that do not obviously migrate in groups. The second part, that the term often excludes birds moving in loose, non-flock groups, is not clearly supported and partly conflicts with the evidence. The same review calls songbirds solitary migrants even though they often migrate at the same time and in the same direction as thousands of other birds. A 2008 ScienceDaily report and WWF also describe 'solitary' songbirds travelling in loose flocks, and paulnoll.com counts birds that sometimes gather loosely as basically solitary. These sources suggest loose-group birds are often included rather than excluded, but no source directly states a rule either way, so the claim is inconclusive.

text: Butterfly fossils have been found in what is now Germany dating back around 200 million years to the time of the Triassic period.
label: supported
reason: Several reliable sources (Sci.News, Live Science, EurekAlert) report the 2018 Utrecht University study of about 70 fossilized lepidopteran wing scales. The scales came from a drill core in Schandelah, northern Germany, and are about 200–201 million years old, dating to the end of the Triassic (the Triassic–Jurassic boundary). These sources describe them as the earliest evidence of butterflies and moths. Strictly speaking, the scales belong to Lepidoptera, the group of butterflies and moths, and are probably from early moths rather than true butterflies. The popular description of them as butterfly fossils is common, so the claim matches the evidence.

text: Abnormally large crystals have grown within the Naica Mine in Chihuahua, Mexico, where one giant selenite crystal reaches 36 feet in length and weighs 55 tons.
label: supported
reason: National Geographic describes the gypsum (selenite) crystals in the Naica Mine's Cave of the Crystals in Chihuahua as being up to 36 feet (11 m) long and weighing up to 55 tons. Atlas Obscura and GeologyScience also describe a single crystal that is over 36 feet long and weighs about 55 tons. Some sources give the largest crystal as 12 m (about 39 ft), but that is consistent with the claim's figure of 36 feet.

text: Scientists estimate that there are approximately 8.7 million identified species on Earth, but the total number of existing species may be significantly higher, with some estimates ranging up to 30 million.
label: contradicted
reason: The 8.7 million figure from Mora et al. (2011, PLoS Biology) is an estimate of the total number of species on Earth, not the number already identified. Only about 1.2 million species had been described and catalogued at that time. Calling 8.7 million the number of "identified" species is therefore wrong. That error also breaks the claim's contrast with a possibly higher total; earlier estimates of that total ranged from 3 million to 100 million.

text: A blue whale can hold up to 2,000 gallons (around 7,500 liters) of krill and small fish in its stomach at a given time.
label: contradicted
reason: WWF says a blue whale's stomach holds about one ton of krill. One ton is roughly 1,000 liters, or about 260 gallons. The claim's 2,000 gallons (about 7,500 liters) is roughly 7.5 times that, so it looks like someone confused about 2,000 pounds with 2,000 gallons. The claim also says the whale eats small fish, but blue whales feed almost entirely on krill. I only managed one search before the search limit ran out, so this verdict depends on that one WWF source.

text: Near the surface of Greenland and Antarctica, scientists have discovered large, ancient freshwater ice shelves containing unfrozen subglacial lakes, frozen meltwater sheets, and frozen waste rock.
label: not_verifiable
reason: I found no reliable source describing large, ancient freshwater ice shelves near the surface of Greenland and Antarctica that contain unfrozen subglacial lakes, frozen meltwater sheets and frozen waste rock. Sources such as Wikipedia, ScienceDaily and Lancaster University describe subglacial lakes as lying beneath the ice sheets, sometimes about 800 m down, not near the surface. The ancient ice shelf that researchers did report was a former marine ice shelf in Baffin Bay, which is not the structure described here. Nothing I found mentions frozen waste rock in this context. The claim seems to mix up unrelated findings, and its central assertion cannot be verified.

text: A giant squid's eyes are said to be the largest of any animal, with some specimens having eyes that are up to 27 centimeters (11 inches) in diameter.
label: supported
reason: The search results back the claim. The peer-reviewed Nilsson et al. (2012) paper in Current Biology says the eyes of giant and colossal deep-sea squid are 27 cm in diameter. ResearchGate's listing of the same paper says the largest eyes, at 27 cm, belong to deep-sea giant squid. A SICB meeting abstract says giant squid (Architeuthis), together with colossal squid, have the largest eyes in the animal kingdom.
