Deep Sea News reports that the largest giant squid eye measured is 27 cm (10.6 in), which matches the claim's 'up to 27 cm (11 in).' One caveat: the giant squid shares the 'largest eye' title with the colossal squid, and some sources give it to the colossal squid alone. The claim's wording ('are said to be'), however, is consistent with the published literature.

text: In New York City, there is a secretly located apartment in the New York Public Library,dımatically decreasing the maintenance  and upkeep cost for the superintendant that is hidden behind a secret shelf.
label: not_verifiable
reason: Only part of this claim can be checked. Reliable sources (Atlas Obscura, Gothamist, 6sqft, Untapped New York) confirm that NYPL buildings had so-called 'secret' live-in apartments for superintendents and custodians. For example, John Fedeler lived in an eight-room apartment on the mezzanine of the Schwarzman Building on 42nd Street from 1911 to 1941, and about 13 abandoned apartments remain in branch libraries. However, no source says any apartment is 'hidden behind a secret shelf.' They were called secret because the public didn't know about them, and the sources describe them being reached through ordinary doors, such as a small door by a staircase or a side door. No source mentions a 'dramatic decrease in maintenance and upkeep cost' either. The reason given for the apartments is that the building needed someone on site around the clock, especially to keep the coal furnaces running. Also, the 42nd Street apartment no longer exists, so 'there is' is misleading for the main library. Because the secret-shelf and cost details can't be verified, the claim as a whole is inconclusive.

text: Aersopatiale Alouette helicopters use a turbine engine which allows for the specially adapted helicopters to be able to dump turbine power put into the engines which enables them to descend near vertically under controlled non thrust power turbine settings.
label: not_verifiable
reason: Reliable sources confirm that Alouette helicopters are powered by turbines: SKYbrary lists the Alouette II's Turboméca Artouste turboshaft, and Wikipedia calls it the first conventional production helicopter with a gas turbine engine. However, no source I found says that specially adapted Alouettes can 'dump turbine power' to descend near vertically under 'non thrust power turbine settings.' That part of the claim is vague and technically unclear, so I couldn't verify it.

text: The Axel Erlandson Tree Circus, located in Felton, California, features a collection of trees that have been carefully pruned and grafted to grow into unique and complex shapes.
label: contradicted
reason: The claim gets the location wrong. The Press Banner reports that Axel Erlandson's Tree Circus was in Scotts Valley, California (on Scotts Valley Drive), not Felton, and that the trees were later moved to Gilroy. Gilroy Gardens confirms the trees were first grown in Scotts Valley and are now shown at Gilroy Gardens. The description of the trees as pruned and grafted into unusual shapes is accurate.

text: Honeybees are able to fly by using their wings to create a whirlpool of air above and below them, which generates lift and allows them to hover and maneuver with incredible agility.
label: supported
reason: Reliable sources broadly back the claim. Altshuler et al. (PNAS, 2005) found that honeybees hover using short, fast wing strokes and that most insects fly by creating a leading-edge vortex. The University of Florida entomology program and McMaster University describe this vortex as a swirling 'mini-hurricane' or 'whirlwind' of air that strongly increases lift and helps bees stay airborne and hover. The claim's wording is a loose popular version: the main lift-generating vortex sits above the wing rather than 'above and below,' and 'incredible agility' is not a precise scientific term. Still, nothing in the sources contradicts the core point that bees generate lift and hover by creating a whirling vortex of air with their wings.

text: Polar bears are excellent swimmers and have been known to swim for over 60 miles without resting, using their powerful front paws to propel themselves through the water.
label: supported
reason: SeaWorld's polar bear adaptations page backs up every part of the claim. It calls polar bears strong swimmers that have been tracked swimming continuously for 100 km (62 mi), which is over 60 miles without rest. It also says their front paws propel them through the water dog-paddle style while the hind legs act as rudders. Other well-known reports, such as a USGS-documented swim of more than 400 miles, are consistent with this.

text: A blue whale's heart is so large that it can pump about 5,000 liters of blood with every beat.
label: contradicted
reason: Several sources put a blue whale's stroke volume far below 5,000 liters. Most say about 220–230 liters per beat, and the Goldbogen/Stanford research estimate is about 80 liters per beat. The 5,000-liter figure is off by more than an order of magnitude. The searches turned up no source that supports it.

text: A fetus develops fingerprints by the time it is three months old in the womb.
label: contradicted
reason: Cleveland Clinic's week-by-week fetal development guide says fingerprints only start to form in month 4 (weeks 13–16). It says the fetus has its own unique set of fingerprints at about week 19, in month 5. For month 3 (weeks 9–12), it mentions nails and external ears but not fingerprints. A Brainly answer, a less authoritative source, gives about 16 weeks. Fingerprints are therefore not fully developed by three months. Some ridge formation may begin earlier, but the claim that a fetus has developed fingerprints by three months goes against the most authoritative source I found.

text: Aersopatiale Alouette helicopters use a turbine engine which allows for the specially adapted helicopters to be able to dump turbine power put into the engines which enables them to descend instantly if required in tough weather conditions.
label: not_verifiable
reason: Reliable sources, including Wikipedia's Turbomeca Artouste and Alouette II/III pages and Airforce Technology, confirm that the Aérospatiale Alouette II and III use turbine (turboshaft) engines. However, no source I found says that specially adapted Alouettes can 'dump turbine power' to descend instantly in bad weather. That part of the claim could not be verified, and it is also not contradicted.

text: Chocolate syrup is the primary topping used over ice cream or frozen yogurt at McDonald's, Dairy Queen, and Wendy's.
label: not_verifiable
reason: I couldn't verify this claim. My first search found only a 1997 Spokesman-Review article. It describes Wendy's Frosty as a 'dairy dessert,' not ice cream or frozen yogurt. That article says nothing about toppings, and nothing I found shows chocolate syrup is the primary topping at McDonald's, Dairy Queen or Wendy's. I hit the tool's search limit before I could search more, so I couldn't rule the claim in or out. The Frosty finding also raises a doubt about whether Wendy's tops ice cream or frozen yogurt this way at all.

text: Didaskaleinophobia is the term used to describe a fear of going to school.
label: supported
reason: I checked several sources and they agree. Wiktionary defines didaskaleinophobia as "the fear of going to school," from the Greek word for school. Klarity Health and a few other sites give the same definition, and none of the results contradict it.

text: Humans and dolphins are the only species known to give themselves names.
label: contradicted
reason: The claim is out of date. In 2024 a Hebrew University study published in Science found that marmoset monkeys use specific "phee-calls" to address each other by name. The press release says this behavior was "previously known to exist only in humans, dolphins, and elephants," and an earlier 2024 study had reported name-like calls in African elephants. So humans and dolphins are not the only species known to use names. One caveat: these studies show animals naming others, which is close to but not exactly the claim's "give themselves names." Dolphins' self-created signature whistles fit that wording best, but the research still contradicts the idea that only humans and dolphins have names.

text: Humans share approximately 60 percent of their DNA with fruit flies, highlighting the deep genetic connections across different species.
label: supported
reason: Several trustworthy sources back the claim. The Max Planck Society (mpg.de) says roughly 60 percent of the fly's genes are also found in humans in a similar form. Arizona State University's Ask A Biologist says 60% of fruit fly DNA code is shared with humans. Strictly speaking, the 60% figure is about similar or conserved genes, not identical DNA. Still, popular-science and educational sources commonly describe it the way the claim does, and they present it as a sign of the deep genetic connections between species.

text: Octopuses have nine brains, with a large central brain and eight smaller "mini-brains" in each of their arms.
label: supported
reason: Several popular science sources (OctoNation, AnimalWised, AnimalsFYI, Discover Wildlife Science) describe octopuses as having "nine brains": one central brain plus a cluster of neurons (ganglia), often called a "mini-brain," in each of the eight arms. Some sources, such as BiologyInsights, point out that "nine brains" is a simplification: strictly, an octopus has one true brain plus dense neural networks in its arms. Still, the anatomy behind the claim is accurate, and the claim puts "mini-brains" in quotes, which signals the loose wording. No source contradicts the basic structure.

text: Seals have a highly developed sense of touch in their whiskers, which helps them navigate and locate prey in dark or murky waters.
label: supported
reason: CBC News reports research from Ruhr-Universität Bochum showing that harbour seal whiskers are extremely sensitive, with 1,000–1,600 nerve fibres per hair, and possibly the most sensitive in the animal kingdom. The same research found that these whiskers let seals track prey in dark, murky water. This backs up the claim that seals have a highly developed sense of touch in their whiskers and use it to navigate and find prey.

text: Honeybees are able to fly by using their wings to create a whirlpool of air above and below them, which generates lift and allows them to hover and maneuver in mid-air.
label: supported
reason: Sources describe honeybee flight the same way the claim does. Scientific American, reporting on the Caltech study, says bees flap and rotate their wings about 240 times a second, creating a vortex that lifts them into the air. UF/IFAS entomology describes this as a leading-edge vortex, a swirling low-pressure 'mini-hurricane' over the wing that boosts lift. A beekeeping source (Blythewood Bee Co.) says that when bees hover, their wings create a vortex above and below the wings that increases lift and lets them hover and steer. One caveat: the scientific research (Altshuler et al., PNAS) adds that honeybees rely on unusually short, high-frequency wing strokes and wing rotation, so 'whirlpool' is a simplified, popular description. The main point of the claim, that vortices generate lift for hovering and maneuvering, still holds up.

text: A blue whale's heartbeat is so loud that it can be detected over 500 miles away underwater.
label: contradicted
reason: The 500-mile figure is not supported by any source I found. Trustworthy sources, including NOAA Fisheries and the Cold Spring Harbor Whaling Museum, say a blue whale's heartbeat can be heard or detected about 2 miles away underwater. Some sources even doubt the 2-mile figure. No source puts the distance anywhere near 500 miles, so this claim overstates the distance by about 250 times.

text: Bees are capable of recognizing human faces and remembering them for later encounters, a unique ability shared by only a handful of animal species.
label: contradicted
reason: The first part of the claim holds up. Dyer et al. (2005, Journal of Experimental Biology) found that honeybees can learn to recognize human faces in photos and still pick them out two days later. The claim that this is a unique ability shared by only a handful of species is wrong, though. Studies show many species can tell human faces apart or recognize individual people, including sheep, dogs, cows, horses, crows, magpies, mockingbirds, pigeons, chickens, archerfish, llamas, seals, rabbits, lizards and octopuses. Medical News Today describes this as backed by 'numerous studies', so the ability is widespread rather than rare.

text: France and Spain have the highest number of time zones with a total of 12 time zones, due mainly to their overseas territories.
label: contradicted
reason: Sources, including an IFLScience article citing Guinness World Records, say France alone has the most time zones of any country: 12, or 13 if its Antarctic claim is counted, mostly because of its overseas territories. Spain is not in that group. It has only two time zones, mainland Spain and the Canary Islands, so the claim that France and Spain together hold the record is false.

text: Higher education students who report using active learning methods in the classroom tend to outperform their peers using more traditional teaching tactics by 3.2%, nationally.
label: not_verifiable
reason: I found no source for the specific figure of 3.2%, for a national comparison, or for a framing based on students reporting their use of active learning. The best-known evidence is the Freeman et al. (2014) PNAS meta-analysis of undergraduate STEM courses. It found that exam scores were about 6% higher (roughly 0.47 SD) under active learning, and that students in traditional lecture courses were 1.5 times more likely to fail. That supports the general idea that active learning outperforms lecturing, but it does not confirm the 3.2% figure or the 'nationally' and 'students who report' parts. Because those details can't be verified, and the main evidence gives a different number for a different design, the claim can't be confirmed.

text: Humans and elephants share several similar physical and emotional characteristics, and their brains also show the largest similarity in structure and function among all mammals.
label: contradicted
reason: Trustworthy sources do describe several similarities between elephant and human brains, including spindle cells, convergent features and a similar ratio of neocortex to corpus callosum. None of them supports the claim that elephant brains are the most similar to human brains among all mammals, and some of the evidence points the other way. A neuroscience study of elephant brains found that the shape and structure of elephant cortical neurons are 'radically different' from those of humans and other primates. An MRI study in The Anatomical Record found that the elephant brain is notably different in shape from human and great ape brains, with large temporal lobes that extend sideways. Wikipedia also notes unique structural differences, and elephants have only about one third as many cortical neurons as humans. Great apes such as chimpanzees, not elephants, have the brains most similar to humans. The superlative part of the claim is therefore contradicted.

text: NASA's Juno spacecraft has revealed that Jupiter's core is unexpectedly large, estimated to be around 10 times the mass of Earth's core.
label: contradicted
reason: Juno did find that Jupiter's core is large, fuzzy and dilute, which surprised scientists, so that part of the claim holds up. The size comparison does not. Juno-based interior models (Wahl et al. 2017, GRL) estimate the core holds about 7–25 Earth masses of heavy elements, and dilute-core models give roughly 10–24 Earth masses. These figures compare the core to the whole Earth, not to Earth's core. Earth's core is only about a third of Earth's mass, so '10 times the mass of Earth's core' works out to roughly 3 Earth masses. That falls well below the published range, which means the claim gets the comparison wrong.

text: Robots can't dance according to human evaluation standards due to the distinct lack of self-expression and fluid movement within current artificial intelligence.
label: contradicted
reason: The claim is contradicted because it says flatly that robots "can't" dance by human standards. Robotics and human–robot interaction research shows otherwise. A 2025 Frontiers survey says human-like robot dance is still "a complex challenge." It also describes growing work on expressiveness and fluid motion, and suggests robots could dance both expressively and responsively. Other studies ("Do You Like Dancing Robots? AI Can Tell You Why" and Frontiers in Neurorobotics/PMC work on humanoid choreography) had human audiences watch and rate robot dance performances. One reports that its model can "vividly imitate human dancers" and create new movements. The research describes limits and ongoing problems, not an inherent inability tied to a missing capacity for self-expression. No reliable source supports the absolute claim.

text: Tarantulas have been around for approximately 120 million years, with fossil evidence dating back to the early Cretaceous period.
label: supported
reason: A peer-reviewed study on tarantula biogeography (Journal of Biogeography, 2023) uses fossil-calibrated phylogenomics to date the origin of tarantulas (stem Theraphosidae) to the early Cretaceous, about 120 million years ago (95% range 109–132 Ma). An earlier estimate by Foley et al. (2021), about 119 Ma, agrees. This supports the claim's age of about 120 million years and its early Cretaceous origin. One caveat: the 120 Ma figure is a molecular-clock estimate, not the age of a fossil. The oldest actual tarantula fossil, from Burmese amber, is about 100 million years old, which is at or just past the end of the early Cretaceous. So the claim's wording about fossil evidence is somewhat loose, but its overall statement matches the evidence.

text: Tarantulas have been on Earth for a long time, with fossil evidence showing that they've remained largely unchanged for over 120 million years.
label: contradicted
reason: Tarantulas are ancient, but the claim gets the fossil evidence wrong. The figure of about 120 million years comes from a 2021 genetic study (transcriptome-based family tree dating). Phys.org and LiveScience report this as the estimated time tarantulas first appeared in Gondwana, not as a fossil finding. True tarantula fossils are extremely rare. LiveScience notes only two amber specimens: one from Mexico, about 16 million years old, and one from Myanmar, about 100 million years old. Neither is older than 120 million years, so fossils cannot show tarantulas staying 'largely unchanged for over 120 million years.' Texas Parks & Wildlife Magazine says fossil records show tarantulas virtually unchanged for 'more than 20 million years,' not 120 million.

text: Tigers have striped skin, not just striped fur, which helps them blend in with their surroundings and remain camouflaged.
label: supported
reason: Several sources say tigers have striped skin, not just striped fur, because the stripe pattern is also in the skin's pigmentation. The Nature Study Society also says the stripes break up the tiger's outline and help it stay hidden. One nuance: the camouflage comes from the visible striped fur, and the skin pigmentation matches it. That matches the claim's general meaning, so I rate it supported.

text: Bass Reef in New Zealand's Hauraki Gulf is home to over 90 shipwrecks, making it one of the largest graveyard of ships in the Southern Hemisphere.
label: not_verifiable
reason: I couldn't find anything showing that a place called 'Bass Reef' exists in New Zealand's Hauraki Gulf, and nothing linking such a reef to more than 90 shipwrecks. Searches for it only turned up general Hauraki Gulf dive pages, Sri Lanka's unrelated Great Basses Reef, and Australia's 'Ships' Graveyard' in Bass Strait off Victoria. The claim may be mixing up that Australian site with New Zealand, but I found no source that directly confirms or disproves it. My search limit ran out before I could check any other candidate sites, such as the Rangitoto ship graveyard.

text: Saturn is the only planet in our solar system that is less dense than water, meaning it could theoretically float if it were placed in a large enough body of water.
label: supported
reason: A NASA Goddard page says that Saturn is less dense than water, that it would float if there were a body of water large enough to hold it, and that no other planet in the Solar System has this property. This matches every part of the claim. It also fits Saturn's well-known average density of about 0.69 g/cm³, which is lower than water's 1 g/cm³.

text: Beehive-shaped structures in the archeological site of one of the earliest human civilizations, Mehrgarh in present-day Pakistan, are estimated to date back around 9,000 years.
label: not_verifiable
reason: The searches confirm that Mehrgarh, in present-day Pakistan, is a Neolithic site dating to about 7000 BCE, roughly 9,000 years ago. However, no result described beehive-shaped structures there. None of the results that mentioned Mehrgarh used the word 'beehive'. The Wikipedia 'Beehive house' page appeared in the results, but its snippet linked beehive houses to other places, such as Harran, not Mehrgarh. Archaeological accounts usually describe Mehrgarh's early houses as rectangular mud-brick buildings divided into rooms, though I recalled this from memory rather than finding it in the searches. I could not finish checking because the search tool limit was reached. The site's age is supported, but the claim about beehive-shaped structures is not confirmed.

text: Plants can make sounds, as research has shown that certain species release distinct ultrasonic frequencies in response to stress or damage.
label: supported
reason: A 2023 study in Cell (Khait et al.) found that tomato and tobacco plants give off ultrasonic clicks when they are short of water or their stems are cut. The sounds are too high-pitched for humans to hear. Each species' sounds were distinct enough that a machine-learning model could tell them apart. This matches the claim that certain plant species release distinct ultrasonic frequencies in response to stress or damage. Science News, a reputable outlet, reported the findings.

text: Plants can make sounds, too, when they are injured or under stress, and these sounds can be too faint for humans to hear.
label: supported
reason: A 2023 Tel Aviv University study published in Cell recorded stressed plants making airborne sounds. Tomato and tobacco plants produced clicking or popping noises when they were dehydrated or had their stems cut. The Washington Post and Science News report that humans can't hear these sounds. That supports the claim's main point. One caveat: the sounds go unheard mainly because they are ultrasonic, meaning too high-pitched for human ears. They are not necessarily too faint, since they were reported to be about as loud as normal conversation at close range. Because the claim only says the sounds "can be" too faint, I still rate it as supported.

text: Scientists estimate that there are approximately 8.7 million identified species on Earth, but up to 80% of all species remain undiscovered and unnamed.
label: contradicted
reason: The 8.7 million figure from Mora et al. (2011) is an estimate of all species on Earth, both known and unknown. It is not a count of identified species. Only about 1.2 million species had been identified and classified, which is less than 15% of the total. That leaves about 86% of land species and 91% of marine species undiscovered. The claim's 'up to 80% undiscovered' part roughly matches this, but calling 8.7 million 'identified species' is wrong.

text: Plants can make sounds, but they are too faint to be heard by the human ear, and scientists use specialized equipment to detect these sounds.
label: contradicted
reason: Plants do make sounds, and scientists pick them up with special equipment. The 2023 Tel Aviv University study in Cell recorded stressed tomato and tobacco plants with ultrasonic microphones. But the claim gives the wrong reason why people can't hear them. Science News says the clicks were "about as loud as a typical conversation, but too high-pitched for humans to hear." Sci.News also says the frequency is too high for human ears. So the problem is the pitch, not that the sounds are faint.

text: Astronomers estimate that there are approximately 100 to 400 billion stars in the Milky Way galaxy.
label: supported
reason: Wikipedia's Milky Way article says the galaxy is estimated to hold 100–400 billion stars. Universe Today also says astronomers estimate 100 to 400 billion stars in our galaxy, while noting that some estimates go as high as a trillion. Both sources match the claim's range.

text: Awitter is a fast and retweet-focused app, from Twitter that connects professionals in the newsroom overnight trending content, placing hashtag threaded tweets in an easy to read format (unordered), leaving communicators with fresh info breaking overnight.
label: not_verifiable
reason: I couldn't find any evidence that an app called "Awitter" exists, from Twitter or anyone else, or that it serves newsrooms by gathering overnight trending or hashtag-threaded content. Searches for "Awitter" only returned a 2001 Rammstein tribute song by Delusion, an inactive X/Twitter handle (@Awitter), an Instructables user profile, a name-pronunciation page and an email address. None of these describe the product in the claim. Nothing on trustworthy sites confirms the claim, and nothing directly disproves it either, so it can't be verified.

text: Japan has the world's oldest known hotel, Nishiyama Onsen Keiunkan, which was initially opened in 705 AD and has been in operation for over 1,300 years.
label: supported
reason: CNN reports that Nishiyama Onsen Keiunkan, in Japan's Yamanashi prefecture, opened in 705 AD and has run continuously for more than 1,300 years. CNN also says Guinness World Records named it the world's oldest hotel in 2011, and Guinness has its own 'Oldest hotel' record page that confirms this. Everything in the claim is backed by these sources.

text: Beehive-shaped structures in Antarctica, known as "blood falls", seep a deep red liquid, which is actually ancient, oxygen-free water rich in iron and salt.
label: contradicted
reason: Reliable sources agree that Blood Falls is iron-rich, very salty (hypersaline), oxygen-free ancient brine that turns red when its iron meets air. However, it is not a set of beehive-shaped structures. It is a single outflow that seeps from fissures at the end of Taylor Glacier, in Antarctica's McMurdo Dry Valleys, into West Lake Bonney. Because the claim gets the physical form wrong, it is contradicted even though the description of the water is accurate.

text: Saturn is the only planet in our solar system that is less dense than water, meaning it could theoretically float if it were placed in a large enough container of water.
label: supported
reason: WorldAtlas says Saturn is the only planet in our solar system with a density lower than liquid water: about 0.687 g/cm³, compared with about 0.997 g/cm³ for water. It adds that, in theory, Saturn would float in a large enough pool. This matches widely accepted NASA figures. The claim says Saturn could float only 'theoretically', which fits the source's point that it couldn't happen in reality.

text: Scientists estimate that there are approximately 8.7 million identified species on Earth, but the total number of species is believed to be much higher.
label: contradicted
reason: The claim gets the 8.7 million figure wrong. It comes from Mora et al. (2011), and it is an estimate of the total number of species on Earth, not the number already identified. According to that paper, only about 1.2 million species had been catalogued, which means roughly 86% of existing species are still undescribed. Calling 8.7 million the number of 'identified species' therefore contradicts the source.

text: Although not visible to the naked eye, there are estimated to be approximately 40 billion billion, or 4 x 10^22, individual stars in the observable universe.
label: contradicted
reason: The figures in the claim don't match each other. "40 billion billion" equals 4 × 10^19, not 4 × 10^22, so it is 1,000 times smaller than the number given in brackets. Reliable sources put the number of stars in the observable universe at about 10^22 to 10^24. One summary gives a range of 6×10^22 to 4.5×10^24, and another gives about 200 sextillion (2×10^23). By those figures, 40 billion billion is far too low. The 4 × 10^22 figure is close to the low end of the range, but no source gives 4 × 10^22 as the estimate. Because the claim's main figure conflicts with the evidence, it is contradicted.

text: In New York City, there is a secretly located apartment in the New York Public Library,dımatically decreasing the maintenance  and upkeep cost for the superintendant that is hidden behind a secret door.
label: not_verifiable
reason: Trustworthy sources such as Atlas Obscura, Gothamist and Untapped Cities confirm that the New York Public Library had hidden apartments. Live-in superintendents and custodians used them, including an eight-room apartment in the main Fifth Avenue building where superintendent John Fedeler lived. Those sources explain that the apartments existed because the buildings needed someone available around the clock. None of the sources I found say that an apartment was hidden behind a secret door. None say that it 'dramatically decreased' the superintendent's maintenance and upkeep costs. Because those parts of the claim can't be verified, the claim is inconclusive.

text: Tarantulas have existed for around 120 million years, with fossil records showing that these large spiders have remained largely unchanged since the Cretaceous period.
label: not_verifiable
reason: The timing is roughly supported. A peer-reviewed biogeography study of tarantulas (Journal of Biogeography, Wiley) puts the origin of modern tarantulas in the early Cretaceous, with one estimate of about 120–105 million years ago. The oldest known tarantula fossil, preserved in Burmese amber, is about 100 million years old. However, these dates come mostly from molecular clock estimates, and the tarantula fossil record is sparse. I found no evidence that fossils show tarantulas have 'remained largely unchanged since the Cretaceous.' Because that part of the claim cannot be verified, the claim is inconclusive.

text: Honeybees are able to fly by using their wings to generate electricity through a process called piezoelectricity, which allows them to take off and land vertically.
label: contradicted
reason: Honeybees fly using aerodynamic lift from their flapping wings, not electricity. A peer-reviewed PNAS study (Altshuler et al., 2005) found that honeybee flight depends on short, very fast wing strokes. It describes the lift-making effects as unsteady aerodynamic mechanisms, including a leading-edge vortex, wing rotation and wake capture, with the wings powered by the flight muscles. No reliable source says bees use piezoelectricity to fly, take off or land. The claim's explanation is false.

text: Astronauts can't cry in space because there is no gravity to help tears flow down their faces.
label: contradicted
reason: Space.com reports that Canadian astronaut Chris Hadfield showed astronauts can cry in space. In his words, "Your eyes will definitely cry in space," but in microgravity the tears don't run down the face. They collect into a ball of water on the eye. Weightlessness changes how tears behave, but it doesn't stop astronauts from crying, so the claim that they can't cry is false.

text: Barely 1% of the approximately 1.5 million known species of animal on Earth have been studied to any extent that would enable humans to predict their medical properties.
label: not_verifiable
reason: My searches turned up nothing that confirms or refutes the claim that only about 1% of roughly 1.5 million known animal species have been studied well enough to predict their medical properties. The results were about biodiversity estimates (phys.org) and traditional animal-based medicine in India (PMC), and neither gives this figure. Similar statements usually describe all species, or plants specifically, such as "less than 1% of tropical plants screened." They are rarely about animals alone. The '1.5 million known animal species' figure also doesn't line up neatly with common estimates of described species. The search limit was reached before I could look further, so the claim cannot be verified either way.

text: Barely 1% of the approximately 1.5 million known species of animal on Earth have been studied to any extent that would enable significant conclusions to be drawn about them.
label: not_verifiable
reason: I could only partly check this claim before I hit the search limit. Wikipedia's Animal article and Earth.com both support the figure of about 1.5 million described animal species. None of the results I retrieved support or contradict the main point, that barely 1% of these species have been studied well enough to draw significant conclusions. The Earth.com piece says research focuses unevenly on vertebrates, but it gives no '1% studied' figure. Because that central figure is unverified, the claim is inconclusive.

text: Fewer than 1% of turtles and tortoises make it to adulthood due to predation.
label: not_verifiable
reason: The sources I found only cover sea turtles, so the claim is broader than the evidence. NOAA, Florida FWC, SEE Turtles and the Olive Ridley Project estimate that about 1 in 1,000 sea turtle hatchlings (0.1%) reach adulthood, and NOAA's range goes as low as 1 in 10,000. That fits 'fewer than 1%' for sea turtles. However, these sources also say deaths come from dehydration and other environmental factors, not just predation. None of the results gave survival rates for tortoises or freshwater turtles. My search limit was reached before I could check those groups, and some reports (not confirmed here) suggest some tortoises survive at higher rates. Because the claim covers all 'turtles and tortoises' and credits predation alone, it cannot be fully verified.

text: Galileo Galilei was the first person to observe the planet Neptune, in 1613, but he did not recognize it as a planet at the time and instead recorded it as a fixed star.
label: supported
reason: NASA says Galileo recorded Neptune as a fixed star during telescope observations in 1612 and 1613. A ResearchGate paper on his notebooks also says he saw Neptune near Jupiter in late 1612 and January 1613 and treated it as a fixed star. These sources support that Galileo saw Neptune in 1613 and did not recognize it as a planet. One nuance: his first recorded sighting was in late December 1612, so '1613' is incomplete rather than wrong. The claim that he was the first person to observe Neptune is not stated directly, but no earlier observer is cited, and Neptune was not officially discovered until 1846.

text: Humans and dolphins are the only mammals known to give themselves names, a trait also shared by some bird species and possibly a few other animal groups.
label: contradicted
reason: Research shows that dolphins are not the only non-human mammals that use name-like calls. A 2024 study on wild African savannah elephants found that they call to each other using individual names they invent, and the researchers suggested elephants are the first non-human animals known to use names that do not involve imitation. Studies on marmosets have reported something similar. This undercuts the claim that humans and dolphins are the only mammals known to have names.

text: Moose are excellent swimmers and have been known to dive to depths of up to 20 feet in search of food.
label: supported
reason: Several sources say moose are strong or excellent swimmers that dive as deep as about 20 feet (6 m) to feed on aquatic plants. These include World Animal Protection, the Ontario Stewardship (osstewardship.ca) page and other wildlife sites. I found no source that contradicts the claim. Most of these are popular wildlife pages rather than scientific studies, but they agree with each other.

text: Spiders have been around for a long time, with fossil evidence showing that they've remained largely unchanged for over 300 million years.
label: contradicted
reason: The first part of the claim holds up: the oldest spider fossils are about 305–315 million years old, from the Carboniferous (e.g., Arthrolycosa in Germany, Eocteniza in England). The 'largely unchanged' part does not. National Geographic says it was daddy longlegs (harvestmen), not spiders, that barely changed over 305 million years. It adds that spiders were 'still evolving into their current shapes' then. Those early spiders still showed traces of segments on their abdomens, which modern spiders lack. Paleontologist Jason Dunlop also suggests the split into modern spider groups likely started later, in the Mesozoic. The claim seems to mix up spiders with harvestmen.

text: Tarantulas have been around for a long time - fossil records show they've remained largely unchanged for over 100 million years.
label: not_verifiable
reason: The first part of the claim holds up: tarantulas are an old group. Molecular studies place their origin about 120 million years ago, and the oldest known theraphosid fossil is in Burmese amber dated to about 100 million years (Live Science; Journal of Biogeography). The second part is not shown. Only two true tarantula fossils are known, one about 16 million years old and one about 100 million years old. That is too sparse to show the group stayed largely unchanged for more than 100 million years. The one source that makes an 'unchanged' claim, Texas Parks & Wildlife Magazine, says 'virtually unchanged, for more than 20 million years', not 100 million. Because the specific 100-million-year claim can't be confirmed, the result is inconclusive.

text: Walking on water is possible for certain animals like the Basilisk lizard and some species of frogs, thanks to their unique adaptations.
label: supported
reason: Biomechanics research on the plumed basilisk lizard says basilisks can run across water from the time they hatch to adulthood. The same sources report that several frog species, including members of Ranidae and cricket frogs, can 'skitter' across the water surface without sinking. The Journal of Experimental Biology describes cricket frog skittering as a form of porpoising, so 'walking on water' is a loose description, but it still fits the claim's general meaning. No source contradicts the claim.

text: In the heart of the Amazon rainforest, there exists a vast, eerie landscape known as the "Meeting of the Waters," where two rivers flow side by side for several miles without mixing due to their different temperatures and densities.
label: supported
reason: Wikipedia and several travel sources describe the Meeting of the Waters near Manaus in the Brazilian Amazon. There, the dark Rio Negro and the sandy Rio Solimões run side by side without mixing for about 6 km (3.7 miles), and the effect continues partially for much farther downstream. Sources attribute this to differences in temperature, speed and density. The core facts match the claim. Calling 3.7 miles 'several miles' is a fair approximation, and 'eerie' is just a subjective description, not something to check.

text: A partitions of the Mandelbrot set can form the swirling patterns which in turn appear similar to Romanesco broccoli under a microscope.
label: not_verifiable
reason: The sources I found only partly back the claim. Several pages describe Romanesco broccoli as a natural fractal made of spirals within spirals, and some put it side by side with the Mandelbrot set, for example Fourmilab's 'fractal food' page. None of them says that parts of the Mandelbrot set form swirling patterns that look like Romanesco 'under a microscope'. The spiral pattern in Romanesco is visible to the naked eye, so the microscope detail can't be verified and doesn't fit the evidence. There is also no source that directly compares the Mandelbrot set's spirals to Romanesco in the way the claim describes.

text: Areatment-free glass, known as 'Prince Rupert's Drops', can withstand extreme pressure on its body but will shatter instantly if the tail is damaged.
label: supported
reason: Purdue University's research news release says the head of a Prince Rupert's drop can withstand hammer blows and very high compressive loads, about 15,000 N. It also says breaking the thin tail with slight finger pressure makes the whole drop shatter into powder within microseconds. New Atlas reports the same thing. That confirms the main claim. The phrase 'Areatment-free' looks like a garbled word, and the drops are actually made by quenching molten glass in water, so 'treatment-free' would be inaccurate if read literally. I treated it as a non-substantive wording error.

text: Astronauts on the International Space Station have reported they can see the Great Barrier Reef from outer space.
label: supported
reason: Several sources say astronauts on the ISS have seen and photographed the Great Barrier Reef from orbit. Sky at Night Magazine describes ISS astronauts, including Kjell Lindgren, capturing shots of the reef. NASA Earth Observatory imagery republished by Earth.com shows the reef in a photo taken by an astronaut on the ISS. Other explainers note that astronauts in low Earth orbit can see parts of the reef when conditions are clear. I found no sources contradicting the claim.

text: A星(is the brightest star in the night sky and is about 63.8 billion miles away from Earth.
label: contradicted
reason: The brightest star in the night sky is Sirius (Sirius A). It is about 8.6 light-years from Earth, which is roughly 50.6 trillion miles, not 63.8 billion miles. The claimed distance is wrong by about a factor of 1,000. Even though the entity is written ambiguously as "A星(", whichever star is meant as the brightest in the night sky is far more than 63.8 billion miles away.

text: Despite its seemingly barren surface, Antarctica is home to several unique species of penguins, seals, and fish that thrive in its freezing climate.
label: supported
reason: Trustworthy sources back the claim. The Australian Antarctic Division (antarctica.gov.au), ASOC and AntarcticGlaciers.org all describe penguins such as the emperor penguin, several seal species (Antarctic fur, leopard, Ross, Weddell and others), and fish that live in the very cold Antarctic waters and are adapted to them. Nothing found contradicts the claim.

text: Despite its seemingly barren surface, Antarctica is home to several unique species of penguins, seals, and fish that thrive in the icy landscape.
label: supported
reason: Reliable sources confirm every part of the claim. National Geographic says notothenioid fish, which make their own antifreeze, live in Antarctic waters. It also notes that emperor penguins live on Antarctica. Wikipedia and wildlife guides list several penguin species, such as emperor and Adélie, and seal species, such as Weddell, crabeater, leopard and Ross, that are native to Antarctica or found there and adapted to the cold.

text: Honey Never Spoils, Archeologists have found pots of honey in ancient Egyptian tombs that are over 3,000 years old and still perfectly edible.
label: supported
reason: Many sources repeat this claim: archaeologists found pots of honey more than 3,000 years old in ancient Egyptian tombs, and it was still edible. They include HistoryFacts, My Modern Met, Dallas Express/Yahoo News (which cites Smithsonian Magazine) and others. They explain it by honey's chemistry: low water content, acidity and hydrogen peroxide stop microbes from growing. None of the results contradicted the claim. However, most of these are popular-science or trivia sites, and none gives a primary archaeological report showing anyone actually tested or ate the honey. So the support comes from widely repeated secondary sources, not direct evidence.

text: Humans and dolphins are the only animals known to give themselves names based on their unique whistles.
label: not_verifiable
reason: The search results support part of the claim but leave the rest unverified. National Wildlife Federation and Science report that bottlenose dolphins develop their own signature whistles, which work like names, and NWF calls this dolphins naming themselves. But dolphins are not the only non-human animals said to use names: researchers have reported that elephants, marmosets and green-rumped parrotlets call each other by name. Those animals seem to learn or be given their names by others (for example, from adults) rather than inventing them, so whether they count against the claim depends on how strictly 'give themselves names' is read. Scientists also still disagree about the evidence for names in those species. Finally, humans don't name themselves with whistles, and no source backs the claim's framing that humans and dolphins are the only two animals that self-name. Because the claim is partly supported, partly undermined and partly unverifiable, it is inconclusive.

text: Katara and the naga, a sea serpent from Polynesian mythology, are believed by some to be the origins for the myth of mermaids.
label: contradicted
reason: Search results consistently say the naga is a serpent being from Hindu, Buddhist and Jain mythology in South and Southeast Asia, not a Polynesian sea serpent. That contradicts the claim's description of it. Nothing I found supports the idea that "Katara" (who has no clear referent) is believed to be an origin of the mermaid myth.

text: Scans of the Egyptian Great Pyramid's internal chamber, created in 2016, suggest the possible presence of a large, undiscovered cavity within its structure.
label: supported
reason: The ScanPyramids project used muon detectors placed in the Great Pyramid's Queen's chamber, and those scans first showed a large unknown space now called the 'Big Void.' The Nature paper says the void was first seen with nuclear emulsion films installed in the Queen's chamber, then confirmed by other detectors. Science News says scientists first identified the void in 2016 using muons. ABC, GeekWire and Smithsonian also describe it as a previously unknown cavity at least 30 metres long. The finding was published in 2017, but the scans that revealed it date to 2016, so the claim matches the evidence.

text: Scientists estimate that there may be between 700,000 to 1 million species on Earth that have not yet been discovered.
label: contradicted
reason: The best-known global estimate puts the number of undiscovered species far higher than the claim. Mora et al. estimated about 8.7 million species on Earth, with roughly 86% of land species and 91% of marine species still undescribed, according to AAAS. That works out to about 7.5 million undiscovered species. The E.O. Wilson Foundation similarly writes of 'the 8 million species we don't know.' The '700,000 to 1 million' range appears to be the estimated total number of species in the oceans only (Appeltans et al. 2012, as reported by LiveScience and US News), with about two-thirds of those undiscovered. That is a marine total, not a count of undiscovered species across all of Earth, so the claim misstates what scientists estimate.

text: Swallows are known for their incredible migratory journeys, with some species traveling over 12,000 miles in a single year.
label: supported
reason: Reputable sources back both parts of the claim. NH Audubon's Barn Swallow handout says the bird's yearly round-trip migration covers 14,000 miles, which is more than 12,000. BBC Discover Wildlife says UK swallows make a 6,000-mile migration to and from South Africa twice a year, which adds up to about 12,000 miles a year. Other sources also call the barn swallow's migration one of the longest for a small bird. This fits the claim that some swallow species travel over 12,000 miles in a year.

text: Millions of trees are accidentally planted upside down each year due to squirrels burying acorns with their stems facing the earth, which can cause the trees to grow roots in the air and potentially die.
label: contradicted
reason: Sources on growing oaks from acorns say it doesn't matter which way up an acorn is planted. The root grows downward on its own because of gravitropism, so trees don't end up with roots in the air. One source notes that jays and squirrels have been planting acorns for thousands of years without the orientation mattering. I found no evidence that millions of trees are 'planted upside down' by squirrels and die as a result.

text: Caterpillars can eat up to 27,000 times their body weight in a single day, which is equivalent to a human consuming around 45,000 pizzas.
label: contradicted
reason: The commonly cited figure is that caterpillars eat about 27,000 times their own body weight over their whole larval stage, which lasts roughly four weeks. It is not a single-day figure. The Naked Scientists says caterpillars eat '27,000 times their own body weight in leaves in the 4 weeks that they're caterpillars.' The claim's 'in a single day' framing gets the timeframe wrong. I found no reliable source for the '45,000 pizzas' comparison either.

text: Astronauts cannot cry in the classical sense in space due to the lack of gravity, which causes their tears to form a ball and cling to their eyes instead of falling.
label: supported
reason: Several sources, including Space.com and Futurism, describe Chris Hadfield's demonstration on the ISS: in microgravity, tears don't fall but stay on the eye as a liquid ball. Futurism even says astronauts 'technically can't cry,' which fits the claim's 'in the classical sense' wording. Some sources say astronauts can still produce tears, but that agrees with the claim's caveat. One small point: sources credit surface tension for holding the ball in place, with the missing gravity being why the tears don't fall.

text: Scientists estimate that there are approximately 8.7 million identified species on Earth, but this number is thought to be only a small fraction of the total number of species that actually exist.
label: contradicted
reason: The claim treats 8.7 million as the number of identified species, which is wrong. In the 2011 study by Mora et al. (PLoS Biology, reported by ScienceDaily), 8.7 million (give or take 1.3 million) is the estimated total number of species on Earth. Only about 1.2 million species had been catalogued at that point, and the study suggests about 86% of existing species are still undescribed. The claim mixes up the estimated total with the count of identified species, so it is contradicted.

text: Scientists have discovered approximately 8.7 million identified species on Earth to date, but it's estimated that up to 80% of the planet's species remain undiscovered.
label: contradicted
reason: The 8.7 million figure (±1.3 million) from Mora et al. (2011) is an estimate of how many species exist on Earth in total, not how many have been identified. Only about 1.2–1.9 million species have actually been catalogued. The same study also estimated that more than 80% of species (about 86%) are still undiscovered, so the claim's 'up to 80%' figure understates that estimate. Because the claim calls the 8.7 million species 'identified', it is contradicted.

text: Schedule 1 of the Indian Constitution initially listed 29 states, but that number has since increased to 28, then to 29 and set back to 28 and currently there are 28 states and 8 union territories in India
label: contradicted
reason: The current figure in the claim is correct: India has 28 states and 8 union territories. The history it gives is wrong. The original 1950 First Schedule (Wikisource copy of the calligraphed Constitution) lists 9 Part A, 9 Part B and 10 Part C states, which makes 28 states. The only other entry was the Part D territory of the Andaman and Nicobar Islands, so the schedule did not list 29 states. Going from 29 to 28 would also be a decrease, not an increase. The claim also leaves out the 1956 reorganisation, which cut the list to 14 states and 6 union territories. From the 14 states the count later rose to 28, then to 29 when Telangana was created in 2014, and fell back to 28 in 2019 when Jammu and Kashmir became a union territory.

text: Astronauts cannot cry in space because their tears don't fall down their cheeks, they instead form a ball and float around.
label: contradicted
reason: Space.com reports Chris Hadfield's demonstration on the ISS, where he said "Your eyes will definitely cry in space." So astronauts can cry. He also showed that tears don't fall but collect into a growing ball of liquid that stays stuck to the eye and can spread across to the other eye. They don't float freely around the cabin. The claim's main point, that astronauts cannot cry, is false.

text: Babies are born without kneecaps; they don't develop and harden until around 3-5 years of age.
label: contradicted
reason: The claim gets the anatomy wrong. Babies are not born without kneecaps. They are born with a kneecap (patella) made of cartilage, which slowly turns into bone during early childhood. HowStuffWorks supports the 3–5 year timeline for the kneecap fully hardening. But it and the other sources agree that the kneecap is already there at birth, just not as bone, so it doesn't show up on X-rays. Several explainers, including one citing NIH research, call 'babies have no kneecaps' a common myth. Some pages, such as Encyclopedia.com and a trivia site, say babies lack kneecaps, but they then clarify that they mean bony kneecaps and that cartilage is present. The claim's main statement is therefore wrong.

text: Cheryl Holder and her team of-sales specialist gifted a Terry Bradshaw over 100 cows during the '80 Super bowl for no reason.
label: not_verifiable
reason: I found nothing that backs up the claim. Reliable sources on Super Bowl XIV (January 20, 1980, Rose Bowl), such as Wikipedia and Britannica, confirm that Terry Bradshaw played and was named MVP. None of them mention a Cheryl Holder, a team of sales specialists, or anyone giving Bradshaw more than 100 cows. The only similar name that came up was Cheryl Ladd, who sang the national anthem at that game. I also found no source that directly disproves the story. The main part of the claim can't be checked, so it is inconclusive, though it looks made up.

text: High-speed cameras have captured the movement of a dragonfly's wings beating at up to 80 times per second.
label: not_verifiable
reason: The evidence conflicts. Several sources, including a scientist's answer based on high-speed video, a Montana FWP publication, and a ResearchGate study, put dragonfly wingbeats at about 27–38 times per second, so 80 would be unusually high. A Purdue engineering document, however, gives a general range of 20–90 Hz, so 80 beats per second is not clearly ruled out. I found no source saying high-speed cameras actually recorded a dragonfly's wings at up to 80 beats per second.

text: Honeybees are able to fly by using electricity generated by the movement of their wings, which helps to attract pollen and improve their aerodynamics.
label: contradicted
reason: Bees do build up a positive electrostatic charge in flight, caused by friction with the air, and that charge helps pollen stick to them. But bees fly by aerodynamic lift from flapping their wings, not by using electricity. Nothing in the sources says the charge powers flight or improves aerodynamics. The research describes the charge as a side effect of flying that helps with pollen collection, which contradicts the main part of the claim.

text: Honeybees are capable of recognizing human faces and remembering them for later encounters, much like some other animal species and even humans.
label: supported
reason: Dyer et al.'s 2005 study in the Journal of Experimental Biology, as reported by Phys.org, found that honeybees could learn to recognize human faces in photos and still remember them at least two days later. Bees tested two days after training kept roughly 76–79% accuracy. The article also compares this with face recognition in humans and other species. One caveat is that the experiments used photographs rather than live faces.

text: Humans and elephants share several similarities in their DNA, with studies showing that they share around 70% of the same DNA.
label: not_verifiable
reason: Sources agree that humans and elephants share a lot of DNA, but none I found supports the specific figure of about 70%. The estimates vary widely depending on what is measured. A geneticist writing in Daedalus (American Academy of Arts & Sciences) says we share roughly 90% of our DNA with elephants, mice, dogs and cattle. A genome-comparison guide gives about 44% of the genome aligned, 83% of human genes with any elephant counterpart, 75.9% with a one-to-one counterpart, and 87% protein identity. A less reliable site claims 97–98% for protein-coding regions. The 70% figure is close to some of these measures but contradicts the reputable 90% estimate, so the evidence is mixed.

text: Humans share about 50% of their DNA with bananas, showing a surprising similarity between species.
label: contradicted
reason: The 50% figure is a popular misreading of an unpublished 2013 NHGRI comparison made for a Smithsonian video. That comparison found that about 60% of human genes have a recognizable counterpart in the banana genome, and that the matched proteins were only about 40% similar on average. It did not find that half of human DNA matches banana DNA. Science outlets including The Naked Scientists ('Mythconception: We share half our DNA with bananas'), IFLScience and HowStuffWorks say the figure is about genes, not DNA, and is wrong or overstated when stated as DNA. Protein-coding genes are only a small part of the genome, and one analysis puts identical coding bases at under 0.1% of the human genome. A few low-authority sites (e.g., factmyth.com) repeat the 50%-DNA claim as fact, but the more credible sources contradict it as worded.

text: Kukoos, also known as Guillemots, are agile flight birds that dive underwater to hunt for their food.
label: contradicted
reason: No source shows that "Kukoos" is another name for guillemots. Wikipedia says guillemot is the common name for several auk (Alcidae) seabirds in the genera Uria and Cepphus. In North America, Uria species are called "murres", not Kukoos. Searches for "Kukoos" mainly return the video game Kukoos: Lost Pets, and the similar name "cuckoo" refers to a different bird family, Cuculidae. Scottish Wildlife Trust does confirm the second half of the claim: guillemots fly fast, dive from the sea surface and swim underwater with their wings to catch fish. Still, the claim that Kukoos are the same as guillemots is wrong.

text: October 10, 1886, marked the day when the first 'talking clock' came into existence.
label: contradicted
reason: Wikipedia and the AES historical pages say the first talking clock was Frank Lambert's experimental machine from about 1878, eight years before 1886. History timelines connect October 10, 1886 with the first tuxedo dinner jacket, worn at Tuxedo Park, New York, not with a talking clock.

text: Octopuses have nine brains, with a large central brain and eight smaller "mini-brains" in each of their eight arms.
label: supported
reason: My search found sources describing the octopus nervous system as one central brain plus neural clusters in each of its eight arms, which is why it is often said to have "nine brains." OctoNation says the answer is "Nine. One central brain and eight mini-brains (satellite-brains) in each arm." AnimalsFYI says the same. OctoNation also notes that these are not nine full brains: the arm "mini-brains" are dense nerve cords and ganglia, and about two-thirds of the octopus's neurons are in its arms. That is a popular nickname, but it still matches how the claim describes the anatomy. Both sources are popular-science sites rather than peer-reviewed research.

text: Researchers estimate that there are around 8.7 million identified species on Earth, but they believe that up to 80% of all species remain undiscovered.
label: contradicted
reason: The 8.7 million figure (Mora et al., 2011) is an estimate of all species on Earth, both known and unknown. It is not a count of identified species. Only about 1.2 million species have actually been identified and catalogued, which is less than 15% of that total. The part about more than 80% of species being undiscovered is roughly right (86% of land species and 91% of marine species), but calling the 8.7 million 'identified species' is wrong.

text: Rome is considered to be the second most populous city in the world with over 3,700,000 residents
label: contradicted
reason: Rome is nowhere near the second most populous city in the world. Wikipedia says the city has about 2.7 million residents and is the third most populous city in the European Union. Statista puts Rome's population at about 2.74 million in 2026, so it does not have over 3.7 million residents either. The world's most populous cities, such as Tokyo, Delhi and Shanghai, are far larger.

text: Rupert, the largest snowman ever recorded, was built in Maine in 1999 and stood at a height of 113 feet 7 inches.
label: contradicted
reason: The 113-foot, 7-inch snowman built in Bethel, Maine in 1999 was called "Angus, King of the Mountain," not "Rupert." It is also no longer the largest snowman on record. In 2008, the "Olympia Snowwoman" beat its record by about 9 feet. The location, year and height in the claim are correct, but the name and the "largest ever" status are wrong.

text: SPiece of the contiguous United States with the lowest recorded temperature is Prospect Creek in Alaska, at 80 degrees below zero Fahrenheit.
label: contradicted
reason: Alaska isn't part of the contiguous United States. Prospect Creek, Alaska, does hold the overall U.S. record of -80°F, set on Jan. 23, 1971. The record for the contiguous U.S. is -70°F at Rogers Pass, Montana, set on Jan. 20, 1954. The claim gives the wrong location and temperature for the contiguous U.S.

text: Space is filled with a giant web of galaxy filaments that stretch across vast distances, with some filaments spanning over 500 million light-years in length.
label: supported
reason: Wikipedia's article on galaxy filaments says they form a web of thread-like structures that border cosmic voids. Most are 50–80 Mpc long (about 160–260 million light-years). Some are much longer: Wikipedia lists Quipu at about 400 Mpc, which is over a billion light-years. It describes the Sloan Great Wall as a galaxy filament or wall about 1.37 billion light-years long. That backs the claim that some filaments are more than 500 million light-years long.

text: Spiders have been around for a very long time, with fossil evidence showing that they've remained largely unchanged for over 300 million years.
label: supported
reason: The fossil record backs both parts of the claim. Spider fossils go back to the Carboniferous, about 305–310 million years ago, and the Australian Museum and Wikipedia also cite Attercopus at about 380 million years ago as an early spider. The Australian Museum says segmented spiders (Mesothelae) have stayed 'virtually unchanged' compared with their ancestors. A geology history blog adds that the basic spider body plan has remained nearly unchanged since the Pennsylvanian, about 300 million years ago. The claim simplifies things, since modern spiders have diversified a great deal, but the overall point holds up.

text: Tarantulas have been on Earth for a long time, with fossil evidence showing they've remained largely unchanged for around 165 million years.
label: contradicted
reason: No source I found supports the 165-million-year figure, and the specific evidence conflicts with it. The oldest known true tarantula (Theraphosidae) fossil is about 100 million years old, from Burmese amber. A phylogenetic study dates the group's origin to about 120 million years ago in the Cretaceous, on Gondwana. Texas Parks & Wildlife magazine says fossils show tarantulas have been "virtually unchanged" for more than 20 million years, not 165 million. Ancestral tarantula-like mygalomorph fossils do go back about 235–240 million years, so the claim that tarantulas are an ancient group is broadly true. However, the claim that fossils show tarantulas largely unchanged for about 165 million years is not supported by these sources and conflicts with the roughly 120-million-year origin date.

text: Black holes are among the densest objects in the universe, with some having a density that is equivalent to the mass of the sun packed into a sphere about 6 miles, or 9.7 kilometers, in diameter.
label: contradicted
reason: The figure in the claim is wrong. Black holes are indeed extremely dense objects, but squeezing the Sun's mass into a black hole gives a sphere about 6 kilometers across, not 6 miles (9.7 km). That comes from the Sun's Schwarzschild radius of about 3 km. The OpenStax astronomy text (UCF Pressbooks) says the Sun would have to shrink to about 6 km in diameter, and other sources describe it as about 3.7 miles wide. The claim mixes up kilometers and miles, so its size is roughly 1.6 times too large.

text: Humans and dolphins are the only known mammals that give birth to their young with their eyes open.
label: contradicted
reason: The claim is false. Many other mammals are also born with their eyes open. A peer-reviewed article on PubMed Central says guinea pigs and spiny mice are precocial, "born with eyes open." It also says rhesus macaque babies are born with their eyes open. Other precocial mammals, such as horses, are well known to be born the same way. So humans and dolphins are not the only ones.

text: The68539-\Traits Eruption, also known as the 'Aeolian Islands eruption in 615 BCE' was a large-scale volcanic eruption which is historically notable because of an extensively documented event during the life of Greek philosopher Thales who is renowned for predicting solar eclipses.
label: not_verifiable
reason: I couldn't identify anything called the "68539-\Traits Eruption"; the name looks garbled, so the claim has no clear referent. Searches found no record of a large-scale "Aeolian Islands eruption in 615 BCE" or any eruption documented in connection with Thales. Reliable sources (NASA Earth Observatory, the Smithsonian Global Volcanism Program, Wikipedia's Vulcano page) give other dates for Aeolian eruptions, such as Vulcanello emerging in 183 BCE and Lipari activity around AD 580–729. Thales is famous for predicting a single solar eclipse, generally dated to 585 BCE, but no source links him to any Aeolian eruption. Because the subject can't be identified and its central details can't be checked, the claim is inconclusive, though it is very likely made up.

text: Tarantulas have been on Earth for a long time, with fossils of these spiders dating back to the Early Cretaceous period, over 100 million years ago.
label: contradicted
reason: Reliable sources show that tarantulas (Theraphosidae) do have Cretaceous fossils, but not from the Early Cretaceous. Wikipedia's Tarantula article says the oldest assigned species, Protertheraphosa spinipes, comes from Burmese amber dated to the "mid and late Cretaceous." Wikipedia's Burmese amber pages date that amber to the early Late Cretaceous (Cenomanian), about 99 million years ago. The Journal of Biogeography study and Live Science both describe the oldest tarantula fossil as about 100 million years old, not more than 100 million. An Early Cretaceous age of about 120 million years appears only as a molecular-clock estimate for when the lineage split off, not as the age of any fossil. So the general point that tarantulas are ancient holds, but the claim's specific details, Early Cretaceous fossils older than 100 million years, are contradicted.

text: Scientists estimate that there may be between 700,000 and 1 million species of insects on Earth, but only about 1 millionth of these have been formally described and named.
label: contradicted
reason: The claim gets both numbers wrong. According to The Conversation, taxonomists have already described about one million insect species. The usual estimate for the total is 5–6 million, and newer research puts it at 13.3–24.7 million. That means the total is far higher than 700,000–1 million, and roughly 1 in 5 to 1 in 20 species have been described, not one millionth. The claim doesn't even work on its own terms, since one millionth of a million would be just one species.

text: One flex of a human eyebrow contains about 1 million individual hairs.
label: contradicted
reason: Sources say the average eyebrow has about 250 hairs, and even eyebrows that have never been plucked top out at around 1,100 hairs in total. That is nowhere near 1 million. Flexing an eyebrow doesn't change how many hairs it has, so the claim is false by several orders of magnitude.

text: One flex of a human eyebrow is made up of more than 10,113 muscles.
label: contradicted
reason: The claim is false. Anatomy sources say eyebrow movement comes from only a handful of named facial muscles: the frontalis lifts the brow, while the corrugator supercilii, procerus, depressor supercilii and orbicularis oculi pull it down or inward. The whole human body has only about 600–650 skeletal muscles, so a single eyebrow flex cannot involve more than 10,113 muscles.

text: Scientists estimate that there are approximately 8.7 million Identified species on Earth, but estimates suggest the actual number could range from 30 to 100 million.
label: contradicted
reason: The claim gets the 8.7 million figure wrong. That number comes from Mora et al. (2011, PLoS Biology), and it is an estimate of all species on Earth, not the number already identified. The same paper puts identified (described) species at only about 1.2 million, and other researchers say about 2 million. So calling 8.7 million the count of identified species is incorrect. Older estimates did range widely, but the main figure is misattributed.

text: Scientists estimate that there are approximately 8.7 million Identified species on Earth, but the actual number could be as high as 30 million.
label: contradicted
reason: The 8.7 million figure from Mora et al. (2011) is an estimate of the total number of eukaryotic species on Earth, not the number already identified. According to the same source, only about 1.2 million species have been described and catalogued, with about 953,000 of the roughly 7.77 million estimated animal species described. That means about 86% of species are still undescribed, so calling 8.7 million "identified" species gets the core fact wrong. Some other estimates of the total do go higher, but that doesn't fix this part of the claim.

text: Scientists estimate that there are approximately 8.7 million identified species on Earth, but the actual number could be much higher, potentially ranging between 30-50 million.
label: contradicted
reason: The 8.7 million figure from Mora et al. (2011, PLoS Biology) is an estimate of the total number of eukaryotic species on Earth, including the ones not yet found. It is not a count of identified species. The study says only about 1.2 million species have been described and catalogued, including 953,434 animals, and it says 86% of land species and 91% of ocean species have not been described yet. So the claim is wrong to call 8.7 million 'identified species'.

text: Scientists estimate that there are approximately 8.7 million identified species on Earth, but the actual number could be significantly higher due to the vast number of unexplored ecosystems.
label: contradicted
reason: The 8.7 million figure (Mora et al., 2011) is an estimate of the total number of species on Earth, both known and unknown. It is not a count of identified species. The same source says only about 1.25 million species had been described and entered into central databases. So calling 8.7 million 'identified species' is wrong, even though the idea that many species remain undiscovered is correct.

text: Scientists estimate that there are approximately 8.7 million identified species on Earth, but the actual number could be significantly higher due to unexplored ecosystems.
label: contradicted
reason: The 8.7 million figure (give or take 1.3 million) from Mora et al. (2011) is an estimate of all species on Earth, most of which have not been found yet. It is not a count of identified species. The same source says only about 1.25 million species have been described and entered into central databases, with roughly 700,000 more thought to be described but not yet in those databases. So calling 8.7 million the number of "identified" species is wrong. The idea that many species are still undiscovered fits the research, but the claim's main number is attached to the wrong thing.

text: Scientists estimate that there are approximately 8.7 million identified species on Earth, but the total number of existing species could be as high as 30 million.
label: contradicted
reason: The claim gets the 8.7 million figure wrong. It comes from Mora et al. (2011) in PLoS Biology, which estimated the total number of eukaryotic species on Earth, both known and unknown, at about 8.7 million (give or take 1.3 million). It is not a count of identified species. The same sources say only about 1.2–1.25 million species had been described and catalogued, roughly 14%, with about 86% still undescribed. Calling 8.7 million the number of identified species directly conflicts with the original study and its press coverage. Some other estimates do run higher, from 3 million up to 100 million or more, but that does not fix the misstated figure.

text: Scientists estimate that there are approximately 8.7 million identified species on Earth, but this number may represent only a small fraction of the total number.
label: contradicted
reason: The claim gets the 8.7 million figure wrong. It comes from Mora et al. (2011), and it is an estimate of all eukaryotic species on Earth, identified or not, give or take 1.3 million. It is not a count of identified species. The same source says only about 1.25 million species had been described and entered into central databases. So the claim mixes up the estimated total with the number identified. If 8.7 million were the identified count, it would not make sense to say that number may be only a small fraction of the total, because 8.7 million is itself the estimated total.

text: British Airways has a 747 jet with the smallest pilot staff as low as 3 plus 3 cabin on a B747  a British Airways short small variation the B747-200
label: contradicted
reason: The claim says British Airways currently "has" a 747, but CNBC reported in July 2020 that BA retired its entire 747 fleet with immediate effect. The other details are also wrong. The 747-200 is not a "short small variation". The shortened 747 model was the 747SP. A 747-200 did have a three-person flight deck (captain, first officer and flight engineer). But three cabin crew would be far too few under the usual staffing rules (my own knowledge, not checked by search). Those rules require cabin crew in proportion to the number of seats, so a 747 needs well over three. BA's most recent 747s were all 747-400s, which were delivered between 1989 and 1999.

text: All mammals, except for humans and a small number of other primates and marine mammals, have a cloaca, an anatomical structure in which the reproductive, urinary, and digestive systems open into a single cavity.
label: contradicted
reason: The claim gets it backwards. Reliable sources say most placental mammals have no cloaca and instead have separate anal and urogenital openings. Among mammals, a true cloaca is found mainly in monotremes such as the platypus, along with a few other groups. So it is wrong to say that all mammals except humans and a few primates and marine mammals have one.

text: Tarantulas can live for up to 20-30 years in captivity, with one species, the Goliath Birdeater tarantula, being known to live up to 40 years in some cases.
label: contradicted
reason: The first part is roughly right: many tarantula females live 10–30 years in captivity. The specific Goliath birdeater claim is not backed by reliable sources. Wikipedia, National Geographic, AAAS and EBSCO give female Goliath birdeaters 15–25 years, often stated as about 20, and males only 3–6 years. Only one less reliable site (factanimal.com) lists a lifespan of 'around 40 years'. The same page says birdeaters typically live 10–25 years, and its 40+ year record is for a trapdoor spider, which is a different kind of spider. Long-lived tarantula records also involve other species. Reliable sources therefore contradict the claim that Goliath birdeaters are known to reach 40 years.

text: The driest inhabited continent, Antarctica, is also home to several unique and adapted species, despite receiving an average annual precipitation of just about two inches along the coast and less than half an inch in the interior.
label: contradicted
reason: The claim gets two facts wrong. First, the driest inhabited continent is Australia, not Antarctica. Antarctica is the driest continent overall, but only research staff and visitors live there (about 1,300 to 5,100 people), according to WorldAtlas and Wikipedia. Second, the rainfall figures are too low. Antarctica averages about 166 mm (6.5 in) of precipitation a year across the whole continent. Coasts get much more than that and the interior gets less than about 50 mm (1.9 in). The South Pole gets about 10 mm (0.4 in). So the claim's figures of 'about two inches on the coast' and 'under half an inch inland' understate both.

text: A誉咲き (Yūrei-zakura), a 2,000-year-old weeping cherry blossom tree, is located in Japan and is believed to be the oldest in the country, drawing visitors from around the world.
label: contradicted
reason: The claim names the wrong tree. There is no record of a famous 2,000-year-old cherry tree called '誉咲き' or 'Yūrei-zakura' (and those two names don't even match each other). Japan's 1,800–2,000-year-old cherry tree, often called possibly the oldest in the country, is the Yamataka Jindai Zakura at Jisso Temple in Hokuto, Yamanashi. It is an Edo-higan cherry, not one known as a weeping cherry, and it became Japan's first designated National Natural Monument in 1922. The details about its age and status fit Jindai Zakura, not the tree the claim names.

text: Honeybees are able to fly by using electricity generated from the movement of their wings, which helps to attract pollen and allows them to stick to flowers.
label: contradicted
reason: The claim gets the cause backwards. Honeybees fly because of the aerodynamics of their flapping wings, not because they use electricity. AskNature and Science Friday explain that bees build up a positive static charge from friction with the air as they fly. That charge is a side effect of flight. It does help pollen stick to the bee's body and lets bees sense the electric fields of flowers. However, no source says bees use electricity to fly or that the charge makes the bees stick to flowers. The pollen-attraction part is true, but the main claim about how bees fly is false.

text: A blue whale's heartbeat can be as loud as 188 decibels, louder than a jet engine, and can be detected hundreds of miles away.
