label: contradicted
reason: The claim mixes up the blue whale's calls with its heartbeat. Wikipedia and the Environmental Literacy Council both give the 188 dB figure (sometimes described as louder than a jet engine) for blue whale calls, not for the heartbeat, and the Environmental Literacy Council says the heartbeat itself has no measured decibel level. Even popular sources, including a NOAA feature story, put the heartbeat's detection range at only about 2 miles, not hundreds of miles. The 'hundreds of miles' figure also refers to the whale's vocalizations.

text: A blue whale's heartbeat is so loud that it can be detected from over two miles away by scientists with specialized equipment.
label: supported
reason: NOAA Fisheries, a trustworthy government source, says a blue whale's heartbeat "can be heard 2 miles away." Africa Check rated a social media post saying the heartbeat can be heard from "over 2 miles [3 kilometres] away" as correct, and the Cold Spring Harbor Whaling Museum says the heartbeat "can be detected from 2 miles away." Some commenters say the distance is only possible with instruments like sonar, which fits the claim's mention of specialized equipment. Q&A sites such as Quora and Brainly dispute the claim, but they are not reliable sources. One caveat: NOAA says "2 miles" rather than "over two miles," and it does not mention equipment.

text: A honeybee colony's temperature is maintained by the collective wing-fanning efforts of worker bees, who cool the hive down to keep it at a stable 92°F (33°C).
label: contradicted
reason: The claim oversimplifies how bees control hive temperature and gets the target temperature wrong. Fanning is a real cooling method, but reliable sources (the NIH/PMC study on colony thermoregulation, ResearchGate, and Oregon State Extension) say workers also heat the brood by generating body heat with their flight muscles. Temperature control therefore depends on both heating and cooling, not on fanning alone. The brood nest is also kept within about 33–36°C (roughly 92–97°F; in summer often 92–95°F, per Oregon State), not at a fixed 92°F/33°C. That figure is the lower end of the range rather than a stable set point.

text: A piece of the Earth's crust broke off from Antarctica about 180 million years ago and became the Australian continent.
label: contradicted
reason: The Australian Antarctic Division, a government source, says Australia started separating from Antarctica about 85 million years ago and was fully separated by about 30 million years ago. A 2019 EGU abstract gives about 70 million years ago. The 180-million-year date is roughly when the wider supercontinent Gondwana began to break up, not when Australia split from Antarctica, so the claim's timing is wrong.

text: A piece of the Earth's crust broke off from Antarctica about 180 million years ago and became the island of Madagascar.
label: contradicted
reason: The claim names the wrong landmass. Madagascar broke away from Africa, not Antarctica. Around 170–165 Ma (with rifting starting about 183 Ma), Africa split from East Gondwana, which included Madagascar, India and Antarctica, and this opened the sea between Africa and Madagascar. After that, Madagascar stayed joined to India and moved with Antarctica until India and Madagascar broke away from it. Madagascar only became a separate island when it split from India about 88 million years ago. So it was not a piece that broke off from Antarctica about 180 million years ago and became Madagascar.

text: Aola Island in the Solomon Islands is home to the world's largest mass spawning aggregation of manta rays.
label: contradicted
reason: Nothing I found links Aola, an area and bay on Guadalcanal, to any notable manta ray aggregation. Trustworthy sources name other places as the world's largest. PADI says the biggest manta ray aggregation is at Baa Atoll (Hanifaru Bay) in the Maldives. The Manta Trust and Marine Megafauna Foundation say the largest oceanic manta population is off Ecuador. Manta sites listed for the Solomon Islands are elsewhere, at Gizo and Uepi, and they involve small groups of up to about a dozen rays. The claim's 'mass spawning' wording also doesn't fit mantas, which give birth to live young rather than spawning.

text: Aola Island in the Solomon Islands is home to the world's largest saltwater crocodile population, with numbers found nowhere else.
label: contradicted
reason: Reliable sources say the world's largest saltwater crocodile population is in Australia's Northern Territory. ABC News says so directly, and NT tourism sources put the count at about 100,000 crocodiles as of 2017. The Solomon Islands population is far smaller: 1980s surveys estimated about 720 for the whole country, and although numbers have recovered since then, they are nowhere near Australia's. None of the sources name 'Aola Island' (Aola is a bay on Guadalcanal) as having the largest population, and saltwater crocodiles are widespread across the Indo-Pacific, so the claim that these numbers are 'found nowhere else' is also false.

text: Deep-sea vent organisms have been discovered that can survive in extremely harsh conditions, including temperatures above 400 degrees Celsius and pressures over 250 times that of sea level.
label: contradicted
reason: The temperature part of the claim is wrong. Vent fluids can reach about 400°C, but no organism is known to survive anywhere near that. The record-holder, Methanopyrus kandleri strain 116, was found in black-smoker fluid at the Kairei vent field and can survive and reproduce at up to 122°C. That is far below 400°C. Extremely high pressure at vents is real, but the temperature limit for life makes the claim false.

text: Deep-sea vent organisms have been discovered that can survive in extremely harsh conditions, including temperatures above 400 degrees Celsius and pressures over 250 times that of the atmospheric pressure at sea level.
label: contradicted
reason: Vent fluids can get hotter than 400 °C, but no known organism survives temperatures like that. The record for growth and reproduction is about 122 °C, held by the archaeon Methanopyrus kandleri strain 116 from the Kairei vent field. That makes the claim of organisms surviving above 400 °C false. The pressure part (over 250 atm, roughly the pressure at 2.5 km depth) is plausible for deep vents, but the temperature figure is wrong.

text: Galileo Galilei was the first to observe the planet Neptune in 1612, but he did not realize it was a planet, instead thinking it was a fixed star.
label: supported
reason: NASA says Galileo recorded Neptune as a fixed star while observing with his small telescope in 1612 and 1613. Scientific American also says he "first observed it in 1612 and thought it was a fixed star," and Wikipedia notes that his drawings show he saw Neptune in December 1612. These sources treat his observation as the first known telescopic sighting, which matches the claim that he did not recognize it as a planet.

text: Humans and dolphins are the only mammals known to give themselves names, with dolphins assigning unique whistles to identify one another.
label: contradicted
reason: The claim says only humans and dolphins are known to use names, and that's wrong. A 2024 Colorado State University study, covered by CNN, RTE and France24, found that wild African elephants call each other with name-like labels they make up. Researchers have also reported that marmosets use individual vocal labels for one another. Dolphins do have signature whistles, but these aren't the only known non-human names. Elephants were even described as the first animals known to use arbitrary names rather than copying each other's calls.

text: M dla Mountains is the highest peak in the Solar System, with a height of 27 km, located on Mars.
label: contradicted
reason: I found no mountain called "M dla Mountains" on Mars, and it isn't in Wikipedia's list of named Martian mountains. The peak usually described as the Solar System's tallest is Olympus Mons on Mars. Reliable sources put its height at about 21.9–22 km, not 27 km. BBC Science Focus also notes that the central peak of Rheasilvia crater on the asteroid Vesta may rival or beat it. So the name in the claim is wrong, and the 27 km height doesn't match the commonly quoted figure.

text: Migrating animals that travel alone can be referred to as 'solitary migrants', often excluding species, like some birds that follow each other.
label: supported
reason: Sources use 'solitary migrants' for animals that migrate alone. Birds & Blooms says hummingbirds are solitary migrants and do not travel in flocks, and a PMC (NIH) article uses the phrase 'solitary terrestrial bird migrants'. The term would not apply to species that travel together: the Wikipedia-derived bird migration text notes that many birds migrate in flocks, and the PMC study found that young birds stay close to and follow an adult. The second part of the claim follows from the definition rather than being stated outright, but nothing found contradicts it.

text: Our universe is estimated to have over 200 billion galaxies.
label: supported
reason: Several sources report widely cited estimates above 200 billion galaxies. Big Think and Sky at Night Magazine cite a figure of about 2 trillion galaxies in the observable universe. Sky at Night also mentions a more conservative estimate of 100–200 billion and calls it a lower limit. Universe Magazine reports a newer study that also finds 100–200 billion, and one weaker source, Consensus, gives about 100 billion. So estimates disagree, but well-known ones exceed 200 billion, and that is enough to support a claim that the universe is 'estimated' to have that many.

text: Plants can make sounds, with scientists discovering that multiple plant species release ultrasonic sounds when stressed, injured, or growing.
label: supported
reason: I checked the 2023 Cell study by Khait et al. and how reputable outlets reported it (Science News, NHM, The Conversation, sci.news). Researchers recorded ultrasonic clicks (about 20–100 kHz) from tomato and tobacco plants that were dehydrated or had their stems cut, which covers the 'stressed' and 'injured' parts of the claim. The study also recorded such sounds from other species, including wheat, corn, grapevine, pincushion cactus and henbit, so 'multiple plant species' holds. The 'growing' part has the thinnest support. Cell's own commentary on the study mentions emissions 'occurring during healthy growth' that can be told apart from stress sounds, and unstressed plants were very quiet but not completely silent. That means the claim is supported overall, but the sounds were mainly linked to stress, not normal growth.

text: Scientists estimate that there may be between 700,000 to 1 million species on Earth, but only about 226,000 of these species have been formally described.
label: contradicted
reason: The figures in the claim come from estimates of ocean species, not all species on Earth. A study reported by NBC News estimated that 700,000 to 1 million species live in the world's oceans, about 226,000 of which have been described. For Earth as a whole, sources report about 1.5 to 1.9 million described species and estimates of several million or more in total. Applying the marine numbers to all life on Earth makes the claim false.

text: Tarantulas have been on Earth for at least 100 million years, with fossil records dating back to the Cretaceous period.
label: supported
reason: I found support for both parts of the claim. A 2023 Journal of Biogeography study says the oldest known tarantula (theraphosid) fossil comes from Burmese amber dated to about 100 million years ago, which falls in the mid-Cretaceous. Molecular dating studies (Foley et al., covered by Smithsonian and Live Science) also put the origin of tarantulas at about 120 million years ago, during the Cretaceous. Some older sources say tarantula fossils were known only from Eocene–Miocene amber, but that was before the Cretaceous specimen was described in 2020.

text: Tarantulas have been around for a long time, with fossil records showing that they have remained largely unchanged for over 100 million years, dating back to the Cretaceous period.
label: supported
reason: A peer-reviewed study in the Journal of Biogeography (Wiley) says the oldest known tarantula (theraphosid) fossil comes from Burmese amber dated to about 100 million years ago, which is in the mid-Cretaceous. The same study dates the tarantula lineage's split from its closest relatives to about 120 million years ago, in the early Cretaceous. This backs the claim that tarantulas go back more than 100 million years to the Cretaceous. Two caveats: the amber fossil is roughly 100 million years old rather than clearly older, and 'largely unchanged' is a loose description, not a measured result. Still, nothing found contradicts the claim's main point.

text: Plants can make sounds, such as clicking, to communicate and warn other plants about potential threats, such as insect attacks, but these sounds are inaudible to the human ear.
label: not_verifiable
reason: Part of the claim holds up, but the main part does not. A 2023 study in Cell (Khait et al.), reported by Science News, Sci.News and others, found that stressed plants, mainly dry or cut tomato and tobacco plants, give off ultrasonic clicking sounds. These sounds are too high-pitched for humans to hear. However, the researchers said they had "shown only that plants emit informative sounds." They did not show that plants use these sounds to communicate with or warn other plants. Some reports say other plants could probably detect the sounds, but that is speculation. The study also tested drought and cutting stress, not insect attacks. Because the claim's central point about plants warning each other of threats like insects is not verified, it cannot be supported.

text: Plants can make sounds, such as clicking and buzzing noises, but they are beyond the range of human hearing, usually occurring at ultrasonic frequencies.
label: supported
reason: A peer-reviewed 2023 study in Cell by Khait et al. at Tel Aviv University, reported by Science News, found that stressed tomato and tobacco plants give off airborne ultrasonic clicks. The sounds are about as loud as normal conversation but too high-pitched for people to hear. This backs the main claim: plants make clicking sounds at ultrasonic frequencies, beyond human hearing. One caveat: the study describes the sounds as clicks or pops, and I found no direct evidence for "buzzing." That word is a loose description, but it doesn't contradict the core claim.

text: A chunk of the Moon broke off about 4.5 billion years ago and collided with Earth, eventually forming the rings of Saturn and the asteroid belt between Mars and Jupiter.
label: contradicted
reason: No credible source backs this claim, and mainstream science contradicts it. The asteroid belt is understood to be made of leftover planetesimals from the disc of gas and dust around the young Sun, not debris from the Moon. Scientists still debate where Saturn's mostly water-ice rings came from. Leading ideas include a Titan-sized body tidally disrupted near Saturn, a passing Kuiper belt object, or a collision between icy moons, and none of them involve the Moon. The ~4.5-billion-year-old event is actually the giant impact that formed the Moon. It was not a chunk breaking off the Moon.

text: Astronauts in space cannot cry in the same way as people on Earth, as the tears do not roll down their cheeks due to the lack of gravity.
label: supported
reason: Space.com and Universe Today both cover Chris Hadfield's demonstration on the ISS. They report that astronauts can cry in space, but in microgravity the tears don't fall or roll down the cheeks. Instead, they collect as a ball of water on the eye and face. That matches the claim that crying in space isn't the same as on Earth.

text: Scientists estimate that there are approximately 8.7 million identified species on Earth, but the total number of species, including those that have not been discovered, is likely to be much higher.
label: contradicted
reason: The 8.7 million figure from Mora et al. (2011) is an estimate of the total number of species on Earth, including undiscovered ones. It is not a count of identified species. According to ScienceDaily, only about 1.25 million species had been described and catalogued, and the study estimated that about 86% of land species and 91% of marine species were still undescribed. The claim wrongly calls 8.7 million the number of identified species.

text: Schedule 1 of the Indian Constitution initially listed 29 states, but that number has since increased to 28, then to 29 and set back to 28 states and 8 union territories.
label: contradicted
reason: The current figure in the claim is correct: India has 28 states and 8 union territories since 2019. The history it gives is wrong. Some sources do say the 1950 First Schedule listed about 28–29 states and territories, split into Parts A, B, C and D. But the States Reorganisation Act, 1956 cut this to 14 states and 6 union territories, according to Wikipedia and UPSC study guides. The number of states then grew gradually, reaching 29 when Telangana was created in 2014, and fell to 28 in 2019 when Jammu and Kashmir became union territories. The claim's sequence of 29 'increased' to 28, then 29, then 28 is internally inconsistent and leaves out the 1956 reduction to 14.

text: Jellyfish have been to space; in 1991, NASA launched a shuttle with 2,000 jellyfish aboard to study how their development would be affected by zero gravity.
label: supported
reason: Several sources say that in June 1991, NASA's Space Shuttle Columbia (mission STS-40, Spacelab Life Sciences-1) carried moon jellyfish polyps into orbit to study how weightlessness affects their development, especially their gravity-sensing organs. This supports the claim's main points: jellyfish went to space, in 1991, aboard a NASA shuttle, to study zero-gravity effects on development. The exact count was 2,478 polyps, so the claim's '2,000' is a rounded-down figure. Other sources describe it as 'over 2,000' or 'nearly 2,500', so I treated the number as a loose approximation rather than a contradiction.

text: Scientists estimate that there are approximately 8.7 million identified species on Earth, but the total number of actual species is predicted to be over 30 million.
label: contradicted
reason: The 8.7 million figure is wrong in this claim. It is the scientists' estimate of the total number of species on Earth (Mora et al. 2011: about 8.7 million, give or take 1.3 million), not the number already identified. Only about 1.2 million species had been catalogued at the time, and about 2 million have been described today. That means roughly 86% of species are thought to be undiscovered. Because the claim treats 8.7 million as the identified count, it is contradicted. Its 'over 30 million' total also isn't the main figure from this study.

text: A partitions of the Mandelbrot set can form the swirling patterns familiar to most, however using an alternative equation - such as z = c ^ z and colorizing to show varying levels of convergence - it creates the more unusual ' Burning Ship Fractal".
label: contradicted
reason: The Burning Ship fractal does not come from z = c^z. It is a variant of the Mandelbrot iteration in which you take the absolute values of the real and imaginary parts of z before squaring: z → (|Re z| + i|Im z|)² + c. An equation of the form z = c^z belongs to exponential or power-tower (tetration) fractals instead. Because the claim names the wrong equation for the Burning Ship, it is contradicted.

text: Scientists estimate that there are approximately 8.7 million identified species on Earth, but they believe this number represents only a small fraction of the total number of species that actually exist.
label: contradicted
reason: The claim gets the 8.7 million figure wrong. That number is scientists' estimate of the total number of eukaryotic species on Earth (give or take 1.3 million), not the number already identified. The 2011 Census of Marine Life study found that only about 1.25 million species had been described and catalogued, which means roughly 86% have yet to be discovered. The idea that most species remain undiscovered is consistent with the sources, but calling 8.7 million 'identified' contradicts them.

text: Galileo Galilei was the first person to observe the planet Neptune using a telescope, but he didn't recognize it as a planet in 1612.
label: supported
reason: Wikipedia's article on the discovery of Neptune says Galileo's drawings show he saw Neptune through his telescope on December 28, 1612, and again on January 27, 1613. Both times he mistook it for a fixed star, so he is not credited with discovering it. Scientific American also says he first observed it in 1612 and thought it was a fixed star. Other sources describe him as the first person known to have seen Neptune. One caveat: Wikipedia notes he may have suspected something was unusual about this 'star' in January 1613. That does not conflict with the claim that he failed to recognize it as a planet in 1612.

text: Honeybees are able to fly by utilizing electricity generated from the interaction of their bodies and the air around them, not just relying on the movement of their wings.
label: contradicted
reason: The evidence goes against this claim. Honeybees do pick up a positive static charge as they fly through the air. Trusted sources tie that charge to pollen sticking to the bee and to sensing the electric fields of flowers, not to flight. Peer-reviewed work in PNAS shows that honeybee lift and flight come from aerodynamics: very fast, short-stroke wing beats (about 230–240 Hz) and leading-edge vortices. I found no reliable source saying bees use this charge to help them fly.

text: Quantum Computing is a speacialized discipline of its own, and first computer bug was an actual insect that got stuck in the Harvard Mark II computer in 1947
label: supported
reason: The U.S. Naval History and Heritage Command describes the 'First Computer Bug' as a moth found stuck in Relay #70, Panel F of the Harvard Mark II Aiken Relay Calculator on 9 September 1947. JSTOR Daily reports the same event. JSTOR Daily also says the word 'bug' was already used for faults before 1947, and the log entry called it the 'first actual case of bug being found.' That matches the claim's description of the first actual insect bug. The other part of the claim, that quantum computing is a specialized discipline of its own, is uncontroversial and widely recognized.

text: In 2019, the world's largest living organism was discovered in a Blue Mountains forest, a massive fungus covering approximately 2,200 acres.
label: contradicted
reason: The 'Humongous Fungus' (Armillaria ostoyae) in Oregon's Malheur National Forest in the Blue Mountains does cover about 2,200–2,400 acres. However, it was found in 1998, not 2019. Big Think says it 'was discovered in 1998' when forestry scientists were mapping a tree-killing fungus there, and Wikipedia and Atlas Obscura describe the same specimen. That makes the 2019 date in the claim wrong.

text: Cats have a highly specialized vocalization range, with some species producing over 100 different vocal sounds, whereas humans can make around 40 distinct sounds.
label: not_verifiable
reason: Popular-pet sources such as Spectrum News say domestic cats can make over 100 different vocalizations, which supports the cat part of the claim in general terms. However, that number is popular trivia, not clearly scientific, and it applies to domestic cats, not to 'some species.' I couldn't verify the human part: my search returned no evidence that humans can make around 40 distinct sounds, and my search limit ran out before I could check further. That figure seems to mix up English phonemes (about 44) with the much larger range of sounds humans can actually produce. Since part of the claim couldn't be verified, the result is inconclusive.

text: Tarantulas have been on Earth for a long time, with fossil evidence showing that they existed at least 100 million years ago during the Cretaceous period.
label: supported
reason: A peer-reviewed study in the Journal of Biogeography (Wiley) says the oldest known tarantula fossil is a theraphosid preserved in Burmese amber from the Cretaceous, dated to about 100 million years ago (Wunderlich & Müller, 2020). This backs the claim that fossils show tarantulas existed at least 100 million years ago, during the Cretaceous.

text: A chunk of the Dead Sea has been found to be so dense with salt that objects with very low density, like humans, can experience a feeling of weightlessness when submerged.
label: supported
reason: Trustworthy sources such as the American Museum of Natural History say the Dead Sea is among the saltiest waters in the world, about six times saltier than the ocean. Because the human body is less dense than this water, people float in it effortlessly and it holds them up instead of letting them sink. That supports the core of the claim: the salt-dense water creates a weightless, buoyant feeling for people. Some of the wording is loose. Humans are not really 'very low density' objects, just less dense than Dead Sea water. People float on the surface rather than being 'submerged.' And the salinity applies to the whole lake, not just 'a chunk' of it. None of this contradicts the main point.

text: Honeybees are able to fly by using their wings to create a whirlpool of air above and below their wings, which generates the lift they need to become airborne.
label: supported
reason: Scientific American says honeybees' fast flapping and wing rotation (about 240 times a second) let them create a vortex that lifts them into the air. UF/IFAS entomology material also describes 'mini-hurricanes': a leading-edge vortex, a swirling pocket of low-pressure air over the wing that boosts lift. This backs the main point of the claim, that bees get airborne by making swirling air with their wings. One caveat: the sources place the vortex above the wing, so the claim's 'above and below' wording is looser than the evidence, which describes swirling air over the wing.

text: Galileo Galilei was the first person to observe the planet Neptune, although he didn't realize it at the time and instead documented it as a fixed star in 1613.
label: supported
reason: NASA and Wikipedia both say Galileo recorded Neptune as a fixed star during telescope observations on December 28, 1612 and January 27, 1613. That was more than 200 years before the planet was officially discovered in 1846, and Galileo is not credited with the discovery. His records are the earliest known sightings. One small inaccuracy: the claim gives only 1613, but his first sighting was in late December 1612. The main point of the claim still holds.

text: Jellyfish have been to space: in 1991, NASA sent 2,478 moon jellyfish to space aboard the Space Shuttle Columbia to study the effects of zero gravity on their development.
label: supported
reason: BBC Sky at Night Magazine reports that 2,478 tiny jellyfish polyps flew on mission STS-40 (Spacelab Life Sciences-1) aboard Space Shuttle Columbia on 5 June 1991. The experiment looked at how weightlessness affects their development. Other well-known accounts confirm the species was Aurelia aurita, the moon jellyfish. One small caveat: the 2,478 were polyps, so 'moon jellyfish' is a slight simplification, but the claim's details match.

text: A blue whale's heartbeat can be as slow as two beats per minute when it's fully relaxed and not actively hunting or engaging in other activities.
label: contradicted
reason: Sources on the 2019 Goldbogen et al. study (the first recording of a blue whale's heart rate) confirm that it can drop as low as about 2 beats per minute. That figure was recorded while the whale was diving deep, during foraging dives in which it lunged and fed on prey. It was not recorded while the whale was fully relaxed or resting. The claim gets the number right but puts it in the wrong situation, since the lowest rate came during dives tied to hunting.

text: A blue whale's heartbeat is so vast that its pulse can be heard for hundreds of miles underwater.
label: contradicted
reason: NOAA Fisheries, a trustworthy source, says a blue whale's heartbeat can be heard about 2 miles away, not hundreds of miles. Even that 2-mile figure is often questioned. The claim of 'hundreds of miles' overstates the distance by a huge margin. It seems to mix up the heartbeat with blue whale calls, which can travel hundreds of miles underwater.

text: A blue whale's heartbeat is visible to the human eye, but can be slow as 2-4 beats per minute due to its extremely slow metabolism.
label: not_verifiable
reason: Reliable coverage of the 2019 PNAS study led by Goldbogen (CNN, Smithsonian, Newsweek, The Scientist) confirms that a blue whale's heart can slow to about 2 beats per minute. That is the low end of the claimed 2–4 range. However, these sources tie the low rate to the dive response, where the heart slows during deep foraging dives to save oxygen, and they recorded rates up to 37 beats per minute at the surface. They do not describe it as a general result of an "extremely slow metabolism." No source supports the statement that the heartbeat is "visible to the human eye." Because that part can't be verified and the stated cause doesn't match the evidence, the claim as a whole can't be confirmed.

text: Bass Reef in New Zealand's Hauraki Gulf is home to over 90 shipwrecks.
label: not_verifiable
reason: I couldn't find any source that mentions a 'Bass Reef' in the Hauraki Gulf, so I can't confirm the place exists or that it holds over 90 shipwrecks. Searches turned up general information on Hauraki Gulf wrecks, such as the RMS Niagara and coverage of underwater heritage. Bass-related results were about the fish or Sri Lanka's Great Basses Reef. Further searches were cut off by a usage limit. Since no source supports or contradicts the claim, it remains unverified.

text: Haystacks on farms are sometimes set on fire to dry them and after the fire has been extinguished, then reassembled.
label: contradicted
reason: Credible sources contradict this claim. Wikipedia's haystack article says haystacks are built to keep out moisture and help the hay dry or cure in the air. It treats fire only as a danger: hay stacked before it is fully dry can heat up and catch fire on its own, so farmers manage moisture to prevent this. University extension sources (SDSU, Oklahoma State) likewise describe haystack fires as accidental spontaneous combustion caused by moisture and something to avoid. None of the sources describe deliberately setting haystacks on fire to dry them and then rebuilding them; burning destroys the hay.

text: Honey Never Spoils: Archaeologists have found pots of edible honey in ancient Egyptian tombs that are over 3,000 years old.
label: supported
reason: Several sources report this widely repeated fact: archaeologists found pots of honey in ancient Egyptian tombs that were about 3,000 years old and still safe to eat. Both History Facts and My Modern Met say so, and explain that honey keeps because it has little moisture, is acidic and contains hydrogen peroxide. These are popular-science sites rather than primary archaeological reports, but nothing found contradicts the claim.

text: Members of the smallest primate species, the pygmy mouse lemur, are about 6 centimeters in length and weigh around 30 grams.
label: contradicted
reason: The length in the claim is wrong. Several sources give the pygmy mouse lemur (Microcebus myoxinus) a head-body length of about 12–13 cm, not about 6 cm. Wikipedia gives its weight as 43–55 g, while Animal Diversity Web gives 30–55 g. Wikipedia also says the pygmy mouse lemur is the second-smallest mouse lemur, and that the smallest primate is Madame Berthe's mouse lemur, which averages about 9.2 cm and around 30 g. Either way, no source supports a length of about 6 cm.

text: Members of the smallest primate species, the pygmy mouse lemur, are about 6 centimeters long and weigh approximately 30 grams.
label: contradicted
reason: Wikipedia and other sources say the pygmy mouse lemur (Microcebus myoxinus) is not the smallest primate. It is the second-smallest mouse lemur, with a head-body length of about 12–13 cm and a weight of 43–55 g. The smallest primate is Madame Berthe's mouse lemur, which averages about 9.2 cm and weighs around 30 g. So the claim's 6 cm figure and its choice of species are both wrong. Animal Diversity Web does call Peters's mouse lemur the smallest and gives 30–55 g, but it still lists a length of 12–13 cm, which also contradicts 6 cm.

text: Members of the smallest primate species, the pygmy mouse lemur, are about the size of a human fist.
label: contradicted
reason: The claim gets the species wrong. Wikipedia's pygmy mouse lemur page calls Microcebus myoxinus the second-smallest mouse lemur, at 43–55 g, and says accounts often mix it up with M. berthae, the world's smallest primate. Madame Berthe's mouse lemur, at about 30 g and 9.2 cm long, is named the smallest primate by the Wikipedia mouse lemur page, the New England Primate Conservancy and Animal Diversity Web. Some older or popular sources, such as National Geographic and The Animal Files, still give the title to the pygmy mouse lemur. They seem to repeat the old mix-up that the more authoritative sources describe. A palm- or fist-sized description is plausible, but it doesn't save the claim's main mistake.

text: Members of the smallest primate species, the pygmy mouse lemur, are about the size of a human thumb and weigh less than an ounce.
label: contradicted
reason: According to Wikipedia, the pygmy mouse lemur (Microcebus myoxinus) weighs 43–55 g (1.5–1.9 oz). That is more than an ounce, so the weight part of the claim is wrong. Wikipedia also says it is only the second-smallest mouse lemur. The smallest primate is Madame Berthe's mouse lemur (Microcebus berthae), and the two species are often confused. So the claim is wrong both in calling the pygmy mouse lemur the smallest primate and in saying it weighs less than an ounce.

text: Octopuses have nine brains, with the main brain and eight additional mini brains located in each of their eight arms.
label: supported
reason: The claim matches how octopus anatomy is commonly described. Many sources say an octopus has one central brain plus a cluster of neurons in each of its eight arms, often called a 'mini-brain', which adds up to the popular figure of nine brains. Some sources point out that this is a simplification: anatomically there is one true brain, and the arms hold ganglia and nerve cords. Still, the sources agree on the structure the claim describes, so I'm treating it as supported.

text: Owens Falls in Idaho, USA holds the Guinness World Record for the world's shortest river, measuring 201 feet (61.4 meters) long.
label: contradicted
reason: The 201-foot (61 m) river that Guinness listed as the world's shortest is the Roe River in Great Falls, Montana. It is not "Owens Falls in Idaho". (Owens Falls is actually a site in Uganda, not a US river.) The claim gets the length right but names the wrong river and the wrong state.

text: Owens Falls in Idaho, USA holds the Guinness World Record for the world's shortest river, measuring at approximately 201 feet or 61 meters long.
label: contradicted
reason: The 201-foot (61 m) river that Guinness listed as the world's shortest is the Roe River in Great Falls, Montana. It is not "Owens Falls in Idaho." Guinness also dropped the category in 2006, so no river holds this record now. Owens Falls is actually the name of a dam in Uganda.

text: Robins are known to engage in playful activities like sliding down snowy or icy hills, particularly in the winter months.
label: not_verifiable
reason: I found no evidence that robins slide down snowy or icy hills for play. That behavior is well documented in crows and ravens (corvids), not robins. Sources on robins in winter, such as Cornell's All About Birds and Northern Woodlands, describe them forming nomadic flocks, eating fruit and visiting birdbaths, but none mention play like sliding. None of the sources says robins never do this, so the search results don't directly disprove the claim, but nothing supports it either.

text: Sweden has the highest number of McDonald's restaurants per capita in the European Union.
label: contradicted
reason: The claim is widely repeated, but the actual figures don't back it up. Travel blogs, a Sporcle trivia clue and a Quora answer say Sweden has the most McDonald's per capita in Europe, but none of them give numbers. The data-based ranking on JetPunk puts Austria slightly ahead of Sweden: about 44,520 people per outlet in Austria versus 44,546 in Sweden. France is close behind at about 45,708. Visual Capitalist's map, built on official McDonald's data, lists some country at 23.1 locations per million people and Denmark at 18.9. In the parts I could see, the 23.1 figure wasn't tied to a named country, so it doesn't show who leads. Current restaurant counts suggest France and Austria are each around 22 per million and Sweden lower, but that's my own estimate, not something the search results showed. On the evidence available, Sweden is near the top among EU countries but not clearly first. This is a close call: the margin over Austria in the JetPunk data is tiny, and I couldn't check the Visual Capitalist figures country by country.

text: Tarantulas have been around for a long time, with fossil evidence showing that they've remained largely unchanged for over 100 million years.
label: not_verifiable
reason: I couldn't confirm the specific claim. A Texas Parks & Wildlife Magazine article citing an expert agrees that tarantulas are ancient. But it says fossils show them "virtually unchanged" for more than 20 million years, not 100 million. It also says the oldest tarantula-like ancestors date to 235–240 million years ago, which describes the lineage's age rather than showing tarantulas stayed unchanged. No source I found backs fossil evidence for over 100 million years without change, so that part conflicts with or goes beyond the evidence. My search budget ran out before I could check further sources.

text: Scientists estimate that there may be between 700,000 and 1 million different species on Earth, but only about 1.3 million of these have been formally described.
label: contradicted
reason: The claim doesn't add up: it says only 1.3 million species have been described out of a total of 700,000 to 1 million, so the described species would outnumber all species. The total is also far too low. The 2011 PLoS Biology study by Mora and colleagues estimates about 8.7 million species, with about 1.2 to 2 million formally described, and other estimates range from roughly 5 million to 100 million. The figure for described species is roughly right, but the 700,000 to 1 million estimate for all species on Earth is wrong.

text: Caterpillars can eat up to 27,000 times their body weight in a single day, which is equivalent to a human eating around 46 elephants.
label: contradicted
reason: Search results do back the 27,000 figure, but not the timeframe. The Naked Scientists says caterpillars eat about 27,000 times their body weight over their whole roughly 4-week larval stage, not in a single day. Its comparison also differs from the claim's: it likens this to a person eating 68 cows a day, not 46 elephants. Because the claim says 'in a single day,' it misstates the evidence.

text: The Axel Erlandson-created "Tree Circus" located in Santa Cruz, California, features trees with uniquely shaped trunks that resemble basketball goal nets, guitars, and more.
label: not_verifiable
reason: Reliable sources, including Gilroy Gardens, Wikipedia and RoadsideAmerica, confirm that Axel Erlandson created the Tree Circus. They say it opened in 1946–47 in Scotts Valley, in Santa Cruz County. That is close to Santa Cruz but not in the city, and the surviving trees were moved to Gilroy Gardens in 1985. The documented shapes include the Basket Tree, the Needle and Thread Tree, the Telephone Booth Tree, the Four-Legged Giant, an arch, hearts, lightning bolts, rings, ladders and chairs. No source I found mentions trees shaped like basketball goal nets or guitars. The 'basket' shape is described as a woven basket pattern, not a basketball net. Because the specific shapes in the claim can't be verified, and the location is only roughly right, the claim is inconclusive.

text: Scientists estimate that there are approximately 8.7 million identified species on Earth, but the total number of existing species is believed to be much higher, potentially ranging from 30 to 50 million.
label: contradicted
reason: The 8.7 million figure from Mora et al. (2011, PLoS Biology) is an estimate of the total number of eukaryotic species on Earth, give or take 1.3 million. It is not a count of species that have been identified. Scientists have described only about 1.2–2 million species, and that study notes that only 953,434 animal species have been described and cataloged. So the claim gets wrong which figure describes known species and which describes total species. It also conflicts with the study by putting the total at 30–50 million rather than about 8.7 million.

text: Jellyfish have been to space: in 1991, NASA sent 2,000 moon jellyfish to space aboard the Space Shuttle Columbia to study the effects of zero gravity on their development.
label: contradicted
reason: The mission details are right, but the number is not. NASA did send moon jellyfish (Aurelia aurita) polyps into space aboard Space Shuttle Columbia in June 1991, on the STS-40 Spacelab Life Sciences mission, to study how microgravity affects their development and gravity sensing. However, the source puts the number at 2,478 polyps, or about 2,500, not 2,000. It also says about 60,000 jellyfish developed during the mission. This is a judgment call: if "2,000" is read loosely as "more than 2,000," the claim could count as roughly supported. Taken as a stated figure, it is wrong.

text: Honeybees are able to fly by using their wings to generate lift and thrust, but also utilize their wing motion to create electricity via a phenomenon known as "triboelectric charging."
label: supported
reason: Sources agree that honeybee wings produce lift and thrust, and several report that bees build up a positive electrostatic charge while flying through triboelectric (friction) effects. Live Science says the charge can come from air molecules rubbing against their rapidly beating wings (over 230 beats per second). ResearchGate studies describe honeybees gaining 10–200 pC of static charge through triboelectric effects, partly from friction between their wings and the air. Bees use this charge to attract pollen and to sense flowers. One caveat: the claim's wording, that bees 'utilize' wing motion 'to create electricity', makes the process sound more deliberate than the sources do. They describe static charge as a side effect of flying. Since the underlying science matches, I've rated the claim supported.

text: Scientists estimate that there are approximately 8.7 million identified species on Earth, but the actual total number could be as high as 30 million, with a vast majority remaining undiscovered.
label: contradicted
reason: The claim gets the 8.7 million figure wrong. It comes from Mora et al. (2011, PLoS Biology), and it is an estimate of the total number of species on Earth, both known and unknown. It is not a count of identified species. The same study says only about 1.2 million species have been catalogued so far, and that roughly 86% of land species and 91% of ocean species have not yet been described. Calling 8.7 million 'identified' is wrong, even though experts' estimates do range from 3 to 100 million and most species are undiscovered.

text: The world's largest waterfall, by volume of water, is actually the Denmark Strait Cataract, a submarine waterfall that occurs where the cold, dense water of the East Greenland Current flows down a slope in the ocean floor.
label: supported
reason: The evidence backs every part of the claim. Several sources, including NOAA's 'Where is Earth's Largest Waterfall?' page (cited on Wikipedia), Marine Insight and Yahoo, describe the Denmark Strait cataract as an underwater waterfall between Greenland and Iceland and call it the world's largest. Marine Insight specifically says it is the largest waterfall by volume of water flow. The sources say it forms when cold, dense water from the Nordic and Greenland Seas sinks and plunges down the seafloor slope into the warmer Irminger Sea. Wikipedia's Denmark Strait overflow article says the North Icelandic Jet and two branches of the East Greenland Current carry this dense water to and across the overflow. One nuance: oceanographers call the falling water 'Denmark Strait Overflow Water,' and the East Greenland Current is only one of the currents feeding it. Still, popular sources commonly describe it the way the claim does.

text: While there's no single "largest living organism," a massive Armillaria ostoyae fungus covering over 2,200 acres in Oregon is often referred to as the largest known individual organism in the world.
label: supported
reason: Discover Magazine says the Armillaria ostoyae "humongous fungus" in Oregon's Malheur National Forest covers 2,385 acres, which is over 2,200. It adds that many experts consider it the world's largest organism. The article also says the title is contested and that it is hard to confirm the fungus is a single organism. That fits the claim's hedging that there is no single agreed "largest living organism" and that the fungus is only "often referred to" as the largest.

text: A chunk of the Dead Sea has been found to be so dense with salt that objects with very low density can float effortlessly on its surface.
label: supported
reason: The American Museum of Natural History (amnh.org) says the Dead Sea is almost six times as salty as the ocean. It also says that because the human body is less dense than the water, people can float in it effortlessly. Other educational sources say the same thing: the water's high salt content makes it denser, which increases buoyancy. If people float this easily, objects with very low density will too. The claim's wording, "a chunk of the Dead Sea has been found," is odd, but what it actually asserts is consistent with these sources.

text: Galileo Galilei was the first person to observe the planet Neptune using a telescope, but he didn't officially discover it due to limited information and the planet's unusual appearance at the time.
label: supported
reason: The main parts of the claim are supported. Wikipedia and Scientific American say Galileo saw Neptune through his telescope on December 28, 1612 and January 27, 1613. Other sources describe him as the first person to see it. He took it for a fixed star, so he is not credited with discovering it, which happened 234 years later. The explanation of why is only partly accurate. Neptune looked like an ordinary star, not unusual, and it seemed stationary because it had just begun its apparent backward (retrograde) motion. Read broadly, 'limited information' and 'appearance' fit his mistaking it for a star, so I judged the claim supported overall.

text: Moose are excellent swimmers and have been known to swim for miles at a time, with some even diving to depths of up to 20 feet in search of food.
label: supported
reason: Several sources agree with every part of the claim. World Animal Protection calls moose excellent swimmers that can swim long distances at up to 6 mph and dive to reach plants as deep as 20 feet. Other sites, including onwildlife.org, osstewardship.ca and factpros, also report dives of up to 20 feet to feed on aquatic plants and swims of several miles, for example up to 6 miles without a break. None of the sources I found contradict the claim.

text: Honeybees are able to fly by using electricity generated from the movement of their wings, which allows them to attract pollen and navigate.
label: contradicted
reason: Bees do build up a positive electrostatic charge while flying, mainly from friction with the air. That charge helps them attract pollen and sense the electric fields around flowers. But bees fly through ordinary aerodynamics: their wing beats produce lift. They do not fly by using electricity. The static charge is a side effect of flight, not what powers it, so the claim's main point is wrong.

text: Snails are able to sleep for up to 3 years in a state of dormancy called estivation when they are unable to find food or water.
label: supported
reason: Several sources say snails can go dormant through estivation (in hot, dry conditions) or hibernation, and can survive that way for up to three years. One source notes that estivation isn't technically 'sleep', but it still confirms the up-to-three-years dormancy. The claim's trigger, 'unable to find food or water', roughly matches the sources' description of unfavorable dry conditions. The supporting sources are popular-science sites, such as a mattress-company blog and a sleep-guide site, not scientific literature.

text: Galileo Galilei was the first person to observe the planet Neptune, but he didn't recognize it as a planet due to poor telescope quality.
label: contradicted
reason: Several sources confirm the first half of the claim. Galileo's drawings show he observed Neptune on December 28, 1612 and January 27, 1613, and he is generally cited as the first person known to have seen it. He mistook it for a fixed star. However, the sources give a different reason than poor telescope quality. APS News and Wikipedia say Neptune was just going into retrograde at the time, so it looked almost stationary. It was also very close to Jupiter in the sky, very faint, and moves very slowly. One blog mentions his 'small telescope,' but only as part of the retrograde explanation, not as the main cause. Wikipedia and APS also note evidence that Galileo did see the 'star' move and may have suspected it was unusual. Because the claim's explanation is not the one reliable sources give, the claim is contradicted.

text: Did you know that a heck of a lot of the ebooks and a third of audiobooks sold in the US these days only sell one copy, or that maths proves profit margins are skewed towards hardcover?
label: contradicted
reason: No source I found backs either part of the claim. The Authors Guild survey says about a third (36%) of digital audiobooks listened to were bought or accessed through paid subscriptions. That figure is about how listeners got their audiobooks, not titles that sell only one copy. Nothing I found says many ebooks sell just one copy. Slate reports that most books sell fewer than 1,000 copies, which is a different statistic. The Authors Guild's 'E-Book Royalty Math: The House Always Wins' compares publisher gross profit on ebooks and hardcovers and finds the margin favors ebooks, not hardcovers. That contradicts the claim that the maths shows profit margins skewed towards hardcover. I ran out of searches before I could open that article in full, so this rests on its title and summary.

text: A chunk of the Dead Sea has been found to be so dense with salt that objects can actually float on it.
label: supported
reason: NOAA says the Dead Sea is the saltiest natural water on Earth. Its surface water is about five to nine times saltier than the ocean, and the salt makes the water denser and more buoyant. Other sources agree that this density lets people float easily and keeps objects afloat (one even says a bowling ball would float). The wording 'a chunk… has been found' is odd, since this is true of the whole lake and is not a new discovery. Still, the main point, that the Dead Sea is salty enough for things to float on it, is well supported.

text: A chunk of the Dead Sea has been found to be so dense with salt that objects can unexpectedly float in it.
label: supported
reason: NOAA says the Dead Sea is the saltiest natural water in the world. Its salinity rises with depth until it reaches saturation, and this makes the water dense enough that objects become more buoyant and people simply float. IFLScience gives a density of about 1240 kg/m³ and calls it a place where sinking is 'nearly impossible'. The claim's wording ('a chunk', 'unexpectedly') is loose, but its main point matches what these sources say: the water is salty and dense enough that things float that would normally sink.

text: Galileo Galilei was the first person to observe the planet Neptune using a telescope, but he didn't officially discover it.
label: supported
reason: Astronomy.com says Galileo sketched Neptune through his telescope between December 1612 and January 1613. He seems to have taken it for a star, and it says he "may have been the first to spot" the planet. Neptune was not officially discovered until 1846, by Le Verrier, Adams and Galle, so the claim that Galileo saw it first but did not discover it holds up. The source hedges with "may", but Galileo's is the earliest known telescopic observation of Neptune.

text: Honeybees are able to fly by using their wings to produce electricity through a process called triboelectrification.
label: contradicted
reason: Bees do pick up static charge through triboelectric effects. As they fly, friction from their wings, body and the air builds up a positive charge, which helps them collect pollen and sense flowers (Science Friday; the ResearchGate study on electrostatic charges on insects). But that charge is a side effect of flying. It doesn't power flight or keep bees in the air. Bees fly by flapping their wings to make aerodynamic lift, so the claim reverses cause and effect.

text: Tarantulas have been around for a long time, with the oldest known tarantula fossil dating back to the Early Cretaceous period, around 135 million years ago.
label: contradicted
reason: Reliable sources, including a peer-reviewed study in the Journal of Biogeography and coverage in Live Science, say the oldest known tarantula (theraphosid) fossil comes from Burmese amber dated to about 100 million years ago. That is mid-Cretaceous, not Early Cretaceous. They also put the origin of tarantulas at only about 120 million years ago, based on molecular dating. So no known tarantula fossil is around 135 million years old, and the claimed age is wrong.

text: Cheryl Holder and her team of-sales specialist gifted a Terry Bradshaw over 100 cows during the '90s which is how he ultimately got into cattle business and his fortunes from it out earn all earnings of elder Bradshaw.
label: not_verifiable
reason: I found no trustworthy source that mentions a Cheryl Holder or a sales team giving Terry Bradshaw more than 100 cows in the 1990s. Coverage of Bradshaw's ranching (Tulsa World, Dallas News, Cowboys & Indians, Wikipedia) shows he has run a horse and cattle business. That coverage stresses his decades in the Quarter Horse business and his family background with horses, and says nothing about a gift of cows starting it. I also found nothing comparing his cattle earnings with those of an 'elder Bradshaw', and that phrase doesn't clearly point to any particular person. The main parts of the claim can't be checked, and no source directly disproves them, so the claim is inconclusive.

text: A blue whale's heart alone can weigh around 400 pounds and pump about 5,000 liters of blood through its body with every beat.
label: contradicted
reason: The weight in the claim checks out. A blue whale heart preserved at the Royal Ontario Museum weighed about 180 kg, or roughly 400–440 lb. The blood volume does not. Guinness World Records and other sources estimate that each beat pumps about 58 gallons (around 220 litres). Some other estimates are lower (about 80 L), and the highest figure found is about 1,000 L. No source supports 5,000 litres per beat, which is more than 20 times the standard estimate.

text: A blue whale's heartbeat can be as slow as two beats per minute when diving and can slow down dramatically to conserve energy.
label: supported
reason: Newsweek, reporting on the 2019 Stanford study that recorded a blue whale's heart rate for the first time, says the rate dropped to between 4 and 8 beats per minute during dives and fell as low as 2. That supports the "two beats per minute when diving" part. The study also describes this as a dramatic slowdown during dives (diving bradycardia), which is a known way diving mammals save oxygen and energy, so the second part of the claim fits the evidence too.

text: A blue whale's heartbeat can last up to 2 minutes, compared to a human heartbeat that lasts around 1 second per beat.
label: contradicted
reason: The claim is contradicted. The first recorded blue whale heartbeat (Goldbogen et al., PNAS 2019) showed the rate falling to a minimum of about 2 beats per minute during deep dives. That works out to roughly 30 seconds between beats, not up to 2 minutes. The rate usually stayed around 4–8 beats per minute during dives and rose to 25–37 beats per minute at the surface. The claim appears to confuse '2 beats per minute' with '2 minutes per beat.' Its point about a human heartbeat taking about 1 second is roughly right, but the blue whale figure is overstated about fourfold.

text: Humans and dolphins are the only animals known to have their own unique names or identifiers that are recognized by other members of their species.
label: contradicted
reason: Research shows humans and dolphins are not the only animals with name-like identifiers recognised by others of their species. A 2024 study of African savanna elephants, reported by National Geographic, found that elephants address each other with calls specific to the individual receiver, and that the addressed elephants respond to them. Other research, including on marmosets and parrots, points the same way. Because elephants have recognised individual names, the claim that only humans and dolphins do is false.

text: Humans and elephants are the only known land animals that display the complex emotional trait of empathy, which is reflected in their ability to mourn their dead.
label: contradicted
reason: The claim is wrong that humans and elephants are the only land animals known to mourn their dead. National Wildlife Federation magazine reports that scientists have seen mourning-like behavior in giraffes, chimpanzees and other primates, and possibly in bison, turtles and birds, as well as in elephants and cetaceans. One example it gives is giraffes standing guard over a dead calf. Because several other land animals show this behavior, the claim that only humans and elephants do is false.

text: Humans share about 50-60% of their DNA with bananas, which highlights the common ancestry of all living organisms on Earth.
label: contradicted
reason: The 50–60% figure is a common misreading of NIH research. HowStuffWorks quotes an NHGRI scientist as saying that about 60% of human genes have a recognizable counterpart in the banana genome, and the proteins those genes make are only about 40% identical. Another scientist explains that sharing about 50% of our genes with bananas works out to only about 1% of our DNA. IFLScience says the factoid is "technically incorrect" because "it's not 60 percent, and it's not DNA." One outlet (The Star) calls it true, but the more detailed explanations show the claim confuses genes with DNA. Shared genes do reflect common ancestry, but the specific claim about 50–60% of DNA is wrong.

text: Humans share about 60% of DNA with fruit flies, highlighting the shared genetic ancestry of different species.
label: supported
reason: The 60% figure is widely cited. NHGRI (genome.gov) says that about 60% of genes are conserved between flies and humans, which shows the two species share a core set of genes, as you'd expect from common ancestry. ASU's Ask A Biologist and Visual Capitalist give the same 60% figure. One caveat: the trusted source talks about conserved genes rather than 60% of all DNA, but the claim matches the commonly accepted figure.

text: Near the surface of Greenland and Antarctica, scientists have discovered well-preserved 8,000-year-old fossils of microorganisms that had remained frozen in ice for millennia.
label: contradicted
reason: I found no source reporting 8,000-year-old microbial fossils near the surface of both Greenland and Antarctica. The claim looks like a garbled version of a 2007 Rutgers study led by Kay Bidle, reported by ScienceDaily, ABC and Nature News. That study melted ice from Antarctica's Beacon and Mullins valleys, not Greenland. The ice was about 100,000 to 8 million years old, not 8,000. The researchers also brought living microbes back to life, rather than finding fossils. A separate 2013 study by Knowlton and colleagues did look at microbes in Greenland and Antarctic ice cores, but those were deep core sections dated about 500 to 157,000 years old. Neither study matches the claim's age, its description of fossils, or its pairing of the two locations. So the main specifics are contradicted, although no source explicitly rules out an 8,000-year figure.

text: Octopuses have been observed displaying a form of playfulness, as they have been known to collect and arrange shiny objects.
label: supported
reason: Reliable sources document play-like behavior in octopuses, such as playing with toys and novel objects (Mental Floss, which cites research). Island Fisherman Magazine says octopuses are drawn to shiny objects and have often been seen collecting and arranging them around their dens, forming 'octopus gardens.' It suggests this may reflect a liking for decoration. Phys.org also reports octopuses arranging shells and other objects around their dens. The idea that collecting shiny objects shows playfulness is an interpretation, but the sources back both parts of the claim, and none of them contradict it.

text: Snails are able to sleep for up to three years in a state of dormancy known as estivation.
label: supported
reason: Several sources say certain land snails can stay dormant in estivation, a summer dormancy triggered by heat and dryness, for up to three years. These include A-Z Animals ("estivation can last for up to three years"), Animal Corner, Lovet and NapLab. Some of them point out that estivation is technically torpor rather than true sleep, and that only some species can do this. The three-year figure for estivation itself is consistent across sources, and none of the results contradict it.

text: Tarantulas have been around for over 120 million years, with some species even preserving their morphology since the Early Cretaceous period.
label: not_verifiable
reason: I could confirm only the age. A 2021 PeerJ study by Foley et al., reported by Phys.org and Live Science, estimates that tarantulas appeared about 120 million years ago in the Cretaceous. That is "about" 120 million years, not clearly "over" 120 million. I found no evidence for the second part, that some species have kept the same body form since the Early Cretaceous. Only two true tarantula fossils are known: a Burmese amber specimen about 100 million years old (mid-Cretaceous) and a Miocene specimen from Mexico. No source says any living species has stayed unchanged since the Early Cretaceous.

text: Tarantulas have existed on Earth for over 100 million years, with some species dating back to the Cretaceous period.
label: supported
reason: A peer-reviewed study in the Journal of Biogeography (Wiley) reports that the oldest known tarantula (Theraphosidae) fossil comes from Burmese amber dated to about 100 million years ago, in the Cretaceous. The same study dates the split between tarantulas and their closest relatives to the early Cretaceous, around 120 million years ago, and places the ancestors of today's tarantulas in the mid-Cretaceous. This supports both parts of the claim: tarantulas have existed for about 100 million years or more, and at least one fossil species dates to the Cretaceous. The oldest fossil itself is about 100 million years old, so 'over 100 million years' rests on the estimated ~120-million-year origin rather than on fossil evidence alone.

text: Galileo Galilei was the first person to observe the planet Neptune using a telescope, but he didn't recognize it as a planet and instead recorded it as a fixed star in 1612.
label: supported
reason: NASA says Galileo recorded Neptune as a fixed star when he looked at it through his small telescope in 1612 and 1613. Scientific American says he first saw it in 1612 and took it for a fixed star, 234 years before it was recognized as a planet. Wikipedia dates his observations to December 28, 1612 and January 27, 1613. A Paul Fraser Collectibles article on Galileo seeing Neptune says he was the first person ever to spot it. No source I found disputes that he was first.

text: The Axel Erlandson's Tre-fontaine tree, also known as the "circus tree," is a natural wonder consisting of three trunks that were cultivated to unite and eventually fuse into a rare single canopy tree.
label: not_verifiable
reason: I found no trustworthy source that mentions a 'Tre-fontaine tree' by Axel Erlandson. Wikipedia, Gilroy Gardens, the American Visionary Art Museum (AVAM) and Raw Vision describe his 'Circus Trees' as a collection of artificially grafted and shaped trees with names like the Basket Tree, Four Legged Giant and Arch Tree. That suggests 'circus tree' is a general name for his works, not another name for one particular tree. Calling the tree a 'natural wonder' also conflicts with the sources, which say his trees were deliberately grafted. Still, because the specific tree can't be identified, the claim can be neither confirmed nor clearly disproved.

text: Galileo Galilei was the first person to observe the planet Neptune using a telescope, but he didn't realize it was a planet at the time, mistaking it for a fixed star in 1613.
label: supported
reason: Wikipedia's article on the discovery of Neptune says Galileo's drawings show he saw Neptune through his telescope on December 28, 1612, and again on January 27, 1613. Both times he mistook it for a fixed star while it was close to Jupiter, which is why he isn't credited with discovering it. These are the earliest known telescopic sightings of Neptune. One detail is a little loose: the claim gives only 1613, but the first sighting was in late 1612, and the 1613 sighting is correct. Wikipedia also notes evidence that Galileo saw something odd when the 'star' appeared to move, but he never identified it as a planet. The main points of the claim hold up.

text: In the United States, there is a library located in Iowa called the Iowa State Fair and Agricultural Exposition where over 600 books are entirely made of butter.
label: contradicted
reason: Reliable sources, including the fair's own site and Wikipedia, describe the Iowa State Fair as an annual fair in Des Moines, not a library. It is famous for butter sculptures, mainly the butter cow carved every year since 1911 plus companion pieces. None of the sources mention a library or a collection of more than 600 books made entirely of butter. The claim seems to mix up the fair's well-known butter cow with a made-up butter-book library.

text: Humans are bioluminescent, meaning they emit a small amount of light, but it is too small to be seen with the naked eye.
label: supported
reason: A 2009 peer-reviewed PLoS ONE study by Kobayashi and colleagues, also on PMC, imaged ultraweak spontaneous photon emission from the human body. It found that the body "literally glimmers." The light is about 1000 times weaker than the naked eye can detect. That supports the claim that humans give off a tiny amount of light that can't be seen unaided. Strictly speaking, the paper calls this ultraweak photon emission (biophotons) rather than classic enzyme-driven bioluminescence like a firefly's. Popular sources call it human bioluminescence, though, and the substance of the claim holds.

text: Octopuses have a highly distributed brain, with nine brains in total including the central brain: a large brain and eight smaller "mini-brains" in their arms.
label: supported
reason: Discovery.com describes the octopus as having a cluster of nerve cells in each arm, which it calls eight independent "mini-brains," plus a larger central brain. Its heading reads "Try Nine Brains." It also says more than half of the octopus's roughly 500 million neurons sit outside the main brain, which fits the "highly distributed" part of the claim. One caveat: strictly speaking, scientists usually describe the arm structures as nerve clusters (ganglia), not true brains. Still, the claim matches this widely used description and the source's own wording.

text: Humans and dolphins are the only animals known to have their own unique names or identifiers that serve as a self-referential tool, in the case of humans, their given names, and in dolphins, their signature whistles.
label: contradicted
reason: The claim says only humans and dolphins are known to have their own names, and that is wrong. A 2024 study in Nature Ecology & Evolution, reported by RTÉ and AFP, found that African elephants call to each other with individual name-like calls. The same reports say parrots also address each other by copying the sounds of others, and that elephants are the first non-human animals known to use names that are not imitations.

text: A blue whale's heart alone can weigh as much as 400 pounds, with some reaching lengths of up to 4 feet, and is considered to be roughly the size of a small car.
label: contradicted
reason: National Geographic Education reports that a blue whale heart weighs about 400 pounds, which matches the claim's weight. The rest of the claim does not hold up. The same source gives the heart's size as about 5 feet long, 4 feet wide and 5 feet tall, so a maximum length of 4 feet is too small. It also says outright that the heart is not the size of a car. That finding comes from scientists who measured a real heart in Canada in 2015, and they compared it to a small golf cart instead. The Cold Spring Harbor Whaling Museum and whalefacts.org also describe it as golf-cart-sized. Some popular sites and videos still repeat the 'small car' comparison, but those are less reliable than the measured result, so the comparison is a myth.

text: Humans are the only species in the world that sleep on average 7-9 hours per day with their brains in a state of complete unconsciousness.
label: contradicted
reason: The claim is wrong on both counts. First, humans aren't the only species that sleeps about 7–9 hours a day: mammal sleep-duration data (Savage & West, PNAS, via Visual Capitalist) and sleep education sources show a wide range across animals, and several, such as pigs, rabbits and some primates, average a similar amount. Second, the brain is not 'completely unconscious' during sleep. Sleep research cited by sleep sources and a Frontiers paper shows the brain stays active, especially during REM sleep (which other animals also have), when some regions are as active as when awake or more so.

text: Scientists estimate that there are approximately 8.7 million identified species on Earth, although the total number, including undiscovered species, is believed to be around 30 million.
label: contradicted
reason: The 8.7 million figure (Mora et al., 2011) is an estimate of all species on Earth, including undiscovered ones. It is not a count of identified species. The study's authors estimated that about 86% of land species and 91% of ocean species have not yet been described. Only about 1.2 million species have been catalogued. The claim wrongly calls the 8.7 million species 'identified' and gives a different total of 30 million.

text: Scientists estimate that there are approximately 8.7 million identified species on Earth, but the total number of existing species, including those that have not been discovered, is believed to be around 30 million.
label: contradicted
reason: The claim gets the 8.7 million figure wrong. It comes from Mora et al. (2011) in PLoS Biology, and it is an estimate of the total number of eukaryotic species on Earth, including ones not yet discovered. It is not a count of identified species. The same study notes that only about 1.2 million species had been catalogued, so roughly 86% of species are still undescribed. Calling 8.7 million 'identified' species contradicts the source. The claim's ~30 million total is also not the estimate from this study, which was 8.7 million ± 1.3 million.

text: A blue whale can hold up to 500 gallons of krill and small fish in its stomach at a time.
label: contradicted
reason: I found no source that gives the stomach's capacity as 500 gallons. WWF says a blue whale's stomach can hold about one ton of krill, and A-Z Animals says about 2,200 pounds of food fills it. Krill is roughly as dense as water, so one ton converts to about 240–265 US gallons, about half the claimed amount. That conversion is my own estimate, since the sources give weight rather than volume. Another answer cites about 200 gallons (760 L) for a large whale's stomach. One older page mentions finding 4 tons of krill in a stomach, which would exceed 500 gallons, but it is a less authoritative outlier. Most sources point to about one ton, so the 500-gallon figure looks overstated.

text: A blue whale's heartbeat is so loud it can be detected from over 500 miles away underwater using specialized equipment.
label: contradicted
reason: NOAA Fisheries says a blue whale's heartbeat can be heard about 2 miles away, not more than 500 miles. The long distances often quoted for blue whales, sometimes hundreds of miles, refer to their calls, not their heartbeat. The 500-mile figure in the claim is therefore wrong.

text: A blue whale's heartbeat is so loud that it can be detected from over 500 miles away, and is louder than any man-made sound on Earth.
label: contradicted
reason: The claim is wrong on both points. NOAA Fisheries, a trusted source, says a blue whale's heartbeat can be heard about 2 miles away, not more than 500 miles. Even that 2-mile figure is disputed as a possible myth. Nothing supports the 500-mile figure or the idea that the heartbeat is louder than any man-made sound. The long-distance detection the claim seems to mix up refers to blue whale vocal calls, not the heartbeat. Man-made sounds such as explosions and seismic airguns are also far louder than a heartbeat.

text: Astronauts in space experience a phenomenon called "space adaptation syndrome," which causes their bodies to temporarily readjust to the lack of gravity.
label: supported
reason: Wikipedia and the Glasgow Science Centre both describe space adaptation syndrome, also called space sickness, as a real condition. Up to about half of space travelers get it while their bodies adapt to weightlessness, and symptoms usually last only the first few days. The claim's wording is a bit loose. The syndrome doesn't cause the readjustment; it's the set of symptoms, such as nausea and disorientation, that appear while the body is still adjusting. The main point of the claim still matches the sources.

text: France and the United States are connected by a 2,000-year-old underwater cave and tunnel system that was recently discovered.
label: contradicted
reason: No credible source reports any ancient cave or tunnel system linking France and the United States. Wikipedia describes a transatlantic tunnel between Europe and North America as only theoretical, and recent coverage, such as Newsweek and Yahoo articles on a proposed tunnel costing around $20 trillion, treats it as a future idea that has not been built. The closest real finds are the Channel Tunnel between England and France, which opened in 1994, and a 7,000-year-old underwater wall off the coast of France. Snopes has also debunked a similar viral claim about a huge ancient tunnel network running across Europe. The search results did not include a fact-check of this exact claim, but what they say about transatlantic tunnels goes against it.

text: Humans and dolphins are the only mammals known to give themselves names, which are communicated through unique whistles in the case of dolphins.
label: contradicted
reason: The claim that only humans and dolphins use names doesn't hold up. A 2024 study found that African elephants call each other with individual, name-like calls. Hebrew University research from August 2024, reported by CNN, found that marmoset monkeys name each other with 'phee-calls'. Both reports describe this ability as previously known in humans, dolphins and elephants, so dolphins are not the only non-human mammal that does it. The part about dolphins using signature whistles is correct, but the 'only mammals' part is wrong.

text: Humans are born without kneecaps, and they typically develop and harden between the ages of 3 and 5 years old through a process called ossification.
label: contradicted
reason: The claim's main point is wrong. Several sources, including HowStuffWorks and a doctor-reviewed article from Acibadem, say babies are born with kneecaps. At birth the kneecaps are made of soft cartilage rather than bone, and they don't show up on X-rays, which is where the myth comes from. The cartilage does turn into bone through ossification, roughly between ages 3 and 5 (some sources say up to about 6). But saying humans are born without kneecaps is a common myth that these sources directly reject.

text: Scientists estimate there are approximately 8.7 million identified species on Earth, but they believe as many as 80% of all species remain undiscovered.
label: contradicted
reason: The 8.7 million figure is an estimate of all species on Earth, both known and unknown. It is not a count of identified species. The study by Mora et al. (2011) found that only about 1.2 million species have been identified and classified, which is less than 15% of the 8.7 million total. The second half of the claim is roughly right: the same study says more than 80% of species are still undiscovered (86% of land species and 91% of marine species). Because the claim calls the 8.7 million species 'identified', it is contradicted.

text: The world's largest known snowflake was recorded in Montana in 1887, measuring an incredible 15 inches in diameter and 8 inches thick.
label: supported
reason: Sources citing Guinness World Records say the largest snowflake on record was reported at Fort Keogh, Montana, on January 28, 1887. They give its size as 15 inches wide and 8 inches thick, matching every detail in the claim. Some sources note that the measurement was never scientifically verified, but this is still the recognized record.

text: urtles have an innate, built-in navigational system that allows them to migrate thousands of miles each year and return to the exact beach where they were born.
label: contradicted
reason: The claim gets the general idea right but two details are wrong. Sea turtles do use the Earth's magnetic field to find their way back to where they hatched, and they migrate long distances. But a Royal Society paper and Florida Fish and Wildlife (FWC) both say females usually nest only every 2–4 years, not every year. They also return to roughly the area where they hatched, not usually the exact beach. Scuba Diving magazine describes this homing as "approximately, not usually exactly" the same place, and Wikipedia says they home to feeding areas near their birthplace rather than the actual beach.
