One more point: researchers think hatchlings learn their beach's magnetic signature (imprinting), so the homing ability isn't entirely built in from birth.

text: urtles have an innate, built-in navigational system that allows them to migrate thousands of miles each year and still return to the exact beach where they were born.
label: supported
reason: Reliable sources support the main idea, though some details are overstated. The Florida Oceanographic Society describes natal homing as sea turtles returning to the stretch of coastline where they hatched. It says they find their way mainly by imprinting on Earth's magnetic field at their birth beach. The Smithsonian says female sea turtles migrate thousands of miles to nest, sometimes on the beach where they were born, and the Sea Turtle Conservancy says most females nest on their birth beach. Three details are less precise than the claim suggests. NOAA says turtles usually return to the general area where they hatched, not always the exact beach. Females usually nest every few years rather than every year. Turtles learn their birth location by imprinting, so the system is not entirely built-in. On balance, the claim is broadly supported.

text: Caterpillars can eat up to 27,000 times their body weight in a single day, which is equivalent to a human eating around 2 elephants.
label: contradicted
reason: Sources say caterpillars eat about 27,000 times their body weight over their whole larval stage, which lasts about 4 weeks, not in a single day. The Naked Scientists article says caterpillars eat this much "in the 4 weeks that they're caterpillars." It also compares this to a person eating dozens of cows, not around two elephants. Two elephants would only be a few thousand times a human's body weight, so that comparison doesn't match the 27,000 figure either.

text: Honeybees are able to fly by using electricity generated from the movement of their wings, which creates a positive charge that aids lift.
label: contradicted
reason: The claim is wrong about why bees build up charge and what that charge does. Bees do pick up a slight positive static charge while flying, as their wings beat and their hairs rub against particles in the air. Sources such as Science Friday say this charge helps them collect pollen, because pollen and flowers carry a negative charge and are drawn to the bee. Bees stay in the air because of the aerodynamic lift their wings produce, not because of electricity. Electrostatic charge is not described as a source of lift, so the claim that bees fly using electricity from their wings is contradicted.

text: A day on Venus is actually longer than its year, with a day lasting around 243 Earth days and a year lasting just 225 Earth days.
label: supported
reason: NASA's Venus facts page says a Venus "day" (one rotation) lasts 243 Earth days, which is longer than a Venus year (one orbit of the Sun), which takes about 225 Earth days. WorldAtlas gives the same numbers. One caveat: 243 days is the sidereal day, meaning one full spin. A solar day on Venus, from one sunrise to the next, is shorter. Still, the claim matches how NASA itself describes it.

text: Astronauts cannot cry in the same way as people do on Earth because the lack of gravity does not allow their tears to flow down their cheeks in the same manner.
label: supported
reason: Space.com and Universe Today both cover Chris Hadfield's ISS demonstration. Astronauts can produce tears in space, but in microgravity the tears don't run down the cheeks the way they do on Earth. Instead they collect as a ball of water on the eye or face. That matches the claim that astronauts can't cry the same way people do on Earth because tears don't flow down their cheeks without gravity.

text: Astronauts cannot cry in the same way they do on Earth, as the lack of gravity in space causes tears to form a ball and float instead of freely falling.
label: supported
reason: Futurism cites astronaut Chris Hadfield, who said that in microgravity your eyes still make tears, but they "stick as a liquid ball." The article adds that astronauts technically can't cry the way they do on Earth, because their tears form wet gobs that hover around the eyes instead of falling. One detail needs care: the ball mostly stays stuck to the eye rather than drifting away. The claim's word "float" fits roughly with tears hovering instead of falling, so the main point is supported.

text: Babies are born without kneecaps, which do not develop and harden into bone until around 3-5 years of age.
label: supported
reason: The claim's main point holds up, though its wording is loose. Babies do have kneecaps at birth, but they are made of cartilage rather than bone and don't show up on X-rays. HowStuffWorks says this cartilage hardens into a fully bony kneecap at about 3 to 5 years of age, which matches the claim's timeline. Encyclopedia.com also says babies are born without bony kneecaps and that the cartilage slowly turns to bone during early childhood. Strictly speaking, 'born without kneecaps' means 'born without bony kneecaps.'

text: Blind people can see dreams similar to sighted people as their brain radar is being trained to navigate spaces using echolocation.
label: contradicted
reason: Reliable sources (BBC Science Focus, Medical News Today) say that people born blind, or who lose their sight early in life, usually do not have visual imagery in their dreams. People who lose their sight later tend to have less visual dreaming than sighted people, and blind people's dreams involve more sounds and smells. Medical News Today describes echolocation only as a waking mobility skill and does not link it to visual dreaming. This contradicts the claim that blind people dream visually like sighted people because echolocation trains their brains.

text: British Airways has a 747 jet with the highest time in the air, at over 115,000 hours.
label: not_verifiable
reason: I found BA 747s with more than 115,000 hours. Simple Flying reports that G-CIVD had flown 115,276 hours, citing UK Civil Aviation Authority data, and a BA press release lists another retired 747 at 118,445 hours. That second figure means G-CIVD was not BA's highest-hour 747. I found no source confirming which BA 747 had the most hours. If the claim means the most of any 747 worldwide, it is wrong: Asiana's 747-400 freighter HL7413 has logged about 149,645 hours. Because the claim is ambiguous and the 'highest' part is either unconfirmed or contradicted, I can't support it.

text: Child prodigy Ruth Lawrence, who entered university at age 10, earned a Ph.D. in mathematics from Harvard University at the age of 18.
label: contradicted
reason: Ruth Lawrence earned her doctorate (a DPhil) in mathematics at Oxford in June 1989, when she was 17. She did not get it from Harvard at 18. Harvard was where she took her first academic job, as a junior fellow, in 1990 at age 19. The claim that she was admitted to university at 10 is roughly right: she was admitted to Oxford in 1981 at 10, although Wikipedia says she started at St Hugh's College in 1983, at 12.

text: Child prodigy Ruth Lawrence, who entered university at age 10, earned her PhD in mathematics from Harvard University at age 18.
label: contradicted
reason: Ruth Lawrence got her DPhil in mathematics from the University of Oxford in June 1989, when she was 17, not from Harvard at 18. She only went to Harvard afterwards, becoming a junior fellow there in 1990 at age 19. The 'age 10' part is roughly right, though: she was admitted to Oxford at 10 in 1981, although Wikipedia says she actually started at St Hugh's College in 1983.

text: Didaskaleinophobia is a type of phobia that refers to an excessive or irrational fear of going to school.
label: supported
reason: Several sources, including a hypnotherapy clinic site and Klarity Health, describe didaskaleinophobia (also called scolionophobia) as a specific phobia: an excessive or irrational fear of going to school, often linked to separation anxiety, school stress or bullying. These are not academic or clinical-reference sources, but they agree with each other and with the claim, and I found nothing that contradicts it.

text: Electric bees (also known as Wallace's giant bee or Megachile pluto) are giant species of bees endemic to Indonesia.
label: not_verifiable
reason: Most of the claim checks out. Wikipedia, iNaturalist and news reports from CNN, NPR and Smithsonian confirm that Megachile pluto is also called Wallace's giant bee, that it is the world's largest known bee, and that it is endemic to Indonesia (the North Moluccas). But none of these sources calls it the 'electric bee.' The names they give are Wallace's giant bee, Wallace's giant resin bee and raja ofu ('king of the bees'). No source directly says the name 'electric bee' is wrong, so this part can be neither confirmed nor ruled out.

text: Germany has the most time zones in a single country, with a total of 14 time zones, since it has several overseas territories that are separated by large distances.
label: contradicted
reason: Guinness World Records, as reported by IFLScience, lists France as the country with the most time zones: 12, or 13 if you count its claim in Antarctica. That's because of its overseas territories. Germany has a single time zone (CET/CEST) and no overseas territories, so both the '14 time zones' figure and the claim that Germany comes first are wrong.

text: Humans are the only known animals capable of producing and comprehending all forms of music.
label: not_verifiable
reason: The sources I found discuss animal musicality, but none tests or confirms this claim. Discover Wildlife, ScienceDaily, MIT Press Reader and MDPI describe animals that have some musical traits or produce something like music: birdsong, whale song, chimpanzee drumming, and animals that can tell musical genres apart. That pushes back on the general idea that only humans make music. However, the claim is narrower: it says only humans can produce and understand "all forms" of music. No source looks at that standard, and it is too vague to verify. It is not clear that even humans can understand every form of music, and no source shows another species meeting that standard. The evidence therefore neither clearly supports nor clearly contradicts the claim.

text: Moisture in certain environments can cause chrome to corrode and rust over time.
label: supported
reason: Chrome-care and plating sources say chrome-plated items can rust when moisture gets through scratches, pores or cracks in the plating and reaches the steel underneath. Over time that rust shows through the chrome. The rust itself forms on the base metal rather than the chromium layer, but chrome surfaces do corrode and rust in moist environments in everyday terms, so the claim holds.

text: povin871% of the Earth's water is found in its oceans.
label: contradicted
reason: The figure in the claim is garbled ("povin871%"), but it seems to say 71% (or possibly 87%). Either way, it is wrong. NOAA, USGS and the U.S. Bureau of Reclamation all say the oceans hold about 96.5–97% of Earth's water. The 71% figure is how much of Earth's surface is covered by water, not the share of Earth's water held in the oceans.

text: France and Spain both claim to be the birthplace of the first restaurant, 'auberge,' with the French claiming it was in the 1760s in Paris, and the Spanish, in 1700s Alicante (where an 'albergue' was opened).
label: contradicted
reason: The sources I found say the first restaurant was in Paris around 1765, when a bouillon seller named Boulanger sold "restoratives." It was called a "restaurant" (from the French word restaurer, to restore), not an "auberge." French sources describe auberges as ordinary inns or taverns, which existed long before that. Spain's claim is also different from what the claim says. It rests on Sobrino de Botín in Madrid, founded in 1725 and listed by Guinness as the world's oldest restaurant. I found nothing about an 'albergue' in 1700s Alicante, so the claim gets both the name and the Spanish location wrong.

text: High-speed camera footage revealed that a mantis shrimp can accelerate its claws at the speed of a .22 caliber bullet, reaching speeds of up to 46 mph (74 km/h) in a matter of milliseconds.
label: contradicted
reason: The bullet comparison and high-speed footage parts check out. Sheila Patek filmed peacock mantis shrimp strikes slowed down more than 800 times, and many sources say the club accelerates about as fast as a .22-caliber bullet. The speed figure is wrong, though. National Geographic and ScubaDiving.com put the club speed at about 50 mph, and Wikipedia gives 23 m/s (83 km/h; 51 mph), with some figures even higher. None of the sources I found give a top speed of 46 mph (74 km/h), so 'up to 46 mph' understates the reported maximum.

text: Scientists estimate that there are approximately 8.7 million identified species on Earth, but the total number of species, including unidentified ones, is believed to be around 30 million.
label: contradicted
reason: The claim gets the 8.7 million figure wrong. It comes from Mora et al. (2011), and it is an estimate of the total number of species on Earth, both known and unknown. It is not a count of identified species. That study found most species have not yet been described: about 86% of land species and 91% of ocean species. Only around 1.2–2 million species have actually been identified. So calling 8.7 million the 'identified' count, with a separate total of about 30 million, misstates the research.

text: A Perez Prado song 'Guantanamera', has an un verifiable connection but is possibly credited to Joseito Fernandez's "Guajira Guantanamera" 1929, but as complied and then popularized through in English as Guantana-Mera 'House of Perez Guantanamera original.
label: not_verifiable
reason: Some parts check out. Pérez Prado and His Orchestra released a 'Guantanamera' album and track in 1976 (Discogs, Apple Music). The song is officially credited to Joseíto Fernández, who popularized it on the radio around 1929 (Wikipedia). It later spread internationally through versions such as Pete Seeger's and The Sandpipers' 1966 recording. Other parts can't be checked, though. The claim is garbled and refers to an 'English' version called 'Guantana-Mera' and a 'House of Perez Guantanamera original,' and no source mentions either one. The claim also never says clearly which connection is 'unverifiable.' Since key parts are unclear or have no supporting evidence, the claim can't be fully verified.

text: In the United States, there is a library with a collection of more than 150 million items: it is called the Library of Congress.
label: supported
reason: Official Library of Congress sources back the claim. Its 225th-anniversary blog post (March 2025) says the Library holds more than 181 million items, and its FAQ says over 178 million. Both figures are well above 150 million. The encyclopedia.com entry gives a much lower count (about 110–120 million), but that article is old, so it doesn't contradict the current numbers.

text: A blue whale's heartbeat can be as loud as 188 decibels, which is louder than a jet engine, and can be heard for hundreds of miles underwater.
label: contradicted
reason: The claim mixes up two different blue whale sounds. Sources say the 188-decibel figure, which is louder than a jet engine and can travel hundreds to over a thousand miles underwater, belongs to the whale's calls, not its heartbeat. NOAA says the heartbeat can be heard about 2 miles away, not hundreds of miles. Other sources also say the heartbeat has no measured decibel level, so the claim's details are wrong.

text: Scientists estimate that there are approximately 8.7 million identified species on Earth, but the total number of existing species is believed to be around 30 million.
label: contradicted
reason: The 8.7 million figure (Mora et al., 2011) is an estimate of the total number of species on Earth, not the number already identified. The same researchers estimated that about 86% of land species and 91% of ocean species have not yet been described, which leaves only about 1.2 million catalogued. So the claim swaps the two figures: it presents the total estimate as the identified count and gives a different 30 million total that the source does not support.

text: Scientists estimate that there are approximately 8.7 million identified species on Earth, but this number is believed to represent only about 10% of the total number of species that actually exist.
label: contradicted
reason: The claim gets the 8.7 million figure wrong. Mora et al. (2011, PLoS Biology) gave 8.7 million (±1.3 million) as an estimate of the TOTAL number of eukaryotic species on Earth, not the number already identified. Only about 1.2 million have been described, so most species (more than 80%) are still undiscovered. The claim calls 8.7 million the identified species and says they are only about 10% of all species. That misstates the estimate and the proportion.

text: Plants can make sounds, too, but they are beyond the range of human hearing; these sounds include the ultrasonic noises produced by photosynthesizing plants.
label: supported
reason: Good sources confirm the main claim. A Tel Aviv University study published in Cell in 2023, covered by EurekAlert, the Natural History Museum and Science News, recorded ultrasonic sounds at about 40–80 kHz from tomato, tobacco, wheat, corn and cactus plants. Adult humans hear only up to about 16 kHz, so these sounds are beyond human hearing. All of these plants photosynthesize, so the claim's wording holds. One caveat: the sources tie the sounds to stress (drought or cut stems) and water-transport processes such as cavitation, not to photosynthesis itself. The claim does not say photosynthesis causes the sounds, so this does not contradict it.

text: Galileo Galilei was the first person to observe the planet Neptune using a telescope, but he didn't recognize it as a planet and documented it as a fixed star in his notes in 1612.
label: supported
reason: Several reliable sources agree on every part of the claim. NASA says Galileo recorded Neptune as a fixed star during observations with his small telescope in 1612 and 1613. Scientific American and Wikipedia's article on the discovery of Neptune say his drawings show he saw it on December 28, 1612, and mistook it for a fixed star. Other sources, such as Paul Fraser Collectibles, describe him as the first person ever to see Neptune. His follow-up observation in January 1613 does not conflict with the claim's 1612 date.

text: Plants can make sounds, such as releasing a high-pitched clicking noise when they are stressed by lack of water.
label: supported
reason: Science News, reporting on a peer-reviewed study (Khait et al., Cell, 2023), says that tomato and tobacco plants without enough water give off distinct ultrasonic clicks. Thirsty tomato plants made about 35 clicks per hour. Ultrasonic means the sound is above the range people can hear, so it fits the claim's 'high-pitched clicking noise' when plants are stressed by lack of water. NBC Bay Area reported the same findings.

text: Plants can make sounds, though inaudible to the human ear, when they are damaged or cut.
label: supported
reason: A peer-reviewed study from Tel Aviv University, published in Cell in 2023 (Khait et al., "Sounds emitted by plants under stress are airborne and informative"), recorded ultrasonic clicks from tomato and tobacco plants after their stems were cut and when they were dehydrated. The clicks were at 40–80 kHz, which is above the range of human hearing, and stressed plants made far more of them than unstressed plants. This matches the claim that plants make sounds we can't hear when they are damaged or cut.

text: Plants can make sounds, too, when they are under stress or when their cells are eating or releasing air bubbles, scientists have discovered.
label: supported
reason: Coverage of the 2023 Tel Aviv University study in Cell reports that plants such as tomato and tobacco give off ultrasonic popping or clicking sounds, especially when stressed by drought or a cut stem. Researchers attribute the sounds to cavitation, where air bubbles form, expand and collapse in the stem. That matches the claim's core: plants make sounds under stress and in connection with air bubbles. The claim's word "eating" is not in the sources and looks like a garbled paraphrase of bubbles forming or being taken in, so it does not change the main point.

text: Plants can make sounds, too, when they're stressed or thirsty, and scientists can record and listen to them using specialized equipment.
label: supported
reason: Reliable sources, including Scientific American, Smithsonian and the Washington Post, report on a 2023 study in the journal Cell by Tel Aviv University researchers. It found that stressed plants, such as tomato and tobacco plants that were short of water or had cut stems, give off ultrasonic popping sounds at about 40–80 kHz. Humans can't hear these sounds, but the researchers recorded them with ultrasonic microphones. This matches the claim that plants make sounds when stressed or thirsty and that scientists can record and listen to them with specialized equipment.

text: Plants can make sounds, with research showing that some plants release ultrasonic sounds when they're stressed by drought.
label: supported
reason: A 2023 Cell commentary on the Khait et al. study, which appeared in a peer-reviewed journal, reports that tomato and tobacco plants give off airborne ultrasonic sounds when stressed by drying out (desiccation/drought) or by being cut. This backs up both parts of the claim.

text: A new discovery in a network of underwater caves in Mexico revealed the bones of an enormous Ice Age creature called a glyptodon, a prehistoric relative of the modern armadillo.
label: not_verifiable
reason: I couldn't confirm the claim before I ran out of searches. My searches turned up related findings but nothing about a specific new glyptodon find in Mexico's underwater caves. Mexico News Daily says glyptodons once lived in Mexico and describes Ice Age megafauna fossils, but those were found in a hard-to-reach cave in San Luis Potosí, not a flooded one. Other reports describe giant sloths, horses, ancient human remains and other fossils in the Yucatán's submerged caves and cenotes (water-filled sinkholes), but none of the results mention a glyptodon. Britannica confirms that glyptodons were giant extinct relatives of armadillos, but no trustworthy source I found reports the specific discovery the claim describes.

text: Bacteria can only grow and reproduce in "ideal" temperatures ranging from 40°F to 140°F (4°C to 60°C).
label: contradicted
reason: USDA FSIS says the 40–140 °F "Danger Zone" is the range where bacteria grow fastest. It does not say this is the only range where they can grow. The same page notes that some bacteria, such as Listeria monocytogenes, thrive at cold temperatures and will multiply in the refrigerator, below 40 °F. Thermophilic bacteria also grow above 140 °F. So the claim that bacteria can "only" grow between 40 °F and 140 °F is wrong.

text: The Axel Erlandson's Tre-fontaine tree, also known as the "circus tree," is a natural wonder consisting of three trunks that were cultivated to unite and eventually fuse into a rare tripod-shaped tree in California, USA.
label: not_verifiable
reason: I found no trustworthy source that mentions a "Tre-fontaine tree" by Axel Erlandson or any tripod-shaped tree of his made from three trunks. Some parts of the claim are true. Erlandson did graft trees together in California, and his work is collectively called the "Circus Trees" (once the Tree Circus in Scotts Valley, now at Gilroy Gardens). His named trees include the Four-Legged Giant, the Basket Tree, the Arch Tree and Squat Curvy Scallops, which is made from three trees but is not called a tripod. However, "circus tree" names the whole collection, not one tree. Calling it a "natural wonder" is also misleading, because these trees were deliberately shaped and grafted by hand. Since the specific tree in the claim can't be found or verified, the claim is inconclusive.

text: Tarantulas have been around for a long time, with fossil records showing that they existed during the Cretaceous period, more than 100 million years ago, at the same time as the dinosaurs.
label: supported
reason: A peer-reviewed study in the Journal of Biogeography says the oldest known tarantula (Theraphosidae) fossil comes from Burmese amber dated to about 100 million years ago, which is in the mid-Cretaceous, when dinosaurs were alive. The same study dates the origin of the tarantula lineage to the Early Cretaceous, about 103–120 million years ago. One caveat: Burmese amber is usually dated to about 99 million years ago, so the fossil itself is roughly 100 million years old rather than clearly more than that. Even so, the claim's main points — a Cretaceous fossil record and coexistence with dinosaurs — are supported.

text: Scientists estimate that there are approximately 8.7 million identified species on Earth, but the actual total is believed to be anywhere between 10 million to 30 million species in total.
label: contradicted
reason: The claim gets the 8.7 million figure wrong. It comes from Mora et al. (2011), and that study gives it as the estimated total number of eukaryotic species on Earth, plus or minus 1.3 million. It is not a count of identified species. Only about 1.2 million species have actually been described and catalogued, including roughly 953,000 animals. The same reporting gives earlier estimates of the total as anywhere from 3 million to 100 million, not 10 to 30 million.

text: Glass can withstand extremely high temperatures, with some types of glass, such as borosilicate, being able to resist thermal shock and maintain its shape and integrity up to 500°C (932°F) or more.
label: supported
reason: DWK Life Sciences, which makes DURAN lab glassware, says the maximum recommended working temperature for 3.3 expansion borosilicate glass is 500°C. It also says this glass has high resistance to thermal shock, and it lists a transformation temperature of about 525°C. Wikipedia likewise says borosilicate resists thermal shock better than any other common glass. One caveat: the 500°C limit applies only for short periods, and the claim's 'or more' slightly overstates it (fused quartz goes higher). Still, the core claim matches reliable sources.

text: Honeybees are able to fly by using their wings to create a whirlpool of air above and below their bodies, generating lift through this unique airflow pattern.
label: supported
reason: The sources support the main point of the claim: honeybees get lift from swirling air created by their wings. AskNature, citing Altshuler et al. 2005 in PNAS, says a vortex (a swirl of air) moves along the bee's wing and delays stall. It adds that rotating the wings at the end of each stroke creates further lift. Dadant, a beekeeping company, describes these leading-edge vortices as tiny tornadoes that create a pressure difference between the tops and bottoms of the wings, which provides lift. The claim's 'whirlpool' is a loose but reasonable way to describe these vortices. One caveat: the research places the vortex along the wing, not 'above and below their bodies'. The studies also say that other unsteady-airflow effects at stroke reversal matter as well.

text: A blue whale's heartbeat can be as loud as 188 decibels, louder than a jet engine taking off, and its heartbeat can also be detected from over 500 miles away.
label: contradicted
reason: The claim mixes up two different things. The 188 dB figure, which is louder than a jet engine, and the ability to be heard hundreds of miles away both describe the blue whale's vocal calls, not its heartbeat. Reliable sources such as the Cold Spring Harbor Whaling Museum, citing Live Science, say a blue whale's heartbeat can be detected from about 2 miles away, not from more than 500 miles.

text: Galileo Galilei was the first person to observe the planet Neptune, but he did not realize it was a planet, in 1613.
label: supported
reason: Galileo's drawings show he saw Neptune near Jupiter on December 28, 1612 and again in January 1613 (Jan 27–28). He mistook it for a fixed star, and his is the earliest known observation. Neptune was only officially discovered in 1846. So the main points hold: he saw it first, didn't recognize it as a planet, and saw it in 1613. Two caveats keep this from being exact. His very first sighting was in late December 1612, not 1613. And sources hedge on whether he was truly first ('may have been the first') and on whether he noticed it moving (a 2009 argument by David Jamieson).

text: Scientists estimate that there may be between 700,000 and 1 million species on Earth that have not yet been formally discovered or described.
label: contradicted
reason: Widely cited scientific estimates put the number of undiscovered species in the millions, not 700,000 to 1 million. The 2011 Mora et al. study in PLoS Biology, reported by ScienceDaily and National Geographic, estimates about 8.7 million eukaryotic species on Earth, with about 86% of land species and 91% of ocean species not yet described. Only about 1.25 million have been catalogued, which leaves roughly 7.5 million still undescribed. The '700,000 to 1 million' range seems to come from estimates of the total number of species in the ocean (for example NOAA's figure and a 2012 marine census). It is not an estimate of undiscovered species across the whole planet, so the claim misstates the numbers.

text: The Axel Erlandson Tree Circus, located in Felton, California, features a collection of trees that have been carefully pruned and grafted into unique shapes and designs.
label: contradicted
reason: The trees really were carefully shaped and grafted, but the location in the claim is wrong. Erlandson opened the Tree Circus in 1947 in Scotts Valley, California, not Felton. In 1985 the surviving trees were bought and moved to Gilroy, where they are now shown at Gilroy Gardens (formerly Bonfante Gardens). Neither source links the Tree Circus to Felton.

text: A blue whale's heartbeat can be as loud as 188 decibels, louder than a jet taking off, and can be heard for hundreds of miles underwater.
label: contradicted
reason: The claim mixes up two different things. Reliable sources such as Enchanted Learning give the 188 dB figure for the blue whale's call. They say this call is louder than a jet (about 140 dB) and can be heard for hundreds of miles underwater. None of this is about the heartbeat. For the heartbeat, NOAA Fisheries says it can be heard about 2 miles away, not hundreds of miles. Some sources even question that 2-mile figure. So pinning the 188 dB and hundreds-of-miles figures on the heartbeat is wrong.

text: Honeybees are able to fly by using their wings to generate electricity and create a positive charge on their bodies, allowing them to attract and collect pollen.
label: contradicted
reason: The sources agree that honeybees pick up a positive electrostatic charge while flying, mainly from friction with the air (triboelectric charging). That charge helps them attract and collect pollen from negatively charged flowers. However, the claim gets cause and effect backwards: bees don't fly by generating electricity. Their wing beats lift them aerodynamically, and the charge is only a side effect of flying. The pollen part is accurate, but the claim that bees fly by using their wings to make electricity is contradicted.

text: Humans are the only species known to experience a condition called 'tetrachromacy,' where the presence of four types of cones in the retina enables them to see a wider range of colors.
label: contradicted
reason: The claim says humans are the only species known to have tetrachromacy, and that is false. A peer-reviewed article in the Journal of Experimental Biology notes that "many birds, reptiles and shallow-water fish are tetrachromatic and use four cone classes." Most humans actually have three cone types; only some people, mostly women, have a fourth.

text: Jellyfish have been to space: in 1991, NASA sent 2,478 moon jellyfish to space aboard the Space Shuttle Columbia to study how weightlessness affects their development.
label: supported
reason: Several sources say that on 5 June 1991, NASA's STS-40 / Spacelab Life Sciences-1 mission on Space Shuttle Columbia carried 2,478 moon jellyfish (Aurelia aurita) polyps into orbit. The goal was to study how microgravity affects their development, especially their gravity-sensing systems. One caveat: they launched as immature polyps, not adult jellyfish. This doesn't contradict the claim. The cited source is a magazine article rather than a NASA document, but the other sources agree with it.

text: A chunk of the Dead Sea has been found to be so dense with dissolved salt that it is literally possible to float effortlessly on the water's surface.
label: supported
reason: Several sources say the Dead Sea is hypersaline. Its salinity is about 34% (around 340 g/L), and its density is about 1.24 kg/L. That makes it denser than the human body, so people float with little effort. This matches the claim that the Dead Sea water is so full of dissolved salt that people can float easily on the surface. The phrase "a chunk of" is odd, but it doesn't change the main point, which is well documented.

text: Galileo Galilei was the first person to observe the planet Neptune using a telescope, but he didn't recognize it as a planet, instead, he recorded it as a fixed star in 1612.
label: supported
reason: NASA says Galileo recorded Neptune as a fixed star while observing with his small telescope in 1612 and 1613. Wikipedia's 'Discovery of Neptune' page says his drawings show he saw it on December 28, 1612, and again in January 1613, and both times took it for a fixed star near Jupiter. Scientific American describes this as Galileo first observing Neptune in 1612 and thinking it was a fixed star, 234 years before it was found to be a planet. No source names anyone who saw Neptune earlier, so the claim that Galileo was the first is consistent with the evidence.

text: Did you know that the world's largest living organism is a fungus called Armillaria ostoyae, a honey mushroom that spans over 2,200 acres in Oregon, USA?
label: supported
reason: The National Wildlife Federation describes Armillaria ostoyae in eastern Oregon as the world's largest living organism and says it covers more than 2,200 acres. The Oregon Encyclopedia and Wikipedia agree that this specimen in Malheur National Forest is believed to be the largest organism. Some sources put its size at about 2,384 acres, which still fits 'over 2,200 acres.' One caveat: this title is usually given with words like 'likely' or 'believed to be,' because other contenders, such as the Pando aspen clone, exist.

text: Galileo Galilei was the first person to observe the planet Neptune, but he didn't recognize it as a planet, instead recording it as a star on January 28, 1613.
label: contradicted
reason: Galileo did see Neptune and mistook it for a fixed star, but the date in the claim is wrong. Wikipedia and Phys.org say he first observed it on December 28, 1612, and again on January 27, 1613. His January 28 notebook entry also undercuts the claim: he wrote that this 'star' seemed to have moved and marked its position in a different ink. That suggests he noticed something unusual rather than simply recording it as a star.

text: Owens Falls Dam, completed in 1931 on the Idaho side but worked by Portland, Oregon is one of the oldest hydroelectric dams in the United States.
label: contradicted
reason: The claim is wrong. Britannica says the Owen Falls Dam, now called the Nalubaale Dam, is in Jinja, Uganda, and was finished in 1954 with Lake Victoria as its reservoir. It is not in Idaho, was not completed in 1931, is not run from Portland, Oregon, and is not a U.S. dam. The search found no source showing an 'Owens Falls Dam' in Idaho that fits the claim.

text: Oil rigs off the coast of California that were once used for extracting oil are now being repurposed as artificial reefs for marine life, helping to increase biodiversity and protect the environment.
label: contradicted
reason: The claim is wrong as stated. No oil rigs off California have actually been turned into artificial reefs. The Congressional Sportsmen's Foundation says none of the more than 20 oil and gas platforms off the California coast have been donated to the Rigs-to-Reefs program, and Wikipedia notes that opposition in California has blocked such a program on the West Coast. The Conversation and PBS SoCal describe conversion only as something California could do in the future and say it has proven difficult. Large-scale rigs-to-reefs conversions have happened in the Gulf of Mexico, not California.

text: A set of human lungs, after being removed from the body and inflated, can float on water due to the air spaces within the lungs.
label: supported
reason: The lung float (hydrostatic) test depends on this principle. Lungs that contain air float in water, while lungs without air sink. Removed and inflated lungs hold air in their alveolar spaces, so they float. The test can give false results in some forensic cases, such as when tissue decomposes, but that doesn't change the basic fact that air-filled lungs float.

text: Bees are capable of recognizing human faces and remembering them for later encounters, a unique ability shared by only a few other animal species.
label: contradicted
reason: The first part of the claim holds up. In a 2005 study published in the Journal of Experimental Biology, Dyer and colleagues found that honeybees could learn to recognize human faces in photos and remember them for at least two days. The second part does not hold up. The claim calls this a unique ability shared by only a few other species, but many species can do it. Sources list sheep, dogs, cows, horses, crows, pigeons, primates and archerfish, and some state outright that many animals have this skill. Because that part of the claim is contradicted, the claim as a whole is contradicted, even though the bee part is accurate.

text: Bees are capable of recognizing human faces and remembering them for later encounters, a unique ability shared by only a few species in the insect world.
label: supported
reason: Reliable sources (Phys.org and Science) report on Dyer et al.'s 2005 study in the Journal of Experimental Biology. Honeybees learned to recognize individual human faces in photos and could still pick out the target face two days later, which shows long-term memory. Dyer said this was, as far as he knew, the first time an invertebrate had been shown to recognize the faces of another species. That fits the claim that only a few insects have this ability. Other insects, like paper wasps, recognize faces of their own species. One caveat: the study used photos, not live people.

text: Bees are capable of recognizing human faces and remembering them for later encounters, a unique ability shared by only a handful of other species.
label: contradicted
reason: The first part holds up. Phys.org reports on Dyer et al. (2005, Journal of Experimental Biology): honeybees learned to recognize human faces in photos and still remembered them at least two days later. The second part does not. Calling this a 'unique ability shared by only a handful of other species' overstates its rarity. Reputable sources show that many animals can recognize human faces. National Geographic covers archerfish and notes the same ability in pigeons, bees and sheep. NBC News says most animals tested so far are mammals with a neocortex, many of them domesticated, such as sheep, dogs, horses and primates. Crows and wasps can do it too. 'A handful' is vague, so this is a judgement call, but the evidence points to a widespread ability rather than a rare one.

text: Bumblebees are able to fly by using electricity generated by the movement of their wings to help them lift off the ground.
label: contradicted
reason: Bumblebees get lift from aerodynamics: their wings beat very fast (about 130 times a second) in a figure-eight, rotating motion and create leading-edge vortices. Electricity plays no part in their lift. Bees do build up static charge, but it helps with things like pollen and sensing flowers, not with getting off the ground. The sources describe flight as purely aerodynamic and say nothing to support electrical lift.

text: Didaskaleinophobia is a type of phobia that refers to a fear of going to school.
label: supported
reason: Several sources describe didaskaleinophobia as an irrational fear of school or of going to school. Klarity Health's library defines it as "the irrational fear of school or going to school," and a phobia wiki gives the same definition. That fully matches the claim, and none of the results I found contradicted it.

text: Owens Falls Dam in Uganda is considered the world's first arch dam, built in 1927, as it was made without an additional fill over its downstream side.
label: contradicted
reason: Britannica and Wikipedia both say the Owen Falls Dam (now the Nalubaale Dam) was built between 1951 and 1954 and completed in 1954, not in 1927. It is a concrete gravity dam, not an arch dam. None of these sources call it the world's first arch dam either; arch dams were built long before then, as far back as Roman times.

text: Plants can only undergo photosynthesis within a specific temperature range of 20-30 °C (68-86 °F).
label: contradicted
reason: The claim mixes up the optimum range with the only possible range. A peer-reviewed review (Sage & Kubien, 2007, Plant, Cell & Environment) measures photosynthesis at 30 and 40 °C and discusses how it declines above about 38–40 °C. That means photosynthesis still happens outside 20–30 °C; it just has an optimum and drops off as temperatures move away from it. An educational source likewise says the temperature needed for photosynthesis varies from about 10 to 40 °C depending on habitat. Both sources describe 20–30 °C as roughly an optimum, not a strict limit, so the word "only" is wrong.

text: Polar bears are excellent swimmers, with some individuals recorded to have swum for hours or even days at a time without resting.
label: supported
reason: A USGS-led study by Durner and colleagues, reported by CBC and others, tracked a GPS-collared female polar bear that swam without stopping for 232 hours, about nine days, covering 687 km of 2–6°C water. That backs up the claim that polar bears are excellent swimmers and that some have swum for hours or even days without resting.

text: Roses arranged in the pattern of a clock in some European parks or a special event form the face of a "Floral Clock" that is actually functional.
label: not_verifiable
reason: Working floral clocks do exist in European parks, such as Geneva's and Edinburgh's, so part of the claim holds. However, the Wikipedia article and Wikimedia Commons describe the faces as made with carpet bedding or succulents, not roses. My searches found no source saying roses are used to form a working floral clock face in European parks or at events, so I couldn't confirm the rose detail. I also found nothing that directly rules it out.

text: Scientists believe that there are approximately 8.7 million identified species on Earth, but the estimated total number, including unidentified species, is around 30 million.
label: contradicted
reason: The 8.7 million figure is an estimate of the total number of species on Earth, including the ones nobody has found yet. It does not count identified species. Mora et al. (2011, PLoS Biology) put the total at about 8.7 million, give or take 1.3 million. ScienceDaily's write-up says about 86% of land species and 91% of ocean species are still undescribed. Only about 1.2 million species had been catalogued. So the claim gets the identified count wrong, and its total of about 30 million doesn't match this estimate either.

text: Scientists estimate that there are approximately 170 billion galaxies in the observable universe.
label: supported
reason: Big Think's 'Starts With a Bang' column, written by astrophysicist Ethan Siegel, says that extrapolating the Hubble eXtreme Deep Field to the whole sky gives an estimate of about 170 billion galaxies in the observable universe. So this figure is a real scientific estimate. It is an older one, though. Later work suggests much higher totals, around 2 trillion or possibly more, while New Horizons data point to a few hundred billion. The claim matches a recognised estimate, but readers should know that more recent figures differ.

text: Tarantulas have been on Earth for a long time, with fossil records indicating they have existed for around 100 million years.
label: supported
reason: A peer-reviewed study in the Journal of Biogeography (Wiley) says the oldest known tarantula (theraphosid) fossil comes from Burmese amber dated to about 100 million years ago. That matches the claim that fossils show tarantulas have existed for around 100 million years.

text: The world's largest snowflake was recorded in Montana in 1887, measuring 15 inches in diameter and 8 inches thick.
label: supported
reason: Several sources, including Guinness World Records as cited in the reports, say the largest snowflake on record was 15 inches (38 cm) wide and 8 inches (20 cm) thick. A rancher reported it at Fort Keogh, Montana, on January 28, 1887. One caveat: this is an unverified eyewitness report that many scientists doubt, but it is the recognized record, which matches what the claim says.

text: Turtles have an innate navigation system that allows them to migrate thousands of miles each year, often returning to the exact beach where they were born.
label: supported
reason: Reliable sources back the main points of the claim for sea turtles. The Smithsonian Ocean Portal says female sea turtles migrate thousands of miles, "sometimes to the same beach where they were born," to nest. It also says they navigate using an inborn magnetic sense and possibly smell. UNC research found that adult sea turtles return to their natal beaches by following unique magnetic signatures along the coast. Wikipedia's sea turtle migration article notes migrations of up to 10,000 miles a year. There are some caveats. The claim says "turtles," but this behavior belongs to sea turtles, not turtles in general. The claim's "often" fits sources saying "sometimes" or "the same stretch of coastline," but sources disagree on the "exact beach" detail: one conservation site says they return to the exact spot, while the natal homing article says they return to the general area. Also, females usually nest every few years, not every year. Overall the claim matches the sources.

text: Turtles have an innate navigational ability that allows them to migrate thousands of miles each year and still return to their birthplace.
label: supported
reason: Sea turtles have this ability, though the claim only fits sea turtles, not all turtles. Research reported by ScienceDaily says they migrate thousands of miles across the ocean and then return to nest on the same stretch of coast where they hatched. They manage this by imprinting on the magnetic field of their home beach as hatchlings, and their navigation is innate. Wikipedia adds that sea turtles can migrate up to 10,000 miles or more per year.

text: cực separation of the Atlantic and Indian Oceans the Mid-Adamant Island Island its located in Mauritius.
label: contradicted
reason: The claim is garbled, and no 'Mid-Adamant Island' could be found. Its main point, that the place separating the Atlantic and Indian Oceans is in Mauritius, is wrong. Britannica says the official boundary between the two oceans is the meridian of Cape Agulhas (20° E) in South Africa. Mauritius lies entirely within the Indian Ocean, far from the Atlantic. No source places this boundary in Mauritius.

text: Walking on water is possible for certain animals like the Basilisk lizard and the Western Grebe, which can run at speeds of up to 18 miles per hour generating enough force to stay on top of the water.
label: not_verifiable
reason: The search results support part of the claim but not the 18 mph figure. Basilisk lizards can run across water for short distances, and research on Western and Clark's grebes describes them running on water. However, no source gave 18 mph for either animal. Wikipedia and A-Z Animals put the basilisk's speed on water at about 15 mph, while a fluid-dynamics summary gives about 1.6 m/s (roughly 3.6 mph) and Science Focus gives about 3 mph for adults. I could not get a grebe speed before my search limit ran out. Because the sources disagree on basilisk speed and none confirms 18 mph, the speed claim cannot be verified.

text: A blue whale's heart alone can weigh up to 400 pounds and pump around 5,000 gallons of blood through the whale's body with each beat.
label: contradicted
reason: NOAA Fisheries backs the weight figure, saying a blue whale's heart weighs about 400 pounds. It contradicts the volume figure, though: NOAA says the heart pumps about 60 gallons of blood with each beat, not around 5,000 gallons.

text: Scientists estimate that there are approximately 8.7 million identified species on Earth, but the actual number could range from 10 to 30 million total species.
label: contradicted
reason: The 8.7 million figure is not a count of identified species. It is the estimated total number of species on Earth (give or take 1.3 million), from Mora et al., 2011. Only about 1.2 million species have actually been described and catalogued. The claim mislabels that estimated total as 'identified' species, so it is contradicted.

text: Humans are born without kneecaps, and they typically begin to develop and appear in a child's early life, between ages 3 to 5.
label: contradicted
reason: Several sources say it's a myth that babies are born without kneecaps. Babies already have kneecaps (patellae) at birth, but they are made of cartilage. What happens later in childhood is ossification, when that cartilage hardens into bone; sources put this at roughly ages 2–6 or 3–6. The age range in the claim is roughly right for ossification, but the statement that humans are born without kneecaps is wrong.

text: Galileo Galilei was the first person to observe the planet Neptune, but he didn't recognize it as a planet; instead, he recorded it as a star in 1612.
label: supported
reason: Wikipedia's article on the discovery of Neptune says Galileo's drawings show he observed Neptune on December 28, 1612, and again on January 27, 1613. Both times he mistook it for a fixed star, because it appeared very close to Jupiter. This is the earliest known recorded observation of Neptune, so it is commonly described as the first. One nuance: Galileo did note that this 'star' seemed to move. However, he never identified it as a planet, so the claim holds.

text: A blue whale's heartbeat can be as slow as two beats per minute when it is fully submerged and diving deep into the ocean.
label: supported
reason: The first heart-rate recordings from a wild blue whale, made by Goldbogen and colleagues in a 2019 study, found that its heart rate fell as low as two beats per minute while diving deep. The usual minimum during dives was about four to eight beats per minute. Newsweek, CNN, Smithsonian and The Scientist all report this result.

text: A blue whale's heartbeat is so loud that it can be detected over 500 miles away using specialized underwater equipment.
label: contradicted
reason: NOAA Fisheries says a blue whale's heartbeat can be heard about 2 miles away, not more than 500 miles. Other sources repeat the 2-mile figure. Some even doubt that it can be heard that far. The long distances of hundreds of miles apply to blue whale calls, not to their heartbeat.

text: Bacteria can survive in extreme environments, such as the Antarctic ice sheets and deep-sea hydrothermal vents.
label: supported
reason: Scientific sources say microbes, including bacteria, live in extreme environments. The Scientist describes microbes thriving in deep-sea hydrothermal vents and in Antarctic settings, such as the ice around Blood Falls. Bacteria have also been widely documented beneath the Antarctic ice sheet, for example in subglacial Lake Whillans, which is consistent with this. Both examples in the claim are well established, and nothing found contradicts it.

text: Cats have a highly specialized vocalization range and can produce over 100 different sounds, whereas humans can only make about 30.
label: contradicted
reason: The well-known piece of trivia compares cats with dogs (cats can make over 100 sounds, dogs about 10), not with humans. A University of Nevada, Las Vegas linguistics page says humans can produce about 600 consonant sounds and 200 vowel sounds. Even English alone uses about 39 meaningful sounds, so the claim that humans can only make about 30 is false.

text: Honeybees are able to fly by using electricity generated from the movement of their wings, which helps reduce air resistance.
label: contradicted
reason: Bees fly through aerodynamics. They beat their wings about 200–300 times per second, which creates pressure differences that generate lift. Bees do pick up a positive electrostatic charge from friction with the air while flying, but the sources say this charge helps them attract pollen and sense the electric fields around flowers. None of the sources say electricity powers their flight or reduces air resistance, so the claim mixes up how bees fly with what their static charge actually does.

text: Honeybees are able to fly by using their wings to generate electricity and create an electric charge that attracts pollen.
label: contradicted
reason: The evidence goes against the claim's main point. A peer-reviewed article on PMC/NIH says bees and other flying animals pick up electrostatic charge while they fly, and that this charge can be strong enough to attract pollen. So the part about charge attracting pollen is broadly accurate. But the charge comes from flying through the air; it is not what makes bees fly. Bees fly because their flapping wings produce aerodynamic lift, not because they generate electricity. The claim gets the cause and effect backwards.

text: Humans and dolphins are the only known species that give themselves names.
label: contradicted
reason: Recent research shows that humans and dolphins are not the only animals with names. Elephants and marmosets also use individual name-like calls. A report on the marmoset study published in Science says humans, dolphins and elephants were the only other species known to use names before marmosets were added. This contradicts the claim that only humans and dolphins do so. One caveat: elephants and marmosets give names to each other, while dolphins develop their own signature whistles, so the wording 'give themselves names' is ambiguous. Even so, the broader claim that only humans and dolphins have names conflicts with current scientific reporting.

text: Humans share about 50% of their DNA with bananas, illustrating the fascinating similarities and connections across different species.
label: contradicted
reason: Snopes, a reliable fact-checker, rates the idea that humans share 50% of their DNA with bananas as false. It says there is "no scenario" where the statement can be read as factual. The number really means that about half of human genes have related counterparts in bananas, not that half of our DNA matches. Comparing whole genomes would put the shared figure well below 1%.

text: Lund in Sweden is home to the world's oldest still-operational restaurant, Stäket, dating back to 1622
label: contradicted
reason: Stäket is a real restaurant in Lund, housed in a 16th-century building (about 1550–1570). The building was renovated in 1957 and has held a restaurant since then. The current Italian restaurant has been run since 2015. Nothing ties it to 1622 or calls it the world's oldest restaurant. Guinness gives that title for continuous operation to Sobrino de Botín in Madrid (1725), and St. Peter Stiftskulinarium in Salzburg (803 AD) is widely cited as the oldest restaurant still operating.

text: Scientists estimate that there may be between 700,000 and 1 million species on Earth that remain undiscovered or unclassified.
label: contradicted
reason: The claim's range of 700,000 to 1 million undiscovered species is far below what scientists actually estimate. Nature reports the widely cited estimate of about 8.7 million species on Earth, with more than 80% still undiscovered, which works out to roughly 7 million. The E.O. Wilson Foundation describes about 8 million unknown species, and other estimates are in the millions or even tens of millions. None of the sources found support the 700,000–1 million figure.

text: Seals use a series of short dives to hunt for prey in the water.
label: supported
reason: The search results back the general claim that seals hunt by making repeated short dives. A Scientific Reports study on harbor seals found they made about 13 foraging dives per hour, averaging 3.3 minutes each. Other harbor seal studies describe foraging in bouts of short, shallow dives. A BBC Discover Wildlife article says common seals forage in shallow coastal waters on brief dives. One caveat: some species, such as elephant seals, make longer dives of about 20–30 minutes, though these are still repeated in a continuous series. Since the claim is a broad generalization, the evidence supports it.

text: Schedule 1 of the Indian Constitution initially listed 29 states, but as of 2023, the number of officially recognized states in India is 28, with the most recent change being the reorganization of Jammu and Kashmir.
label: supported
reason: Several sources (Vedantu and Testbook explainers) say the 1950 Constitution grouped India's states into Parts A, B, C and D, for a total of 29. Other sources say India has 28 states and 8 union territories. They add that the most recent change to the number of states came from the Jammu and Kashmir Reorganisation Act, 2019, which split the former state into two union territories on 31 October 2019 and lowered the count from 29 to 28. One caveat: strictly speaking, Part D (the Andaman and Nicobar Islands) was a territory rather than a state. However, commonly cited sources still give the original total as 29.

text: Humans are the only species known to experience a condition called 'tetrachromacy,' where the presence of four types of cones in the retina allows a person to see an increased range of colors.
label: contradicted
reason: The claim is false. Humans are not the only species known to have tetrachromacy. A Journal of Experimental Biology paper says that many birds, reptiles and shallow-water fish are tetrachromatic and use four cone classes. Wikipedia and Color Matters also describe tetrachromacy in non-human animals, including fish and turtles. Only some humans, mostly some women, may be tetrachromats.

text: Scientists estimate that there are approximately 8.7 million identified species on Earth, but the total number of species is believed to be significantly higher.
label: contradicted
reason: The 8.7 million figure is not a count of identified species. It comes from Mora et al. (2011), who estimated the total number of eukaryotic species on Earth at about 8.7 million, give or take 1.3 million. Only about 1.2 million species had been described or catalogued at the time, which suggests that roughly 86% are still undiscovered. The claim calls 8.7 million the identified species and says the total is much higher, so it gets the relationship wrong.

text: Glass can withstand extremely high temperatures, with some types of glass, such as borosilicate, being able to resist thermal shock and maintain its shape and integrity up to 500 degrees Celsius.
label: supported
reason: DWK Life Sciences, a laboratory glassware maker and a reliable technical source, gives 500°C as the maximum recommended working temperature for 3.3 borosilicate glass. It also says the glass resists thermal shock well. Wikipedia likewise says borosilicate resists thermal shock better than any other common glass. One caveat: DWK says the 500°C limit applies only for short periods, and the safe temperature difference for thermal shock is much smaller (about 166°C). Still, the claim's main points match the sources.

text: Tarantulas have been on Earth for a long time, with fossil evidence showing they existed over 120 million years ago during the Cretaceous period, a time when dinosaurs roamed the planet.
label: contradicted
reason: The 120-million-year date is real, but it doesn't come from fossils. ScienceDaily and Smithsonian report on a phylogenomic (molecular dating) study, which concluded that tarantulas first appeared about 120 million years ago in the Cretaceous. That supports the claim's timing and the overlap with dinosaurs. The fossil record shows something different. A peer-reviewed biogeography study in the Journal of Biogeography says the oldest known tarantula (theraphosid) fossil comes from Burmese amber and is dated to about 100 million years ago. Older mygalomorph fossils, such as Rosamygale from the Triassic, belong to a broader spider group, not to true tarantulas. So there is no fossil evidence that tarantulas existed more than 120 million years ago, and the claim's 'fossil evidence' detail is wrong.

text: A fossilized sea lizard discovered in the Yucatan Peninsula in Mexico was found to have a large block of amber lodged in its stomach, suggesting that these lizards ingested large amounts of the pine tree resin.
label: not_verifiable
reason: My searches found no report of a fossil sea lizard (such as a mosasaur) from the Yucatán Peninsula with a block of amber in its stomach. The amber-and-lizard finds that did come up are different things. One is a small 23-million-year-old Anolis lizard preserved inside amber from Simojovel, Chiapas, not the Yucatán, and it had not eaten amber. Others are amber lizards from the Dominican Republic and Myanmar. Sea-reptile stomach-content finds involve eaten animals, not resin. Nothing confirms the claim, but nothing directly disproves it either, so it cannot be verified.

text: A blue whale's heart is so large that it can pump around 5,000 liters of blood with every beat.
label: contradicted
reason: The 5,000-liter figure is far too high. Sources put a blue whale's output at about 220 liters (58 gallons) per beat. The Politecnico di Milano (iheart.polimi.it) says the heart can pump "up to 220 liters of blood at each beat," and several other sources give the same number. A study of one young whale, reported by Inverse, estimated only about 80 liters per beat. Both figures are a small fraction of 5,000 liters, and no source supported the claim.

text: A blue whale's heartbeat can be as loud as 188 decibels, louder than a jet taking off, and can be detected for hundreds of miles underwater.
label: contradicted
reason: The claim mixes up the blue whale's call with its heartbeat. Monterey Bay Aquarium, Live Science, Enchanted Learning and Cool Antarctica all give the 188-decibel figure, the comparison to a jet, and the detection range of hundreds of miles for the whale's vocal calls, not its heartbeat. Even popular sources that make bold heart claims say only that the heartbeat can be heard about 2 miles away underwater, which is far from 188 dB or hundreds of miles. Because the claim gives these call figures to the heartbeat, it is contradicted.

text: A blue whale's heartbeat can be as slow as two beats per minute when it is resting and can produce almost 1,000 pounds of sound with each beat from its heartbeat.
label: contradicted
reason: Newsweek's report on the Stanford study (Goldbogen et al., published in PNAS) confirms that a blue whale's heart rate can drop as low as two beats per minute. However, that low rate was measured during deep foraging dives, not while the whale was resting; at the surface its heart rate rose to 25–37 beats per minute. The rest of the claim doesn't hold up either. Sound is not measured in pounds, so 'almost 1,000 pounds of sound with each beat' has no meaning. The claim seems to garble the commonly reported weight of the heart (about 400 lbs) or the popular idea that the heartbeat can be heard from far away. Because the two-beat figure is placed in the wrong context and the second part is inaccurate, the claim is contradicted.

text: A blue whale's heartbeat can be as slow as two beats per minute when it's deep in the ocean, allowing it to conserve energy.
label: supported
reason: Reliable outlets (Science, Newsweek, Live Science) cover the Stanford-led study by Goldbogen et al., published in PNAS. The study found that a blue whale's heart rate can fall to as low as two beats per minute during deep foraging dives. This slowing of the heart during dives (bradycardia) is a recognised way of conserving oxygen and energy, and the coverage describes the whale surviving on just two beats per minute while diving. Strictly speaking, the sources frame the benefit as saving oxygen rather than 'energy', but the claim matches the evidence.

text: A veutric, an eversion of a sphere turning itself inside out is made up entirely of circles, calculated by Bill Thurston in 1980
label: contradicted
reason: I found nothing on a sphere eversion called a "veutric". The term doesn't appear in any source I checked. Bill Thurston's eversion does exist, but the claim gets two things wrong. First, the method: Thurston's eversion works by corrugation, wrinkling the sphere into wavy strips, and the Geometry Center's "Outside In" pages describe it that way. That video does suggest picturing the sphere as a stack of circles, but nothing says the eversion is made up entirely of circles. Second, the date: sources place Thurston's eversion in the mid-1970s, not 1980. A ruled-surface eversion by Adam and Witold Bednorz came much later and is a different construction. Overall the sources contradict the claim's description and date.

text: Astronauts on the Moon lose about 1 inch of their height due to the Moon's lower gravity when they return to Earth.
label: not_verifiable
reason: The evidence I found covers astronauts in orbit, not on the Moon. A Medium explainer, which is not a highly authoritative source, says astronauts in Earth orbit temporarily grow about 2 inches taller because their spinal discs expand in microgravity, and that the change is temporary. Low gravity therefore makes people taller, not shorter. I found no source giving a Moon-specific figure such as 'about 1 inch' for astronauts in lunar gravity, which is one-sixth of Earth's. The claim's wording is also unclear: it may mean that low gravity shrinks people, which conflicts with the general evidence, or that astronauts lose height they gained once they return to Earth. Because there is no Moon-specific data, and my searches hit the tool limit, I can neither confirm nor refute the claim.

text: Caterpillars can consume up to 27,000 times their body weight in a single day, which is equivalent to a human eating around 2 elephants.
label: contradicted
reason: Reliable sources say the 27,000-times figure covers a caterpillar's whole larval stage, not a single day. The Naked Scientists puts it at 27,000 times body weight over the roughly 4 weeks of caterpillar life, and 13abc says the same applies before pupation, about 3–4 weeks after hatching. KidsKonnect calls it a lifetime total. Only one low-quality page (thingscope) says 'in a single day'. The elephant comparison is also unsupported: the only human comparison found is Naked Scientists' '68 cows... a day', not 2 elephants.

text: Honeybees are able to fly by using electricity generated from friction created by the movement of their wings, in a process known as "triboelectric charging".
label: contradicted
reason: Research shows honeybees do pick up static charge through triboelectric effects, for example when their wings rub against their bodies or the air. That charge has other effects, such as helping them detect electric fields and pick up pollen. But no source says the electricity powers flight. Bees fly by aerodynamics, generating lift with their muscle-driven wingbeats. So the claim that bees fly by using electricity from wing friction gets the mechanism wrong, even though the triboelectric charging itself is real.

text: Honeybees are able to fly by using electricity generated from friction created by the movement of their wings, in a process known as "triboelectric charging."
label: contradicted
reason: Honeybees do pick up static charge through triboelectric charging when they fly, from friction with the air and from body parts rubbing together. Research describes this charge as useful for things like sensing electric fields and collecting pollen, not for powering flight. The trustworthy sources I found (a ScienceDirect primer on aerial electroreception and studies of bee charge on ResearchGate) treat it as a side effect of flying, and none say bees use electricity to fly. Bees fly by aerodynamics, generating lift with their flapping wings and flight muscles. So the claim gets the cause backwards: triboelectric charging comes from flight rather than powering it.

text: Human babies are born without kneecaps, and they do not begin to develop fully until they are around 3-5 years old.
label: contradicted
reason: The claim that babies are born without kneecaps is a common misconception. HowStuffWorks says that although bony kneecaps do not show up on X-rays, babies do have kneecaps; at birth they are made of cartilage. Grownsy calls the no-kneecaps idea a myth, and another health answer site likewise says infants are born with kneecaps. The age part is roughly right: HowStuffWorks says the cartilage becomes a fully hardened patella between ages 3 and 5, though other sources say bone formation starts around age 2 to 6. Because the main premise is wrong, the claim is contradicted. Some sites, such as Pampers and Encyclopedia.com, say babies are born 'without kneecaps', but they mean without bony ones and agree that cartilage kneecaps are present.

text: Owens Falls Dam, located in New York, was the first hydroelectric power plant in the United States when it was completed in 1886 to power a manufacturing business.
label: contradicted
reason: Britannica says the Owen Falls Dam, now called the Nalubaale Dam, is on the Victoria Nile at Jinja, Uganda, not in New York. It was finished in 1954, not 1886, and it was not the first US hydroelectric plant. That title usually goes to the Vulcan Street Plant in Appleton, Wisconsin (1882), which I know from background knowledge rather than this search.

text: Scientists estimate that there are approximately 8.7 million identified species on Earth, but up to 80% of all species remain undiscovered and undescribed.
label: contradicted
reason: The 8.7 million figure from Mora et al. (2011) is an estimate of the total number of species on Earth, both known and unknown. It is not a count of identified species. Only about 1.2 million species have actually been identified and catalogued, which is less than 15% of that total. The claim is right that over 80% of species remain undiscovered, but calling the 8.7 million 'identified' is wrong.

text: Scientists estimate that there may be between 700,000 and 1 million plant species on Earth, but only about 10% of them have been formally described.
label: contradicted
reason: Credible sources put the total number of plant species far below the claim's 700,000 to 1 million. They also say most plant species, not about 10%, have already been described. BioNumbers (Harvard), citing primary literature, reports that about 350,000 plant species have been named, which is an estimated 80–90% of the global total. Kew's State of the World's Plants report counted about 390,900 known plant species. Mora et al. (2011) also estimated that roughly 80% or more of plant species are described.

text: Spiders have been on Earth for approximately 318 million years, with the earliest known spider-like arachnid fossil dating back to the Devonian period.
label: supported
reason: Both parts of the claim check out, though the first part depends on what counts as a spider. The oldest fossils of true spiders come from the Carboniferous, about 315–319 million years ago. A British Arachnological Society paper cites a fossil of about 318 Ma from Hagen-Vorhalle, Germany, and fossils of the related ricinuleid arachnids go back to about 319 Ma. The earliest spider-like arachnid is Attercopus fimbriunguis from the Devonian (about 380–390 Ma). It was once called the oldest spider but has been reclassified into the extinct silk-producing order Uraraneida, which is close to the origin of spiders. One caveat: Wikipedia says spiders have existed for 'at least 380 million years,' and molecular-clock estimates put their origin at 375–328 Ma. So 318 Ma is the date of the oldest true-spider fossils, not necessarily when spiders first appeared. Read that way, the claim matches the sources.

text: Tarantulas have been around for a long time - fossil evidence shows they've remained largely unchanged for over 120 million years.
label: contradicted
reason: The 120-million-year figure doesn't come from fossils. It comes from a genetic (phylogenomic) study by Foley et al. (2021), which estimated that tarantulas first appeared about 120 to 105.5 million years ago. That is an estimate of when the group originated, not proof that it has stayed the same since. Only two tarantula fossils are known, both in amber: one from Mexico (about 16 million years old) and one from Myanmar (about 100 million years old). So no fossil evidence covers more than 120 million years. Texas Parks & Wildlife magazine says fossils show tarantulas 'virtually unchanged' for more than 20 million years, not 120. Older tarantula-like ancestor fossils (235–240 million years) exist, but they are not tarantulas. The idea that tarantulas are ancient is reasonable, but the claim's specific fossil statement is wrong.

text: Tarantulas have been on Earth for a long time, with fossil evidence showing they existed at least 120 million years ago during the Cretaceous period.
label: contradicted
reason: The 120-million-year date is real, but it doesn't come from fossils. It comes from a 2021 genetic study (Foley et al.) that used transcriptome data to estimate when tarantulas first appeared: about 120 million years ago in the Cretaceous. Live Science reports that only two tarantula fossils are known, both in amber. One from Mexico is about 16 million years old, and the oldest, from Myanmar, is about 100 million years old. A Journal of Biogeography paper also calls the Burmese amber specimen (~100 Mya) the oldest tarantula fossil. So it is true that tarantulas are ancient and date to the Cretaceous, but no fossil shows they existed at least 120 million years ago.

text: The Boiling River of the Amazon, a natural river in Peru, remains at a constant boiling temperature of around 91°C (196°F) throughout the year, despite being located far from any volcanic activity.
label: contradicted
reason: Sources confirm that Shanay-Timpishka, Peru's "Boiling River," stays hot even though it is far from any volcano (about 700 km by one account). The claim's description of the temperature is wrong, though. Geoscientist Andrés Ruzo found an average of about 86°C (186.8°F) and said it was "not quite boiling." The temperature also changes along the river: it starts as a cold stream, and the hottest stretches reach roughly 94–99°C. So the river is not at a constant boiling temperature of around 91°C, and none of the sources support it staying the same all year.

text: Turtles have an innate navigation system that allows them to migrate thousands of miles across oceans and return to the exact beach where they were born to lay their own eggs.
label: supported
reason: Several reliable sources support the claim when it is read as being about sea turtles. National Geographic, UNC and Live Science report research showing that female sea turtles migrate across thousands of miles of ocean. They then return to nest at the beach or stretch of coastline where they hatched, guided by Earth's magnetic field and the coast's unique magnetic signature, which they imprint on as hatchlings. National Geographic describes them returning to the exact spot where they were born. One caveat: EarthSky notes that turtles do not always reach the exact beach and sometimes nest on beaches with similar magnetic fields. The scientific consensus is natal homing to the same general area, so 'exact beach' slightly overstates the precision, but the main claim holds.

text: Walking on water is possible for certain animals like the Basilisk lizard and some species of fish, due to their special adaptations that allow them to generate enough force and speed to stay above the water's surface.
label: supported
reason: National Geographic and Wikipedia confirm that basilisk lizards run across water. They do it with high speed and specially shaped feet that push down hard enough to keep their bodies above the surface and upright. The fish part is weaker. I found one video description saying mudskippers can 'dance' across the water surface using special adaptations, but no stronger source confirmed this. My search limit ran out before I could check further. On balance the claim looks broadly right, but the 'some species of fish' part rests on thinner evidence.

text: setSize is a feature that only some programming languages use to define array size.
label: supported
reason: Sources show that setSize is a library method in certain languages, not something all languages have. In PHP, SplFixedArray::setSize() sets the size of a fixed array. In Java, setSize() changes the size of Vector and Stack collections. Other languages set array size in different ways, for example when the array is declared. This matches the claim's point that only some languages use setSize. One caveat: setSize is a method in a library, not a core language feature, so 'feature' is used loosely.

text: Scientists estimate that there are approximately 8.7 million identified species on Earth, although it's believed that up to 80% of all species remain undiscovered.
label: contradicted
reason: The 8.7 million figure from Mora et al. (2011) is an estimate of all species on Earth, both described and undescribed. It is not a count of identified species. Only about 1.2 to 1.9 million species have actually been described, and the study estimated that about 86% of land species and 91% of ocean species are still undiscovered. So calling 8.7 million 'identified' species is wrong. It also doesn't fit with the claim's own statement that up to 80% remain undiscovered.

text: Tortoises have an exceptional lifespan, with the longest recorded lifespan being that of Jonathan, a Seychelles giant tortoise who lived to the age of 187.
label: contradicted
reason: Jonathan the Seychelles giant tortoise did not die at 187. He is still alive: he turned 190 in 2022 and 191 in 2023, and recent coverage describes him as the oldest living land animal at about 194. The claim's wording that he 'lived to the age of 187', and that this is his final recorded lifespan, is therefore wrong. Guinness World Records, CNN, Smithsonian and Live Science all describe him as still living. The general point that tortoises live exceptionally long lives is accurate.
