text: Honeybees are able to recognize human faces, using the same areas of their brains that humans use for face recognition, and are even able to differentiate between unknown and familiar faces.
label: contradicted
reason: Research supports part of the claim. Dyer et al. (2005) showed that honeybees can learn to tell apart and recognise images of human faces, and later studies found they use configural or holistic-like processing. But the claim that bees use 'the same areas of their brains' as humans is false. Bees have a tiny insect brain with no human-like face areas. The research is notable precisely because it shows face recognition does not need the specialised neural circuitry humans have. The sources also do not show that bees tell familiar faces from unknown ones; they show bees can recognise faces they were trained on.

text: The world's largest snowflake was recorded in Montana in 1887 and measured an astonishing 15 inches in diameter and 8 inches thick.
label: supported
reason: Several sources, including NC State University News and pieces citing the Guinness World Records entry, say the largest reported snowflake fell at Fort Keogh, Montana, in January 1887 and measured 15 inches (38 cm) wide and 8 inches thick. Some sources point out that the report was never verified, but no source contradicts any detail in the claim.

text: Humans and elephants share a similar rate of gestation, with human pregnancies lasting approximately 280 days and elephant pregnancies lasting nearly 22 months, which equals about 640-660 days.
label: contradicted
reason: The figures in the claim are about right: human pregnancy lasts about 280 days, and elephant pregnancy lasts about 18–22 months, or roughly 640–660 days. But those same numbers disprove the main point that the two gestation periods are 'similar.' Elephants are pregnant more than twice as long as humans, and their gestation is described as one of the longest of any mammal on Earth.

text: Cats have a highly specialized vocalization range that includes over 100 different sounds, while humans can make around 450 sounds and dogs can make around 10.
label: not_verifiable
reason: The cat and dog figures check out against popular pet sources. Purina, petdoors.com and AMAC all repeat that cats can make about 100 or more sounds while dogs make only about 10. That said, this is pop-trivia and the sources don't give a scientific basis for it. The human figure is the problem: nothing I found supports 'around 450 sounds.' The sources give other numbers, such as about 44 sounds in English, and one Quizlet study card says humans can make about 4,000 sounds. Because the human part can't be verified and other figures conflict with it, the claim as a whole is inconclusive.

text: Galileo Galilei was the first person to observe the planet Neptune using a telescope, but he didn't realize it was a planet at the time.
label: supported
reason: Astronomy.com reports that Galileo sketched Neptune between December 1612 and January 1613 using his telescope. It describes him as possibly the first person to see the planet, and says he seems to have taken it for a star. In 2009, physicist David Jamieson argued that Galileo knew he had spotted a planet, but the article concludes that the available evidence shows Galileo probably didn't work out what the object really was. This is the accepted account among historians, so both parts of the claim hold up: he made the first telescopic observation and didn't recognize Neptune as a planet.

text: The Axel Erlandson's TREE CIRCUS, in California, features intricately shaped and grafted trees, some of which form complex patterns and designs created by the late farmer Axel Erlandson.
label: supported
reason: Wikipedia and a gardening blog both say Axel Erlandson (1884–1964) was a Swedish American farmer who shaped trees as a hobby. In 1947 he opened 'The Tree Circus' in Scotts Valley, California. He used grafting to create shaped trees, such as the Basket Tree, whose sycamores were approach-grafted into diamond patterns. His trees still exist, with about 20 surviving at Gilroy Gardens, so the claim's present-tense wording is broadly acceptable even though the original roadside attraction is no longer run in its original form.

text: The68539-\Traits Eruption, also known as the 'Aeolian Islands eruption in 615 BCE  was likely the result of the largest volcanic eruption in the last 6,000 years on the planet.
label: contradicted
reason: The claim doesn't hold up. First, the name 'The68539-\Traits Eruption' looks garbled and doesn't match any known eruption. My searches also found no record of a major 'Aeolian Islands eruption in 615 BCE'. The Smithsonian's Global Volcanism Program describes the Aeolian volcanoes (Lipari, Vulcano, Stromboli) mainly in terms of small and moderate (Vulcanian/Strombolian) eruptions, not very large events. Second, the 'largest eruption in the last 6,000 years' title belongs to Indonesian volcanoes, not Italian ones. VolcanoDiscovery and Britannica name Tambora's 1815 eruption as the largest of the past 10,000 years or of recorded history, and other sources list Samalas (Rinjani) in 1257 as larger still. Wikipedia's list of large Holocene eruptions also shows no Aeolian eruption from 615 BCE among the biggest.

text: Owens Falls Dam, located on the Niagara River in New York, was the first power station in the world that used alternating current (AC) to transmit electricity over a significant distance.
label: contradicted
reason: The claim gets the dam's location wrong. Owen Falls Dam, now called the Nalubaale Power Station, is a hydroelectric station in Jinja, Uganda. It sits on the White Nile where it leaves Lake Victoria, not on the Niagara River in New York, and it was finished in 1954. That is decades after the first long-distance AC power transmission, so the claim about being first in the world doesn't hold either.

text: Researchers at the University of California, San Diego, and Google have identified that honeybees improve their learning by sleeping and even have cycles similar to REM and non-REM sleep seen in humans.
label: not_verifiable
reason: I found no evidence for this claim before my search limit ran out. The search turned up a UC San Diego study from James Nieh's lab, led by Ashley Kim. That study found artificial light disrupts honeybee circadian rhythms and sleep. It does not mention Google, a link between sleep and better learning, or sleep cycles like REM and non-REM. From what I already know, rather than from these search results, the best-known research tying bee sleep to memory came from groups in Germany, not UC San Diego and Google. I found nothing that directly disproves the claim, but its main details are unverified.

text: A large percentage of human brains are actually more active and 'right-brained' in both creative, or 'mathematical' or 'non-creative' or other tasks, showing most brains are inaccurately described by such generalisation.
label: contradicted
reason: The claim's conclusion matches the evidence: the 'left-brained/right-brained' label does not describe people accurately. But the reason it gives is wrong. In a 2013 University of Utah study of resting brain scans from 1,011 people, researchers found no evidence that anyone is right-brained or left-brained overall. They did not see the whole right-brain network more connected in some people than others. That contradicts the claim that a large percentage of brains are more 'right-brained' in creative, mathematical and other tasks. The study found that lateralization depends on specific networks, not on whole-brain dominance in a person.

text: Plants can make sounds, too, as scientists have found that certain plants release distinct ultrasonic clicks or sounds when stressed or under attack by pests.
label: supported
reason: A 2023 peer-reviewed study in Cell (Khait et al., Tel Aviv University) found that stressed tomato and tobacco plants give off airborne ultrasonic popping or clicking sounds at about 40–80 kHz. They were tested under drought stress and after their stems were cut. Stressed plants made far more of these sounds than unstressed ones, and a machine-learning model could tell the type of stress from the sounds alone. That supports the main claim that plants release distinct ultrasonic clicks when stressed. One caveat: the study did not test pest attack directly, but the claim says 'stressed or under attack,' so the 'stressed' part is enough to support it.

text: Caterpillars can eat up to 27,000 times their body weight in a single day, which is equivalent to a human eating around 50,000 pizzas.
label: contradicted
reason: Sources describe the 27,000-times figure as the total a caterpillar eats over its whole larval stage, not in one day. The Naked Scientists says caterpillars eat 27,000 times their body weight in leaves "in the 4 weeks that they're caterpillars." That contradicts the claim's "in a single day." The source also gives a different human comparison (68 cows a day), and no search result supports the 50,000-pizza figure.

text: A blue whale can hold its breath for around 20 minutes and dive to depths of up to 3,288 feet in search of food.
label: contradicted
reason: The breath-holding part checks out, but the depth is wrong. Britannica says blue whales usually dive for about 10–20 minutes, and other sources give similar figures. However, 3,288 feet (about 1,000 m) is far deeper than any reported blue whale dive. SIMoN/NOAA puts the maximum at about 500 m (1,640 feet) and says blue whales usually stay shallower than 100 m. A tagging study recorded a maximum depth of 204 m. Several other sources put the limit at about 1,000 feet (about 305 m), not 3,288 feet. The 3,280-foot figure in Britannica refers to sperm whales.

text: A blue whale can hold its breath for around 20 minutes when it dives deep into the ocean in search of food.
label: supported
reason: Britannica says blue whales usually dive for about 10 to 20 minutes and can stay under for up to half an hour when needed. A whale-watching blog (futurismo.pt) gives an average dive time of 20 minutes, with a maximum of about 35–36 minutes. Together these support the claim that a blue whale holds its breath for around 20 minutes on deep feeding dives.

text: A blue whale's heartbeat is so powerful that scientists have found it possible to detect the heartbeat from over two miles away.
label: supported
reason: NOAA Fisheries, a trusted government science agency, says a blue whale's heartbeat "can be heard 2 miles away." The Cold Spring Harbor Whaling Museum and other sources say it can be detected from 2 miles away underwater, and many popular sources phrase this as "over 2 miles." Only an unreliable crowd-sourced answer site (Brainly) disputes it. Two caveats: NOAA says "2 miles" rather than "over" two miles, and I found no primary study behind the figure. Still, the credible evidence broadly supports the claim.

text: A blueprint is typically a large-scale detailed drawing or diagram that is often used in planning, construction, and architecture to provide a visual representation of a project.
label: supported
reason: The claim matches how trustworthy sources define a blueprint. MasterClass calls it "a detailed visual representation of how an architect wants a building to look" and says it specifies dimensions, materials and where each component goes. Cambridge Dictionary says blueprints are "used especially in the building industry." Merriam-Webster and Dictionary.com say they are used for copying architectural and mechanical drawings and architects' plans. Wikipedia describes a blueprint as a reproduction of a technical drawing. Other sources (Archisoup, Live Home 3D) confirm their role in construction and architecture, and Britannica notes they are often large sheets. Strictly, the word first meant a white-on-blue photographic copy, but the claim reflects the common meaning, and none of the sources contradict it.

text: A fetus can develop its unique fingerprints as early as 3 months into a pregnancy.
label: supported
reason: Trustworthy sources put the start of fingerprint formation at about 3 months of pregnancy. The Lozier Institute says fingerprints start forming around gestational week 12, and Cleveland Clinic says they begin to form around week 14. Other sources give weeks 10 to 13. One caveat is that the fingerprints are not complete at that point. Cleveland Clinic says the fetus has its own unique set by about week 19. Still, these sources support the claim that fingerprint development can begin as early as about 3 months.

text: A fetus can develop its unique fingerprints as early as 3-4 months into a woman's pregnancy.
label: supported
reason: Several reliable sources back this up. A Cell paper says fingerprint patterns are set by primary ridges that form at about gestational week 13, with sweat glands appearing by week 16. A U.S. Department of Justice (NIJ) document says friction ridges start forming at about 10.5 weeks and keep maturing into the second trimester. Other sources put the formation of secondary ridges at weeks 15–17. That puts the pattern-forming stage at roughly 3–4 months of pregnancy. The ridges continue to mature after that, up to about 25 weeks.

text: Gbetos, also known as plastic kayak-like boats, were used in West Africa as early as the 1400s to transport people.
label: contradicted
reason: Reliable sources say that 'Gbeto' is a Fon word for the female elephant hunters of the Dahomey kingdom. They served under King Houegbadja around 1645–1685 and were later folded into Dahomey's corps of women soldiers. Nothing describes Gbetos as boats. The claim that they were plastic kayak-like boats used to carry people in the 1400s is also anachronistic, since plastic did not exist then.

text: Humans and dolphins are the only mammals known to give themselves names, according to a study that noted dolphins have specific whistles that act as identifiers.
label: supported
reason: A 2013 PNAS study by King and Janik, reported by AFP via Phys.org and Rappler, found that wild bottlenose dolphins invent their own signature whistles to identify themselves. The reports say dolphins answer when they hear their own whistle and call them the only non-human mammals known to use names this way. The Sarasota Dolphin Research Program also says dolphins are the only animals besides humans shown to have names of this kind. One caveat: 2024 studies suggest elephants and marmosets use name-like calls for each other. Those calls are names given by others, not ones the animals make for themselves, so they don't clearly contradict the claim about self-chosen names or what the study reported.

text: Humans and elephants share the longest pregnancy periods, with a gestation period of nearly 22 months in elephants and approximately 9 months in humans.
label: contradicted
reason: The figures are right: elephants carry for about 22 months and humans for about 9. The claim is still wrong because humans don't share the longest pregnancy periods with elephants. Sources such as Discover Magazine and A-Z Animals say the African elephant alone has the longest gestation of any mammal. They also list many animals with longer pregnancies than humans, including rhinos, giraffes and sperm whales, which carry for 14 to 16 months.

text: Humans share approximately 50% of their DNA with bananas, highlighting the common ancestry of many living organisms.
label: contradicted
reason: Reliable science sources say the claim confuses genes with DNA. The Naked Scientists calls "we share half our DNA with bananas" a myth. Humans share roughly 50–60% of their genes with bananas, meaning the genes have recognisable counterparts, and those counterpart proteins are only about 40% identical (Lawrence Brody of NHGRI, quoted by HowStuffWorks). Because genes make up only about 2% of the genome, the actual share of DNA is around 1%, not 50%. IFLScience also says the popular statement is technically wrong because "it's not DNA." Some sites such as factmyth.com repeat the 50% figure, but they are less reliable and they also mix up genes and DNA. The common-ancestry part of the claim is right, but the central 50% DNA figure is contradicted.

text: Level 1 is the highest international classification level of wheelchair basketball in the International Wheelchair Basketball Federation.
label: contradicted
reason: IWBF classes run from 1.0 to 4.5 points. A 1.0 player has the most severe impairment and the least function, so 1.0 is the lowest class, not the highest. The highest functional class is 4.5. The British Wheelchair Basketball page confirms this: players are scored from 1.0 to 4.5, and the more impaired a player is, the fewer points they get.

text: Our brains are more active while we sleep and more creative than when we are awake.
label: not_verifiable
reason: The evidence is mixed. A Notre Dame article on sleep researcher Jessica Payne's work comes closest to backing the claim. It says many brain regions, especially those for learning and emotion, are more active during sleep than when awake. It also says sleep encourages creativity that might not happen during waking hours. However, that is about certain regions and about sleep supporting creativity afterward. It does not say the whole brain is more active or that we are more creative while asleep. Other trustworthy sources describe the brain in REM sleep as about as active as when awake (MIT Picower Institute, Karolinska Institutet). Harvard's sleep education site says activity depends on the stage: it is high and variable in REM but lower and more stable in non-REM sleep. A Science Advances study found a creative 'sweet spot' only in the light stage just as sleep begins, not across sleep as a whole. Because the sources partly support and partly contradict the claim's broad wording, it cannot be confirmed or ruled out.

text: Our brains are more active while we sleep and more creative when we daydream.
label: supported
reason: Reputable sources back both parts of the claim, with some caveats. On sleep, Notre Dame (Jessica Payne's research) says many brain regions, especially those for learning, information processing and emotion, are "more active during sleep than when you're awake." Harvard's sleep medicine division adds that the brain in REM sleep can be even more active than when awake, and MIT Picower and ZOE report similar findings. These sources also note the effect varies by sleep stage and region: the brain is less active in NREM sleep, so it is not more active across the board. On daydreaming, the Association for Psychological Science reports a Psychological Science study suggesting that mind wandering boosts creativity. Frontiers and PMC reviews support the link but call the evidence mixed. Overall the claim matches what reputable sources say, though it simplifies the science.

text: Plants are capable of producing flowers in response to the direction of sunlight, a phenomenon known as heliotropism or phototropism.
label: contradicted
reason: Heliotropism isn't about plants producing flowers. Wikipedia defines it as the daily or seasonal motion of plant parts, such as flowers or leaves, in response to the Sun's direction. Phototropism means growth toward or away from light. Neither one means making flowers because of where sunlight comes from. Flowering triggered by light is controlled by day length, which is called photoperiodism. So the claim gets wrong what these phenomena are.

text: Scientists estimate that there are around 8.7 million identified species on Earth, but the true number could be as high as 30 million.
label: contradicted
reason: The 8.7 million figure from Mora et al. (2011, PLoS Biology) is an estimate of the total number of species on Earth, including the ones nobody has found yet. It does not count identified species. The same study says only about 1.2 million species have been described and catalogued, including about 953,000 animals. So calling 8.7 million 'identified species' is wrong. Older estimates did run from 3 million to 100 million, so a total of up to 30 million is possible, but the main figure in the claim is mislabeled.

text: Tarantulas have been on Earth for a long time, with fossil evidence showing that they've remained largely unchanged for over 200 million years.
label: contradicted
reason: Tarantulas have been around a long time, but the '200 million years largely unchanged' part is wrong. A 2021 PeerJ study, reported by Live Science, Smithsonian and Phys.org, dates their origin to about 120 million years ago on Gondwana. The tarantula fossils it cites are amber specimens about 16 and about 100 million years old. Texas Parks & Wildlife magazine says the fossil record shows tarantulas 'virtually unchanged' for more than 20 million years, not 200 million. Only 'tarantula-like' ancestral fossils, broader mygalomorph spider relatives, go back about 235–240 million years. None of the sources I checked support true tarantulas staying largely unchanged for over 200 million years.

text: Tarantulas have lived on Earth for a long time, with fossil evidence showing they've remained largely unchanged for over 100 million years.
label: not_verifiable
reason: The search results don't support the claim's specific statement about fossils. Tarantulas are old: molecular studies put their origin around 105–120 million years ago, so the general idea of a long history holds up. But Live Science reports that only two tarantula fossils are known, both in amber: one from Mexico, about 16 million years old, and one from Myanmar, about 100 million years old. That oldest fossil is about 100 million years old, not clearly over it, and the claim's 'over 100 million years' rests mostly on molecular estimates rather than fossils. With only two specimens, the fossil record can't show that tarantulas have stayed 'largely unchanged' over that span. Some evidence points the right way, but the specific claim about fossil evidence can't be verified and is somewhat overstated.

text: When heated to extremely high temperatures, certain types of glass can actually be molded and shaped into a variety of forms.
label: supported
reason: Search results back the claim. Several glass-shaping patents describe heating glass to its softening or deformation point, where it can be molded into a new shape. This is also the basis of well-established processes like glassblowing, slumping and mold pressing, where heated glass is formed into many shapes.

text: Caterpillars can eat up to 27,000 times their body weight in a single day, which is equivalent to a human eating around 2.5 elephants daily.
label: contradicted
reason: The 27,000-times-body-weight figure is real, but it covers a caterpillar's whole larval stage, not one day. Kidskonnect says caterpillars eat about 27,000 times their body weight 'in its lifetime,' and Twinkl, Durham Wildlife Trust and The Naked Scientists say the same thing (Naked Scientists puts it at about 4 weeks). Guinness World Records likewise gives its record for the polyphemus moth caterpillar over a period of weeks, not a single day. I found no reliable source for the '2.5 elephants daily' comparison. Because the claim turns a lifetime total into a daily amount, it is contradicted.

text: A blue whale's heartbeat can be as slow as two beats per minute when the whale is resting or sleeping underwater.
label: not_verifiable
reason: The 2 bpm figure is real, but the sources tie it to a different situation than the claim. They say a tagged blue whale's heart rate dropped as low as two beats per minute during deep foraging dives, when it was diving for food, with typical dive rates of 4–8 bpm. That is active feeding at depth, not resting or sleeping. None of the results report heart rates for a resting or sleeping blue whale, so the claim's 'resting or sleeping' condition can't be confirmed. It also isn't directly ruled out, which is why this is inconclusive rather than contradicted.

text: A giant squid's eyes are the largest of any animal, with some specimens having eyes that are up to 27 centimeters (11 inches) in diameter.
label: contradicted
reason: The record for the largest eyes of any animal goes to the colossal squid (Mesonychoteuthis hamiltoni), not the giant squid (Architeuthis). CNN, IFAW, Wikipedia, Mission Blue and Live Science all link the roughly 27 cm (about 11 inch) eye measurement to a colossal squid specimen. Giant squid eyes are also very large, but reliable sources say they are the largest 'except perhaps the colossal squid.' So calling the giant squid's eyes the largest of any animal attaches the record to the wrong species.

text: A person who collects or studies antique clocks is known as an horologist.
label: supported
reason: Wikipedia's Horology article says people interested in horology are called horologists. It adds that the term covers professionals who work with timekeeping devices as well as enthusiasts and scholars of horology. Merriam-Webster defines a horologist as someone skilled in the practice or theory of horology. Together these back the idea that a person who studies or collects antique clocks, as an enthusiast or scholar, can be called a horologist. One caveat: the core dictionary sense is closer to clockmaker or expert, and the word isn't only for antique-clock collectors. The claim's grammar ('an horologist') doesn't change what it means.

text: Awitter is a fast and retweet-focused app, from Twitter that connects professionals in the newsroom overnight trending content producer.
label: not_verifiable
reason: I found no reliable evidence that an app called "Awitter" exists. Searches only turned up unrelated Twitter/X accounts with the handles @Awitter and @awitter_, plus similarly named third-party clients such as AeroWitter. Nothing shows a fast, retweet-focused app from Twitter that connects newsroom professionals or overnight trending-content producers. The claim's wording is also garbled and doesn't point to a clear subject.

text: Awitter is a fast-growing, rare condition where animals and even people have the sensation of swallowing when there is nothing inside their mouth.
label: not_verifiable
reason: I found no reliable source that describes "awitter" as a medical or veterinary condition. Searches turned up nothing that defines it as a fast-growing, rare condition where animals or people feel like they are swallowing with nothing in their mouth. The results only covered unrelated swallowing disorders, such as dysphagia and aerophagia, and unrelated words like "awit" and "awaj." Since nothing supports or directly contradicts the claim, the evidence is inconclusive. The term seems to be made up or a misspelling, possibly of "atwitter," meaning agitated or excited.

text: Bionic limbs can be controlled directly by the user's thoughts, using electroencephalography (EEG) technology to detect the brain activity that normally triggers muscle movement.
label: supported
reason: Several sources show that prosthetic or bionic arms can be controlled by thought through EEG. Peer-reviewed work by Beyrouthy et al. (IEEE 2016; ASTESJ) describes a smart prosthetic arm 'controlled by the brain commands, obtained from an electroencephalography (EEG) headset.' A paper in IJACSA on an EEG-based brain-computer interface prosthetic hand describes the same approach, and Smithsonian Magazine reports a low-cost mind-controlled prosthetic arm that runs on EEG brain-wave data. Most commercial bionic limbs use EMG (muscle signals) or implanted interfaces rather than EEG, but the claim only says limbs 'can be' controlled this way. That is supported, and nothing found contradicts it.

text: C Rustan wasOnce the only country in the world whose inhabitants were required to have a 'registered profession.'
label: not_verifiable
reason: I couldn't tell what "C Rustan" refers to. No country with that name turned up in my searches. The results only showed unrelated things: Rustan's (a Philippine department store chain), Dom Rustan (a village in Iran) and Rust (a town in Austria). I also found no reliable source saying any country was once the only one that required its inhabitants to have a "registered profession." Because the subject has no clear referent and the claim itself can't be checked, it can't be confirmed or ruled out.

text: Finland has a "forest library" called Kirjasaari, a large woodland area in which books are exchanged for trees to help create more opportunities for reading.
label: contradicted
reason: The search results show that Kirjasaari is real, but it is not a forest library. Official City of Oulu library pages (ouka.fi, kirjastossatavataan.fi) describe it as a yearly event series open to everyone, where library staff present new books for children, young people and adults, plus music, games and films. It has run for about 20 years at Oulu's central library, Saari. None of the results mention a woodland area or swapping books for trees, so the claim gets what Kirjasaari is wrong.

text: France and the United States are the only countries in the world withSending 'physicians to nearly every corner of the globe.
label: contradicted
reason: The claim says France and the United States are the only countries sending physicians to nearly every corner of the globe, and the evidence shows this is false. Human Rights Watch reports that, according to the Cuban government, Cuba has sent over 400,000 health workers to 164 countries over nearly 60 years. Al Jazeera, Time and ABC News also describe Cuba's long-running medical missions abroad. Since at least one other country does this on a global scale, France and the US are not the only ones. (The claim's wording is garbled, but its meaning is clear enough to check.)

text: Giraffes are the only animals born with their eyes open, and they are also able to walk within their first hour of birth, although they can't run immediately.
label: contradicted
reason: The claim says giraffes are the only animals born with their eyes open, and that is false. Oxford Reference describes precocial mammals as young born with their eyes and ears open and able to stand and walk, and it names cattle, sheep and horses as examples. Merriam-Webster adds that hares are born with their eyes open. Because many other species share this trait, the claim's main assertion is contradicted, whatever the truth of the details about walking and running.

text: Honeybees are able to fly by using electricity generated by the movement of their wings to attract pollen from flowers.
label: contradicted
reason: Reliable sources such as AskNature and Science Friday say that a bee picks up a positive electrostatic charge as it flies and flaps its wings, and that this charge helps pull pollen onto its body. So the charge comes from flight; it does not power flight. Bees fly using aerodynamic lift from beating their wings. Static electricity is a side effect that helps them collect pollen, not how they stay in the air. The claim gets this backwards when it says bees are able to fly by using electricity.

text: Humans and dolphins are the only mammals known to give themselves names, as demonstrated by observations of dolphins assigning unique whistles to identify one another.
label: contradicted
reason: The claim that humans and dolphins are the only mammals known to use names is out of date. A 2024 study, reported by AFP/France24, found that wild African elephants call each other by individual names they invent, without imitating the other animal's sound. That makes elephants a mammal besides humans and dolphins with name-like calls. Research on marmosets has reported similar individual-specific calls. Dolphins do use signature whistles to identify each other, but the 'only mammals' part of the claim is wrong.

text: In the United States, the shortest war ever fought was between the United States and the Hawaiian Islands, lasting only 45 minutes.
label: contradicted
reason: No 45-minute war between the United States and Hawaii was ever fought. The 1893 overthrow of the Hawaiian Kingdom was a coup backed by U.S. Marines, not a declared war between the two countries. The war that is known as the shortest ever recorded, lasting 38 to 45 minutes, was the Anglo-Zanzibar War of 1896, fought between the United Kingdom and the Sultanate of Zanzibar. The claim gets the countries involved wrong.

text: Polar bears are excellent swimmers and have been known to swim for hours or even days at a time in search of food or shelter.
label: supported
reason: National Geographic, Guinness World Records, and the CBC all report that polar bears swim long distances. A USGS study recorded one female swimming for 9 straight days (687 km), and Guinness says she did it in search of food. The CBC reports a median long-distance swim of about 3.4 days, and these swims happen as bears travel between land and sea-ice floes to hunt seals or find stable ice. That backs up both parts of the claim: hours-to-days swims, and swimming to find food or shelter.

text: Roses arranged in a specific pattern can be used to create a compass, as the head of the rose turns south, giving rough directional indications.
label: contradicted
reason: No source I found supports the idea that rose heads turn south or that roses can be arranged to work as a compass. The claim seems to mix up the 'compass rose', a direction diagram on maps and charts, with real roses. Reliable sources (Wikipedia, gisnet/Leonardtown) say the compass rose is called a 'rose' only because its points look like a rose's petals; it was originally a wind rose showing wind directions. The plant actually known for pointing in a direction is the compass plant (Silphium laciniatum), whose leaves tend to line up north–south. That is a different plant, not a rose. So the claim's premise goes against what the sources say about where the 'compass rose' idea comes from.

text: Some mushrooms, specifically the Armillaria ostoyae fungus, can grow to be over 2,200 acres in size, making them one of the largest living organisms in the world.
label: supported
reason: The Oregon Encyclopedia says the Armillaria ostoyae colony in Oregon's Malheur National Forest, nicknamed the Humongous Fungus, covers 2,385 acres, or about 3.7 square miles. That is more than 2,200 acres. The same source says it is believed to be the largest single living organism on earth by biomass, which supports calling it one of the largest living organisms in the world.

text: Spiders have been around for a long time, with the oldest known spider fossil dating back approximately 318 million years to the Carboniferous period.
label: supported
reason: Reliable sources agree that the oldest true spider fossils date to the Carboniferous. A British Arachnological Society paper names a Russian Arthrolycosa sp. as the oldest unequivocal spider, from the late Carboniferous Bashkirian stage at about 315 million years ago. Paul Selden's paper on the Russian spiders says the fossil is 'slightly older than 315 Ma' and calls it the oldest spider currently known. None of the sources I found gives exactly 318 million years. Popular sources round the age to about 300 million years. Still, about 315+ Ma is close enough to 'approximately 318 million years,' so the claim holds up overall. The Devonian Attercopus, once called the oldest spider, has since been reclassified as a non-spider.

text: Spiders have been around for a remarkably long time, with fossils of ancient spiders dating back to over 318 million years ago during the Carboniferous period.
label: supported
reason: Several sources confirm that the earliest true spider fossils come from the Carboniferous period. Guinness World Records puts the earliest fossil spiders in the Carboniferous, at about 300 million years ago, and reports on Arthrolycosa wolterbeeki describe a Carboniferous spider dated to 310–315 million years ago. The searches I could run did not show the exact figure of "over 318 million years ago." My search limit ran out before I could check it directly. I'm relying on my own background knowledge for that number: references such as the Wikipedia spider article place the oldest known true spiders at about 318–319 million years ago in the Carboniferous. The overall claim fits the evidence I found, but that specific date is not directly confirmed by these search results.

text: Tarantulas have been on Earth for a long time, with fossil evidence showing they existed around 150 million years ago during the Cretaceous period.
label: contradicted
reason: The claim conflicts with the evidence on both the fossil date and the geologic period. Live Science, reporting on the 2021 Foley et al. study, says only two tarantula fossils are known, both in amber: one from Mexico, about 16 million years old, and one from Myanmar, about 100 million years old. No fossil shows tarantulas 150 million years ago. Genetic studies reported by SciTechDaily, Big Think and Smithsonian place the origin of tarantulas at about 120 million years ago in the Cretaceous. The date and period in the claim also don't match each other: 150 million years ago falls in the Late Jurassic, since the Cretaceous began about 145 million years ago.

text: Tarantulas have existed for millions of years, with fossil records dating back to the Early Cretaceous, over 135 million years ago.
label: contradicted
reason: Tarantulas have existed for millions of years, but the fossil date in the claim is wrong. Scientific sources, including a 2023 Journal of Biogeography paper and Live Science reporting on a phylogenomic study, say the oldest known tarantula fossil comes from Burmese amber dated to about 100 million years ago (mid-Cretaceous). Live Science says only two tarantula fossils are known, the other about 16 million years old. Molecular-clock studies estimate tarantulas arose around 105–120 million years ago, but that is an inferred origin, not a fossil, and it is still well under 135 million years. No source supports a tarantula fossil from the Early Cretaceous older than 135 million years.

text: giànhamas are a type of small, single-seated sled originating in the Andes Mountains of South America.
label: not_verifiable
reason: I couldn't find any trustworthy source showing that "giànhamas" is a real term. I searched for "giànhamas," "gianhamas" and "giànhamas sled Andes." The results were unrelated: Wikipedia disambiguation pages for Hama and Gian, and a History.com article about the 1972 Andes plane crash. Nothing describes a small single-seat sled from the Andes by this name. The term may be made up or garbled, so the claim can't be confirmed or disproved.

text: British Airways has a 747 jet with the smallest pilot staff as low as 3 plus 3 cabin on a B747  a British Airways short small variation the B747-200.
label: contradicted
reason: British Airways did fly 747-200s, and those had a three-person flight deck (captain, first officer and flight engineer). The rest of the claim is wrong. BA retired all 31 of its remaining 747s in 2020, so it no longer has any 747 jets. Its 747-200s were also not crewed by 3 pilots plus 3 cabin crew: on BA Flight 009, a 747-236B, there were 15 crew in total, a 3-person flight deck plus a full cabin crew. Three cabin crew would be far too few for a jumbo jet.

text: Butterfly eggs can range in size from as small as 0.1 millimeters in diameter for the Western Pygmy Blue, to about 2 millimeters in diameter for the monarch butterfly.
label: contradicted
reason: Both sizes in the claim are wrong. A Western Pygmy Blue egg is described as "almost exactly 0.5 millimeters across" (socalbutterflies.com), not 0.1 mm. Monarch eggs are about 0.9 mm wide and 1.2 mm high according to UC ANR and other sources, which is far smaller than the 2 mm diameter claimed.

text: France and the United States are the countries with the most time zones, with a total of 12 and 11 time zones, respectively, across their territories.
label: supported
reason: Several sources agree that France has the most time zones, with 12 across its overseas territories (13 if its Antarctic claim is counted). They also agree that the United States has 11 when its territories are included. Both figures in the claim are correct. One caveat: Russia also has 11, so it ties the US for second place. The claim leaves Russia out, but it doesn't say only France and the US hold these top spots, so the statement still holds.

text: Humans and elephants share several similarities, including that they both have the longest gestation periods among all mammals, with nearly 22 months of pregnancy, but for elephants it's almost 2 full year with 640 days almost 95 weeks of gestation
label: contradicted
reason: Science reports that elephants carry a fetus for about 22 months, which is the longest gestation of any mammal. Humans do not share that record, since human pregnancy lasts about 9 months, so the claim that both have the longest gestation (about 22 months) is false. The numbers for elephants also don't add up: 640 days is about 91 weeks, not almost 95.

text: Bionic limbs are being developed to give paralysed people the ability to control their prosthetic limbs by using signals from the brain with the help of sensors.
label: supported
reason: Several reliable sources (Science, UCSF via Neuroscience News, and a Scientific Reports paper on PMC) describe brain-computer interfaces that read brain signals through implanted or external sensors. Paralysed patients have used these to control robotic arms and a neuroprosthetic hand, which backs the general claim. One caveat: the claim says 'their prosthetic limbs', but in these studies the patients controlled external robotic or neuroprosthetic arms and hands rather than prostheses replacing missing limbs. The core point still holds: sensors pick up brain signals so paralysed people can control bionic limbs.

text: Caterpillars can eat up to 27,000 times their body weight in a single day, which is equivalent to a human eating around 2,000 pizzas in one sitting.
label: contradicted
reason: Reliable sources say the 27,000-times figure covers a caterpillar's whole larval stage, not a single day. The Naked Scientists says caterpillars eat 27,000 times their body weight "in the 4 weeks that they're caterpillars," and other sources describe it as happening over several weeks or a lifetime. Only one low-quality page (statustest.amherst.edu, which looks like a generated test page) says "in a single day." The claim's daily timeframe is therefore wrong. The pizza comparison is not backed by any credible source.

text: Researchers at the University of California, San Diego, and Google have identified that honeybees improve their learning by sleeping and even have cycles of deeper (slow-wave) and lighter (rapid eye movement) sleep periods.
label: contradicted
reason: I found no evidence of any study by UC San Diego and Google showing that honeybees learn better through sleep or have slow-wave and REM sleep cycles. The real UC San Diego bee-sleep study, from 2024 by the Nieh Lab, was about artificial light disrupting bees' sleep and daily rhythms. It did not involve Google, and it did not report REM-type sleep. The research on honeybee sleep stages and memory came from other groups, such as Zwaka et al. in Berlin, and it describes deep and light sleep stages, not REM sleep. The claim gets both the researchers and the findings wrong.

text: Bernard Bartalan, an Austrian-language teacher, holds the Guinness World Record for the longest duration without sleep, staying awake for 264.4 hours (11 days), albeit under close medical observation.
label: contradicted
reason: The claim gets the record holder wrong. Wikipedia credits the 264.4-hour (about 11-day) stay-awake record to Randy Gardner, a high school student from San Diego, in 1964. Searching for "Bernard Bartalan" turned up nothing linking that name to any sleep-deprivation record. Guinness also no longer monitors this category, so nobody currently holds a Guinness record for it. Its earlier recognised record was Toimi Silvo's 276 hours in Finland.

text: Honeybees are able to fly by using electricity, with the beat of their wings generating a positive static electric charge, allowing them to attract pollen which carries a negative charge.
label: contradicted
reason: The second half of the claim holds up. Flying bees build up a positive static charge from friction with the air, and flowers and pollen carry a negative charge, which helps pollen jump onto the bee (Quanta Magazine; a USPTO document). But the main assertion, that honeybees fly by using electricity, is wrong. The charge is a side effect of flight that helps with pollen collection and sensing flowers. It doesn't power or enable flight, which comes from aerodynamic lift produced by the wings. No reliable source says electricity lets bees fly.

text: In the heart of the Amazon rainforest, there's a species of jellyfish that's immortal - the Turritopsis dohrnii, a type of jellyfish that can transform its body into a younger state through a process called transdifferentiation.
label: contradicted
reason: Turritopsis dohrnii is called the 'immortal jellyfish', and it can return to a younger polyp stage through transdifferentiation. That part of the claim is accurate. But it is a marine species that lives in the Mediterranean Sea and in temperate to tropical ocean waters around the world. It does not live in the Amazon rainforest, so the claim's location is wrong.

text: Galileo Galilei was the first person to observe the planet Neptune, but he didn't recognize it as a planet and instead documented it as a fixed star in 1612.
label: supported
reason: Wikipedia's 'Discovery of Neptune' article and Scientific American both say Galileo's drawings show he observed Neptune on December 28, 1612, and mistook it for a fixed star close to Jupiter, so he did not recognize it as a planet. Other sources call him the first person to see Neptune, and no earlier observation is recorded. Wikipedia adds that he saw it again in January 1613 and even noted it seemed to move, but this does not contradict the claim.

text: Owens Falls Dam, completed in 1931 on the Idaho side but worked by Portland, Oregon is the deepest hydroelectric dam in the world northwest of Lewiston, and near the lower Arrow of Arrow Lakes, the deepest lake of the three Columbia River Arrow Lakes.
label: contradicted
reason: The claim is false. The Owen Falls Dam, now called the Nalubaale Dam, is on the Victoria Nile near Jinja in Uganda. It was completed in 1954 and is about 31 m high. It is not in Idaho, it is not operated by Portland, Oregon, it was not completed in 1931, and it has nothing to do with Lewiston or the Arrow Lakes on the Columbia River in British Columbia.

text: A blue whale can hold up to 2,000 gallons of krill and small fish in its stomach at a time.
label: contradicted
reason: Reliable sources give the blue whale's stomach capacity by weight, not volume: about one ton of krill, or roughly 2,000–2,200 pounds. WWF says its stomach "can hold up to a ton at a time," and Oregon State says about 2,200 pounds (1 metric ton) fills it. The claim's "2,000 gallons" looks like a mix-up with pounds. My own estimate, based on krill being about as dense as water, is that 2,000 gallons of krill (about 7,570 liters) would weigh around 7.5 tonnes, roughly seven times the documented figure. None of the sources I found supports a stomach capacity of 2,000 gallons. The sources also describe the diet as mainly krill, with small fish only occasionally mentioned.

text: Galileo Galilei was the first person to observe the planet Neptune using a telescope, but he didn't officially discover it due to limited information and documentation of his observation.
label: contradicted
reason: Part of the claim holds up: Galileo's drawings show he saw Neptune through his telescope on December 28, 1612 and January 27, 1613, and he is often called the first person to spot it. The reason the claim gives for why he didn't discover it is wrong, though. He did record his observations in drawings and notebook entries. On January 28 he even noted that the 'star' seemed to have moved. He didn't get credit because he mistook Neptune for a fixed star, not because his records were thin.

text: Glass can withstand extremely high temperatures, with some types of glass, such as borosilicate, being able to resist thermal shock and maintain its shape and integrity up to 500°C (932°F).
label: supported
reason: DWK, the maker of DURAN labware, says 3.3 expansion borosilicate glass has high thermal shock resistance and a maximum recommended working temperature of 500°C, though only for short periods. SCHOTT says DURAN borosilicate glass is stable up to 525°C with high resistance to thermal shock. Both are manufacturer sources, and together they back the claim's 500°C (932°F) figure.

text: A blue whale's heartbeat is so loud that it can be detected from over 500 miles away using underwater listening devices called hydrophones.
label: contradicted
reason: NOAA Fisheries says a blue whale's heartbeat can be heard about 2 miles away, not more than 500 miles. Blue whale calls, not heartbeats, are the sounds known to travel hundreds of miles. Even the 2-mile figure is debated, so the claim's 500+ mile range is a big exaggeration.

text: Galileo Galilei was the first person to observe the planet Neptune using a telescope, but he didn't realize it was a planet, mistaking it for a star in 1613.
label: supported
reason: Wikipedia's article on the discovery of Neptune and Astronomy.com both say Galileo observed Neptune through his telescope, on December 28, 1612 and again in January 1613. Both sources say he mistook it for a fixed star near Jupiter, and Astronomy.com says he may have been the first to see the planet. The claim's date of 1613 is slightly imprecise, since his first sighting was in late December 1612, but he did see it again in January 1613, so the date doesn't contradict the record. Some scholars, notably David Jamieson in 2009, have argued that Galileo noticed the object moving. Still, the consensus these sources describe is that he did not realize it was a planet.

text: Galileo Galilei was the first person to observe the planet Neptune, but he did not realize it was a planet, on January 28, 1613.
label: contradicted
reason: Galileo did see Neptune without realizing it was a planet, but the claim gets the date of his first sighting wrong. Wikipedia's 'Discovery of Neptune' article and a 1980 Nature paper (Kowal & Drake, indexed on ADS) say his drawings show Neptune first on December 28, 1612. He saw it again in January 1613 and noted on January 28 that it seemed to have moved. So January 28, 1613 was a later sighting, not his first. It is also not certain that Galileo was the first person ever to see Neptune.

text: Honeybees are able to fly by using their wings to generate lift, but also by generating additional lift and thrust from the movement of the air over and under the wing itself due to their unique wing motion.
label: supported
reason: Altshuler et al. (2005, PNAS) found that honeybees fly with a distinctive wing motion: short strokes of about 90° beaten at roughly 230 Hz. Their study and later work cited alongside it describe lift coming not only from the basic flapping stroke but also from unsteady airflow effects. Two of these are extra forces produced when the wing flips over at the end of each stroke, and wing flexing that keeps a positive camber and adds thrust. That matches the claim's broad wording that extra lift and thrust come from air moving over and under the wing because of the bees' unusual wing motion. Because the claim is vague, this rests on a general match rather than a point-by-point check.

text: Migrating animals that travel alone can be referred to as 'solitary migrants', often excluding species, like some birds that follow each other in line, using aerodynamic benefits called 'aerodynamic drafting' but flying in formation alone.
label: not_verifiable
reason: The first part checks out. A ScienceDirect review, "Viewing animal migration through a social lens," uses the term 'solitary migrants' for species that do not obviously migrate in groups. Research on bird formation flight also confirms that birds flying in V-formations or lines save energy through aerodynamic interactions, compared with flying alone. The second part can't be judged, though, because it contradicts itself and isn't clear. It says these species are 'often excluded' while also saying they are 'flying in formation alone.' I found no source that describes such an exclusion or uses this framing. Since part of the claim is unclear and can't be verified, the result is inconclusive.

text: Plants can make sounds, albeit not like animals, when they are cut or injured, as the sudden release of pressure causes vibrations that create ultrasonic clicking noises.
label: supported
reason: A peer-reviewed 2023 study in Cell (Khait et al.), also covered by Science News, Smithsonian and Sci.News, found that tomato and tobacco plants give off airborne ultrasonic clicks when their stems are cut or when they dry out. Hadany describes the sounds as 'very short clicks,' like popcorn, and they are beyond the range of human hearing. The researchers think the cause is cavitation: air bubbles form and then pop or collapse in the xylem, the tissue that carries water under tension. The claim's 'sudden release of pressure causes vibrations' is a looser way of saying this, but it fits the proposed mechanism. The sources also present cavitation as a likely explanation rather than a proven one.

text: Scientists estimate that there are approximately 8.7 million identified species on Earth, but the actual number of total species, including unidentified ones, could be anywhere between 10 and 30 million.
label: contradicted
reason: The 8.7 million figure from Mora et al.'s 2011 PLoS Biology paper is an estimate of all species on Earth, both known and unknown. It is not a count of identified species. Only about 1.2 to 2 million species have actually been described. The claim also gets the logic backwards: it treats 8.7 million as the identified count and then puts the total at 10 to 30 million.

text: Honeybees are able to fly by using their wings to create a whirlpool of air above and below their wings, generating the lift needed to become airborne.
label: supported
reason: Reliable sources back the main idea: bees get lift from swirling air (vortices) created by their flapping wings. Scientific American reports that honeybees flap and rotate their wings about 240 times a second. This lets them 'create a vortex that lifts it into the air.' Nature and McMaster's Synopsis describe this as a leading-edge vortex, a 'tiny tornado' or 'whirlwind of air' that produces lift. The detail 'above and below' is loose wording: sources say the vortex sits on the wing's upper surface, and the lift comes from the pressure difference between the top and bottom of the wing (Dadant). No source contradicts the claim's main point.

text: Plants can make sounds, too, when they're thirsty or stressed, a phenomenon that scientists have recorded using special equipment sensitive to ultrasonic frequencies.
label: supported
reason: A study by Tel Aviv University researchers, published in Cell in 2023, found that tomato and tobacco plants give off airborne ultrasonic popping sounds when they are dehydrated or their stems have been cut. The sounds were mostly at 40–80 kHz, above the range humans can hear, so the team recorded them with ultrasonic microphones. Scientific American, Smithsonian and the Washington Post all report the finding, and Scientific American says plants make these sounds 'when thirsty or stressed.'

text: A large percentage of the world's underwater mountains, which are volcanoes, are still unexplored.
label: supported
reason: A Scripps Institution of Oceanography release on ScienceDaily says more than 99% of all seamounts are still unexplored by scientists. It also describes seamounts as underwater mountains, including volcanoes. Seamounts are generally recognized as volcanic in origin, so the claim matches the evidence.

text: Astronomers estimate there are approximately 100-400 billion stars in the Milky Way galaxy.
label: supported
reason: Wikipedia's Milky Way article says the galaxy is estimated to contain 100–400 billion stars, and its infobox lists the same figure ((1–4)×10^11). This matches the claim exactly. It is also the widely cited range in the astronomical literature.

text: Bacteria are capable of surviving in extremely cold temperatures, with some species found to thrive even in Antarctic ice sheets.
label: supported
reason: Reliable sources (Science News, ScienceNordic, reporting on peer-reviewed work about Subglacial Lake Whillans) say active bacterial communities, including thousands of microbial species and methane-eating bacteria, live 800 m beneath the West Antarctic Ice Sheet. This backs the claim that bacteria survive extreme cold and that some thrive in Antarctic ice-sheet environments. Strictly speaking, these bacteria were found in a lake under the ice sheet rather than in the ice itself, but this is a minor wording difference and still matches what the claim means.

text: France and the United States are the two countries with the most time zones, each with a total of 12 time zones.
label: contradicted
reason: France does have 12 time zones, the most of any country, but the United States does not. Reliable sources, including Geography Realm and Vajiram & Ravi, say the US has 11 time zones and is tied with Russia for second place. That contradicts the claim that the US and France each have 12.

text: Humans and dolphins are the only known mammals that give themselves names.
label: contradicted
reason: Bottlenose dolphins do develop their own signature whistles, which work like self-chosen names. But the claim says humans and dolphins are the only known mammals with names, and a widely reported 2024 study contradicts that. It found that wild African elephants call each other by individual, name-like calls that they invent and that do not imitate the recipient's own call. A separate 2024 study reported something similar in marmosets. The claim's exact wording, "give themselves names," is slightly narrower, since elephant names appear to be given by others. Even so, the claim that only humans and dolphins have names is out of date.

text: Humans are the only known species in the world that possess the unique ability to produce tears in response to emotions.
label: supported
reason: Reliable sources say humans are the only known animals that shed emotional tears. University of Utah Health says, "Humans are the only species that cry emotional tears." Discover Magazine quotes Vassar psychologist Randolph Cornelius: "We appear to be the only animal that sheds tears for emotional reasons." These sources also note that other mammals do produce tears, but only to lubricate their eyes or flush out irritants. That matches the claim, which is specifically about emotional tears and is qualified with "known" species.

text: Humans share about 50-60% of their DNA with bananas, highlighting the surprising genetic similarities between seemingly unrelated species.
label: contradicted
reason: The 50–60% number is a popular misreading of the research. HowStuffWorks, quoting an NHGRI scientist, explains that about 60% of human genes have a recognizable counterpart in the banana genome. The proteins those genes make are only about 40% identical, and the overall DNA sequences of humans and bananas would not line up. The Star's QuickCheck rates the claim 'true' in a loose sense, but its own explanation agrees: the gene overlap amounts to only about 1–2% of the whole human genome. Since both sources show that humans do not share 50–60% of their DNA with bananas, the claim is contradicted.

text: Octopuses have nine brains, with one main brain and eight miniature brains located in each of their arms.
label: supported
reason: Many sources, including PBS Nature's "Giant Pacific Octopus: 8 Arms and 9 Brains", describe octopuses as having one main brain in the head plus a brain-like cluster of nerves in each of the eight arms, for nine in total. A few science-explainer sites point out that "nine brains" is a simplification: the arms hold dense nerve cords and ganglia rather than true separate brains. Still, they confirm the structure the claim describes (one central brain plus neural control centres in each arm), which is the common way of putting it.

text: Polar bears are excellent swimmers and have been known to swim up to 60 miles without resting.
label: supported
reason: Several reliable sources (the San Diego Zoo Wildlife Alliance, NHPBS NatureWorks and Ocean Conservancy) describe polar bears as very good swimmers. They also say polar bears can swim 60 miles (about 100 km) or more without resting. NHPBS gives the figure as 'as far as 60 miles.' Some of these sources say 'more than 60 miles' and mention a recorded 426-mile swim, so 60 miles is not a true upper limit. Still, nothing found contradicts the claim's main point.

text: Scientists estimate that there may be between 700,000 to 1 million species on Earth that haven't been discovered yet.
label: contradicted
reason: The claim's range is much too low. The most widely cited estimate (Mora et al., 2011, reported by ScienceDaily and the University of Hawaii) puts the number of species on Earth at about 8.7 million, give or take 1.3 million. That study found about 86% of land species and 91% of ocean species had not yet been described, which means millions of species are still undiscovered, not 700,000 to 1 million. Other estimates are also higher than the claim: one recent simulation suggests 1 to 3 million undiscovered land animal species alone. I found no credible source giving a total of 700,000 to 1 million undiscovered species.

text: dortmund has the highest density of bridges in the world, with over 1,000 bridges within the city limits.
label: contradicted
reason: My searches found no source that names Dortmund as the world's bridge-density leader or puts its bridge count above 1,000. The City of Dortmund's own bridge-engineering pages give no such count or claim. Several sources say Hamburg holds the bridge record with about 2,300–2,500 bridges, more than any other city. They list Amsterdam second with roughly 1,281, and Dortmund is not among the leaders. Because these sources count total bridges rather than density, they do not disprove the density claim directly. However, a rough calculation makes it implausible. Even if Dortmund had 1,000 bridges, they would be spread over about 280 km², or roughly 3.6 per km². Amsterdam's approximately 1,281 bridges over about 219 km² come to roughly 5.8 per km², and Venice's historic centre is much denser. The land areas are approximate figures from my own knowledge, not from the search results. The claim conflicts with the available evidence about which cities lead in bridges.

text: Tarantulas have been on Earth for a long time, with fossils of early tarantula-like spiders dating back to the Early Cretaceous period, around 135 million years ago.
label: contradicted
reason: The claim's dating doesn't match the evidence. A 2023 Journal of Biogeography study says the oldest known tarantula fossil comes from Burmese amber and is about 100 million years old (mid-Cretaceous), not 135 million. Molecular-clock studies (Carnegie Mellon, reported by ScienceDaily and Smithsonian) estimate tarantulas first appeared about 120 million years ago, and that date comes from genetic modeling rather than a fossil. If 'tarantula-like' is read more broadly to mean mygalomorph spiders, their fossils go back at least 240 million years (Triassic), so 135 million is wrong under that reading too. No source supports early tarantula-like fossils at about 135 million years ago, though the general point that tarantulas are ancient and date to the Cretaceous is accurate.

text: When heated to extremely high temperatures, certain types of glass can be molded into detailed forms, due to the facts that hot glass has the viscosity of a fluid.
label: supported
reason: The sources back the claim. A glass-industry explainer says molten glass viscosity depends heavily on temperature. It needs to flow properly to fill molds during pressing, blowing or casting, and molding typically happens at about 1,000–1,200°C. Other sources describe hot working glass (around 2,100°F) as viscous like honey, which means it flows like a fluid and can be shaped. None of the results contradict the claim. One caveat: the main source is a commercial explainer on alibaba.com, not a scientific or museum reference, but what it says matches standard glassmaking knowledge.

text: Scientists estimate that there are around 8.7 million identified species on Earth, but the total number of species, including those that have not been discovered, is believed to be significantly higher.
label: contradicted
reason: The 8.7 million figure from Mora et al. (2011) is an estimate of all species on Earth, including the ones not yet found. It is not a count of identified species. Only about 1.2 million species have actually been identified and catalogued, which is under 15% of the 8.7 million estimate. The same study suggests about 86% of land species and 91% of marine species are still undiscovered. So the claim gets wrong what the 8.7 million number means.

text: Schedule 1 of the Indian Constitution initially listed 29 states, but that number has since increased to 28, and then to 36, with the state of Jammu and Kashmir reorganised into two separate union territories in 2019.
label: contradicted
reason: The claim doesn't hold up. Going from 29 to 28 would be a decrease, not an increase, so the sequence it describes makes no sense. The number of states also never rose to 36. Today the First Schedule lists 28 states in Part A and 8 union territories in Part B, and 36 is only the total of the two. The original 1950 Schedule did not list 29 states of the same kind: it grouped states into Parts A, B and C, with territories in Part D. The only accurate part is that Jammu and Kashmir was split into two union territories (J&K and Ladakh) in 2019, which is how the count reached 28 states and 8 union territories.

text: Honeybees are able to fly by using electricity generated from the movement of their wings, which creates a positive charge that attracts the negatively charged air particles around them, allowing for more efficient flight.
label: contradicted
reason: Research shows honeybees fly through aerodynamics, not electricity. A Caltech study explains their lift as coming from short, very fast wing strokes (about 230 per second), quick wing rotation and leading-edge vortices. Bees do pick up a positive static charge as they fly, mostly from friction with air and collisions with charged particles. That charge helps with pollen attraction and communication between bees, as reported by National Geographic. No evidence shows it powers flight or makes flight more efficient by attracting negatively charged air particles.

text: Roses arranged in a specific pattern can be used to create a compass, as the head of the rose turns south due to the interesting way they react with the Earth's magnetic field and the effects of sunlight.
label: contradicted
reason: No reliable source says that rose flowers turn south or react to Earth's magnetic field. The 'compass rose' (Wikipedia) is just the direction diagram printed on maps and compasses, not real roses. The plant actually known for this is the compass plant (Silphium laciniatum), whose leaves tend to line up north–south. Botanical sources explain that orientation by sunlight, not magnetism, and say nothing about roses pointing south. The claim looks like a mix-up of the 'compass rose' and the compass plant, and it is not a real property of roses.

text: Galileo Galilei was the first person to observe the planet Neptune, but he didn't recognize it as a planet, instead documenting it as a fixed star in 1612.
label: supported
reason: Scientific American says Galileo first saw Neptune in 1612 and took it for a fixed star, 234 years before it was identified as a planet. Wikipedia's Discovery of Neptune page agrees: his drawings show he observed it on December 28, 1612 (and again in January 1613) and mistook it for a fixed star. These are the earliest known observations of Neptune. Wikipedia also notes some evidence that Galileo saw the object seemed to move, but he never identified it as a planet, so the claim still holds.

text: In 2019, the world's largest living organism was discovered in a Blue Mountains forest, a massive fungus that spans about 2,200 acres in New South Wales, Australia.
label: contradicted
reason: The record-holding 'Humongous Fungus' (Armillaria ostoyae), about 2,200 acres in size, is real. But it grows in Malheur National Forest in the Blue Mountains of Oregon, USA, not in the Blue Mountains of New South Wales, Australia. It also wasn't discovered in 2019: it has been widely reported since the 1990s and is estimated to be at least 2,400 years old.

text: In the heart of the Amazon rainforest, there exists a type of jellyfish which is immortal, known as the Turritopsis dohrnii, also called the "immortal jellyfish."
label: contradicted
reason: Turritopsis dohrnii is indeed called the "immortal jellyfish," but it does not live in the Amazon rainforest. It is a small marine hydrozoan. Simple Wikipedia, iNaturalist and a PubMed paper all say it lives in the Mediterranean Sea and in waters off Japan, and related sources say Turritopsis species occur in temperate to tropical oceans worldwide. None of the sources places it in the Amazon rainforest or in any freshwater or forest habitat, so the location part of the claim is wrong.

text: In 2019, the world's largest living organism was discovered in a Blue Mountains forest in Australia, and it's a giant fungus covering over 2,200 acres.
label: contradicted
reason: The giant fungus covering more than 2,200 acres, often called the world's largest living organism, is real. But the claim gets the place and the date wrong. The fungus is an Armillaria ostoyae (honey fungus) in the Blue Mountains of eastern Oregon, USA, not Australia. Sources date its discovery to around 1998, not 2019. It covers about 2,384 acres.

text: The Axel Erlandson's Tree Circus, also known as the "Basket Tree," was created by an American farmer who grafted various tree branches together to grow a single tree with multiple trunks.
label: contradicted
reason: The claim is wrong on two points. First, the Tree Circus was not "also known as" the Basket Tree. According to Wikipedia, the Tree Circus was the roadside attraction Axel Erlandson opened in 1947, and the Basket Tree was one of the most famous trees in it. Second, he did not graft branches onto a single tree. He planted six separate sycamore trees in a circle, topped them, and approach-grafted them to one another to form a woven, diamond pattern. The claim gets one thing right: Erlandson was a Swedish-American farmer.

text: Galileo Galilei was the first person to observe the planet Neptune, although he didn't recognize it, in 1613, over 230 years before the official discovery.
label: supported
reason: Britannica says Galileo's sketches, the first of them dated Dec. 28, 1612, suggest he saw Neptune near Jupiter but did not recognize it as a planet. It also notes that no one saw Neptune before telescopes, so Galileo was effectively the first observer. Discover Magazine reports that he observed Neptune in 1612 and again in 1613, mistaking it for a star. The official discovery came in 1846, which is 233 years after 1613, so 'over 230 years' holds. The claim gives only 1613, but his first sighting was actually in late December 1612. Since he did observe Neptune again in 1613, the claim is essentially supported.

text: Tarantulas have been around for a long time, with the oldest known tarantula fossil dating back to the Early Cretaceous period, approximately 125 million years ago, during the time of the dinosaurs.
label: contradicted
reason: The claim gets the age wrong. Peer-reviewed sources (Journal of Biogeography, 2023, and a tarantula phylogenomics paper) say the oldest known tarantula fossil is a protertheraphosine preserved in Burmese amber, dated to about 100 million years ago (Wunderlich & Müller, 2020). That is mid-Cretaceous, not Early Cretaceous about 125 million years ago. Live Science also reports the Myanmar amber fossil as about 100 million years old. Molecular studies estimate that tarantulas themselves originated about 120–105 million years ago, but that is a date inferred from genetic data, not the age of a fossil. Tarantulas did live alongside dinosaurs during the Cretaceous, but the claim's fossil date of about 125 million years is not supported.

text: The world's largest waterfall, by volume of water, is actually located underwater, with the Denmark Strait Cataract, a submarine waterfall that occurs where cold, dense water sinks down a slope in the ocean floor between Iceland and Greenland.
label: supported
reason: Live Science says the Denmark Strait cataract is an underwater waterfall in the channel between Iceland and Greenland, and calls it technically the world's largest waterfall. It describes cold water from the Nordic Seas being funneled down a sloping section of the seafloor into the Irminger Sea. The article highlights its height, but it is also widely documented (NOAA, for example) as the largest waterfall by volume, carrying about 175 million cubic feet per second. That covers every part of the claim.

text: Honeybees are able to fly by using electricity generated from the movement of their wings, which helps attract pollen and dust particles to their bodies through a process called 'triboelectric charging'.
label: contradicted
reason: Bees do pick up a static charge through triboelectric effects while flying (friction with the air and surfaces), and this charge helps pull pollen onto their bodies. That part of the claim is true. But the charge is a side effect of flight, not what powers it. Bees fly using aerodynamic lift from flapping their wings. A ResearchGate paper on bee electric ecology says bees acquire static charge "by virtue of triboelectric effect during flight," which treats charging as a consequence of flying. No source says bees use electricity to fly, so the central claim is wrong.

text: Glass can withstand extremely high temperatures, with some types of glass, such as borosilicate, being able to resist thermal shock and maintain its shape and integrity up to 400-500 degrees Fahrenheit.
label: contradicted
reason: The claim puts borosilicate glass's limit at 400-500°F, which is much too low. Wikipedia gives a typical maximum service temperature of about 500°C (930°F), and MakeItFrom lists a mechanical maximum of 360°C (680°F). Both sources agree that borosilicate glass resists thermal shock, handling temperature differences of about 160-166°C (320-330°F). The 400-500°F figure appears to mix up Celsius and Fahrenheit. Because the glass does stay intact at 400-500°F, this is a judgment call, but the claim presents that range as the upper limit, and it is not.

text: Astronauts Robert B. Lawrence and Joe Engle on June 5th 1965, were the first American's to sleep in space, aboard the 84 orbital flight of Gemini 4.
label: contradicted
reason: NASA says Gemini 4 carried James McDivitt and Edward White, not Robert Lawrence and Joe Engle. It launched on June 3, 1965, not June 5, and flew 62 orbits (Wikipedia gives 66 orbits / 62 revolutions), not 84. Lawrence never flew in space, and Engle did not fly on Gemini.

text: The Axel Erlandson's Tre-fontaine tree, also known as the "circus tree," is a natural wonder consisting of three trunks that were cultivated to unite and eventually fuse into a rare natural formation.
label: contradicted
reason: I couldn't find any Erlandson tree called the "Tre-fontaine" tree. His documented trees have names like the Basket Tree, Four-Legged Giant, Telephone Booth, Needle and Thread and Cathedral Window. "Circus Trees" is the name for his whole collection, not for one tree. More importantly, the claim calls it a natural wonder and a rare natural formation. Reliable sources, including Gilroy Gardens, Wikipedia and the Santa Cruz Public Library, say these trees were deliberately shaped and grafted by Erlandson starting in the 1920s. That makes them man-made tree sculptures, not natural formations, which contradicts a key part of the claim.

text: Scientists estimate that there are approximately 8.7 million identified species on Earth, but the total number of species, including those that have not been discovered yet, is believed to be around 30 million.
label: contradicted
reason: The claim treats 8.7 million as the number of species already identified, and that is wrong. The 8.7 million figure (give or take 1.3 million) comes from Mora et al. 2011 in PLoS Biology, and it estimates the total number of species on Earth, including undiscovered ones. Only about 1.2 million species had been described at that time; for example, about 953,000 of an estimated 7.77 million animal species. The same source does not describe the total as being around 30 million.

text: A oku, or hundred trillion, is 100 trillion in the Japanese number system, and in English represents the number 100,000,000,000,000.
label: contradicted
reason: The claim gets the value of oku wrong. In Japanese, 億 (oku) means 100 million (10^8, or 100,000,000), not 100 trillion. Coto Academy's guide to Japanese numbers lists man (万) as 10,000, oku (億) as 100 million, chou (兆) as 1 trillion and kei (京) as 10 quadrillion. The number 100,000,000,000,000 (100 trillion) would be 百兆 (hyaku-chou), not oku.

text: Astronauts can cough in space but the cough doesn't sound like a typical cough on Earth as the sound waves don't have enough air molecules to travel and transfer the noise.
label: contradicted
reason: Astronauts do cough in space; HowStuffWorks says real astronauts sneeze, cough and blow their noses. The rest of the claim is wrong. Astronauts live and work inside pressurized spacecraft and spacesuits that are filled with air. The Indianapolis Children's Museum says sound inside the space station travels as it does on Earth, and that astronauts can talk or yell inside their own spacesuits. A blog on hearing in space likewise says sound can be heard inside spacecraft because there is air. Only the vacuum outside lacks a medium for sound, so a cough inside a spacecraft or spacesuit has plenty of air to travel through and would not sound different for the reason the claim gives. No source found supports the idea that astronauts' coughs sound abnormal because of too few air molecules.

text: A hanging astronaut's body would immediately freeze and eventually disintegrate in the extreme environment of outer space.
label: contradicted
reason: The claim says the body would freeze immediately, and reliable sources say that's wrong. RealClearScience explains that a person "would not instantly freeze because heat does not transfer away from the body very quickly." Other explanations agree that freezing in a vacuum takes hours, not moments. The 'disintegrate' part is also doubtful. Sources such as Live Science and ScienceABC describe the body losing surface liquids, then freezing or freeze-drying and being preserved, mummy-like. Radiation might slowly degrade it, but none of them describe it disintegrating.

text: A partitions of the Mandelbrot set can form the swirling patterns which in turn appear similar to Romanesco broccoli as well as other types of vegetables.
