label: not_verifiable
reason: I found many sources that put the Mandelbrot set and Romanesco broccoli side by side as examples of fractals. One page describes a Mandelbulb render as reminiscent of Romanesco, but the Mandelbulb is a 3D relative of the Mandelbrot set, not part of the set itself. I found no reliable source saying that parts of the Mandelbrot set form swirling patterns that look like Romanesco. A UMB correspondence page suggests the opposite: someone asked where to find a cauliflower-like image in the Mandelbrot set, and the question was still open. Nothing I found supports the part about 'other types of vegetables.' I couldn't open the UMB page in full because the search limit ran out, so I'm judging it from a snippet.

text: Aolphin calves are born with a thick layer of blubber that helps them stay afloat, and they can swim within the first hour of being born.
label: contradicted
reason: Taking "Aolphin" to mean dolphin, the claim is partly right and partly wrong. Newborn dolphins can swim within minutes, so the swimming part is supported. The blubber part is not. SeaWorld's page on bottlenose dolphin calves says the mother's rich milk "helps the baby rapidly develop a thick blubber layer," which means calves do not have one at birth. Other sources say calves are born with much thinner blubber than adults, and a NOAA study describes cetacean newborns as having a "relatively thin blubber layer" that grows quickly while they nurse. The claim that calves are born with a thick layer of blubber is therefore contradicted.

text: A星(is the brightest star in the night sky and is about 8.6 lightyears away from Earth
label: supported
reason: The claim's subject is garbled ("A星("), so I'm assuming it means Sirius A, the main star of Sirius. Only Sirius matches the description, but that identification is my inference rather than something stated in the claim. On that assumption, EarthSky confirms both parts: it calls Sirius "the brightest star in the night sky" and says it lies 8.6 light-years away. Sirius A is the visible star of the pair, and EarthSky also notes Sirius is an A-type star, which may be what "A星" refers to. If the subject were read as having no clear referent, the label would be inconclusive instead.

text: Despite its seemingly barren surface, Antarctica is home to several unique species of flora and fauna that have adapted to its harsh environment.
label: supported
reason: Reliable sources such as the AMNH say Antarctica's plants, lichens and animals, including penguins, seals and orcas, have developed physical, behavioral and chemical adaptations to its harsh environment. Antarctica also has endemic species such as the emperor penguin and two native flowering plants, which supports the claim that it has unique, adapted flora and fauna.

text: Humans share about 50-60% of their DNA with bananas, indicating a distant evolutionary connection between the two species.
label: supported
reason: The usual meaning of this popular claim holds up, with one caveat. HowStuffWorks quotes an NHGRI geneticist, and The Star rates the claim 'TRUE': about 60% of human genes have a recognisable counterpart in the banana genome. These shared genes do basic jobs such as cell growth, DNA replication and energy production, which fits a distant common ancestry. The caveat is that the figure counts genes, not all of our DNA. The shared proteins are only about 40% identical, and genes make up only about 1–2% of the human genome. So 'share 50–60% of DNA' is an oversimplification, but the trustworthy sources back the claim as it is commonly meant.

text: Large corporations like IBM, Microsoft, and Google have been using artificial intelligence (AI) for various purposes including problem-solving, since the 1960s.
label: contradicted
reason: The claim can't be true as stated. Google's own history page says Larry Page and Sergey Brin founded the company in 1998, and Microsoft was founded in 1975. Neither company existed in the 1960s, so neither could have been using AI then. IBM did do early AI work in that period, but the claim puts all three companies in the 1960s, so it is contradicted.

text: Large corporations like IBM, Microsoft, and Google have been using artificial intelligence (AI) for various purposes including problem-solving.
label: supported
reason: The search results back this widely known fact. IBM describes its AI work, including AI used for cybersecurity vulnerability discovery and its AI consulting services, as building systems that copy human problem-solving and decision-making. A patent analysis comparing Google, IBM and Microsoft shows that all three are actively developing AI. Microsoft and Google are also well documented as using AI in many products and services. Nothing in the results contradicts the claim.

text: Scans of the Egyptian Great Pyramid's internal chamber, created in 2017, revealed a substantial previously undiscovered void or cavity.
label: supported
reason: In November 2017, the ScanPyramids team published muon imaging results in Nature reporting a large, previously unknown void above the Grand Gallery in Khufu's Great Pyramid. They called it the 'Big Void' and described it as the first major inner structure found in the pyramid since the 19th century. Some of the detectors sat in the Queen's Chamber. The claim's wording about scanning the 'internal chamber' is a bit loose, but its main point matches the evidence: 2017 scans revealed a substantial undiscovered void.

text: Scientists estimate that there are approximately 8.7 million identified species on Earth, but up to 80% of all species remain undiscovered and undocumented.
label: contradicted
reason: The 8.7 million figure is not a count of identified species. It is the estimated total number of species on Earth (give or take 1.3 million), from Mora et al. (2011). Only about 1.2 million species have actually been identified and catalogued, which is less than 15% of that total. The study found that 86% of land species and 91% of marine species remain undiscovered, so more than 80% of species are undescribed overall. The claim's description of 8.7 million as 'identified species' is therefore false, and its 'up to 80%' undiscovered figure is also too low.

text: Tarantulas have been on Earth for a long time, with fossil evidence showing they existed over 120 million years ago during the Cretaceous period.
label: contradicted
reason: The claim conflicts with the evidence on the fossil part. Tarantulas are old, and their origin is dated to the Early Cretaceous at about 120 million years ago. However, that date comes from molecular-clock studies built from genetic data (Foley et al., PeerJ 2021: about 120 to 105.5 million years ago). These studies note that tarantula fossils are extremely rare. A 2023 Journal of Biogeography study says the oldest known tarantula fossil comes from Burmese amber and is about 100 million years old (Wunderlich & Müller, 2020). That study dates the family's origin to a mean of about 120 million years ago (range 109–132) using molecular dating, not fossils. So fossils do not show tarantulas existing more than 120 million years ago.

text: A chunk of the Dead Sea has been found to be so dense with salt that objects with lower densities, like humans, naturally float when submerged in the water.
label: supported
reason: The American Museum of Natural History says Dead Sea water is almost six times as salty as the ocean. It also says that because human bodies are less dense than this water, people can float in it effortlessly. That matches the main point of the claim. The phrase "a chunk of" is odd wording, but it doesn't change the basic fact.

text: Beehive-shaped structures in Antarctica, known as "blood falls", seep a deep red liquid, which is actually ancient saltwater rich in iron, that has been sealed off for millions of years, beneath Taylor Glacier.
label: not_verifiable
reason: Most of the claim checks out. SCAR and National Geographic both say Blood Falls flows out of Taylor Glacier, and that its color comes from iron-rich salty brine that turns red when it meets air. They also say the water comes from a saltwater lake that has been trapped under the glacier for more than a million years, at least 1.5 million by one estimate. The problem is the description of Blood Falls as "beehive-shaped structures." None of the sources describe it that way. They call it a waterfall-like reddish stain or outflow spilling from the front edge of the glacier, about five stories high. A search pairing "beehive" with Blood Falls found nothing linking the two. Because that part can't be verified and seems to mix up the feature's appearance, the claim as a whole can't be fully supported.

text: Abnormally large crystals have grown within the Naica Mine's Cave of the Crystals in Chihuahua, Mexico, with some selenite crystals reaching over 36 feet in length.
label: supported
reason: The sources agree that the Cave of the Crystals, which connects to the Naica Mine in Chihuahua, Mexico, contains giant selenite (gypsum) crystals. Reported lengths for the largest ones run from about 11.4 m (37.4 ft) to 12 m (39 ft). Either figure is over 36 feet, so the claim holds.

text: Beneath the waves of the Indian Ocean, near Taiwan, lies the South China Sea's deepest point: the Challenger Deep's counterpart, the 'Tonga Trench' is incorrect however the 'South China Sea Trough' in this ocean is the correct answer and its nearly five miles down to the bottom.
label: contradicted
reason: The South China Sea is a marginal sea of the Pacific Ocean, not the Indian Ocean. Wikipedia and Baidu Baike give its maximum depth as about 5,559–5,563 m, which is roughly 3.5 miles, not 'nearly five miles' (about 8 km). The 'South China Sea Trough' named as its deepest point also doesn't match any recognized feature in the search results.

text: Scientists estimate that there are approximately 8.7 million identified species on Earth, but the total number of species, including those that have not been discovered, is believed to be around 30 million.
label: contradicted
reason: The 8.7 million figure is not a count of identified species. Mora et al. (2011, PLoS Biology), as reported by ScienceDaily, give about 8.7 million (±1.3 million) as the estimated total number of species on Earth, and that includes undiscovered ones. Only about 1.2 million species have actually been described. The claim also treats about 30 million as the accepted total, when the study's best estimate is 8.7 million. Older estimates ran anywhere from 3 million to 100 million.

text: Tarantulas have been on Earth for a long time, with the oldest known species dating back to the Cretaceous period, which was over 135 million years ago.
label: contradicted
reason: The evidence supports the Cretaceous part of the claim, but not the date of more than 135 million years ago. Live Science, reporting on a phylogenetic study, says there are only two known tarantula fossils, both in amber. The older one, from Myanmar, is about 100 million years old (Cretaceous). Molecular dating in the same study puts the group's origin at about 120 million years ago, also in the Cretaceous. The Cretaceous period did begin about 145 million years ago, but the oldest known tarantula is not shown to be more than 135 million years old. Both the fossil age and the estimated origin are well below that figure.

text: Humans and dolphins are the only mammals known to give themselves names or have a sense of self-awareness in the form of unique identifiers, such as signature whistles in dolphins.
label: contradicted
reason: The claim is false because humans and dolphins are not the only mammals known to use name-like identifiers. A 2024 study in Science found that marmoset monkeys use distinct "phee calls" to address specific individuals, and another 2024 study found that African elephants appear to name each other through differences in their rumbles. The Washington Post and CNN both reported these findings and say marmosets join a short list of name-using animals. Other mammals, such as great apes and elephants, have also shown signs of self-awareness.

text: Listing ship, known as heel, and slipping slowly sideways into the open waters is, historically one of many ways old vessels were deliberately scuttled to an intentional early retirement under ocean.
label: not_verifiable
reason: The sources I found describe scuttling as sinking a ship on purpose by letting water into the hull, usually by opening seacocks, cutting holes or using charges (Wikipedia, Dictionary.com). None of them say that listing and slipping sideways into open water was a recognised scuttling method. The claim also treats listing as the same as heel, but naval stability sources draw a clear line between them: heel is a temporary tilt caused by wind, waves or turning, while list is a lasting tilt caused by weight inside the ship. A scuttled ship may list as it floods, so the claim's main point can't be confirmed or ruled out, and part of its wording conflicts with standard terminology.

text: Tarantulas have been on Earth for a long time, with fossil evidence showing that they have remained largely unchanged for over 100 million years.
label: not_verifiable
reason: Part of the claim holds up and part doesn't. Tarantulas are clearly an old group. Molecular dating estimates the lineage at about 120 million years (Cretaceous), and Wunderlich & Müller (2020) describe a possible tarantula fossil in Burmese amber at about 100 million years old. Triassic 'tarantula-like' mygalomorph fossils go back 235–240 million years. However, the specific claim that fossils show tarantulas 'largely unchanged for over 100 million years' isn't backed up. True tarantula fossils are extremely rare: most are Miocene amber specimens from about 16–23 million years ago. The Texas Parks & Wildlife source says fossils show tarantulas virtually unchanged for 'more than 20 million years,' not 100 million. The 120-million-year figure comes from molecular dating, not from fossils showing morphological stability. The single roughly 100-million-year fossil does not establish that tarantulas stayed largely unchanged for that long.

text: France and Spain both claim to be the birthplace of the first restaurant, 'auberge,' with the French claiming Procope's established in 1686 and the Spanish claiming its 'they invented ' the concept of the restaurant ' inn's during 1386.
label: contradicted
reason: The search results don't match the claim's framing. Café Procope was founded in Paris in 1686, but sources call it the oldest café in Paris and France's first business to call itself a café. They don't describe it as France's claim to the first restaurant or 'auberge.' Spain's well-known claim is Sobrino de Botín in Madrid, founded in 1725, which Guinness World Records lists as the oldest restaurant. No result shows Spain claiming to have invented restaurants or inns in 1386. The claim's description of both countries' positions conflicts with the evidence, and the 1386 date has no support.

text: Saturn is the only planet in our solar system that is less dense than water, making it the only planet that would float if it were placed in a large enough body of water.
label: supported
reason: I found that the density part of the claim is well supported. WorldAtlas says Saturn is "the only planet in our solar system with a density lower than that of liquid water," and NASA material backs this up. Saturn's average density is about 0.69 g/cm³, and every other planet is denser than water. Because of that low density, NASA and others use the hypothetical image of Saturn floating in a big enough body of water. An IFLScience article argues that this picture doesn't hold up physically. However, the claim is the standard thought experiment based on density, and the evidence supports it.

text: Wertheim's discovery of two new chemical elements in 1783 led to the understanding that tungsten and barium (then called baryta) are indeed separate elements.
label: contradicted
reason: Trustworthy element-history sources say the Spanish brothers Juan José and Fausto de Elhuyar isolated tungsten in 1783, after Carl Wilhelm Scheele found tungstic acid in 1781. They do not credit anyone named Wertheim with discovering two new elements in 1783. Barium (from baryta) is historically linked to Scheele in the 1770s and to Humphry Davy, who isolated it in 1808. It was not identified through a 1783 discovery that showed tungsten and baryta were separate elements. The claim gives the discovery to the wrong person and misstates what happened.

text: A ball of glass will float in the Dead Sea due to the extremely high salt concentration in the water, which is approximately 33.7% salinity.
label: contradicted
reason: Wikipedia gives Dead Sea water a density of about 1.24 kg/L (salinity about 34%). Patent sources list common glass at about 2.2–2.5 g/cm³, roughly twice as dense. A solid glass ball is denser than Dead Sea water, so it would sink despite the high salt concentration. The salinity figure in the claim is roughly correct, but the main claim that the glass ball floats is false. Only a hollow, air-filled glass ball could float, and the claim doesn't say that.

text: A blue whale's heart can pump around 5,000 liters (1,320 gallons) of blood with every beat.
label: contradicted
reason: Reliable sources, including Guinness World Records and the Royal Ontario Museum heart specimen coverage, put a blue whale's output at about 220 liters (58 gallons) of blood per heartbeat. A 2019 study estimated about 80 liters per beat for a 70-tonne whale. Even the highest figure found, from a social media post, was about 1,000 liters. That is far below the claimed 5,000 liters (1,320 gallons) per beat.

text: A blue whale's heartbeat is so loud that it can be detected by a satellite in space even though it lives deep beneath the ocean's surface.
label: contradicted
reason: No reliable source supports the claim that a satellite can detect a blue whale's heartbeat. The first-ever recording, reported by Stanford in 2019, was made with an electrode sensor tag attached to the whale by suction cups. The sensors bobbed at the surface until researchers collected them, so this was not remote detection. Even the popular claim about range only says the heartbeat can be picked up about 2–3 miles away with instruments like sonar, and fact-checkers note that even this needs special equipment. Satellites cannot pick up underwater sound, so the claim is a myth that the sources contradict.

text: A blue whale's heartbeat is so powerful it can be detected from over two miles away by using specialized equipment.
label: supported
reason: NOAA Fisheries, a trustworthy government source, says a blue whale's heartbeat "can be heard 2 miles away." The Cold Spring Harbor Whaling Museum also says it can be "detected from 2 MILES AWAY." Many other sources say "over 2 miles," and some note that it takes instruments such as sonar rather than the human ear. There are caveats. NOAA gives a flat figure of 2 miles and does not say "over" two miles or mention specialized equipment; those details come only from less authoritative sources. There is also no primary scientific study behind the figure. Some low-quality Q&A answers dispute it, but they cite no evidence. On balance, reputable sources support the claim.

text: A giant squid's eyes are said to be the largest of any animal, with some specimens having eyes that are up to 27 cm (11 inches) in diameter.
label: supported
reason: Reliable sources back both parts of the claim, though there is a caveat. Wikipedia says the giant squid has the largest eyes of any living creature except perhaps the colossal squid, measuring up to at least 27 cm (11 in) across. Britannica gives up to 27 cm (10.6 in). A BMC Evolutionary Biology paper says giant and colossal squid eyes are the largest of any living organism, reaching 27 cm. A PubMed-indexed study documents a giant squid eyeball of about 27 cm with a 9 cm pupil. The caveat: Britannica, Te Papa and Guinness rank the colossal squid's eyes as equal or larger. The claim only says giant squid eyes 'are said to be' the largest, and that hedged wording matches how sources describe them, so the claim holds overall.

text: A lavender shortbread cookie was a favorite of Queen Elizabeth II, and it is said that she would often have the cookies shipped from theANI farm in Scotland to II.
label: not_verifiable
reason: I found nothing showing that lavender shortbread was one of Queen Elizabeth II's favourites, or that she had cookies shipped from a farm in Scotland. What the sources do say is that she liked plain buttery shortbread (recipes adapted from the Buckingham Palace chef) and, most of all, chocolate biscuit cake. One source says outright that we don't know which type of biscuits she preferred. The claim is also garbled: "theANI farm" and "to II" don't refer to anything identifiable, so that part can't be checked.

text: Honey Never Spoils; Archaeologists have found pots of honey in ancient Egyptian tombs that are over 3,000 years old and still perfectly edible
label: supported
reason: Many sources report that archaeologists found pots of honey in ancient Egyptian tombs that are about 3,000 years old and still edible. These include History Facts, My Modern Met, and WBAP/Dallas Express. They explain this with honey's low moisture, high acidity and hydrogen peroxide content, which back up the 'honey never spoils' part of the claim. None of the results contradicted it. Two caveats: these are mostly popular-science outlets rather than primary archaeological reports, and the sources say honey only stays good if it is sealed properly, so 'never spoils' is a simplification.

text: Honeybees are able to fly by using electricity generated by the flapping of their wings to attract and attach pollen to their bodies.
label: contradicted
reason: Honeybees fly because of the aerodynamic lift produced by their wings. Electricity does not make them fly. Sources such as AskNature and Science Friday say a bee builds up a positive electrostatic charge as a side effect of flying and flapping, and that charge helps pull pollen onto its body. The claim gets the cause backwards by saying bees fly by using that electricity. The part about pollen sticking to the charge is right, but no source says the charge lets bees fly.

text: Honeybees are able to fly by using their wings to generate electricity, with the movement creating a positive static electric charge.
label: contradicted
reason: Reliable sources, including Current Biology on ScienceDirect and a ResearchGate paper on insect electrostatics, confirm that honeybees pick up a positive static charge when their bodies and wings rub against the air in flight. But that charge is a side effect of flying. It is not what lets bees fly. Bees stay airborne because their wings create aerodynamic lift. No source says bees fly by generating electricity, so the claim's main point gets cause and effect backwards.

text: Honeybees are capable of recognizing human faces and remembering them for later encounters, much like some other animals and even some primates.
label: supported
reason: Research led by Adrian Dyer (published in 2005 and reported by Phys.org) found that honeybees can be trained to recognize human faces in photos and remember them for at least two days. Scientific American also reports that honeybees can tell individual human faces apart, an ability long thought to be limited to large-brained mammals such as primates. The study shows bees can retain the faces for days, which fits the claim that they remember faces for later encounters. Note that the bees were trained in a lab using photographs, not tested on real people in the wild.

text: Humans and dolphins are the only known mammals that give themselves names, with dolphins using a unique whistle to identify themselves.
label: contradicted
reason: The claim says humans and dolphins are the only known mammals that use names. That is outdated. A 2024 Hebrew University study, reported on EurekAlert, found that marmoset monkeys use specific "phee-calls" to name each other. The same report says this kind of naming was previously known in humans, dolphins and elephants, so elephants already broke the "only humans and dolphins" idea before the marmoset finding. The claim's detail about dolphins identifying themselves with unique signature whistles is accurate. One caveat: the claim is about animals giving themselves names, while the elephant and marmoset studies show them using names for each other. Even so, the evidence undercuts the claim that only humans and dolphins are known to have names.

text: Humans and dolphins are the only mammals known to have their own unique names for identifying themselves and other individuals within their social groups.
label: contradicted
reason: Humans and dolphins aren't the only mammals known to use names for each other. A 2024 study in Nature Ecology & Evolution, led by Colorado State University researchers, found that wild African elephants call to specific individuals with name-like calls. Unlike dolphin signature whistles, these calls don't imitate the receiver's own sounds, which makes them more like human names. Research published the same year also reported that marmosets use individual-specific calls.

text: Humans share approximately 50-60% of their DNA with bananas, illustrating the remarkably common genetic heritage between species.
label: contradicted
reason: The 50–60% figure is a common misunderstanding. HowStuffWorks, IFLScience and a Star fact-check all trace it to research finding that about 60% of human genes have a recognisable counterpart in the banana genome, and those matching proteins are only about 40% identical. Since genes make up only about 2% of human DNA, sources estimate the actual DNA overlap at roughly 1–2% or less. So saying humans share 50–60% of their DNA with bananas is incorrect. The idea of a shared, distant genetic heritage is accurate, but the specific DNA percentage in the claim is wrong.

text: Kukoos, also known as Guillemots, are agile flight birds that dive underwater to hunt for fish and other small aquatic animals.
label: contradicted
reason: The claim is false on two counts. First, my searches found no source that uses "Kukoos" as another name for guillemots. The name only turns up as the creatures in the video game "Kukoos: Lost Pets" (Steam, PlayStation Store). Guillemots' recorded alternative names include murre and tystie (Wikipedia). Second, guillemots do dive underwater for fish, but Wikipedia says common murres (common guillemots) are fast in direct flight yet "not very agile," which contradicts the claim that they are agile fliers.

text: Kukoos, also known as Guillemots, are agile flight birds that dive underwater to hunt for food.
label: contradicted
reason: I found no source that calls guillemots "Kukoos." Wikipedia's Guillemot page explains where the name comes from and gives "murre" as the alternative name. Wikipedia also gives "tystie" as another name for the black guillemot. A search for "Kukoos" only turned up unrelated birds, such as cuckoos and the kōkako. It is true that guillemots are auks that dive underwater for food. However, the claim that they are "agile" fliers also conflicts with Wikipedia's Common murre page, which says they are fast in direct flight but not very agile. Because the claimed name, Kukoos, is wrong, the claim as a whole is contradicted.

text: Listing ship, known as heel, and slipping slowly sideways into the open waters is, historically one of many sinking scenarios.
label: supported
reason: The Wikipedia article on sailing ship accidents describes cargo shifting that gives a ship a list to one side. It says a heavy enough list can make the ship capsize, and a ship heeled past its stability limit is vulnerable to flooding and sinking. It gives the Pamir (1957) as a historical example. This backs the general claim that listing (or heeling) and going over sideways is one of several historical ways ships sink. Strictly speaking, 'list' and 'heel' are different terms, and the 'slipping slowly sideways' wording is loose, but the claim's main point holds.

text: Norway has a public library system where citizens can borrow an e-book for free.
label: supported
reason: Norway's public libraries are free for all residents (bibliotekutvikling.no, Trondheim library). Library websites such as Nordland county library (bibliotek.nfk.no) also say that every library in Norway lends e-books and audiobooks through the BookBites app, now being replaced by Biblio, and that borrowing is completely free with a library card. Sources from Bergen, Sølvberget and BookBites support say the same, and Oslo's Deichman library lends e-books through OverDrive.

text: Octopuses have nine brains in total, with one central brain and eight smaller brains located in each of their arms.
label: supported
reason: Popular-science sources such as OctoNation and AnimalWised say octopuses have "nine brains": one central brain in the head plus eight smaller ones, one in each arm. This matches the claim. The same sources add that the eight "arm brains" are really clusters of nerve tissue (ganglia and nerve cords) that work as local control centres, not full separate brains. So the claim is a common simplification, but it matches how these sources describe octopus anatomy.

text: Octopuses have nine brains, with eight of them located in their arms and one central brain, allowing them to process information and make decisions independently.
label: supported
reason: Many sources say octopuses have 'nine brains.' By that count there is one central brain between the eyes and eight ganglia ('mini-brains'), one in each arm. These let each arm sense, process information and act independently of the central brain. Some sources (e.g., Biology Insights) point out that 'nine brains' is a simplification: scientists more precisely describe one brain plus eight large neural clusters. Even these sources confirm the structure and the independent arm control the claim describes. So the claim's substance holds, though its wording is popularized.

text: Plants can produce flowers and seeds without undergoing pollination through a process known as apomixis, also referred to as "virgin birth."
label: supported
reason: Reliable sources describe apomixis as asexual seed production that skips meiosis and fertilization and gives seeds that are clones of the mother plant (ScienceDirect; Nature Biotechnology; PMC review). One study of Ficus gasparriniana found that fig trees made apomictic seeds without their pollinating wasps, which shows seeds can form without pollination. Spillane et al. call apomixis 'virgin births' in their Nature Biotechnology title, and the term is in common use. Plants flower whether or not they are pollinated, so the flower part of the claim is uncontroversial. One caveat: some apomicts still need pollination to trigger seed development (pseudogamy), but that does not contradict the general claim.

text: Plants can produce flowers and seeds without undergoing pollination through a process known as apomixis, resulting in seeds genetically identical to their parent.
label: supported
reason: ScienceDirect's overview defines apomixis as making seeds without fertilization, and says the resulting seeds are genetically identical to the mother plant. That matches the claim. One caveat: some apomictic plants still need pollination to form the endosperm (called pseudogamy), and the same source notes that apomicts differ in this requirement. Other apomicts are autonomous and need no pollination, so the claim's wording that plants "can" do this still holds.

text: Tarantulas have been around for a long time - fossil records show that they existed at least 120 million years ago during the Cretaceous period.
label: contradicted
reason: The 120-million-year figure comes from genetic (molecular-clock) studies, not from fossils. Live Science, Phys.org and SciTechDaily report that genetic and transcriptome analyses put the origin of tarantulas in the Early Cretaceous, about 120 million years ago. The fossil evidence is younger. Live Science says only two tarantula fossils are known: one in Mexican amber about 16 million years old and one in Burmese amber about 100 million years old. A 2023 Journal of Biogeography study also calls the roughly 100-million-year-old Burmese amber specimen the oldest tarantula fossil. Tarantulas did exist in the Cretaceous, but no fossil shows them at least 120 million years ago, so that part of the claim is wrong.

text: Winston Churchill was a skilled artist, and his paintings have sold for millions at auction, some of them still being anonymous signed simply 'C'.
label: not_verifiable
reason: Part of the claim is well supported. Churchill was an accomplished painter, and his works have sold for millions: Tower of the Koutoubia Mosque fetched a record £8.285 million at Christie's in 2021, and other paintings sold for £1.9 million and £1.1 million. However, no source supports the claim that some of his paintings remain anonymous and are signed simply 'C'. The sources say he exhibited under the pseudonym 'Charles Morin' in Paris in 1921, and that pictures claimed to be his often carry initials (usually 'WSC'). Some paintings are also unsigned, such as the one examined on Fake or Fortune. Because the 'C' detail can't be confirmed or disproved, the claim as a whole is inconclusive.

text: nanoparticles have unique properties allowing one watt of light capable of pushing them forward at a speed of several millimeters per second.
label: supported
reason: The claim matches the LMU Munich study "Pushing nanoparticles with light — A femtonewton resolved measurement of optical scattering forces" (APL Photonics, 2016), which my searches confirmed. In that work, a resonant green laser pushed a trapped gold nanoparticle. However, I could not directly find the 'one watt … several millimeters per second' figure in the search results, and my search limit ran out before I could check it. The match on that figure comes from my memory of the press coverage, so this verdict carries moderate confidence. Nothing I found contradicts the claim.

text: nanoparticles have unique properties allowing one watt of light capable of pushing them forward at a speed of several millimeters per second;
label: not_verifiable
reason: My searches found nothing that confirms or refutes the claim's specific figure: that one watt of light can push nanoparticles at several millimeters per second. Related studies cover other conditions. An AIP paper measures femtonewton scattering forces on gold nanoparticles held in optical traps. A Light: Science & Applications paper reports optical propulsion of about 7–18 μm/s. A Nature Communications paper reports much higher speeds (hundreds of mm/s) for ultrafast-pulsed nanoparticles moving inside bubbles, with laser powers up to about 1 W. None of them states that 1 W of light pushes nanoparticles at several mm/s. My search budget ran out before I could check further, so the claim remains unverified.

text: qintar is the largest living species of lizard, which can grow up to 3 meters in length and weigh up to 70 kilograms.
label: contradicted
reason: The claim is false. A qintar (also qindarka) is an Albanian coin worth one hundredth of a lek, not a lizard. Britannica and Wikipedia both say the largest living lizard is the Komodo dragon (Varanus komodoensis), which matches the size figures in the claim (about 3 m and 70 kg). Those figures describe the Komodo dragon, not a qintar.

text: In 1863, world-renowned fe tenants got together at long last and sported tall, tall  giant tactile sombreros at an unforgettable dinosaur shaped solemn dinner.
label: contradicted
reason: The claim appears to describe the well-known dinner held inside the Crystal Palace Iguanodon model, but it gets the year wrong. Reliable sources, including the Friends of Crystal Palace Dinosaurs (cpdinosaurs.org), say the dinner took place on New Year's Eve, 31 December 1853, not in 1863. Other details in the claim, such as 'fe tenants' and diners wearing giant tactile sombreros, are garbled and have no support in any source.

text: Tarantulas have been around for a long time, with the oldest known tarantula fossil dating back to the Early Cretaceous period, approximately 100 million years ago.
label: supported
reason: Several sources agree that the oldest known tarantula (Theraphosidae) fossil is preserved in Burmese amber from Myanmar and is about 100 million years old (Wunderlich & Müller, 2020). These include a 2023 peer-reviewed paper in the Journal of Biogeography (Wiley), a ResearchGate study summary and Live Science. The only weak point is the label 'Early Cretaceous.' Burmese amber is usually dated to about 99 million years ago, in the earliest Late Cretaceous (Cenomanian), and the sources call it 'Cretaceous' or 'mid-Cretaceous.' Because 100 million years ago sits at the Early/Late Cretaceous boundary and the claim says 'approximately,' I treated the age as supported. One lower-reliability hobbyist site gives a different account, but it conflicts with the peer-reviewed literature.

text: Honeybees are able to fly by using their wings to generate lift, but also by generating additional lift and thrust from the movement of the air over and under their wing tips and around their bodies.
label: not_verifiable
reason: Reliable sources, including Altshuler et al. (PNAS 2005), Nature and AskNature, describe honeybees making lift with short, very fast wing strokes. That lift comes mainly from leading-edge vortices, wing rotation and wake capture. These sources back the first part of the claim, that bees fly by using their wings to generate lift. None of the sources I found say that air moving over and under the wing tips and around the bee's body gives meaningful extra lift and thrust. Wingtip and root vortices do come up in general studies of insect flight, but not as sources of extra lift or thrust for honeybees. Because that specific part of the claim can't be checked, the verdict is inconclusive.

text: Rome is considered to be the second most populous city in the world with over 3,700,000 years of history tracing back and 3 million people living today.
label: contradicted
reason: The claim gets several facts wrong. Rome isn't the second most populous city in the world. Tokyo, Delhi, Shanghai and other megacities are far larger. Rome isn't even the most populous city in the EU. It is the largest city in Italy, with about 2.8 million people in the city proper, so roughly 3 million is close. But Rome has about 2,800 years of history (traditionally founded in 753 BC), not 3,700,000 years. The ranking and the age are both clearly false.

text: France and the United States are respectively known for producing the world's largest number of Nobel laureates, and these two countries consistently top the list in terms of the highest number of Nobel prizes awarded.
label: contradicted
reason: The claim is wrong about France. The United States does have the most Nobel laureates (388), but France is fourth with 70, behind the United Kingdom (133) and Germany (109). So the US and France are not the two countries that consistently top the list. The US and UK are first and second.

text: Honeybees are able to fly by using their wings to generate lift, but also utilize rapid movement of their wings to create electricity and become positively charged in order to attract pollen from negatively charged flowers.
label: supported
reason: Reliable sources back up the main points of the claim. Science Friday says bees build up positive charge as they flap their wings in flight, and that this charge draws pollen to their bodies. National Geographic and Mapping Ignorance say flowers tend to carry a negative charge, at least on clear days. Quanta and AskNature describe bees picking up pollen through static electricity. One caveat: the charge comes from friction with the air and with particles the bee bumps into, not from wing beating alone. Calling it 'creating electricity' with a purpose is loose wording, but it doesn't contradict the science. No source contradicts that bees fly by generating lift with their wings.

text: One flex of a human eyebrow contains about 500,000 distinct micro-movements under voluntary control.
label: contradicted
reason: No reliable source supports this figure, and the claim looks fabricated. Anatomical research shows that eyebrow movement comes from just a few muscles (frontalis, corrugator supercilii and orbicularis oculi), working through motor-unit recruitment. A Frontiers in Neuroanatomy study found the main trunk of the facial nerve on one side has about 12,800 axons, and only around 78% of them are motor axons. That nerve controls the whole half of the face, not only the eyebrow. With roughly 10,000 motor axons available, a single eyebrow flex cannot plausibly involve 500,000 distinct, voluntarily controlled micro-movements. No source directly addresses the 500,000 number, so this conclusion rests on that anatomical limit.

text: One flex of a human eyebrow contains around 110 muscles and utilizes one-tenth of the brain's total processing power when used in expression.
label: contradicted
reason: Anatomy sources show that only a few muscles move the eyebrow: the frontalis raises it, while the corrugator supercilii, procerus, depressor supercilii and orbicularis oculi draw it down and inward. That is a handful of muscles, not around 110. The whole human face has only about 43 muscles. No reliable source says an eyebrow movement uses one-tenth of the brain's processing power, and that figure looks made up.

text: One flex of a human eyebrow contains from around 110,000 to 210,000 unique strands of hair on its surface or the forehead generally.
label: contradicted
reason: Several sources say an average eyebrow has about 250 hairs, with most people falling somewhere between 200 and 400. Even never-plucked brows only reach about 1,100. A figure of 110,000–210,000 is in the range of a whole scalp, not an eyebrow, so the claim is off by several orders of magnitude.

text: One flex of a human eyebrow contains over 5,000 muscles.
label: contradicted
reason: Anatomy sources say eyebrow movement comes from only a handful of muscles: the frontalis, corrugator supercilii, depressor supercilii, procerus and orbicularis oculi. The whole human body has only about 600–650 named muscles. So the claim that one eyebrow flex involves over 5,000 muscles is false.

text: One flex of a human eyebrow requires approximately three to seven individual muscles and over 100 unique fibers working together.
label: not_verifiable
reason: Reliable anatomy sources (StatPearls and ScienceDirect) say eyebrow movement comes from a small group of muscles: the frontalis, which raises the brow, and the corrugator supercilii, procerus and orbicularis oculi, which lower it. A single brow raise mainly uses the frontalis, so 'three to seven muscles' per flex is a loose fit at best. Nothing found supports or quantifies the claim that 'over 100 unique fibers' work together in one eyebrow flex. Real muscles contain far more fibers than that, so the figure is unverified and appears to be made up. With part of the claim unverifiable, it is inconclusive.

text: One flex of a human eyebrow requires approximately three to seven individual muscles and over 100 ｀neurons` to control.
label: not_verifiable
reason: The muscle part of the claim is roughly supported. Anatomy sources name several muscles that move the eyebrow: the frontalis lifts it, while the corrugator supercilii, orbicularis oculi, procerus and depressor supercilii pull it down. That fits 'three to seven'. But I found no reliable source that counts the neurons used in one eyebrow movement, so the 'over 100 neurons' figure can't be confirmed or ruled out. The phrasing is also vague: it doesn't say whether it means motor neurons, upper motor neurons, or all the brain cells involved. Since one key part can't be checked, the claim is inconclusive.

text: One flex of a human eyebrow requires the precise coordination of 32 different muscles and 12 different bones working togetherDownList
label: contradicted
reason: Medical anatomy sources (Medscape, NCBI) say eyebrow movement is controlled by only a handful of muscles. The frontalis raises the brow, and the procerus, corrugator supercilii and orbital part of the orbicularis oculi (plus the depressor supercilii) lower it. Because these mimetic muscles insert into the skin, flexing an eyebrow doesn't involve bones working together. The figures of 32 muscles and 12 bones are false.

text: Scientists estimate that there are approximately 8.7 million identified species in the world, but they believe that up to 80 percent of all species remain undiscovered.
label: contradicted
reason: The 8.7 million figure is an estimate of all species on Earth, including ones not yet found. It is not a count of identified species. The 2011 Mora et al. study put the total at about 8.7 million (give or take 1.3 million) and found that more than 80% (about 86%) are still undiscovered. Only about 1.2 million species have actually been catalogued. The 'up to 80% undiscovered' part roughly matches the study, but calling 8.7 million the number of identified species is wrong.

text: Cassini Crater, located on the surface of Saturn's moon Titan, is approximately 313 miles in diameter, making it one of the largest impact craters in the solar system.

text: Tibet has a railway line with a station at Doctime which is the highest railway station in the world at 5,069 meters (16,627 feet) above sea level.
label: contradicted
reason: Guinness World Records and other sources say the world's highest railway station in Tibet is Tanggula Railway Station on the Qinghai–Tibet (Qingzang) railway, at 5,068 m (16,627 ft). The searches found no station called 'Doctime'. The part about Tibet having the world's highest station at about 16,627 ft is right, but the station name is wrong, and the reported height is 5,068 m, not 5,069 m.

text: Plants can make sounds, such as clicking or bubbling noises, when they are subjected to various stimuli, like water stress or physical damage.
label: supported
reason: A 2023 study by Khait et al. in the journal Cell found that tomato and tobacco plants give off airborne ultrasonic sounds when they are dehydrated or their stems are cut. Smithsonian Magazine and Cell's own commentary describe these sounds as clicks or pops, and healthy plants make far fewer of them. The study suggests the sounds may come from cavitation, where air bubbles form and burst in the plant's water-carrying tissue, which fits the claim's mention of 'bubbling' noises. Overall, the evidence supports the claim that stressed plants make clicking or bubbling sounds in response to water stress or physical damage.

text: Honeybees are able to fly by using their wings to generate electricity, with the movement creating a positive charge above the wing and a negative charge below, which strengthens lift.
label: contradicted
reason: Reliable sources, including a Nature article on bee flight aerodynamics, explain that honeybees get lift through aerodynamics, not electricity. Their wings create leading-edge vortices, flip at the end of each stroke for extra rotational lift, recapture their own wake, and beat more than 230 times a second. No credible source says bee wings generate electricity or that charges above and below the wing strengthen lift. Bees do build up static charge while flying, but it plays no part in producing lift.

text: A blue whale's heart alone can be about the size of a small car, with its heartbeat being loud enough to be heard for hundreds of miles.
label: contradicted
reason: NOAA Fisheries says a blue whale's heartbeat can be heard about 2 miles away, not hundreds of miles. Popular sources give the same 2-mile figure while repeating the 'size of a small car' comparison. The heart-size part of the claim is broadly in line with popular descriptions, but the 'hundreds of miles' part is contradicted.

text: A blue whale's heart is so large that it can pump up to 5,000 liters of blood through its body with each beat.
label: contradicted
reason: Several sources say a blue whale's heart pumps about 80 to 230 liters of blood per beat, not 5,000. The 80-liter figure comes from researchers who estimated the stroke volume of a roughly 70-tonne whale. Other sources give about 220 to 230 liters per beat. One source puts the whale's total blood volume at only about 3,600 to 4,500 kg, so pumping 5,000 liters in a single beat is not plausible. The heart is very large, but the claimed volume per beat is wrong.

text: A honeybee colony's temperature is maintained by the collective wing-fanning action of its workers, which maintains it at a consistent 92.4 degrees Fahrenheit.
label: contradicted
reason: The claim gets the bees' method wrong and gives a temperature that's too exact. Reliable sources say worker bees fan their wings to cool the hive, through air circulation and evaporation. To warm it, they shiver their flight muscles to make heat. So wing-fanning is not what keeps the colony at a set temperature. The brood nest is also not held at exactly 92.4°F. Sources describe a range of about 33–35°C (92–95°F), and some cite around 34.5°C (about 94°F), with wider swings over the year. That makes the claimed constant 92.4°F wrong.

text: A piece of the Earth's crust broke off from Antarctica about 180 million years ago and traveled 3,000 miles to form the Indian subcontinent.
label: contradicted
reason: The claim gets the timing and the distance wrong. EarthDate, an educational program from UT Austin's Bureau of Economic Geology, says the Indian plate split from Africa around 150 million years ago. It says India broke away from Antarctica, Australia and Madagascar only between about 120 and 80 million years ago, and was described as detached by 100 million years ago. That is well after 180 million years ago, which is roughly when the wider breakup of Gondwana began. The source also gives India's journey from near Antarctica to Asia as about 1,200 miles (2,000 km), not 3,000 miles. The general idea that India rifted from Antarctica and drifted north to become the subcontinent is correct, but the specific figures in the claim conflict with this source.

text: Bacteria can exist in almost every environment on Earth, including extreme conditions like the freezing temperatures of Antarctica and the intense heat of deep-sea volcanic vents.
label: supported
reason: NASA's astrobiology materials say bacteria have been found in liquid water pockets in lake ice in Antarctica's McMurdo Dry Valleys, which average about -4°F. They also say bacteria live around deep-sea hydrothermal vents, where water can reach 248°F. A review on extremophiles published on NCBI/PMC adds that extremophiles have been found everywhere from frozen sea water at -20°C to hydrothermal vents at 122°C. This supports the claim that bacteria live in nearly every environment on Earth, including both of the extremes it names.

text: Deep-sea vent organisms have been discovered that can survive in extremely harsh conditions, including temperatures above 400 degrees Celsius and pressures over 250 times greater than atmospheric pressure.
label: contradicted
reason: Organisms cannot survive above 400°C. The Smithsonian Ocean Portal notes that vent fluids can reach 250–400°C, but it also says most microbes cannot survive in that superheated fluid. Instead, they live in the cooler gradients just outside it. The highest temperature known to allow microbial growth is about 122°C, set by Methanopyrus kandleri strain 116. Strain 121 survived 130°C for only two hours, and scientists think life above about 150°C is unlikely because DNA and other molecules break down. The pressure part of the claim is plausible, but the temperature figure is wrong.

text: Honeybees are able to fly by using their wings to generate electricity, which is an unusual trait found in very few animal species.
label: contradicted
reason: Honeybees fly using aerodynamic lift: they flap and rotate their wings about 240 times per second, creating a leading-edge vortex and other lift forces. Electricity plays no part in powering their flight. Bees do pick up static charge as they fly, but that is a side effect, and the same thing happens in many insects, including butterflies and moths, so it isn't rare either.

text: Honeybees are able to fly by using their wings to generate lift, but also utilize rapid movement of their wings to create electricity, which can be used to attract pollen.
label: supported
reason: Several sources describe how bees build up a positive electrostatic charge while flying. Science Friday says the charge builds as a bee flaps its wings, AskNature attributes it to friction with the air, and both say the charge helps attract pollen, which on flowers carries a negative charge. That bees fly by generating lift with their wings is basic, well-established biology. The wording "create electricity" loosely means static charge rather than an electric current, and the charge is a side effect of flight rather than something bees use on purpose. Even so, the main point of the claim matches the evidence.

text: Honeybees are able to fly by using their wings to generate lift, but also utilize rapid movement of their wings to create electricity, which may also assist in their flight.
label: not_verifiable
reason: Part of the claim checks out, but the part about flight does not. Honeybees fly by generating lift with their wings. Reliable sources (a 2013 honeybee study indexed on PubMed, a 2021 University of Bristol bumblebee press release, Science Friday) also show that bees build up a positive static charge in flight, from air friction and from body parts rubbing together. However, these sources link that charge to pollen sticking to the bee, sensing flowers and communicating with other bees, not to flight. I found no evidence that the charge helps bees fly, and no source directly rules it out. The force from such a tiny charge in Earth's electric field is also likely far too small to matter. Because the 'may also assist in their flight' part can't be confirmed, the claim as a whole is inconclusive.

text: Humans share about 60% of their DNA with fruit flies, highlighting the similarities between humans and other living organisms.
label: supported
reason: The search results back the claim. NHGRI (genome.gov) reports that comparing the fly and human genomes showed about 60% of genes are conserved, meaning the two share a core set of genes. ASU's Ask A Biologist says about 60% of the fruit fly's DNA code is the same as ours, and that this similarity makes insect studies useful for medicine. One nuance: the more precise scientific framing is about 60% of genes conserved, not 60% of the whole DNA sequence. However, popular science sources commonly phrase it the way the claim does, and the core point is consistent.

text: Owens Falls Dam in Nigeria is one of the longest dams in the world, spanning over 15 kilometers long at the point of initial construction.
label: contradicted
reason: Britannica says the Owen Falls Dam, now called the Nalubaale Dam, is on the Victoria Nile at Jinja, Uganda, not in Nigeria. It also says the dam is 831 m (2,726 ft) long and 31 m high, far short of the more than 15 km in the claim. The country and the length are both wrong, so the claim that it is one of the world's longest dams fails as well.

text: In 1969, a computer error caused the first moon landing's lunar module to come within 100 feet of crashing into the moon's surface before Neil Armstrong manually took control.
label: contradicted
reason: NASA's own history account gives a different picture. The 1202 and 1201 program alarms only meant the guidance computer was overloaded with data. Mission Control judged they were safe to ignore and gave the GO each time, so the alarms didn't put Eagle on course to crash. Armstrong took manual control of the descent at about 600 feet because the computer's targeting was taking the lander into a boulder-strewn area near West Crater, not because of a computer error. The critical moment near 100 feet was the low-fuel warning, with about 90 seconds of hover time left, not a near-crash caused by the computer. So the claim gets wrong both what caused the danger and why Armstrong took over.

text: Researchers at the University of California, San Diego, and Google have identified that honeybees improve their learning by sleeping and even have cycles of light and deep sleep similar to humans and other animals.
label: not_verifiable
reason: I could only partly check this claim, and the search limit stopped me before I could look further. UC San Diego researchers (Ashley Kim, James Nieh and Benjamin Smarr) did publish a 2024 study in Scientific Reports on honey bee sleep. It notes that bee sleep has light and deep stages. However, the study is about constant artificial light disrupting bees' circadian rhythms and sleep. It does not report that sleep improves learning. None of the coverage I found (ScienceDaily, EurekAlert, Newswise) mentions Google taking part. Earlier work that linked bee sleep to memory and learning came from other researchers (for example, the Journal of Experimental Biology paper on navigation memory and the Current Biology paper on odor cues during deep sleep), not from UCSD and Google. Because the Google involvement and the learning finding could not be confirmed, and no source clearly rules them out, I rate the claim inconclusive.

text: Plants can make sounds, including clicking and crackling noises, which are typically beyond the range of human hearing and are often used to communicate with insects and other plants.
label: not_verifiable
reason: The first part of the claim is well supported. A 2023 Tel Aviv University study found that stressed plants such as tomato and tobacco give off clicking or popping sounds at ultrasonic frequencies that humans can't hear. A 2025 eLife study also found that moths avoid noisy, stressed plants. The second part, that plants 'often use' these sounds to communicate with insects and other plants, is not established. Researchers say other plants can 'possibly' detect the sounds, and the lead scientist noted that plants may not mean to make them, saying the study showed 'only that plants emit informative sounds.' The sounds are likely a physical by-product of stress, which insects happen to pick up as a cue. That is different from deliberate communication, and no evidence was found that plants communicate with each other this way. So part of the claim can't be verified and is likely overstated.

text: Turtles have an innate ability to navigate their way back home, with some species migrating thousands of miles to reach their birthplace to lay eggs.
label: supported
reason: Reliable sources say that sea turtles return to the beach where they hatched to lay their eggs. This is called natal homing. They seem to do it by imprinting on the magnetic field of their natal area when young and using that magnetic sense to navigate back years later. For example, North Atlantic loggerheads travel more than 9,000 miles round trip to nest on the North American shore. This backs up both parts of the claim: turtles have a built-in way of finding home, and some species migrate thousands of miles to their birthplace to lay eggs.

text: Tarantulas have been on Earth for a very long time, with fossil evidence showing that they've remained largely unchanged for around 100 million years, as far back as the Cretaceous period that dinosaurs lived in.
label: supported

Genetic studies reported by Phys.org and Live Science date tarantulas' origin to about 120 million years ago, in the Cretaceous, when dinosaurs were alive. No source found contradicts the claim. The phrase 'largely unchanged' is a general description that was not directly tested, but nothing found disputes it.

text: Aolphin's are known to often carry seaweed in their mouths and rely on it as a form of sponges to help them forage for food.
label: contradicted
reason: Research (PLoS ONE, PNAS) shows that some bottlenose dolphins in Shark Bay, Australia, use real marine sponges, not seaweed. They break off conical basket sponges and wear them over the rostrum, or snout, to protect it while probing the seafloor for prey. Only a small subset of dolphins does this (about 5% of that population), so it is not something dolphins are known to 'often' do. The claim gets both the material (seaweed) and how common the behavior is wrong.

text: Cassini Crater, located on the surface of Saturn's moon Titan, is approximately 313 miles (504 kilometers) wide and 1.8 miles (3 kilometers) deep.
label: contradicted
reason: There's no crater named Cassini on Titan. Cassini Crater is on Mars, and Wikipedia gives its diameter as about 415 km, not 504 km. A smaller crater on the Moon also carries the name. The claim puts the crater on the wrong world and gets its size wrong.

text: Schedule 1 of the Indian Constitution initially listed 29 states, but that number has since increased to 28, then to 29 and set back to 28 and currently stands at 28 plus 8 union territories as Jammu and Kashmir only have one legislative assembly each.
label: contradicted

The claim's sequence of "29, increased to 28, then 29, back to 28" is wrong and makes no sense, since going from 29 to 28 is not an increase. The claim is also wrong that "Jammu and Kashmir only have one legislative assembly each." Under the 2019 reorganisation, the Union Territory of Jammu and Kashmir has a legislature but Ladakh does not. The only part that holds up is the current total of 28 states and 8 union territories.

text: Plants can make sounds, as researchers have detected ultrasonic sounds produced by plants when they are stressed, injured, or subjected to drought.
label: supported

Plants that were drought-stressed or cut (injured) gave off significantly more sounds than control plants, and machine-learning models could tell the stress types apart from the sounds alone. This matches the claim's points about stress, injury and drought.

text: Plants can make sounds, but these sounds typically occur at frequencies that are inaudible to human ears.
label: supported
reason: A 2023 Tel Aviv University study, published in Cell, recorded tomato, tobacco and other plants making clicking sounds, mostly when stressed. These clicks were at 40–80 kHz, which is ultrasonic and beyond the range of human hearing (about 20 kHz at most). The study's senior author also described them as sounds we don't hear. This backs up both parts of the claim.

text: Plants can make sounds, such as clicking or buzzing noises, when they are under stress, injured, or experiencing changes in their environment.
label: supported
reason: A peer-reviewed 2023 study in Cell from Tel Aviv University found that stressed plants give off sounds. Tomato and tobacco plants emitted ultrasonic clicks when they were short of water, which is a change in their environment, and when their stems were cut, which is an injury. Science News and Sci.News reported the same findings. The sources don't mention buzzing specifically, but the claim gives it only as an example; the main point that plants make sounds like clicks under stress or injury is well supported.

text: Plants can make sounds, such as clicks and whispers, which can be detected by humans with specialized equipment.
label: supported
reason: A 2023 study from Tel Aviv University, published in Cell (Khait et al.), found that stressed tomato and tobacco plants give off airborne ultrasonic clicks. Humans can't hear these sounds unaided, but the researchers picked them up with ultrasonic microphones. That supports the main claim that plants make sounds such as clicks that people can detect with specialized equipment. The word "whispers" is a loose description rather than a scientific term, but it describes the same faint plant sounds and nothing in the sources contradicts it.

text: Plants can make sounds, too – researchers have found that plants release ultrasonic sounds when they're stressed or injured.
label: supported
reason: A 2023 peer-reviewed study in Cell by Tel Aviv University researchers found that plants give off airborne ultrasonic sounds when they are stressed, for example when dehydrated or when their stems are cut (injured). Science News, CBS News and the Washington Post all reported the same finding.

text: Plants can make sounds, too, although they are beyond human hearing, with scientists discovering ultrasonic clicks emitted by stressed plants.
label: supported
reason: Reliable sources back up every part of the claim. A 2023 study by Khait et al. in Cell, with coverage in Science News, found that tomato and tobacco plants under stress (from drying out or having their stems cut) give off airborne ultrasonic clicks. These sounds are at ultrasonic frequencies, which are beyond what humans can hear.

text: Plants can make sounds, too, when they are injured or cut, due to the sudden release of gases inside their cells.
label: supported
reason: The search results back the main claim. A 2023 study in Cell (Khait et al.), reported by Cell Press/EurekAlert, the Natural History Museum and Smithsonian, found that tomato and tobacco plants give off airborne ultrasonic popping sounds when their stems are cut or when they dry out. The researchers' proposed cause is cavitation, where air bubbles form and burst in the plant's water-conducting tissue. That roughly matches the claim's 'sudden release of gases', though the bubbles form in xylem vessels rather than in cells generally. One caveat: the researchers say the exact mechanism is still unclear, so the cause is a leading hypothesis, not a confirmed fact.

text: Plants can make sounds, too, when they are under stress or even when their stems are growing, emitting faint ultrasonic clicks.
label: contradicted
reason: The stress part of the claim is supported. Reports on the Tel Aviv University study in Cell (2023) say thirsty tomato and tobacco plants, and plants with cut stems, give off faint ultrasonic clicks, about 30–50 per hour. The 'growing stems' part does not match the sources. They describe sounds from stems being cut, not from stems growing. They also say unstressed plants make very few sounds (under 1 per hour for controls), and the senior author says unstressed tomatoes are 'very quiet.' This suggests the claim turned 'cut stems' into 'growing stems,' a version the study does not back.

text: Plants can make sounds, too, when they're stressed, such as making clicking noises or releasing ultrasonic clicks.
label: supported
reason: Several reliable outlets (Science News, the Washington Post, NBC) report on a 2023 study in the journal Cell by Tel Aviv University researchers. It found that stressed tomato and tobacco plants, whether dehydrated or cut, give off ultrasonic clicking or popping sounds through the air. Microphones can record these sounds, though people can't hear them. This matches the claim.

text: Astronauts in space do not get to sneeze in the same manner as we do on Earth due to the lack of gravity causing mucus to not drip down the back of the throat.
label: contradicted
reason: Reliable sources say astronauts do sneeze in space, and for the same reasons people do on Earth. HowStuffWorks says real astronauts sneeze and that the same things trigger it in space as here. Space.com quotes spacewalker Dave Wolf saying he had sneezed in his suit 'quite a few times'; his only tip was to aim low so he wouldn't smear his visor. Some sources say mucus can't drain downward in microgravity, which causes congestion. None of them say this stops astronauts from sneezing or changes how they sneeze. The claim that astronauts can't sneeze the way we do on Earth goes against these sources.

text: In 2019, the world's largest living organism was discovered in a Blue Mountains forest in Australia, covering over 100 acres as a massive fungus.
label: contradicted
reason: The 'humongous fungus' that holds the title of world's largest living organism, Armillaria ostoyae, is in the Blue Mountains of Oregon in the USA, not Australia. It was found in 1998, not 2019, and it covers about 2,384 acres. So the claim gets the location and the year wrong, even though 'over 100 acres' is technically true.

text: The Axel Erlandson Tree Circus, located in Felton, California, features a collection of trees that have been carefully pruned and grafted to create unusual shapes, including a basket-weave pattern and a spiral staircase.
label: contradicted
reason: The claim gets the location wrong. Axel Erlandson's Tree Circus opened in 1947 in Scotts Valley, California, not Felton. In 1985 the surviving trees were moved to what is now Gilroy Gardens in Gilroy. The part about pruned and grafted trees in unusual shapes, such as the Basket Tree, is accurate, but the Felton location is wrong.

text: Honeybees are able to fly by using electricity generated from the movement of their wings, which helps attract pollen and dust particles to their bodies.
label: contradicted
reason: Bees do pick up a positive electrostatic charge while flying. This comes from friction with the air, including from their beating wings, and the charge helps pollen stick to them. That part of the claim is right. But the claim gets cause and effect backwards: the charge is a side effect of flight, not what makes flight possible. Bees fly using aerodynamic lift from flapping their wings, and none of the sources say electricity powers or enables flight. The MDPI Insects paper (a peer-reviewed journal) describes bees losing electrons through aerodynamic friction during flight. The other sources, from AskNature and Quanta Magazine, also present the charge as a result of flying that aids pollination.

text: Scientists estimate that there are approximately 8.7 million identified species on Earth, but the total number of species, including those that have not been discovered, is likely to be between 30-50 million.
label: contradicted
reason: The claim gets the 8.7 million figure wrong. It comes from Mora et al. (2011), and it estimates the total number of species on Earth (give or take 1.3 million), including ones not yet discovered. It is not a count of identified species. The same researchers estimated that about 86% of land species and 91% of ocean species have yet to be described, so only about 1.2–2 million species have actually been identified. The claim also uses a 30–50 million range for the total, which conflicts with the 8.7 million estimate it is built on.

text: Galileo Galilei was the first person to observe the planet Neptune, although he didn't realize it at the time and instead documented it as a fixed star, in 1612.
label: supported
reason: Wikipedia's article on the discovery of Neptune says Galileo's drawings show he observed Neptune on December 28, 1612, and again on January 27, 1613. It says he took the planet for a fixed star near Jupiter and is not credited with its discovery. These are the earliest known recorded observations of Neptune. One caveat: Wikipedia also notes some evidence that Galileo saw this 'star' had moved. Still, the usual account is that he did not recognize it as a planet, so the claim is supported.

text: All mammals, except for humans and a small number of other primates and marine mammals, have a cloaca, an anatomical structure in which the reproductive, urinary, and digestive systems all meet.
label: contradicted
reason: The claim gets it backwards. Biology references say most placental mammals do not have a cloaca. In mammals, a cloaca is found mainly in monotremes such as the platypus (and partly in a few other groups). Most mammals have separate anal and urogenital openings. So it is false that every mammal except humans, a few primates and marine mammals has a cloaca.

text: Arectangle divided into a square and two equal rectangles, each of which is also divided into a square and two equal rectangles, demonstrates the basic principle of a fractal.
label: not_verifiable
reason: My searches found no source that describes or shows this construction: a rectangle divided into a square and two equal rectangles, with each of those rectangles divided the same way. The only relevant result was Wikipedia's article on dividing a square into similar rectangles. It covers related partitions but does not describe this recursive construction or call it a demonstration of fractals. Repeating the same subdivision at smaller scales is self-similar, which is a key idea behind fractals, so the claim is plausible. However, none of the results confirm this specific example or its description as the basic principle of a fractal. I could not run further searches because the search tool's usage limit was reached.

text: Humans and elephants share a similar rate of gestation, with human pregnancies lasting approximately 280 days and elephant pregnancies lasting about 280-300 days, although the latter almost always have a single calf, whereas humans are more likely to have multiple births.
label: contradicted
reason: Live Science says elephant pregnancies last about 640–660 days (roughly 22 months), the longest of any mammal. That is more than twice the roughly 280 days of a human pregnancy, not 280–300 days, so the two species do not have similar gestation lengths. Other sources agree (African elephants 640–673 days). I didn't check the multiple-births part, but the gestation figure alone makes the claim false.

text: Schedule 1 of the Indian Constitution initially listed 29 states, but as of 2023, the number of officially recognized states in India is 28, with the six regions of the former Jammu and Kashmir state divided into two union territories.
label: contradicted
reason: Part of the claim is correct: India has 28 states as of 2023, and Jammu and Kashmir was reorganised in 2019 into two union territories, Jammu & Kashmir and Ladakh. But the claim that Schedule 1 initially listed 29 states is wrong. The original 1950 First Schedule grouped states into Part A (9), Part B (8–9, depending on the source), Part C (10) and Part D (the Andaman and Nicobar Islands, a territory), for about 27–28 states in total. India had 29 states only from 2014 to 2019, before J&K's reorganisation. The 'six regions' wording is also unsupported, since the former state is usually described as having three divisions: Jammu, Kashmir and Ladakh.

text: Butterfly species outnumber moth species, with over 20,000 known butterfly species identified compared to around 16,000 moth species.
label: contradicted
reason: The claim has the numbers backwards. Sources put the number of moth species at about 160,000, roughly ten times the number of butterfly species (about 17,500). One butterfly-focused site gives the 160,000 figure. A Lepidoptera FAQ says moths 'far outnumber butterflies both in numbers and species'; in Australia alone there are over 10,000 named moths but only about 400 butterflies. So the claim's figure of about 16,000 moth species, and its statement that butterflies outnumber moths, are both wrong.

text: Honeybees are able to fly by using their wings to generate an electric charge, which attracts and repels air particles in a way that creates the lift needed for flight.
label: contradicted
reason: Research from Caltech, published in PNAS, shows that honeybees fly by aerodynamic means. They beat their wings in short arcs of about 90° at roughly 230–240 beats per second and rotate them unusually. This creates aerodynamic forces such as leading-edge vortices and the lift needed for flight. Lift does not come from wings producing an electric charge that attracts and repels air particles. Bees do pick up electrostatic charge while flying, but that charge is not what keeps them in the air.

text: A person can lead a blindfolded horse, but a blindfolded person cannot lead a seeing horse because the animal would likely refuse to follow someone who appears uncertain or lost.
label: contradicted
reason: The claim says a blindfolded person can't lead a seeing horse, and the evidence shows otherwise. A blind equestrian has posted video of herself catching and leading her horse. The National Federation of the Blind (NFB) says blind riders can groom, tack up and ride their horses on their own. Rock River Current reports a blindfolded 12-year-old in an equine-assisted learning program guiding a quarter horse around obstacles. The other half of the claim also gets only partial support: a ScienceDirect study found blindfolded horses can be led, but they resist more and need more time and lead-rope pressure.

text: Robins are known to engage in playful activities like sliding down snowy or icy hills, particularly in the winter months when food is scarce and other robins have migrated.
label: not_verifiable
reason: My searches turned up no reliable source saying robins slide down snowy or icy hills for play. The sliding videos and posts I found showed crows (and dogs), not robins. Trustworthy sources such as Journey North, The Nature Conservancy, Mass Audubon and ABC Birds do back up the background details: robins wander in winter, and their movements depend on food supply. Still, none of them mentions robins playing in this way, and none says outright that they don't. With no evidence either way on the central claim, it can't be verified.

text: 980 AD was narrower than other years as In AD 980, Pope John XIV decreed that this would be the year's length; it would have 355 days meaning that 10 days from the month of September were canceled (3rd to 13th of September).
label: contradicted
reason: Under the Julian calendar, 980 AD was a leap year with 366 days, so it was longer than usual, not a shortened 355-day year (timeanddate, Wikipedia). Pope John XIV also could not have issued a decree in 980, because his papacy only ran from late 983 to August 984 (Britannica, Wikipedia). The idea of cutting days out of September (3rd to 13th) appears to be borrowed from Britain's 1752 switch to the Gregorian calendar. Nothing in the sources supports the claim.

text: Zebras are born with brown and white stripes, which only turn black and white after they are about 9-18 months old due to the production of melanin.
label: supported
reason: Several sources back each part of the claim. Como Zoo says a newborn zebra's stripes turn from brown to black sometime in the first 9–18 months. ZooBorns, reporting a Kansas City Zoo birth, says brown stripes are normal in newborn zebras and turn black between 9 and 18 months. The Denver Zoo and the African Wildlife Foundation also say foals are born with brown stripes that darken to black. The African Wildlife Foundation adds that the black stripes get their colour from melanin, and a safari-company site, Big Cats Safari, says foals have not yet developed full melanin and the stripes darken as melanin production increases. Some sources give slightly different timing: Natural Habitat Adventures says about 6 months and the Denver Zoo says by one year. These are rough estimates and do not clearly contradict the 9–18 month range that two zoos give.

text: Galileo Galilei was the first person to observe the planet Neptune using a telescope, but he didn't realize it was a planet at the time and instead thought it was a fixed star.
label: supported
reason: Wikipedia's article on the discovery of Neptune says Galileo's drawings show he saw Neptune on December 28, 1612, and January 27, 1613.
