Both times he took it for a fixed star while it sat close to Jupiter in the sky, and he did not recognise it as a planet, so he is not credited with discovering it. These are the earliest recorded telescope sightings of Neptune, which fits the claim that he was the first to see it. There is one complication: Galileo noted that the 'star' seemed to move, so he may have suspected something was unusual. Still, he never identified it as a planet.

text: A blue whale's heart is so large that it can pump around 50 gallons of blood with every beat.
label: contradicted
reason: Reliable sources give a larger figure than the claim. NOAA Fisheries says a blue whale's heart pumps about 60 gallons of blood with each beat, and Guinness World Records estimates around 58 gallons (220 litres) per beat. Other sources also say about 60 gallons (227 L). The claim's 'around 50 gallons' is roughly 15–17% below this figure. Because the claim says 'around,' this is a borderline call, but I found no source that gives 50 gallons, so I'm treating the number as contradicted.

text: A blue whale's heart is so massive that it can pump over 5,000 liters of blood with every beat.
label: contradicted
reason: Inverse, reporting on the 2019 study that recorded a wild blue whale's heartbeat, says researchers estimated the whale's 319 kg heart pumps about 80 liters of blood with each beat. Other commonly cited figures are around 220 liters per beat. Both are far below 5,000 liters, which is closer to the whale's entire blood volume than to the amount moved in one beat. The heart is very large, but the 'over 5,000 liters per beat' figure is wrong.

text: A blue whale's heartbeat can be as slow as two beats per minute when the animal is at rest underwater.
label: supported
reason: Reporting on the 2019 Stanford study by Goldbogen and colleagues, the first recording of a blue whale's heart rate, says it fell to as low as 2 beats per minute while the whale was diving underwater. During dives it usually ran at 4–8 bpm, and it rose to 37 bpm at the surface. One detail is off: the whale was on deep foraging dives, not strictly 'at rest.' The main point of the claim, that the heartbeat can drop to about two beats per minute underwater, is still supported.

text: Bees are able to fly by using electricity generated from their wing movements and the surrounding air to create a force field around their bodies that adds lift.
label: contradicted
reason: Bees fly because of aerodynamics, not electricity. Nature's explainer and the University of Florida entomology article both say the lift comes from fast wing strokes at changing angles. These create leading-edge vortices, along with rotational lift and wake recapture. Bees do pick up a static charge in flight, but this is a side effect. It does not create a force field that lifts them, so the claim is wrong.

text: Denmark has the highest number of traffic lights and cycles in Europe, and the lowest number of traffic deaths in the world.
label: contradicted
reason: The search results show that Norway, not Denmark, has the lowest rate of road traffic deaths in the world, at about 1.5 deaths per 100,000 people. Norway, Iceland and Sweden are the usual top performers. That contradicts the claim that Denmark has the lowest number of traffic deaths in the world. I also found nothing to back up the claim that Denmark has the most traffic lights in Europe.

text: Galaxies in the observable universe are moving away from each other at speeds of up to 90% of the speed of light.
label: contradicted
reason: The claim sets a ceiling of 90% of light speed, but cosmology sources say recession speeds have no such limit. Peer-reviewed papers on arXiv (Davis & Lineweaver) explain that galaxies farther away than the Hubble distance c/H recede faster than light, and that we can still observe some of these galaxies. Scientific American likewise notes that the most distant galaxies in JWST deep fields are receding faster than light because space itself is expanding. So galaxies in the observable universe recede at speeds well beyond 90% of c, which contradicts the 'up to 90%' limit.

text: Geokinetics refers to the study of the flow and movement of tectonic plates, as well as the processes that shape the Earth's lithosphere.
label: not_verifiable
reason: I found no reliable source that defines "geokinetics" as the study of tectonic plate flow and movement or of the processes that shape the lithosphere. Most search results use "Geokinetics" as the name of a Houston-based seismic data company (Wikipedia, SEG wiki, LinkedIn). One result, the P2P Foundation wiki, describes it as a philosophical theory of Earth as material flow. Several sources describe plate tectonics as the large-scale motion of the lithosphere, but none link that field to the term "geokinetics." The search did not show the claim to be false, so the evidence is insufficient either way.

text: Honeybees are able to fly by using electricity generated from the friction of their wings beating, with the static electricity helping their wings to lift.
label: contradicted
reason: Research published in PNAS (Altshuler et al., 2005) shows that honeybees get their lift from aerodynamics. They beat their wings in short, very fast strokes, and the resulting unsteady airflow, including leading-edge vortices, keeps them in the air. Bees do pick up a positive static charge from friction with the air while flying, but sources such as AskNature link that charge to sensing flowers' electric fields and moving pollen, not to producing lift. The claim that static electricity from wing friction lets bees fly is false.

text: Humans and dolphins are the only mammals known to give themselves names, although dolphins name themselves using a unique series of clicks and whistles.
label: contradicted
reason: The claim is wrong on two counts. First, humans and dolphins are not the only mammals known to use names. A 2024 Colorado State University study found that wild African elephants address each other with name-like calls. A 2024 Hebrew University study reported by EurekAlert, CNN and ScienceAlert found that marmoset monkeys name each other with 'phee-calls', and these reports describe the behavior as previously known in humans, dolphins and elephants. Second, dolphins identify themselves with signature whistles, not a series of clicks and whistles.

text: Humans and dolphins are the only mammals known to give themselves names, although dolphins name themselves using unique clicking sounds called "sig whistles".
label: contradicted
reason: The claim gets two things wrong. First, dolphin 'names' are signature whistles, which are whistles and not clicking sounds, and they aren't called 'sig whistles'. Second, research says elephants and marmosets (plus green-rumped parrotlets, which are birds) also appear to use names, so humans and dolphins are not the only mammals reported to do this. Some researchers question the evidence for elephants and marmosets, but the dolphin description is wrong either way.

text: Humans share about 60% of their DNA with fruit flies, indicating a common genetic ancestor.
label: supported
reason: Sources broadly back the claim. The Max Planck Society says that about 60% of fruit fly genes have a similar counterpart in humans. Popular-science pieces such as The Gazelle describe this as humans and flies sharing 60% of their DNA or genome. NIH's NIGMS says most human genes have counterparts in flies, which fits with descent from a common ancestor. One caveat: the 60% figure strictly refers to conserved or similar genes, not 60% identical DNA sequence. Still, the claim matches the commonly cited fact, and I found no source that contradicts it.

text: Members of the smallest primate species, the pygmy mouse lemur, are about the size of a human middle finger.
label: not_verifiable
reason: The sources disagree on which species is the smallest primate, and I couldn't check the size comparison. Wikipedia, Animal Diversity Web and a PMC study say Madame Berthe's mouse lemur (Microcebus berthae, about 9.2 cm and 30–33 g) is the smallest. Wikipedia calls the pygmy mouse lemur (M. myoxinus, about 12–13 cm head-body and 43–55 g) the second smallest, noting the two are often confused. National Geographic and The Animal Files, however, still name the pygmy mouse lemur as the smallest. My searches found nothing comparing either species to a human middle finger, and I ran out of searches before I could look further. Because one part of the claim has evidence on both sides and the other part is unverified, I can't call it supported or contradicted.

text: Members of the smallest primate species, the pygmy mouse lemur, are about the size of a human thumb and weigh around 30 grams.
label: contradicted
reason: The claim names the wrong species. Wikipedia, Britannica and Guinness World Records all say the smallest primate is Madame Berthe's mouse lemur (Microcebus berthae), which averages about 9.2 cm long and weighs around 30 g. The pygmy mouse lemur (Microcebus myoxinus) is a different species: Wikipedia lists it at 43–55 g, calls it the second-smallest mouse lemur, and notes the two species are often confused. An older Animal Diversity Web page still calls Peters's (pygmy) mouse lemur the smallest primate at 30–55 g, but the more recent and authoritative sources contradict it.

text: Octopuses have a highly distributed brain, with nine brains in total including the central brain and eight separate mini-brains in each of their eight arms.
label: supported
reason: My search turned up reliable sources, including Discovery's coverage of University of Washington research, that describe the claim the same way. Each octopus arm has its own cluster of nerve cells that controls movement and can act without the central brain, so the octopus is commonly said to have eight independent mini-brains plus a larger central brain, nine in all. OctoNation adds that 'nine brains' is a nickname for one integrated nervous system with arm control centers, not nine full brains, but this nuance does not contradict the claim.

text: Research has shown thatreno have a unique type of three-chambered stomach, an organ that started evolution some time before dinosaurs became extinct.
label: contradicted
reason: Reading "reno" as the Spanish word for reindeer, the claim is wrong. Reliable sources, including a University of Alaska Fairbanks reindeer physiology publication and a PMC study, describe reindeer as ruminants with a four-chambered stomach (rumen, reticulum, omasum and abomasum). Their stomach is not a unique three-chambered type. Three-chambered stomachs belong to pseudo-ruminants such as camelids, not reindeer. Because the stomach structure is contradicted, the claim fails whatever is true about when the organ evolved. One caveat: "reno" could be a typo for something else, but reindeer is the most plausible meaning.

text: Scientists estimate that there are approximately 8.7 million identified species on Earth, but the actual number could be closer to 30 million.
label: contradicted
reason: The 8.7 million figure (Mora et al., 2011, PLoS Biology) is an estimate of the total number of eukaryotic species on Earth, both known and unknown. It is not a count of identified species. Only about 1.2 million species had been described and catalogued at the time. For example, the study counted only 953,434 described animal species out of an estimated 7.77 million. Calling the 8.7 million species "identified" is therefore wrong, so the claim is contradicted even though some older estimates did range up to 30 million or more.

text: Tarantulas have been around for a long time, with fossil evidence showing they existed over 100 million years ago during the Cretaceous period.
label: supported
reason: The search results back the claim. Live Science reports that one of the only two known tarantula fossils is a specimen in amber from Myanmar that is about 100 million years old. Scientific papers on ResearchGate describe it as the oldest known tarantula fossil, dating to the Cretaceous (~100 Ma; Wunderlich & Müller, 2020). Phylogenetic dating also puts the origin of tarantulas in the early Cretaceous, around 120 million years ago. One caveat: Burmese amber is usually dated to about 99 Ma, so 'over 100 million years' rounds up slightly, but sources consistently describe the fossil as roughly 100 million years old.

text: Tarantulas have been on Earth for a long time, with fossil records showing that they existed over 100 million years ago during the Cretaceous period.
label: supported
reason: A peer-reviewed study in the Journal of Biogeography (Wiley) says the oldest known tarantula fossil, Protertheraphosinae in Burmese amber, dates to about 100 million years ago, in the Cretaceous. The same study dates the split between tarantulas (Theraphosidae) and their closest relatives to the early Cretaceous, about 120 million years ago. Together this supports the claim that tarantulas have existed for a long time, going back to the Cretaceous. The one caveat is that Burmese amber is usually dated to about 99 million years, so the fossil itself is roughly 100 million years old. The age of over 100 million years comes from the molecular dating estimate rather than the fossil.

text: Tarantulas have been on Earth for a long time, with fossil records showing they existed at least 100 million years ago during the Cretaceous period.
label: supported
reason: A peer-reviewed paper in the Journal of Biogeography (Wiley) says the oldest known tarantula (Theraphosidae) fossil comes from Burmese amber dated to about 100 million years ago (Wunderlich & Müller, 2020). That age falls in the Cretaceous period, so the fossil record matches the claim that tarantulas existed at least 100 million years ago.

text: Walruses are able to slow down their heart rate dramatically when diving, from 100 beats per minute to just 4-10 beats per minute.
label: contradicted
reason: A peer-reviewed study of wild adult male Atlantic walruses found a mean resting heart rate of about 36 beats per minute, with a range of 29–43. That conflicts with the claim's starting rate of 100 beats per minute. The 100-to-about-5 bpm figures appear in the Smithsonian's description of seals, not walruses. The only source I found for the 4–10 bpm diving range is a low-reliability animal-facts site. SeaWorld confirms that walruses slow their heart rate when diving but gives no numbers. The claimed drop from 100 bpm to 4–10 bpm is not backed by reliable walrus data and conflicts with the measured resting rate.

text: Water can exist in three distinct states at the same time, a phenomenon known as the triple point of water, which occurs at a specific temperature and pressure.
label: supported
reason: Fluke's explainer says the triple point of water is the specific temperature and pressure (0.01 °C and about 0.006 atm) at which water's solid, liquid and gas phases coexist in thermodynamic equilibrium. That matches every part of the claim: three states at once, the name 'triple point', and a specific temperature and pressure.

text: velit Solis or the voice of the Sun is a proposed planet considered for loose debris outside our solar system.
label: not_verifiable
reason: I found nothing about a proposed planet called "velit Solis" or "the voice of the Sun". Searches turned up only unrelated things: fan-fiction worlds named Solis, Solis Lacus (a dark surface feature on Mars), the Warframe quest Vox Solaris, and a Star Trek episode called Vox Sola. Wikipedia's list of hypothetical Solar System objects doesn't include such a name either. The translation is also wrong: in Latin, "velit" means "wants", not "voice". Because no source mentions this object, the claim can't be confirmed, and there's no direct evidence that it's false.

text: velit Solis or the voice of the Sun is a proposed planet considered for loose debris outside the planetary orbit of Neptune.
label: not_verifiable
reason: I found no trustworthy source that mentions a proposed planet called "velit Solis" or "voice of the Sun" beyond Neptune. Searches for the name only returned unrelated hits, such as a heater brand, the Martian feature Solis Lacus and a Scorn album. The proposed planets beyond Neptune that searches did turn up are Planet Nine and Planet Y, and neither goes by this name. The search snippets I could see of Wikipedia's list of hypothetical Solar System objects did not mention it either, but they were too short to rule it out completely. Since nothing confirms or directly disproves the name, the claim can't be verified.

text: िरफ is the largest living structure on Earth, according to the Guinness World Records, spanning more than 2,300 kilometers off the coast of Australia.
label: supported
reason: "िरफ" looks like a garbled spelling of "रीफ" (reef), and the rest of the claim clearly points to the Great Barrier Reef. Guinness World Records lists the Great Barrier Reef, off Queensland, Australia, as the largest structure ever built by living creatures, about 2,300 km long and covering 207,000 km². Other sources commonly describe it as the largest living structure on Earth, spanning about 2,300 km. Two small caveats: Guinness's exact wording is "largest marine animal structure" rather than "largest living structure," and it gives the length as 2,300 km, not "more than" 2,300 km. These differences don't change the substance of the claim.

text: Jellyfish have been to space: in 1991, NASA sent 2,000 moon jellyfish to space aboard the Columbia space shuttle to study their development in microgravity.
label: contradicted
reason: Most of the claim is accurate. In June 1991, NASA's STS-40 Spacelab Life Sciences mission on the shuttle Columbia carried moon jellyfish (Aurelia aurita) to study how they develop in microgravity. The number is wrong, though. Futura-Sciences and BBC Sky at Night both report 2,478 polyps, which is about 2,500, not 2,000.

text: High-speed camera footage revealed that a mantis shrimp can accelerate its claws at the speed of a .22 caliber bullet, which is around 25 feet per second squared.
label: contradicted
reason: Several sources agree that high-speed filming by Sheila Patek and colleagues (published in Nature in 2004) showed the mantis shrimp's strike reaching an acceleration of about 10,400 g, which they compare to a .22 caliber bullet. The strike also reaches a speed of about 23 m/s (around 50 mph). That much of the claim holds up. But 10,400 g works out to roughly 102,000 m/s², or about 335,000 ft/s². That is nowhere near the claim's '25 feet per second squared,' which is about 0.8 g. The claim also confuses speed with acceleration, so its numbers are wrong.

text: France and the United States are the two countries with the most time zones, with France having a total of 12 time zones and the United States having a total of 11 time zones when including its insular areas.
label: supported
reason: Several sources agree on both numbers. France has 12 time zones because of its overseas territories (13 if its Antarctic claim is counted). The United States has 11 when its territories and insular areas are included. One caveat: Russia also has 11 time zones, so the US is tied with Russia for second place rather than being the clear runner-up. The claim's figures are correct, and France and the US do rank first and second-equal, but saying they are 'the two' countries with the most leaves out the tie with Russia.

text: Honeybees are able to fly by using their wings to create electricity through a process known as triboelectrification, allowing them to attract pollen, which aids in the pollination process.
label: contradicted
reason: Research does show that bees pick up a static charge through the triboelectric effect while flying, mostly from friction with the air, and that this charge helps pollen move to them and supports pollination. However, the claim gets the cause backwards. The charge is a side effect of flying. Bees fly because their wing beats generate aerodynamic lift, and electricity plays no part in it. Because the claim says bees fly by using their wings to create electricity, it misstates the mechanism.

text: Plants can make sounds, too - when they're stressed or under attack from insects, some plants release ultrasonic clicks that are beyond human hearing, which can be used to warn nearby plants.
label: not_verifiable
reason: Part of the claim holds up. Khait et al. (Cell, 2023) found that stressed tomato and tobacco plants give off ultrasonic clicks that humans can't hear. However, the stresses tested were drought and stem cutting, not insect attack. The researchers also say they have only shown that plants emit informative sounds. No study has shown that these clicks warn nearby plants, and later work suggests other plants would have trouble hearing them. Because the insect-attack and warning parts can't be verified, the claim as a whole is not confirmed.

text: Honeybees are able to fly by using their wings to generate electricity and create an electrical charge that helps to propel them through the air, along with traditional aerodynamic forces.
label: contradicted
reason: Research on honeybee flight, such as the PNAS study by Altshuler et al. (2005), shows that bees stay aloft through aerodynamic forces alone. They use short, very fast wing strokes (about 240 beats per second) and unsteady mechanisms when the stroke reverses direction. The study concludes that this wing motion is enough to hold up the bee's weight. Bees do pick up a static charge while flying, which helps with things like collecting pollen and sensing flowers. However, no reliable source I know of says this charge is made by the wings or helps push the bee through the air, so the claim's main mechanism is contradicted.

text: Astronauts initially used pencils in space, but later shifted to pens as they are more reliable and don't make a mess, however, today many prefer using digital tools with styluses or just their fingers on touchscreens.
label: not_verifiable
reason: The history part checks out. Several sources, including Wikipedia, ZME Science and pen retailer blogs, say NASA astronauts first used pencils, such as the mechanical pencils on Gemini in 1965. They then switched to the Fisher Space Pen, which NASA ordered for Apollo, because graphite dust, broken tips and shavings could float around, conduct electricity or burn. That fits the claim's 'reliable / no mess' explanation. The last part is not established. Space.com, NASA Watch, AppleInsider and other coverage show that astronauts on the ISS and Crew Dragon do use iPads and tablets. However, no source says that 'many prefer' digital tools with styluses or fingers over pens. The Space Foundation also notes that Fisher Space Pens are still used aboard the ISS. Since the preference claim can't be checked, the overall claim is inconclusive.

text: A chunk of the Dead Sea has been found to be so dense with salt that objects with a density lower than the water can easily float on the surface.
label: supported
reason: Reliable sources say the Dead Sea is extremely salty, roughly 10 times saltier than average ocean water. That salt makes its water very dense, so people and objects less dense than the water float easily. This matches the claim's main point. The phrase "a chunk of the Dead Sea has been found" is oddly worded, but nothing contradicts it: the high salinity and density apply to the sea as a whole.

text: A blue whale's heartbeat can last up to 2 minutes, or about 30 seconds slower than the average human heartbeat, due to the massive size of its heart.
label: contradicted
reason: The claim gets the numbers wrong. Goldbogen's PNAS study, as reported by Newsweek, found that a blue whale's heart rate drops to as low as 2 beats per minute during dives. That means the longest gap between beats is about 30 seconds, not 2 minutes. The claim also doesn't hold together on its own terms: a human heartbeat lasts about 1 second, so a 2-minute beat could not be only "about 30 seconds slower" than a human's.

text: The Axel Erlandson's Tre-fontaine tree, also known as the "circus tree," is a natural wonder consisting of three trunks that were cultivated to unite and eventually fuse into a rare and single, multi-trunked tree.
label: not_verifiable
reason: Reliable sources, including Wikipedia, Gilroy Gardens and Roadside America, confirm that Axel Erlandson shaped and grafted trees, some with several trunks fused together. He showed them at his attraction 'The Tree Circus', and they are now called the 'Circus Trees'. However, none of the sources I found mention a 'Tre-fontaine' tree, or any tree by that name made of three trunks fused into one. The names that do appear include the Basket Tree, the Four-Legged Giant, the Two-Legged Tree/Arch and the Telephone Booth Tree. Calling it a 'natural wonder' is also misleading, because these trees were artificially grafted. Since the specific tree in the claim can't be verified, the claim is inconclusive.

text: Arectangle divided into a square and two equal rectangles, each of which is also divided into two more equal rectangles is a layout called a Harmonic Division and results in a pattern of integral proportions used in painting and composition.
label: not_verifiable
reason: My searches turned up general sources on compositional armatures, rabatment, dynamic symmetry and "harmonic divisions" of the rectangle, including Wikipedia, harmonicarmature.com and art blogs. These show that harmonic proportions and rectangle divisions are used in painting composition. None of them confirms that the specific layout in the claim is called a "Harmonic Division": a square plus two equal rectangles, each split again into two equal rectangles. None says this layout produces a pattern of integral proportions either. A similar construction, a square flanked by two golden rectangles, makes a root-5 rectangle, which is not an integral proportion. That casts some doubt on the claim, but it doesn't clearly contradict it. My search limit ran out before I could check further.

text: Rome is considered to be the second most populous city in the world with over 3,700,000 residents within city limits at its peak, but it is now the most populated city within the Italian Republic with about 2.8 million people.
label: contradicted
reason: The second half of the claim checks out: Rome is Italy's most populous city, with roughly 2.75 to 2.87 million residents. The first half is wrong. I found no source calling Rome the world's second most populous city, and none showing it ever had over 3.7 million people within city limits. At its ancient peak, estimates put Rome at about 1 million people. In modern times its population has stayed under about 2.9 million (2,805,109 in 1981, about 2.88 million in 2017). Sources rank Rome as the third or fourth most populous city in the EU by city-limits population, not second in the world.

text: Scientists estimate that there may be between 700,000 and 1 million species of insects on Earth, but only about 1 million of the estimated 8.7 million total species on the planet have been formally described.
label: contradicted
reason: The insect estimate in the claim is wrong. Stork's 2018 Annual Review of Entomology analysis puts the number of insect species at about 5.5 million, and more than 1 million insect species have already been described. That means a total of 700,000 to 1 million insect species is lower than the number already known. The 8.7 million total-species figure (Mora et al. 2011) is correct, but that paper counts about 1.2 million catalogued species, and other experts put the figure nearer 1.5 to 2 million.

text: Astronauts cannot cry in space because tears do not roll down their faces due to the lack of gravity, instead they tend to gather in their eyes and form a film.
label: contradicted
reason: The second half of the claim is right: without gravity, tears don't run down the face and instead collect in the eye as a ball of water. But the first part, that astronauts "cannot cry" in space, is wrong. Space.com reports that astronaut Chris Hadfield said "Your eyes will definitely cry in space," and explained that the difference is only that the tears don't fall. Astronauts can cry; the tears just stay where they form.

text: QImage, a NASA spacecraft launched in 1983 to study Halley's comet but now deemed an Earth quasi-satellite, has recently made a transition from being a spacecraft to becoming the most stable quasi-satellite Earth has ever known.
label: contradicted
reason: The searches turned up no NASA spacecraft called "QImage"; the name belongs to an image class in the Qt programming toolkit. The spacecraft that studied Halley's Comet (the "Halley Armada") were Giotto, Vega 1 and 2, Suisei, Sakigake and the international ISEE-3/ICE. ICE was the only one with NASA as operator, and it launched in 1978, not 1983. It also went into orbit around the Sun and did not become an Earth quasi-satellite. Earth's known quasi-satellites are natural asteroids such as Kamo'oalewa. The claim's main details, a 1983 NASA Halley probe named QImage that turned into Earth's most stable quasi-satellite, conflict with this record.

text: A Perez Prado song 'Guantanamera', covered by Celia Cruz, became Cuba's second most-recognized song worldwide.
label: contradicted
reason: The claim gets the songwriter wrong. 'Guantanamera' (originally 'Guajira Guantanamera') was written by Joseíto Fernández, not Pérez Prado. It was composed around 1929 and first recorded by Cuarteto Caney in 1938. The 'second most-recognized song' ranking is also unsupported, but the songwriter error alone is enough to contradict the claim.

text: A blue whale can hold up to 2,000 gallons (around 7,500 liters) of krill in its stomach.
label: contradicted
reason: WWF, a trustworthy source, says a blue whale's stomach holds about one ton of krill, while the whale needs about four tons a day. Krill is roughly as dense as water, so one ton works out to about 1,000 liters, or around 265 gallons. The claim's figure of 2,000 gallons (about 7,500 liters, which would be roughly 7.5 tons) is more than seven times that and is also more than the whale's whole daily intake. I didn't find any credible source for the 2,000-gallon figure, though a tool limit cut my search short.

text: A blue whale's heartbeat can last up to 2 minutes, compared to a human's 1 second, allowing the large mammal to conserve oxygen underwater.
label: contradicted
reason: In the first recording of a wild blue whale's heartbeat (Goldbogen et al., 2019, reported by Futurity, CNN, Newsweek and Smithsonian), the heart rate fell to about 2 beats per minute at its lowest during dives. That means roughly 30 seconds between beats, not a heartbeat lasting up to 2 minutes. The slowing does help the whale conserve oxygen, but the 2-minute figure is wrong.

text: A blue whale's heartbeat can last up to 2 minutes, compared to a human's 1 second, allowing the whale to conserve energy while it's underwater.
label: contradicted
reason: Stanford's Goldbogen Lab recorded the first heart rate from a wild blue whale. During dives its heart slowed to a low of 2 beats per minute, which works out to roughly 30 seconds between beats at the most. That is far short of the claimed 2 minutes. The general idea that the heart slows to save oxygen during dives is right, but the 'up to 2 minutes' figure goes against the measured data.

text: A blue whale's heartbeat can last up to 2 minutes, compared to a human's 1 second, allowing the whale to conserve energy while sleeping.
label: contradicted
reason: The only direct measurement of a wild blue whale's heart rate comes from Stanford's Goldbogen Lab (2019). It found the slowest rate was about 2 beats per minute, which works out to roughly 30 seconds between beats. Nothing like a 2-minute heartbeat was recorded. That low rate also happened during deep foraging dives, not during sleep. At the surface the heart beat 25–37 times per minute. So both the 2-minute figure and the link to sleep are contradicted.

text: A blue whale's heartbeat is so loud that scientists claim it can be detected over 500 miles away underwater.
label: contradicted
reason: The search results contradict the claim. NOAA Fisheries, a trustworthy government source, says a blue whale's heartbeat "can be heard 2 miles away," and the Cold Spring Harbor Whaling Museum gives the same 2-mile figure. Nothing found supports a distance of over 500 miles. Distances in the hundreds of miles usually describe blue whale calls (their songs), not heartbeats.

text: A combination lock contains multiple components that must be precisely aligned (usually a correct numerical sequence, letters, or both) for the lock to disengage.
label: supported
reason: Wikipedia says a combination lock is opened by entering a sequence of symbols, usually numbers. It also says the sequence is entered with a rotating dial that works with several discs or cams, or with a set of rotating discs, so the lock has multiple internal parts that must line up. LockWiki and the Britannica and Cambridge dictionaries describe opening the lock with a particular sequence of numbers, letters, or symbols. This fits the claim that several components must be aligned using a correct sequence of numbers, letters, or both before the lock releases.

text: Baby sloths are born with their eyes open and a thin layer of fur, and can even start eating leaves within the first 24 hours of life.
label: contradicted
reason: The part about open eyes is correct: several sources, including Wikipedia and A-Z Animals, say baby sloths are born with their eyes open. The rest of the claim doesn't hold up. Those same sources describe newborns as fully furred or having a full coat of fur, not a thin layer. Nothing I found says they eat leaves within the first 24 hours. Reported ages for first solid food are at least four days (Kiddle/critterbabies), about one week (A-Z Animals, Teach Starter), about 10 days (San Diego Zoo), and 10 weeks to 2 months (Denver Zoo and others).

text: Honeybees are able to recognize human faces and remember them for later encounters, much like some other animals and even primates.
label: supported
reason: A 2005/2006 study led by Adrian Dyer, published in the Journal of Experimental Biology and reported by Phys.org, found that honeybees can learn to recognize human faces in photos and remember them for at least two days. Later studies also showed that bees can tell face-like images apart. The comparison to other animals and primates is a general framing, and nothing in the sources contradicts it. One caveat: the bees were trained with sugar rewards and tested on photographs, not real people in the wild.

text: Humans and dolphins are the only mammals known to give names to themselves and others within their species.
label: contradicted
reason: The claim is out of date. A 2024 study in Nature Ecology & Evolution (Pardo et al.) found that African elephants address each other with individual, name-like calls and respond to calls aimed at them. The researchers say elephants are the first non-human animals known to use names that are not imitations of the other animal's own sound. Separate 2024 research also reported that marmosets use calls directed at specific individuals. So humans and dolphins are not the only mammals known to use names for others in their species.

text: Humans share approximately 50% of their DNA with bananas, highlighting the remarkable similarity between the genetic makeup of humans and many other living organisms.
label: contradicted
reason: The claim is false. Snopes, in a fact-check republished by Yahoo News, rated "Humans share 50% of their DNA with bananas" as False. It calls the idea a long-circulating internet "fact" and says there is no scenario in which the statement could be read as factually true. The figure comes from a mix-up between genes and DNA: some human genes have recognizable counterparts in bananas, but that is not the same as half our DNA sequence being shared. Snopes notes that ortholog-inference methods find at most about 25% of human genes with banana counterparts. Protein-coding genes also make up only about 2% of the human genome. The one source backing the claim, factmyth.com, is a low-reliability site, and a comment on its own page disputes it.

text: Humans share approximately 50% of their DNA with bananas.
label: contradicted
reason: This is a popular myth. Snopes says there is no reading under which humans and bananas sharing 50% of their DNA is factually true. The Naked Scientists also call it a 'mythconception' and note that the only people you share 50% of your DNA with are your parents and children. IFLScience and HowStuffWorks explain where the figure comes from: about 60% of human genes have a recognizable counterpart in the banana genome, and the proteins those genes make are only about 40% similar. That compares genes and proteins, not the full DNA sequence. Most of the human genome does not match banana DNA. Some low-quality sites such as factmyth.com repeat the claim, but they misread this gene comparison.

text: Japan has the world's oldest known hotel, Nishiyama Onsen Keiunkan, which was initially built in 705 AD.
label: supported
reason: CNN reports that Guinness World Records named Nishiyama Onsen Keiunkan in Yamanashi, Japan, the world's oldest hotel in 2011. CNN also says the hotel opened in 705 AD and has operated continuously since then. Guinness World Records has its own 'Oldest hotel' record page for it, which backs this up.

text: Quantum Computing is a speacialized discipline of computing where computation is trasnsacted using.bio"]).
label: not_verifiable
reason: The claim is cut off and garbled. It ends with 'computation is trasnsacted using.bio"]).' and never says what the computation actually uses, so there is no complete statement to check. Sources (an arXiv paper and Telefónica's explainer) confirm the first part: quantum computing is a specialized field of computing that uses quantum-mechanical properties such as superposition and entanglement. The rest of the claim can't be judged true or false.

text: Researchers at the University of California San Diego have trained AI chatbots that revolutionize communication process with people that have a speech or language disorder.
label: not_verifiable
reason: I found no evidence that UC San Diego researchers trained AI chatbots that transform how people with speech or language disorders communicate. Searches only turned up UCSD's toxic-prompt detection research for chatbots, UCSD Health speech therapy services, and AI-for-aphasia studies from other institutions, such as the University of Maryland and studies on ChatGPT's use in aphasia. None of these connects UCSD to the described chatbots, so the claim can't be confirmed or ruled out, and 'revolutionize' is a subjective description that couldn't be verified either way.

text: Sweden has the most islands of any country in the world, with approximately 221,800 islands along its coast.
label: supported
reason: Several sources say Sweden has the most islands of any country. A 2005 peer-reviewed fact sheet in Geografiska Annaler (via Taylor & Francis) gives a count 'as high as 221 800,' and WorldAtlas says Sweden has about 221,831 islands, so the approximate figure checks out. Two caveats apply: Statistics Sweden's newer 2013 count is higher at 267,570, and that total includes lake and river islands, not just coastal ones. These caveats concern the wording rather than the main facts, so the claim's central points are supported.

text: Turtles have an innate navigational ability, allowing some species to migrate thousands of miles each year and still return to the exact beach where they were born.
label: supported
reason: Reliable sources back the main points of the claim. The Smithsonian Ocean Portal says female sea turtles migrate thousands of miles, sometimes back to the same beach where they were born, and that they use an inborn magnetic sense to navigate. UNC and ScienceDaily report research showing that hatchlings imprint on the magnetic signature of their natal beach and later use it to return. Wikipedia notes that sea turtles can migrate up to 10,000 miles or more per year. One caveat: the sources describe a return to the natal beach or 'same stretch of coastline', and say it happens 'sometimes'. Also, females usually nest every few years rather than every year. Still, the claim's core statements are consistent with the evidence.

text: Zebras are born with brown and white stripes, which only turn black and white after a period of about two weeks.
label: contradicted
reason: The sources agree that zebra foals are born with brown and white stripes, but none support the claim that the stripes turn black after about two weeks. The Denver Zoo says the stripes turn black by about one year of age. Biologyinsights.com puts the change at 9 to 18 months, and other sources say it happens gradually as the foal grows to full size. That is far longer than two weeks.

text: Honeybees are able to fly by using their wings to generate electricity and create a difference in air pressure above and below their wings, allowing them to lift and propel themselves through the air.
label: contradicted
reason: The claim is wrong about how honeybees fly. Research in PNAS (Altshuler et al. 2005, Caltech) shows that honeybees stay aloft through aerodynamics. They beat their wings very fast, about 230 times per second, in short strokes of roughly 90°. This creates unsteady airflow, including leading-edge vortices and lift peaks when the wing changes direction. Bees do pick up electrostatic charge, but it plays no part in lift or propulsion. The pressure-difference part of the claim is broadly true, but saying the wings generate electricity to produce it is false.

text: Galileo Galilei was the first person to observe the planet Neptune, but he didn't recognize it as a planet, instead documenting it as a star, in 1613.
label: supported
reason: Galileo's drawings show he saw Neptune in December 1612 and again in January 1613, when it was near Jupiter. Both times he recorded it as a fixed star rather than a planet. Neptune wasn't officially discovered until 1846, and Galileo's sightings are considered the earliest recorded ones. Two caveats: his first sighting was actually December 28, 1612, so the claim's 1613 date only covers the January observations. Also, Astronomy.com says he only 'may have been' the first to see it, and some evidence suggests he noticed it moving. Still, the main points of the claim match the sources.

text: Bees are able to fly by using electricity generated from their wing movements and the surrounding air, helping to create an electric charge which contributes to their ability to defy gravity.
label: contradicted
reason: Bees do pick up a small positive static charge as they fly, mostly from friction with the air. Research shows this charge helps them attract pollen and sense the electric fields of flowers, not fly. Peer-reviewed aerodynamic studies (Altshuler et al., PNAS, Caltech) and Nature explain that bees get their lift from aerodynamic forces: short-amplitude, high-frequency wing strokes, leading-edge vortices, rotational lift and wake recapture. No credible source says the electric charge helps bees overcome gravity, so the claim's main mechanism is wrong.

text: Dragonflies have been in existence for over 300 million years, with some of the oldest known fossils dating back to the Paleozoic Era.
label: supported
reason: Several sources say dragonflies and their close ancestors go back more than 300 million years. Fossils of large dragonfly ancestors about 325 million years old have been found in Upper Carboniferous rocks, and the Carboniferous is part of the Paleozoic Era. One caveat: the oldest of these fossils are early relatives such as Protodonata or griffinflies, not modern dragonflies. Popular and educational sources still treat them as early dragonflies, so the claim holds up.

text: Researchers at the University of California San Diego have trained AI chatbots that revolutionize communication for individuals with severe speech or language disorders, allowing them to interact more easily with others.
label: not_verifiable
reason: I found no evidence that UC San Diego researchers trained AI chatbots that transform communication for people with severe speech or language disorders. The UCSD results I found were about unrelated chatbot work: detecting toxic prompts, a medical triage chatbot, and the TritonGPT campus assistant. Other AI-for-speech projects I found came from UTS, the University of Maryland, Cambridge, Vienna, and UCSF/UC Berkeley, not UCSD. Nothing directly contradicts the claim, but nothing supports it either. I ran out of searches before I could try more queries.

text: Japan has a vending machine for everything, from live crabs to umbrellas, with over 5.5 million vending machines across the country.
label: contradicted
reason: Japan's actual vending machine count doesn't match the claim. The Japan Vending System Manufacturers Association (JVMA) reports about 3.93 million machines at the end of 2023, and the 2022 figure was 3.97 million. The 5.6 million figure was the peak in 2000, and the number has fallen steadily since then. So "over 5.5 million" is outdated and wrong today. Live-crab vending machines are also best documented in China (a 2010 machine at a Nanjing station), not Japan. A few blogs, such as Bokksu, still repeat the 5.5 million figure, but Yano Research and the JVMA data are more reliable sources.

text: A-type main-sequence stars, also known as A stars, are among the brightest and most massive stars in the universe, with lifespans of approximately 100 million to 1 billion years.
label: contradicted
reason: Wikipedia calls A-type main-sequence stars a "class of moderate-large main-sequence star" with a mass range of only about 1.6 to 2.3 solar masses. O-type stars, B-type stars and supergiants are far more massive and luminous, so A stars are not among the brightest and most massive stars in the universe. The lifespan range in the claim is roughly in line with known A-star ages; for example, an A0 star 317 million years old is described as about 40% through its main-sequence life. Still, the main part of the claim about mass and brightness is false.

text: Aolphin calves are born with a temporary, waxy layer coating their bodies, called lanugo, that helps insulate them for their first few weeks of life.
label: contradicted
reason: Dolphin calves are not born with a waxy, insulating lanugo coat. Dolphins Plus, a dolphin facility whose marine biologists provide the information, says newborn calves have only a few hairs on their rostrum (beak). These fall out soon after birth, are thought to be an evolutionary leftover from land-dwelling ancestors, and aren't needed for warmth because dolphins rely on blubber. The claim also gets the term wrong: lanugo is fine body hair, not a waxy layer (the waxy coating on newborns is called vernix). There is no evidence of an insulating layer that lasts for the first few weeks.

text: High-speed camera footage revealed that a mantis shrimp can accelerate its claws at the speed of a .22 caliber bullet, reaching speeds of up to 46 mph (74 kph) in just 0.01 seconds.
label: contradicted
reason: Patek's 2004 high-speed footage did show that a mantis shrimp's strike accelerates like a .22-caliber bullet, so that part holds up. The numbers in the claim do not. National Geographic and Discover put the club's speed at about 50 mph, and other reports give 23 m/s, which is about 51 mph or 83 km/h. Wikipedia lists strikes as fast as about 68 mph (110 km/h) for some species. These figures conflict with the claim's maximum of 46 mph (74 kph). The timing is also off: reports say the whole strike takes about 3 milliseconds, not 0.01 seconds. I found no reliable source that gives 46 mph in 0.01 seconds.

text: A single strand of spaghetti is not strong enough to support its own weight and will snap under its own tension when it reaches a certain length, known as the "spaghetti length."
label: contradicted
reason: Hanging materials do have a maximum length before they break under their own weight, and that applies to spaghetti too. But the claim gets the name wrong and overstates the point. In Randall Munroe's What If? 2, the engineering term for this limit is the "free-hanging length," a ratio of a material's tensile strength, density and gravity. No source calls it the "spaghetti length." The claim also says a single strand is "not strong enough to support its own weight," yet strands of ordinary length hold their own weight without trouble. They only break past a material-dependent critical length. Because the named term appears to be made up and the framing is wrong, the claim is contradicted.

text: A blue whale can hold up to 500 gallons of krill and small fish in its stomach at one time.
label: contradicted
reason: WWF and A-Z Animals say a blue whale's stomach holds about one ton of krill, or roughly 2,200 lb. That is about 1,000 litres, or roughly 260 US gallons. The claim's figure of 500 gallons is about twice that. Answers.com, a less reliable source, gives about 200 gallons (760 L) for a large whale's stomach, which also falls well short of 500. Blue whales also eat almost only krill, not small fish. No source I found supports 500 gallons. However, none of the reliable sources states the capacity in gallons, so this verdict depends on my volume conversion.

text: A blue whale's heart can beat as loud as 188 decibels, louder than a jet engine taking off.
label: contradicted
reason: Reliable sources such as the Monterey Bay Aquarium put the 188-decibel figure on blue whale calls, not on the heartbeat. Several sources say the calls are louder than a jet engine (about 140 dB). Sources that talk about the heartbeat only say it can supposedly be detected about 2 miles away, and none give it 188 dB. The claim takes the vocalization figure and wrongly applies it to the heart.

text: A blue whale's heart can pump over 5,000 gallons of blood through its body with every beat.
label: contradicted
reason: NOAA Fisheries says a blue whale's heart pumps about 60 gallons of blood with each beat. That is nowhere near the 5,000+ gallons per beat in the claim.

text: A blue whale's heartbeat is so loud that it can be detected from over 500 miles away, and is louder than any other animal sound.
label: contradicted
reason: NOAA Fisheries and other sources say a blue whale's heartbeat can be heard about 2 miles away, not over 500 miles. Even the 2-mile figure is disputed. Blue whale calls can travel hundreds of miles, and sperm whale clicks are generally considered the loudest animal sounds. The heartbeat is not the loudest animal sound.

text: A oku, or hundred trillion in Japanese counting system, is a 1 followed by 28 zeros, which is 100 times larger than an American quadrillion.
label: contradicted
reason: Several Japanese dictionaries and learning sites (JapanDict, Nihongo Master, JapanesePod101, JLPT Sensei) define 億 (oku) as 10^8, which is one hundred million, or a 1 followed by 8 zeros. It is not a hundred trillion, and it does not have 28 zeros. The math in the claim is also wrong on its own terms: a 1 followed by 28 zeros (10^28) is 10^13 times an American quadrillion (10^15), not 100 times.

text: Astronauts cannot cry in the classical sense in space due to the lack of gravity, which prevents tears from falling down their faces.
label: supported
reason: Several sources, including Space.com's coverage of Chris Hadfield's demonstration, ScienceABC and Futurism, say that in microgravity the eyes still make tears but the tears do not fall. Instead they stick to the eye as a liquid ball. Futurism even concludes that astronauts 'technically can't cry.' This fits the claim's wording 'cannot cry in the classical sense': astronauts can still produce tears, but the usual sight of tears running down the face doesn't happen without gravity.

text: Beehive-shaped structures in Mexico, known as "sweat houses," have been discovered to date back over 2,000 years.
label: not_verifiable
reason: My searches didn't turn up any report of beehive-shaped "sweat houses" found in Mexico and dated to more than 2,000 years ago, and the search limit was reached before I could look further. What I did find is related but doesn't confirm the claim. Reports from Smithsonian, Archaeology magazine and Gizmodo describe a 14th-century temazcal (steam bath) in Mexico City, which is only about 600–700 years old and isn't described as beehive-shaped. A Penn Museum bulletin covers Maya sweat baths in general. A paper on Chechem Ha cave links sweat baths to the Late Preclassic period (around 120 BC), but that site is in Belize, not Mexico. A Cambridge paper describes a clay beehive dated around 100 BC–AD 250, but it's an actual beehive for keeping bees, not a sweat house. None of this confirms the claim, and none of it clearly contradicts it either.

text: Black bears are excellent climbers and have been known to climb trees to escape danger, protect themselves from extreme weather, and even hibernate in tree cavities.
label: supported
reason: Wildlife agencies and extension services back each part of the claim. The Vermont Fish & Wildlife and University of Missouri Extension pages say black bears are built for climbing and go up trees to escape danger. The North Shore Black Bear Society says climbing is their instinctive retreat and that bears shelter from summer heat in the tree canopy. The University of Arkansas Extension says bears in bottomland hardwood habitats den in raised tree cavities to escape seasonal flooding, which also counts as protection from harsh conditions. One less authoritative site says adult bears don't usually den in trees, but that only means tree dens are uncommon, not that they never happen, so it doesn't contradict the claim. The weather part is backed less directly than the rest: the sources mention escaping summer heat and avoiding floods by denning in tree cavities, not extreme weather in general.

text: Blind people who have never seen often develop heightened senses of smell and hearing due to the brain reorganizing itself in a process known as neuroplasticity.
label: supported
reason: A 2017 study led by Massachusetts Eye and Ear (published in PLOS ONE and reported by ScienceDaily and others) found that the brains of people born blind form new connections when they get no visual input. The press release says this produces compensatory abilities, including a heightened sense of hearing, smell and touch, and calls it structural and functional neuroplasticity. Other peer-reviewed work, such as a 2015 PMC study, also reports better olfactory abilities in people blind from birth. Some research finds the smell advantage less consistent than the hearing one, but the claim's hedged wording ('often') fits the evidence.

text: Chocolate syrup was originally invented by Milton Hershey in 1894 as a topping for ice cream, but it eventually became popular for other desserts.
label: contradicted
reason: Milton Hershey did not invent chocolate syrup in 1894. The Hershey Community Archives says the Hershey Chocolate Company did not start making and selling chocolate syrup until 1926. Even then it was sold to commercial users, mainly for soda fountain drinks, not as an ice cream topping. Smithsonian Magazine also dates Hershey's syrup to 1926 and describes chocolate syrup as having earlier roots in medicine, so Hershey was not its original inventor.

text: Dragonflies have been around for a remarkable 300 million years, with fossils dating back to the Paleozoic era.
label: supported
reason: Britannica says odonates have an unusually long fossil record, with ancestors dating back more than 300 million years to the Late Carboniferous, which is part of the Paleozoic era. NatureNorth likewise describes Carboniferous fossils of early dragonflies that are over 300 million years old. One caveat: these early fossils are dragonfly ancestors (protodonates and griffinflies such as Meganeura), not modern dragonflies. Popular usage commonly counts them as dragonflies, though, so the claim holds up.

text: Honeybees are able to fly by using their wings to generate electricity through a process called piezoelectricity, as well as using muscle power.
label: contradicted
reason: Reliable sources, including ASU's Ask A Biologist and beekeeping and biology sites, say honeybees fly by flapping their wings with flight muscles. The wingbeats are fast and the wings rotate and twist to create lift. None of these sources mentions piezoelectricity as part of bee flight. Bees can pick up an electrostatic charge from friction (triboelectric charging), but that charge does not power or lift them. The claim that bees generate electricity with their wings to fly therefore goes against the accepted explanation of how they fly.

text: Honeybees are able to fly by utilizing electricity generated from the interaction of their bodies and the air around them, not just through traditional muscular movements.
label: contradicted
reason: The sources say honeybees pick up a positive static charge while flying, through contact with charged air molecules and friction from their wing beats. The charge is a byproduct of flight, not a power source. It helps pollen stick to bees and lets them sense the electric fields of flowers. No source says electricity powers or helps bee flight; bees fly by beating their wings with their flight muscles. So the claim gets cause and effect backwards.

text: In New York City, there is a secretly located apartment in the New York Public Library,dımatically designed to accommodate the library's superintendent.
label: supported
reason: Several sources describe a little-known apartment inside the New York Public Library's main building on Fifth Avenue (the Schwarzman Building). It had eight rooms and was built so the building's superintendent could live there and deal with problems at any hour. Superintendent John Fedeler lived there with his family from 1911 to 1941. One caveat: the apartment is no longer lived in and has been turned over to other library uses, so it would be more accurate to say there 'was' such an apartment. The main point of the claim still holds.

text: Qatar is scheduled to host the 2030 Asian Games, making it the third time in 15 years that Qatar would be hosting the games.
label: contradicted
reason: Doha, Qatar is confirmed as host of the 2030 Asian Games. However, Qatar has hosted the Asian Games only once before, in Doha in 2006. That makes 2030 the second time, not the third, and the two editions are 24 years apart, not within 15 years. Wikipedia's 'Doha Asian Games' disambiguation page lists only the 2006 and 2030 Games.

text: Qatar is scheduled to host the 2030 Asian Games, making it the third time in 17 years the country will host the event.
label: contradicted
reason: Qatar (Doha) is set to host the 2030 Asian Games, but reliable sources such as The Peninsula Qatar and Inside the Games say it will be the second time, not the third. Doha's only previous Asian Games was in 2006, 24 years before 2030, so the claim of 'the third time in 17 years' is wrong on both counts.

text: Robots and artificial intelligence have been used to study and mimic the intricate movements of animals, ranging from hummingbirds in flight to the complex swarm behavior of insects.
label: supported
reason: Purdue University researchers built hummingbird-like flying robots trained with machine-learning algorithms to copy the bird's flight (reported by EurekAlert and Futurity). Swarm robotics also draws on social insects: for example, Harvard's termite-inspired robots (covered by National Geographic and CNN) and work modeled on ants and bees. Together these sources back both parts of the claim.

text: Robots and artificial intelligence have been used to study and mimic the intricate movements of animals, ranging from hummingbirds in flight to walking spiders.
label: supported
reason: Several reliable sources back both examples in the claim. Purdue University built a hummingbird-like robot that uses machine learning (AI) to mimic the bird's flight (ScienceDaily, Tech Briefs, Futurity). For spiders, Festo made BionicWheelBot, which copies a spider that can both walk and roll (TechXplore), and Fraunhofer built the eight-legged Arachno-Bot, with joints modelled on spider legs. Other projects have also built spider-inspired legged robots that use evolved walking algorithms. Together, these show that robots and AI have been used to study and imitate animal movement, from hummingbird flight to walking spiders.

text: уванніTarantulas have been around for a long time, with fossil records showing they existed at least 120 million years ago, during the Cretaceous period.
label: contradicted
reason: The claim gets the age roughly right but credits the wrong evidence. Tarantulas probably did originate about 120 million years ago in the Cretaceous, but that date comes from molecular-clock (transcriptome) studies, not from fossils. Live Science reports that only two tarantula fossils are known, both in amber: one about 16 million years old from Mexico and one about 100 million years old from Myanmar. Wiley's Journal of Biogeography and related papers also name the roughly 100-million-year-old Burmese amber specimen as the oldest tarantula fossil. No fossil shows tarantulas existed at least 120 million years ago. (The stray 'уванні' at the start of the claim was ignored.)

text: The Axel Erlandson's Circus Trees, located in Santa Cruz, California, is a collection of bent and grafted trees created by the Swedish farmer Axel Erlandson between 1925 and 1957.
label: contradicted
reason: The claim gets the location wrong. Erlandson was a Swedish-born farmer who began shaping trees around 1925, but his Tree Circus was in Scotts Valley, not the city of Santa Cruz. Scotts Valley is in Santa Cruz County, and the trees were moved to Gilroy Gardens in Gilroy, California, in 1985, where they are today. The 1925–1957 span is also not supported. 1957 is the year of a Life magazine article about the trees, not the end of his work: the attraction opened in 1946–47 and he kept it going until close to his death in 1964.

text: Wentworth Wooden Puzzles, established in 1994, introduced a product that was the first to allow users to personalize and create their own jigsaw puzzles.
label: not_verifiable
reason: Part of the claim checks out, but the main part can't be verified. Wikipedia, LinkedIn, Made in Britain and thejigasaurus.com all say Kevin Wentworth Preston founded the Wentworth Wooden Jigsaw Company in 1994, with production starting in September 1994. However, the company's own website now says it was founded in 1991, so the founding year itself is disputed. Several sources confirm that Wentworth offers personalised puzzles, where customers can upload their own photos and choose whimsy pieces. None of the sources I found say Wentworth was the first company to let people personalise or create their own jigsaw puzzles. That 'first' claim is unverified.

text: A blue whale's heartbeat can be as low as 2 beats per minute when the whale is deep in the ocean, allowing it to conserve energy while diving.
label: supported
reason: Newsweek and Live Science both report a 2019 Stanford study, the first to record a blue whale's heartbeat. It found the heart rate can drop as low as two beats per minute at the deepest point of a dive. The slowdown, part of the diving reflex, helps the whale save oxygen and energy so it can stay underwater longer on a single breath.

text: A day on Venus is actually longer than its year, lasting 243 Earth days while its orbital period is just 225 Earth days.
label: supported
reason: NASA Science says a day on Venus lasts 243 Earth days, which is "longer even than a Venus year" of 225 Earth days. That matches every part of the claim. One caveat: the 243-day figure is Venus's sidereal day (one full spin relative to the stars). Its solar day is about 117 Earth days, but the claim reflects the standard way this fact is stated.

text: Apronicious clouds, a rare atmospheric phenomenon, are formed when a meteor punches a hole through a layer of clouds.
label: not_verifiable
reason: I found no trustworthy source that mentions "Apronicious clouds." A search for the term returned only general Wikipedia pages about cloud types, so it seems to have no real referent and may be made up. The closest real phenomenon is the hole-punch cloud (fallstreak hole or cavum). NASA, EarthSky and Wikipedia say these form when aircraft fly through layers of supercooled cloud, not when meteors pass through. Because the main term can't be verified, the claim is inconclusive. The meteor explanation also doesn't match how the related real phenomenon forms.

text: Astronauts in space cannot cry in the same way they do on Earth because the microgravity environment prevents tears from falling.
label: supported
reason: Space.com reports Chris Hadfield's demonstration on the ISS. He showed that your eyes still produce tears in space, but they don't fall. In microgravity the tears gather into a ball of water on the eye. On Earth, tears run down the face only because of gravity. This matches the claim that crying in space is not the same as on Earth because tears can't fall. ScienceABC says the same thing: astronauts can cry, but the tears don't fall.

text: Babies are born without kneecaps, which do not develop and harden into bone until they are around three to five years old.
label: contradicted
reason: The age range is right, but the main premise is wrong. HowStuffWorks says babies do have kneecaps at birth. They are made of cartilage, which is why they don't show up on X-rays. That cartilage then hardens into bone, becoming a fully bony patella by about age 3 to 5. So the claim that babies are "born without kneecaps" is a common myth.

text: Giraffes are the only animals born with their eyes open, this helps them to quickly respond and protect themselves from predators.
label: contradicted
reason: The claim says giraffes are the only animals born with their eyes open, and that is false. Many animals are born with their eyes open. Oxford Reference defines precocial young mammals as born with eyes and ears open and lists cattle, sheep and horses as examples. Merriam-Webster notes that hares are born fully furred with their eyes open. Wikipedia says most ungulates are precocial. Giraffes may be born with open eyes, but they are not the only ones.

text: Japan has a vending machine for everything, from umbrellas and underwear to live crabs and pizza, with over 5.5 million machines across the country.
label: contradicted
reason: The machine count in the claim is wrong. Yano Research, citing the Japan Vending System Manufacturers Association, reported that Japan had 3,969,500 vending machines and automated service machines at the end of 2022. That is below 4 million, and the end-2023 figure was expected to be about 3.94 million. Other sources also give about 3.93 million. The 'over 5.5 million' figure is outdated: it matches the count from around the early 2000s, not today. The claim that there are machines selling unusual items like umbrellas and crabs may be true, but the number contradicts current data.

text: Ocean waves can travel at speeds of up to 35 miles per hour, with the longest waves able to travel thousands of miles without losing much energy.
label: contradicted
reason: The second half of the claim holds up. Scripps and other sources say swells can travel thousands of miles with little energy loss, and the longest-period waves travel fastest. The 'up to 35 mph' limit is wrong, though. About 35 mph (30 knots) is only the group speed of a 20-second wind swell, according to Surfertoday. Individual crests of such swells move about twice as fast. Tsunamis are also ocean waves, and they cross the deep ocean at about 500–600 mph, according to Scripps and National Geographic. So ocean waves can go far faster than 35 mph, which contradicts the claim's top speed.

text: Ocean waves can travel at speeds of up to 35 miles per hour, with the longest waves sometimes spanning over 1,700 miles.
label: contradicted
reason: The speed limit in the claim is wrong. The NOAA/NWS Tsunami Warning Center (tsunami.gov) says tsunamis in the deep ocean can travel at over 500 mph, so ocean waves are not limited to 35 mph. A Miracosta oceanography text gives wind-wave speeds of 10 to 75 mph. The 35 mph number seems to come from a non-authoritative site (bikehike.org) describing only near-shore surf waves. The wavelength figure is also unsupported. Tsunami wavelengths are about 125 miles, wind waves and swells are a few hundred to about 2,600 feet, and Guinness lists tides as the longest at about 7,500 miles. No source I found supports 1,700 miles as the size of the longest waves.

text: Polar bears are excellent swimmers and have been known to swim for hours or even days at a time, covering distances of up to 60 miles or more without resting.
label: supported
reason: National Geographic and the Deseret News (reporting a USGS study) say a female polar bear swam for nine days straight without a break and covered 426 miles (687 km). That record backs every part of the claim: polar bears are strong swimmers, they can swim for hours or days, and they can cover 60 miles or more without resting. Polar bears have also been spotted as far as 65 miles offshore.

text: Turtles have an innate navigational system that allows them to migrate thousands of miles across oceans and return to the exact beach where they hatched.
label: supported
reason: Reliable sources (a Current Biology study reported by Cell Press/EurekAlert and ScienceDaily, plus UNC and Wikipedia) say sea turtles migrate hundreds to thousands of miles and come back to nest at the beaches where they hatched. They find their way using an inborn magnetic sense, imprinting on the magnetic signature of their home coast. Two caveats: the claim says 'turtles' when the evidence is about sea turtles, and some sources say turtles return to the same stretch of coastline, not always the exact beach. Overall, the evidence supports the claim.

text: Tweeting birds and specifically, the Northern Cardinal, are known for complex songs with up to 24 variations and some even up to 200 different song variations.
label: contradicted
reason: Popular sources such as NRCM and Birds & Blooms say Northern Cardinals sing "more than 24 different songs." That makes the claim's "up to 24" a misstatement, since those sources give 24 as a minimum, not a maximum. The "200" figure in the same NRCM source is about how often males sing: during the breeding season they may sing 200 or more songs per hour. It is not a count of 200 different song variations. Scientific sources point to much smaller repertoires: individual males use 8–21 syllable types (Birds of the World, Halkin & Linville), and a University of Cincinnati study found a maximum of about 9 song types per bird. No source credits cardinals with 200 song variations. The 200-song figure turned up only in an anecdotal comment about mockingbirds.

text: Bacteria have been found to thrive in even the most inhospitable locations, including the freezing cold temperatures of Antarctica and the scorching hot temperatures of deep-sea hydrothermal vents.
label: supported
reason: Reliable sources back both parts of the claim. Wikipedia's Extremophile article reports bacteria living in a lake buried under Antarctic ice. A review on PubMed Central (PMC4187170) says extremophiles, including bacteria, form microbial mats "from Antarctic ice to continental hot springs" and thrive in extremely hot niches. Other sources describe extremophiles living at scorching deep-sea hydrothermal vents as well as in polar ice. No source found contradicts the claim.

text: Scientists estimate that there are approximately 8.7 million identified species on Earth, but the total number, including those that have not been discovered, is believed to be around 30 million.
label: contradicted
reason: The claim mixes up two numbers. The 8.7 million figure comes from Mora et al. (2011, PLoS Biology), and it is an estimate of all species on Earth, including undiscovered ones. Only about 1.2 to 2 million species have actually been identified and described. The claim calls 8.7 million the identified count and gives about 30 million as the total, which misstates the main scientific estimate.

text: British Airways has a 747 jet with the smallest pilot staff as low as 3 plus 3 cabin on a B747  a British Airways short small variation the B747-200, a business jet variant often referred to as the 747-200C.
label: contradicted
reason: The 747-200C is the convertible version of the 747-200, not a business jet. It could be set up to carry all cargo, all passengers, or a mix of both. It was not a short or small variant either; it was a full-size jumbo jet. British Airways' 747s were standard models such as the 747-136 and 747-236B, and there is no evidence that BA flew a 747-200C business-jet version. The 747-200 did have a three-person flight deck (captain, first officer and flight engineer), but a crew of just 3 cabin staff on a BA airliner is not supported by any source.

text: Plants can make sounds, such as clicking, as a response to their environment and as a way to communicate with each other and even other species.
label: supported
reason: The sources back each part of the claim. Tel Aviv University research published in Cell (2023) recorded ultrasonic clicking sounds from plants under stress, such as dehydration or being cut, so the sounds are a response to their environment. Gagliano et al. (Trends in Plant Science) recorded clicking from corn roots and was reported as evidence that plants communicate with each other through sound. A later Tel Aviv University study found that female moths pick up these plant distress sounds and avoid laying eggs on stressed plants, which the researchers describe as the first evidence of acoustic communication between plants and animals. One caveat: the idea that plants communicate with each other by sound is still more tentative than the evidence that they make sounds at all.

text: Astronauts can't cry in the same way on Earth because the microgravity environment of space prevents tears from falling and flowing in the same manner.
label: supported
reason: Space.com reports Chris Hadfield's demonstration: tears only run down the face on Earth because of gravity, so in microgravity they don't fall. Instead, surface tension holds them in a liquid ball on the eye. ScienceABC and Futurism say the same thing. The claim's wording is a little awkward, but it means that astronauts can't cry in space the way they do on Earth because tears don't fall or flow in microgravity, and the sources back that up.

text: Tarantulas have been around for a long time, with the earliest known tarantula fossil dating back to the Cretaceous period, around 100 million years ago.
label: supported
reason: Peer-reviewed studies in PeerJ (Foley et al. 2021) and the Journal of Biogeography (2023) say the oldest known tarantula (Theraphosidae) fossil comes from Burmese amber dated to about 100 million years ago, which is in the Cretaceous (Wunderlich & Müller, 2020). One hobbyist site (birdspiders.ch) instead names a Miocene Dominican amber specimen as the earliest. That site is outdated and less reliable than the peer-reviewed literature. The PeerJ paper also notes that the Burmese fossil cannot be firmly placed on the tarantula family tree, but it still treats it as a tarantula fossil.

text: Mathematicians used a combination of over 13 billion computational hours and approximately 6,000 processors at the University of California, Los Angeles, to verify a mathematical equation known as the Kepler Conjecture, also called the Hales-Ferguson proof, showing an 18-sided and 12-sided solid optimally stacking
label: contradicted
reason: The proof of the Kepler conjecture (Hales and Ferguson, 1998), which says the face-centred cubic 'cannonball' packing of equal spheres is the densest, was formally verified by Hales's Flyspeck project. The authoritative paper (Hales et al., arXiv 1501.02155, published by Cambridge) says checking the nonlinear inequalities took about 5,000 processor-hours on the Microsoft Azure cloud, plus a second check of about 9,370 processor-hours. That is nowhere near 13 billion hours, and the work was not done on about 6,000 processors at UCLA. The conjecture is also about stacking spheres, not about 18-sided and 12-sided solids.

text: France and the United States share the only international border that is to the north and south poles, due to their claims to the region surrounding the geographic North Pole known as the Arctic France or French Guiana and the North and South Poles region being within the Coastal pollution virgin islands near populations that belong, do the coast lines
label: contradicted
reason: Most of this claim is garbled nonsense, and the parts that can be checked are false. France has no claim to the area around the geographic North Pole, and there is no place called 'Arctic France.' French Guiana is a French overseas department in South America, near the equator. The Arctic Ocean around the North Pole is governed by UNCLOS, and the only countries with Arctic coastlines are Canada, Russia, the US, Norway and Denmark (through Greenland). Antarctica is governed by the Antarctic Treaty, which freezes territorial claims. France claims Adélie Land there, but the US makes no claim. So France and the US do not share any border at or near either pole. Their real maritime borders are in the Caribbean (for example, between Saint Martin/Saint Barthélemy and the US Virgin Islands and Puerto Rico) and off Saint Pierre and Miquelon. These are not polar borders. The rest of the claim ('Coastal pollution virgin islands near populations that belong, do the coast lines') is incoherent and can't be checked.

text: Owens Falls Dam, completed in 1931 on the Idaho side but worked by Portland, Oregon is one of the biggest Hydroelectric dams in the world's 5,141 hydroelectric facility industry (per/wiki list in 2021).
label: contradicted
reason: The claim is false. Britannica says the Owen Falls Dam, now called the Nalubaale Dam, is on the Victoria Nile at Jinja, Uganda, and was completed in 1954. It is not on the Idaho side, it was not completed in 1931, and it is not run from Portland, Oregon. It is also a fairly modest dam, about 31 m high, so it is not one of the world's biggest hydroelectric dams.

text: Honeybees are able to fly by using their wings to create electricity through a process known as triboelectrification, and they are also able to collect the pollen from flowers which becomes the honey.
label: contradicted
reason: Bees do pick up static charge through triboelectrification while flying, but the charge comes from flight. It doesn't power flight, which works by aerodynamic lift. So the claim gets cause and effect backwards. The claim also says the pollen bees collect becomes honey. The National Honey Board says honey is made from flower nectar, not pollen, and any pollen in honey gets there by accident.

text: Plants can make sounds, and researchers have found that some plants release clicking or popping sounds when stressed or damaged, which can even warn other nearby plants of potential threats.
label: not_verifiable
reason: The first part of the claim checks out.
