A 2023 Tel Aviv University study published in Cell found that tomato and tobacco plants give off ultrasonic clicks or pops when they are dehydrated or their stems are cut (Science News, ScienceAlert, Asian Scientist). The part saying these sounds can warn nearby plants of threats has not been shown, though. The researchers said they had 'shown only that plants emit informative sounds.' They added that whether other plants or insects respond to the sounds is still being studied, so the warning idea remains speculation.

text: A chunk of the Dead Sea has been found to be so dense with salt that objects can be suspended in it, allowing people to effortlessly float on its surface.
label: supported
reason: The American Museum of Natural History (AMNH) says the Dead Sea is almost six times saltier than the ocean. Because the human body is less dense than its water, people "can float in it effortlessly." An ocean-sciences education resource (JPL Aquarius workshop) also says the Dead Sea's high salinity makes its water very dense, so people float easily. The claim's wording about "a chunk" of the sea is odd, but the main point — the water is dense enough with salt to hold objects and people up so they float easily — is well documented.

text: One flex of a human eyebrow contains from around 110,000 to 210,000 individual hairs, which work together to allow a single eyebrow to form more than 10,000 unique expressions.
label: contradicted
reason: Several sources, including Bosley as cited by pleijsalon, put the average eyebrow at about 250 hairs. Even never-plucked brows only reach around 1,100 hairs. The claimed 110,000 to 210,000 hairs is off by orders of magnitude and is closer to the number of hairs on a whole scalp. I didn't check the figure of more than 10,000 expressions, but that doesn't matter because the hair count is clearly wrong. The sources aren't top-tier, but they agree with each other and with well-known figures.

text: Jellyfish have been to space: in 1991, NASA sent 2,000 moon jellyfish to space aboard the Columbia space shuttle to study their development in zero gravity.
label: contradicted
reason: Most of the claim checks out. In June 1991, NASA's STS-40 mission (SLS-1) aboard Space Shuttle Columbia carried moon jellyfish (Aurelia aurita) to study how weightlessness affects their development. The number is wrong, though. Sources say 2,478 polyps were launched, roughly 2,500, not 2,000. They also say the population grew to nearly 60,000 during the flight.

text: Bees are able to fly by using electricity produced from the movement of their wings, which helps them to stay aloft while foraging for pollen, rather than generating lift solely through muscular power.
label: contradicted
reason: Reliable sources, including ASU's Ask A Biologist and beekeeping science explainers, say bees fly by using powerful flight muscles in the thorax to beat their wings rapidly, and those wingbeats create aerodynamic lift. Bees do pick up static charge in flight, which can help pollen stick to them, but no source says electricity powers their flight or keeps them in the air. The idea that bees fly using electricity instead of muscle-driven lift contradicts the established explanation.

text: Scientists estimate that there are approximately 8.7 million identified species on Earth, but this number only represents a small fraction of the estimated total 30 million species on the planet.
label: contradicted
reason: The 8.7 million figure (Mora et al., 2011) is scientists' estimate of the total number of species on Earth, not the number already identified. The same study estimates that about 86% of land species and 91% of ocean species have not yet been discovered or described. Only around 1.2 million species have actually been catalogued. The claim treats 8.7 million as the identified count and adds a 30 million total that the study does not give, so it gets the core facts wrong.

text: Bacteria have been found to thrive in even the most inhospitable locations, including the freezing cold temperatures of Antarctica and the extremely high temperatures surrounding deep-sea hydrothermal vents.
label: supported
reason: Reliable sources back both parts of the claim. A review on PMC (NCBI) says extremophiles, bacteria among them, live everywhere from hydrothermal vents at 122 °C to sea water frozen at −20 °C. A ChemRxiv paper names the frozen deserts of Antarctica and scorching hydrothermal vents as places where extremophiles thrive. LCO's astrobiology resource notes that researchers were surprised to find bacteria thriving in deep-sea vents despite the extreme heat and pressure. NOAA also describes organisms thriving at hydrothermal vents. None of the results contradict the claim.

text: Citadel, a medieval walled city, located in the old city of Derinkuyu, Turkey, is home to an extensive network of underground tunnels and rooms, accommodating up to 20,000 people.
label: not_verifiable
reason: Discovery.com confirms part of the claim: Derinkuyu in Turkey is an ancient underground city with many levels of tunnels and rooms, large enough for about 20,000 people. The rest of the claim doesn't hold up. I found no source describing a 'Citadel' that is a medieval walled city in an 'old city of Derinkuyu.' Derinkuyu is known as an underground city cut into volcanic tuff, not a walled citadel. Because 'Citadel' has no clear referent and that part can't be verified, the claim as a whole is inconclusive.

text: Caterpillars can eat up to 27,000 times their body weight in a single day, which is equivalent to a human eating about 46,000 pizzas.
label: contradicted
reason: The claim's timeframe is wrong. A Naked Scientists article says caterpillars eat about 27,000 times their body weight over the roughly four weeks they spend as caterpillars, not in a single day. That article compares this to a person eating 68 cows, and I found no source for the '46,000 pizzas' figure. Because the 27,000-times amount applies to the whole larval stage, saying it happens in one day contradicts the evidence.

text: A chunk of the Dead Sea has been found to be so dense with salt that objects can unexpectedly float in it, due to its elevated density.
label: supported
reason: NOAA's JetStream page on the Dead Sea backs up the main point of the claim. It says the Dead Sea's surface water is about 5–9 times saltier than the ocean, and that below about 100 m the water is saturated with salt. It also says the high salinity makes the water denser, so objects in it are more buoyant and people can simply lie back and float. Some of the claim's wording is odd ('a chunk', 'unexpectedly'), but the central idea, that the Dead Sea is so salty and dense that things float in it, is well documented and nothing in the sources contradicts it.

text: Scientists estimate that there are approximately 8.7 million identified species on Earth, but the total number of species, including those that have not been discovered, is likely between 10 and 30 million.
label: contradicted
reason: The claim gets the 8.7 million figure wrong. In the 2011 PLoS Biology paper by Mora et al., 8.7 million is the estimated total number of species on Earth, including undiscovered ones. It is not the number already identified. Only about 1.2 to 2 million species have actually been described, so most of the 8.7 million are still unknown.

text: Tarantulas have been around for a long time, with the oldest known tarantula fossil dating back to the Cretaceous period, over 100 million years ago.
label: supported
reason: A 2023 tarantula biogeography study in the Journal of Biogeography (Wiley) says the oldest known theraphosid (tarantula) fossil is from Burmese amber and is about 100 million years old (Wunderlich & Müller, 2020). That places it in the Cretaceous and supports the claim. Older sources say tarantula fossils were known only from Eocene–Miocene amber, but the Cretaceous find is newer and replaces that view. The claim's wording 'over 100 million years ago' is slightly loose, because the fossil is dated to roughly 100 million years (Burmese amber is usually put at about 99 million years).

text: Plants can make sounds, such as clicking, to communicate and warn other plants about potential threats, such as insect attacks, but these sounds are in the ultrasonic range and inaudible to humans.
label: not_verifiable
reason: Part of the claim holds up, but the main point can't be confirmed. A 2023 study in Cell by Khait et al. found that stressed tomato and tobacco plants make ultrasonic clicking or popping sounds that humans can't hear. Those plants were stressed by drought or by having their stems cut, not by insect attacks. The researchers did not show that plants use these sounds to communicate or to warn other plants. Science News quotes them saying they've shown only that plants emit informative sounds. ScienceAlert reports that whether other plants sense and respond to the sounds is still unknown. Most likely the clicks are a physical side effect: water columns inside the plant snap under strain (cavitation). The purpose stated in the claim, communicating and warning about insect attacks, is unverified rather than proven false.

text: A partitions of the Mandelbrot set can form the swirling patterns familiar to most, however using an alternative equation Maple it seems the partition produced looks more like a giant squid.
label: not_verifiable
reason: I couldn't find anything confirming that an alternative equation in Maple produces a Mandelbrot partition that looks like a giant squid. The only relevant result I found was a 2008 jwz.org blog post. In its comments, a reader jokingly calls a fractal image a 'Giant Fractal Squid', and another says the image looks more like a Julia set than the Mandelbrot set. That post doesn't mention Maple or an alternative equation. My search tool hit its usage limit after this one query, so I couldn't look any further. The claim is also vaguely worded and doesn't say what 'Maple' or 'partition' refers to. The search results neither support nor contradict it.

text: Lower Antarctica is home to several unique lakes that remain frozen for the majority of the year, with Lake Vida holding the record for the coldest and saltiest of these lakes.
label: contradicted
reason: Lake Vida in Antarctica's McMurdo Dry Valleys does have very cold brine. DRI calls it the coldest, most stable cryo-environment on Earth, at about −13°C. But the claim that it is the saltiest of these lakes is wrong. Lake Vida's brine is about six times saltier than seawater. Don Juan Pond, in the same Dry Valleys, has about 40–44% salinity and is widely described as the saltiest body of water in Antarctica, and possibly on Earth. Two smaller problems: 'Lower Antarctica' is not a standard geographic term, and Lake Vida's ice cover is permanent, not just present for most of the year.

text: France and Spain both claim to be the birthplace of the first restaurant, 'auberge,' with the French claiming it was in the 1760s and the Spanish stating it was earlier in the 1520s.
label: contradicted
reason: Part of the claim is right: France dates the first modern restaurant to the 1760s, specifically Boulanger's in Paris in 1765. The Spanish part is wrong. Spain's claim rests on Sobrino de Botín in Madrid, which opened in 1725, not the 1520s. Guinness World Records lists it as the world's oldest restaurant. Neither claim is about an 'auberge' either. That French word means an inn, and it was not the name of the first restaurant in either country.

text: Honeybees are able to fly by using their wings to generate lift and thrust, but also utilize their body hair to trap a boundary layer of air close to their body and gain additional lift and thrust.
label: not_verifiable
reason: The first part of the claim holds up: honeybees fly by flapping their wings to produce lift and thrust, which is well documented in insect flight research. I found no reliable source for the second part, that body hair traps a boundary layer of air to give extra lift and thrust. Sources on bee hair describe other jobs, such as collecting pollen, keeping warm, grooming and sensing air movement or electric fields. Nachtigall's study of honeybee trunk aerodynamics found that lift from the body (not the wings) is only a few percent of body weight in fast flight, and it credits that to body shape, banking and the legs, not to hair. The evidence doesn't directly rule out the hair mechanism, but nothing supports it, so this part of the claim can't be verified.

text: Honeybees are able to fly by using electricity generated from the movement of their wings, which helps attract pollen and increase the bees' overall flying efficiency.
label: contradicted
reason: Bees do not fly using electricity. Their flight comes from the aerodynamic lift produced by their wing beats. Research does show that bees pick up a static (mostly positive) charge while flying, mainly through friction with the air, and that this charge helps pollen move between flowers and bees without direct contact. None of the sources say this charge powers flight or improves flight efficiency. So the pollen part is partly supported, but the main claim that bees fly using electricity from their wing movement is wrong.

text: Caterpillars can eat up to 27,000 times their body weight in a single day, which is equivalent to a human eating around 49,000 pizzas.
label: contradicted
reason: Several sources, including The Naked Scientists and a 13abc science segment, give the 27,000-times-body-weight figure for a caterpillar's whole larval stage of about 3–4 weeks, not for a single day. One low-quality page (a statustest.amherst.edu page) says "in a single day," but it doesn't look like a credible source. The more trustworthy sources contradict the daily timeframe. None of the results supports the 49,000-pizza comparison.

text: Scientists estimate that there are approximately 8.7 million identified species on Earth, but the actual number could be significantly higher, with some estimates ranging up to 30 million.
label: contradicted
reason: The claim treats 8.7 million as the number of species that have already been identified. That is wrong. The figure comes from Mora et al. (2011, PLoS Biology), and it is an estimate of all eukaryotic species on Earth, give or take 1.3 million. Only about 1.2 million species had actually been described and catalogued at the time, including about 953,000 animals. The claim that the true number could be higher, up to 30 million, is plausible, since earlier estimates ranged from 3 million to 100 million. But the core statement about 8.7 million identified species is false.

text: Galileo Galilei was the first person to observe the planet Neptune, but he didn't recognize it as a planet, instead mistaking it for a star in 1613.
label: supported
reason: Wikipedia's article on the discovery of Neptune says Galileo's drawings show he observed Neptune on December 28, 1612, and again on January 27, 1613. Both times he mistook it for a fixed star near Jupiter, which is why he isn't credited with discovering it. His observations are generally treated as the earliest recorded sightings of Neptune. One detail is imprecise: the claim dates the mistake to 1613, but his first sighting was in late December 1612. He did also misidentify it in January 1613, though, so the claim still holds overall.

text: Scientists estimate that there are approximately 8.7 million identified species on Earth, but the total number of existing species is believed to be much higher, with estimates ranging from 10 million to 30 million.
label: contradicted
reason: The claim gets the 8.7 million figure wrong. That number, from Mora et al. (2011), is the estimated total number of species on Earth (give or take 1.3 million). It is not a count of identified species. Only about 1.2 to 2 million species have actually been described and catalogued. Calling 8.7 million 'identified' therefore contradicts the source.

text: Galileo Galilei was the first person to observe the planet Neptune, but he didn't recognize it as a planet, instead recording it as a star in 1613.
label: supported
reason: Wikipedia's 'Discovery of Neptune' article says Galileo's drawings show he saw Neptune on December 28, 1612, and again on January 27, 1613. Both times he mistook it for a fixed star while it sat close to Jupiter, which is why he isn't credited with discovering it. These are the earliest known sightings of Neptune, so he is generally treated as the first to observe it, though 'first' means first on record. He did record it as a star in January 1613, so that date fits, even though his first sighting was in late 1612. The same article notes some evidence that he saw the 'star' had moved, but he still never identified it as a planet.

text: Owens Falls Dam, completed in 1931 on the Idaho side but worked by Portland, Oregon is one of the biggest Hydroelectric dams in the world's power generation in terms of percentage at about 21% per water.
label: contradicted
reason: The Owen Falls Dam, now called the Nalubaale Dam, is on the Victoria Nile at Jinja in Uganda. It was finished in 1954, not 1931. It has nothing to do with Idaho or Portland, Oregon. It is also a fairly small dam, not one of the world's biggest hydroelectric producers, and the claim's '21% per water' figure doesn't make sense.

text: A fossilized sea lizard discovered in the Yucatan Peninsula in Mexico was found to have a large block of amber lodged in its stomach, containing what is now the only known example of a mammal hair trapped in amber that dates back to the time of the dinosaurs.
label: contradicted
reason: I found no trustworthy report of a fossil sea lizard from the Yucatan with amber containing mammal hair in its stomach. Peer-reviewed studies directly contradict the claim that such hair would be the only known example from the age of dinosaurs. A 2010 paper in Naturwissenschaften (Springer) describes two mammal hairs in roughly 100-million-year-old Early Cretaceous amber from France. A 2020 paper in Scientific Reports describes hair strands in Early Cretaceous amber from Spain. The amber finds from Mexico that did turn up are unrelated, such as a 23-million-year-old lizard preserved in amber.

text: Honeybees are able to fly by using electricity generated by their bodies to electrostatically charge the tiny hairs on their bodies, creating a natural force that aids in their lift-off and overall flight capabilities.
label: contradicted
reason: Research from Caltech (Dickson, Altshuler, Dickinson and colleagues) shows that honeybees fly by aerodynamics. They beat their wings in short, very fast strokes, which creates leading-edge vortices and unsteady lift. Bees do pick up an electrostatic charge on their bodies, mostly from friction with the air in flight, but studies (e.g., Clarke et al. 2013 in Science, and Quanta's coverage of electrostatic ecology) tie that charge to collecting pollen and sensing the electric fields around flowers, not to lift. No credible source says static charge on bee hairs helps them take off or fly.

text: A blue whale's heartbeat can be as loud as 188 decibels, louder than a jet engine, which is approximately 140 decibels.
label: contradicted
reason: WWF says blue whale calls (their vocalizations) reach 188 decibels, compared with 140 decibels for a jet. That figure is about their calls, not their heartbeat. So the claim takes a real vocalization statistic and wrongly attaches it to the heartbeat. WWF mentions the heart only to compare its size to a Volkswagen Beetle, and gives no heartbeat volume.

text: A blue whale's heartbeat can be detected from over two miles (about 3.2 kilometers) away due to its unique physiological features.
label: supported
reason: NOAA Fisheries, a trustworthy government source, says a blue whale's heartbeat "can be heard 2 miles away." It ties this to the whale's very large heart, which weighs about 400 pounds and pumps about 60 gallons of blood per beat. That covers the claim's reference to physiological features. The Cold Spring Harbor Whaling Museum and several fact sites also say the heartbeat can be detected from 2 miles away. Two caveats: these sources give "2 miles" rather than "over two miles," and some commenters note that detection at that range would need instruments such as sonar. Neither point contradicts the claim's main assertion. I found no strong, reliable rebuttal; the only disagreement came from user-generated Q&A sites like Brainly, which gave conflicting answers.

text: A plug of superheated, pressurized water can shoot out of a metal bottle if it is shaken and then opened.
label: supported
reason: The sources I found back up the main idea, though none uses the exact wording 'a plug of superheated, pressurized water' or says 'metal bottle' outright. A guide on shaker bottles says that shaking hot liquid in a sealed container builds steam pressure. That pressure can force the lid open and cause an explosive spray of hot liquid that can burn skin. Forum and Q&A posts about Thermos and Stanley flasks say that shaking hot water in a sealed flask raises the internal pressure, and several users report lids popping off and spraying hot water. Wikipedia's 'Superheating' article says that disturbing superheated water can cause a dangerous eruption of hot water and burns. My searches were cut off by a tool limit before I could find a source matching the exact wording. Taken together, the evidence supports the claim and none of it contradicts it.

text: A plug of superheated, pressurized water can shoot out of a metal bottle if it is shaken vigorously while being heated.
label: not_verifiable
reason: I couldn't find a source describing this situation: a metal bottle shaken hard while being heated, with a plug of superheated, pressurized water shooting out. Wikipedia's Superheating article says water can superheat in an undisturbed container. It also says that when that water is disturbed, part of it flashes to steam and can spray boiling water out. That backs the general idea that disturbed superheated water can erupt. But the claim's specific conditions don't match. Shaking while heating would usually prevent superheating rather than cause it, and no source covered the metal-bottle or 'plug' details. Some of the claim is plausible, but the specific scenario is neither confirmed nor clearly ruled out. My search budget ran out before I could look further.

text: A set of human lungs, after being removed from the body and inflated, can float on water due to the air inside.
label: supported
reason: Several sources describe the lung float (hydrostatic) test, which is based on the principle that lungs filled with air float in water while lungs without air sink. These include Wikipedia's article on the test and forensic and medical literature hosted by the BU Law Review, the Unpad medical journal and NCBI/PMC. Aerated or inflated lungs therefore float because of the air inside them, which matches the claim.

text: All mammals, except for humans and a small number of other primates and marine mammals, have a cloaca: an opening used for reproduction, digestion, and excretion.
label: contradicted
reason: The claim has it backwards. Most mammals, including nearly all placental mammals, do not have a cloaca. They have separate openings for the anus and the urogenital tract. Wikipedia's Cloaca article says that apart from a few exceptions, mammals have no cloaca. The main exception is the monotremes (egg-laying mammals such as the platypus), which have a true cloaca, and some marsupials also show a cloaca-like arrangement. The cloaca is not a general mammalian trait that only humans, a few primates and marine mammals lack.

text: Bacteria have been found in almost every habitat on Earth, including extreme environments such as deep-sea vents and radioactive waste sites.
label: supported
reason: Wikipedia's Bacteria article says bacteria "are present in most of its habitats" and lists radioactive waste and the deep biosphere among them. Britannica says bacteria have been found in extreme environments, including the hot hydrothermal vents of the seafloor, and have "evolved to live in every habitat on Earth." A Springer review also describes diverse bacterial communities at radioactive waste repositories. Together these support every part of the claim, and no source contradicts it.

text: Firefighters use Dalmatians to clear a path and keep the horses calm when they used horse-drawn carriages.
label: supported
reason: FireRescue1, a fire-service publication, says Dalmatians ran alongside horse-drawn fire apparatus, barked to clear pedestrians from the road and stayed with the horses at fire scenes to keep them calm. The claim says firefighters "use" the dogs, but this was a historical practice. It ended when motorized trucks replaced horse-drawn engines.

text: Galileo Galilei was the first person to observe the planet Neptune, but he didn't discover it as he initially thought it was just a star.
label: supported
reason: Wikipedia's article on the discovery of Neptune says Galileo's drawings show he observed Neptune on December 28, 1612 and January 27, 1613. Both times he mistook it for a fixed star, which is why he is not credited with discovering it. Scientific American also says he first observed it in 1612 and thought it was a fixed star, and other sources call him the first person to see Neptune. Wikipedia adds that Galileo may later have noticed the 'star' seemed to move. That detail fits the claim's word 'initially' and does not contradict it.

text: Galileo Galilei was the first person to observe the planet Neptune, but he didn't discover it as it was initially thought to be a fixed star.
label: supported
reason: Reliable sources back the claim. Wikipedia and NASA say Galileo observed Neptune in December 1612 and January 1613 and recorded it as a fixed star. Scientific American and Astronomy.com add that this was centuries before it was recognized as a planet in 1846. One caveat: Galileo is the first person known to have observed Neptune, as most sources word it. That does not prove nobody saw it earlier, but it matches the claim as normally stated.

text: Honeybees are able to fly by using electricity generated by the movement of their wings, which creates an electric charge that helps them beat their wings faster and more efficiently.
label: contradicted
reason: Scientific studies, such as Altshuler et al. in PNAS, show that honeybee flight works through aerodynamics and muscle power. Bees beat their wings in short, fast strokes (about 90° at around 230 Hz), and their flight muscles drive the wings. This creates lift through effects at the end of each stroke, rotation of the wing, and vortices along the leading edge. Bees do pick up static charge, but no reputable source says electricity from wing movement powers their flight or makes their wingbeats faster or more efficient. The established mechanism contradicts the claim.

text: In 2019, the world's largest living organism was discovered in a Western Australia forest, covering over 2,200 acres, identified as a massive Armillaria ostoyae fungus.
label: contradicted
reason: The record-holding Armillaria ostoyae, often called the "Humongous Fungus" and listed by Guinness as the largest living organism, is in the Malheur National Forest in Oregon, USA, not in Western Australia. It covers about 2,385 acres (965 hectares). It was identified in the late 1990s, not in 2019. The claim gets the location and the date wrong. It seems to blend this fungus with a different 2022 finding: a giant seagrass (Posidonia australis) in Shark Bay, Western Australia.

text: In the United States, the shortest war was between the United States and the Seminole Indians lasting nine hours.
label: contradicted
reason: Reliable sources such as Britannica, Wikipedia and the Seminole County museum say the Seminole Wars were among the longest US conflicts, not the shortest. The three wars ran from roughly 1816/1817 to 1858, and the Second Seminole War alone lasted from 1835 to 1842. Britannica calls it the longest of the wars of Indian removal. No source describes any US–Seminole war as lasting nine hours. The war usually cited as the shortest in history is the Anglo-Zanzibar War of 1896, which lasted about 40 minutes.

text: Jellyfish have been to space; in 1991, NASA launched a shuttle with 2,000 jellyfish aboard to study their behavior in zero gravity.
label: supported
reason: Reliable sources confirm that on 5 June 1991, NASA launched Space Shuttle Columbia on mission STS-40 (Spacelab Life Sciences 1) carrying 2,478 moon jellyfish polyps. Researchers wanted to see how microgravity affects the jellyfish's development, how they sense gravity, and how they swim. So jellyfish have been to space, and the year, agency and shuttle are correct. The claim's figure of '2,000' is a rounded-down version of the real 2,478 (more than 2,000), and 'study their behavior' is a simplified description of the research. Neither detail contradicts the sources.

text: Many species of jellyfish are biologically immortal, meaning they can transform their bodies into a younger state through a process called transdifferentiation.
label: contradicted
reason: The sources say this ability is rare, not common. A genome study of Turritopsis dohrnii on PMC/NCBI says that most jellyfish species do not show life-cycle reversion. It says only a couple of hydromedusan species, mainly T. dohrnii and one close relative, can repeatedly rejuvenate. The Scientist also reports that a related species, Turritopsis rubra, is not biologically immortal. Transdifferentiation is the right name for the process, but saying that "many species" of jellyfish are biologically immortal goes against the evidence.

text: Owens Falls Dam, in Kenya, was the world's first major dam to incorporate a fish ladder designed to allow fish to migrate upstream.
label: contradicted
reason: The claim gets the country wrong. Owen Falls Dam (often written "Owens Falls"), now called Nalubaale Power Station, is at Jinja in Uganda, not Kenya. Wikipedia, Britannica and the University of Wisconsin–Milwaukee photo archive all place it in Uganda. None of the sources I checked mention a fish ladder or describe it as the world's first major dam to have one, and fish ladders were in use well before the dam was finished in 1954. The location is clearly wrong, so the claim is contradicted.

text: Polar bears are excellent swimmers, and they have been known to swim for hours or even days at a time in search of food or shelter.
label: supported
reason: National Geographic reports that polar bears make long-distance swims. One female swam for a record nine days straight, covering 426 miles, and another swam for more than 12 days. These swims happen as bears travel between sea ice and land, which they need for hunting and resting. This supports the claim that polar bears are strong swimmers that can swim for hours or even days at a time.

text: Polar bears are excellent swimmers, with some individuals known to swim for hours or even days at a time, covering distances of up to 60 miles without rest.
label: contradicted
reason: Polar bears are strong swimmers, and some swim for days. The problem is the claim's limit of "up to 60 miles." San Diego Zoo Wildlife Alliance says polar bears have swum "more than 60 miles" without rest. National Geographic, Live Science, UPI and Deseret News all report a GPS-tracked female that swam nonstop for nine days and covered 426 miles (687 km). That tracking data shows 60 miles is a low figure, not the maximum, so the distance part of the claim is wrong.

text: Researchers at Stanford University successfully created the first mouse with a computer chip in its brain.
label: not_verifiable
reason: I found no trustworthy source saying Stanford researchers created the "first" mouse with a computer chip in its brain. Stanford has published related work: a 2020 device that connects silicon microwires to the brain, and a wireless optogenetic implant tested in mice. Neither is described as a first mouse with a brain chip. The searches also turned up unrelated Stanford work on mice with human neurons and Neuralink's human implants. Electronic brain implants in rodents almost certainly predate the Stanford work, which makes the "first" part doubtful. Still, I found no source that directly rules it out, so the claim can't be confirmed or refuted.

text: Robots can't dance according to human evaluation standards due to the distinct lack of self-expression and fluid movement within their mechanical responses.
label: contradicted
reason: The claim says robots can't dance by human standards, but reputable outlets say otherwise. CNN, CBS/AP, Smithsonian and Boston Dynamics itself report that the Atlas, Spot and Handle robots danced fluidly to "Do You Love Me?" in a widely praised viral video. CNN wrote that the robots "can boogie down better than most humans." That evidence goes against the claim's sweeping statement that robots can't dance and lack fluid movement. No reliable source found supports the claim.

text: Roses arranged in a particular pattern and left in a vase for a long time can ferment and create an alcoholic drink, often referred to as "rose wine".
label: contradicted
reason: There's no evidence that roses arranged in a pattern and left in a vase ferment into a drink called "rose wine." The drink known as rosé wine is made from red grapes. Winemakers take only part of the colour from the grape skins and ferment the juice on purpose. Roses play no part. Homemade rose-petal wines do exist, but they are made deliberately with added sugar and yeast. Flowers rotting in vase water don't produce them, and how the roses are arranged makes no difference.

text: Scientists believe that there are approximately 8.7 million identified species on Earth, but the estimated total number, including undiscovered species, is around 30 million.
label: contradicted
reason: The 8.7 million figure (Mora et al., 2011, PLOS Biology) estimates the total number of eukaryotic species on Earth, including undiscovered ones. It is not a count of identified species. Only about 1.2 million species had been catalogued, and the authors suggest that around 86% of land species and 91% of ocean species have not been described yet. The claim wrongly treats 8.7 million as the identified count, and its 30 million figure is not the scientists' estimate of the total in that study.

text: Scientists estimate that there are approximately 8.7 million identified species on Earth, but this number only represents a small fraction of the total number thought to exist.
label: contradicted
reason: The 8.7 million figure (Mora et al., 2011, PLoS Biology) is an estimate of all species thought to exist on Earth, not the number already identified. Only about 1.2 to 2 million species have actually been described. So the claim gets it wrong when it calls 8.7 million the identified count.

text: Snails are able to sleep for up to 3 years in a state of dormancy called 'estivation' during periods of extreme drought or heat.
label: supported
reason: Several sources say that some land snails can stay dormant in estivation for up to three years when it is too hot or dry. These include A-Z Animals, Tuft & Needle, Lovet and NapLab. One less reliable site gives a much lower figure (79 days), but the widely reported 'up to 3 years' figure for estivation in drought or heat matches the claim. Note that the 3-year figure applies to some species in extreme cases, not to all snails.

text: Spiders have been on Earth for over 300 million years, with the oldest known spider fossils dating back to the Devonian period.
label: contradicted
reason: The first part of the claim holds up: true spiders have been around for more than 300 million years. The second part is outdated. Attercopus fimbriunguis, a Devonian fossil about 386 million years old, was once called the oldest spider. The scientists who first described it later reclassified it as a silk-making relative of spiders, not a true spider. Wikipedia and Smithsonian both say the oldest known true spiders come from the Carboniferous period (roughly 300–315 million years ago), not the Devonian.

text: The largest snowflake ever recorded fell in Montana, USA, in 1887, and it measured an astonishing 15 inches in diameter and 8 inches thick.
label: supported
reason: Several sources, including Guinness World Records as cited by Mystic Stamp, say the largest snowflake on record was reported at Fort Keogh, Montana, on January 28, 1887. It was said to be 15 inches wide and 8 inches thick. That matches every detail of the claim. The report came from a rancher and was never scientifically verified, but it is still the recognised record, which is what the claim states.

text: Turtles have an innate navigational system that allows them to migrate thousands of miles across oceans and return to the exact beach where they were born.
label: supported
reason: Reliable sources back the claim for sea turtles specifically, though not for turtles in general. National Geographic and a Current Biology study by Brothers & Lohmann report that sea turtles such as loggerheads make migrations of thousands of miles. They also say the turtles use an inborn magnetic sense and imprint on their birth beach's magnetic field to return there and nest. National Geographic says the turtles go back to the 'exact spot' where they hatched. Some sources describe the return more loosely: scientific papers call it the 'same stretch of coastline,' and one source says turtles return to approximately, 'not usually exactly,' the same place. Even so, the main claim matches the mainstream scientific account.

text: Wombat burrows typically have just one underground entrance and can extend up to 20 meters in length.
label: contradicted
reason: The length is roughly right: Wikipedia gives common wombat tunnels as 2–20 m long, and an SA government source says burrows can be more than 20 m (NSW says up to 30 m). The claim that burrows typically have just one entrance is wrong, though. Wikipedia says common wombat burrows have many side tunnels and 'often more than one entrance,' and Toronto Zoo says southern hairy-nosed wombat burrows can have up to 23 entrances. I found no source saying burrows typically have one entrance.

text: In the heart of the Amazon rainforest, there's a unique species of jellyfish called the Turritopsis dohrnii, also known as the "immortal jellyfish," which has a remarkable ability to transform its body into a younger state through a process called transdifferentiation.
label: contradicted
reason: Turritopsis dohrnii is called the "immortal jellyfish," and it can revert to a younger stage through transdifferentiation, so that part is correct. But it is a marine species. Sources place it in the Mediterranean Sea and the waters around Japan, and the genus lives in the world's oceans. It does not live in the Amazon rainforest, so the location in the claim is wrong.

text: A誉咲き (Yūrei-zakura), a 2,000-year-old weeping cherry blossom tree, is located in Japan and is said to be one of the oldest and most sacred trees in the world.
label: contradicted
reason: Japan's roughly 2,000-year-old weeping cherry, an Edo-higan cherry, is the Jindai-zakura (Yamataka Jindai Zakura) at Jisso-ji Temple in Hokuto, Yamanashi. It is described as possibly the oldest cherry tree in Japan and one of the Three Great Cherry Trees. The searches turned up no record of a 2,000-year-old tree called 'Yūrei-zakura' or '誉咲き'. The kanji 誉咲き don't match the reading 'Yūrei-zakura' either, since yūrei means 'ghost', usually written 幽霊. The claim gives the wrong name for this tree. Its 'oldest and most sacred trees in the world' description is also stronger than the sources' 'possibly oldest cherry in Japan'.

text: Blind people often develop a heightened sense of echolocation and hearing to compensate for their lack of vision, allowing them to navigate through obstacles more effectively.
label: supported
reason: A PLOS ONE study (Kolarik et al., 2017) found that blind participants navigated around obstacles using sound faster, more fluidly and more accurately than sighted participants. The authors say this fits the hypothesis that people with severe visual loss develop better hearing to compensate. Other research also links blind people's use of echolocation to easier mobility. The study notes that echolocation skill varies a lot from person to person, but that does not contradict the claim's hedged word "often."

text: Scientists estimate that there may be between 700,000 and 1 million distinct species of insects that exist on Earth, although only about 1 million out of an estimated 8.7 million total species have been formally described and named so far.
label: contradicted
reason: The insect numbers in the claim are far too low. Scientists usually put the number of insect species at about 5.5 million (Stork 2018), with other estimates ranging from about 2 to 30 million. Around 1 million insect species have already been named, so a total of 700,000 to 1 million cannot be right. The claim also says about 1 million of the estimated 8.7 million species on Earth have been described, but the usual figure is 1.2 to 1.5 million, and insects alone make up more than half of that.

text: A-type main-sequence stars, also known as A stars, are among the brightest and most massive stars in the universe, with lifespans of approximately 100 million to a billion years.
label: contradicted
reason: A-type main-sequence stars have only about 1.6 to 2.4 solar masses, so they are not among the most massive or brightest stars in the universe. O- and B-type stars are much more massive and luminous. Their main-sequence lifetimes are also longer than the claim says: about 0.7 billion years for a 2.4-solar-mass star and about 2.2 billion years for a 1.6-solar-mass star, not 100 million to 1 billion years.

text: France and the United States are the only countries in the world where the Mississippi River and the Seine River do not act as international boundaries.
label: contradicted
reason: The claim doesn't hold up logically. The Mississippi flows entirely within the United States (it rises in Minnesota and empties into the Gulf of Mexico). The Seine flows entirely within France (from Burgundy to the English Channel at Le Havre). Neither river forms an international boundary anywhere, so no country uses either one as a border. Saying France and the US are the 'only' countries where these rivers aren't international boundaries wrongly implies they are boundaries elsewhere.

text: France and Spain both claim to be the birthplace of the first restaurant, 'auberge,' with the French claiming Procope's established in 1686 was the first one.
label: contradicted
reason: Sources describe Café Procope, founded in Paris in 1686, as France's first café and the oldest café in Paris, not as the 'first restaurant' or an 'auberge.' In French tradition, the first restaurant is usually credited to Boulanger's establishment around 1765, and 'auberge' means an inn, not the first restaurant. Spain's claim refers to Sobrino de Botín in Madrid, founded in 1725, which Guinness recognises as the world's oldest restaurant still operating. That is a different kind of claim from being the birthplace of the first restaurant. Because the claim misdescribes what Procope is and what France claims, it is contradicted.

text: A誉咲き (Yūrei-zakura), a 2,000-year-old weeping cherry blossom tree is located in the cemetery of the Kiyota ward in the Hanshin region of Japan
label: contradicted
reason: The sources show that Japan's well-known roughly 2,000-year-old weeping cherry (an Edo-higan/itosakura tree) is the Jindai-zakura, also called Yamataka Jindai Sakura. It stands on the grounds of Jissō-ji temple in Hokuto, Yamanashi Prefecture. It is not called 'Yūrei-zakura' and is not in a cemetery in a 'Kiyota ward' in the Hanshin region. Kiyota Ward is actually in Sapporo, Hokkaido, not in Hanshin. The claimed name, 誉咲き, also doesn't match the reading 'Yūrei-zakura'. No source supports a tree like this in Hanshin, so the claim's details conflict with the documented location of Japan's 2,000-year-old cherry.

text: Space is filled with a mysterious type of sound known as the "Oh-My-God Particle" that is made up of extremely high-energy cosmic rays which are still not fully understood by scientists.
label: contradicted
reason: The "Oh-My-God particle" is not a sound, and space is not filled with it. It was one ultra-high-energy cosmic ray, probably a proton, detected in Utah on 15 October 1991 with about 300 million TeV of energy. The claim is right that scientists still don't know where it came from. But calling it a mysterious sound that fills space, and saying it is made up of many cosmic rays, is wrong. It was a single particle detection.

text: Scientists estimate that there are approximately 8.7 million identified species on Earth, but the total number of species, including those that are not discovered or documented, is believed to be much higher.
label: contradicted
reason: The 8.7 million figure is wrong for what the claim says. It comes from Mora et al. (2011, PLoS Biology), which estimates the total number of species on Earth, including undiscovered ones. It is not a count of identified species. The same study says only about 1.2 million species had been catalogued, and that roughly 86% of species on land and 91% in the oceans have not yet been described. So the claim mixes up the estimated total with the number already identified.

text: Schedule 1 of the Indian Constitution initially listed 29 states, but that number has since increased to 28, then to 29 and set back to 28 and now has 28 and increased now to the 29th- formerly the number became 28 with  rejoining and has now become formally as
label: not_verifiable
reason: I can't verify this claim because it is garbled and cut off: it ends with "has now become formally as" and never states a final number. Some sources do say the 1950 Constitution grouped the states into Parts A, B, C and D with 29 in total (Vedantu), but the 1950 count varies by source. India has 28 states today. The claim's sequence of changes (from 29 "increased" to 28, then 29, then back to 28, then to a 29th) does not match the documented history of state reorganisation and makes no sense as written. Since the claim is incoherent and incomplete, it cannot be judged as supported or contradicted.

text: A blue whale's heartbeat can be as slow as 4-8 beats per minute when it is in a state of relaxation.
label: contradicted
reason: Stanford's report on the 2019 Goldbogen study, which made the first recording of a blue whale's heart rate, found that the heart slowed to an average minimum of about 4–8 beats per minute while the whale was diving, with a low of 2 beats per minute. The 4–8 bpm figure therefore describes the diving reflex during foraging dives, not a state of relaxation. The rate also went lower than 4–8 bpm, so 'as slow as 4–8' understates the minimum. Newsweek reports the same findings, and also notes a maximum of 37 bpm when the whale surfaced after deep dives.

text: A day on the planet Venus is longer than a year on Venus, with a day lasting approximately 243 Earth days and a year lasting approximately 225 Earth days.
label: supported
reason: NASA's Venus facts page says a Venus "day" (one full rotation) lasts 243 Earth days, which is longer than a Venus year of about 225 Earth days. WorldAtlas gives the same figures. One caveat: the solar day on Venus (from one sunrise to the next) is only about 117 Earth days. The claim's 243-day figure is the rotation period, which is how NASA describes a Venus day, so the claim holds.

text: A veutric, an eversion of a sphere turning itself inside out consists of 14 movements within this full inversion impeccability
label: not_verifiable
reason: I couldn't find any source that uses the term "veutric" for sphere eversion. Searching for it only turned up an unrelated e-bike brand (Velotric), so the term has no clear referent. Reliable sources such as Wolfram MathWorld and Wikipedia describe sphere eversion as turning a sphere inside out through a regular homotopy. None of the results I found say an eversion has exactly 14 movements, and the phrase "full inversion impeccability" doesn't match any known concept. The basic idea of a sphere turning itself inside out is accurate, but the specific claims can't be verified.

text: Astronauts cannot actually cry in space because the microgravity prevents tears from flowing downwards and out of the eyes.
label: contradicted
reason: Space.com reports that astronaut Chris Hadfield showed astronauts do cry in space. In his words, "Your eyes will definitely cry in space," but the tears don't fall. Instead they collect in a ball of water on the eye. Microgravity only changes how tears behave. It doesn't stop astronauts from crying, so the claim that they "cannot actually cry" is false.

text: Astronauts' footprints on the moon can remain intact for millions of years due to the lunar surface's vacuum-like environment.
label: supported
reason: Several sources agree with the claim. In his Starts With A Bang column on Medium, astrophysicist Ethan Siegel concludes that astronaut footprints and rover tracks "will likely persist for millions of years in most instances." Space Daily and Little Astronomy say the same and explain why: the Moon has no atmosphere, so there is no wind, rain or erosion to wipe the prints away. Having essentially no atmosphere is the same thing as the 'vacuum-like environment' in the claim. Siegel also notes slow wear from micrometeorite impacts, moonquakes and heating and cooling, but he still expects most prints to last millions of years.

text: Barely 1% of the approximately 1.5 million registered charities in the United States account for around 50% of all charitable giving in the country.
label: not_verifiable
reason: The searches did not turn up a reliable source that confirms or rules out the claim that about 1% of roughly 1.5 million US charities get about 50% of all charitable giving. The results covered related but different measures. Several sources (Institute for Policy Studies (IPS) and Inequality.org) say the top 1% of income earners account for about half of all charitable deductions. That figure describes donors, not the charities that receive the money. Another source says the top 1% of charities hold about 69% of all sector revenue. Most of that revenue is not donations, so it doesn't test the claim either. The National Council of Nonprofits counts more than 1.3 million charitable nonprofits, not 1.5 million. With nothing directly confirming or contradicting the 1%-of-charities, 50%-of-giving figure, the claim can't be judged.

text: Beneath the ice of Antarctica lies a network of hundreds of subglacial lakes, with the largest being Lake Vostok, which is about the size of Lake Ontario.
label: supported
reason: Several sources back up every part of the claim. NASA Astrobiology says over 400 subglacial lakes have been found in Antarctica and calls Lake Vostok the largest known one, the size of North America's Lake Ontario. Study.com says that "There are hundreds of subglacial lakes in Antarctica, but Lake Vostok is the largest, approximately the size of Lake Ontario." EBSCO and HowStuffWorks also describe Vostok as about the size of Lake Ontario. One caveat: Vostok covers about 12,500 km² and Ontario about 18,960 km², so "about the size" is a rough but standard comparison.

text: Burning entirely in space, without any visible evidence, there is a giant star that is about three billion times larger than our Earth called VY Canis Majoris.
label: contradicted
reason: Sources put VY Canis Majoris's radius at about 1,420 solar radii. That makes its volume roughly 3 billion times the Sun's (space.fandom says 'a volume of three billion suns'), not 3 billion times Earth's. Since the Sun's volume is about 1.3 million Earths, VY CMa is quadrillions of times larger than Earth by volume. The claim mixes up Earth and the Sun. Saying the star leaves 'no visible evidence' is also wrong: it is an observed star in Canis Major whose apparent size astronomers have measured with telescopes such as the VLTI.

text: Caterpillars can consume up to 27,000 times their body weight in a single day, which is equivalent to a human eating around 40,000 pizzas in one sitting.
label: contradicted
reason: The 27,000-times figure is real, but it covers a caterpillar's whole larval stage, not one day. The Naked Scientists says caterpillars eat 27,000 times their body weight over the roughly 4 weeks they spend as caterpillars. 13abc and KidsKonnect also describe it as the total before pupation or over a lifetime. text: Cleanor, the longest recorded flight of a chicken, is a hen that achieved 13 seconds of sustained flight in 1973.

reason: I couldn't find any source that names a chicken called "Cleanor" or dates a record chicken flight to 1973. The 13-second figure is widely repeated, but where sources tie it to a specific bird, they name Sheena, a bantam owned by Bill and Bob Knox. text: Galileo Galilei was the first person to observe the planet Neptune, although he didn't realize it, mistaking it for a star in 1612.
label: supported
reason: Reliable sources back the claim. Scientific American says Galileo first saw Neptune in 1612 and took it for a fixed star, about 234 years before it was identified as a planet. Astronomy.com says he may have been the first to spot it and apparently mistook it for a star. Wikipedia's article on the discovery of Neptune notes that only telescopes could reveal it and that Galileo's drawings show it from late December 1612. One caveat: Astronomy.com is more cautious and says he "may" have been the first.

text: Galileo Galilei was the first person to observe the planet Neptune, in 1613, but he did not recognize it as a planet and instead documented it as a fixed star.
label: supported
reason: NASA's Neptune facts page says Galileo recorded Neptune as a fixed star during telescope observations in 1612 and 1613, more than 200 years before it was discovered as a planet in 1846. A ResearchGate paper on Galileo's observations of Neptune also says he took it for a 'fixed star' and shows sightings in his notebooks from late December 1612 and January 1613. So the claim's main points hold: he was the first known person to see Neptune, he observed it in 1613, and he recorded it as a fixed star rather than a planet. One detail is off: his first sighting was in late December 1612, not 1613. The claim doesn't actually say he first saw it in 1613, so I don't count this as a contradiction.

text: Humans share about 50-60% of their DNA with bananas, due to the common ancestry of all living organisms on Earth.
label: contradicted
reason: The figure is real, but it describes genes, not DNA. A 2013 NHGRI estimate found that about 60% of human genes have a recognizable counterpart in the banana genome. The proteins those genes make are only about 40% identical. Genes make up just a small part of the genome, so the shared share of human DNA is only about 1–2%. HowStuffWorks and IFLScience both say the popular 'we share 60% of our DNA with bananas' line is wrong: it is not 60%, and it is not DNA. A protein-database analysis (proteiniq) puts it lower still, at about 18% of genes and about 0.08% of the genome. Shared ancestry does explain why the two share genes, but saying humans share 50–60% of their DNA with bananas is false. Some lower-quality pages repeat the 60% DNA figure, and a Star fact-check rates the idea 'true' while adding that it is really about 1–2% of the genome.

text: Humans share approximately 50-60% of their DNA with bananas due to the common ancestral origin of all living organisms.
label: contradicted
reason: The claim treats a misreading of the research as fact. Fact-checks from HowStuffWorks and IFLScience, and an analysis by Dessimoz's genomics lab, trace the "50–60%" figure to a 2013 NHGRI comparison. That comparison found that about 60% of human genes have a recognizable counterpart in the banana genome. It did not find that 60% of human DNA is shared. Even among the matching genes, the encoded proteins are only about 40% identical. Protein-coding genes make up less than 2% of the human genome, so the shared portion of the whole genome is far smaller than 50–60%. Orthology-based analyses put the share of human genes with a banana counterpart at roughly 17–24%. Humans and bananas do share some genes because all life has a common ancestor, but the figure that humans share about 50–60% of their DNA with bananas is wrong.

text: Owens Falls Dam, located in New York, was the first hydroelectric power plant in the United States when it was completed in 1881.
label: contradicted
reason: The claim is wrong on both location and date. The Owen Falls Dam (now called Nalubaale Dam) is on the Victoria Nile near Jinja in Uganda, not in New York. It was built between 1951 and 1954, not in 1881. It powers the Nalubaale Hydroelectric Power Station, which supplies Uganda and Kenya, so it was not the first hydroelectric plant in the United States.
