text: Rubber ducks were originally made from rubber, but most modern rubber ducks are now made from plastic, specifically polyvinyl chloride.
label: supported
reason: Histories of the toy say the first rubber ducks really were made of rubber. Fatherly notes that they weren't made of rubber for long: manufacturers switched to softened plastic and then to vinyl plastic. Vinyl here means polyvinyl chloride (PVC), so this matches the claim that most modern ducks are PVC. Wikipedia's rubber duck article, which I'm recalling rather than citing from this search, says the same thing.

text: Scientists estimate that there are approximately 8.7 million identified species on Earth, but it's estimated that up to 80% of all species remain undiscovered.
label: contradicted
reason: The claim says 8.7 million species have been identified, but that's wrong. 8.7 million (±1.3 million) is Mora et al.'s 2011 estimate of the total number of species on Earth. Only about 1.2 million species have actually been identified and catalogued, which is less than 15% of that estimate. The source also says more than 80% of species remain undiscovered (86% of land species and 91% of marine species), so the claim's 'up to 80%' figure is also too low.

text: Scientists estimate that there are approximately 8.7 million identified species on Earth, but the total number of species, including unidentified ones, is believed to be between 11 and 30 million.
label: contradicted
reason: The 8.7 million figure (Mora et al., 2011) is an estimate of the total number of eukaryotic species on Earth, identified and unidentified together. It is not a count of identified species. Only about 1.2 million species have been described and catalogued. The claim mislabels 8.7 million as the number of 'identified' species, and its '11–30 million' total range does not come from this source either.

text: Tarantulas have been around for a long time, with fossil records showing that they existed over 100 million years ago during the Cretaceous period.
label: supported
reason: A 2023 Journal of Biogeography study (Wiley) cites the oldest known theraphosid (tarantula) fossil, found in Cretaceous Burmese amber and dated to around 100 million years ago (Wunderlich & Müller, 2020). Molecular studies published in PeerJ and reported by Smithsonian and Live Science also put the origin of tarantulas at about 120 million years ago, in the Cretaceous. One caveat: the fossil is dated to about 100 million years (Burmese amber is usually put at roughly 99 Ma), so 'over 100 million' is slightly loose. Older sources list only Miocene amber tarantulas, but the newer Cretaceous find replaces that record. Overall, the claim holds up.

text: Tarantulas have been around for a long time, with fossil records showing that they've remained largely unchanged for over 200 million years.
label: contradicted
reason: Peer-reviewed research on tarantula evolution (Journal of Biogeography, 2023) says the oldest known tarantula (Theraphosidae) fossil comes from Burmese amber and is about 100 million years old. It also notes that fossils within Theraphosidae are scarce, so the authors had to calibrate their dating with fossils from other spider groups. The ~242-million-year-old Rosamygale is a more distant mygalomorph relative, not a tarantula. Molecular estimates also put the origin of tarantulas at well under 200 million years ago. Because the fossil record does not show tarantulas staying largely unchanged for over 200 million years, the claim is contradicted.

text: Tarantulas have been on Earth for over 100 million years, with fossil evidence showing they existed during the Cretaceous period.
label: supported
reason: Molecular-dating studies (Foley et al., reported by Smithsonian, Live Science and Futurity) estimate that tarantulas first appeared about 120 million years ago, during the Cretaceous. For the fossil part of the claim, a 2023 paper in the Journal of Biogeography (Wiley) uses what it calls the oldest theraphosid fossil, found in Burmese amber and dated to around 100 million years ago (Wunderlich & Müller, 2020), which places it in the Cretaceous. One caveat: older sources say tarantula fossils are extremely rare and list only Miocene/Eocene amber specimens. Those sources came out before the Burmese amber fossil was described and are not a direct contradiction, so the claim holds overall.

text: Walking on water is possible for certain animals like the Basilisk lizard and water striders, due to their unique weight distribution, powerful leg muscles, or surface tension manipulation capabilities.
label: supported
reason: Wikipedia's article on animal locomotion on the water surface says the basilisk lizard is too heavy for surface tension to hold it up, so it runs across water using strong, fast leg movements. Water striders do rely on surface tension: their feet are water-repellent and covered in tiny hairs, which keeps them from breaking through. The claim's phrase "surface tension manipulation" is a loose wording, but its main points match the source.

text: Galileo Galilei was the first person to observe the planet Neptune, but he did not realize it was a planet, on January 28, 1613, and instead mistook it for a fixed star.
label: contradicted
reason: The claim gets the date wrong. Wikipedia's Discovery of Neptune article says Galileo's drawings show him observing Neptune on December 28, 1612, and again on January 27, 1613. Paul Fraser Collectibles and Scientific American also say his first sighting was in December 1612. The sources do agree that he was the first person to see Neptune and that he mistook it for a fixed star. However, his first observation came about a month before the claimed January 28, 1613, and the later sighting Wikipedia gives is January 27, not January 28.

text: Honeybees are able to fly by using electricity generated from the movement of their wings, which helps to interact with charged particles in the air.
label: contradicted
reason: Bees do pick up a static (positive) charge as they fly, partly from their wings and body hairs rubbing against the air. That charge helps them attract pollen and sense the electric fields around flowers. They do not use it to fly, though. Bee flight comes from the aerodynamic lift their flapping wings produce. Sources such as Science Friday describe the charge only as an aid for collecting pollen and judging flowers, not as a way of flying. The claim that bees fly using electricity from their wing movement is therefore a misstatement of the science.

text: Cassie is the deep-diving, deep-sea submersible that holds the Guinness World Record for the longest human dive, which reached 35,853 feet (10,928 meters) in the Mariana Trench in 1960 with Jacques Piccard and US Navy Lieutenant Don Walsh.
label: contradicted
reason: Reliable sources, including the US Navy's history site, the US Naval Institute and Wikipedia, say Jacques Piccard and Lt. Don Walsh made the 1960 Challenger Deep dive in the bathyscaphe Trieste, not in a vessel called 'Cassie'. They give the depth as about 10,911–10,916 m (roughly 35,800 ft), not 10,928 m. No source names a submersible called 'Cassie' in connection with this dive or record.

text: Galileo Galilei was the first person to observe the planet Neptune, but he didn't recognize it as a planet at the time, in 1612.
label: supported
reason: Several sources agree with the claim. Scientific American says Galileo first saw Neptune in 1612 and took it for a fixed star, about 234 years before it was recognized as a planet. Astronomy.com says he sketched it between December 1612 and January 1613, calls him possibly the first to spot it, and says he probably mistook it for a star. One caveat: in 2009 the physicist David Jamieson argued that Galileo may have noticed it moving. Astronomy.com reports this view but concludes that the evidence indicates Galileo most likely did not realize what the object was.

text: Owens Falls Dam, a hydroelectric dam in Uganda, harnesses the energy of the Owen Falls, and is Africa's largest power station in terms of capacity, providing over 90% of the country's electricity.
label: contradicted
reason: Wikipedia and an engineering paper both list the Owen Falls Dam, now called Nalubaale Power Station, at 180 MW. That is much smaller than other African power stations such as the Aswan High Dam (about 2,100 MW). It isn't even Uganda's largest: the 250 MW Bujagali station is bigger, and Karuma and Isimba are also on the same river. So the claim that it is Africa's largest power station by capacity is false, and the 'over 90%' share of Uganda's electricity is also unlikely today.

text: A blue whale's heartbeat is so loud that it can be detected from over 100 miles away, and its pulse rate can be as slow as 4-8 beats per minute.
label: contradicted
reason: Sources, including the Cold Spring Harbor Whaling Museum and an Africa Check fact-check, put the popular estimate for hearing a blue whale's heartbeat at about 2 miles (3 km), not over 100 miles. The heart-rate part of the claim is right: during dives, a blue whale's heart slowed to 4–8 beats per minute, and once dropped as low as 2. But the 100-mile figure is wrong, so the claim as a whole is contradicted.

text: Arectangle divided into a square and two equal rectangles, each of which is also divided into two more equal rectangles is a layout called a Harmonic Division and results in a layout of traditional Din A sizes of paper in Germany.
label: contradicted
reason: Trustworthy sources (Wikipedia's Paper size article and explanations of ISO 216 / DIN 476) say DIN A sizes come from a √2:1 aspect ratio. Each sheet is simply cut in half into two equal sheets of the next size, and no square is taken off. If you cut a square from a √2 rectangle, the strip left over has a ratio of about 2.414:1, so it is not an A-size sheet. I found no source calling the described square-plus-rectangles layout a 'Harmonic Division' or linking it to DIN paper sizes. In geometry, 'harmonic division' means something else entirely: a set of collinear points with a cross-ratio of −1. The claim gets how DIN A sizes are made wrong.

text: Honey Never Spoils is a fact - Archaeologists have found pots of honey in ancient Egyptian tombs that are over 3,000 years old and still perfectly edible.
label: supported
reason: Several sources, including My Modern Met citing Smithsonian Magazine and a Yahoo News science article, say archaeologists found unspoiled, edible honey in Egyptian tombs about 3,000 years old. They say honey resists spoilage because it is low in moisture, acidic and contains hydrogen peroxide. Honey can spoil if it absorbs moisture or is stored badly, so 'never spoils' is a simplification, but the claim matches what these sources report.

text: Plants can make sounds, although they are usually inaudible to the human ear, as research has shown that plants respond to injuries or environmental changes by releasing bursts of ultra-high-frequency clicks.
label: supported
reason: A 2023 study in Cell by Khait et al. found that tomato and tobacco plants make ultrasonic clicks when they are dehydrated or their stems are cut. The clicks are about as loud as normal conversation but too high-pitched for people to hear. This matches the claim that plants make sounds we usually can't hear, releasing ultra-high-frequency clicks in response to injury or environmental stress.

text: While they are often perceived to be slow-moving animals, sloths in the wild are capable of swimming at speeds of up to three times faster than they move on land.
label: supported
reason: The Sloth Conservation Foundation, a specialist group, says sloths can swim three times faster than they can move on the ground. The Washington Post reports the same thing: sloths move three times as fast in water as on land. Both line up with the claim that sloths swim up to three times faster than they move on land, even though people think of them as slow.

text: Researchers at the University of California, Riverside, have successfully created a battery that runs on air and can power devices for days, using zinc and oxygen to react and produce electricity.
label: not_verifiable
reason: I couldn't find any trustworthy source saying that University of California, Riverside researchers built a zinc-air battery that 'runs on air' and powers devices for days. My searches found unrelated UCR battery news, including its 2012 lithium-ion battery bank and 2025 solid-state battery studies. They also found zinc-air battery work from other institutions, such as Waterloo, TU Darmstadt, Donghua University and a team in Mexico. The only UCR link was that the Waterloo researcher got his PhD there. I ran out of searches before I could finish checking, so the claim can't be confirmed or ruled out.

text: Astronauts cannot cry in the classical sense in space due to the lack of gravity, which causes their tears to form a ball and cling to their eyes.
label: supported
reason: Several sources back this up, including astronaut Chris Hadfield's own account. In microgravity, tears don't fall. Surface tension pulls them into a liquid ball that sticks to the eye. Futurism quotes Hadfield, "your eyes make tears but they stick as a liquid ball," and concludes that astronauts "technically can't cry" in the usual sense. ScienceABC, Sciencing and other outlets describe the same thing. Some sources say astronauts can still cry, just without falling tears, but that matches the claim's 'classical sense' wording. One nitpick: the cause is microgravity (free fall), not an actual absence of gravity, though this is commonly simplified.

text: Gbetos, also known as plastic kayak-like boats, were invented by the Nauruan people of the equatorial Pacific island nation to help fisherman ride and break waves more easily.
label: not_verifiable
reason: I found nothing that links 'gbetos' to Nauru or to kayak-like boats. The sources I found use 'Gbeto' in other ways: it is a Fongbe word from Benin meaning 'human being' or 'person', and the name of a Malian unit in Age of Empires II. That makes the claim doubtful, but no source directly rules it out. The Wikipedia page on Nauru's culture says local fishermen wait for fish in small light boats, but it does not call them gbetos or say they were invented to ride waves. Some evidence also argues against the claim: plastic boats would hardly be a traditional invention. Since nothing directly confirms or refutes it, the claim is inconclusive.

text: Honeybees are able to fly by using electricity generated from the movement of their wings, which allows them to attract pollen, a process known as "triboelectric charging".
label: contradicted
reason: Research shows that bees pick up static charge through triboelectric charging while they fly, and this charge helps attract pollen. But that charge is a side effect of flying, not what makes flight possible. Bees fly using ordinary aerodynamic lift from flapping their wings, not electricity. The claim gets this backwards by saying bees fly by using electricity from their wing movement.

text: Scientists estimate that there are approximately 8.7 million identified species on Earth, but the total number of species is believed to be much higher, potentially exceeding 30 million.
label: contradicted
reason: The claim is wrong about what the 8.7 million figure means. It comes from Mora et al. (2011, PLoS Biology), and it is an estimate of the total number of eukaryote species on Earth, give or take 1.3 million. It is not a count of species already identified. Scientists have described only about 1.2 million species, including roughly 953,000 animals. Calling 8.7 million 'identified species' therefore contradicts the source. Estimates higher than 30 million do exist, since earlier ranges ran from 3 million to 100 million, but that doesn't fix the core error.

text: A large percentage of human brains are actually more active and 'right-brained' in both creative, or 'right-brained' functions, but also left-brained, mathematical functions.
label: contradicted
reason: A 2013 University of Utah study (Nielsen et al., PLoS ONE) looked at brain scans from more than 1,000 people. It found no evidence that people use one hemisphere more than the other or can be described as 'right-brained' or 'left-brained.' The specialized functions are handled by separate networks on each side, with no person-level dominance. That goes against the claim that a large share of brains are more active or 'right-brained' in both creative and mathematical functions. The claim's wording is also internally confused, and no reliable source supports it.

text: Beehive-shaped structures in the archeological site of one of the earliest human civilizations, Mehrgarh in present-day Pakistan, were discovered with evidence of bee domestication around 2500 BC.
label: contradicted
reason: I found no source that mentions beehive-shaped structures or bee domestication at Mehrgarh. Sources on Mehrgarh describe it as an early farming site known for barley, wheat and cattle, with nothing about bees. Reports on the 2010 Tel Rehov discovery in Israel (about the 10th–9th century BC) said archaeologists had never before found physical evidence of beekeeping in the ancient Near East. They called those hives the oldest evidence for beekeeping ever found. Wikipedia places the earliest evidence of beekeeping in Egypt (about 3100 BC), not in South Asia. This evidence goes against the claim of a Mehrgarh find from around 2500 BC. However, none of these sources directly addresses Mehrgarh.

text: Honeybees are able to fly by using their wings to create electricity, which helps to reduce air resistance through a process known as "triboelectric charging".
label: contradicted
reason: Honeybees do pick up a positive static charge through friction as they fly (triboelectric charging), but that charge has nothing to do with how they stay in the air. Sources describe the charge as a side effect that helps bees attract pollen and sense the electric fields around flowers. They explain bee flight by aerodynamics instead: rapid wingbeats, unusual wing mechanics, unsteady vortex-based lift and strong thorax muscles. None of the results say bees fly by making electricity to reduce air resistance, so the claim's account of how bees fly is wrong.

text: Beehive-shaped structures in the archeological site of one of the earliest human civilizations, Mehrgarh in present-day Pakistan, were discovered with evidence of bee domestication dating back to around 2500 BCE.
label: contradicted
reason: No source reports beehive-shaped structures or evidence of bee domestication at Mehrgarh. Mehrgarh is well documented as an early farming site known for domesticated plants and animals and early cotton. Reliable sources instead say the oldest known remains of human-made beehives were found at Tel Rehov in Israel, dated to about 3,000 years ago (around 900 BCE). The earliest evidence of beekeeping comes from Egyptian depictions, not from finds in South Asia. That conflicts with the claim of hives used for bee domestication at Mehrgarh around 2500 BCE.

text: Quantum Computing is a speacialized discipline of its own, and first computer bug was an actual insect that got stuck in the Harvard Mark II computer in 1947.
label: supported
reason: The U.S. Naval History and Heritage Command describes the photo as "The First Computer Bug": a moth found stuck in Relay #70, Panel F, of the Harvard Mark II on 9 September 1947. The operators taped it into the log as the "First actual case of bug being found." JSTOR Daily confirms the same event. One caveat is that "bug" was already engineering slang before 1947, so the moth was the first actual insect bug, not the first use of the word. Quantum computing being a specialized field is widely accepted and not in dispute.

text: Cats have a special talent for recognizing and mimicking the sounds of their human caregivers, with some even imitating the sounds of their owners' voices.
label: supported
reason: Both parts of the claim have some backing, though the evidence for mimicry is much weaker than the evidence for recognition. Recognition is well established: a 2013 Animal Cognition study (Saito & Shinozuka) found that domestic cats tell their owners' voices apart from strangers' voices, and later work found the same in cats responding to familiar caregivers. For mimicry, Lund University phonetics researcher Susanne Schötz says cats can imitate their owners' voices. She means they copy nuances such as melody patterns to communicate better. That claim comes from her book for cat owners, not from a peer-reviewed study. Calling this a 'special talent' overstates the evidence, but nothing found contradicts the claim.

text: Cassini Crater, located on the surface of Saturn's moon Titan, is approximately 313 miles in diameter and is named after Giovanni Cassini, a French astronomer.
label: contradicted
reason: The claim puts Cassini Crater on the wrong world. Cassini Crater is on Mars, in the Arabia quadrangle, not on Saturn's moon Titan. Its diameter is about 415 km, or roughly 258 miles, not 313 miles. It is named after Giovanni Domenico Cassini, but sources describe him as Italian (or Italian-French) rather than simply French. A separate Cassini crater on the Moon is only about 57 km across, so it doesn't match the claim either.

text: Plants can make sounds, a phenomenon known as 'plant bioacoustics,' where research has identified a variety of clicks, buzzing noises, and even what sounds like 'howling' emissions in certain plant species when they are under stress.
label: not_verifiable
reason: Reliable sources back the main idea. Plant bioacoustics is a recognized field (Wikipedia), and stressed plants do give off ultrasonic clicks or pops: Khait et al. 2023 in Cell, reported by Science News, CNN, Smithsonian and NHM. Gagliano's work also recorded clicks from corn roots. But I found no research showing that stressed plants make 'buzzing' noises. The buzzing in this literature comes from bees and other pollinators that plants respond to, not sounds the plants produce. I also found no research describing plant sounds as 'howling'. Popular articles call the sounds 'screams', but the studies describe them as pops or clicks. Because those parts of the claim can't be verified, the verdict is inconclusive.

text: Galileo Galilei was the first person to observe the planet Neptune, but he didn't recognize it as a planet and instead documented it as a star.
label: supported

text: The Axel Erlandson's Treasury Gardens in California is home to a unique collection of 17 grafted tree specimens, featuring elaborate designs, manifestations of the delicate art of postural pruning and tree grafting.
label: contradicted
reason: Axel Erlandson's trees, known as the Tree Circus, are displayed at Gilroy Gardens Family Theme Park (formerly Bonfante Gardens) in California. My search found no place called "Treasury Gardens." The count is also wrong: sources say 29 surviving trees were moved there in 1985 and about 25 are still alive and on display, not 17. The claim is right that the trees are shaped by grafting and training, but its name and number are contradicted.

text: Scientists estimate that there may be between 700,000 to 1 million species on Earth, but we have formally described and named only around 1.3 million, with many more awaiting discovery.
label: contradicted

text: Apa is among the world's largest family of flying foxes and is a type of large fruit bat native to forests and mangrove swamps in New Zealand.
label: contradicted
reason: New Zealand has no native flying foxes. The NZ Department of Conservation says the country has only two native bat species, the long-tailed bat and the lesser short-tailed bat, and neither is a flying fox or large fruit bat. Flying foxes (Pteropus) are native to places such as Australia and Asia, not New Zealand. The name "Apa" also doesn't clearly match any known flying fox species.

text: Humans and elephants share several physical and behavioral similarities, including gestation periods of almost two years, with human pregnancies lasting about 280 days and elephant pregnancies lasting nearly 700 days.
label: contradicted
reason: The claim says humans and elephants both have gestation periods of almost two years, but that is not true. Live Science reports that elephant pregnancies average about 640–660 days (about 95 weeks), while human pregnancies average 280 days (40 weeks), or about nine months. So only elephants have pregnancies close to two years. The 280-day figure in the claim also undercuts its own statement that the two species share a gestation period of almost two years. The 'nearly 700 days' figure for elephants is also a little higher than the usual 640–660 days.

text: A blue whale's heart alone can weigh as much as 400 pounds, with some reaching lengths of up to 5 feet and pumping around 5,000 liters of blood with a single beat.
label: contradicted
reason: The weight and length in the claim check out. text: Honeybees are able to fly by using their wings to generate electricity through a process called piezoelectricity, which is created by the movement of their wings beating around 200 times per second.

reason: Honeybees fly because of aerodynamics, not electricity. That finding comes from Caltech research published in PNAS in 2005. Bee flight has nothing to do with piezoelectricity. The '200 times per second' figure is also off: that is the fruit fly's wingbeat rate, while honeybees flap about 230–240 times per second.

text: Beehive-shaped structures in the ocean called fulgurites are created when lightning strikes the water's surface and rapidly heats it, forming a glass tube around the strike area.

text: Honeybees are able to fly by using their wings to generate electricity and create an electric charge which aids in their lift-off and overall flight.

Their flight comes from aerodynamics: very fast wingbeats, the way the wing moves and powerful thorax muscles produce lift through unsteady airflow. They don't use their wings to generate electricity to help them take off or stay in the air.

text: Galileo Galilei was the first person to observe the planet Neptune, but he didn't recognize it as a planet and instead documented it as a star in 1613.

text: Plants can make sounds, such as clicking or buzzing, by using a process called ultrasonic sound production which typically happens in plant cells when under stress.

text: Honeybees are able to fly by using their wings to generate lift and thrust, but also utilize their body hair to trap a boundary layer of air close to their body and generate additional lift.

text: Beneath the waves of the Indian Ocean, near Taiwan, lies the South China Sea's deepest point: the Manila Trench's Challenger Deep's rival is actually called the Philippine Trench - but the lowest point is actually called Emden Deep at about nearly 36,000 feet deep.

But the claim gets the cause backwards when it says bees fly by using their wings to make electricity. The charge is a side effect of flying, not how they fly. Bees fly because their wing movements create aerodynamic lift. None of the sources say electricity powers or enables bee flight.

text: Humans and elephants share several physical and behavioral similarities, including gestation periods of almost two years, with human pregnancies lasting around 280 days and elephant pregnancies lasting almost 660 days.
label: contradicted
reason: The claim calls a gestation period of almost two years something humans and elephants share, but that is wrong. The UFV Cascade source says an elephant pregnancy lasts about 22 months, or almost two years (about 660 days). It contrasts this with the roughly nine-month human pregnancy, which matches the claim's own 280 days. Only elephants have the near-two-year pregnancy, so it is not a shared similarity.

text: In the United States, there is a library located in Iowa called the Iowa State Fair and Agricultural Exposition where it lends out vegetables, fruits, and flowers instead of books.
label: contradicted
reason: The Iowa State Fair is an annual fair held in Des Moines, not a library. Its horticulture competitions put flowers, fruits and vegetables on display, and it runs farmers markets, but nothing shows it lending produce the way a library lends books. The closest real thing is the Des Moines Public Library's seed library, which lets people check out seed packets for fruits, vegetables and flowers. That is a different organization, and it lends seeds, not produce.

text: France and the United States are respectively known for producing the world's largest number of Nobel laureates, and these two countries consistently top the list.
label: contradicted
reason: The United States does have the most Nobel laureates (388 on the list I found), but France does not. It ranks fourth with 70, behind the United Kingdom (133) and Germany (109). So France and the US do not "consistently top the list" together.

text: Bees are able to fly by using electricity generated from the friction of their wings beating and the static electricity in the air to help lift and propel them.
label: contradicted
reason: The claim is wrong. Nature's reporting on bee flight research describes it as purely aerodynamic. Bees beat their wings up to 240 times a second at steep, constantly changing angles. This creates leading-edge vortices, rotational lift and wake recapture, which together produce the lift. Bees do pick up static charge, but scientists link that to pollen collection and to sensing the electric fields of flowers. No credible source says bees use friction electricity or static in the air to lift or propel themselves.

text: Beneath the waves of the Indian Ocean, near Taiwan, lies the South China Sea's deepest point: the Manila Trench's Challenger Deep's rival is actually named the 'Tonga Trench no', called the 'Challenger Deep's cousin', named the 'Marina Trench', known as the '
label: contradicted
reason: The claim is garbled and partly unreadable, but its main facts are wrong. The South China Sea and the Manila Trench are in the western Pacific, not the Indian Ocean. The Manila Trench lies off western Luzon, about 5,400 m deep, in the northeastern South China Sea. Challenger Deep is in the Mariana Trench, not the Manila Trench, and the Tonga Trench has no connection to the South China Sea. The claim's 'Marina Trench' is also a misspelling of 'Mariana Trench'.

text: The Boiling River of the Amazon, a natural river in Peru, is a six-kilometer-long section of water that is unusually and consistently hot, with temperatures reaching as high as 91°C (196°F).
label: contradicted
reason: Most of the claim checks out. The Boiling River (Shanay-Timpishka) is in Peru's Amazon, and its hot stretch runs for roughly 6 km. IOP Spark says it stays hot for over 6 km, and Wikipedia-derived sources give about 6.3–6.4 km. It is also consistently hot, with Andrés Ruzo citing an average of about 86°C. The maximum temperature is wrong, though. Wikipedia-derived sources (Wikiwand, Kiddle) report a hottest measurement of 99.1°C (210.4°F) in a hot spring feeding the river and a hottest average river temperature of nearly 95°C (203°F). Other sources describe the water as ranging up to about 93°C or nearly 100°C. None of the sources I found gives 91°C (196°F) as the peak. My searches ran out before I could check specifically for a 91°C figure. The river does exceed 91°C, but stating it as the maximum understates the documented peak.

text: The stravinsky fountain in Paris, created by sculptors François-Xavier Lalanne, is actually a faux water feature that recycles a small amount of water, and it is built over a parking garage.
label: contradicted
reason: The claim names the wrong artists. Reliable sources, including the official Paris tourism site and an art-history image archive, say the Stravinsky Fountain was created by Jean Tinguely and Niki de Saint Phalle, not François-Xavier Lalanne, and was inaugurated in 1983. The sources also describe a real fountain whose 16 sculptures spray jets of water. It sits directly above IRCAM's underground music centre, not a parking garage.

text: British Airways has a 747 jet with the smallest pilot staff as low as 3 plus 3 cabin on a B747  a British Airways short small variation the B747-200, normally holding 3 plus 7 cabin using this novel method
label: not_verifiable
reason: I couldn't verify this claim. It's garbled and refers to "this novel method" without saying what the method is. Sources do say the 747 Classic (-100/-200/-300) needed at least 3 flight-deck crew (two pilots plus a flight engineer). However, no source I found mentions a British Airways 747-200 flying with 3 flight crew and 3 cabin crew, normally carrying 7 cabin crew, or any special crewing method. The present-tense "has" is also doubtful: British Airways retired the 747-200 around 2001 and its whole 747 fleet in 2020.

text: Plants can make sounds, such as loud clicking noises, when they're under stress or dying, a phenomenon that is not yet fully understood by scientists.
label: supported
reason: The 2023 Tel Aviv University study in Cell found that tomato and tobacco plants give off airborne clicking or popping sounds when stressed, either by drought or by having their stems cut. Stressed plants made more sounds than healthy ones, and reports say the clicks are about as loud as a human conversation (roughly 60–65 dB at 10 cm). One caveat: the sounds are ultrasonic, so people can't hear them without equipment. The authors also point to open questions, for example that only a few species were tested, and the likely cause (bubbles forming in the plant's water-transport tissue, called cavitation) is still a hypothesis. That fits the claim that scientists don't yet fully understand it. The claim's mention of 'dying' is a loose reading: the study covers severe stress such as dehydration and cut stems, not death itself.

text: A Heller whale, also known as a dwarf sperm whale, holds the Guinness World Record as the world's largest toothed predator on Earth, and is known for growing teeth up to 10 cm long.
label: contradicted
reason: Guinness World Records names the sperm whale (Physeter macrocephalus) as the largest living toothed mammal, and other sources call it the largest toothed predator. Males can reach about 20.5 m long. The dwarf sperm whale (Kogia sima) is a separate, small species, usually only about 2 to 2.7 m long, so it cannot hold this record. No source supports 'Heller whale' as another name for it.

text: Tarantulas have lived on Earth for a long time, with fossil evidence showing that they existed over 150 million years ago, during the Cretaceous period.
label: contradicted
reason: The claim doesn't hold together. The Cretaceous period ran from about 145 to 66 million years ago, so 'over 150 million years ago' would fall in the Jurassic, not the Cretaceous. The fossil record also doesn't back the date: according to a Journal of Biogeography study, the oldest known tarantula (Theraphosidae) fossil is from Burmese amber dated to about 100 million years ago. The same study's molecular dating puts the split between tarantulas and their closest relatives in the early Cretaceous, around 120 million years ago. That matches the 'Cretaceous' part of the claim but contradicts 'over 150 million years ago.' Only the wider mygalomorph spider group, which includes tarantulas, goes back about 240 million years.

text: Scientists estimate that there are approximately 8.7 million identified species on Earth, but the actual number could be much higher, potentially ranging from 30 to 100 million.
label: contradicted
reason: The 8.7 million figure from Mora et al. (2011) is an estimate of the total number of eukaryotic species on Earth, not the number already identified. The same study says only about 1.2 million species had been catalogued, and that roughly 86% of species on Earth have yet to be described. Calling 8.7 million "identified" species is therefore wrong. Earlier estimates did range from about 3 million to 100 million total species, but that doesn't fix the misstatement about identified species.

text: Humans are the only species in the world that sleep on average 7-9 hours per day with their brains in a state of complete unconsciousness, known as REM sleep.
label: contradicted
reason: The claim gets REM sleep wrong. REM sleep isn't a state of complete unconsciousness: the brain is highly active, close to how it behaves when awake, and it's when most vivid dreams happen. Humans also aren't unique in having it. Many mammals (such as monkeys, dogs and cats), birds and some reptiles have REM sleep, and REM-like states have been reported in cuttlefish. The sources I found don't cover the 7–9 hour figure.

text: Blind people can see through technology that translates light into sound through a process called "sensory substitution," allowing them to perceive their surroundings in new ways.
label: supported
reason: Reliable sources, including a Nature npj Science of Learning article, describe visual-to-auditory sensory substitution devices such as The vOICe. These devices turn camera images (that is, captured light) into sound: a pixel's vertical position becomes pitch and its horizontal position becomes time. Blind users can learn to perceive their surroundings this way, and their visual cortex becomes active after training. This backs the claim, with the word "see" read loosely, as it usually is in this field.

text: A blue whale's heartbeat can be as slow as two beats per minute when it's not excited or scared.
label: supported
reason: Several reliable sources report on the 2019 Stanford-led study that put a heart-rate tag on a wild blue whale (published in PNAS, available on PMC). They agree that its heart can slow to as little as two beats per minute. The main part of the claim, 'as slow as two beats per minute', is confirmed. However, the sources link the lowest rate to deep foraging dives (diving bradycardia), not to the whale being calm, 'not excited or scared'. They don't say anything that rules out the claim's wording, but it describes the condition imprecisely. I rated it supported because the figure is right and nothing contradicts it.

text: A chunk of the Dead Sea has been found to be so dense with salt that objects with lower densities than it float instead of sinking.
label: supported
reason: NOAA describes the Dead Sea as the saltiest natural water in the world, with salinity rising with depth until the water is saturated below about 100 m. Other sources say the extra salt makes the water dense enough that people and objects float more easily. The physics is simple: anything less dense than the water floats. The claim's wording ("a chunk… has been found") is unusual, but its content matches these well-established facts.

text: A rolling ball of glass can melt in extreme heat without shattering due to itsirse uniformly conducting heat.
label: contradicted
reason: The claim says the glass ball avoids shattering because it conducts heat uniformly, but glass is actually a poor conductor of heat. ASM International's thermal shock material and Berlin Packaging both say so. Because glass spreads heat poorly, it heats unevenly, which creates stress and thermal-shock cracking. Glass can soften and melt when heated gradually, but not because it conducts heat evenly. The reason the claim gives is therefore wrong.

text: Bacteria can only grow and reproduce in "moist" environments,  typically requiring a relative humidity of at least 90%.
label: supported
reason: Food-science sources on water activity say that most bacteria need a minimum water activity of about 0.91, the same as an equilibrium relative humidity of about 91%. Only salt-tolerant (halophilic) bacteria grow at lower levels, down to about 0.75, and no microbe grows below 0.6. This matches the claim that bacteria need moist conditions and typically need about 90% relative humidity or more. The word "typically" leaves room for the halophilic exceptions.

text: The Axel Erlandson's Tree Circus, also known as the "Basket Tree," was created by a Swedish immigrant and consists of a distinctive "basket-weaved" tree sculpture formed by training multiple trees into a woven shape.
label: supported
reason: The sources back the claim's main points. Gilroy Gardens and Wikipedia both say Axel Erlandson was a Swedish immigrant (Swedish American) who opened 'The Tree Circus' in 1947. Wikipedia also says he made the 'Basket Tree' by planting six sycamores in a circle and approach-grafting them together into a woven diamond pattern, and Gilroy Gardens calls it the iconic centerpiece. One wording problem: the 'Basket Tree' is a single tree in the Tree Circus, not another name for the whole attraction. I read the claim as referring to the Tree Circus's Basket Tree, so this is loose phrasing and I don't count it as a real contradiction.

text: Humans are the only species known to experience a condition called 'tetrachromacy,' where the presence of a fourth type of cone cell allows some people, mostly women, to see more nuanced colors.
label: contradicted
reason: The claim says humans are the only species known to have tetrachromacy, and that is false. Wikipedia's Tetrachromacy article says tetrachromacy has been shown in several species of birds, fish and reptiles. In humans, it is only suspected in a small percentage of people. The rest of the claim is broadly accurate: a fourth cone type is involved, and it is reported mostly in women. But the 'only species' part is wrong.

text: Galileo Galilei was the first person to observe the planet Neptune, but he didn't recognize it as a planet, instead documenting it as a star in 1613.
label: supported
reason: Wikipedia's article on the discovery of Neptune says Galileo's drawings show he observed Neptune on December 28, 1612, and again on January 27, 1613, and both times he mistook it for a fixed star. Astronomy.com and Scientific American agree that Galileo was likely the first person to see Neptune and thought it was a star, about 234 years before it was identified as a planet. The claim gives only 1613, but the first sighting was in December 1612. Because one of his documented observations was in January 1613, the claim is still essentially accurate.

text: Honeybees are able to fly by using their wings to generate electricity and create a positive charge on their bodies, allowing them to attract and collect pollen from flowers.
label: contradicted
reason: The claim gets the cause backwards. Bees do pick up a positive static charge while flying, mostly from friction with the air, and that charge helps pollen stick to them. But the charge is a side effect of flying. It isn't what lets them fly. Bees stay in the air through aerodynamics: they beat their wings very fast, flex them in unusual ways, rely on strong thorax muscles, and create small leading-edge vortices that produce lift. So the claim's core statement, that bees fly by using their wings to generate electricity, is contradicted by the sources on bee flight.

text: The Axel Erlandson "Tree Circus" in California, USA, features 62 trees, including an arch of eucalyptus and a basket-weave sycamore, all grown and pruned in unusual shapes.
label: contradicted
reason: Several details don't match the sources. Gilroy Gardens, the park that now owns the surviving trees, says the Arch Tree was grown from two American sycamores, not eucalyptus. Sources also put the Tree Circus at about 70 trees at its peak (or '60-70'), falling to about 40 by 1977, with 29 later moved to Gilroy; none gives a count of 62. The Basket Tree was made of sycamores, so that part is correct, but the eucalyptus arch and the figure of 62 trees are contradicted or unsupported.

text: Astronauts cannot cry in the same way they do on Earth, as the lack of gravity in space causes tears to form a ball and float instead of freely flowing down their faces.
label: supported
reason: Several sources, including Futurism, HuffPost and IBTimes, cover astronaut Chris Hadfield's demonstration on the ISS. They report that in microgravity tears don't run down the face but gather into a liquid ball. Futurism quotes Hadfield saying tears 'stick as a liquid ball' and concludes that astronauts 'technically can't cry' the way people do on Earth. One detail is slightly off: the ball mostly clings to the eye or face rather than floating away, though it can drift around the face as it grows (IBTimes). The claim's main point is still accurate.

text: Cassini Crater, located on the surface of Saturn's moon Titan, is approximately 313 miles in diameter and is considered one of the largest and most prominent polar craters in the Saturnian system.
label: contradicted
reason: Cassini Crater is not on Titan. It's a crater on Mars, in the Arabia quadrangle, and it's about 415 km (roughly 258 miles) across, not 313 miles. The only other Cassini crater is a small one on the Moon (about 57 km across). Neither is in the Saturnian system, so the location, the size and the claim that it is a major polar crater around Saturn are all wrong.

text: Blue whales can hold up to 2,000 gallons, or about 5,000 liters, of food in their stomachs at any given time due to their massive size.
label: contradicted
reason: Reliable sources give a much smaller stomach capacity. WWF says a blue whale's stomach holds about one ton of krill at a time, and the UW-La Crosse biology page says the stomach chambers hold up to 1,000 kg of food. That works out to roughly 1,000 liters (about 260 gallons), nowhere near 2,000 gallons or 5,000 liters. The claim's own figures also don't match: 2,000 gallons is about 7,570 liters, not about 5,000.

text: Bernard Bartalan, an Austrian-language teacher, holds the Guinness World Record for the longest duration without sleep, staying awake for 264.4 hours (11 days), from December 24 to January 4, 1964
label: contradicted
reason: The searches turned up no record holder named Bernard Bartalan. The 264.4-hour (about 11-day) feat belongs to Randy Gardner, a 17-year-old San Diego high school student who stayed awake for a science fair project around Christmas break 1963–64. He was not an Austrian-language teacher. Guinness World Records also says the record it last recognised was Robert McDonald's 453 hours 40 minutes in 1986, and it stopped monitoring the category in 1997. So the claim gets the person and the record holder wrong. One search failed to run, but the evidence found is enough to contradict the claim.

text: Galileo Galilei was the first scientist to observe the planet Neptune, albeit unintentionally, in 1613, but he didn't recognize it as a planet at that time.
label: supported
reason: Astronomy.com reports that between December 1612 and January 1613, Galileo sketched a "point" near Jupiter that sat exactly where Neptune was, and that he probably took it for a star. He was likely the first to see Neptune. The planet wasn't officially discovered until 1846. This matches the claim's main points: he was first, he saw it by accident, the observations include January 1613, and he didn't realize it was a planet. One caveat on dates: his first sighting was in December 1612, not 1613. Another: physicist David Jamieson argued in 2009 that Galileo may have noticed the object moving. Still, the article says the evidence suggests Galileo probably didn't work out what it really was.

text: Mathematicians used a combination of over 13 billion calculations in a multitude of methods to prove that the الطب 42 is the answer to the famous related categories or "Colatz math topic named related.
label: contradicted
reason: The 2019 result about the number 42 had nothing to do with the Collatz conjecture. Andrew Booker of the University of Bristol and Andrew Sutherland of MIT found a solution to x³ + y³ + z³ = 42, a long-standing sum-of-three-cubes puzzle. They did it with Charity Engine, a distributed network of more than 500,000 home PCs. The source does not mention '13 billion calculations' or 'a multitude of methods'. 42 is also not 'the answer' to the Collatz conjecture, which remains unproven. The claim misidentifies the problem.

text: Tarantulas have been around for a long time, with the earliest known tarantula fossils dating back to the Cretaceous period, around 135 million years ago.
label: contradicted
reason: The claim gets the period right but the date wrong. Sources agree that the oldest known tarantula (Theraphosidae) fossil is from the Cretaceous: it is Protertheraphosinae, preserved in Burmese amber from Myanmar. But that fossil is dated to about 100 million years ago, not 135. A 2023 Journal of Biogeography study and Live Science, reporting on a separate study, both give the ~100 Ma age. Molecular estimates also put the origin of tarantulas at only about 120–105 Ma. Since no source supports a 135-million-year-old tarantula fossil, that figure is contradicted.

text: Honeybees are able to fly by using their wings to produce electricity through a process called triboelectrification, which helps to attract pollen.
label: contradicted
reason: The evidence does not support the cause-and-effect in this claim. Studies show that honeybees and other flying insects pick up static charge through triboelectric effects, such as friction with air and plants, while they fly. That charge may help attract or transfer pollen. But the charge is a side effect of flying, not the way bees fly. Bees stay in the air because their flapping wings create aerodynamic lift. The claim says bees fly by using their wings to make electricity, which reverses this relationship and gets the mechanism of flight wrong.

text: Humans and elephants share several physical and behavioral similarities, including gestation periods of almost two years, with human pregnancies lasting around 280 days and elephant pregnancies lasting almost 700 days but taking nearly two years to start showing outward signs of conception.
label: contradicted
reason: The claim says humans and elephants both have gestation periods of almost two years, but that's false. Human pregnancy lasts about 266 days from conception (usually counted as 280 days, or 40 weeks), which is about nine months. Only the elephant's pregnancy comes close to two years: about 640–660 days, or roughly 22 months. So the claimed shared 'almost two years' gestation is wrong, and the claim even contradicts itself by also giving 280 days for humans. The extra statement that elephants take nearly two years to show outward signs of conception would mean the whole pregnancy passes before any sign appears, and no source supports it.

text: Scientists estimate that there may be between 700,000 and 1 million species on Earth, but we have formally described only about 1.3 million, with most estimates suggesting around 75% of all species remain undiscovered.
label: contradicted
reason: The claim doesn't add up and conflicts with the main scientific estimate. It says Earth may hold only 700,000 to 1 million species, yet also says about 1.3 million have already been described. That would mean more species are described than exist. The widely cited 2011 PLoS Biology study, reported by National Geographic and The Scientist, puts the total at about 8.7 million species (range 7.4 to 10 million). About 1.2 million have been described, which leaves roughly 86% undiscovered, not around 75%.

text: Astronauts Robert B. Willingham, on Space Shuttle Columbia in 1982, and Nick Hague, on Soyuz MS-10 in 2018, initially set to go to space on their 40th birthday.
label: contradicted
reason: The claim is wrong about Nick Hague. Wikipedia gives his birth date as 24 September 1975. Soyuz MS-10 launched on 11 October 2018, when he was 43, and the launch was not set for his 40th birthday. I also found no record of an astronaut named Robert B. Willingham. Columbia's 1982 missions were STS-3, STS-4 and STS-5, and their crews (for example Lousma, Fullerton, Mattingly, Hartsfield, Brand, Overmyer, Allen and Lenoir) include no one by that name.

text: Bees are able to fly by using electricity that is generated from the friction of their wings beating, but it is a small portion of the overall energy they expend.
label: contradicted
reason: Bee flight is powered by muscles, not electricity. Sources on bee flight say large indirect flight muscles in the thorax drive wingbeats of about 200–300 per second. These wingbeats create lift through aerodynamic vortices. Bees do pick up a small electrostatic charge from air friction, but none of the sources say this charge helps them fly or supplies any of the energy they use. Since the claim says bees fly using electricity from wing friction, it is contradicted.

text: Honeybees are able to fly by using their wings to generate lift and thrust, but also utilize their body hair to trap a boundary layer of air close to their body and increase efficiency.
label: not_verifiable
reason: The first part of the claim holds up: honeybees fly by beating their wings at high frequency, which produces lift and thrust through unsteady aerodynamics (Nature; studies of honeybee flight aerodynamics). I found no reliable source for the second part, that body hair traps a boundary layer of air to make flight more efficient. Sources describe other jobs for bee hair: capturing pollen, thermal insulation and sensing air movement or electric fields. Royal Society Interface notes boundary layers only to explain why short hairs are less sensitive to airflow. Honeybees do reduce drag, but by streamlining their posture (raising the abdomen), not with their hair. A beekeeping site raises the idea that hair might reduce drag but says the author is unsure. Because the hair claim can be neither confirmed nor clearly ruled out, the verdict is inconclusive.

text: Plants can make sounds, too, when they experience stress, such as releasing ultrasonic clicking sounds when they're thirsty or stressed out by insects eating them.
label: supported
reason: The claim's main point is supported. A peer-reviewed 2023 Cell study (Khait et al.), reported by Science News, Nature, Scientific American, the Natural History Museum and CNN, found that stressed tomato and tobacco plants give off ultrasonic clicks or pops. They did this when they were thirsty and when their stems were cut. Stressed plants clicked far more often (about 30–50 clicks per hour) than unstressed ones. One caveat: the study tested drought and stem cutting, not insects eating the plants. The insect example is a loose extension of the physical-damage result rather than something the study measured directly. This makes the supported label somewhat uncertain.

text: Plants can make sounds, too; when they're stressed, cut or pulled from the soil, plants issue ultrasonic squeaks that are beyond human hearing.
label: not_verifiable
reason: Most of the claim is backed by trustworthy sources. Khait et al.'s 2023 Cell study, covered by Smithsonian, the Natural History Museum and Science News Explores, found that tomato and tobacco plants give off ultrasonic pops, at roughly 20–150 kHz, when they are drought-stressed or their stems are cut. Human ears can't hear these sounds. However, none of the sources I found say the plants were pulled from the soil. The experiments tested only dehydration and stem cutting. Because that part of the claim can't be checked, the claim as a whole is inconclusive.

text: Astronauts in space do not get to sneeze in the same manner as we do on Earth due to the lack of gravity causing mucus to not drip down the back of the throat, which often causes sneezes.
label: contradicted
reason: My sources say the opposite of the claim. HowStuffWorks says real astronauts do sneeze and that "the things that make an astronaut sneeze in space are the same things that make all of us sneeze on Earth." Space.com and Live Science describe astronauts sneezing normally, including inside spacesuit helmets, where they can't stop the sneeze. What changes in space is what happens after a sneeze: droplets float around instead of falling. Microgravity does make mucus collect in the nose and cause stuffiness, but no reliable source I found says that missing post-nasal drip changes or stops sneezing. My last search hit a tool limit, so I didn't check that mechanism further.

text: Galileo Galilei was the first person to observe the planet Neptune, but he didn't realize it was a planet, instead mistaking it for a star in 1613.
label: supported
reason: Reliable sources back the claim. Wikipedia says Galileo's drawings show he observed Neptune on December 28, 1612 and again on January 27, 1613, and both times he mistook it for a fixed star near Jupiter. Astronomy.com says Galileo may have been the first to spot Neptune and seems to have mistaken it for a star. There are two small caveats. His first sighting was in late December 1612, so it was not only in 1613. Also, some researchers argue he noticed that the 'star' had moved. The overall evidence still says he did not realize it was a planet.

text: Plants can make sounds, such as clicking or cracking noises, although these sounds are typically too subtle for human ears to detect, and scientists use specialized equipment to detect them.
label: supported
reason: A 2023 Tel Aviv University study published in Cell (Khait et al.) found that stressed tomato and tobacco plants give off clicking or popping sounds. The sounds are ultrasonic, so they're above what human ears can hear. The researchers picked them up with special ultrasonic microphones, then shifted them into the audible range so people could hear them. Science News and Sci.News both report this, which backs up every part of the claim.

text: Plants can make sounds, too, when they are under stress, and a recent study areas used special tools to discover that different plants make different sounds, such as ultrasonic clicks, to release water vapor and warn nearby plants.
label: contradicted
reason: The Tel Aviv University study (Khait et al., Cell, 2023) supports the basic claim. Using ultrasonic microphones and machine learning, the researchers found that stressed plants such as tomato and tobacco give off ultrasonic clicks. How the plants sound depends on the species and on the kind of stress, such as drying out or being cut. The claim goes wrong when it says why the plants make these sounds. The clicks are explained as a side effect of cavitation: stretched water columns in the plant's water-carrying tissue break, a bit like a rubber band snapping. They are not described as a way to release water vapor. The study also did not show that the sounds warn nearby plants. Its author said 'we've shown only that plants emit informative sounds,' and other scientists only raised the open question of whether insects or other animals might pick up on the sounds. So the claim's stated purpose, releasing water vapor and warning neighbouring plants, is not what the study found.

text: A blue whale's heart alone can weigh as much as 400 pounds, with some reaching lengths of up to 5 feet and pumping over 5,000 liters of blood with every beat.
label: contradicted
reason: Parts of the claim about size are close to commonly cited figures. The preserved blue whale heart was reported at about 400 lb (180 kg), and blue whale hearts are often described as about 5 feet long. The blood-volume figure is wrong, though. A study reported by Inverse estimated that a roughly 70-tonne blue whale's heart pumps about 80 liters per beat, and other commonly cited figures are around 220 liters (58 gallons). Both are far below the more than 5,000 liters per beat in the claim.

text: France and Spain both claim to be the birthplace of the first restaurant, 'auberge,' with the French claiming Procope's established in 1686 and the Spanish pointing to Julianas in 1787 in Laredo, as a more permanent equivalent.
label: not_verifiable
reason: I couldn't fully verify this claim because my searches hit the tool limit after only a few results. The evidence I found is about Le Procope in Paris (opened 1686), which is usually described as a café, not as the first restaurant or an 'auberge' (an inn). I found nothing showing that Spain claims 'Julianas' in Laredo (1787) as the first restaurant. Spain's best-known claim is Sobrino de Botín in Madrid (1725), which is from general knowledge, not something these searches confirmed. Several details look wrong or fabricated, but the searches did not clearly confirm or refute the Laredo part.

text: Despite their size difference, the largest mammal, the blue whale, and the smallest mammal, the Etruscan shrew, both share a similar number of chromosomes, with 44 in the blue whale and 42 in the Etruscan shrew (the number of chromosomes varies among species).
label: supported
reason: Both chromosome counts check out. A cytogenetic study of a female blue whale found a diploid number of 2n=44, and other sources also give 44 chromosomes for the blue whale. Karyotype studies (Folia Zoologica 2014, Mammalian Biology 2025, GBIF) give Suncus etruscus 2n=42. The blue whale is the largest mammal, and the Etruscan shrew is widely recognized as the smallest mammal by mass; the bumblebee bat is sometimes named instead, depending on how size is measured. The note that chromosome numbers vary among species is accurate.

text: Galileo Galilei was the first person to observe the planet Neptune using a telescope, but he didn't recognize it as a planet at the time and instead documented it as a fixed star.
label: supported
reason: Reliable sources back the claim. Wikipedia's 'Discovery of Neptune' page says Galileo's drawings show he observed Neptune through his telescope on December 28, 1612, and again on January 27, 1613. Both times he mistook it for a fixed star while it sat close to Jupiter, so he is not credited with discovering it. Scientific American also reports that he first saw Neptune in 1612 and took it for a fixed star, 234 years before it was identified as a planet. Other sources call him the first person to see Neptune. One caveat: Wikipedia notes that on January 28 Galileo recorded that this 'star' seemed to have moved. That suggests he may have suspected something unusual, but he still never recognized it as a planet.

text: Scientists estimate that there may be between 700,000 and 1 million species of insects on Earth, but they have formally described only around 1 million out of an estimated total of 8.7 million on the planet.
label: contradicted
reason: Scientists estimate there are about 5.5 million insect species, likely somewhere between 2.6 and 7.2 million (Stork 2018, reported by Live Science and Annual Reviews). The claim's figure of 700,000 to 1 million is far too low. It is closer to the roughly 1 million insect species that have already been described, which makes the claim contradict itself. The 8.7 million figure is an estimate for all eukaryotic species on Earth, not for insects. Overall, about 1.5 million species of all kinds have been described.

text: Honeybees are able to fly by using their wings to produce electricity through a process called triboelectrification, which allows them to attract pollen and other particles.
label: contradicted
reason: Bees do pick up static charge through triboelectric charging while they fly, mostly from friction with the air and surfaces, and that charge helps pull pollen onto them. But the causation in the claim is backwards. Bees don't fly by making electricity with their wings: they fly using normal aerodynamic lift from beating their wings. The charge is a side effect of flying, not what lets them fly. So the claim's main statement is contradicted by the research.

text: Plants can make sounds, too - when they're stressed or under attack from insects, some plants release ultrasonic clicks that are beyond human hearing, which researchers call 'plant screams'.
label: supported
reason: The main claim checks out. A 2023 peer-reviewed study in Cell (Khait et al., Tel Aviv University) found that stressed plants, including tomato and tobacco, give off airborne ultrasonic popping or clicking sounds at about 20–100 kHz. These sounds are too high for humans to hear, and stressed plants click much more often than unstressed ones. Popular coverage (ScienceAlert, SciTechDaily, Asian Scientist, Yahoo News) widely calls these sounds plant 'screams.' The claim goes too far in two places. First, the study tested drought, cut stems and infection, not insect attack specifically. Second, the 'scream' label comes mostly from media headlines rather than from the researchers. Because the claim says 'stressed or under attack,' the stress part is enough to make the core statement true.

text: Abnormally large crystals have grown within the Naica Mine in Chihuahua, Mexico, where one giant selenite crystal measured over 36 feet long and weighed more than 55 tons.
label: supported
reason: Several sources agree that the Naica Mine's Cave of the Crystals in Chihuahua, Mexico contains giant selenite crystals. They put the largest at about 11.4 to 12 m long (roughly 37 to 39 ft), which is more than 36 feet, and its weight at about 55 tons. Wikipedia describes them as some of the largest natural crystals ever found. Some sources say the crystals weigh 'over 55 tons', while others give exactly 55 tons, so 'more than 55 tons' slightly overstates the commonly cited figure. That gap is small, and the claim is supported overall.

text: Members of the smallest primate species, the pygmy mouse lemur, are about the size of a human fist, with a typical body length of around 6 centimeters (2.4 inches).
label: contradicted
reason: Wikipedia says the pygmy mouse lemur (Microcebus myoxinus) is only the second-smallest mouse lemur. The smallest primate is Madame Berthe's mouse lemur (M. berthae). Wikipedia, Earth.com and Animal Diversity Web all give the pygmy mouse lemur's head-body length as about 12–13 cm, not about 6 cm. The 6 cm (2.4 inch) figure appears only on a fan wiki, which is not a reliable source. ADW does call it the smallest primate, but that reflects older classification and still gives 12–13 cm.

text: Scientists estimate that there are around 8.7 million identified species on Earth, but the total number of species, including those that have not been discovered, is estimated to be between 13 and 30 million.
label: contradicted
reason: The 8.7 million figure from Mora et al. (2011, PLoS Biology) is an estimate of the total number of eukaryotic species on Earth, including undiscovered ones. It is not a count of identified species. The same study notes that only about 1.2 million species had been catalogued, which means around 86% of species have not yet been described. The claim gets this wrong by calling 8.7 million the 'identified' species, and its 13–30 million total is not the figure this study gives.

text: In 2019, the world's largest living organism was discovered in a Blue Mountains forest in Australia, and it's estimated to be around 4,560 years old, covering approximately 100 acres.
label: contradicted
reason: The organism usually called the world's largest is the Armillaria ostoyae "humongous fungus" in the Blue Mountains of Oregon, USA, not Australia. It lies in Malheur National Forest, covers thousands of acres (about 3.7 km²), not around 100, and is estimated to be up to about 8,650 years old, not 4,560. It was also not discovered in 2019. The claim gets the location, size, age and date wrong.

text: Plants can make sounds, too, when they're under stress - for instance, scientists found that ultrasonic clicks are detectable when a plant is cut or injured.
label: supported
reason: A peer-reviewed study by Khait et al. (Cell, 2023) found that tomato and tobacco plants give off ultrasonic airborne sounds when stressed, including when their stems are cut. Cut and drought-stressed plants made far more sounds than control plants. Science news coverage describes the sounds as clicks, which matches what the claim says.

text: Honeybees are able to fly by using their wings to generate electricity and create an electric charge that helps to lift them into the air and propel them forward.
label: contradicted
reason: Honeybees fly by aerodynamics, not electricity. Peer-reviewed work, including a PNAS study and a Nature feature, shows that they get lift and thrust from short, very fast wing strokes. These produce leading-edge vortices, rotational lift and wake recapture, and bees also adjust stroke amplitude. Bees do build up a small static charge from friction with the air, which can help with picking up pollen, but nothing shows it lifts them or pushes them forward.

text: Seals are able to slow down their heart rate dramatically to conserve energy, with some species experiencing a heart rate reduction from 100 beats per minute to just 4 beats per minute while they dive underwater and sleep.
label: not_verifiable
reason: The diving part is well supported. SeaWorld says a harbor seal's heart rate falls from 75–120 bpm to 4–6 bpm when it dives. The Smithsonian National Zoo gives 80–120 down to 3–4 bpm, and the National Park Service says elephant seals go from 55–120 bpm to 4–15 bpm. However, I found no source showing a drop to about 4 bpm during sleep. The sleep studies I found report much smaller drops: in elephant seal pups, about 54–60 bpm while breathing and 41–44 bpm during breath-holding pauses in sleep, with brief lows of 25–35 bpm. Sleeping adults went from about 65 to 54 bpm. I couldn't check whether rates fall that low when seals sleep during deep dives, so the 'and sleep' part of the claim is unverified.

text: The Axel Erlandson, a Swedish farmer, had 29 specially grafted trees known as the " Tree Circus", one being a trunk with six different types of citrus, due to grafting.
label: contradicted
reason: Several sources confirm that Axel Erlandson was a Swedish(-American) farmer who grafted and shaped trees for an attraction called "The Tree Circus." But the claim's count of 29 trees is wrong. Dave's Garden and Boing Boing say the Circus had about 70 trees at its peak. Only 29 were left by 1985 (other sources say 25). The surviving trees at Gilroy Gardens are sycamores, box elders, ash and Spanish cork. No source mentions a trunk grafted with six types of citrus. The well-known 'six' tree is the Basket Tree, which was made from six sycamores grafted together.

text: Astronauts can cough in space but the cough doesn't sound like a typical cough on Earth as the sound waves don't have enough air molecules to travel and transfer the noise effectively.
label: contradicted
reason: Astronauts do cough, as well as sneeze and blow their noses, according to HowStuffWorks. The claim's reason for why the cough would sound different is wrong, though. Spacecraft like the ISS keep their air at about 14.7 psi, the same pressure as at sea level on Earth. So there are plenty of air molecules to carry sound, and a cough inside the station sounds normal. Low pressure only limits certain sounds, such as whistling inside a spacesuit, where the pressure is much lower. None of the sources say a cough sounds different because there isn't enough air.

text: Bacteria can only grow and reproduce in "moist" environments,  typically requiring a relative humidity of at least 80% to survive.
label: contradicted
reason: Search results confirm that water/moisture is needed for bacterial growth, but they contradict the specific thresholds in the claim. Microbiology and food-science sources state that most bacteria require a minimum water activity (equivalent to equilibrium relative humidity) of about 0.90–0.91 (90–91% RH), well above the claimed 80%, while some bacteria grow below that level — Staphylococcus aureus grows down to aw ~0.86 and halophilic bacteria can grow at aw ~0.75 (75% RH). The claim's assertion about needing ≥80% humidity 'to survive' is also contradicted, since bacteria (notably endospore-formers such as Bacillus and Clostridium) can survive desiccation and remain dormant for years or centuries in dry conditions, even though they cannot actively grow. Thus the stated humidity requirement and the conflation of growth with survival are both inaccurate.

text: Beehive-shaped structures in Mexico, known as "sweat houses," have been discovered to date back over 2,000 years to the Mayans or the Aztecs.

The sources disagree on how old temazcales are. One blog says the evidence goes back at least 1,200 years, while a non-scholarly Medium post says more than 3,000 years. The Aztecs also flourished centuries after 2,000 years ago, so that part of the claim is doubtful. The 2,000-year date in the search results belongs to an unrelated Maya beehive found at Nakum, in Guatemala. Because the specific discovery and its date could not be verified, the claim is inconclusive.

text: Plants can make sounds, although they are too faint for humans to hear, and researchers have recorded ultrasonic clicks from plants under stress.

text: Owens Falls Dam, completed in 1931 on the Idaho side but worked by Portland, Oregon is now known as one of the prime sites for Fall Chinook Salmon viewing in the State.

text: Beneath the waves of the Indian Ocean, near Taiwan, lies the South China Sea's deepest point: the Philippine Trench, but actually the lowest point is the "Lowell Seamount", but the lowest point, the 'lowell Seamount' is unknown and was never discovered or was priorly went underwater

The Philippine Trench lies east of the Philippines, outside the South China Sea. No reliable source names a 'Lowell Seamount' as the sea's deepest point, and a seamount is a rise in the seafloor, so by definition it cannot be the lowest point. text: Galileo Galilei was the first person to observe the planet Neptune using a telescope, but he didn't recognize it as a planet.

text: A partitions of the Mandelbrot set can form the swirling patterns familiar to most, however using a tiny zoom creates patterns familiar to every domain in mathematics including statistical mechanics, information theory, quantum mechanics and beyond.
label: not_verifiable

text: Honeybees are able to fly by using their wings to produce electricity through a process called triboelectrification, which helps to attract and trap pollen.
label: contradicted
reason: Bees do pick up a positive static charge while flying, and this is partly due to the triboelectric effect (charge transfer through friction or contact). That charge helps draw negatively charged pollen onto their bodies. However, the claim gets the cause backwards. Bees fly because their wing beats create aerodynamic lift. The charge is a side effect of flight, not what makes flight possible. The research describes bees gaining charge 'by virtue of triboelectric effect during flight,' not producing electricity in order to fly. The claim also overstates the role of the wings: one review says the cause of the charge 'is not yet fully understood' and is only partly triboelectric. Because the claim says triboelectrification is how bees fly, it is contradicted.

text: Astronauts on the International Space Station have reported they can see the Great Barrier Reef from outer space, but this is a common myth; in reality, it is not visible.
label: contradicted
reason: The claim says it's a myth that the Great Barrier Reef can be seen from space, and that's wrong. ESA has published a photo of the reef that astronaut André Kuipers took from the ISS. ABC News reported on photos of the reef that astronaut Kjell Lindgren shared from the station. NASA Earth Observatory and Sky at Night magazine also say the reef can be seen from space. (The well-known 'visible from space' myth is actually about the Great Wall of China.)

text: While there's no single largest living organism, a massive fungus, Armillaria ostoyae, spans over 2,200 acres in Oregon, USA, and is estimated to be around 2,400 years old.

Some sources give higher estimates, up to roughly 8,000–8,650 years, so 2,400 is the low end of the range. Since "estimated around 2,400 years" is a common published figure, this does not contradict the claim. The opening line, that there is no single largest living organism, is framing rather than a factual dispute. It reflects that the record depends on how you measure: by area, mass or other criteria.

text: In 2019, the world's largest living organism was discovered in a Blue Mountains forest, a massive fungus that spans about 2,200 acres and is estimated to be over 2,400 years old.

text: Scientists estimate that there may be between 700,000 and 1 million species of insects on Earth, but they have formally described only around 1 million out of an estimated total of 8.7 million animal species.

text: Humans and elephants share several physical and behavioral similarities, including gestation periods of almost two years, with human pregnancies lasting around 280 days and elephant pregnancies lasting almost 22 months.
label: contradicted
reason: Live Science says elephant pregnancies average about 640–660 days, which is close to 22 months, and that human pregnancies average about 280 days (40 weeks). Elephants have the longest pregnancy of any land animal, roughly 2.4 times as long as a human's, so the two species do not share a near-two-year gestation period. The central claim is false.

text: Honeybees are able to fly by using electricity generated from the movement of their wings, which allows them to attract pollen and other particles.

But electricity is not what keeps them in the air. Honeybees fly using aerodynamics: muscles flap their wings and the moving air creates lift. The charge is a side effect of flying, not how they fly, so the claim's main point is false.

text: In the heart of the Amazon rainforest, there exists a type of jellyfish which is immortal, known as the Turritopsis dohrnii, also called the "immortal jellyfish," because it can transform its body into a younger state through a process called transdifferentiation.
label: contradicted

Britannica says it comes from the Mediterranean Sea and has spread through the world's oceans, probably carried in ships' ballast water. A PubMed review also places it in the Mediterranean Sea. None of the sources mention it in the Amazon rainforest.

text: Honeybees are able to fly by using their wings to produce electricity through a process called triboelectrification, which allows them to attract pollen.

text: Plants can make sounds, too, with scientists recording ultrasonic clicks and murmurs coming from stressed-out plants, including cabbage and corn stalks.
label: supported

text: In 2019, the world's largest living organism was discovered in a Western Australia forest, covering over 2,200 acres and estimated to be around 4,500 years old.

The area of about 2,200–2,385 acres belongs to the honey mushroom (Armillaria ostoyae) in Oregon's Malheur National Forest.

text: Did you know that the world's largest living organism is a fungus called Armillaria ostoyae, a honey mushroom that covers over 2,200 acres in Oregon, USA?
label: supported

text: Scientists estimate that there are approximately 8.7 million identified species on Earth, but the total number of species, including undiscovered ones, is believed to be around 30 million.
label: contradicted
reason: The claim misstates the 8.7 million figure. That number comes from Mora et al. (PLoS Biology, 2011) and is an estimate of all species on Earth, including undiscovered ones. It is not a count of identified species. Only about 1.2 to 2 million species have actually been described. The claim also gives about 30 million as the total, which is not the widely cited estimate from that work.

text: Honeybees are able to swim by using the surface tension of water to stay afloat and their wings to propel themselves through the water.
