No source supports tarantula or tarantula-like fossils from about 145 million years ago. If 'tarantula-like' were read broadly to include all mygalomorph spiders, that record goes back much further, so 145 million years still would not fit.

text: Cassini Crater, located on the surface of Saturn's moon Titan, is approximately 313 miles in diameter, making it one of the largest impact craters in the Saturn system.
label: contradicted
reason: Cassini Crater is on Mars, not on Saturn's moon Titan. It sits in the Arabia quadrangle and is about 415 km (roughly 258 miles) across, not 313 miles. Titan's largest impact crater is Menrva, about 425 km wide, and the second largest, Forseti, is about 140 km. The impact-crater list for Titan does not include any Cassini crater.

text: Tarantulas have been around for a long time - the oldest known tarantula fossil is estimated to be over 135 million years old.
label: contradicted
reason: The 135-million-year figure is wrong. Live Science, reporting on a 2021 study, says only two tarantula (Theraphosidae) fossils are known, both in amber: one from Mexico about 16 million years old and one from Myanmar about 100 million years old. The same research dates the group's origin to about 120 million years ago. The first part of the claim, that tarantulas are old, holds up. Fossils of related mygalomorph spiders go back about 240 million years, but those are tarantula-like relatives, not tarantulas.

text: A large percentage of human brains are actually more active and often at their most creative when we're asleep, which is why many people report waking up with innovative ideas or solutions.
label: supported
reason: Reliable sources broadly support the claim. University of Notre Dame research coverage says many brain regions, especially those involved in learning, information processing and emotion, are more active during sleep than when awake. TIME reports research suggesting the brain may be at its most inventive and creative during sleep, with better answers having a chance to emerge. A Science Advances study (PMC) found that the sleep-onset stage triples the chance of discovering a hidden rule after waking. Wikipedia's article on sleep and creativity also notes that sleep promotes insight. One caveat: the claim's wording 'a large percentage of human brains' is vague. Not all brain activity rises during sleep; NREM sleep shows reduced activity, and the increase is mainly in REM and certain regions. Even so, the general point that many brain regions are more active and creative during sleep, leading to waking insights, matches the evidence.

text: Tarantulas have been on Earth for a long time, with the oldest known tarantula fossil dating back around 165 million years to the Jurassic period.
label: contradicted
reason: My searches ran out before I could get full results, so this verdict rests mostly on background knowledge, not on retrieved text. I know of no 165-million-year-old Jurassic tarantula fossil. The oldest fossils attributed to tarantulas (Theraphosidae) are Cretaceous at most, such as material in Burmese amber about 100 million years old. Undisputed ones are much younger, such as Miocene Dominican amber. Molecular dating, including the 2024 Foley et al. study, puts the group's origin at roughly 120 million years ago, in the Cretaceous. A result I could only partly see (The Tarantula Collective, 'Did Tarantulas Live with Dinosaurs?') appears to cover this, but I could not read it. Tarantulas are indeed ancient, but the specific claim of a ~165-million-year Jurassic fossil does not match the known record.

text: A blue whale can hold up to 2,000 gallons of krill and small fish in its mouth alone.
label: contradicted
reason: The claim's figure doesn't match reliable sources. The Aquarium of the Pacific says a blue whale's throat grooves expand so it can take in as much as 64,252 L (about 17,000 gallons) of food and water in one mouthful. Other common estimates put a mouthful at about 90 tons. The claim's 'up to 2,000 gallons' is far below these figures, so it misstates the maximum. Blue whales also feed almost entirely on krill rather than 'krill and small fish.' The search did not turn up any reliable source for the 2,000-gallon figure. One caveat: the sources measure food and water together, while the claim describes only krill and fish. Even so, '2,000 gallons' is not a documented maximum, so the claim is best judged contradicted.

text: A blue whale's heartbeat can be as loud as 188 decibels, which is louder than a jet taking off, despite the sound being made underwater.
label: contradicted
reason: The 188-decibel number comes from the blue whale's call, not its heartbeat. Enchanted Learning says the blue whale's call reaches up to 188 dB and can be heard for hundreds of miles underwater, and a GMAT Club item likewise links 188 dB to the whale's vocalization. No source says the heartbeat reaches 188 dB, so the claim credits the call's loudness to the heartbeat.

text: A blue whale's heartbeat is so strong that scientists claim they can be detected from over 500 miles (800 km) away.
label: contradicted
reason: Common sources, including the Whaling Museum blog, put the distance at about 2 miles (roughly 3.2 km), not more than 500 miles. Even the 2-mile figure is a popular fact that hasn't been firmly verified. The very long distances (hundreds of miles or more) usually refer to blue whale calls, not their heartbeats. So the 500-mile/800 km figure for a heartbeat is wrong.

text: A fetus can develop its unique fingerprints as early as 3 months in the womb, and these prints remain unchanged for a person's entire life.
label: supported
reason: Several sources say fingerprint ridges start forming around weeks 10–13 of pregnancy, which is about 3 months, and develop their unique patterns between roughly weeks 13 and 19. The same sources say fingerprints stay essentially unchanged for life once they form. One caveat: the patterns are not fully complete at 3 months; that happens later (around weeks 17–24). Read as 'starts developing as early as 3 months', the claim matches the evidence.

text: A fetus can develop its unique fingerprints as early as 3 months into pregnancy.
label: supported
reason: Several sources agree that fingerprints start to form around the end of the first trimester, which matches the claim's 'as early as 3 months.' LiveScience says the patterns begin forming in about the 10th week of gestation and are set by week 17. EHD.org says fingerprints begin to emerge at around 9–10 weeks. Pregnancy sites such as CloudNine and minymemos give 10–13 weeks, which is about 3 months. The patterns are not final until roughly 17–24 weeks, and one less reliable source (Brainly) says 16 weeks. Still, the claim is about when development starts, and the reliable sources back that up.

text: A giant squid's eyes are the largest of any animal, with some specimens having eyes that reach up to 10 inches in diameter.
label: supported
reason: The Smithsonian's Ocean Portal says giant squid have the largest eye in the animal kingdom, measuring up to 10 inches in diameter, which matches the claim. NBC News reports the same figure. Other sources give the record to the colossal squid, whose eyes reach about 27 cm (11 inches). However, the peer-reviewed research by Nilsson and Warrant (PMC) finds that the eyes of both giant and colossal squid grow to about 27 cm, roughly three times larger than any other animal's eyes. Since both squids share the top size range, the claim still holds as stated.

text: A recent study suggests that trees that live in areas where there are more birds and bats have more fruit and higher seed production.
label: supported
reason: Several peer-reviewed studies back the main point. Ocampo-Ariza et al. (2023, Ecological Applications) kept birds, bats and ants away from cacao trees in Peru and found that "cacao yield was higher in the presence of birds and bats" than on any tree where they were excluded. Maas et al. (2013) found that keeping birds and bats away from cacao trees in Indonesia cut yield by 31%. Cacao yield is measured as beans, which are the seeds, so this covers both more fruit and more seeds. Two caveats: these are exclusion experiments on a crop tree rather than comparisons of areas with more or fewer birds and bats, and one study (Wiley-hosted, via ResearchGate) found mixed results, where bird effects depended on shade and bats had no effect. The claim also doesn't name its study, so I can't confirm it means these exact papers. Still, the general finding matches, so I've rated it supported.

text: Barlow's Wheel is an optical illusion invented in 1825 by British physician Peter Barlow, which creates the appearance of a spinning wheel due to the way our brains process patterns in motion.
label: contradicted
reason: The claim is wrong on several points. Barlow's Wheel was not an optical illusion. It was an early demonstration of a homopolar electric motor: current runs through the wheel's hub to a mercury contact, and the wheel really does rotate because of the electromagnetic (Lorentz) force. Peter Barlow built it in 1822, not 1825, and he was an English mathematician and physicist, not a physician.

text: Beehives are maintained at a constant temperature of around 92°F (33.3°C) to ensure the health and productivity of the colony.
label: supported
reason: Several sources support the claim. Loudoun Beekeepers says bees keep their central brood nest at 92–93°F whatever the weather outside. Oregon State Extension says honey bees keep their hives between 32–36°C (89.6–96.8°F), and outside that range the colony suffers. Research sources describe a remarkably constant brood nest temperature of about 33–35°C, which is critical for normal larval and pupal development. One caveat: many sources put the figure slightly higher, around 93–95°F (34–35°C), and the tight control applies mainly to the brood area rather than the whole hive. Still, 'around 92°F (33.3°C)' falls within the reported ranges, so the claim holds.

text: Bionic limbs are being developed to give paralysed people the ability to control their prosthetic limbs by simply thinking of the action.
label: supported
reason: Science magazine (science.org) reported that two people who were almost completely paralysed used a brain implant to control a robotic arm with their thoughts alone. They could reach for and grasp objects, such as a thermos of coffee. This shows that thought-controlled bionic or robotic limbs are being developed for paralysed people. The wording "prosthetic limbs" is a bit loose, since the study used a robotic arm, but the main point of the claim matches the evidence.

text: Did you know that the world's largest waterfall, by volume of water, is actually located underwater and is called the Denmark Strait Cataract?
label: supported
reason: HowStuffWorks, which agrees with other popular science sources like NOAA and EarthSky, says the Denmark Strait cataract between Greenland and Iceland is the world's largest waterfall. It lies entirely underwater and carries about 5 million cubic meters of water per second, roughly 2,000 times more than Niagara Falls. That backs up the claim that the largest waterfall by volume is underwater and goes by this name.

text: Female mangrove crabs can change sex from female to male after reaching a certain age or size.
label: contradicted
reason: The sources contradict the claim. I found no evidence that female mangrove crabs naturally change from female to male as they get older or bigger. In mud crabs (Scylla serrata, S. paramamosain and S. tranquebarica), sex is set genetically by a WZ/ZZ chromosome system, and most malacostracan crustaceans, the group that includes crabs, have separate, fixed sexes. Researchers have only tried to masculinize mud crabs artificially with hormone treatments, and one 17α-methyltestosterone trial found no significant effect. None of this points to natural sex change. The search did turn up the 'mangrove rivulus', but that is a fish, not a crab, so it does not support the claim.

text: Female mangrove crabs can change sex from female to male as they mature.
label: contradicted
reason: I found no evidence that any mangrove crab changes sex from female to male. The studies I found on mangrove crabs (Ucides cordatus) and mangrove mud crabs (Scylla serrata and S. olivacea) treat males and females as fixed sexes and compare their sexual dimorphism, sex ratios and sex-specific growth. One source says malacostracan crustaceans, the group that includes crabs, are generally gonochoristic, meaning each animal is one sex for life, with sex set genetically. The source says some decapods and isopods are an exception: they change from male to female, the opposite direction to the claim, and mangrove crabs are not named among them. In my searches, the sex-changing animals linked to mangroves were other species, such as the mangrove rivulus fish, and I found no source supporting the claim. One caveat is that I found no source that directly says mangrove crabs cannot change sex, so this verdict rests on the general rule for crabs and the lack of any supporting evidence.

text: Honeybees are able to fly by using electricity, with the beat of their wings generating a positive static electric charge.
label: contradicted
reason: Reliable sources, including a ScienceDirect review on aerial electroreception and a ResearchGate study, confirm part of the claim: honeybees build up a positive static charge through friction between their wings and body and the air. These sources describe that charge as a byproduct of flight. It helps bees pick up pollen and sense the electric fields of flowers. None of the sources say bees use electricity to fly. Bee flight depends on aerodynamics, so the claim's main point, that bees fly by using electricity, is false.

text: Honeybees are able to fly by using their wings to generate lift, but also by generating additional lift through the movement of their entire body.
label: supported
reason: A peer-reviewed study, Nachtigall & Hanauer-Thieser (1992), J Comp Physiol B, 'Flight of the honeybee V', measured forces on honeybee bodies and found that 'the body is able to generate dynamic lift.' This non-wing lift comes from the body's shape and banking as it moves through the air. The effect is small: only a few percent of body weight in fast flight, or about 8.4% of body weight at the speed reported in the paper. The wings still produce most of the lift, through short, high-frequency strokes (Altshuler et al. 2005, PNAS). Together, these sources support the claim that wings provide lift and the moving body adds a small amount more.

text: Honeybees are able to recognize and remember human faces, and they are also able to use this information to identify potential threats.
label: not_verifiable
reason: The first part of the claim holds up. Dyer et al. (2005, Journal of Experimental Biology) found that honeybees can be trained with sugar rewards to tell human face photos apart and remember them for at least two days, and Science, Scientific American and Phys.org all reported the result. The second part, that bees use face recognition to spot threats, has no clear support. These were lab tasks with rewards, and the studies say bees have no evolutionary reason to recognise faces. NC State bee expert David Tarpy said there is 'no real need for them to distinguish one big mammal from another,' and noted that bees rely mainly on smell. He did say bees can anticipate threats such as bears or humans robbing honey, but he linked this to learning by time of day (circadian rhythms), not to recognising faces. Since the threat part can't be verified, the claim as a whole is inconclusive.

text: Humans share about 50% of their DNA with bananas, highlighting the shared ancestry of all living organisms.
label: contradicted
reason: Several reliable sources say the '50% of DNA' figure is a myth. The Naked Scientists (University of Cambridge), IFLScience and the Dessimoz lab explain that people mix up shared genes with shared DNA. Bananas have counterparts for very roughly 18–60% of human genes, depending on the method, but genes make up only about 2% of the genome, so the overlap in actual DNA is about 1% or less. Shared ancestry is real, but the claim's central figure is wrong.

text: Reindeer are excellent swimmers, and some populations in the Arctic migrate annually by swimming through icy waters to reach their summer habitats.
label: supported
reason: Reputable sources back both parts of the claim. The US Fish & Wildlife Service says caribou (the North American name for reindeer) are effective swimmers. Their hollow, buoyant hair and paddle-like hooves help them in water, and they cross rivers and other bodies of water during their long migrations. Animal Corner adds that they are very strong swimmers that swim through icy waters on seasonal migrations between winter ranges and calving and summer grounds. In northern Norway, reindeer also swim across sounds each year to reach summer pastures on islands, which matches the claim; I'm drawing that example from general knowledge, as it didn't come up in my search.

text: Roses arranged in a specific pattern can be used to encode secret messages through a technique known as floriography, which was popular during the Victorian era.
label: supported
reason: Sources say floriography, the language of flowers, was used in the Victorian era to send coded, covert messages. Invaluable notes that Victorian guides explained how to decipher the color, quantity and arrangement of flowers, and Antique Trader says roses carried specific meanings and that even how ribbons were tied on an arrangement mattered. That supports the idea that roses, including how they were arranged, could encode messages through floriography. One caveat: floriography covered many kinds of flowers, so it was not a technique limited to arranging roses in patterns.

text: Scientists have successfully trained bees to detect certain diseases, such as cancer, through scent recognition.
label: supported
reason: Several reputable sources back the claim. ABC News and Entomology Today (2013) report that bees can be trained by scent conditioning, linking an odour to a food reward, to react to the breath odours of diseases such as cancer, tuberculosis and diabetes. The person behind the glass bee device is Susana Soares, a Portuguese designer, and her work was a proof-of-concept rather than a validated diagnostic. Separately, Michigan State University researchers reported in 2024 that honeybees can detect lung-cancer biomarkers in breath. That study measured the bees' brain responses rather than training them, so it supports scent recognition but not the training part. Taken together, the evidence supports the general claim that bees have been trained to recognise disease odours, including cancer.

text: Spiders have been around for a long time, with fossil evidence showing they existed at least 318 million years ago, during the Carboniferous period.
label: supported
reason: The sources I found support the main point: the oldest known spider fossils come from the Carboniferous period, in coal measures of Europe and North America. The British Arachnological Society's review of spider origins mentions Upper Carboniferous material from Hagen-Vorhalle, Germany, dated to about 318 million years ago (Namurian). However, the same review names the oldest unequivocal spider as an Arthrolycosa specimen from about 315 million years ago, and other sources say the oldest spiders are about 300 million years old. So the exact figure of 'at least 318 million years' is borderline. Spiders clearly existed in the Carboniferous, but whether firm spider fossils reach 318 rather than about 315 million years ago depends on which fossils are accepted as true spiders. I couldn't finish further checks because the search limit ran out.

text: Tarantulas have been around for a long time, with fossil evidence showing that they've remained largely unchanged for over 120 million years.
label: contradicted
reason: The sources don't back the claim that fossils show tarantulas unchanged for over 120 million years. The 120-million-year figure comes from molecular dating: Foley et al. 2021 built a genetic family tree and estimated that tarantulas first appeared about 120 million years ago (Phys.org, Live Science, Smithsonian). Phys.org also notes that tarantula fossils are extremely rare. A 2023 paper in the Journal of Biogeography says the oldest known tarantula fossil is from Burmese amber and is only about 100 million years old. So no fossil goes back more than 120 million years. Texas Parks & Wildlife magazine says fossils show tarantulas virtually unchanged for more than 20 million years, not 120. Tarantulas are still an old group, but the claim's fossil basis and 'unchanged for over 120 million years' are contradicted.

text: Tarantulas have existed on Earth for at least 120 million years, with some species remaining largely unchanged since the time of the dinosaurs.
label: not_verifiable
reason: The first part checks out. Several reputable outlets (Live Science, Smithsonian, Big Think, IFLScience) report a Carnegie Mellon phylogenetic study that dates the first tarantulas to about 120 million years ago, in the Cretaceous, when dinosaurs were alive. I found no reliable evidence for the second part, that some species have stayed largely unchanged since the dinosaurs. The closest source, TPW Magazine, quotes a fossil record showing tarantulas 'virtually unchanged' for more than 20 million years. That is far short of the end of the dinosaur era about 66 million years ago. A hobbyist site goes further and says evolution 'absolutely reshaped them' while keeping their basic body plan. Because the 'unchanged since the dinosaurs' part can't be verified, the claim as a whole is inconclusive.

text: The short-lived ULONG glass frog, discovered in 2015, is capable of turning transparent when it sleeps or is under duress.
label: not_verifiable
reason: I found no record of a glass frog called the "ULONG" glass frog, so it is unclear what species the claim refers to. The glass frog described in Costa Rica in 2015 is Hyalinobatrachium dianae (the "Kermit" frog), and the sources describing it don't call it "ULONG." The ability to turn transparent while sleeping was documented in a different species, Fleischmann's glass frog (H. fleischmanni), in a 2022 study. None of the sources I found say this happens under duress or describe any such frog as short-lived. Because the frog can't be identified and several parts of the claim can't be checked, the evidence is not enough to support or contradict it.

text: Tigers have striped skin, not just striped fur, as the stripes are visible even when their fur is shaved.
label: supported
reason: Several sources agree with the claim. Wikipedia's White tiger article says a tiger's stripes are a pigmentation of the skin, and that if one were shaved its distinctive coat pattern would still be visible. Biology Insights and other sources say the same thing: shave a tiger and the stripes still show on its skin. One trivia source thinks the visible skin pattern may come from pigmented hair follicles, a bit like beard stubble. That is a possible caveat about the cause, but it doesn't change the claim that the stripes stay visible after shaving.

text: When heated to extremely high temperatures, certain types of glass can be molded and transformed into a metallic form, a process known as "glass metalization".
label: contradicted
reason: In the sources I found, 'glass metallization' means putting a thin metal coating on the surface of glass, for example by sputtering, silvering or spraying metal onto it. It does not mean heating glass until it turns into a metal. Wikipedia describes metallizing as coating metal on the surface of objects, and patents describe glass metallization as depositing a metal seed layer or coating on glass. Heated glass can be molded, but it stays glass. So the claim's description of how the process works is wrong.

text: When heated to extremely high temperatures, certain types of glass can be molded and transformed into a metallic form, a process known as "metallic glass."
label: contradicted
reason: Metallic glass (also called amorphous metal) does not come from heating ordinary glass until it turns metallic. It is a metal alloy that is cooled so quickly from its molten state, on the order of millions of degrees a second, that crystals never form. The metal ends up locked in a disordered, 'glassy' structure. It can also be made by vapor deposition, mechanical alloying and similar methods. The 'glass' in the name describes the atomic structure, so the claim gets the process backwards.

text: When heated to extremely high temperatures, certain types of glass can be molded into a dependent shape that can hold its form when cooled.
label: supported
reason: I treated "dependent shape" as a garbled "desired shape," since "dependent" doesn't make sense here. Read that way, the claim matches standard glass-forming practice. The Wikipedia article on warm (kiln-formed) glass and a USPTO glass-molding patent both describe heating glass until it softens, shaping it in a mold, and cooling it so it holds the molded shape. Different glass types need different softening temperatures, which fits the claim's "certain types of glass" and "extremely high temperatures." Nothing found contradicts the claim.

text: When heated to extremely high temperatures, certain types of glass can be molded into desired shapes and then rapidly cooled and annealed to create works of art.
label: supported
reason: The searches back up the main idea. Glass softened at high temperatures can be shaped, including with molds and by glassblowing, and is then annealed to relieve internal stress so finished pieces, including art glass, don't crack. One wording issue: annealing itself is controlled slow cooling through the annealing range, and sources warn that cooling molten glass too fast causes uneven stress. Still, in practice the piece does drop quickly from working temperature to the annealing temperature, and a patent source notes that faster cooling follows once the glass is through the annealing range. So I don't treat 'rapidly cooled and annealed' as a real contradiction, but this part of the wording is imprecise.

text: A UK network of hidden ' thicker' Garden-style allotments secret paths built during WW2, allowed people living locally, to move unseen.
label: not_verifiable
reason: I found no reliable source for a WW2 network of hidden 'thicker' garden- or allotment-style secret paths in the UK that let local people move unseen. Searches turned up only unrelated wartime features, such as secret bunkers, Auxiliary Unit hideouts and underground tunnels, and wartime allotments in general. None of these confirm the claim, and none clearly disprove it. The claim is also vague and unclear, especially the word 'thicker'.

text: A blue whale can produce over 1,000 gallons of saliva on a daily basis.
label: contradicted
reason: Baleines en direct (GREMM), a whale-science source, reports that cetaceans' salivary glands are shrunken or missing. Researchers it cites say whales make little or no saliva: they have no use for it under water, and making it could waste fresh water. I found no reliable source saying a blue whale makes more than 1,000 gallons of saliva a day. Big daily figures do exist for blue whale milk (about 50–150 gallons) and whale urine, but not for saliva, so the claim conflicts with what is known about whale biology.

text: A blue whale's heartbeat can be as loud as 188 decibels, louder than a jet taking off, and can be detected for hundreds of miles.
label: contradicted
reason: The 188-decibel figure, and the idea that the sound carries for hundreds of miles, describe the blue whale's call, not its heartbeat. Enchanted Learning says the call reaches up to 188 dB and can be heard for hundreds of miles underwater. NOAA Fisheries says the blue whale's heartbeat can be heard about 2 miles away, which is far short of 'hundreds of miles.' The claim mixes up the call and the heartbeat.

text: A blue whale's heartbeat can be as slow as two beats per minute when the animal is at rest.
label: contradicted
reason: The 2 beats-per-minute figure is real, but the claim gets the circumstances wrong. In the 2019 Goldbogen study, a tagged wild blue whale's heart rate fell to about 4–8 bpm, and sometimes as low as 2 bpm, at the deepest part of its feeding dives. When the whale surfaced to breathe and recover, its heart rate rose to 25–37 bpm. So the very slow heartbeat was linked to deep diving, not to the animal being at rest.

text: Astronauts cannot cry in space because tears do not fall down their faces due to the microgravity environment.
label: contradicted
reason: Space.com reports astronaut Chris Hadfield saying "Your eyes will definitely cry in space" but "tears don't fall." In microgravity, tears gather into a ball of water on the eye instead of running down the face. The claim gets this part right, but it is wrong to say astronauts cannot cry, because they do.

text: Astronauts cannot cry in the classical sense while in space because the microgravity environment prevents tears from flowing downward.
label: supported
reason: Several sources say that in microgravity, tears form but don't run down the face. Instead, surface tension holds them as a liquid ball on the eye until they're wiped away. Chris Hadfield's demonstration shows this, and outlets including Space.com and CBS describe it the same way; Futurism and Grunge go as far as saying astronauts "technically can't cry." That backs the claim's qualified wording, "cannot cry in the classical sense," along with its reason. Tears are still produced, but the claim's qualifier allows for that.

text: Astronomers estimate that there are approximately 100-400 billion stars in the Milky Way galaxy alone.
label: supported
reason: Wikipedia's Milky Way article says the galaxy is estimated to contain 100–400 billion stars ((1–4)×10^11), which matches the claim. Other astronomy sources commonly give the same range.

text: Awitter is a fast-growing, rare condition where animals and even people have the sensation of swallowing when there is nothing in their mouth, but little understanding is prevalent.
label: not_verifiable
reason: I found no reliable source that describes a medical condition called "Awitter" in animals or people. In my searches, "Awitter" showed up only as a masculine first name on howtopronounce.com and as a song title ("Awitter" by The Delusion, on Spotify and Deezer). The swallowing-disorder results, such as Penn Medicine's dysphagia page, never use the term. Nothing confirms the claim that it is a fast-growing, rare condition causing a phantom swallowing sensation, but no source directly refutes it either. The term looks fabricated, though the evidence isn't enough to call the claim contradicted.

text: A跪 on the planet Mars, scientists discovered water in the form of large ice caps in 2004.
label: supported
reason: The claim's opening word is garbled ("A跪"), but its core statement checks out. A March 18, 2004 Washington Post report says ESA's Mars Express confirmed a vast expanse of water ice at Mars' south pole. Universe Today reported the same in March 2004. Both describe a large water-ice cap found by scientists in 2004. One caveat: water ice in the north polar cap was known earlier, and earlier indirect observations had suggested ice at the south pole. Still, the 2004 discovery of water as large polar ice is well documented.

text: Bernard Bartalan, a Brazilian, holds the Guinness World Record for being the largest popcorn consumer, having eaten 267 handfuls in 8 minutes.
label: contradicted
reason: I found nothing at all about a 'Bernard Bartalan' setting a popcorn-eating record. Searches only turn up the name Bartalan as a Hungarian given name. The well-reported 8-minute popcorn-eating world record belongs to American competitive eater Joey Chestnut. He ate 32 servings of 24 oz each at Victory Field in Indianapolis in 2022, then beat that with 42 servings in 2025. One caveat: these are competitive-eating records, not Guinness World Records listings. Guinness's popcorn records found in the search go to other people, such as David Rush (USA) for catching popcorn. No source mentions a Brazilian eating 267 handfuls. Since a different person holds the 8-minute record and nothing backs Bartalan's, the claim is contradicted.

text: Bernard Bartalan, a Brazilian, holds the Guinness World Record for being the largest popcorn consumer, having eaten 850 pounds of popcorn in 2015
label: not_verifiable
reason: I found nothing that confirms this claim. The searches turned up only unrelated Guinness popcorn records: the largest popcorn sculpture (Sri Chinmoy Centre, 2006), popcorn balls, and popcorn containers. None of them mentioned anyone named Bernard Bartalan, a 'largest popcorn consumer' record, or 850 pounds eaten in 2015. My targeted searches for 'Bernard Bartalan' returned no results before the search limit was reached. The claim is probably fabricated, but I found no source that directly contradicts it, so it can't be verified either way.

text: Bernard Bartalan, an Austrian-language teacher, holds the Guinness World Record for the longest duration without sleep, staying awake for a total of 264.4 hours (11 days).
label: contradicted
reason: Bernard Bartalan didn't set the 264.4-hour (11-day) sleep-deprivation record. Reliable sources, including Wikipedia, credit it to Randy Gardner, a 17-year-old student from San Diego, in 1963–64. He wasn't an Austrian-language teacher. Guinness also no longer tracks this record, and Robert McDonald held a longer one of 453 hours. No source links Bartalan to this record.

text: Did you know that a blue whale's heart can beat around 4-8 beats per minute and pump approximately 5,000 liters of blood with every beat?
label: contradicted
reason: The heart rate part checks out. Reporting on Goldbogen's 2019 PNAS study, which tagged a wild blue whale, describes a heart rate of about 4–8 beats per minute during dives, dropping as low as 2. The volume per beat is badly overstated, though. Sources put each heartbeat at roughly 80 to 227 liters (about 60 gallons), and even the highest figure found, from a social media post, was about 1,000 liters. None comes close to 5,000 liters per beat, so the claim is contradicted.

text: Did you know that a heck of a lot of the ebooks and a third of audiobooks sold in the US are from romance novels.
label: not_verifiable
reason: The ebook part has partial support. Statistics aggregators (Gitnux, BestWriting) report that romance makes up about 30% of US ebook sales, and Zipdo puts it at 40%, which fits "a heck of a lot." However, I found no source supporting the specific claim that romance accounts for a third of US audiobook sales. The one genre breakdown I found (Coolest-Gadgets, citing Audio Publishers Association categories) puts romance at about 11% of audiobook revenue, well short of a third. That conflicts with the claim, but the source is a low-reliability aggregator. My searches hit their limit before I could check stronger industry data. With unreliable sources and the audiobook figure unconfirmed, the claim can't be called supported or clearly contradicted.

text: Dragonflies have existed for over 300 million years, and during the Paleozoic Era, some species had a wingspan of over 2 feet.
label: supported
reason: The search results support the claim. Smithsonian Gardens and the National Park Service say dragonflies, or their direct ancestors, go back about 300 million years. Sources usually give 'about 300 million' rather than 'over,' but the earliest dragonfly relatives (griffinflies) date to the Carboniferous, roughly 300–325 million years ago. ASU's Ask a Biologist and other sources describe Paleozoic dragonfly relatives such as Meganeura (Carboniferous) with wingspans of up to 65 cm, about 2.1 ft, which is over 2 feet. The Permian species Meganeuropsis was similarly large. One caveat: these giants were griffinflies (Meganisoptera), close relatives of modern dragonflies rather than true Odonata, but they are commonly called giant dragonflies.

text: Dragonflies have existed for over 300 million years, and during the Paleozoic Era, some species had a wingspan of up to 2 feet in length.
label: supported
reason: Discover Magazine says dragonfly-like 'griffinflies' with wingspans of up to 27 inches (70 cm), which it rounds to about 2 feet, lived around 300 million years ago in the Paleozoic era. ABC News also describes Paleozoic dragonflies from 300 million years ago with wingspans of roughly two to two and a half feet, and notes that dragonflies are still around today. One caveat: these Paleozoic giants were close relatives of modern dragonflies (griffinflies, or protodonates), not true dragonflies. Popular sources commonly call them dragonflies, though, so the claim holds in general terms.

text: Finland has a "forest library" called Kirjasaari, a large woodland area in which books are exchanged and left for others to read among the trees.
label: contradicted
reason: Kirjasaari exists, but it is not a forest library. Official Oulu city sources (ouka.fi and kirjastossatavataan.fi) describe it as a yearly event that has run since 2007. At the event, staff from Oulu City Library and the Kaipo libraries present the past year's new books for children, young people and adults, along with music, games and films, and authors appear as guests. It is held indoors at the Saari central library, and recent editions have also been streamed on YouTube. No source describes Kirjasaari as a woodland area where people exchange books among the trees, so that part of the claim is contradicted.

text: Fortaleza in Brazil is home to the world's largest cashew tree, which has become a UNESCO World Heritage site and is over 100 years old.
label: contradicted
reason: The world's largest cashew tree, the Cajueiro de Pirangi, is at Pirangi beach in Parnamirim, about 12 km south of Natal in Rio Grande do Norte. It is not in Fortaleza, which is in Ceará. The other tree that sometimes claims the title, Cajueiro da Praia, is in Piauí, so it is not in Fortaleza either. The Pirangi tree is recognized by Guinness World Records, but it is not a UNESCO World Heritage site.

text: Giraffes are the only animals born with their eyes open, and they are also able to walk within their first hour of birth, although they can't run for a bit.
label: contradicted
reason: The claim says giraffes are the only animals born with their eyes open, and that part is false. Many animals are born that way. These are called precocial young: cattle, sheep, horses, most other hoofed mammals, and hares are all born with their eyes open and are soon able to move around. The giraffe calf does walk within about an hour of birth, but the 'only animals' part is contradicted by reliable reference sources.

text: Giraffes are the only animals born with their eyes open, and they are also able to walk within their first hour of birth, although they can't run for about ten weeks.
label: contradicted
reason: The claim says giraffes are the only animals born with their eyes open, and that part is false. Oxford Reference, Wikipedia and Merriam-Webster all describe precocial young, which are born with their eyes open. These include grazing animals such as cattle, sheep and horses, as well as hares, and most hoofed mammals in general. Giraffe calves do stand and walk soon after birth, but because the 'only animals' part is wrong, the claim as a whole is contradicted. I did not check the 'can't run for ten weeks' detail.

text: Honey NeverSpoils, an archaeological team found pots of honey in an ancient Egyptian tomb that were over 3,000 years old and still edible.
label: supported
reason: Several sources, including History Facts, Smithsonian-style science write-ups and Yahoo News, report that archaeologists found pots of honey in ancient Egyptian tombs. They say the honey was about 3,000 years old and still edible. This matches the claim. Note that these are popular-science sources rather than primary archaeological reports, and the story is often repeated without detailed documentation.

text: Honeybees are able to fly by using electricity generated by the movement of their wings to create a positive charge that helps counteract the weight of their bodies.
label: contradicted
reason: Honeybees fly because of aerodynamics, not electricity. A Caltech study published in PNAS (Altshuler et al., 2005) found that they stay aloft with short wing strokes of about 90° at roughly 230 beats per second, plus rapid wing rotation when each stroke reverses. The authors conclude that this rapid wing motion alone 'is sufficient to maintain the weight of the animal.' Bees do build up a positive static charge in flight, but no research shows that charge helping to lift them or offset their weight. The claimed electrical mechanism goes against the established science.

text: Honeybees are able to fly by using electricity generated by their bodies to electrostatically charge the tiny hairs on their bodies, creating a natural force that aids in lift-off.
label: contradicted
reason: Research published in PNAS (Altshuler et al., 2005) shows that honeybees get their lift from wing aerodynamics: short wing strokes of about 90° at roughly 230 Hz, which create force peaks during each stroke. Bees do pick up a positive electrostatic charge, but they don't generate it with their bodies to help them fly. The charge builds up on their hairs from friction as they fly, and it helps pollen stick to them and lets them sense flowers' electric fields. No source says static electricity helps bees take off or stay in the air.

text: Honeybees are able to fly by using their wings to generate electricity and create an electric charge that helps to reduce air resistance.
label: contradicted
reason: Peer-reviewed research (Altshuler et al., PNAS 2005) shows honeybees fly using aerodynamics. They beat their wings very fast (about 230–240 Hz) with short strokes, and lift comes from a leading-edge vortex plus unsteady forces at the ends of each stroke. Bees do pick up static charge in flight, which helps them sense flowers and attract pollen. But no credible source says flight works by generating electricity or that the charge reduces air resistance.

text: Honeybees are able to fly by using their wings to generate electricity through a process called "triboelectric charging," which attracts pollen grains to their bodies.
label: contradicted
reason: The claim gets cause and effect backwards. Scientific sources confirm that bees build up static charge through the triboelectric effect, mostly from friction with the air while flying, and that this charge helps pull pollen onto their bodies. But that charge is a side effect of flying, not what keeps them in the air. Bees fly because their flapping wings create aerodynamic lift. They do not fly by using their wings to generate electricity, so the claim's central point is false.

text: Humans and dolphins are the only mammals known to give themselves names, with dolphins using a unique whistle to identify themselves.
label: contradicted
reason: The claim says humans and dolphins are the only mammals known to use names. That is no longer true. Dolphins do have signature whistles, but 2024 studies found that African elephants call each other with individual name-like calls. Another 2024 study found that marmoset monkeys use 'phee-calls' to name each other. A Hebrew University press release on EurekAlert and a CNN report both describe naming as a behavior seen in humans, dolphins, elephants and now marmosets.

text: Humans share about 50-60% of their DNA with bananas, highlighting the similarity in genetic structures across different species.
label: contradicted
reason: The claim confuses genes with DNA. Several sources, including HowStuffWorks, IFLScience and The Star, explain where the figure comes from: about 60% of human genes have a recognizable counterpart in the banana genome, and the proteins those genes encode are only about 40% identical. Because genes make up only around 1–2% of the genome, these sources put the real shared DNA at only about 1–2% of the human genome, or less. IFLScience calls the popular statement "technically incorrect – mostly because it's not 60 percent, and it's not DNA." So the claim that humans share 50–60% of their DNA with bananas is a misconception.

text: NASA's Juno spacecraft has revealed that Jupiter's Great Red Spot storm has been raging continuously for at least 187 years.
label: supported
reason: The 187-year figure checks out, but Juno isn't what established it. Spaceflight Now's July 2017 report on Juno's first close-up images of the Great Red Spot described its winds as "howling for at least 187 years." That figure comes from NASA saying in 2017 that the storm had been monitored since about 1830. NASA/JPL and other sources likewise say the storm has raged since at least the 1800s, and a 2024 study puts its age at more than 190 years, dating it to 1831. These sources agree with the claim's core fact. However, the age comes from historical telescope records, not from Juno's own measurements. The claim's wording that Juno "revealed" the age is therefore loose, though it reflects how Juno-era coverage reported the storm's age.

text: Owens Falls Dam, located in Idaho, is one of the world's first hydroelectric dams.
label: contradicted
reason: The claim is wrong on two counts. The Owen Falls Dam, now called the Nalubaale Dam, is in Jinja, Uganda, on the Victoria Nile, not in Idaho. It was also completed in 1954, long after the first hydroelectric plants were built in the 1880s, so it is not one of the world's first hydroelectric dams.

text: Polar bears are classified as excellent swimmers, and have been known to swim for hours or even days at a time, covering distances of up to 60 miles without resting.
label: supported
reason: The sources back each part of the claim. Several describe polar bears as exceptional or powerful swimmers that can swim for hours or days without a break. PolarBears.com says some bears have reportedly swum up to 60 miles (96 km) without stopping, which matches the claim's figure. One caveat: GPS tracking reported by LiveScience and The World shows much longer swims, including one of about 426 miles (687 km) over 9 days. So '60 miles' is a common conservative figure, not the true maximum. It understates what bears can do rather than overstating it, so I don't treat it as a contradiction.

text: Polar bears are classified as excellent swimmers, with some individuals recorded swimming over 60 miles non-stop without resting.
label: supported
reason: A U.S. Geological Survey study, reported by Defenders of Wildlife, tracked a radio-collared female polar bear in the Beaufort Sea. She swam 426 miles (687 km) without stopping over nine days, about 232 hours, before reaching an ice floe to rest. That is far more than 60 miles. The sources also say polar bears regularly swim between land and ice floes, which fits the claim that they are excellent swimmers.

text: Polar bears are excellent swimmers and have been known to swim for hours or even days at a time in search of food or to migrate.
label: supported
reason: National Geographic reports that a GPS-collared female polar bear swam for a record nine days straight, covering 426 miles (687 km). Another bear in the same study swam for more than 12 days, though she appears to have found places to rest along the way. The study looked at more than 50 swims longer than 50 km. This backs up the claim that polar bears are excellent swimmers that can swim for hours or even days. Their reasons for swimming, such as reaching sea ice where they hunt and moving between areas as the ice shrinks, are widely documented and fit the claim's 'in search of food or to migrate.'

text: Roses arranged in a specific pattern in the shape of " corpuscular roses" by Robert Hooke in 1661, were the first object viewed under an improved microscope.
label: contradicted
reason: I found no source that mentions Robert Hooke viewing roses arranged as "corpuscular roses" in 1661. Hooke's microscope observations were published in Micrographia in January 1665, and the book's first observation is the point of a sharp needle, not roses. The cells he is known for were seen in cork. Neither the 1661 event nor the claim that roses were the first object viewed is supported, and the record of his first observation contradicts it.

text: Roses arranged in a specific, intricate pattern on a stem can actually form a naturally occurring, mathematical concept called a "Fibonacci spiral."
label: supported
reason: Sources on phyllotaxis say rose petals, like other plant parts arranged around a stem or central point, follow a spiral pattern linked to the Fibonacci sequence and the golden angle. Study.com names 'the spiral pattern of rose petals as they open' as an example of a Fibonacci spiral in nature, and a separate investigation of spiral phyllotaxis in roses makes the same link. The claim's wording is loose, since it is the petals or leaves rather than whole roses that form the spiral, but its main point is backed by these sources.

text: Roses arranged in a specific, intricate pattern on a stem can actually form a naturally occurring, mathematical concept called a Fibonacci spiral.
label: supported
reason: The sources I found agree that rose petals grow in a spiral pattern linked to Fibonacci numbers. An arXiv paper on the Fibonacci lattice calls it a mathematical idealization of repeated plant elements "such as rose petals," and other sources say a rose's overlapping petals form a logarithmic spiral, with wild roses having five petals, a Fibonacci number. The claim's wording is loose (it says roses are arranged 'on a stem'), but its main point holds: the spiral arrangement in roses can form a naturally occurring Fibonacci-type spiral.

text: Some mushrooms, specifically the Armillaria ostoyae fungus, are known to be the largest living organisms in the world, covering over 2,200 acres in Oregon, USA.
label: supported
reason: The National Wildlife Federation describes the Armillaria ostoyae fungus in eastern Oregon as the world's largest living organism, covering "more than 2,200 acres." The Oregon Encyclopedia says the Humongous Fungus in Malheur National Forest covers 2,385 acres and is believed to be the largest single living organism by biomass. Both sources support every part of the claim.

text: Some mushrooms, specifically the Armillaria ostoyae fungus, are known to be the largest living organisms in the world, covering over 2,200 acres in a single colony.
label: supported
reason: Guinness World Records names a single honey mushroom (Armillaria ostoyae) in Oregon's Malheur National Forest as the largest living organism. It covers 965 hectares (2,385 acres), which is more than the 2,200 acres in the claim. Other sources give the same 2,385-acre figure.

text: Some mushrooms, specifically the Armillaria ostoyae fungus, can grow to be over 2,200 acres in size, making them among the largest living organisms on Earth.
label: supported
reason: Several reliable sources, including Discover Magazine, Scientific American and Wikipedia, say the Armillaria ostoyae 'humongous fungus' in Oregon's Malheur National Forest covers about 2,385 acres, which is more than 2,200 acres. They also describe it as one of the largest known living organisms on Earth. This backs up both the size and the 'among the largest organisms' parts of the claim.

text: Spiders have been present on Earth for at least 318 million years, with ancient fossils of spider-like creatures found during the Devonian period.
label: supported
reason: Reliable sources back both parts of the claim. Wikipedia's 'Evolution of spiders' page says spiders have existed for at least 380 million years, which fits 'at least 318 million years.' It also places the oldest reported true spiders in the Carboniferous. Devonian fossils of spider-like arachnids are well documented: Attercopus fimbriunguis, about 380–390 million years old, was once claimed as the oldest spider. It was later reclassified into Uraraneida, an extinct order of spider-like arachnids that could make silk, and the Royal Society paper and British Arachnological Society material support this. I couldn't confirm the exact 318-million-year figure in the search results, but the claim only sets a minimum age, and the evidence meets it. Nothing I found contradicts the claim.

text: Spiders have been present on Earth for at least 318 million years, with fossil records showing that they existed during the Devonian period.
label: contradicted
reason: The evidence contradicts the Devonian part of the claim. The roughly 318–319 million-year figure points to the Carboniferous period, which came after the Devonian (about 419–359 million years ago). Attercopus, a Devonian fossil from about 380–386 million years ago, was once called the oldest spider. Its discoverers later reclassified it as a proto-spider without spinnerets, placing it in the extinct group Uraraneida. Smithsonian and the PNAS/Royal Society research indicate that the oldest true spider fossils are Carboniferous. Some sources, including one Wikipedia line, still say spiders are at least 380 million years old, but they rely on the reclassified Attercopus. So the fossil record does not show true spiders in the Devonian.

text: Tarantulas have been around for a long time, with fossils of these eight-legged creatures dating back to the Early Cretaceous period, over 135 million years ago.
label: contradicted
reason: The claim's dates don't match the fossil record. A peer-reviewed study in the Journal of Biogeography (Wiley) says the oldest known tarantula (Theraphosidae) fossil comes from Burmese amber and is about 100 million years old. That is mid-Cretaceous, not Early Cretaceous more than 135 million years ago. The same study puts the earlier split between tarantulas and their relatives at about 120 million years ago (range 109–132), but that date comes from molecular-clock estimates, not from fossils, and still falls short of 135 million years. Most other tarantula fossils are from Miocene amber, which is much younger.

text: Tarantulas have been on Earth for a long time, with fossil evidence dating back around 135 million years to the Jurassic period.
label: contradicted
reason: The figure and the period don't fit the evidence. Live Science says only two tarantula fossils are known, both in amber: one from Myanmar about 100 million years old and one from Mexico about 16 million years old. The 2021 Carnegie Mellon study, reported by Phys.org, Smithsonian and Big Think, dates the first tarantulas to about 120 million years ago, in the Cretaceous period. That is not 135 million years ago, and not the Jurassic. The claim also contradicts itself: 135 million years ago falls in the Early Cretaceous, because the Jurassic ended about 145 million years ago. It is true that tarantulas are an old group, but no reliable source supports 135-million-year-old Jurassic fossils.

text: Tarantulas have been on Earth for over 100 million years, with fossil records showing they existed even in the Cretaceous period.
label: supported
reason: Molecular-clock studies reported by Phys.org, Smithsonian and Live Science (Foley et al. 2021) place the origin of tarantulas about 120 million years ago, in the Cretaceous. On the fossil side, a 2023 Journal of Biogeography study includes what it calls the oldest theraphosid fossil, found in Burmese amber and dated to about 100 million years ago (Wunderlich & Müller, 2020). Live Science also mentions a Myanmar fossil. Together these back both the 'over 100 million years' age and Cretaceous fossil evidence. One caveat: tarantula fossils are extremely rare, and most known specimens come from much younger Eocene–Miocene amber. The ~100-million-year Burmese fossil is roughly at the threshold, while the 120-million-year figure comes from molecular estimates.

text: Turtles have an innate navigation system that allows them to migrate thousands of miles each year and return to their exact birthplace to lay eggs.
label: contradicted
reason: Part of the claim holds up. Sea turtles navigate using Earth's magnetic field, migrate long distances, and come back to their natal area to nest (Cell/Current Biology, National Geographic). But the claim says they make this trip "each year," and reliable sources say otherwise. The Sea Turtle Conservancy says females typically don't nest in consecutive years and often skip one or two years. The Olive Ridley Project says they usually nest only every 2–3 years. Cell/Current Biology says they return to the same stretch of coastline, the Sea Turtle Conservancy says "most" females return to their natal beach, and the Sea Turtle Conservancy notes many migrations are hundreds of miles, only occasionally thousands. text: Turtles have an innate navigational system that allows them to migrate thousands of miles across oceans and return to their birthplaces to lay eggs.
label: supported
reason: I'm reading "turtles" here as sea turtles. UNC biologists (Lohmann lab) report that sea turtles migrate thousands of miles across the ocean and then come back to nest on the same stretch of coast where they hatched. They do this by sensing Earth's magnetic field. Hatchlings imprint on the magnetic signature of their home beach and use it to find their way back as adults. The magnetic sense itself is built in, though the beach-specific signature is learned through imprinting. Overall, the evidence supports the claim.

text: When heated to extremely high temperatures, certain types of glass can be molded and transformed into a metallic form, a process often referred to as "metallic glass."
label: contradicted
reason: The claim gets metallic glass backwards. Metallic glass is not ordinary glass that turns into metal when heated. It is a metal or metal alloy that is cooled so quickly, often at millions of degrees per second, that crystals cannot form. The metal is left with a disordered, glass-like (amorphous) structure. It can also be made by methods such as vapor deposition and mechanical alloying. Heating glass does not transform it into a metal.

text: Beehive-shaped structures in the Australian Outback, known as "termite mounds", are built by millions of termites working together and can be up to 20 feet tall and last for decades.

That fits 'can be up to 20 feet tall and last for decades.' Since the tallest reported mounds are 8 m, 'up to 20 feet' undersells the maximum, but no source contradicts it. text: Scientists estimate that there may be between 700,000 and 1 million species on Earth, but we have formally described only about 1.3 million, however only 14% of all described species have been assessed by the International Union for Conservation of Nature (IUCN).
label: contradicted
reason: The claim doesn't hold together, and it conflicts with mainstream estimates. A total of 700,000 to 1 million species can't be right if about 1.3 million species have already been formally described. The widely cited PLoS Biology study (Mora et al. 2011) puts the number of species on Earth at about 8.7 million, with about 1.2 million described. That makes the claimed 700k–1M range far too low. I also have doubts about the 14% IUCN figure. From memory, about 170,000 species have been assessed out of roughly 2 million described, which is under 10%. I didn't confirm that number with a search, though. The species-count error alone is enough to contradict the claim.

text: All mammals, except for humans and a small number of other primates and marine mammals, have a cloaca, an opening that is used for reproduction, digestion, and excretion.
label: contradicted
reason: The claim gets this backwards. Wikipedia says that "with a few exceptions noted below, mammals have no cloaca." Most placental mammals don't have one. A true cloaca is found mainly in monotremes, and marsupials and a few other mammals have cloaca-like openings. So it is false that all mammals except humans, a few primates and marine mammals have a cloaca.

text: Galileo Galilei was the first person to observe the planet Neptune using a telescope in 1613, but it wasn't recognized as a planet at that time.
label: supported
reason: Wikipedia and Astronomy.com say Galileo sketched Neptune with his telescope, including on January 27, 1613, but mistook it for a fixed star. He is considered the first known telescopic observer, and the planet was not recognized until it was formally discovered in 1846. One correction: his first recorded sighting was on December 28, 1612, so the observations ran from late 1612 into 1613. This does not overturn the main claim.

text: Honeybees are able to fly by using their wings to produce electricity through a process called "triboelectric charging," which allows them to attract pollen from flowers.
label: contradicted
reason: Bees build up a static charge through triboelectric charging, mostly from friction with the air while they fly, and that charge helps pollen move onto them electrostatically. But this is a side effect of flying, not how they fly. Bees fly by aerodynamics, flapping their wings fast to make lift. The claim gets this backwards when it says bees fly by using their wings to produce electricity.

text: In the heart of the Amazon rainforest, there exists a type of jellyfish which is immortal, known as the Turritopsis dohrnii, however it doesn't live in the Amazon, this 'immortal' creature is found within the oceans worldwide.
label: contradicted

That is false, since the species lives only in the sea. The claim then says the jellyfish doesn't live in the Amazon, so it contradicts itself. Because the claim does assert a false Amazon location, I labeled it contradicted rather than supported.

text: Honeybees are able to fly by using electricity generated by their bodies to attract and manipulate pollen grains and create lift, a phenomenon known as 'triboelectric charging'.
label: contradicted
reason: Honeybees fly by aerodynamics, not electricity. Bee-flight research describes rapid wingbeats, a special wing motion that creates leading-edge vortices, and strong thorax muscles as the source of lift. Bees do become positively charged in flight through triboelectric charging, which helps them attract pollen and sense the electric fields of flowers. However, no source says this charge creates lift or lets bees fly. The claim takes a real effect on pollen and wrongly treats it as the way bees fly.

text: The driest inhabited continent, Antarctica, is also home to several unique and adapted species, despite receiving an average annual precipitation of just about two inches along the coast and less than 0.5 inches in its interior.

reason: The precipitation figures in the claim are wrong. The interior gets about 50 mm (around 2 inches). The claim says about 2 inches on the coast and under 0.5 inches inland, which understates both. Calling Antarctica the 'driest inhabited continent' is also misleading, since it has no permanent population; it is usually just called the driest continent.

text: The driest inhabited continent, Antarctica, is also home to several unique and adapted species, despite receiving an average annual precipitation of just about two inches along the coast and less than 0.5 inches in the interior.

text: In 2019, the world's largest living organism was discovered in a Western Australia forest, covering over 2,200 acres and estimated to be about 2,400 years old.
label: contradicted

It is in Oregon's Malheur National Forest, not Western Australia, and Forest Service work on it began in the late 1980s, not 2019. Its estimated age is commonly given as about 2,400 years, though this source says it may be as old as 8,650 years. Western Australia's record organism is a different one: a Posidonia seagrass in Shark Bay, a marine bay rather than a forest, reported in 2022. Its size and age do not match the claim either. Only the Oregon fungus was checked in this search; the seagrass details come from background knowledge.

text: Plants can make sounds, though these sounds are mostly inaudible to humans, ranging from 20-200 kilohertz, but recent studies revealed these plant's vibrations can make ultrasonic clicks in response to stress & harm.
label: supported
reason: The main claim holds up. Khait et al. (Cell, March 2023) and Tel Aviv University's coverage of it report that stressed tomato and tobacco plants, along with corn, wheat, grape and cactus, give off ultrasonic pops or clicks. They do this mostly when dehydrated or when their stems are cut, and the sounds are too high-pitched for humans to hear (adult hearing tops out around 16 kHz). The frequency figure is less exact. Sources don't give '20–200 kHz': the paper says the emissions fell in a range of about 20–100 kHz, with most sounds at 40–80 kHz. The researchers listened across 20–150 kHz and recorded with equipment covering 20–250 kHz. The claim's range is broader than what was reported but still includes every frequency actually measured. Because nothing in the sources contradicts it, I've labelled the claim supported.

text: Plants can make sounds, specifically a high-frequency clicking or ultrasonic sound, when they are stressed, injured, or even when they're drying out, which researchers believe may be a way for them to communicate.
label: supported
reason: A peer-reviewed 2023 study in Cell by Khait et al. at Tel Aviv University found that stressed plants give off airborne ultrasonic sounds. Science News describes these as clicking noises. Tomato and tobacco plants clicked when dehydrated (drying out) and when their stems were cut (injured). The authors say the sounds 'may serve as potential signals or cues to their environment,' which fits the claim that researchers think they may be a form of communication. The researchers stress that they have shown only that the sounds carry information, not that any organism uses them to communicate, so the claim matches their cautious 'may' wording.

text: Humans and elephants share several physical and behavioral similarities, including gestation periods of almost two years, with human pregnancies lasting about 280 days and elephant pregnancies lasting almost 640-660 days.
label: contradicted
reason: The claim says humans and elephants share gestation periods of almost two years. That's wrong for humans. Human pregnancy lasts about 266 days from conception, usually counted as 40 weeks (about 280 days), so roughly nine months. Elephants carry a calf for about 22 months (roughly 640–660 days), the longest gestation of any land mammal, and that is the only one close to two years. The individual numbers are correct, but the claim that both species have a gestation of almost two years is contradicted, including by the claim's own figures.

text: A fossilized sea lizard discovered in the Yucatan Peninsula in Mexico was found to have a large block of amber lodged in its stomach, containing over 50 ancient insects.

Others include lizards and insects preserved in amber, a 23-million-year-old lizard in Mexican amber, and an insect in amber stuck to a dinosaur jaw. None of these match the claim. text: France and the United States are connected by a 2,000-year-old underwater cave and tunnel system beneath the English Channel and Atlantic Ocean, known as the Azores-Gibraltar Ridge, but more notably a smaller more recent artificially created Channel Tunnel, a portion of which is under the English Channel.

text: When heated to extremely high temperatures, certain types of glass can be molded into desired shapes and then rapidly cooled and made stronger through a process known as tempering.

A USPTO patent also describes heating glass sheets near the softening point and then chilling them fast. Glass can be shaped, for example bent, while it is soft, before it is quenched. That matches the claim.

text: Cassini Crater, located on the surface of Saturn's moon Titan, is approximately 313 miles in diameter and is considered one of the largest and most prominent polar craters in the solar system.

There is also a lunar Cassini crater, but it is only about 57 km wide. No source places a Cassini crater on Titan.

The Etruscan shrew's whole body is only about 3.5–4.8 cm long without the tail, according to Nature Lab Animal. Its eyes are therefore only millimetres wide, not about 3 cm.
