text: Plants can make sounds, too, when they are under stress or injured, as scientists have detected ultrasonic sounds emitted by plants with the help of specialized equipment.
label: supported
reason: A peer-reviewed study published in Cell (Khait et al., 2023) found that plants under stress, both drought-stressed and cut (injured), give off ultrasonic airborne sounds. The researchers picked these up with microphones in acoustic boxes and in greenhouses, which matches the claim's mention of specialized equipment. Stressed plants made significantly more sounds than control plants.

text: Honeybees are able to fly by using their wings to generate electricity and create an electric charge that helps to lift them into the air and sustain their flight.
label: contradicted
reason: Honeybees fly using aerodynamics, not electricity. Flight research shows that their fast wingbeats and unusual wing movements, driven by strong thorax muscles, create lift through unsteady airflow around flapping wings. Bees do pick up a static electric charge while flying, which helps them collect pollen, but none of the sources say that charge produces or sustains lift. The claim that bees stay in the air by generating electricity is therefore false.

text: Plants can make sounds, too, when they're under stress - for instance, scientists found that ultrasonic clicks are detectable when a plant is drying out.
label: supported
reason: A peer-reviewed study by Khait et al., published in Cell in March 2023, found that stressed plants give off ultrasonic airborne sounds. Tomato and tobacco plants under drought stress made far more of these click-like sounds than unstressed control plants. The sounds could be recorded from a distance, and they were distinct enough to tell drought-stressed, cut and control plants apart. This backs both parts of the claim: plants make sounds under stress, and ultrasonic clicks can be detected when a plant dries out.

text: Tarantulas can live for up to 20-30 years in captivity, with one species, the Goliath Birdeater tarantula, being known to live up to 35 years.
label: contradicted
reason: Reliable sources do back the general idea that female tarantulas of some species can live about 20–30 years in captivity. The specific part about the Goliath birdeater is not backed up. Wikipedia, EBSCO, and caresheets say females of this species live about 15–25 years on average or at most. AAAS says up to 20 years, and Dimensions.com gives 10–20 years. No reliable source supports a 35-year lifespan for the Goliath birdeater. One low-quality fact site says 'around 40 years', which conflicts with the authoritative sources and does not confirm 35. Because the reliable evidence puts the maximum well below 35 years, the claim is contradicted.

text: Plants can make sounds, ranging from barely detectable clicks and chirps to loud cracking noises, in response to environmental stimuli such as injury or drought.
label: supported
reason: Reliable sources back the main claim: plants give off sounds when stressed by drought or injury. A 2023 study in Cell found that tomato and tobacco plants made clicking or popping sounds when they were dried out or had their stems cut. Science News, the Natural History Museum, Scientific American, CNN and ScienceDaily all reported the result. The sounds are ultrasonic, so people can't hear them, which fits 'barely detectable clicks.' But they are roughly as loud as normal speech, and Scientific American calls them 'crackles.' The sources don't describe 'chirps' or 'loud cracking noises' audible to humans, so that part of the claim is a loose description. The central claim is still well supported.

text: Scientists estimate that there are approximately 8.7 million identified species on Earth, but they believe this number may represent only about 10% of the total number of species that actually exist.
label: contradicted
reason: The 8.7 million figure from Mora et al. (2011) is an estimate of all species on Earth, both known and unknown. It is not a count of identified species. The same study found that about 86% of those species have not yet been described, which puts the number identified at roughly 1.2 million. The claim treats the total estimate as the identified count, and its 'about 10%' figure doesn't match the study's numbers either.

text: Turtles have an innate navigation system that allows them to migrate thousands of miles each year and return to the exact beach where they were born.
label: not_verifiable
reason: The search results back the core idea, but only for sea turtles. A Current Biology study and National Geographic report that sea turtles likely imprint on the magnetic signature of their natal beach and use Earth's magnetic field to find it after long migrations. Other details in the claim don't hold up as stated. It says 'turtles' in general, but the evidence covers only sea turtles. It also says they migrate 'each year.' The Sea Turtle Conservancy says females typically skip one or two years between nesting migrations, and SWOT (seaturtlestatus.org) says they return 'a couple years later.' NOAA, however, says some females nest every year. The 'exact beach' part is also disputed: National Geographic says 'exact spot,' while Wikipedia's natal homing article cites evidence that turtles return to the natal area rather than the actual beach. With some parts supported and others contradicted or overstated, the claim as a whole is inconclusive.

text: A誉咲き (Yūrei-zakura), a 2,000-year-old weeping cherry blossom tree, is located in Japan's inset, Fukushima Prefecture.
label: contradicted
reason: My searches turned up no 'Yūrei-zakura' (and nothing named '誉咲き') in Fukushima. The name in the claim looks garbled. Japan's well-known roughly 2,000-year-old cherry tree is the Yamataka Jindai-zakura, an Edo-higan cherry at Jissoji Temple in Hokuto, Yamanashi Prefecture. Its age is estimated at 1,800 to 2,000 years. Fukushima's famous weeping cherry is the Miharu Takizakura, which is about 1,000 years old, not 2,000. The claim mixes up these two trees, so the evidence contradicts it.

text: Plants can make sounds, when they are cut or injured, and scientists have identified that when trees are damaged they release sounds classified as clicks or ultrasonic sounds, which are above human hearing range.
label: supported
reason: Several reliable sources back the main points of the claim. The 2023 Khait et al. study in Cell, along with coverage by Science News, the Natural History Museum and Cell's own preview, found that tomato and tobacco plants give off airborne ultrasonic clicks or pops when their stems are cut or they are dehydrated. These sounds are above the range of human hearing (about 20–100 kHz). Peer-reviewed tree research, including work in New Phytologist and by Milburn & Johnson and Tyree & Dixon, has also recorded ultrasonic acoustic emissions, described as 'clicks', from tree xylem. The tree studies involve stress such as drought-induced cavitation and xylem embolism rather than physical injury, so 'when trees are damaged' is a loose description. The claim's general point still matches the evidence, and no source contradicts it.

text: A partitions of the Mandelbrot set can form the swirling patterns familiar to most, however using a tiny zoom creates patterns familiar to every domain in mathematics including statistical mechanics, topology and even Timoshenko centroids.
label: not_verifiable
reason: I found no source backing the main parts of this claim. Sources do say that zooming into the Mandelbrot set reveals complex and self-similar patterns, and that the set is studied in topology. But nothing says that zoomed-in regions show patterns from "every domain in mathematics," which is a sweeping overstatement. I also found no link to statistical mechanics, and "Timoshenko centroids" is not a recognised idea connected to the Mandelbrot set. The opening phrase "A partitions of the Mandelbrot set" is also too vague to check. Because these parts can't be confirmed, the claim is inconclusive.

text: Honeybees are able to fly by using their wings to generate electricity, which creates a positive charge allowing the wings to repel the air and lift off the ground.
label: contradicted
reason: Reliable sources say honeybees fly using aerodynamics, not electricity. Their wings beat about 230 times per second, twist and rotate, and create leading-edge vortices. These form low-pressure zones that lift the wings, with extra lift from wing rotation and from the wing catching its own wake (Nature; beekeeping and science explainers). Bees do pick up a positive static charge while flying, but none of these sources says the charge makes the wings repel air or produces lift. Lift comes entirely from the flapping motion.

text: Beehive-shaped structures in the Australian Outback, known as "termite mounds", are built by millions of termites working together and can be up to 20 feet tall and survive for decades in the arid environment.
label: supported
reason: Several sources back up the main parts of the claim. On height, aussieanimals.com says cathedral termite mounds (Nasutitermes triodiae) in northern Australia can be up to 20 feet tall, and other sources put the figure at 6 to 8 m. On colony size, colonies can number in the millions of termites. On age, park signs and trail descriptions say mounds about 5 m high can be over 50 years old, and some magnetic termite mounds are about 100 years old. The 'beehive-shaped' wording is only descriptive and doesn't conflict with anything found. One caveat: some sources give a maximum of about 8 m (roughly 26 ft), which is taller than 20 feet. That makes 'up to 20 feet' conservative rather than wrong, and other sources state 20 feet directly.

text: A blue whale's heart alone can pump around 5,000 liters of blood with every beat.
label: contradicted
reason: The 5,000-liter figure is far too high. Reliable sources put a blue whale's output per heartbeat at about 80 to 230 liters. A study covered by Inverse estimated about 80 liters per beat, and Azores Whale Watch says about 230 liters. A figure in the thousands of liters is closer to estimates of the whale's total blood volume, not the amount pumped in one beat.

text: A blue whale's heartbeat can be as loud as 188 decibels, making it the loudest animal on Earth.
label: contradicted
reason: The 188-decibel figure comes from the blue whale's call (its vocalizations), not its heartbeat. Sources such as Enchanted Learning say the blue whale's call can reach up to 188 dB. Its heartbeat is much quieter: monitoring studies picked it up with sensors placed on the whale, and popular claims only say it can be heard from about 2 miles away. Calling the blue whale the loudest animal is also disputed, since sperm whale clicks have been measured at around 230 dB. Because the claim attributes the 188 dB level to the heartbeat, it is contradicted.

text: A blue whale's heartbeat can be as slow as two beats per minute when the whale is at rest underwater.
label: supported
reason: Reliable reports on the 2019 Stanford study, the first recording of a wild blue whale's heart rate, say its heartbeat can drop to as low as two beats per minute while underwater. The heart rate averaged about 4–8 bpm during dives, and the 37 bpm maximum came at the surface. The main figure and the underwater setting are confirmed. One caveat: the low rate was recorded during deep foraging dives, not while the whale was strictly at rest, so the claim's wording is slightly loose.

text: A blue whale's heartbeat is so powerful that it can be detected over 500 miles away using specialized equipment.
label: contradicted
reason: Sources that repeat this popular fact, such as the Cold Spring Harbor Whaling Museum blog, say a blue whale's heartbeat can be detected from about 2 miles away, not more than 500 miles. Even the 2-mile figure is a popular claim that hasn't been well verified. The 'hundreds of miles' distance actually belongs to blue whale calls, not their heartbeats. The 500-mile heartbeat claim is therefore contradicted.

text: A fetus develops its fingerprints by the time it is 24 weeks old, and these fingerprints are unique to each individual.
label: supported
reason: ScienceABC says fingerprints form between about weeks 10 and 24 of fetal development, so they are in place by week 24. The same source says each print is shaped by genes plus the conditions in the womb. That is why fingerprints are unique, even between identical twins. Other well-known sources agree that ridge patterns are set by roughly 17 to 24 weeks.

text: A fossilized sea lizard discovered in the Yucatan Peninsula in Mexico was found to have a large block of amber lodged in its stomach, which was likely ingested hundreds of millions of years ago.
label: not_verifiable
reason: My searches found no report of a fossil sea lizard from the Yucatan Peninsula with a block of amber in its stomach. Related Mexican finds don't match the claim. A 23-million-year-old Anolis lizard was found encased in amber from Chiapas, not with amber in its stomach. Documented mosasaur stomach contents include fish, bivalves and plesiosaurs, but no amber. The timeline is also doubtful: sea lizards (mosasaurs) lived about 66–98 million years ago, not 'hundreds of millions' of years ago. Since nothing confirms the event, the claim can't be verified.

text: Apple trees can live for more than 100 years, but they typically stop producing fruit after about 50 years.
label: not_verifiable
reason: The first part holds up: several sources (Harvest to Table, Outdoor Guide, and a tree-surgeon site) say apple trees can live 100 years or more. The second part, that they typically stop fruiting after about 50 years, is disputed. One low-authority blog (plantids) says this almost word for word. Peppers Home & Garden says there is no set age at which apple trees stop producing. Other sources say old trees keep producing, though less reliably: the Bramley original tree was still alive at around 180–200 years, and one source says espaliered apple trees stay productive for more than 150 years. Because the sources conflict and the support comes from an unreliable site, the 50-year cutoff can't be confirmed or clearly ruled out.

text: Astronauts cannot cry in space because there is no gravity to pull the tears down their cheeks.
label: contradicted
reason: Astronauts can cry in space. Chris Hadfield, a Canadian Space Agency astronaut, said on the ISS that "Your eyes will definitely cry in space." Without gravity, the tears don't run down the cheeks. Instead, they collect as a ball of water on the eye. So the claim gets the part about gravity right but is wrong to say astronauts cannot cry.

text: Cats have a special talent for recognizing and imitating the sounds of their owners' voices.
label: not_verifiable
reason: The evidence is mixed. The recognition part holds up: research from Paris Nanterre University (reported by My Modern Met) found that cats can tell their owner's voice from a stranger's. The imitation part does not. Lund University phonetics researcher Susanne Schötz says in a book that cats may copy their owners' intonation, but that is one researcher's claim, not established science. Other experts say cats' vocal anatomy can't produce human speech sounds, so they can't really copy it (Adoptapet). Because the sources disagree on imitation, and nothing backs calling it a 'special talent', the full claim can't be confirmed.

text: Humans and dolphins are the only known species in the animal kingdom that give themselves names.
label: contradicted
reason: The claim is out of date. Scientists now know of other animals that use names. A 2024 study in Science found that marmoset monkeys use specific "phee-calls" to name each other. Reports on that study (EurekAlert, CNN) say this ability was previously known in humans, dolphins and elephants, and a separate 2024 study had already found that African elephants address each other with name-like calls. So humans and dolphins are not the only known species with names. One caveat: the claim says animals give "themselves" names, but this research is about vocal labels used for other individuals. Even so, it still counts against the idea that only humans and dolphins have names.

text: Humans share about 50-60% of their DNA with bananas due to their common ancestor that lived billions of years ago.
label: contradicted
reason: The Naked Scientists calls the claim a myth. About 50–60% of human genes have counterparts in bananas, but protein-coding genes make up only about 2% of human DNA. That means we share roughly 1% of our DNA with bananas, not 50–60%. The common ancestor of plants and animals was a single-celled organism that probably lived about 1.6 billion years ago, so the claim's ancestry part is roughly right. The 'DNA' percentage is what makes it wrong.

text: Humans share about 50-60% of their DNA with bananas, despite being very distinct species.
label: contradicted
reason: Reliable explainers say the popular "50–60% of our DNA" figure is wrong. It comes from a 2013 NHGRI comparison showing that about 60% of human genes have a recognizable counterpart in the banana genome. Since genes make up only a small part of the genome, the shared portion is roughly 1–2% of human DNA at most. IFLScience says nearly every detail of the factoid is technically incorrect, partly because "it's not 60 percent." HowStuffWorks says there is "some truth" to the figure but that it is misleading. A ProteinIQ orthology analysis also puts the share well below 50–60%. Some popular sites repeat the 60% figure, and The Star rates the claim "true" even though its own explanation says the overlap is in genes, about 1–2% of the genome. The more reliable sources show the claim is wrong as stated.

text: Humans share approximately 60% of their DNA with fruit flies, highlighting the surprising genetic similarity between two distinctly different species.
label: supported
reason: NHGRI (genome.gov) reports that a 2000 comparison of the fruit fly and human genomes found about 60% of genes are conserved between the two species. Other sources repeat the same figure, though it is often loosely stated as 60% of DNA. Strictly, the 60% refers to shared or conserved genes, not the full DNA sequence. Since this is the widely accepted meaning of the claim, the evidence supports it.

text: Rats are extremely skilled swimmers and can even tread water for up to three days under certain conditions.
label: supported
reason: Several sources say rats are excellent swimmers that can tread water for up to three days. These include BBC Discover Wildlife, Wikipedia's 'Rats in New York City' article, and pest-control companies such as Terminix, Rentokil and Western Exterminator. None of the results I found disputes this. One caveat: the figure gets repeated a lot, but none of these pages points to the original study behind it.

text: Tarantulas have been on Earth for around 120 million years, long before dinosaurs roamed the planet.
label: contradicted
reason: The 120-million-year figure is right. Live Science and Smithsonian report that tarantulas first appeared about 120 million years ago, in the Cretaceous, on Gondwana. The claim that this was "long before dinosaurs" is wrong, though. Dinosaurs appeared about 230 million years ago and were still around throughout the Cretaceous, so tarantulas arose during the age of dinosaurs, not before it.

text: _seqs2Peer, a program released the world's first de-extinction womb transplant.
label: not_verifiable
reason: I found nothing on a program called "_seqs2Peer", so the claim's subject has no clear referent. Searching for it only returned unrelated bioinformatics tools such as Seq2science and seq2seq. I also found no report of any "de-extinction womb transplant". The womb-transplant firsts that came up are human medical cases, like the 2002 Saudi transplant and the 2018 birth from a deceased donor, and none involve de-extinction. The claim can't be verified either way.

text: Orient Drinks, a Japanese beverage company, teamed up with convenience store chain, Lawson, to sell a hot, bubble tea drink in the winter, calling it ' Matcha Hot Tea with Boba'.
label: not_verifiable
reason: I couldn't find any evidence for this claim. My searches for 'Orient Drinks', Lawson and a hot matcha boba drink returned nothing relevant. I couldn't confirm that a Japanese beverage company called 'Orient Drinks' exists, that it partnered with Lawson, or that a winter product called 'Matcha Hot Tea with Boba' was sold. The search tool then hit its usage limit, so I couldn't search further. Nothing I found contradicts the claim either.

text: Honeybees are able to fly by using their wings to generate lift, but also by generating additional lift and thrust from the movement of the air over and under their wing as they rotate.
label: supported
reason: Caltech's record of the Altshuler et al. PNAS study supports the claim. Bees beat their wings in short, very fast strokes, about 230 times a second. Tests on a scaled robot wing showed that the wings make lift during each stroke. They also produce extra force peaks at the start and end of each stroke, when the wing flips over. The authors put those peaks down to 'additional unsteady mechanisms at stroke reversal.' That matches the claim's point that bees get extra lift and thrust from air moving over and under the wing as it rotates. No source I found says otherwise. The claim's wording is loose, but its core is consistent with this peer-reviewed work.

text: In New York City, there is a secretly located apartment in the New York Public Library,dımatically decreasing the maintenance  and upkeep costs of employee housing nearby the  adjacent Bryant Park.
label: not_verifiable
reason: Reliable sources confirm the first part of the claim. The New York Public Library's 42nd Street (Schwarzman) building had a hidden apartment where live-in superintendent John Fedeler and his family lived. Several other branches also had custodian apartments, which have since been turned over to other library uses. However, I found nothing showing that this apartment cut the maintenance or upkeep costs of employee housing near Bryant Park, dramatically or otherwise. That part of the claim appears to be unsupported, so the claim as a whole cannot be verified.

text: Plants can make sounds, too, when they lose a significant amount of water, and studies have found that some trees release hundreds to thousands of clicks when they're dehydrated under a drought.
label: supported
reason: Reporting on the 2023 Tel Aviv study (ScienceAlert, The Conversation, ABC) says dehydrated plants make ultrasonic popping or clicking sounds, which become more frequent as water stress increases. LiveScience and Phys.org (2013) say living trees make noises when they run out of water, because air bubbles form and pop in the water-conducting tubes. ResearchGate studies of 'ultrasonic acoustic emissions in drought-stressed trees' show these tree sounds are measured as countable events. One less authoritative source also describes thousands of these tiny ruptures producing clicks together. I couldn't confirm the exact 'hundreds to thousands' range in a primary paper because my search limit ran out, but nothing I found contradicts it, and it fits the research on drought-related tree sounds.

text: Rome is considered to be the second most populous city in the world with over 3,700,000 residents within the administrative limits, it was the most populated city in Europe by 2021
label: contradicted
reason: The claim is wrong on several points. Wikipedia says Rome's municipality has about 2.7 million residents, not more than 3.7 million. That makes it the third most populous city in the EU by city limits and 8th in Europe. It is not the second most populous city in the world, and it was not Europe's most populated city in 2021.

text: Honeybees are able to fly by using their wings to create electricity through a process known as triboelectrification, which helps them attract pollen to facilitate the pollination process.
label: contradicted
reason: Honeybees do pick up static charge through the triboelectric effect while flying, and that charge helps pollen stick to them. But the charge comes from flying, not the other way around. Bees fly by aerodynamics: they make short, fast wing strokes that create a leading-edge vortex, which produces lift. Saying bees fly by making electricity with their wings gets cause and effect backwards, so the claim is false.

text: Scientists estimate that there may be between 700,000 and 1 million distinct species of insects that exist on Earth, although only about 1 million out of an estimated 8.7 million total species have been formally described.
label: contradicted
reason: The claim's estimate for insects is too low. Wikipedia's 'Insect biodiversity' article, citing Stork (2018), says there are about 5.5 million insect species in total. It also says about 1 million insect species have already been described. A range of 700,000 to 1 million describes roughly the known species, not the estimated total. The 8.7 million figure for all species is a real estimate (Mora et al. 2011), and about 1.2 million species were described at that time, so the rest of the claim is roughly right. The insect estimate is still wrong, so the claim as a whole is contradicted.

text: Plants can make sounds, too, although we can't hear them with our ears; they use a variety of methods like clicking roots, and vibrating leaves to communicate with insects and even other plants.
label: not_verifiable
reason: Part of the claim holds up. A 2023 study, reported by The Conversation and SciTechDaily, found that stressed tomato and tobacco plants make ultrasonic clicks too high-pitched for human ears. Young corn roots also give off click-like acoustic signals (Gagliano et al., 2012). The communication part is not established. A New Phytologist review says there is so far no evidence of plants communicating with each other through sound. Researchers say the sounds 'may' be detectable by insects or other plants. The closest evidence is a 2025 study in which moths avoided laying eggs on plants making distress sounds, but that shows insects reacting to a cue, not plants deliberately signalling. No source supports 'vibrating leaves' as a way plants communicate. Popular outlets like National Geographic describe plants as 'talking', but the scientific review contradicts the idea of plant-to-plant sound communication. Because the sources conflict and some parts of the claim can't be verified, the claim is inconclusive.

text: Plants can make sounds, ranging from gentle whispers to loud clicks, as a means of communication and defense, although these sounds are typically beyond the range of human hearing.
label: contradicted
reason: Part of the claim holds up. The 2023 Cell study found that stressed tomato and tobacco plants give off ultrasonic clicks that humans can't hear, likely caused by air bubbles bursting in their water-carrying tissue (cavitation). But the claim that plants make these sounds 'as a means of communication and defense' is contradicted. Reports on the study (CNN via ABC15 and WRAL) say 'there is no evidence that the noise produced by the plants is intentional or a form of communication.' Independent experts at UC Davis and the Natural History Museum also warn against reading the sounds as active communication, since the researchers suggest they may simply be a byproduct of cavitation. No source describes a range of sounds 'from gentle whispers to loud clicks' either. The studies describe only ultrasonic clicks or pops.

text: Japan has the world's oldest known hotel, Nishiyama Onsen Keiunkan, which was initially built in 705 AD and has been in continuous operation for over 1,300 years.
label: supported
reason: CNN reports that Guinness World Records named Nishiyama Onsen Keiunkan, in Japan's Yamanashi prefecture, the world's oldest hotel in 2011. CNN also says it opened in 705 AD and has operated continuously since then, which is about 1,300 years. The Guinness World Records 'Oldest hotel' page also appeared in the search results, but only its title and opening words were checked, not the full entry. CNN alone supports every part of the claim.

text: Galileo Galilei was the first person to observe the planet Neptune, but he didn't realize it was a planet, cataloging it instead as a star in 1613.
label: supported
reason: I found reliable sources that back the claim. Astronomy.com says that between December 1612 and January 1613, Galileo sketched a 'point' near Jupiter that was actually Neptune, and that he 'seems to have mistook the planet for a star.' Space.com says the honour of being first to observe Neptune 'goes to' Galileo, who drew it twice when it was near Jupiter in early 1613. One small caveat: his first sighting was in late December 1612, and a 2009 hypothesis suggests he may have noticed it moving. Even so, the mainstream account matches the claim.

text: Scientists estimate that there may be between 700,000 and 1 million species of insects on Earth, but only about 1 million animal species of all kinds have been formally described.
label: contradicted
reason: Both numbers in the claim conflict with reliable sources. A PNAS study and other sources estimate about 5.5 million insect species on Earth, with a range of roughly 2.6 to 7.8 million, not 700,000 to 1 million. About 1 million insect species have already been described. Described animal species of all kinds number more than 1.5 million (insects alone are about 950,000 to 1 million), not about 1 million.

text: Plants can make sounds, too, as researchers have found that a plant can generate clicks, or other loud noises, when it's stressed or needs water and making those noises by releasing air bubbles through its roots.
label: contradicted
reason: Researchers did find that stressed plants make clicking sounds. A Tel Aviv University study recorded clicks from tomato and tobacco plants that were dehydrated or cut. But two parts of the claim don't match the research. First, the sounds aren't 'loud noises': they are ultrasonic, mostly 40–80 kHz, which is above what humans can hear. Second, the researchers don't link the sounds to air bubbles released through the roots. They think the cause is cavitation, where air bubbles form and burst inside the plant's water-carrying tissue (xylem) in the stem.

text: A blue whale's heartbeat can be as loud as 188 decibels, making it louder than a jet engine taking off.
label: contradicted
reason: The 188-decibel figure is real, but it describes the blue whale's calls, not its heartbeat. WWF says blue whale "calls reach 188 decibels, while a jet reaches 140 decibels." Wikipedia's whale vocalization page and IFLScience also tie the 155–188 dB range to the whale's vocal sounds. The blue whale heart sources found give only size and heart rate, with no decibel level for the heartbeat. Because the claim credits the heartbeat with a loudness that belongs to the call, it is contradicted.

text: A day on Venus is actually longer than a year on Venus.
label: supported
reason: Snopes rates this claim as true. It cites NASA and Royal Museums Greenwich: Venus takes about 243 Earth days to spin once on its axis (its sidereal day) but only about 225 Earth days to go around the Sun (its year). Snopes also quotes NASA saying a day on Venus is "a little longer than a year on Venus." One caveat: the solar day on Venus (sunrise to sunrise) is about 117 Earth days, which is shorter than its year. But the claim uses the standard definition of a day as one rotation, so it holds.

text: Aolphin calves are born with a thick layer of blubber that helps them stay afloat, as they can't swim right away.
label: contradicted
reason: The claim is wrong on both points. Scientific American reports that newborn dolphin calves do not have enough body fat or blubber to float easily, so a calf starts to sink if its mother stops swimming. The claim says the opposite, that calves are born with thick blubber that keeps them afloat. Calves also swim from birth, travelling alongside the mother in her slipstream, so the idea that they can't swim right away is also false. ('Aolphin' is read here as a typo for 'dolphin'.)

text: Honeybees are able to fly by using electricity generated by the movement of their wings, and the spin of their bodies, to create an electric charge.
label: contradicted
reason: Scientific sources say honeybees fly by aerodynamics, not electricity. They flap and rotate their wings about 240 times a second, and the lift comes from leading-edge vortices, rotational lift and wake recapture. Bees do pick up a static electric charge while flying, but that charge does not hold them up in the air.

text: Humans share approximately 50-60% of their DNA with bananas, highlighting the common ancestry and genetic similarity among living organisms.
label: contradicted
reason: Several explainers, including HowStuffWorks quoting NHGRI geneticist Lawrence Brody, say the popular '50–60%' figure is a misreading. It means that about 60% of human genes have a recognizable counterpart, or homolog, in the banana genome. It does not mean that 50–60% of our DNA is shared. The proteins made by those matching genes are only about 40% similar on average. Because protein-coding genes make up only about 1–2% of the human genome, the share of total DNA in common is very small. One analysis puts identical coding bases at about 0.08% of the genome. A few popular sites repeat the figure loosely, but they also say it refers to genes, not the whole genome. The part of the claim about common ancestry is reasonable, but the specific '50–60% of DNA' statement is wrong.

text: Large corporations like IBM, Microsoft, and Google have been using artificial intelligence (AI) for decades in their internal operations and to optimize processes.
label: not_verifiable
reason: I found partial support, but not for the whole claim. IBM has clearly worked on AI for decades, though the sources mostly describe research and products such as checkers programs, Deep Blue and Watson, not use in its own operations. Google used DeepMind's AI to cut the cooling energy in its own data centres by about 40%, which shows it uses AI to optimize processes, but that was reported in 2016, not decades ago. One commentary piece says Microsoft was 'nowhere with AI' twenty years ago, which cuts against the 'for decades' part for Microsoft. No source confirmed that all three companies have used AI in their internal operations for decades.

text: Norway is home to the world's longest tunnel, the Lærdal Tunnel, which spans 24.5 kilometers in length.
label: contradicted
reason: The Lærdal Tunnel is in Norway and is 24.5 km long, but it holds the record for the world's longest road tunnel, not the world's longest tunnel overall. Visit Norway, the official tourism site, calls it "the world's longest road tunnel." Several other tunnels are much longer, including the Gotthard Base Tunnel (about 57 km) and the Channel Tunnel (about 50 km), so the claim's unqualified "world's longest tunnel" is wrong.

text: Polar bears are excellent swimmers, and they have been known to swim distances of up to 60 miles (97 kilometers) without resting.
label: supported
reason: Several reliable sources back the claim. The San Diego Zoo Wildlife Alliance says polar bears have been known to swim more than 60 miles (100 km) without resting, and Ocean Conservancy, NH PBS and others give the same figure while describing polar bears as strong swimmers. One caveat: the documented record is much longer, a nonstop swim of about 426 miles over nine days, so calling 60 miles the upper limit understates their range. The 60-mile figure itself is still widely reported.

text: Scans of the Egyptian Great Pyramid's internal chamber, created in 2016, suggest the possible presence of a previously undiscovered void.
label: supported
reason: I found two reliable sources. Smithsonian says the first signs of the 'Big Void' showed up in spring 2016 in muon data from detectors placed inside the pyramid, in the Queen's Chamber area. Science News also says ScanPyramids scientists first spotted a void with muon scans in 2016. That matches the claim that 2016 scans from an internal chamber pointed to a possible undiscovered void. The wording 'created in 2016' is a little loose, but nothing I found contradicts the claim.

text: Scans of the Egyptian Great Pyramid's internal chamber, created in 2017, revealed a substantial previously undiscovered void within the pyramid.
label: supported
reason: GeekWire (2 Nov 2017) reports that the ScanPyramids team announced in Nature that muon imaging had found a large, previously unknown void inside the Great Pyramid. It was nicknamed the "Big Void" and could be as large as an art gallery space. Part of the imaging was done with detectors placed in the Queen's Chamber, which matches the claim that the scans came from inside a chamber. Some of the scanning began before 2017, but the results were published that year, so the claim is substantially accurate.

text: Scientists estimate that there are approximately 8.7 million identified species on Earth, but the total number of species is believed to be between 30-50 million.
label: contradicted
reason: The claim gets the 8.7 million figure wrong. In Mora et al. (PLoS Biology, 2011), 8.7 million is the estimated total number of species on Earth, not the number already identified. That study puts described species at about 1.2 million, and other estimates put it at around 2 million. The claim treats 8.7 million as the identified count and gives a separate 30–50 million total, which misstates what the sources say.

text: Tarantulas have been around for a long time, with fossil evidence showing they've remained largely unchanged for over 100 million years.
label: not_verifiable
reason: Part of the claim holds up: tarantulas are an old group. A Journal of Biogeography paper (Wiley) and Live Science both say the oldest known tarantula fossil, preserved in Burmese amber, is about 100 million years old, and molecular studies date the group's origin to about 120 million years ago. However, Live Science notes that only two tarantula fossils are known, one about 100 million years old and one about 16 million. The amber fossil is dated at about 99–100 million years, so it does not clearly show 'over' 100 million years. With so few fossils, the evidence cannot show that tarantulas stayed 'largely unchanged' for that long. Texas Parks & Wildlife magazine makes a much smaller claim: fossils show tarantulas 'virtually unchanged' for more than 20 million years. Only a hobbyist blog supports the 100-million-year version. The age is roughly supported, but the claim that fossils show they stayed unchanged for over 100 million years is not reliably confirmed.

text: Tarantulas have existed for approximately 120 million years, with fossil evidence showing they have remained largely unchanged since the Cretaceous period.
label: not_verifiable
reason: The age is supported, but the fossil part isn't. A Carnegie Mellon–led study (PeerJ, 2021) estimated that tarantulas first appeared about 120 million years ago, during the Cretaceous. That figure comes from a family tree built from genetic data, not from fossils, and only some fossil dates were used to calibrate it. Researchers describe tarantula fossils as extremely rare: only two are known, a roughly 100-million-year-old amber fossil from Myanmar and a roughly 16-million-year-old one from Mexico. No source found says fossil evidence shows tarantulas have stayed largely unchanged since the Cretaceous, so that part can't be verified.

text: Tarantulas have existed for approximately 120 million years, with fossil evidence showing they have remained largely unchanged since the early Cretaceous period.
label: not_verifiable
reason: The roughly 120-million-year age is supported. Reporting on a 2022 phylogenomic study (Live Science, Big Think) says tarantulas first appeared about 120 million years ago, during the Cretaceous. However, that date came from a molecular family tree calibrated mostly with fossils of other spiders, not from a tarantula fossil record. Tarantula fossils are very rare: Live Science reports only two known ones, both in amber, one about 100 million years old from Myanmar and one about 16 million years old from Mexico. No source found shows fossil evidence that tarantulas have stayed largely unchanged since the early Cretaceous, so that part of the claim cannot be verified.

text: The68539-\Traits Eruption, also known as the 'Aeolian Brown-Tail' volcano, is a large region of volcanoes, but actually it is Paricutin that is more famously known as the cinder cone volcano that erupted in a cornfield in Mexico in 1943, famously within one
label: not_verifiable
reason: The Parícutin part checks out: it is a cinder cone that suddenly appeared in a Mexican cornfield in 1943. The rest of the claim can't be verified. I found no record of a "68539-\Traits Eruption" or an "Aeolian Brown-Tail" volcano. Searches only returned unrelated geology papers on the "Brown Tuffs" ash deposits of Italy's Aeolian Islands. The claim also breaks off mid-sentence ("famously within one"), so its full meaning is unclear.

text: Plants can make sounds, as researchers have discovered that when certain plants, such as corn and sunflowers, are under stress or injured, they release ultrasonic sounds that are beyond human hearing.
label: not_verifiable
reason: I couldn't verify the claim in full. The core of it is well supported. Khait et al.'s 2023 study in Cell found that tomato and tobacco plants give off airborne ultrasonic clicks, too high for humans to hear, when they are dried out or cut. The researchers also recorded sounds from wheat, corn, grapevines and cactus, so the corn example holds up. However, none of the coverage of the study, including reports from Science News and the Natural History Museum, lists sunflowers among the plants tested. I also found no other source showing that sunflowers make ultrasonic sounds under stress. The only sunflower result was a Snopes fact-check of a viral 'sounds of a sunflower' video, which found the audio was not produced by the plant. That is not a scientific test, so it neither confirms nor rules out the sunflower example.

text: Plants can make sounds, too, and researchers have discovered that certain types like tomatoes and tobacco can produce ultrasonic clicks to communicate and even summon beneficial insects when under attack.
label: contradicted
reason: The basic finding is correct. Khait et al. (Cell, March 2023) recorded ultrasonic clicks from tomato and tobacco plants that were dry or had cut stems. The rest of the claim goes beyond the evidence. CNN and ABC15, reporting on the study, say there is no evidence the noises are intentional or a form of communication. Researchers think the clicks likely come from cavitation, where air bubbles collapse in the plant's water column. Lead researcher Hadany told Science News that calling it 'screaming' jumps to a conclusion her team has not reached. No source shows plants using these sounds to call in helpful insects when attacked. The stress was drought or cutting, not insect attack. A 2024 bioRxiv preprint found that moths react to the sounds of drought-stressed plants, which is a pest picking up on the sound, not the plant summoning allies.

text: A partitions of the Mandelbrot set can form the swirling patterns familiar to most, however using a tiny zoom creates patterns familiar to every domain in mathematics including statistical mechanics, evolution, and fluid dynamics.
label: not_verifiable
reason: The evidence doesn't settle this claim. Sources confirm that zooming into the Mandelbrot set reveals intricate, self-similar, swirling patterns at every scale (Mathigon, Quanta). Britannica says fractal geometry in general is used in statistical mechanics, fluid mechanics and other fields. No trustworthy source says that a tiny zoom into the Mandelbrot set produces patterns familiar to every domain of mathematics, or names evolution as one of them. The claim also has problems of its own: its wording is unclear ('A partitions'), it overgeneralizes to 'every domain', and it treats physics and biology as branches of mathematics. Key parts therefore can't be verified.

text: Apa is among the world's largest family of flying foxes and is a type of large fruit bat native to forests and mangrove swamps of the Indo-Australian region.
label: not_verifiable
reason: I couldn't verify this claim. The description fits large flying foxes, such as the genus Pteropus (for example, Pteropus vampyrus): large fruit bats that live in forests and mangroves across the Indo-Australian region. But I found nothing showing that "Apa" is a recognized name for any flying fox or fruit bat species. My first search returned only general flying-fox pages, and later searches hit the tool limit before I could check further. The wording "among the world's largest family of flying foxes" is also unclear. Because "Apa" has no clear referent, the claim can't be confirmed or ruled out.

text: Plants can make sounds, such as clicking or bubbling noises, when they are under stress, injured, or growing, which can be detected using specialized equipment.
label: supported
reason: Science News reported on a 2023 study in Cell (Khait et al.). It found that tomato and tobacco plants made ultrasonic clicks when they were short of water or had their stems cut. The researchers picked these up with ultrasonic microphones, and the clicks sound like popping bubble wrap. That covers the stress, injury and special-equipment parts of the claim. The growing part is supported separately: Gagliano's research (reported by NBC News and Science Illustrated) found that young, growing corn roots give off clicking sounds around 220 Hz that people can't hear. 'Bubbling' is the only loose wording, but the bubble-wrap-like clicks match what the claim describes.

text: The Axel Erlandson's Tre-fontaine tree, also known as the "circus tree," is a natural wonder and the world's first known example of a tree grown into a triple-fluted column.
label: contradicted
reason: Search results do not support this claim. No source mentions a "Tre-fontaine" tree. "Circus Trees" (or "The Tree Circus") is the name of Erlandson's whole collection, not another name for one tree. Reliable sources, including Wikipedia, Gilroy Gardens, AVAM and Raw Vision, say Erlandson deliberately shaped these trees by planting, bending, pruning and grafting them starting in the 1920s. That contradicts calling it a "natural wonder." No source describes a triple-fluted column tree or says any of his trees was the world's first of that kind.

text: Beehive-shaped structures in the Australian Outback, known as "termite mounds", are built by millions of termites working together and can be up to 20 feet tall and 30 feet wide.
label: not_verifiable
reason: The sources partly match the claim but don't confirm all of it. Australian cathedral termites in the Outback do build very large mounds. Some reach about 8 m (26 ft), so mounds 20 ft tall or taller are plausible, though 20 ft isn't the maximum. However, I found no source saying Australian Outback termite mounds reach 30 ft wide. The very wide mounds I found were elsewhere: Brazil's murundus are about 9 m across, and Wikipedia gives a general 30 m figure that isn't specific to Australia. Australian sources describe the mounds as tall and narrow. I also found no direct confirmation that each mound is built by 'millions of termites'. Finally, the 'beehive-shaped structures in the Australian Outback' are usually the Bungle Bungle Range sandstone domes, not termite mounds, which makes the claim less reliable.

text: Scientists estimate that there are approximately 8.7 million identified species on Earth, but the total number of species is believed to be significantly higher, ranging from 30 to over 100 million.
label: contradicted
reason: The 8.7 million figure (Mora et al., 2011) is an estimate of all eukaryotic species on Earth, not the number already identified. Only about 1.2 to 2 million species have been described and catalogued. The same source says earlier estimates of the total ranged from 3 million to 100 million, so it does not support the claim's framing of 8.7 million identified species with a true total of 30 to 100+ million.

text: Plants can make sounds, though these sounds are inaudible to human ears, as researchers have discovered that plants release ultrasonic clicks when they are injured or under drought stress.
label: supported
reason: Khait et al. (Cell, 2023), along with a Cell commentary on that study, report that tomato and tobacco plants give off airborne ultrasonic clicks when they are dried out (drought stress) or have their stems cut. Ultrasonic sounds are above the range of human hearing, but insects and other ultrasound-sensitive organisms can detect them. Every part of the claim matches these findings.

text: Plants can make sounds, too, when they are injured, but these sounds are not range-friendly, as most plants making a sound falls in the ultrasonic frequency.
label: supported
reason: A peer-reviewed study (Khait et al., Cell, 2023) found that stressed tomato and tobacco plants, including ones whose stems had been cut, give off airborne sounds. Healthy plants make few or none. These sounds are ultrasonic clicks at about 40–80 kHz, which is above the range of human hearing. That backs the claim that injured plants make sounds and that the sounds fall in the ultrasonic range. I read the claim's odd phrase "not range-friendly" as meaning "outside the range people can hear."

text: Azerbaijan is home to the oldest known human habitation and reveals a unique glimpse into prehistoric human civilization, featuring tools and artifacts dating as far back as around 1.5 million years.
label: contradicted
reason: Sources confirm that Azykh Cave in Azerbaijan holds tools dated to about 1–1.5 million years ago, so that part of the claim holds up. They do not support calling it the oldest known human habitation. Wikipedia describes it as a habitation site of prehistoric humans, and other sources call it 'one of the oldest' sites in Eurasia or the world. They note that older or equivalent finds come from Olduvai Gorge in Tanzania, and an official Azerbaijani source ranks the Azykh jaw bone only fourth oldest in the world. Showcaves.com also dates the oldest layer to about 1.19 million years.

text: In 2019, the world's largest living organism was discovered in a Blue Mountains forest in Australia, covering over 100 acres as a massive fungus growth.
label: contradicted
reason: The fungus known as the world's largest living organism is the Armillaria ostoyae 'Humongous Fungus' in the Blue Mountains of Oregon, USA, in Malheur National Forest, not Australia. It covers about 9.65 km² (roughly 2,385 acres). Studies from 1998 and 2000 identified it, not a 2019 discovery. The claim gets the country and the year wrong.

text: Hexagons are the strongest shape in nature and appear in the structure of beehives, tortoise shells, and rock formations such as the Giant's Causeway in Ireland.
label: contradicted
reason: The examples in the claim hold up. Hexagons do show up in honeycombs and tortoise shells, and in the basalt columns of the Giant's Causeway (in Northern Ireland, on the island of Ireland). The central claim, that hexagons are 'the strongest shape in nature', does not. Engineering sources say a regular hexagon on its own is not the strongest shape, and that triangles are usually considered the strongest because they are rigid. Sources credit hexagons with efficiency: they tile space with the least perimeter. Some popular sites repeat the 'strongest shape' line, but reliable sources contradict it.

text: A new discovery in a network of underwater caves in Mexico revealed the bones of an enormous Ice Age creature called a glyptodon, an ancient relative of the armadillo, that's estimated to be around 13,000 years old.
label: not_verifiable
reason: My searches turned up only partial evidence before the search limit cut me off. A Mexico News Daily article says fossils of Ice Age animals, including a glyptodon, were found in a cave in San Luis Potosí, Mexico, and some of its passages were flooded. But that cave is described as hard to reach and partly water-filled, not as a network of underwater caves. The article also gives no estimate of about 13,000 years and doesn't present the find as a new glyptodon discovery. I found nothing that confirms the claim's specific details: the underwater cave network, the age estimate, or that this was a recent discovery.

text: A blue whale has a heartbeat so loud that it can be detected from over 500 miles away under ideal conditions.
label: contradicted
reason: Sources that cite a distance for detecting a blue whale's heartbeat put it at about 2 miles, not more than 500 miles. The Whaling Museum blog, for example, says the heartbeat "can be detected from 2 MILES AWAY." Even that figure is widely seen as an exaggeration. Distances of hundreds of miles apply to blue whale calls (vocalizations), not to their heartbeats.

text: A blue whale's heart alone can weigh as much as 400 pounds, with some reaching lengths of up to 5 feet.
label: supported
reason: Reliable sources back both numbers. NOAA Fisheries says a blue whale's heart weighs about 400 pounds. Guinness World Records reports that a heart taken from a blue whale stranded in Newfoundland in 2014 weighed 440 lb and measured about 5 feet (1.5 m) long. Reuters and National Geographic also describe the heart as about 5 feet long and weighing roughly 400 pounds. The claim's wording ('as much as 400 pounds', 'up to 5 feet') fits these figures.

text: A blue whale's heartbeat is so loud that it can be detected almost 500 miles away by the right equipment.
label: contradicted
reason: NOAA Fisheries and other popular sources say a blue whale's heartbeat can be heard about 2 miles away, not almost 500 miles away, and even the 2-mile figure has been questioned. The 'hundreds of miles' range refers to blue whale calls, not heartbeats. The claim mixes up these two facts and greatly overstates the distance.

text: A blue whale's heartbeat is so loud that it can be detected by a satellite in space even though it's deep within the ocean.
label: contradicted
reason: No source says a blue whale's heartbeat can be picked up by a satellite, and the evidence points against it. NOAA's fact sheet gives the most generous figure, saying the heartbeat can be heard about 2 miles away, which is nowhere near space. Even that popular figure is disputed. The first recorded blue whale heart rate (Stanford/Scripps, 2019) needed a sensor tag stuck to the whale with suction cups near its flipper, which shows the heartbeat is hard to detect even up close. Sound also cannot travel through the vacuum of space. The satellite claim is an exaggeration of the '2 miles' factoid.

text: A blue whale's heartbeat is so loud that it can be detected from over 600 miles away under ideal conditions.
label: contradicted
reason: NOAA Fisheries and the Cold Spring Harbor Whaling Museum both say a blue whale's heartbeat can be heard about 2 miles away, not more than 600 miles. The very long distances often quoted (hundreds of miles or more) refer to blue whale vocalizations, not heartbeats. Even the 2-mile figure is a popular claim rather than a measured value, but no source supports a 600-mile range for a heartbeat.

text: A person can lead a blindfolded horse with just the sound of their voice and a gentle tug on the halter.
label: supported
reason: I could only partly check this claim because the search tool limit was reached. The one result I found (EquiSearch) shows that horses can be trained to respond to voice commands while being led on a halter and lead line, but it does not mention blindfolds. The blindfold part is not supported by any source I found. It rests on common horse-handling knowledge: horses are blindfolded to lead them out of burning barns, and blind horses are routinely led by voice and halter cues. Nothing I found contradicts the claim, and it is plausible, but the evidence is thin.

text: Astronomers have discovered a massive galaxy made almost entirely of dark matter, known as Dragonfly 44.
label: supported
reason: In 2016, W. M. Keck Observatory, Space.com and GeekWire all reported that astronomers had found Dragonfly 44, a massive galaxy estimated at about 99.99% dark matter, with a total mass similar to the Milky Way's. Space.com's wording almost exactly matches the claim. Some later studies, such as one with fewer globular clusters reported by ScienceAlert, dispute how much dark matter the galaxy has. Those revisions don't change the fact that the reported discovery happened as described.

text: Bloom County, Doonesbury, and Calvin and Hobbes, were all Physiology or Notable Awards Finalists illustrated comic strips from the USA.
label: not_verifiable
reason: The category the claim names, "Physiology or Notable Awards Finalists," is not a recognizable award or list, so there is nothing clear to check it against. All three are American comic strips. Sources say Bloom County won a Pulitzer Prize in 1987, and Doonesbury is also widely known as a Pulitzer winner. Calvin and Hobbes is not known to have won a Pulitzer. None of the search results ties the three strips to any award called "Physiology or Notable Awards," and since the label is garbled, the claim can't be confirmed or ruled out.

text: Finland has a "forest library" where trees are carved with passages from literature and poetry, creating a living, breathing library that grows with time.
label: contradicted
reason: I found no trustworthy source for a Finnish "forest library" where trees are carved with passages from literature. The well-known forest library is the Future Library (Framtidsbiblioteket) by Katie Paterson, and it is in Norway's Nordmarka forest near Oslo. It works differently: 1,000 trees were planted to supply paper for 100 manuscripts that will be printed in 2114. No text is carved into the trees. The closest Finnish project is IC-98's IÄI at the Hyytiälä Forestry Field Station. It is a poetry installation of 38 words or syllables carved on trees, rocks and stones, not literary passages, and it is not described as a library. The claim seems to mix up these two projects. Strictly speaking, the searches cannot prove that no such site exists in Finland, but the evidence points against the claim.

text: Honey Never Spoils: Archaeologists have found pots of honey in ancient Egyptian tombs that are over 3,000 years old and still perfectly edible
label: supported
reason: Several sources describe archaeologists finding pots of honey in ancient Egyptian tombs that were about 3,000 years old and still safe to eat. They include History Facts and My Modern Met, and the claim also matches widely cited Smithsonian reporting. They explain this by honey's low moisture, acidity and natural hydrogen peroxide, which stop it from spoiling. Some caveats: 'perfectly edible' is popular wording, and the original excavation records behind this story are rarely cited. Still, the search results consistently support the claim and none contradict it.

text: Honeybees are able to fly by using their wings to create electricity, beating them around 200 times per second to generate the lift needed.
label: contradicted
reason: The wingbeat figure is about right: sources put honeybees at roughly 200–240 beats per second, with 230 often cited. The main point is wrong, though. Bees don't fly by making electricity with their wings. Arizona State University's Ask A Biologist, UC ANR and the 2005 PNAS research describe lift as aerodynamic, coming from short, fast wing strokes, the angle of the wings and powerful thorax muscles. Bees do pick up a static charge as they fly, but that charge doesn't produce lift.

text: Humans and elephants share several similarities in their DNA, with studies showing that they share around 70% of their genetic makeup.
label: contradicted
reason: I couldn't find any source that backs the 70% figure. A geneticist's essay in Daedalus, published by the American Academy of Arts & Sciences, says humans share roughly 90% of their DNA with elephants, along with mice, dogs and cattle. A less reliable animal website puts the figure at about 98%. Both numbers are well above 70%. My last search, aimed specifically at finding a 70% claim, failed because I hit the tool's usage limit, so a source using that figure may exist that I didn't find. Still, the most credible source I found contradicts the claim's specific percentage, even though the general point that the two species share a lot of DNA holds up.

text: Humans share approximately 50% of their DNA with bananas, highlighting the surprising genetic similarities between seemingly distant species.
label: contradicted
reason: This is a common myth, and trustworthy fact-checks say it's wrong. Snopes rates the claim that humans share 50% of their DNA with bananas as 'False'. Snopes and The Naked Scientists both explain that the figure confuses genes with DNA: roughly half of human genes have a counterpart in bananas, but genes make up only about 2% of our DNA. That puts the actual shared DNA at around 1% or less. Computational biologist Natasha Glover found that the 50% figure doesn't come from any published research. A few low-quality sites repeat the claim, but the reliable sources clearly contradict it.

text: Plants can produce flowers and seeds without undergoing pollination through a process known as apomixis, a rare form of asexual reproduction.
label: supported
reason: A Current Biology (ScienceDirect) quick guide defines apomixis as asexual reproduction through seeds that produces clonal offspring. It says that in apomictic dandelions, "seed production is completely independent of male reproduction and pollination." It also calls apomixis rare, "less than 0.1% of plant species" can do it. Other sources agree that apomixis forms seeds without fertilization. One caveat: some apomicts (pseudogamous ones) still need pollination to form the endosperm, but the general claim, that plants can make seeds without pollination through this rare asexual process, is supported.

text: Rome is considered to be the second most populous city in the world with over 3,700,000 inhabitants in the metropolitan area inside the city limits.
label: contradicted
reason: Rome is not the second most populous city in the world. Its city limits (the comune) hold about 2.86 million people, which makes it Italy's most populous comune and the third most populous city in the EU by population within city limits. Wikipedia ranks it 8th in Europe. The 'over 3,700,000' figure doesn't fit either measure: the city itself has about 2.86 million, and the Metropolitan City of Rome has about 4.36 million.

text: Rome is considered to be the second most populous city in the world with over 3,700,000 residents in Rome itself.
label: contradicted
reason: Wikipedia puts Rome's city population at about 2.7 million. It calls Rome the third most populous city in the EU, and its outline page says fourth. Either way, Rome is nowhere near the second most populous city in the world, and the city itself has fewer than 3.7 million residents. Even the whole Metropolitan City of Rome has only about 4.3 million people.

text: Rome is considered to be the second most populous city in the world with over 3,700,000 residents living in the metropolitan area.
label: contradicted
reason: Wikipedia puts Rome at about 2.7 million people within city limits and about 4.2 million in the Metropolitan City. That makes it the third most populous city in the EU by city-limits population and the most populous metropolitan city in Italy. It is nowhere near second in the world, since cities like Tokyo, Delhi and Shanghai are far larger. The population figure is also off, though not in a way that saves the claim: 4.2 million is technically "over 3.7 million", but the claim understates it.

text: Rome is considered to be the second most populous city in the world with over 3,700,000 residents.
label: contradicted
reason: The claim is wrong on both counts. Rome is the most populous city in Italy and the fourth largest in the EU, but it is nowhere near second in the world. Its population is about 2.75 million (Statista and Vikidia), well under 3.7 million. The wider metropolitan area has about 4.2 million people, which still wouldn't make it second in the world.

text: Rupert, the largest snowman ever recorded, was built in Maine in 1999 and stood at an impressive 113 feet 7 inches tall.
label: contradicted
reason: The 113-foot, 7-inch snowman built in Bethel, Maine, in 1999 is real, but it was named "Angus, King of the Mountain" after then-Governor Angus King, not "Rupert." It also isn't the largest ever recorded: Bethel's Olympia SnowWoman beat it in 2008. Both mistakes go against the claim.

text: Rupert, the largest snowman ever recorded, was built in Maine in 1999 and stood at an incredible 113 feet 7 inches tall.
label: contradicted
reason: Reliable Maine news sources say the 113-foot, 7-inch snowman built in Bethel, Maine, in 1999 was named "Angus, King of the Mountain," not "Rupert." The claim also calls it the largest snowman ever recorded, but its record was beaten in 2008 by the "Olympia SnowWoman," which was about 9 feet taller. The location, year and height in the claim are right, but the name and the all-time record are wrong.

text: Scientists estimate that there are approximately 8.7 million identified species on Earth, but the total number of species is estimated to range from 10 to 30 million.
label: contradicted
reason: The claim misstates what the 8.7 million figure means. It comes from Mora et al. (2011, PLoS Biology), and it is the estimated *total* number of eukaryotic species on Earth (give or take 1.3 million), not the number already identified. Only about 1.2 million species have been described and catalogued, including roughly 953,000 animals. The same study says earlier estimates of the total ranged from 3 million to 100 million, not 10 to 30 million. So the claim treats the estimated total as if it were the count of species already identified.

text: Scientists estimate that there are approximately 8.7 million identified species on Earth, but the true number could range up to 30 million.
label: contradicted
reason: The claim gets the meaning of the 8.7 million figure wrong. In Mora et al. (2011, PLOS Biology), 8.7 million (±1.3 million) is the estimated total number of eukaryotic species on Earth, not the number that have been identified. Only about 1.2 million species had been catalogued, which leaves about 86% still undescribed. The coverage of that study also gave earlier estimates of the total as ranging from 3 to 100 million, so the claim's 'up to 30 million' upper bound is not what these sources say either.

text: Scientists estimate that there are around 8.7 million identified species on Earth, but they believe that up to 80% of all species remain undiscovered.
label: contradicted
reason: The 8.7 million figure (give or take 1.3 million) from Mora et al. (2011) is an estimate of all species on Earth, both known and unknown. It is not a count of species already identified. About 1.2 million species have actually been described, and the same study suggests roughly 86% (more than 80%) are still undiscovered. The 'more than 80% undiscovered' part matches the sources, but calling the 8.7 million 'identified' species is wrong, and it doesn't fit with the claim's own statement that most species remain unknown.

text: Scientists estimate that there may be between 700,000 and 1 million species on Earth, but only about 226,000 have been formally described.
label: contradicted
reason: The figures in the claim are real, but they describe ocean species only, not all species on Earth. UNESCO and the Appeltans et al. study say about 226,000 marine species have been described, out of an estimated 700,000 to 1 million in the ocean. For all life on Earth, the estimate is about 8.7 million species, of which only about 1.2 million have been described (Mora et al., PLoS Biology). So the claim gets the scope wrong.

text: Scientists estimate that there may be between 700,000 and 1 million species on Earth, but only about 226,000 of these have been formally described.
label: contradicted
reason: The figures are real, but they describe ocean species only, not all life on Earth. UNESCO and a 2012 study led by Appeltans (reported by NBC News and LiveScience) put about 226,000 described marine species against an estimated 700,000 to 1 million species in the oceans. Estimates for all species on Earth are far higher, commonly around 8.7 million. Saying 'on Earth' misstates the scope of the estimate.

text: Tarantulas have been around for a long time, with fossil records showing they've remained largely unchanged for over 140 million years.
label: contradicted
reason: Reliable sources don't back the 140-million-year figure. Texas Parks & Wildlife Magazine, citing tarantula expert Rick West, says fossil records show tarantulas have stayed 'virtually unchanged' for more than 20 million years, not more than 140 million. Most confirmed tarantula (Theraphosidae) fossils come from Miocene amber about 16 million years old. The oldest tarantula fossil, from Burmese amber, is about 100 million years old, and molecular studies date the group's origins to about 120 million years ago. Tarantulas are an ancient group, but the claim that fossils show them largely unchanged for over 140 million years conflicts with the evidence.

text: Tarzon, or giant water lilies, are capable of supporting up to 70 pounds due to their unique leaf structure and waxy underside.
label: not_verifiable
reason: I found no source that uses "Tarzon" as a name for giant water lilies (Victoria species), so it's unclear what the claim refers to. Even reading it as Victoria amazonica, the details don't match. Sources commonly say a mature leaf can hold about 45 kg (about 99 lb) when the weight is evenly spread, not "up to 70 pounds." They also credit the leaf's strength to the network of ribs underneath, not a waxy underside. Because the main subject has no clear referent and the specifics are unsupported or inconsistent, the claim can't be confirmed.

text: Tarzon, or giant water lilies, are capable of supporting up to 70 pounds due to their web-like underside structure which disperses the weight it holds.
label: not_verifiable
reason: Some of the claim checks out: Bok Tower Gardens says giant Victoria water lily leaves can support about 70 pounds, and AskNature and other sources credit the ribbed underside for the structural support. However, I found no source that uses "Tarzon" as a name for giant water lilies. Searches for it only turned up people's surnames, so that part of the claim cannot be verified. The "up to 70 pounds" limit is also disputed: Smithsonian reports a pad held 183 pounds in a weigh-off contest, and Denver Botanic Gardens says the pads can hold an adult. Since one part can't be verified and the evidence on the weight limit conflicts, the claim is inconclusive.

text: Turtles have an innate navigation system that helps them migrate thousands of miles across oceans to reach their birthplace or specific breeding grounds.
label: supported
reason: Reliable sources back the claim. ScienceDaily and LiveScience report on a 2015 UNC study in Current Biology showing that sea turtles migrate thousands of miles and return to nest where they hatched by following magnetic signatures along the coast. A review in the Journal of Experimental Biology describes magnetic navigation as the main way they find their way home over long distances. Earth.com reports that hatchlings with no experience sense the Earth's magnetic field to cross thousands of miles of ocean, which points to an inborn ability. Two caveats: the claim is really about sea turtles, not all turtles, and Wikipedia notes that adults may also learn parts of the magnetic map rather than rely only on instinct. Overall, though, the evidence supports the claim's main point.

text: Winston Churchill was a skilled artist, and his paintings have sold for millions at auction, some of them even fetched higher prices than those by renowned artists of his time.
label: not_verifiable
reason: Most of the claim is supported, but I couldn't verify the comparison with other artists before my search limit ran out. The sources call Churchill an accomplished painter, and Sotheby's praised his "exceptional ability as a painter." His paintings have sold for millions: The Goldfish Pool at Chartwell fetched about £1.8m in 2014, and Tower of the Koutoubia Mosque, sold by Angelina Jolie at Christie's in 2021, fetched £8.2m (about $11.5m). No source I found says his works sold for more than paintings by renowned artists of his time, such as Lavery or Sickert. An Artnet headline hints the 2021 sale set a record in Modern British art, but I couldn't confirm the details, so that part of the claim remains unverified.

text: Zebras are born with their eyes open and can walk within the first hour of birth.
label: supported
reason: Both parts of the claim check out. A-Z Animals says newborn zebra foals have their eyes and ears open and can stand within 10 to 20 minutes of birth. Sciencing says most foals can walk, and even run, within an hour of being born. Other sources say the same thing: zebrafacts.net reports walking at about 15 minutes and running by one hour, and Petmojo reports foals standing within 15 to 20 minutes and running within an hour. These are popular-science sites rather than primary research, but they all agree and nothing contradicts them.

text: Arectangle divided into a square and two equal rectangles, each of which is also divided into square and two rectangles, and so on, can help to illustrate the visual depiction of a continued fraction.
label: supported
reason: I could only run a few searches before hitting the search limit, so this verdict rests on limited evidence. Reliable math sites, Ron Knott's Surrey continued-fractions page and cut-the-knot's 'Square Root of 2 as a Continued Fraction', present continued fractions visually by repeatedly cutting a rectangle into squares and smaller rectangles. That matches the claim's main point that this kind of recursive dissection illustrates a continued fraction. I could not find a source that describes the exact 'square plus two equal rectangles' layout, so that specific detail is unconfirmed. Nothing I found contradicts it, and the general idea is well supported.

text: Reindeer are excellent swimmers, and some populations in the Arctic migrate annually by swimming through icy waters to reach their summer habitats, with some making swims of up to five miles at a time.
label: not_verifiable
reason: Most of the claim is supported, but the five-mile figure is not. Reliable sources say reindeer and caribou are strong swimmers: the Smithsonian National Zoo says they can swim "strongly for miles at a time," and the San Diego Zoo says they cross rivers during migration. Swimming is part of their seasonal migrations, including herds swimming fjords and sounds in Norway. However, no source confirms swims of "up to five miles" during migration. That number seems to come from swimming speed (about 4–6 mph, per the San Diego Zoo) rather than distance. Other evidence suggests five miles is not the upper limit: a Movement Ecology study recorded a caribou swimming more than 25 km (about 15.5 miles) across Lake Bienville, and another source reports swims of about 35 miles. Because the specific distance is unconfirmed and partly conflicts with this evidence, the claim cannot be fully supported.

text: QImage, a NASA spacecraft launched in 1985, was originally an Earth-orbiting satellite that a team repurposed in 2004 to orbit the Sun and act as a gravitational 'listening post' to observe the Sun-Earth connection.
label: contradicted
reason: I found no record of a NASA spacecraft called "QImage". The 1985 launch records (astronautix's 1985 chronology and NASA's NSSDCA catalog) and searches for a repurposed Sun-orbiting "listening post" don't turn one up. Searches for the name only return the QImage image class in the Qt software framework, documented at doc.qt.io. Since QImage is a software class, not a spacecraft launched in 1985 and repurposed in 2004, the claim misidentifies what it is.

text: In 2019, the world's largest living organism was discovered in a Blue Mountains forest in Australia, covering over 2200 hectares as a giant fungus.
label: contradicted
reason: The record-holding giant fungus, the 'Humongous Fungus' (Armillaria ostoyae), grows in the Blue Mountains of eastern Oregon in the US, under the Malheur National Forest. It was not found in Australia. It was discovered in 1998, not 2019, and it covers about 2,384 acres, which is roughly 965 hectares, not more than 2,200 hectares. The claim seems to mix up Oregon's Blue Mountains with Australia's and treat acres as hectares.

text: Abnormally large crystals have grown within the Naica Mine's Cave of the Crystals in Chihuahua, Mexico, with the largest crystal, a selenite, measuring approximately 36 feet long and weighing 55 tons.
label: supported
reason: Several sources describe the Naica Mine's Cave of the Crystals in Chihuahua as holding giant selenite (gypsum) crystals. Stormchaser.ca says the largest are over 11 m (36 ft) long and weigh 55 tons. Atlas Obscura gives up to 12 m (over 36 ft) and about 55 tons for one crystal. Some sources, including Wikipedia, put the length at 12 m (39 ft), so the size estimates vary a little. Still, "approximately 36 feet" and 55 tons match the published figures.

text: British Airways has a 747 jet with the smallest pilot staff as low as 3 plus 3 cabin on a B747  a British Airways short small variation the B747-200LR
label: contradicted
reason: British Airways flew the 747-100, 747-200 (passenger and one freighter) and 747-400. There is no '747-200LR' variant in its fleet history, and no '747-200LR' model exists. BA also retired all its 747s in 2020, so it no longer 'has' a 747. Nothing supports the claimed '3 pilots plus 3 cabin crew' figure either. Because the claim rests on an aircraft BA never operated, it is contradicted.

text: Plants can make sounds, albeit too quiet for human ears, when they undergo stress or injury, with researchers using specialized equipment to detect and record these sounds.
label: supported
reason: A 2023 Tel Aviv University study published in Cell recorded tomato, tobacco and other plants making airborne popping sounds when they were short of water or had their stems cut. Stressed plants made about 30–50 pops per hour, far more than unstressed plants. Researchers captured the sounds with microphones in a soundproof acoustic chamber and a greenhouse, then used machine learning to tell the sounds apart. Bees do pick up a positive electrostatic charge, but National Geographic reports that it comes from colliding with charged particles in the air, which strip electrons from their waxy outer shell. That charge is linked to sensing and communication (and is known to help with pollen), not to staying aloft. None of the sources say electricity from wing movement reduces air resistance or helps bees fly.
