text: Honeybees are able to fly by using their wings to generate electricity and then using that electricity, along with their wings beating at 200 times per second, to generate lift.
label: contradicted
reason: Reliable sources (ASU Ask A Biologist, Live Science, UC ANR) say honeybees fly using their thoracic flight muscles. These muscles drive short, rapid wing strokes, about 230–240 beats per second, that create lift through aerodynamic effects such as leading-edge vortices. Bees do pick up static charge, but none of these sources say they make electricity with their wings or use it to generate lift. The claim's flight mechanism is wrong, and 200 beats per second is also a little below the reported figure.

text: Honeybees are able to fly by using their wings to generate lift, but also utilize rapid movement of their wings to create electricity and become statically charged to attract pollen.
label: supported
reason: Several sources (AskNature, Quanta Magazine, Bumblebee Conservation Trust) say that bees build up a positive electrostatic charge while flying, from friction as their wings beat rapidly through the air. Pollen and flowers tend to carry a negative charge, so static forces help pull pollen onto the bee, sometimes even across a small air gap. The claim that bees fly by generating lift with their wings is basic, well-established science. One caveat: the claim says bees "utilize" their wings to make this charge, which suggests intent, but the research describes the charge as a side effect of flight that bees then benefit from.

text: Honeybees are able to fly by using their wings to generate lift, but also utilize rapid movement of their wings to create electricity and propel themselves through the air more efficiently.
label: contradicted
reason: The first part is right: honeybees fly by beating their wings very fast (about 230–240 Hz) to produce lift, which comes from vortices forming around the wings. The electricity part is wrong. Bees do pick up a positive static charge, but it comes from friction with the air as they fly, not from using their wings to generate electricity. Sources describe that charge helping bees attract pollen and sense flowers. None say it helps propel bees or makes their flight more efficient. Ordinary aerodynamics already explains how bees fly. No source I found denies the propulsion idea in so many words, but the evidence on what the charge actually does goes against it.

text: Honeybees are able to fly by using their wings to generate lift, but also utilize rapid movement of their wings to create electricity through a process called "triboelectric charging."
label: supported
reason: Honeybees fly by generating lift with their wings. Studies of insect electrostatics report that flying insects such as honeybees build up a positive electric charge from the friction of their bodies and wings against the air, which is triboelectric (contact/friction) charging. Other sources similarly describe bees gaining a faint positive charge as their wings beat against the air. One caveat: the charge comes from friction while flying rather than being deliberately "utilized" to make electricity. Bees do use the charge, for example to sense floral electric fields and to help pollen stick to them, so the claim is broadly accurate.

text: Japan has the world's oldest known living tree, a white pine called 'Jōmon Sugi,' estimated to be approximately 2,000 to 7,000 years old.
label: contradicted
reason: The 2,000–7,000-year age range is right, but the rest of the claim is wrong. Nippon.com and Wikipedia both say Jōmon Sugi on Yakushima is a Japanese cedar (sugi, Cryptomeria japonica), not a white pine. It is also not generally recognised as the world's oldest known living tree. Its age is uncertain, and that title usually goes to Great Basin bristlecone pines such as Methuselah in California, at roughly 4,800+ years.

text: Japan has the world's oldest known living tree, a white pine called 'Jōmon Sugi,' estimated to be approximately 2,000 to 7,200 years old.
label: contradicted
reason: The age range is right, but the claim gets two other things wrong. Jōmon Sugi on Yakushima is estimated at about 2,000 to 7,200 years old. However, it is a Japanese cedar (sugi, Cryptomeria japonica), not a white pine. Sources also call it Japan's oldest and largest cedar, or 'one of the world's oldest trees', not the world's oldest known living tree. Its lower dendrochronology-based estimate of about 2,000 years is far younger than the roughly 4,800-year-old Great Basin bristlecone pines, which are generally treated as the oldest known individual trees.

text: Japan has the world's oldest known living tree, a white pine called 'Jōmon Sugi,' estimated to be approximately 2,000-7,200 years old.
label: contradicted
reason: The claim gets the species wrong and overstates the tree's record. Wikipedia and Monumental Trees both say Jōmon Sugi is a Cryptomeria japonica, a Japanese cedar known as sugi or yakusugi, not a white pine. Wikipedia calls it the oldest and largest tree in Japan, not in the world. Age estimates of about 2,000 to 7,200 years do appear in some sources, but Monumental Trees gives roughly 3,000 years. Other trees, such as the Great Basin bristlecone pines, are generally recognised as the world's oldest known living trees.

text: Migrating animals that travel alone can be referred to as 'solitary migrants', often excluding species, like some birds that follow each other in groups during migration periods.
label: supported
reason: Birds and Blooms uses the term "solitary migrants" for animals that migrate alone. It says hummingbirds "are solitary migrants, so you won't see them traveling in flocks." That supports the term and its definition. It also matches the contrast in the claim: species that migrate in flocks are not described as solitary migrants. The claim's wording is loose, but the search results contradict none of it.

text: Roses arranged in the pattern of a clock on a compass, naturally grow in a north-south direction to attract pollinating bees more efficiently.
label: contradicted
reason: The claim mixes up the 'compass rose' with real roses. A compass rose is a drawing on compasses and maps that shows the cardinal directions. It is called a 'rose' only because its radiating points look like a flower, not because roses grow in that pattern. I found no evidence that rose plants grow in a north-south direction to attract bees. The plant that actually lines up north-south is the unrelated compass plant (Silphium laciniatum), and sources say its leaves do this to manage sun exposure (catching morning and evening sun while avoiding the harsh midday sun), not to attract pollinators. No source supports the claim's link between roses, compass alignment and bees.

text: Scientists estimate that there are approximately 8.7 million identified species on Earth, but this number is likely a small fraction of the total variety of life on our planet.
label: contradicted
reason: The 8.7 million figure (Mora et al. 2011, PLoS Biology) is an estimate of the total number of eukaryotic species on Earth, not the number that have been identified. Only about 1.2 million species had been catalogued, and the study suggests about 86% of species have not yet been described. Calling 8.7 million 'identified species' therefore misstates the figure. The claim also says 8.7 million is a small fraction of all life; that conflicts with the study, which presents 8.7 million (±1.3 million) as its estimate of the total.

text: Scientists estimate that there may be between 700,000 and 1 million species on Earth, but we have formally described only about 300,000 of those species.
label: contradicted
reason: The claim's numbers are far too low for all life on Earth. A widely cited 2011 study (Mora et al.) puts the total at about 8.7 million eukaryotic species, give or take 1.3 million, and says about 1.25 million have already been described. Earlier estimates ranged from 3 to 100 million. The figures in the claim (700,000 to 1 million estimated, about 300,000 described) look closer to estimates for ocean species only, not all species on Earth.

text: Scientists estimate that there may be between 700,000 to 1 million described species of insects on Earth, but the actual number could be much higher.
label: supported
reason: Reliable sources put the number of described insect species at roughly 900,000 to 1 million. The Smithsonian figure is about 900,000 known species, and Wikipedia, citing Stork 2018, gives 950,000 to 1,000,000. Both fall within the claimed range of 700,000 to 1 million, although the claim's lower bound of 700,000 is wider than the usual figures. Sources also agree that the real total is much higher. Stork's averaged estimate is about 5.5 million insect species (likely between 2.6 and 7.2 million), and a 2026 Cornell study suggests 14 to 20 million. This supports the claim that the actual number could be much higher.

text: Scientists estimate that there may be between 700,000 to 1 million species on Earth, but only about 226,000 of these have been formally described and named.
label: contradicted
reason: The figures are real, but they describe ocean species, not all species on Earth. UNESCO and ABC report a 2012 Current Biology study estimating 700,000 to about 1 million marine species, with about 226,000 marine species described. Estimates for all life on Earth are much higher: about 8.7 million species, with almost 2 million described. Applying the marine numbers to the whole planet makes the claim wrong.

text: Tarantulas have existed for around 120 million years, dating back to the Cretaceous period.
label: supported
reason: Phys.org's coverage of a 2021 PeerJ study reports that tarantulas first appeared about 120 million years ago, during the Cretaceous period, in the landmass that is now the Americas. Smithsonian Magazine covered the same study. Both sources match the claim.

text: Near the surface of Greenland and Antarctica, scientists have discovered well-preserved 8,000-year-old fossils of microorganisms that can survive in environments lacking water, life force and light.
label: not_verifiable
reason: I found no reliable source for this specific discovery. What turned up was different research: a 2007 Rutgers study that revived bacteria up to 8 million years old from ice 3–5 m deep in an Antarctic glacier, microbial studies of Greenland and Antarctic ice cores dated from 500 to 157,000 years old, and microbes living in dark, oxygen-poor buried Antarctic lakes. None of these reports well-preserved 8,000-year-old fossils found near the surface in both Greenland and Antarctica. None describes organisms that survive without water, 'life force' and light. The claim looks like a distorted mix of separate studies, but no source directly contradicts it, so it can't be confirmed or refuted.

text: Plants can make sounds, such as clicking and bubbling noises, when they are subjected to stress, injury, or drying out, although these sounds are typically inaudible to the human ear.
label: supported
reason: A 2023 Tel Aviv University study published in Cell found that tomato and tobacco plants give off airborne ultrasonic sounds when they are dried out (desiccated) or cut. Reports describe these sounds as clicking or popping noises in ultrasonic frequencies that humans cannot hear, and they increase when the plant is stressed. The research links them to cavitation, which is the forming and bursting of air bubbles in the plant's water-conducting tissue. That fits the claim's 'bubbling' description. Science News, ScienceAlert and Cell's own summary all agree on the main points.

text: A blue whale's heartbeat is so slow and loud that scientists can use specialized underwater tools to detect and study the sounds of its heartbeat from miles away.
label: supported
reason: NOAA Fisheries, a trusted government source, says a blue whale's heartbeat "can be heard 2 miles away." WWF Australia gives a similar figure of three kilometres. The Cold Spring Harbor Whaling Museum says the heartbeat can be detected underwater from about 2 miles away, and that it slows sharply during dives, to as low as 2 beats per minute. Only unreliable sources, such as Brainly community answers, dispute the distance. One caveat: no source describes scientists actually using underwater acoustic tools to study heartbeat sounds from miles away. The first recording of a blue whale's heartbeat (2019) used a monitor attached to the whale with suction cups. The core claim about distance is backed by reputable sources, but the detail about how scientists study the sound goes further than the evidence.

text: Denmark has the highest number of traffic crossings over the country's coastline with a 7.4km Drogden tunnel and nearly 25% of railway tracks over water in Europe.
label: contradicted
reason: Wikipedia's Øresund Bridge article says the Øresund Tunnel under the Drogden channel is about 4 km long, not 7.4 km. The 7.4 km figure is close to the bridge's 7,845 m length, so the claim seems to mix up the bridge and the tunnel. I found no evidence for the other parts of the claim: that Denmark has the most coastline crossings in Europe or that nearly 25% of its railway tracks run over water. The wrong tunnel length is enough to contradict the claim.

text: Abnormally large crystals have grown within the Naica Mine's Cave of the Crystals in Chihuahua, Mexico, with the largest crystal, a selenite, measuring approximately 36 feet long.
label: supported
reason: Sources agree that the Naica Mine's Cave of the Crystals in Chihuahua holds giant selenite (gypsum) crystals, among the largest natural crystals ever found. HowStuffWorks gives the largest as about 36 feet (11 m) long, which matches the claim exactly. Other sources, including Wikipedia, Geology In and the Lizzadro Museum, put the largest at about 12 m (39 feet). That is close enough to fit the claim's 'approximately 36 feet', so the evidence supports the claim overall.

text: Werth, a small village in North Rhine-Westphalia, Germany, is home to the largest Easter egg museum in the world, featuring a collection of over 4,000 eggs and egg-related artifacts.
label: contradicted
reason: Nothing in the search results links Werth to an Easter egg museum. Werth is part of Isselburg in North Rhine-Westphalia, and the museum listed there is a local history museum, the Heimatmuseum Werth. Atlas Obscura says Germany's only Easter egg museum is in Sonnenbühl, Baden-Württemberg, and that museum is described as holding about 1,000 eggs. Tripadvisor describes the Pysanka Easter Egg Museum in Kolomyia, Ukraine, as holding more than 12,000 decorated eggs, so a 4,000-egg collection would not be the world's largest.

text: A blue whale, with its massive size, has a blue-gray color and a heart so large that it can pump up to 5,000 liters (1,320 gallons) of blood with each beat.
label: contradicted
reason: The blue-gray color and the huge size are accurate, but the stroke volume in the claim is far too high. Several sources (Politecnico di Milano's iHeart project, IFLScience, Ocean Action Hub) put a blue whale's heart output at about 220 liters (58 gallons) per beat. A Stanford-based study cited by Inverse estimated about 80 liters per beat for a 70-ton whale. None of the sources support 5,000 liters (1,320 gallons) per beat, which is more than 20 times the reported figure.

text: A chunk of the Moon broke off about 4.5 billion years ago and collided with Earth, eventually merging with our planet and forming the mountains that make up its core.
label: contradicted
reason: Scientists' leading explanation, the giant impact hypothesis, says that about 4.5 billion years ago a Mars-sized protoplanet called Theia hit the early Earth, and the Moon formed from the debris. The claim gets this backwards: the Moon did not exist yet, so no piece of it could have broken off and hit Earth. Earth's core is made of iron and nickel, not mountains. Some research suggests remnants of Theia may sit deep in Earth's mantle, but those remnants came from Theia, not from the Moon.

text: Plants can make sounds, as research has shown that they release ultrasonic clicks when they are stressed, injured, or communicating with other plants and even insects.
label: not_verifiable
reason: The 2023 Tel Aviv University study published in Cell (Khait et al.) supports part of the claim. It found that plants give off airborne ultrasonic clicks when stressed by drought or when their stems are cut. But the research does not show that plants make these sounds to communicate with other plants or insects. Coverage of the study says insects and possibly other plants might be able to detect the sounds, but that whether plants use them to communicate is still unclear. Because the communication part of the claim is unverified speculation, the claim as a whole cannot be confirmed.

text: Honeybees are able to fly by using electricity generated from the flapping of their wings, which creates a positive charge around the bee, and a negative charge from the air around it.
label: contradicted
reason: The sources say honeybees pick up a positive electrostatic charge while flying, mainly from friction with the air. They use this charge to sense flowers' electric fields and to move pollen. Nothing says bees fly by using electricity. Bee flight works through wing aerodynamics (lift), and the charge is a side effect of flying, not what powers it. The claim also gets the cause and purpose of the charge wrong, so its central assertion is contradicted.

text: Scientists estimate that there may be between 700,000 and 1 million species on Earth, but only about 1.3 million of these have been formally described.
label: contradicted
reason: Scientific estimates put the total number of species on Earth far higher than 700,000 to 1 million. The widely cited 2011 PLoS Biology study (Mora et al.) estimated about 8.7 million species, give or take 1.3 million, with roughly 1.2 to 1.3 million formally described. The claim also contradicts itself: 1.3 million described species could not be a subset of a total of only 700,000 to 1 million.

text: Plants can make sounds, too, but they are beyond the range of human hearing; these sounds include the ultrasonic noises produced by photosynthesizing plants and the hissing sound of snapping cucumbers.
label: not_verifiable
reason: I ran several searches before reaching the search limit. Trustworthy sources, including the 2023 Cell study and reports from NHM, Washington Post and Science News, back the general point: stressed plants such as tomato and tobacco make ultrasonic clicks that humans can't hear. However, these sounds come from drought stress or cutting, not from photosynthesis as such. A Frontiers review links ultrasonic emissions to transpiration, and the only photosynthesis-related sound I found was a passing mention of marine algae. I found no evidence of a 'hissing sound of snapping cucumbers.' The squirting cucumber's seed ejection is a well-known plant, but nothing I found describes it as hissing or beyond human hearing. Because these specific examples can't be verified, the claim is inconclusive.

text: Plants can make sounds, too, in the form of ultrasonic clicking noises that occur when they're under stress, such as when a branch or stem is about to break.
label: not_verifiable
reason: The main claim holds up. A 2023 Tel Aviv University study in Cell, reported by Science News, CNN and Sci.News, recorded tomato and tobacco plants making ultrasonic clicks under stress. The researchers caused that stress in two ways: they withheld water (dehydration) or cut the stems. The example in the claim does not hold up. No source says plants click 'when a branch or stem is about to break.' The clicks are thought to come from cavitation, when air bubbles form and the water column in the xylem breaks, not from a branch or stem failing. Since this part can't be verified and seems to misstate the trigger, the claim is not fully supported.

text: Honeybees are able to fly by using electricity generated by the movement of their wings to create an electrostatic charge that helps them lift off the ground and stay aloft.
label: contradicted
reason: Reliable sources, including Nature, research on honeybee takeoff, and beekeeping suppliers, say honeybees fly using aerodynamics. Their wings beat very fast through short, sweeping strokes and rotate at the end of each stroke. This creates unsteady airflow effects such as leading-edge vortices, which produce the lift. Powerful muscles in the thorax drive the wings. Bees do pick up electrostatic charge while flying, but that charge helps with things like pollen sticking to them, not with lift. No credible source says electricity from wing movement keeps bees aloft.

text: France and Spain both claim to be the birthplace of the first restaurant, 'auberge,' with the French claiming it was in the 1760s in Paris and the Spanish dating it back as far as 1268.
label: not_verifiable
reason: I couldn't verify the claim as a whole. The French part holds up: Britannica and other sources credit Boulanger's soup shop, opened in Paris in 1765, as the first restaurant. Nothing I found supports the Spanish part, though. No source mentions a Spanish claim going back to 1268. The Spanish record usually cited is Sobrino de Botín in Madrid, open since 1725, which Guinness lists as the oldest continuously operating restaurant. Rival Spanish claims such as Casa Pedro in Madrid, Cal Xarina from 1550, and Can Culleretes from 1786 also say nothing about 1268. Sources also describe the first restaurant as a Paris broth shop, not an 'auberge', which means inn. I ran out of searches before I could fully rule out the 1268 date, so the evidence leans against the claim but doesn't firmly contradict it.

text: A Perez Prado song 'Guantanamera', was the first song to be transmitted from Earth into deep space, on November 16, 1974, as part of the 'Arecibo Message'.
label: contradicted
reason: The Arecibo Message did go out on November 16, 1974, but it was not a song. It was a 1,679-bit binary picture sent at 2380 MHz toward the globular cluster M13. The image showed a counting scheme, the numbers of key chemical elements, a DNA diagram, a human figure, the solar system and the telescope itself. No reliable source says it contained Perez Prado's 'Guantanamera' or any other music, so the claim gets the content of the message wrong.

text: Plants can make sounds, too, when they are injured, but these sounds are not range-friendly, as most plants making a sound falls in the range of 10-80 Hz, beyond the range of human hearing ability.
label: contradicted
reason: The claim gets the frequency wrong. The Tel Aviv University study (Khait et al., 2023, in Cell) found that stressed and cut tomato and tobacco plants make ultrasonic clicks at about 40–80 kHz, not 10–80 Hz. Those sounds are too high-pitched for people to hear. A 10–80 Hz range would be very low and mostly inside human hearing, which runs from about 20 Hz to 20 kHz, so that part of the claim is false.

text: Water can exist in all three states of matter - solid, liquid, and gas - at the same time when it reaches its triple point at 0.01 degrees Celsius and 611.73 pascals of pressure.
label: supported
reason: Reliable sources agree that water's triple point is 273.16 K (0.01 °C), where ice, liquid water and water vapour coexist in equilibrium. ScienceNotes gives the pressure as about 611.7 Pa and notes that some sources list 611.73 Pa while others give 611.657 Pa. The claim's value of 611.73 Pa is one of these commonly cited figures, so it is acceptable. The small difference between those values is not enough to call the claim wrong.

text: Plants can make sounds, including a faint hissing sound when they're stressed due to a lack of water, which researchers have been able to detect using specialized equipment.
label: supported
reason: Khait et al. (Cell, 2023) found that tomato, tobacco and other plants give off airborne sounds when they are short of water or their stems are cut. The researchers picked these up with ultrasonic microphones, and Science News, the Natural History Museum and Smithsonian all reported the study. That supports the main claim: plants make sounds under drought stress, and specialized equipment can detect them. One caveat is the word "hissing." Reports describe the sounds as ultrasonic clicks or pops that humans can't hear, not a hiss. Because the core claim matches the evidence, I'm calling it supported, but the description of the sound itself is inaccurate.

text: Orient Drinks, a Japanese beverage company, teamed up with convenience store chain, Lawson, to sell a vending machine coffee, and Kraft Foods, to test a soft-serve ice cream dispensing vending machine.
label: not_verifiable
reason: My searches turned up no trace of a Japanese beverage company called "Orient Drinks." I also found nothing on a Lawson partnership for vending-machine coffee or a Kraft Foods trial of a soft-serve ice cream vending machine. The results only covered general topics: Lawson's in-store MACHI café coffee and other soft-serve vending machines in Japan. Without a clearly identifiable company or any source for these partnerships, the claim can't be confirmed or disproved.

text: Roses arranged in a specific pattern of 14, the number associated with Valentine's Day, can also be called a baker's dozen plus one.
label: supported
reason: Dictionary.com says a baker's dozen is 13, or "a dozen plus one." So a baker's dozen plus one is 14, and Valentine's Day falls on February 14, which is why 14 is linked to the holiday. The claim is correct as arithmetic. No source shows florists actually using "baker's dozen plus one" as a name for 14 roses, but the claim only says the arrangement can be called that, and it can. The phrase "specific pattern" is vague but doesn't affect the count.

text: In the heart of the Amazon rainforest, there exists a type of jellyfish which is immortal, known as the Turritopsis dohrnii or the 'immortal jellyfish.'
label: contradicted
reason: Turritopsis dohrnii, called the 'immortal jellyfish' because it can revert to an immature polyp stage, is a small marine species. Sources such as iNaturalist, Simple Wikipedia and a PubMed paper place it in the Mediterranean Sea and the waters off Japan. Nothing places it in the Amazon rainforest, so the location in the claim is wrong.

text: A blue whale's heartbeat can be as loud as 188 decibels, louder than a jet engine, and can be detected over 500 miles away underwater.
label: contradicted
reason: The claim pins figures that belong to blue whale vocalizations onto the heartbeat. Blue whale calls are the sounds that reach about 188 decibels and can be heard hundreds of miles away. NOAA Fisheries says the heartbeat can be heard about 2 miles away, which is nowhere near 500 miles. Some researchers think even the 2-mile figure for the heartbeat is exaggerated. No credible source says a heartbeat reaches 188 dB.

text: Honeybees are able to fly by using their wings to create electricity through a phenomenon called "triboelectric charging," which helps to attract and trap pollen.
label: contradicted
reason: The sources confirm that bees pick up static charge through the triboelectric effect while flying, and that this charge helps them attract pollen. But the claim gets the cause and effect backwards. Bees don't fly because they make electricity. Flight comes from aerodynamic lift produced by flapping their wings, and the charge is only a side effect of moving through the air (with body hairs and the air rubbing together). The idea that bees fly by generating electricity is false.

text: Aersopatiale Alouette helicopters use a turbine engine which allows for the specially adapted helicopters to be able to dump turbine power put into the engines which enables them to descend nearly vertically.
label: not_verifiable
reason: The search results confirm only the first part of the claim. Aérospatiale Alouette II and III helicopters do use a turbine (turboshaft) engine, the Turbomeca Artouste. I found no reliable source saying that specially adapted Alouettes can "dump turbine power" so they can descend nearly vertically. That part of the claim can't be checked, so the claim as a whole is inconclusive.

text: Plants can make sounds, including clicking and crackling noises, which are typically beyond the range of human hearing and are often used to communicate with insects or other plants nearby.
label: not_verifiable
reason: The first part of the claim checks out. A 2023 Cell study found that stressed tomato and tobacco plants give off ultrasonic clicking or popping sounds outside the range of human hearing, and Science News and ScienceAlert reported the same finding. The claim that plants "often use" these sounds to communicate with insects or nearby plants is not established. The researchers and news coverage only say the sounds are loud enough for insects to hear and could be a way of signalling distress. They describe how insects respond as a question for future research. The sounds are thought to be a byproduct of water stress rather than proven communication. Because this part cannot be verified, the claim as a whole is inconclusive.

text: Barlow's Wheel is an optical illusion invented in 1825 by British physician Peter Barlow, which creates the appearance of a spinning wheel due to the way our brains process patterns.
label: contradicted
reason: The claim gets the device, the date and the inventor's job wrong. Barlow's Wheel was not an optical illusion. It was an early demonstration of a homopolar motor: a real electromagnetic device that spins because an electric current runs through the wheel inside a magnetic field. Peter Barlow built it in 1822, not 1825, and he was an English mathematician and physicist, not a physician. The source is a science-education page for school experiments.

text: A person was able to stay inside an airtight coffin for 27 days before suffocating, because of the algae that formed inside and started to break down carbon dioxide into oxygen.
label: contradicted
reason: I found no record of anyone lasting 27 days in an airtight coffin because algae made oxygen. Credible sources, including Popular Science, put survival in a sealed coffin at about 5.5 hours at most, and many guides say one to two hours. Algae also need light to turn carbon dioxide into oxygen, and a closed coffin is dark. Mick Meaney's 61-day buried-coffin stunt had an air supply, so it doesn't support this claim. The evidence contradicts the claim.

text: A single strand of spaghetti is not strong enough to support its own weight and will snap under its own tension when it reaches a certain length, known as the "spaghetti length".
label: contradicted
reason: The basic physics is right: any material, spaghetti included, will snap under its own weight once a hanging piece gets long enough. But the name in the claim is wrong. A note quoting Randall Munroe's book 'What If? 2' says engineers call this the 'free-hanging length' (also known as breaking length or self-support length), a ratio of tensile strength, density and gravity. My searches turned up no source using 'spaghetti length' as a term for this. The claim's parenthetical name is contradicted, and the evidence suggests it was made up.

text: Apa is among the world's largest family of flying foxes and is a type of large fruit bat native to forests and mangrove swamps in Southeast Asia.
label: not_verifiable
reason: I couldn't find any bat called "Apa". Searches turn up no flying fox species, common name or genus by that name, so it's unclear what the claim is about. The description matches the large flying fox (Pteropus vampyrus), a Southeast Asian megabat in the family Pteropodidae. But nothing links the name "Apa" to that species. The phrase "largest family of flying foxes" is also muddled. Since the subject can't be identified, the claim can't be checked.

text: Astronauts in space do not get to sneeze in the same manner as we do on Earth due to the lack of gravity causing mucus to not drip down the back of the throat, as it would normally.
label: contradicted
reason: HowStuffWorks says real astronauts do sneeze in space, and that the same things trigger sneezes in space as on Earth. Astronaut Dave Wolf has sneezed several times during spacewalks. Sources agree that microgravity stops mucus from draining downward, which causes congestion. But none of them say this changes how astronauts sneeze or keeps them from sneezing the way people do on Earth. The claim's central point, that sneezing works differently in space, goes against these sources.

text: The Axel Erlandson's Tre-fontaine tree, also known as the "circus tree," is a natural wonder consisting of three trunks that were cultivated to unite and eventually fuse into a rare formation resembling one with three-branched upper portion.
label: not_verifiable
reason: I found no evidence that Axel Erlandson made a tree called the "Tre-fontaine." Sources from Wikipedia, Gilroy Gardens, RoadsideAmerica and the Santa Cruz Public Library describe his "Tree Circus" and list trees such as the Four-Legged Giant, Basket Tree, Telephone Booth, Spiral Staircase, Zig-Zag and Arch. None of them mentions a "Tre-fontaine." "Circus tree" is the general name for all of his shaped trees, not a nickname for one tree. Gilroy Gardens does list some trees made from three trees, such as Squat Curvy Scallops, but none is described as three trunks fused under a three-branched top. The sources also say the trees were shaped and grafted by hand, so calling one a "natural wonder" is misleading. Because the specific tree in the claim cannot be identified or confirmed, the claim is inconclusive.

text: Near the surface of Greenland and Antarctica, scientists have discovered large, ancient freshwater ice shelves known as "ice slabs," hidden beneath the snow for millions of years, offering a glimpse into Earth's ancient past.
label: contradicted
reason: Scientists use the term "ice slabs" for thick, low-permeability layers of ice that form near the surface of the Greenland Ice Sheet when meltwater seeps into the firn (old, porous snow) and refreezes. Research describes them forming and thickening in recent decades, during extreme melt years such as 2010–2012. They are not ancient freshwater ice shelves, they have not been hidden beneath the snow for millions of years, and they do not offer a glimpse into Earth's ancient past. Instead, they are a sign of current warming that increases surface runoff. The search did not check the Antarctica part of the claim, but the rest of it misrepresents what ice slabs are.

text: The Axel Erlandson "Tree Circus" in California, USA, features 62 trees, including an arch of eucalyptus and a basket-weave sycamore, all shaped by grafting multiple trunks together.
label: contradicted
reason: The tree count in the claim is wrong. Several sources say Erlandson shaped about 70 trees (one says 60–70) and that the Tree Circus had 'nearly 70' when it opened. About 25 survivors were later moved and are now shown at Gilroy Gardens. No source gives 62. Wikipedia does confirm that the Basket Tree was made by approach-grafting six sycamores together. I found nothing confirming a eucalyptus arch, and my search limit ran out before I could check it. The claim that every tree was made by grafting multiple trunks is also too broad, since the sources mention other techniques such as pleaching. Because the number of trees is contradicted, the claim as a whole is contradicted.

text: Rome is considered to be the second most populous city in the world with over 3,700,000_possible inhabitants in the city proper, but is actually ranked as number 53 with "only" 2.8 million.
label: contradicted
reason: Rome is not considered the world's second most populous city. Wikipedia says the Roma Capitale municipality has about 2.7 million residents and ranks third or fourth in the European Union for population within city limits. It is the largest city in Italy, not the second largest in the world, and no source puts 3.7 million people in the city proper. Even the metropolitan area has only about 3.4 million. The 'rank 53' figure is also unsupported.

text: Scientists estimate that there are approximately 8.7 million identified species on Earth, but it's believed that up to 80% of the planet's total species remain undiscovered.
label: contradicted
reason: The 2011 study by Mora, Worm and colleagues puts the *estimated total* number of species on Earth at about 8.7 million, give or take 1.3 million. That figure is not a count of identified species. Only about 1.2 million species have actually been catalogued, which is why the study says more than 80% (about 86%) of species are still undiscovered. The part about 80% being undiscovered matches the study, but calling 8.7 million 'identified' species gets the main number wrong.

text: France and Spain both claim to be the birthplace of the first restaurant, 'auberge,' with the French claiming it was in the 1760s, and Spain locating their first in the 1610s.
label: contradicted
reason: The French part is right: Paris is widely credited with the first restaurant, opened in 1765 by Boulanger or Roze de Chantoiseau. The Spanish part is wrong. Spain's claim is Sobrino de Botín in Madrid, which Guinness lists as the oldest restaurant and which dates its founding to 1725, not the 1610s. Botín's own history page puts 1606 next to the French cook Jean Botín, but it says the inn itself opened in 1725, and Wikipedia says it actually opened as a restaurant in 1865. The claim also gets the terms wrong: 'auberge' is French for an inn, not the name of the first restaurant, and Spain's claim is to the oldest restaurant still operating, not to being where restaurants were born.

text: Scientists estimate that there may be between 700,000 and 1 million species on Earth, but we have formally discovered and named only around 300,000 of these.
label: contradicted
reason: The claim's numbers are far too low for species on Earth. ScienceDaily, reporting the widely cited 2011 study, puts the estimate at about 8.7 million eukaryote species (give or take 1.3 million). It says about 1.25 million have been described, not around 300,000. Earlier estimates ran from 3 million to 100 million. The claim's figures look closer to estimates for marine species alone, where up to about 1 million species are thought to exist and roughly 250,000 have been described.

text: Honeybees are able to fly by using electricity generated by their bodies, with research showing that bees can generate an electric charge of around 200-400 volts when in flight.
label: contradicted
reason: The claim is wrong about how bees fly. Bees fly by beating their wings with their flight muscles, not by using electricity. Research does show that bees pick up a static electric charge, usually positive, through friction with the air during flight. That charge helps them interact with pollen and flowers. Measurements of foraging honeybees suggest it can reach hundreds of volts, so the 200–400 V figure is roughly in line with the research. But the charge is a side effect of flying, not the thing that powers it, so the main part of the claim is contradicted.

text: A blue whale's heartbeat can be as loud as 188 decibels, which is louder than a jet engine, and can be detected hundreds of miles away.
label: contradicted
reason: The claim mixes up two different facts. Live Science says the 188-decibel figure, which is louder than a jet engine and can carry up to about 1,000 miles, describes the blue whale's calls or songs, not its heartbeat. For the heartbeat, NOAA and other popular sources say it can be heard about 2 miles away, not hundreds of miles, and some sources doubt even that. So the claim wrongly gives the vocalization's loudness and range to the heartbeat.

text: A 대학, or 'daycare university' in Japan is essentially a room the elderly rent to care for each other as if at university, as a replacement for a social interaction lifestyle.
label: not_verifiable
reason: I found no reliable source that describes a Japanese 'daycare university' (대학) where elderly people rent a room to care for each other as a substitute for a social life. 대학 is a Korean word, not a Japanese one, which makes the claim's framing doubtful. Searches did turn up Japanese adult day-care services, including a Korean article likening day-care centres to an elderly version of kindergarten and a casino-style day-care centre. None of them mention a 'university' model or elderly people renting a room to look after one another. With no evidence for or against the specific concept, the claim can't be verified.

text: A blue whale's heartbeat can actually be heard from over 200 miles away, which is louder than a jet plane taking off.
label: contradicted
reason: The usual popular claim is that a blue whale's heartbeat can be detected about 2 miles away, not more than 200 miles. Even the 2-mile figure is loosely sourced. The "louder than a jet plane" comparison is about blue whale calls, not their heartbeat. In the first heart-rate study, scientists recorded the heartbeat with a sensor attached to the whale. So the claim's 200-mile figure is contradicted.

text: A blue whale's heartbeat can actually be heard from over 200 miles away, which is louder than a jet taking off.
label: contradicted
reason: Even the most generous popular sources, like the Whaling Museum blog, say a blue whale's heartbeat can be detected from about 2 miles away, not over 200 miles, and that 2-mile figure is itself disputed. The 'hundreds of miles' and 'louder than a jet' facts are about blue whale calls (vocalizations), not their heartbeat. So the claim mixes up the two, and its heartbeat figure is wrong.

text: A blue whale's heartbeat can actually be heard from over 200 miles away, which is roughly the distance from Chicago, Illinois to St. Louis, Missouri.
label: contradicted
reason: Even the most generous popular claim, which appears on NOAA Fisheries' page, is that a blue whale's heartbeat can be heard about 2 miles away. Fact-check-style sources say even that figure is doubtful. No source supports anything close to 200 miles, which is about 100 times the commonly cited distance, so the claim exaggerates the figure. The Chicago to St. Louis distance (roughly 260–300 miles) doesn't matter, because the main claim is wrong.

text: A blue whale's heartbeat can be as loud as 188 decibels, louder than a jet engine, which is typically around 140 decibels.
label: contradicted
reason: The claim is wrong about where the 188 dB figure comes from. Reliable sources give 188 dB as the loudness of a blue whale's call, the low-frequency sound it makes to communicate, not its heartbeat. Wikipedia lists blue whale calls at 155–188 dB (measured underwater, re 1 µPa at 1 m), and Enchanted Learning and WorldAtlas say the same thing. Enchanted Learning compares the call with a jet at 140 dB. No credible source says the whale's heartbeat reaches 188 dB. The comparison is also loose, because underwater and in-air decibels use different reference levels and can't be compared directly.

text: A blue whale's heartbeat is so loud, it can be detected over 500 miles away with the correct equipment.
label: contradicted
reason: NOAA Fisheries says a blue whale's heartbeat can be heard about 2 miles away, not more than 500 miles. Distances of hundreds of miles usually refer to blue whale calls, not their heartbeats. Even the 2-mile figure is doubtful, but nothing reliable supports a distance anywhere near 500 miles.

text: A blue whale's heartbeat is so slow in some cases that it averages 2-8 beats per minute while it is sleeping or resting.
label: contradicted
reason: The numbers are roughly right, but the setting is wrong. In the 2019 Goldbogen et al. study published in PNAS, a blue whale's heart rate averaged about 4–8 beats per minute and dropped as low as 2 at the bottom of deep foraging dives. Smithsonian, CNN, Newsweek and The Scientist all report these low rates while the whale was diving for food, not while it was sleeping or resting. Its heart rate was highest at the surface, at 25–37 beats per minute, while it recovered between dives. No source links the 2–8 bpm range to sleeping or resting.

text: Astronauts cannot cry in the same way people do on Earth because tears in space do not fall due to the lack of gravity.
label: supported
reason: Space.com says tears only run down the face on Earth because of gravity, so in microgravity they don't fall. Chris Hadfield's demonstration showed tears staying on the eye as a ball of liquid held by surface tension. Astronauts can still produce tears, but they don't cry the way people do on Earth because the tears don't fall. That matches what the claim says. Futurism and ScienceABC say the same thing.

text: Astronauts in space cannot cry in the same way as people on Earth, as the lack of gravity prevents tears from flowing down their cheeks.
label: supported
reason: Space.com covered Chris Hadfield's video from the International Space Station, where he said "Your eyes will definitely cry in space... But the big difference is, tears don't fall." The article explains that tears run down your face on Earth only because of gravity. In microgravity they stay on the eye as a growing ball of water instead. That matches the claim: astronauts can produce tears, but they don't cry the way people on Earth do, because the tears can't flow down their cheeks.

text: Bearable Cave, located in the Canadian Rockies, holds the record for the longest cave in North America, spanning over 11 miles.
label: contradicted
reason: No cave called "Bearable Cave" shows up in the searches. Mammoth Cave in Kentucky, not a Canadian Rockies cave, is the longest cave in North America and the world, with about 426 miles of mapped passages. Even in Canada, the longest caves are ARGO Cave (about 25 km) and Castleguard Cave (about 21 km). A cave of about 11 miles is far from the North American record.

text: Cats have a special talent for recognizing and responding to the tone and pitch of their owner's voice.
label: supported
reason: Studies back the claim. A 2022 paper in Animal Cognition, reported by ScienceDaily (Springer) and Cats Protection, found that cats changed their behaviour when their owner spoke in the higher-pitched tone people use with pets, but not when the owner spoke in a normal adult-directed way or when a stranger spoke. Earlier research reported by National Geographic also showed that cats can tell their owner's voice apart from strangers' voices and respond to it. Calling this a 'special talent' is subjective, and the studies were small, but the main point that cats recognise and respond to the tone and pitch of their owner's voice is supported.

text: Didaskaleinophobia is a type of phobia that is defined as a persistent and irrational fear or anxiety of school.
label: supported
reason: Several sources, including Klarity Health, YourDictionary and fearof.net, define didaskaleinophobia as an irrational fear of school or of going to school. Klarity Health describes it as an "irrational and excessive fear" of school situations that causes serious difficulty attending school. No source contradicts the claim.

text: Haystacks on farms are sometimes set on fire to dry them and after the fire has broken out it is allowed to smoulder slowly.
label: contradicted
reason: Agricultural extension sources say haystack fires are accidents, not a drying method. They describe these fires as spontaneous combustion that happens when hay is stacked too wet: microbial activity and chemical heating raise the temperature until the hay ignites. Farmers are told to prevent this by baling hay dry and to call the fire department right away if they suspect a fire. None of the sources describe setting haystacks alight on purpose to dry them, or letting such a fire smoulder on purpose. The claim seems to confuse spontaneous combustion, which is a hazard, with a deliberate practice.

text: Honeybees are able to fly by using electricity generated by the movement of their wings to attract oppositely charged pollen, which helps them gain lift.
label: contradicted
reason: Bees do build up a positive static charge while they fly, and that charge pulls pollen onto their bodies. Science Friday explains that the charge "offers the pollen-hungry bee an incredible advantage" for gathering pollen. But the charge is only for collecting pollen and sensing flowers. It doesn't produce lift. Bees fly by beating their wings to create aerodynamic lift, not through electrostatic attraction. So the claim's main point, that bees use electricity and pollen attraction to fly, is wrong.

text: Honeybees are able to fly by using their wings to generate electricity, but more accurately they generate both lift and thrust using a figure-eight wing motion.
label: contradicted
reason: The claim's first part is wrong. Honeybees do not fly by using their wings to generate electricity. Reliable sources on bee flight mechanics, including a bioRxiv study of honeybee wing kinematics and a PMC paper on figure-eight wing motion in insects, explain flight through aerodynamics. Bees flap their wings very fast, about 180–260 beats per second, with wide strokes, and often trace a figure-eight path that produces lift. Bees can pick up static electric charge, but that is not what keeps them in the air. The second part of the claim, about lift and thrust from a figure-eight wing motion, is broadly accurate. Because the claim still asserts the false electricity mechanism, it counts as contradicted.

text: Humans and dolphins are the only mammals known to give themselves names, although dolphins name themselves using a unique whistle.
label: contradicted
reason: The claim says only humans and dolphins are known to have names, and that part is false. Studies from 2024 found that African elephants address each other with individual name-like calls, and that marmoset monkeys use "phee-calls" to name each other. Reports from Hebrew University (via EurekAlert) and CNN say vocal naming is now documented in humans, dolphins, elephants and marmosets, not just humans and dolphins. The part about dolphins using a unique signature whistle is correct.

text: Humans share approximately 50-60% of their DNA with bananas, which demonstrates the shared ancestry of living organisms through evolution.
label: not_verifiable
reason: The sources disagree on the key number. The 50–60% figure comes from a 2013 National Human Genome Research Institute analysis, which found that about 60% of human genes have a recognizable counterpart in bananas. The Star's fact-check rates the claim 'TRUE', and a fun-fact site repeats it as evidence of common ancestry. But the Star itself adds that these genes make up only about 1–2% of the whole human genome. IFLScience says the 'share 60% of our DNA' wording is technically incorrect. ProteinIQ reports that matching coding DNA is about 48% identical, but that this is only about 0.08% of the full genome. So the evidence supports shared ancestry and the 'about 60% of genes' version, but not the claim's wording that humans share 50–60% of their DNA with bananas.

text: In 1969, a computer error caused the first moon landing's lunar module to come perilously close to running out of fuel.
label: contradicted
reason: Part of the claim is true: in 1969 Apollo 11's lunar module did land with only about 25–30 seconds of fuel left. It also had 1201/1202 computer alarms, which meant the computer was overloaded. But reliable sources don't say the alarms caused the fuel shortage. NASA-based accounts say the alarms were judged safe ('GO'), and the software's priority scheduler dropped low-priority tasks so the landing could continue. The fuel ran low because the planned landing spot turned out to be a crater and boulder field. Armstrong took semi-manual control and flew farther downrange looking for a smooth place to land, and that extra flying used up the fuel. So the claim gets the cause wrong.

text: Japan has a vending machine for everything, from umbrellas and underwear to fresh eggs and live crabs.
label: supported
reason: My searches found several travel sources saying Japanese vending machines sell these items. Japan Wise Life describes crab vending machines in Hakodate and Kanazawa that sell 'live crabs or packaged cooked crab.' Other sources say Japanese machines sell umbrellas, fresh eggs and live crabs (list25, vendbuddy, vendingmachinepapa), and underwear (YouTube and vending-machine guides). The live-crab part is the weakest: the best-known live-crab vending machine, reported by NPR and TechCrunch, was in a Nanjing subway station in China, and the Japanese live-crab claims come from less authoritative travel and listicle sites. 'For everything' is an exaggeration, but the claim's examples are generally backed by these sources, so I rate it supported with moderate confidence.

text: Members of the smallest primate species, the pygmy mouse lemur, are about the size of a human fist and weigh approximately 30 grams.
label: contradicted
reason: Wikipedia says the pygmy mouse lemur (Microcebus myoxinus) weighs 43–55 g and is the second-smallest mouse lemur. The smallest primate is Madame Berthe's mouse lemur (Microcebus berthae), which weighs about 30 g, and Wikipedia notes that accounts of the two species are often confused. So the claim gets two things wrong: the pygmy mouse lemur is not the smallest primate, and it does not weigh about 30 g. The 'human fist' size comparison was not checked.

text: Octopuses have a highly distributed brain, with nine brains in total including the central brain and eight mini-brains in their arms.
label: supported
reason: Many sources say octopuses have a highly distributed nervous system, with a central brain plus a large cluster of nerve cells (ganglia) in each of the eight arms. Popular sources commonly describe this as "nine brains": one central brain and eight mini-brains in the arms (e.g., A-Z Animals, Wondereo). One caveat: some sources (e.g., Biology Insights) say "nine brains" is a simplification, because the arm clusters are neural ganglia rather than true brains. Still, the distributed setup the claim describes is well supported.

text: Octopuses have nine brains, with the main brain and eight additional mini brains located in their arms, allowing them to make decisions independently.
label: supported
reason: Popular science sources say each octopus arm has a cluster of nerve cells (a ganglion) that works like a mini-brain. That gives the animal a central brain plus eight smaller 'brains', and the arm clusters can control movement and make decisions without going through the central brain. Discovery's article says this outright under the heading 'Nine Lives? Try Nine Brains'. One caveat: biologists usually describe an octopus as having one true brain plus nerve clusters in the arms, so 'nine brains' is a loose popular description rather than a strict anatomical term. Recent research (ScienceDaily, 2020) also suggests the arms and central brain are more connected than once thought. Still, the claim matches how reputable sources commonly describe octopus anatomy.

text: Plants can make sounds when distressed or when their stems are being cut, using a process called ultrasonic vocalizations.
label: supported
reason: Reliable sources back the main claim. A 2023 Tel Aviv University study published in Cell recorded tomato and tobacco plants giving off airborne ultrasonic sounds, described as popping or clicking noises, when they were dehydrated or their stems were cut. The Natural History Museum and other outlets reported the same findings. One part of the claim is loosely worded: scientists don't use 'ultrasonic vocalizations' as the name of a process. Plants have no vocal organs, and the sounds are thought to come from cavitation (air bubbles forming in the plant's water-carrying tissue). Still, the sounds are ultrasonic, so the claim's substance holds.

text: Plants can make sounds when distressed or when their stems are being cut, using a process in which rapid airflow through their xylem creates small vibrations.
label: supported
reason: Khait et al. (2023, Cell) found that tomato and tobacco plants give off airborne ultrasonic clicks when they are drought-stressed or have their stems cut. Cell's commentary and a Trends in Plant Science review both point to cavitation in the xylem as the likely source of at least some of these sounds. Cavitation means air bubbles forming and collapsing inside the xylem's water columns, which produces small vibrations. The claim calls this 'rapid airflow through the xylem,' which is a loose way to put it but describes the same xylem air-and-vibration mechanism. The studies themselves say cavitation probably explains at least part of the sounds, not all of them.

text: Roses arranged in a bouquet have the longest shelf life and are typically freshest if placed in cool, dry environments at a 45-degree angle.
label: contradicted
reason: Rose-care guides like Kremp Florist say bouquets last longest when you cut the stems at a 45-degree angle so they take up more water, keep them in a fresh vase of water with no leaves below the waterline, and put them somewhere cool and shady. The claim gets these tips wrong in two ways. First, the 45-degree angle is about how you cut the stems, not how you position the bouquet. Second, roses need constant water, so 'dry environments' runs against the advice. Only the 'cool' part matches the sources.

text: Tarantulas can live up to 20-30 years in captivity, with some species reported to have lived into their 40s.
label: supported
reason: Hobbyist and popular sources say female tarantulas commonly live about 20–30 years in captivity. The Tarantula Collective lists species such as the Mexican red knee and curly hair at about 25–30 years. A-Z Animals says tarantulas have been reported living up to about 40 years and that females 'in some exceptional cases, can exceed 40 years.' It also lists female Oklahoma brown tarantulas as living up to 40. These sources support both parts of the claim as worded ('reported'). One caveat: the best-documented 43-year-old spider, 'Number 16', was a wild Australian trapdoor spider (Gaius villosus), not a captive theraphosid tarantula. Coverage of that record also said the previous record holder was a 28-year-old tarantula, so lifespans in the 40s rest mainly on popular-source reports rather than verified records.

text: Tarantulas have been around for a long time, with the earliest known tarantula fossil dating back approximately 165 million years to the Middle Jurassic period.
label: contradicted
reason: Reliable sources do not support the claimed date of about 165 million years ago in the Middle Jurassic. A peer-reviewed study in the Journal of Biogeography (2023) calls a theraphosid from Burmese amber, dated to about 100 million years ago in the Cretaceous, the oldest tarantula fossil. Live Science says only two tarantula fossils are known, both in amber: one about 16 million years old and one about 100 million years old. One hobbyist site lists Rosamygale as a Triassic "tarantula" from about 240 million years ago, but that is not a Middle Jurassic date either. No source supports 165 million years.

text: Tarantulas have been around for a very long time, with fossil evidence showing that they've remained largely unchanged for over 100 million years.
label: not_verifiable
reason: The first part of the claim holds up: tarantulas are an old group. A molecular study published in PeerJ in 2021 and reported by Live Science and Phys.org dates their origin to about 120 million years ago. A Wiley paper says the oldest known tarantula fossil comes from Burmese amber and is about 100 million years old. The second part does not hold up as well. Tarantula fossils are extremely rare, and only a few true tarantulas have been described, mostly from Miocene amber. The 120-million-year figure comes from genetic dating, not from fossils showing the animals stayed the same. Texas Parks & Wildlife Magazine says the fossil record shows them 'virtually unchanged' for more than 20 million years, not over 100 million. No source I found shows fossils proving tarantulas stayed largely unchanged for over 100 million years.

text: Tarantulas have been on Earth for a long time, with fossil evidence showing that they existed at least 165 million years ago during the Middle Jurassic period.
label: contradicted
reason: The scientific sources contradict the claim. The oldest known tarantula (Theraphosidae) fossil comes from Burmese amber and is about 100 million years old, from the Cretaceous. Only two tarantula fossils are known: that one and a much younger one from Mexican amber (about 16 million years old). Phylogenomic studies estimate that tarantulas first appeared about 120 million years ago, in the Early Cretaceous. No fossil shows tarantulas living 165 million years ago in the Middle Jurassic. Older mygalomorph fossils such as Rosamygale exist, but they are not tarantulas.

text: Tarantulas have been on Earth for a long time, with fossil records showing that they existed over 120 million years ago during the Cretaceous period.
label: contradicted
reason: The claim mixes up two kinds of evidence. Tarantulas did appear in the Cretaceous, and genetic (molecular-clock) studies estimate they arose about 120 million years ago. That figure is an estimate, not fossil evidence. Tarantula fossils are extremely rare, and only two are known. The older one, from Burmese amber in Myanmar, is about 100 million years old, and the other, from Mexico, is about 16 million years old. No known fossil shows tarantulas living more than 120 million years ago, so the part of the claim citing the fossil record is wrong.

text: Tarantulas have been on Earth for around 100 million years longer than dinosaurs, with fossil records showing they existed as far back as the Early Cretaceous period.
label: contradicted
reason: Live Science, reporting on a published study, says tarantulas first appeared about 120 million years ago, in the Early Cretaceous. That fits the claim's Early Cretaceous fossil date, since the oldest tarantula fossil is a roughly 100-million-year-old specimen in Myanmar amber. But dinosaurs appeared about 230–245 million years ago, so tarantulas came more than 100 million years after dinosaurs, not 100 million years before them. Even the oldest tarantula-like ancestors, dated to 235–240 million years ago, are described as 'as old as dinosaurs', not older. The claim also contradicts itself: animals first known from the Early Cretaceous cannot predate dinosaurs, which arose in the Triassic.

text: The world's largest snowflake was 15 inches in diameter and 8 inches thick, recorded in Montana on January 28, 1887.
label: supported
reason: The sources back every detail in the claim. Guinness World Records, as cited by Mystic Stamp, lists the largest snowflake as 15 inches wide and 8 inches thick, reported at Fort Keogh, Montana, on January 28, 1887. One caveat: the report came from a rancher's account and was never scientifically verified. Still, it is the recognized record, so the claim matches the documented record.

text: Turtles have an innate navigation system that allows them to migrate thousands of miles each year to reach their exact birthplace to lay their own eggs.
label: contradicted
reason: Sea turtles do have magnetic navigation abilities. Research by Lohmann and colleagues suggests they imprint on the magnetic field of the area where they hatched and use it to return to nest there, so that part of the claim holds. Two parts of the claim are wrong, though. First, the same research says female turtles usually nest every 2–4 years, not every year (another source says every 2–3 years). Second, natal homing works on a regional scale, so turtles return to the general area where they hatched, not to the 'exact birthplace.' The claim also says 'turtles' in general, but this behavior is documented for sea turtles specifically.

text: Water can exist in three distinct states at the same time, a phenomenon known as the triple point, at a specific temperature and pressure.
label: supported
reason: Science Notes defines the triple point as the temperature and pressure at which three phases of a substance exist in equilibrium. For water, it says that ice, liquid water and water vapor coexist stably at about 0.01 °C and roughly 611.66–611.73 Pa, depending on the source. The same source notes that water also has other triple points that involve different ice phases. That does not contradict the claim, which describes the familiar solid–liquid–vapor triple point.

text: A blue whale's heartbeat can be as slow as one to four beats per minute when the animal is fully submerged underwater and using a physiological response called "bradycardia" or "bradyarrhythmia".
label: supported
reason: The claim mostly holds up. In the 2019 study by Goldbogen and colleagues, the first recording of a wild blue whale's heart rate, the heart slowed to as few as 2 beats per minute during dives. That figure falls within the claimed range of one to four. The resting rate predicted for an animal that size is about 15 beats per minute. Slowing the heart during a dive is the diving response known as bradycardia, and the study also noted irregular heart rhythms (arrhythmias). One caveat: no source reports a rate as low as 1 beat per minute, so the bottom of the claimed range goes beyond the published data.

text: Plants can make sounds, such as clicking, when they undergo stress, and researchers can interpret these sounds to better understand plant behavior and detect potential health issues.
label: supported
reason: A 2023 study in Cell (Khait et al.), covered by Science News, found that stressed tomato and tobacco plants make ultrasonic clicking sounds when they are dehydrated or their stems are cut. Using machine learning, the researchers could tell from the sounds alone whether a plant was drought-stressed or injured. They suggested that listening for these sounds could become a new way to monitor water stress in crops, which supports the claim's point about interpreting the sounds to understand plant condition and spot health problems.

text: Plants can make sounds, such as clicking or popping, when they're going through stressful situations, as they release gases or react to environmental changes.
label: supported
reason: A 2023 Cell study by Khait et al. at Tel Aviv University found that stressed tomato and tobacco plants make ultrasonic popping or clicking sounds. The plants were stressed by dehydration or by having their stems cut, and they made up to about 35–40 clicks per hour. Science News and Asian Scientist both report this. The sounds are thought to come from cavitation, where air bubbles form and burst in the plant's water-carrying tissue (xylem) under stress. That broadly matches the claim's wording about gases and reactions to environmental change, though 'release gases' is a loose description of the mechanism.

text: 980 AD was narrower than other years as In AD 980, Pope John XIV decreed that this would be the year's length; it exempted leap year for lack of calenders astroubled briefly.
label: contradicted
reason: The claim is false. Britannica says John XIV was pope only from late 983 to 984, so he could not have issued a decree in 980. Benedict VII was pope in 980. No source records any papal decree that shortened 980 or skipped its leap day. Under the Julian calendar then in use, 980 was a normal leap year because it divides by 4, so it was not shorter than other years.

text: The Axel Heiberg Island in Canada is home to a unique "glass forest" created by a natural phenomenon where permafrost causes tree roots to freeze and subsequently shatter, giving off a "glassy" appearance.
label: contradicted
reason: Reliable sources, including the Canadian Encyclopedia, UBC's Beaty Museum and peer-reviewed research, describe the special forest on Axel Heiberg Island as a fossil forest. It dates from the Eocene, about 40–50 million years ago, and its stumps, logs and leaves are mummified and so well preserved that they still contain organic material. None of these sources mention a "glass forest," and none say permafrost freezes and shatters tree roots to make them look glassy. The claim gets the nature of the phenomenon wrong.

text: A person was able to stay inside an airtight coffin for 27 days before suffocating, because of the algae that fell on the coffin from the palm tree above, produced oxygen through photosynthesis; this event took place in 1940.
label: not_verifiable
reason: No source I found mentions anyone surviving 27 days in an airtight coffin in 1940 because algae from a palm tree produced oxygen. The closest real case is Soviet researcher Evgenii Shepelev in 1961. He sealed himself in a steel capsule with about eight gallons of chlorella algae and lasted only about 24 hours before the air went bad. That doesn't match the claim's date, length of time or setup. The claim also doesn't add up on its own terms: Popular Science estimates the air in a sealed coffin runs out in about 5.5 hours, and algae outside a truly airtight coffin couldn't get oxygen inside. Still, no source directly addresses or debunks this specific story, so it can't be confirmed or firmly refuted.

text: A blue whale's heartbeat can be as loud as 188 decibels, which is louder than a jet taking off and can be heard hundreds of miles away underwater.
label: contradicted
reason: The figures in the claim are real, but they describe the wrong sound. Reliable sources give 188 decibels, louder than a jet at about 140 dB and audible for hundreds of miles underwater, for the blue whale's call or vocalization, not its heartbeat. Saying the heartbeat is that loud is a common mix-up. The heartbeat is much quieter: popular accounts say it might be heard about 2 miles away at most, and scientists measured it with an electrocardiogram tag attached to the whale, not by listening from far away.

text: Plants can make sounds, such as clicking or bubbling noises, in response to stress, injury, or certain environmental changes, which scientists have been studying to better understand plant behavior.
label: supported
reason: Science News, reporting on a 2023 study in Cell (Khait et al.), says that tomato and tobacco plants give off ultrasonic clicks when they are short of water or have their stems cut. It describes the noises as sounding like popping bubble wrap. That backs up the claim's main points: plants make clicking or bubbling-type sounds in response to stress or injury, and scientists are studying these sounds, for example as a possible way to monitor water stress in crops. The underlying mechanism is thought to be cavitation, where air bubbles form in the plant's water-carrying tissue, which fits the 'bubbling' description, though the excerpt I checked doesn't state this.

text: Plants can make sounds, typically in the range of 10-240 Hz, which is within human hearing range, when they are under stress or communicating, although these sounds are usually extremely quiet.
label: contradicted
reason: The 2023 study on stressed tomato and tobacco plants found that they give off ultrasonic popping sounds at about 40–80 kHz. That is far above the roughly 16 kHz limit of adult human hearing, and the sounds could only be heard after researchers shifted them into an audible range. This contradicts the claim's 10–240 Hz range and its statement that these sounds fall within human hearing.

text: Plants can make sounds, typically in the range of 20-200 Hz, when they are subjected to stress, damage, or other environmental stimuli.
label: contradicted
reason: Plants do make sounds when they are stressed, but the frequency range in the claim is wrong. The main study on this (Khait et al., 2023, published in Cell) found that drought-stressed and cut plants make ultrasonic clicks. These are roughly 40–80 kHz, far higher than human hearing, not low-frequency sounds of 20–200 Hz. Because the claim gives a frequency range that is off by orders of magnitude, it is contradicted.

text: A Bolt of lightning can reach temperatures of up to 50,000 degrees Celsius during its formation, which is five times hotter than the surface of the sun.
label: contradicted
reason: The claim gets the temperature unit wrong. Britannica says lightning heats the air around it to about 50,000 °F (roughly 27,760 °C), and that this is five times hotter than the Sun's surface. The claim says 50,000 °C instead, which is close to twice the actual peak. The 'five times hotter than the Sun' part matches the Fahrenheit figure, not the Celsius one.

text: A Perez Prado song 'Guantanamera', was the first song to be transmitted from Earth into deep space, in 1977.
label: contradicted
reason: Guinness World Records says the first song beamed into deep space was The Beatles' 'Across the Universe', which NASA sent on 4 February 2008. It was not a Pérez Prado 'Guantanamera' in 1977. NASA-related reporting from 2024 adds that the Deep Space Network had sent only one other song (the Beatles track) before Missy Elliott's. I found no source tying Pérez Prado or 'Guantanamera' to a deep-space transmission.

text: A blue whale can hold up to 2,000 gallons (around 7,500 liters) of krill and small fish in its mouth at one time.
label: contradicted
reason: Reliable sources put a blue whale's mouthful far above 2,000 gallons. The Aquarium of the Pacific says a blue whale can take in up to about 64,252 L (17,000 gal) of food and water in a single mouthful. Other sources give similar figures, such as more than 13,000 or about 15,000 gallons. Blue whales also feed almost entirely on krill, not small fish. A cap of "up to 2,000 gallons" therefore greatly understates the real capacity, and no reliable source supports it.

text: A blue whale can hold up to 2,000 gallons (around 7,500 liters) of krill and small fish in its stomach.
label: contradicted
reason: Reliable sources put the blue whale's stomach capacity much lower than the claim. WWF says its stomach "can hold one ton of krill," and Oregon State University says about 2,200 pounds (1 metric ton) of food fills it. Since krill is roughly as dense as water, one ton is about 1,000 liters, or around 260 gallons. The claim's 2,000 gallons (about 7,500 liters, or 7.5 tonnes) is roughly 7.5 times that figure. The higher numbers I found don't help the claim: the 10,000–15,000 gallon and 80,000 liter figures describe water taken into the mouth in one gulp, not stomach contents. An older UNM page says a stomach might contain 4 tons, which is still well short of the claimed 7.5 tonnes.

text: A blue whale's heartbeat can last up to 2 seconds, its pulse is around 8-10 beats per minute.
label: not_verifiable
reason: The 8–10 beats-per-minute figure is common in popular sources, and an Africa Check fact-check rated a post making that claim as correct. But the first measurement of a wild blue whale's heart rate, published in PNAS in 2019 by Goldbogen and colleagues, found a much wider range. The rate fell to about 4–8 bpm during dives, went as low as 2 bpm, and rose to 25–37 bpm at the surface. No reliable source says a single heartbeat lasts 'up to 2 seconds.' The claim may be mixing up the 2-beats-per-minute minimum, which would mean about one beat every 30 seconds. Because the 2-second part can't be verified and the 8–10 bpm figure is only partly backed by the measured data, the claim can't be confirmed or clearly ruled out.

text: A якості fact is that humans share about 50% of their DNA with bananas, indicating a common ancestor in the distant past.
label: contradicted
reason: Snopes rates the popular "50% of DNA shared with bananas" claim as false. It says there is no reading of that statement that makes it factual. The figure comes loosely from the idea that about half of human genes have counterparts in bananas, which is not the same as sharing half our DNA. A whole-genome comparison would put the shared DNA well below 1%.

text: Aersopatiale Alouette helicopters use a turbine engine which allows for the specially adapted helicopters to be able to dump turbine power put into the engines which enables them to descend from any altitude and land running the engine at nearly the same RPM.
label: not_verifiable
reason: The sources confirm that Alouette helicopters use Turbomeca turboshaft engines, and forum posts say the Alouette II's fixed-shaft Artouste runs at a near-constant speed, with the fuel control adjusting power to hold the set RPM. I found no reliable source for the rest of the claim. Nothing describes "specially adapted" Alouettes that can "dump turbine power" so they can descend from any altitude and land with the engine at about the same RPM. A record flight even cuts against it: in Jean Boulet's 1972 altitude record in an SA 315 Lama (an Alouette II derivative), the engine flamed out at altitude and he came down in autorotation. Because a core part of the claim can't be verified, I'm rating it inconclusive.

text: Baby sloths are born with their eyes open and a thin layer of fur, and they can start climbing trees in as little as 2 weeks.
label: not_verifiable
reason: The evidence backs the first half of the claim. Biodôme (Espace pour la vie), San Diego Zoo factsheets and other sources say baby sloths are born with their eyes open and with fur. Sources describe them as covered in fur except on the chest, or as fully furred, so 'a thin layer' isn't quite how they put it. The 2-week climbing figure is not supported. Biodôme and the San Diego Zoo say infants first hang from branches at about 3 weeks (20–25 days), and A-Z Animals says they can climb on their own within 20–25 days. Other sources go the other way, saying babies can climb or cling to their mother from birth. Because the sources disagree and none mentions 2 weeks specifically, that part can't be confirmed.

text: Baby sloths are born with their eyes open and a thin layer of fur, and they can start climbing trees in as little as 48 hours after birth.
label: not_verifiable
reason: I could only partly verify this claim. Several sources say baby sloths are born with their eyes open, including the Montreal Espace pour la vie fact sheet and A-Z Animals, so that part is supported. The fur part doesn't match well: sources describe newborns as 'fully furred', with a 'full coat of fur', or 'covered in fur, except on its chest', not as having a thin layer. I found no source for the '48 hours' climbing figure. Sources disagree on timing: some popular sites say babies can climb within minutes or hours of birth, which would make 48 hours too long to be the minimum. Another says they can hang and climb on their own only after 20–25 days, and newborns mainly cling to the mother. Because the evidence is mixed and the specific figure is unverified, the claim is inconclusive.

text: France and the United States have the most time zones, with 12 time zones each.
label: contradicted
reason: The sources say France alone has the most time zones, with 12. The United States has 11 and is tied with Russia for second place. The claim's statement that the US also has 12 and ties France for first is wrong.

text: Galileo Galilei was the first person to observe the planet Neptune, although he didn't realize it was a planet at the time, in 1613.
label: supported
reason: Astronomy.com says Galileo sketched Neptune between December 1612 and January 1613, likely mistook it for a star, and may have been the first person to see it.
