A second source also says he first saw it on December 28, 1612 and again on January 27, 1613. One caveat is that his first sighting was in late December 1612, not 1613, but he did observe it again in January 1613, so the date is close enough. The "didn't realize" part is the standard account, though in 2009 physicist David Jamieson argued that Galileo may have noticed it moving.

text: Government scientists at the US Army base in Fort Detrick invented the first fluoride toothpaste in 1950.
label: contradicted
reason: Reliable sources say the first fluoride toothpaste came out of a project Procter & Gamble started in 1950. Dr. Joseph Muhler led the team at Indiana University, and the product became Crest with Fluoristan, test-marketed in 1955 and sold nationwide in 1956. Crest's own history page and P&G's dentalcare.com both give this account. Neither source mentions government scientists or the US Army base at Fort Detrick, so the claim gets both the inventors and the place wrong.

text: Humans and elephants are the only known land animals that display the complex emotional trait of empathy, which is reflected in their ability to express and feel deep compassion and grief.
label: contradicted
reason: The claim says only humans and elephants show empathy, and the evidence contradicts that. Peer-reviewed research describes consolation behaviour in chimpanzees, a recognised sign of empathy, based on nearly ten years of observing 44 animals. Other sources report empathy-related behaviour in rats, dogs, capuchin monkeys and other apes. Elephants do show grief and compassion, but they are not the only land animals besides humans that do.

text: Near the surface of Greenland and Antarctica, scientists have discovered large, ancient freshwater ice shelves containing unfrozen subglacial lakes.
label: contradicted
reason: The claim mixes up two different things. Scientists have found many subglacial lakes in Greenland and Antarctica, including 56 newly mapped lakes in Greenland, bringing its total to 60. Those lakes lie beneath the ice sheets, at their base. The sources do not describe them as lying near the surface, and they say nothing about finding "large, ancient freshwater ice shelves" that contain unfrozen lakes. The evidence matches only the general idea that such lakes exist and contradicts where the claim puts them.

text: Parts of the Great Barrier Reef in Australia have been dated as far back as 20 million years.
label: not_verifiable
reason: The sources disagree. WorldAtlas says some sections of the reef are 20 million years old, and tourism sites also give ages of about 20 million years. However, Science magazine reports drilling data that date the reef's oldest coral remains to between about 490,000 and 1.05 million years. Another site notes that only older sources gave an age of 18 million years. It adds that the reefs older than 10 million years grew on the Queensland Plateau, which is separate from the Great Barrier Reef. The scientific evidence points against the claim, but some search results support it, so the evidence is mixed rather than a clear contradiction.

text: Polar bears are skilled swimmers, with some individuals recorded swimming for hours or even days at a time, covering distances of up to 60 miles without resting.
label: contradicted
reason: My searches support the first part of the claim: polar bears are strong swimmers and can swim for hours or even days. The 60-mile limit is the problem. National Geographic, CBC and Live Science report a GPS-tracked female polar bear that swam nonstop for nine days and covered about 426 miles (687 km). Ocean Conservancy and the San Diego Zoo Wildlife Alliance say polar bears can swim more than 60 miles without rest. One less authoritative source, NHPBS, does say they can swim 'as far as' 60 miles, but the documented 426-mile swim shows that 60 miles is not the upper limit.

text: Quantum Computing is a speacialized discipline of Mathematics and Physics.
label: supported
reason: Reputable sources such as AWS, Indiana University's Luddy School, Springer and an arXiv introduction describe quantum computing as a multidisciplinary field that draws on physics and mathematics, as well as computer science. They back the claim that it is a specialized field rooted in mathematics and physics. The claim leaves out computer science, which makes it incomplete, but nothing in the sources contradicts it.

text: Researchers at the University of California San Diego have trained AI chatbots that revolutionize communication for individuals with severe speech or motor disorders.
label: not_verifiable
reason: I couldn't find a trustworthy source showing that UC San Diego researchers trained AI chatbots for people with severe speech or motor disorders. The UC San Diego AI work that came up is about other things: a patient-portal chatbot built with Epic, a symptom-triage chatbot based on American Medical Association care flowcharts, and AI drafting replies to patient messages. Studies on using large language models to speed up communication for people with ALS or severe motor impairments do exist (Nature Communications and arXiv papers), but the results I saw didn't tie them to UC San Diego. A medRxiv preprint combines muscle-signal (sEMG) sensors with language models for assistive communication, but I hit my search limit before I could check who wrote it. Nothing confirms the UC San Diego link or the claim that the technology is 'revolutionary', but nothing directly contradicts it either.

text: Researchers at the University of California San Diego have trained AI chatbots that revolutionize communication process with people that have a speech and language disorder.
label: not_verifiable
reason: I searched for the specific UC San Diego project described in the claim, AI chatbots trained to change how people with speech and language disorders communicate, and found nothing about it. UCSD results covered unrelated chatbot work: ToxicChat for detecting toxic prompts, a medical triage chatbot, simulated patients for training clinicians, and Dr. Chatbot. Research on AI or large language models for augmentative and alternative communication (AAC) and aphasia turned up only from other institutions, such as Cornell and a team in China. The searches don't confirm or rule out the claim, and the search limit was reached before I could check more specific angles such as stuttering or dysarthria.

text: Spiders have been around for a long time, with fossil evidence showing that they existed as far back as the Devonian period, about 318 million years ago.
label: contradicted
reason: The claim gets its dates wrong. The Devonian period ran from about 419 to 359 million years ago, so 318 million years ago falls in the Carboniferous. Wikipedia and the Kentucky Geological Survey both place the Devonian spider fossil (Attercopus, which has been claimed as the oldest spider) at about 380 million years ago, not 318. Wikipedia separately dates the oldest reported true spiders to the Carboniferous. Spiders are ancient, and Devonian spider-like fossils are known, but 'Devonian, about 318 million years ago' cannot be right as stated.

text: Spiders have been around for a long time, with fossil evidence showing that they existed over 318 million years ago during the Carboniferous period.
label: supported
reason: The search results support the claim that spiders existed during the Carboniferous period. Guinness World Records says the earliest fossil spiders date to about 300 million years ago in Carboniferous coal measures. Another source describes the German spider Arthrolycosa wolterbeeki as 310–315 million years old. A British Arachnological Society paper places the oldest unequivocal spider, an Arthrolycosa, in the late Carboniferous Bashkirian stage (roughly 323–315 million years ago). None of the results I retrieved stated the exact figure of 318 million years. That number matches the Wikipedia Spider article's statement (recalled from memory, not retrieved) that true spider fossils come from Carboniferous rocks dated 318 to 299 million years ago. Nothing I found contradicts the claim, so I consider it supported, though the exact '318 million years' figure is the least directly confirmed part.

text: Tarantulas have been on Earth for a long time, with the oldest known tarantula fossil dating back around 155 million years.
label: contradicted
reason: The claim's broad point holds, since tarantulas are an ancient group, but the 155-million-year figure is wrong. Live Science, reporting on a 2024 study, says there are only two known tarantula fossils, both in amber. The older one, from Myanmar, is about 100 million years old, and the other, from Mexico, is about 16 million. The same study dates the origin of tarantulas to roughly 120 million years ago in the Cretaceous. Fossils older than 155 million years, such as the Triassic Rosamygale, belong to the wider mygalomorph group rather than to tarantulas, so they don't support the figure either.

text: Turtles have an innate navigational ability, allowing some species to migrate thousands of miles each year and still return to their birthplace to lay eggs.
label: supported
reason: I rated this supported. Reliable sources (Live Science, EarthSky, UNC, and Wikipedia on natal homing) report that sea turtles, such as loggerheads, swim thousands of miles and then return to the beaches where they hatched to lay eggs. They find their way using Earth's magnetic field, which acts as a built-in compass and map. Two details are looser than the evidence: most sea turtles nest every 2–3 years rather than every year, and their homing also relies on imprinting on the magnetic signature of their home beach, which is learned rather than purely innate. Neither point changes the core of the claim.

text: Turtles have an innate navigational ability, allowing some species to migrate thousands of miles each year and still return to their exact birthplace to lay eggs.
label: supported
reason: Reliable science reporting on a Current Biology study (Brothers et al.), carried by EurekAlert and UNC, says sea turtles travel thousands of miles of ocean and then return to nest on the stretch of coastline where they hatched. They find it using Earth's magnetic field, imprinting on their home beach's magnetic signature as hatchlings. This supports the claim's main point. Three details are overstated, though. Turtles return to the same general stretch of coast, not their exact birthplace. Most individuals nest every two to three years rather than every year. And homing relies partly on learned imprinting, so it is not purely innate.

text: tabela consists of a type of prehistoric cave art that has been discovered in caves in Europe and North America.
label: contradicted
reason: No source I found describes "tabela" as a type of prehistoric cave art. Dictionaries give it entirely different meanings. In Portuguese, Polish and Romanian it means a table or chart for organizing data. Wiktionary's English entry gives it as a borrowing from Hindi तबेला, which means a stable. Searches for "tabela" together with cave art turned up only general pages about cave painting, with no link to this word. Since the established meanings don't match the claim, it is contradicted.

text: A person was able to stay inside an airtight coffin for 27 days before suffocating, because of the algae growing inside the coffin and turning the carbon dioxide into oxygen.
label: contradicted
reason: I found no report of anyone surviving 27 days in an airtight coffin, with or without algae. A science piece on how long a person can survive in a sealed coffin says estimates run from about ten minutes to six hours, and up to 36 hours at the most optimistic. It bases this on roughly 170 liters of available oxygen and about 0.5 liters used per minute at rest. 27 days is far beyond that. The algae explanation also fails: algae need light to turn carbon dioxide into oxygen, and a closed coffin is dark. Note that I could only run a few searches before hitting the search limit, so the verdict rests on that one source plus basic biology.

text: Haystacks on farms are sometimes set on fire to dry them and after the fire has been extinguished, any sparks remaining that have not yet died out are put out by urinating on them.
label: contradicted
reason: This claim is wrong. Reliable agricultural sources describe hay drying in the field, either in small haystacks or by curing before baling. Fire in haystacks is a hazard, not a drying method. It usually comes from spontaneous combustion when hay is stored too wet, which is why extension services warn about it. No credible source says farmers set haystacks on fire to dry them, or that they put out leftover sparks by urinating on them. Burning would destroy the hay.

text: Plants can make sounds, when they are injured or stressed, using ultrasonic clicks, squeaks, and other noises in order to communicate with other plants.
label: not_verifiable
reason: The Khait et al. (2023) study in Cell, reported by Science News, supports the first part of the claim: stressed plants, such as thirsty or cut tomato and tobacco plants, give off ultrasonic clicks. But the researchers say they have only shown that plants emit "informative sounds." They have not shown that plants make these sounds in order to communicate with other plants. Whether other plants or insects pick up on the sounds is still being investigated. The study also describes clicks or pops, not squeaks. Because the purpose the claim gives is unverified, the claim is inconclusive.

text: Plants can make sounds, albeit sounds that are too faint for human ears to detect, such as ultrasonic clicks produced by some plants when they are stressed or injured.
label: supported
reason: A peer-reviewed 2023 study in Cell by Tel Aviv University researchers found that plants under stress, either from drought or from being cut, give off ultrasonic airborne sounds described as 'clicks'. These sounds can be recorded from a distance but are outside the range of human hearing. That backs up the claim that plants make sounds people can't hear, including ultrasonic clicks when stressed or injured. One detail is a bit off: humans can't hear these sounds because their frequency is too high, not mainly because they are faint. This doesn't change the main point of the claim.

text: Plants can make sounds, too, when they are stressed or in pain; scientists have detected ultrasonic clicks coming from plants like tomatoes and corn when they are injured or thirsty.
label: supported
reason: Science News, reporting on the peer-reviewed study by Khait et al. in Cell (2023), says scientists used ultrasonic microphones to record clicks from tomato and tobacco plants when they were dehydrated or had their stems cut. The same article says wheat and corn made similar sounds. A commentary in Cell confirms that stressed tomato and tobacco plants give off airborne ultrasonic sounds. One caveat: the sources do not say plants feel 'pain'. That word is loose wording, but the claim's factual core about ultrasonic clicks from stressed (injured or thirsty) tomatoes and corn is backed up.

text: British Airways has a 747 jet with the smallest pilot staff as low as 3 plus 2 reserve pilots or 1 Captain and A relief Captain to fly with at 2 crew along with a triple reserve fund.
label: contradicted
reason: The claim says British Airways currently has a 747, but reliable sources (CNBC, AirlineGeeks, InsideFlyer) report that BA retired its entire Boeing 747-400 fleet with immediate effect in July 2020. The airline said the jet was unlikely ever to fly commercially for it again. The crew figures in the claim (3 pilots plus 2 reserves, or a captain and relief captain flying as 2 crew, plus a 'triple reserve fund') are garbled, and no search result supports them.

text: Scientists estimate that there are approximately 8.7 million identified species on Earth, but the actual number is thought to be much higher, with estimates ranging from 30 to over 100 million.
label: contradicted
reason: The 8.7 million figure from Mora et al. (2011) is an estimate of all species on Earth. It is not a count of identified species. Most of those species have not been described yet: about 86% on land and 91% in the oceans, with only about 1.2 million catalogued. The claim also gets the range wrong. Earlier estimates ran from 3 million to 100 million, not from 30 to over 100 million.

text: In the heart of New York City, there is a small piece of land called Building 20 at Bryant Park that technically is a part of Bryant Park but has its own unique history, as was originally a timing square left over from the construction of nearby buildings that occurred during the 1800s.
label: not_verifiable
reason: I found no reliable source that mentions a parcel called "Building 20 at Bryant Park." Searches turned up only nearby buildings, such as the Bank of America Tower, The Bryant and Bryant Park Studios. Official histories from the Bryant Park Corporation and NYC Parks say the land was set aside as public property in 1686. It later became a potter's field and then Reservoir Square, next to the Croton Distributing Reservoir, and finally the park. None of these sources mentions a 'timing square' left over from 1800s construction. The claim appears to be made up, but because the parcel it describes has no clear referent, the sources can't directly prove or disprove it.

text: Honeybees are able to fly by using their wings to generate electricity through a process called piezoelectricity, and then using that electricity to generate lift.
label: contradicted
reason: The evidence contradicts this claim. Research on honeybee flight (Altshuler et al., PNAS 2005, summarized by AskNature) shows that bees get lift from aerodynamics: they flap their wings in short, very fast strokes, and they rotate the wings when each stroke reverses, which adds rotational, acceleration and wake-capture forces. Bees do not use wing-generated piezoelectricity to create lift, and electricity is not how any insect produces lift.

text: A blue whale's heartbeat is so loud that scientists can detect it from over 500 miles away with a specialized underwater microphone.
label: contradicted
reason: The search results don't back the 500-mile figure. The popular claim, repeated on the Cold Spring Harbor Whaling Museum blog and on fun-fact sites, is that a blue whale's heartbeat can be detected from about 2 miles away. Some sources call even that distance unproven, and say that only the whale's calls carry hundreds of miles, not its heartbeat. Nothing found says the heartbeat can be detected from over 500 miles away, so the claim seems to mix up the range of the whale's calls with its heartbeat.

text: A blue whale, with its massive size, can hold up to 2,000 gallons of blood, which is roughly 5% of its total body weight.
label: not_verifiable
reason: I couldn't confirm this claim because the sources disagree. NPS says a blue whale's heart pumps "10 tons of blood" through its body, which works out to roughly 2,400 gallons. A physician's post on X puts total blood volume at about 5,300 liters, or 1,165 gallons. NOAA only gives the volume per heartbeat (about 60 gallons), not the total. None of the sources I found says blood makes up about 5% of a blue whale's body weight. The arithmetic is roughly plausible: 2,000 gallons weighs about 8 tons, which is around 5% of a 150–200-ton whale. However, no source directly supports either the 2,000-gallon figure or the 5% share.

text: A blue whale, with its massive size, has a blue-gray color and a heart so large that it can pump around 50 gallons of blood with every beat.
label: contradicted
reason: The claim gets the colour right but the heart figure wrong. Blue whales are well known to be mottled blue-gray, but trustworthy sources put the blood pumped per heartbeat at about 58 to 60 gallons, not around 50. NOAA Fisheries says a blue whale's heart pumps about 60 gallons with each beat. Guinness World Records estimates about 58 gallons (220 litres), and Salon and WorldAtlas also give about 60. A search for a 50-gallon figure found nothing supporting it.

text: A oku, or hundred trillion in Japanese counting system, is a 1 followed by 28 zeros, which is 100 trillion times greater than a trillion.
label: contradicted
reason: Several Japanese dictionaries and language-learning sites give oku (億) as one hundred million: 100,000,000, or 10^8. That is a 1 followed by 8 zeros. It is not a hundred trillion, not a 1 followed by 28 zeros, and not 100 trillion times a trillion. Japanese groups large numbers in units of four digits: man (万) is 10^4, oku (億) is 10^8 and chō (兆) is 10^12.

text: Beehive-shaped structures in the ocean called fulgurites are created when lightning strikes the water and instantly melts the sand, forming long glass tubes.
label: contradicted
reason: Reliable sources, including the Oxford University Museum of Natural History, a PMC/NCBI research article and ResearchGate, say fulgurites form when lightning strikes sand or soil on the ground. The heat fuses the silica into hollow glass tubes. They are not beehive-shaped structures in the ocean, and they do not form when lightning hits water. The part about melted sand forming glass tubes is accurate, but the ocean and beehive details are wrong.

text: Beehive-shaped structures in the ocean called fulgurites are created when lightning strikes the water and vaporizes the sand into a tube.
label: contradicted
reason: Fulgurites are not beehive-shaped structures in the ocean. Reliable sources describe them as natural glass tubes, often cylindrical, that form when lightning strikes sand, soil or rock on the ground. The lightning heats, melts and fuses the sand into glass rather than vaporizing it. The claim therefore gets the location, the shape and the way they form wrong.

text: Bees are able to fly by using electricity generated from their wings to attract and repel other bees, as well as to maneuver and steer through the air.
label: contradicted
reason: Reliable sources such as UF/IFAS entomology and Nature say bees fly by flapping their wings very fast, up to about 200 beats per second. They control airflow by changing the angle of their wings, and lift comes from leading-edge vortices. Electricity plays no part in how bees fly or steer. Bees do pick up a static electric charge while flying. Research shows they use it to sense the electric fields around flowers and to help move pollen, not to fly, steer, or attract or repel other bees. The claim misstates what this charge does.

text: Black bears are excellent climbers and have been known to climb trees to escape danger, protect themselves from extreme weather, or even just to catch a nap.
label: supported
reason: Every part of the claim is backed by sources I found. Vermont Fish & Wildlife says black bears climb trees to escape danger, and several sources call them excellent climbers. Bear.org (North American Bear Center) reports that black bears often climb trees during thunderstorms, and mothers with cubs climb big pines for safety in storms. That supports climbing to shelter from bad weather, though the evidence covers storms rather than "extreme weather" in general. Other sources (A-Z Animals, BiologyInsights, the North Shore Black Bear Society, and Yahoo) say black bears climb trees to rest, relax, sleep or nap on branches. I found nothing contradicting the claim.

text: Blind people often develop a stronger sense of hearing and smell due to their brain's ability to reorganize and compensate for the loss of sight.
label: supported
reason: Harvard Medical School's Mass. Eye and Ear reported a PLOS ONE study showing that the brains of people born blind form new connections. These changes are linked to compensatory abilities such as sharper hearing, smell and touch, which matches the brain reorganization described in the claim. The research focuses mostly on people blind from birth or early in life, and some studies on smell have found mixed results, but the general claim, hedged with "often", is consistent with what reputable sources report.

text: Galileo Galilei was the first person to observe the planet Neptune, but he didn't realize it was a planet and instead thought it was a star.
label: supported
reason: Wikipedia's article on the discovery of Neptune says Galileo's drawings show he saw Neptune on December 28, 1612, and again on January 27, 1613, which is the earliest recorded sighting. Both times he took it for a fixed star, and he is not credited with discovering it. Scientific American gives the same account. Wikipedia also notes evidence that he saw this 'star' appear to move, but it still says he did not recognize it as a planet. One caveat: 'first person to observe' is only supported in the sense of the first recorded observation, since earlier unrecorded sightings can't be ruled out.

text: Hippopotamuses can hold their breath underwater for up to five minutes and can also sleep with their eyes and nostrils closed while submerged.
label: supported
reason: Trusted sources back both parts of the claim. National Geographic and Britannica say hippos can hold their breath for up to five minutes underwater, and that their nostrils and ears shut tight when they go fully under. National Geographic also says hippos nap in the water, using a reflex that lifts them to the surface to breathe without waking up. AfricaFreak describes hippos sleeping underwater with their eyes closed, and they would be closed nostrils while submerged. One small caveat: the San Diego Zoo and Newsweek say "five minutes or longer," and one smaller site reports up to six minutes. Still, the widely cited typical maximum is five minutes, so the claim holds.

text: Humans share approximately 50% of their DNA with bananas, highlighting the shared ancestry of all living organisms.
label: not_verifiable
reason: The sources disagree. Some popular sites, such as FactMyth and The Star, say humans share about 50–60% of their DNA with bananas. More careful explainers, including IFLScience, KnowYourDNA and MetaQuest, say this is a muddle. The roughly 50–60% figure refers to genes that have a counterpart in bananas, not to DNA. At the sequence level we share much less, only about 1% according to MetaQuest, and one source puts matching genes closer to 25%. The general point about shared ancestry is accepted, but the evidence both supports and contradicts the specific claim of about 50% of DNA.

text: Tarantulas have been around for a long time, with the oldest known tarantula fossil dating back around 165 million years to the Middle Jurassic period.
label: contradicted
reason: No source I found supports a 165-million-year-old Middle Jurassic tarantula fossil. My search tool hit its usage limit, so this verdict relies mostly on established references such as Wikipedia's tarantula and Theraphosidae articles. They say only a few fossils can be firmly assigned to tarantulas (Theraphosidae), and these are much younger: specimens in Miocene amber from the Dominican Republic and Chiapas, Mexico, about 16–24 million years old. Fossil mygalomorphs (the broader group that includes tarantulas) go back to the Triassic, but they are not tarantulas. Molecular dating also places the origin of tarantulas around the Cretaceous (about 120 million years ago), not the Middle Jurassic. The age and period in the claim therefore conflict with the known fossil record.

text: Tarantulas have been on Earth for a long time, with fossil records showing that they've remained largely unchanged for over 120 million years.
label: contradicted
reason: The claim says fossils show tarantulas unchanged for over 120 million years, and the sources don't back that. A 2021 Carnegie Mellon study, reported by Live Science, Phys.org and Futurity, estimated that tarantulas first appeared about 120 million years ago. That figure comes from a molecular family tree calibrated against fossils, not from tarantula fossils themselves. Tarantula fossils are rare, and the oldest known one is in Myanmar amber about 100 million years old, so the fossil record can't show more than 120 million years of anything. Texas Parks & Wildlife Magazine, citing an expert, says fossils show tarantulas virtually unchanged for more than 20 million years, not 120 million. The rough 120-million-year origin is supported, but the claim's fossil detail is wrong.

text: Tarantulas have been on the planet for a long time, with fossil records showing they've remained largely unchanged for over 100 million years.
label: not_verifiable
reason: The first part holds up: tarantulas are an old group. A peer-reviewed study (Journal of Biogeography) says the oldest known tarantula fossil, preserved in Burmese amber, is about 100 million years old. Live Science and Smithsonian report that, based on molecular dating, tarantulas appeared about 120 million years ago. The part about being 'largely unchanged for over 100 million years' according to fossil records is not well supported. Live Science reports that only two tarantula fossils are known, one about 16 million years old and one about 100 million years old. That is too few to show the group stayed the same for more than 100 million years. Texas Parks & Wildlife Magazine says the fossil record shows tarantulas 'virtually unchanged' for more than 20 million years, not 100 million. Only a hobbyist blog suggests they stayed recognizably the same for over 100 million years, and it is not a reliable source. So the 'over 100 million years unchanged' detail can't be confirmed, though it isn't clearly disproven either.

text: butcher-robots, built and run by companies like Ross, Moley, and Makr, are specially designed robots that are capable of preparing, this includes cleaning, and also even of cooking high-quality restaurant meals.
label: not_verifiable
reason: Only Moley is backed by the sources I found. They describe Moley Robotics' robotic kitchen as cooking meals from scratch and cleaning up afterward, and say it was aimed at restaurants and hotels. However, Moley calls it a robotic kitchen, not a 'butcher-robot', and Robb Report notes it can't peel or dice, so users still do some prep work themselves. I found nothing on 'Ross' or 'Makr' as companies that build cooking robots, and my search limit ran out before I could check them. 'Makr' may refer to Makr Shakr, which I believe makes robot bartenders rather than cooking robots, but I could not confirm this. Since key parts of the claim can't be verified and some are questionable, the evidence is inconclusive.

text: уванніTarantulas have been around for a long time, with fossil records showing they existed at least 165 million years ago during the Jurassic period

reason: Reliable scientific sources contradict the claim. The oldest known tarantula (Theraphosidae) fossil is from Burmese amber dated to about 100 million years ago, in the Cretaceous, and the other known fossil is a roughly 16-million-year-old Miocene specimen from Mexico. The 165-million-year-old Jurassic spiders that sometimes get mentioned, Mongolarachne and 'Nephila' jurassica, are not tarantulas. Mygalomorph spiders in general go back much further, about 240 million years, but that is the wider group tarantulas belong to, not tarantulas themselves.

text: Honeybees are able to fly by using their wings to generate electricity through a process called piezoelectricity, allowing them to charge pollen and other particles with static electricity.
label: contradicted
reason: This claim is false. Honeybees fly using aerodynamic lift: they flap their wings about 230 times a second. Electricity does not keep them in the air. Bees do pick up a positive static charge in flight, which helps pollen stick to them. But reliable sources say the charge comes from triboelectric charging, meaning friction between the bee and the air as it moves. It does not come from piezoelectricity generated by the wings.

text: Three of the ocean's zones - the hadal, abyssal, and bathyal zones - are characterized by extreme conditions and have limited accessibility.
label: supported
reason: Several sources describe the bathyal, abyssal and hadal zones as having extreme conditions: total darkness, crushing pressure and near-freezing temperatures. They also say these depths are among the least explored parts of the planet because these conditions make exploration hard. Globe Composite says the deep zones below 1,000 m are among the least explored places on Earth and that the bathyal zone's pressure makes exploration difficult. Wikipedia notes that pressure of up to 600 atmospheres makes exploring these depths difficult. Articles on the hadal zone describe immense pressure, frigid temperatures and complete darkness.

text: Clouds can weigh more than a million pounds, as a single cumulus cloud can contain up to 1 million pounds of water.
label: supported
reason: The USGS says an average 1 km × 1 km cumulus cloud weighs about 1.1 million pounds, and Science Notes and EarthDate give the same figure. That supports the claim's main point that clouds can weigh more than a million pounds. Calling 1 million pounds the upper limit ("up to") is a little imprecise, since the average cloud already weighs slightly more than that. Still, the figure is close, and some outlets phrase it the same way, so the claim's gist holds.

text: Galaxies in the observable universe are moving away from each other due to a phenomenon called dark energy, resulting in an accelerating expansion of the universe.
label: supported
reason: Trustworthy sources back the claim. The US Department of Energy says dark energy "pushes them [galaxies] apart", and Space.com and NASA's Hubble pages say dark energy drives the accelerating expansion of the universe. American Scientist also says dark energy is pushing galaxies away from one another. Strictly speaking, galaxies were already moving apart because space has been expanding since the Big Bang; dark energy explains why that expansion is speeding up. Nearby galaxies held together by gravity, such as those in our Local Group, are also not moving apart. Still, mainstream science sources describe the claim's overall picture the same way.

text: Germany has the most time zones in a single country, with a total of 14 time zones across its various territories and islands around the world.
label: contradicted
reason: France, not Germany, has the most time zones of any country: 12, or 13 if you count its Antarctic claim, thanks to overseas territories such as French Polynesia. Germany uses a single time zone (Central European Time) and has no overseas territories that would give it 14.

text: Humans and dolphins are the only mammals known to give themselves names, in the form of unique whistles that serve as identifiers.
label: contradicted
reason: 2024 research shows the claim is out of date. A Colorado State University study published in June 2024 found that wild African elephants address each other with name-like calls. A Hebrew University study published in August 2024 found that marmoset monkeys use 'phee-calls' to name each other. The Hebrew University release says this behavior was 'previously known to exist only in humans, dolphins, and elephants.' So humans and dolphins are not the only mammals known to use names. The claim is also wrong that these names take the form of whistles for humans.

text: Humans share approximately 50-60% of their DNA with bananas, highlighting the shared ancestry of all living things on Earth.
label: contradicted
reason: Fact-checks from IFLScience, HowStuffWorks and The Star trace the popular "50–60%" figure to a gene comparison: about 60% of human genes have a recognizable counterpart in the banana genome. That is not the same as sharing 50–60% of our DNA. Genes make up only a small part of the genome, so The Star puts the actual overlap at about 1–2% of the human genome. IFLScience says the statement is technically wrong because "it's not 60 percent, and it's not DNA." The shared-ancestry point is fair, but the core claim about the share of DNA is contradicted. Some sources, including The Star's lenient "TRUE" verdict, accept the figure loosely, but only by reading it as genes rather than DNA.

text: NASA's Mars Curiosity Rover, launched in 2011, has traveled over 29 kilometers on the Martian surface since its landing in 2012.
label: supported
reason: Curiosity launched in November 2011 and landed in Gale Crater in August 2012. NASA's 10-year anniversary article (2022) said it had already driven nearly 29 km. A Universe Magazine report later said it had passed 30 km. A recent Earth.com article, published around NASA/JPL's news on Perseverance's distance record, says Curiosity has now logged more than 38 km. That is well over 29 km, so every part of the claim holds.

text: Our solar system is not perfectly aligned with the Milky Way galaxy, with Earth tilted at about 60 degrees relative to the galactic plane.
label: supported
reason: Reliable sources say the Solar System's plane (the ecliptic, which is Earth's orbital plane) is tilted about 60° to the Milky Way's galactic plane. Wikipedia lists the invariable-plane-to-galactic-plane inclination as about 60°, and Oikofuge and other sources give the same figure. The claim's wording is a little loose: it says "Earth tilted", but the ~60° figure applies to Earth's orbital plane, which matches. Earth's equator is tilted about 63° to the galactic plane, which still rounds to "about 60 degrees".

text: Plants can make sounds when they're stressed or growing, as researchers have detected faint clicks and murmurs emanating from plants' roots and stems.
label: supported
reason: Several reliable sources back this up. A 2023 study in Cell, covered by Science News, CNN and the Natural History Museum, recorded ultrasonic clicks or pops from tomato, tobacco and other plants when they were short of water or had their stems cut. Separately, Monica Gagliano's research at the University of Western Australia found that young, growing corn roots make regular clicking sounds at around 220 Hz. Together these support the claim that plants make sounds when stressed or growing, and that the sounds come from roots and stems. The word "murmurs" is loose wording, but it doesn't conflict with the evidence.

text: Polar bears are excellent swimmers and have been known to swim for hours or even days at a time, covering distances up to 60 miles without resting.
label: supported
reason: The claim holds up. Several reputable sources describe polar bears as excellent swimmers that can swim about 60 miles (around 100 km) without resting. These include NH PBS NatureWorks, San Diego Zoo Wildlife Alliance and Ocean Conservancy. USGS GPS tracking reported by Live Science shows swims lasting from 17 hours to nearly 10 days, which backs the 'hours or even days' part. One caveat: the same research recorded swims of up to 427 miles. So 60 miles is a commonly cited figure, not the true maximum, but the sources still describe bears covering that distance without rest.

text: Tarantulas have existed on Earth for at least 100 million years, with fossil evidence showing that early species of these spiders lived during the Cretaceous period.
label: supported
reason: A peer-reviewed study in the Journal of Biogeography (Wiley) says the oldest known tarantula (theraphosid) fossil comes from Burmese amber dated to about 100 million years ago, which is in the mid-Cretaceous. The study also places the ancestors of modern tarantulas in the mid-Cretaceous. Both parts of the claim are backed by this evidence.

text: WERAM (WEPOS, WEEEOS) is an old fossillized French underground ocean circa "540 Million Years ago."
label: contradicted
reason: No search result describes WERAM, WEPOS or WEEEOS as a fossilized underground ocean in France from about 540 million years ago. WERAM is a bioinformatics database of proteins that write, erase and read histone acetylation and methylation marks, published in Nucleic Acids Research. It is also the name of a South African IT company. WEPOS is Windows Embedded for Point of Service, and wePOS is a point-of-sale plugin for WooCommerce. The searches for WEPOS also returned Microsoft's Windows Embedded Industry page. Fossil results from about 540 million years ago are unrelated to these names. These sources show the claim misidentifies what these terms refer to.

text: Plants can make sounds, such as clicking or buzzing, that can be heard by humans or other organisms, although these sounds are often too quiet to be detected without specialized equipment.
label: supported
reason: Peer-reviewed research in Cell (Khait et al., 2023), reported by Science News and CNN, found that stressed tomato and tobacco plants make airborne popping or clicking sounds. Researchers detected them with ultrasonic microphones. The sounds are outside the range of human hearing, but some animals such as bats, mice and moths could likely hear them. This supports the core claim that plants make clicking sounds that other organisms can hear and that people need special equipment to detect. Two details are not exact. The study found the sounds are hard to hear mainly because their pitch is ultrasonic, not because they are quiet. The sources describe clicks and pops, not buzzing.

text: Water can exist in all three states (liquid, solid, and gas) at the same time, a rare occurrence known as the "triple point," which occurs at a very specific temperature and pressure.
label: supported
reason: Fluke's explainer says the triple point of water is the single combination of temperature and pressure (0.01 °C and about 0.006 atm) at which ice, liquid water and water vapor exist together in equilibrium. It also notes that these conditions are not usually found outside controlled laboratory settings. That backs up both the 'very specific temperature and pressure' and the 'rare occurrence' parts of the claim.

text: Beehive-shaped structures in Mexico, known as "sweat houses," have been discovered to date back over 2,000 years to the ancient Mayans.
label: not_verifiable
reason: I found no source reporting a discovery in Mexico of beehive-shaped Maya "sweat houses" dated to more than 2,000 years ago. The related finds don't match the claim: the Maya sweat baths I found were at Piedras Negras and Xultun, both in Guatemala, and the Xultun bath was in use around 300–600 AD. The temazcal (steam bath) found in Mexico City dates to the 14th century and was built by the Mexica (Aztecs), not the Maya. The roughly 2,000-year-old 'beehive' was a ceramic object from Nakum, Guatemala, possibly an actual beehive, not a building. Sweat baths have a long history among the Maya, but none of these sources confirm the claim's combination of a beehive shape, a site in Mexico and an age of more than 2,000 years. My searches were cut short by a tool limit, so a matching report may exist that I didn't find.

text: Astronauts who stay in space long enough can experience a condition called 'space adaptation syndrome', which causes a range of symptoms including space motion sickness, fatigue, and disorientation.
label: supported
reason: The claim holds up. WikEM's page on space adaptation syndrome lists its common symptoms as space motion sickness, dizziness and disorientation, nausea, headaches and fatigue. Quironsalud's medical page also names disorientation and fatigue as common symptoms and says the condition comes from microgravity. Wikipedia adds that it affects up to about half of space travelers while they adjust to weightlessness. One wording issue doesn't change the verdict: the syndrome usually starts in the first few days of a flight rather than only after a long stay, and it typically fades within 2–3 days.

text: A veutric, an eversion of a sphere turning itself inside out, is a theoretical concept that cannot be visualized in reality, however its concept serves the purpose to get international attention to topological deformations in intrinsic spatial arrangements.
label: contradicted
reason: I couldn't find "veutric" used as a name for sphere eversion in any source. The concept itself is real. Wolfram MathWorld and Wikipedia describe sphere eversion as turning a sphere inside out by a regular homotopy. But the claim says it "cannot be visualized," and that is wrong. Sphere eversion is a well-known subject for mathematical visualization: the Geometry Center's video "Outside In," the 1998 video "The Optiverse," computer-generated eversions on Scientific American covers, and Bednorz's simulation all show it. Nothing I found supports the claim's stated purpose of drawing "international attention to topological deformations in intrinsic spatial arrangements" either.

text: Plants can make sounds, too, when they are stressed or even happy, at a frequency that's undetectable to the human ear, using specialized equipment scientists have discovered ultrasonic sounds produced by plants.
label: not_verifiable
reason: The search results support part of the claim. A 2023 Tel Aviv University study published in Cell (Khait et al.) used specialised microphones to record ultrasonic clicks at about 40–80 kHz, which humans cannot hear, from stressed tomato and tobacco plants. Those plants had been left unwatered or had their stems cut. The results do not support the idea that plants make sounds when 'happy'. The study found that unstressed plants emit far fewer sounds, and no evidence ties plant sounds to a positive or 'happy' state. Because that part of the claim cannot be verified, the claim as a whole is inconclusive.

text: Plants can make sounds, which are typically too low for humans to hear, using methods like changing gas pressure in their cells or producing high-frequency clicks as they undergo stress.
label: contradicted
reason: Plants do make sounds under stress. The 2023 Cell study found that stressed tomato and tobacco plants make click-like sounds. However, the claim says these sounds are typically too low for humans to hear, and the study shows the opposite: they are ultrasonic, at about 40–80 kHz, which is too high in frequency for humans to hear. The study attributes the sounds to likely cavitation, meaning air bubbles forming and bursting in the plant's water-carrying xylem, not to gas-pressure changes in cells. The claim's mention of 'high-frequency clicks' matches the study, but its 'too low' description and its account of how the sounds are made do not.

text: Plants can make sounds, like clicking and popping noises, that are typically beyond the range of human hearing and are often used for communication and defense.
label: not_verifiable
reason: The first part of the claim is supported. A 2023 peer-reviewed study in Cell by Khait et al. found that stressed tomato and tobacco plants make ultrasonic clicking or popping sounds, compared to bubble wrap, that are beyond the range of human hearing. Science News, Earth.com, and a Cell commentary report the same finding. The second part, that plants 'often' use these sounds for communication and defense, is not established. The researchers say they don't know exactly what causes the sounds, which may simply be air bubbles forming and popping in the plant's water-carrying tissue. They describe insect responses and plant communication only as possibilities for future study. Since part of the claim is supported and part is not verified, the claim as a whole is inconclusive.

text: Astronauts on the International Space Station have reported they can see the Great Barrier Reef from outer space, but this is a common myth; in reality, it is not as visible as often described.
label: contradicted
reason: Trustworthy sources show the Great Barrier Reef really can be seen from space, so calling it a myth is wrong. ESA published a photo of the reef taken from the ISS by astronaut André Kuipers. NASA's Earth Observatory has shared astronaut photos of it taken from the ISS, and Sky at Night Magazine says it is the only living thing that can be seen from space. The myth the claim seems to have in mind is about the Great Wall of China, not the reef.

text: Beehive-shaped structures in Mexico, known as "sweat houses," have been discovered to be around 1,000 years older than previously thought, dating back to around 700 AD.
label: not_verifiable
reason: I found nothing confirming this claim. My searches on Mexican sweat lodges (temazcales) brought up reports of a 14th-century Aztec temazcal found in Mexico City's La Merced district, Classic Maya sweat baths, and a note that temazcales existed in the Americas at least 700 years before 1519. None of these sources describe beehive-shaped 'sweat houses' in Mexico being redated to around 700 AD, or as 1,000 years older than previously thought. Beehive-shaped 'sweat houses' are more typically associated with Ireland, so the claim may be mixing up separate stories. I hit the search limit before I could check that possibility. With no source that supports or directly contradicts the claim, I can't verify it.

text: Bees are able to fly by using their wings to create electricity through a process known as triboelectrification, where the wings create a static charge and are then attracted to oppositely charged particles in the air.
label: contradicted
reason: Bees fly by aerodynamics, not electricity. Their large thorax muscles beat the wings about 200 to 300 times per second, and the flapping motion makes swirling air currents (vortices) that produce lift. Bees do pick up static charge as they move, which is triboelectric charging, but that charge is linked to things like collecting pollen and sensing flowers. It does not keep them in the air. No reliable source says that being attracted to charged particles in the air is how bees fly, so the claim's explanation is wrong.

text: Tarantulas have been around for a long time, with the oldest known tarantula fossil dating back to the Early Cretaceous period, over 135 million years ago.
label: contradicted
reason: A peer-reviewed study in the Journal of Biogeography (Wiley) describes the oldest known theraphosid (tarantula) fossil as coming from Burmese amber dated to about 100 million years ago (Wunderlich & Müller, 2020). That puts it in the mid-Cretaceous, around the Early/Late Cretaceous boundary, not the Early Cretaceous more than 135 million years ago. Much older mygalomorph fossils, such as Rosamygale from about 242 million years ago, are not tarantulas, so they do not support the claim.

text: Near the surface of Greenland and Antarctica, scientists have discovered large, ancient freshwater ice shelves known as "ice slabs" or "ice dams," up to 130 meters thick and containing trillions of tons of frozen water.
label: contradicted
reason: The 2019 Nature study by MacFerrin et al. describes Greenland's near-surface ice slabs as 1 to 16 meters thick. They are recently formed layers of refrozen meltwater in the firn, not ancient ice shelves up to 130 meters thick holding trillions of tons of water. They also aren't called "ice dams," and the study maps them in Greenland, not Antarctica. The claim gets the thickness, age and nature of the ice slabs wrong.

text: Plants can make sounds, as research has detected that plants release clicks, pops, and other noises, often inaudible to humans, when they are stressed or in need of water.
label: supported
reason: Research published in Cell in 2023 found that stressed tomato and tobacco plants make ultrasonic clicks and pops. They did this when dehydrated or when their stems were cut, at about 30–50 pops per hour. The sounds are too high-pitched for humans to hear. Reports from the Natural History Museum, Science News and Cell Press back the claim that plants make sounds when stressed or short of water.

text: Honeybees are able to fly by using their wings to generate electricity and create lift through a process called piezoelectricity, beating them around 200 times per second.
label: contradicted
reason: Honeybees do not fly by using piezoelectricity. Their flight muscles squeeze the thorax up and down and side to side, which makes the wings beat. The lift comes from aerodynamic effects of the rapid, short wing strokes, not from generating electricity. Research reported by LiveScience found that honeybees beat their wings about 230 times per second, and ASU's Ask a Biologist says it's over 230. So the piezoelectric mechanism in the claim is wrong, and its figure of about 200 beats per second is also a little low.

text: Plants can only undergo photosynthesis within a specific temperature range of 20-30 °C (68-86 °F), with most species experiencing reduced growth or death outside of this range.
label: contradicted
reason: The sources show plants photosynthesize across a much wider temperature range than 20–30 °C. A Vedantu study guide (an educational site, not a primary research source) gives a range of about 10–40 °C depending on habitat, with an optimum around 25–35 °C. Peer-reviewed research (ScienceDirect, Arctic journal) records lichen photosynthesis below -10 °C and CO2 exchange near -20 °C, with polar species doing best at 0–15 °C. Lichens are not true plants, but the habitat-dependent range for plants still refutes the claim that photosynthesis is only possible between 20 and 30 °C.

text: Near the surface of Greenland and Antarctica, scientists have discovered large, ancient freshwater ice shelves known as "ice slabs" or "ice dams," up to 130 meters thick.
label: contradicted
reason: The research contradicts the main details of this claim. "Ice slabs" are layers of refrozen meltwater in the firn (compacted old snow) of the Greenland Ice Sheet. MacFerrin et al. (Nature, 2019) and Jullien et al. (GRL, 2023) describe them as only metres thick, roughly 1 to 16 m, not up to 130 m. They are also not ancient. They formed and spread recently as surface melting increased, and have been documented since at least 2002. They are not ice shelves, and the term "ice dams" does not refer to them. The studies focus on Greenland, not Antarctica.

text: Three of the ocean's zones - the hadal, abyssal, and bathyal zones - are characterized by extreme conditions and have limited accessibility to humans and animals alike.
label: supported
reason: My searches support the core of the claim. Vedantu and Fiveable say the bathyal and abyssal zones have permanent darkness, cold and very high or crushing pressure. Britannica, PMC and Wikipedia describe the hadal zone as the deepest and least explored part of the ocean. Wikipedia's Deep sea article notes that the deep sea is the least explored biome because its 'extreme conditions make the environment difficult to access and explore.' On the animal side, Wikipedia calls the hadal zone 'sparsely inhabited,' and other sources say only specially adapted organisms survive in these zones. That fits the idea that animals also have limited access. The 'animals alike' wording is loose, though, since many adapted species do live in these zones. Read broadly, the claim matches the evidence.

text: Cheryl Holder and her team of-sales specialist gifted a Terry Bradshaw over 100 cows during the 'Hard Knocks' show; his then teammate PatTokenizer indicated envy.
label: not_verifiable
