The results only covered unrelated news about Bradshaw's ranches and his memoir. The claim also looks garbled: 'PatTokenizer' doesn't point to any real teammate, so that part can't be checked at all.

text: Orient Drinks, a Japanese beverage company, teamed up with convenience store chain, Lawson, to sell a Pepsi "Ice Cream" that is actually a frozen, creamy version of the popular cola.
label: not_verifiable
reason: I couldn't find any source that confirms this claim. My searches turned up a Lawson drinkable soft-serve product called "Nomu Soft Cream" and some general articles about Pepsi flavours in Japan. None of them mentioned a company called "Orient Drinks", a Pepsi "ice cream" sold at Lawson, or a frozen, creamy cola. Pepsi in Japan is generally made and sold by Suntory, so the claim that "Orient Drinks" is the Japanese partner looks doubtful. I hit the search tool's usage limit before I could check further, so I can't confirm or rule out this claim.

text: Plants can make sounds, when injured or cut, at a frequency inaudible to human ears; these sounds are in the range of 20-240 Hz.
label: contradicted
reason: The main study on this is Khait et al., Cell, 2023. It found that stressed plants, both cut and drought-stressed, give off airborne sounds that humans can't hear. However, these sounds are ultrasonic: the researchers recorded in the 20–150 kHz range, and the mean peak frequencies were about 50–55 kHz. That doesn't match the claim's range of 20–240 Hz. Frequencies of 20–240 Hz also sit inside the range of human hearing (about 20 Hz to 20 kHz), so the claim contradicts itself as well.

text: Plants can make sounds, such as clicks or even what is perceived as screaming, when they are injured or under stress, and scientists have developed devices to record and study these sounds more closely.
label: supported
reason: A 2023 study from Tel Aviv University, published in Cell (Khait et al.), backs up every part of the claim. The researchers placed ultrasonic microphones near living plants and recorded ultrasonic clicks from tomato and tobacco plants that were dehydrated or had their stems cut. Science News reported the findings. The team then slowed the recordings down into the range of human hearing so they could be studied, which matches the claim that scientists use devices to record these sounds. Popular coverage widely described the sounds as plants 'screaming'. The claim only says the sounds are 'perceived as' screaming, so it doesn't conflict with the scientific description of them as clicks.

text: The68539-\Traits Eruption, also known as the 'Aeolian Brown-Tail' volcano, is a volcano that is actually a submerged seamount rather than an Olympic-standard volcano structure on the sites mountains.
label: not_verifiable
reason: I found no evidence that a volcano called "The68539-\Traits Eruption" or the "Aeolian Brown-Tail" volcano exists. Searches only turned up unrelated results, such as the Brown Tuffs ash deposits on Italy's Aeolian Islands and real seamounts like Axial and Ahyi. The claim is also garbled ("Olympic-standard volcano structure on the sites mountains") and has no clear referent, so it can be neither supported nor contradicted.

text: The Axel Erlandson's Tree Circus, also known as the "Basket Tree," was created by an American farmer who grafted various tree branches together to grow a single tree into a basket shape.
label: contradicted
reason: Wikipedia and Futility Closet both say the Tree Circus was the name of Erlandson's roadside attraction, which opened in 1947 and showed many shaped trees. The "Basket Tree" was just one of those trees, not another name for the Tree Circus. It also wasn't one tree grown into a basket shape: Erlandson planted six sycamore trees in a circle and approach-grafted them together to form diamond patterns. The sources do confirm that he was a Swedish-American farmer.

text: Plants can make sounds, such as a high-pitched clicking noise, that are usually undetectable to humans and have even been found to warn other plants of danger or stress through these sounds.
label: not_verifiable
reason: Reliable reports on the 2023 Cell study by Tel Aviv University (Science News, Asian Scientist) back the first part of the claim. Stressed plants, such as thirsty tomato and tobacco plants, give off ultrasonic clicking or popping sounds at 20–100 kHz, which humans cannot hear. The second part, that these sounds have been found to warn other plants of danger, is not backed up. The researchers say they have only shown that plants emit informative sounds. They are still trying to learn how other plants and animals respond to them. So the warning part can't be confirmed, and the evidence doesn't directly disprove it either.

text: A blue whale's heartbeat can be as loud as 188 decibels, which is louder than a jet taking off, but not loud enough to be heard by humans outside of the water.
label: contradicted
reason: The 188-decibel figure is for blue whale calls (vocalizations), not their heartbeat. WWF says blue whale "calls reach 188 decibels, while a jet reaches 140 decibels." Wikipedia's list of whale vocalizations likewise puts blue whale sound source levels at 155–188 dB re 1 µPa. No reliable source gives the heartbeat a loudness anywhere near 188 dB, so the claim credits the wrong sound with that figure.

text: Plants can make sounds, as research has shown that they release ultrasonic clicks when they are stressed, injured, or communicating with other plants and even animals nearby.
label: not_verifiable
reason: Research supports the core of the claim. Khait et al. (Cell, 2023) found that tomato, tobacco, and other plants make ultrasonic clicks at 40–80 kHz when stressed by drought or a cut stem, and that stressed plants click much more than unstressed ones. The claim goes further, though, by saying plants click when 'communicating with other plants and even animals nearby.' That part hasn't been shown. Coverage of the study says it is still unclear whether the sounds are used to communicate with other organisms; the researchers only suggest animals or other plants might detect them. Because the communication part can't be verified, the claim is only partly supported.

text: Polar bears are excellent swimmers, and they have been known to swim for hours or even days at a time, covering distances of up to 60 miles (97 kilometers) without resting.
label: supported
reason: Several reputable sources back the claim. NH PBS NatureWorks says polar bears are very good swimmers that can swim 'as far as 60 miles (96.6 km) without resting.' The San Diego Zoo Wildlife Alliance and Ocean Conservancy say they can swim more than 60 miles (about 100 km) without rest. National Geographic, CBC and Guinness report a tracked female that swam nonstop for nine days, which supports swims lasting 'hours or even days.' One caveat: that record swim covered 687 km (426 miles), so 'up to 60 miles' understates the longest distance on record. It still matches the commonly cited figure, and nothing contradicts the claim's main point.

text: Plants can make sounds, too, when they are stressed or in pain; scientists have detected ultrasonic clicks coming from plants like tomatoes and corn when the plants are subjected to drought or physical harm.
label: supported
reason: The 2023 Cell study by Khait et al., reported by Science News and other outlets, recorded ultrasonic clicks from tomato and tobacco plants that were drought-stressed or had their stems cut. Similar sounds also came from stressed wheat, corn, grapevines and cacti. The phrase "in pain" is loose wording: the study is about physical stress, not about plants feeling pain. The claim's core facts still hold up.

text: Honeybees are able to fly by using their wings to generate electricity through a process called piezoelectricity, allowing them to charge pollen and other particles with an electric current.
label: contradicted
reason: The claim gets both flight and charging wrong. Bees fly through aerodynamics, meaning lift from flapping their wings, and not by generating electricity. Scientific reviews say bees pick up static charge mainly through the triboelectric effect, which is friction with the air and with surfaces as they fly. That is not piezoelectricity. The charge that results is static, not an electric current, and it helps pollen stick to the bee by electrostatic attraction.

text: A partitions of the Mandelbrot set can form the swirling patterns familiar to most, however using an alternative equation Maple it seems the partition produced looks more like a giant squid than anything else.
label: not_verifiable
reason: I couldn't find any source that backs up this claim. The only search result that mentions a squid is a 2008 comment on the jwz blog, where a reader jokingly calls a fractal image a 'Giant Fractal Squid'. That image had nothing to do with a Maple partition of the Mandelbrot set or an 'alternative equation'. The Maple-related results (MaplePrimes's 'Mandelbrot Mania with Maple', Maple Help, and RWTH Aachen's Maple V fractal pages) only show standard ways of drawing and colouring the Mandelbrot set. None of them mention a partition from another equation that looks like a giant squid. The search tool hit its usage limit before I could look further. The wording of the claim is also garbled and vague, so the specific result it describes can't be confirmed or ruled out.

text: Plants can make sounds, too, as researchers have found that a plant can generate clicks, or other loud noises, when it's stressed or needs something, such as water.
label: supported
reason: A peer-reviewed 2023 study in Cell by Tel Aviv University researchers found that stressed plants, such as tomato and tobacco plants that were dehydrated or had their stems cut, give off airborne ultrasonic clicks. These sounds can be recorded from a distance. Science News, Smithsonian and NBC also reported the findings. This backs the main claim that plants make clicking sounds when stressed or short of water. One caveat: the sounds are ultrasonic, so humans can't hear them, and calling them 'loud noises' is loose wording. They have been reported as reaching volumes similar to a normal conversation, though, so the claim is broadly supported.

text: Plants can make sounds, too, and researchers have discovered that certain types like tomatoes and tobacco can produce ultrasonic clicks to communicate and even summon beneficial insects.
label: not_verifiable
reason: I couldn't verify the second half of the claim. The first part holds up: a 2023 Cell study by Tel Aviv University researchers found that tomato and tobacco plants give off airborne ultrasonic clicks when stressed by drought or cutting. But the sources describe these clicks as signs of stress that some animals might be able to hear. None of the results show that the plants make the sounds to communicate, and none show that the sounds attract beneficial insects. Researchers only speculated that animals might react to them. Since the 'communicate and summon beneficial insects' part isn't supported by the evidence, the claim as a whole can't be confirmed.

text: Moisture in certain environments can cause chrome and most metals to corrode over time, and some researchers suggest that the ancient Library of Alexandria was damaged not by the burning of the scrolls, but by a moisture buildup and certain environmental factors, pre-dating the scroll fires.
label: not_verifiable
reason: Part of the claim is supported. Reliable sources agree that moisture causes corrosion, and scholarly accounts say the Library of Alexandria likely declined slowly instead of being destroyed in one fire. The UChicago Encyclopaedia Romana says its papyrus scrolls were exposed to the 'humidity of a coastal Mediterranean climate' and to mice and insects, and other summaries point to papyrus decaying in a humid climate. However, no source says this moisture damage happened before the fires. The decline described by scholars mostly comes after Caesar's fire in 48 BC, during the Roman period. Researchers also do not describe a 'moisture buildup' that replaced fire as the cause of damage. They list humidity as one factor alongside neglect and lost funding. Because the claim's timing and framing cannot be confirmed, it is inconclusive.

text: Haystacks on farms are sometimes set on fire to dry them and after the fire has been extinguished, any sparks remaining that have not yet died out are put out with heavy sod or by trampling on them with people's feet or their animals.
label: contradicted
reason: I found no evidence that farmers set haystacks on fire to dry them. Wikipedia says haystacks dry naturally in the meadow. Agricultural extension sources from NDSU and Oklahoma State describe haystack fires as an unwanted hazard. These fires usually start by spontaneous combustion when hay is stored too wet, and farmers work to prevent them. The sources also say nothing about putting out leftover sparks with sod or by trampling.

text: Plants can make sounds, with researchers discovering over 300 different types of ultrasonic sounds produced by various plant species that signal stress and other biological functions.
label: not_verifiable
reason: The main idea checks out. A 2023 study in Cell (Khait et al.), reported by Science News and the Natural History Museum, found that tomato and tobacco plants under stress make airborne ultrasonic clicks. A machine-learning model could tell those sounds apart by stress type (drought or cutting) and by species. However, I found no source saying researchers discovered 'over 300 different types' of ultrasonic sounds. The study described clicks from a few plant species, with tomato plants making about 35 clicks per hour, sorted into a small number of categories. The '300 types' figure can't be verified, so the claim as a whole is unverified rather than supported.

text: Plants can make sounds, as research has shown that when a plant is injured or cut, it can produce clicking or bubbling sounds at a frequency inaudible to humans.
label: supported
reason: Research published in Cell in 2023 (Khait et al.) supports the claim. It found that tomato and tobacco plants give off airborne ultrasonic sounds when stressed by drought or a cutting injury. Coverage such as Science News describes these sounds as clicks. They are ultrasonic, roughly 20–100 kHz, which is above the range humans can hear. The researchers think cavitation, meaning air bubbles forming and bursting inside the plant's water-carrying tissue, may produce them. That fits the claim's 'clicking or bubbling' description well enough.

text: Plants can make sounds, as research has shown that when a plant is injured or cut, it can produce clicking or bubbling sounds at a frequency inaudible to the human ear.
label: supported
reason: The claim matches published research. A 2023 study in Cell (Khait et al., Tel Aviv University) found that tomato and tobacco plants give off airborne ultrasonic sounds when stressed by drying out or by being cut. Science News and Cell Press coverage describe these as ultrasonic clicks or popping sounds, like bubble wrap popping, likely caused by air bubbles forming and bursting in the plant's water-carrying tissue. The sounds are above the range of human hearing.

text: A person was able to stay inside an airtight coffin for 27 days before suffocating, because of the algae that fell on the coffin from the palm tree above, that produced oxygen for him to breath.
label: contradicted
reason: I found no record of anyone surviving 27 days in an airtight coffin because algae from a palm tree supplied oxygen. The story does not appear in any search results, including well-documented cases like Angel Hays, Mick Meaney and David Blaine. Science also rules it out. Popular Science estimates the air in a sealed coffin lasts only about 5.5 hours, and other sources say an hour or two. The claim also contradicts itself: if the coffin was airtight, oxygen made by algae on the outside could not get in. Credible sources point to survival of hours, not 27 days.

text: Honeybees are able to fly by using their wings to generate electricity through a process called piezoelectricity, allowing them to defy the normal laws of aerodynamics.
label: contradicted
reason: Honeybees don't fly by making electricity through piezoelectricity, and they don't break the laws of aerodynamics. A 2005 PNAS study by Altshuler et al. shows they stay airborne through ordinary aerodynamic lift. They do it with short wing strokes (about 90°) at a very high wingbeat frequency (about 230 Hz). The idea that bees 'defy aerodynamics' is an old myth that this research explained away.

text: A blue whale can hold up to 5,000 liters (1,320 gallons) of blood in its body at any given time.
label: contradicted
reason: The 5,000 L to 1,320 gallon conversion is correct. The problem is the word "up to": no source I found treats 5,000 L as the most a blue whale's blood can measure. Most of the estimates are higher. One post puts an adult's blood volume at about 5,300 L. A site gives 1,500 gallons, about 5,700 L. Another says the total blood can weigh 14,000 lb (6,400 kg), which works out to roughly 6,000 L or more. One educational PDF gives a much lower figure, about 58 gallons, but that looks like an error, since one heartbeat alone pumps about 60 gallons (NOAA). The sources are informal (a social media post, fact sites and a classroom handout), and my searches ran out before I could check a more authoritative one. Still, the available estimates point to more than 5,000 L, which conflicts with calling it the maximum.

text: A blue whale's heartbeat can be as loud as 188 decibels, louder than a jet engine during takeoff.
label: contradicted
reason: WWF says the 188-decibel figure belongs to blue whale calls (vocalizations), not their heartbeat. Those calls are louder than a jet, which reaches about 140 dB. No reliable source puts a blue whale's heartbeat at 188 dB, so the claim pins the call's loudness on the heart. The heartbeat is a quiet sound by comparison, only picked up from a short distance with special equipment.

text: A blue whale's heartbeat can be as loud as 188 decibels, louder than a jet taking off, and can be detected hundreds of miles away.
label: contradicted
reason: The 188-decibel figure, which is louder than a jet engine and carries hundreds to thousands of miles, describes blue whale calls, not the heartbeat. NOAA says a blue whale's heartbeat can be heard about 2 miles away, not hundreds of miles. The Environmental Literacy Council says the heartbeat has no decibel rating and that the 188 dB figure belongs to the whale's calls. The claim mixes up the heartbeat with the calls.

text: A blue whale's heartbeat can be detected from over two miles (about 3.2 kilometers) away due to the massive size of its heart.
label: supported
reason: The claim is supported, though not by any direct measurement I found. NOAA Fisheries, a trustworthy government source, says a blue whale's heart weighs about 400 pounds and that its heartbeat 'can be heard 2 miles away.' The Cold Spring Harbor Whaling Museum also says the heartbeat 'can be detected from 2 MILES AWAY.' Africa Check reviewed a post that said the heartbeat can be heard from over 2 miles (3 km) away and headlined its fact-check 'Yes, impressive claims about blue whales correct,' though the excerpt I retrieved did not discuss the distance part. A children's book adds that this requires 'the right equipment,' which fits the claim's wording of 'detected.' Some disagreement exists: crowd-sourced Brainly answers call the claim false, but they are not reliable sources. There is also a small wording gap, since NOAA says 2 miles and the claim says over two miles.

text: A blue whale's heartbeat is so loud that it can be detected by scientists using underwater microphones from hundreds of miles away.
label: contradicted
reason: No reliable source backs the claim that a blue whale's heartbeat can be picked up by underwater microphones hundreds of miles away. The most widely repeated figure, including on NOAA Fisheries' page, is that the heartbeat can be heard about 2 miles away, and some sources dispute even that. When scientists first recorded a wild blue whale's heart rate (Goldbogen lab, 2019), they used an ECG tag stuck to the whale with suction cups, not distant hydrophones. The 'hundreds of miles' distance seems to come from blue whale calls, which do travel that far, not from the heartbeat.

text: A set of human lungs, after being removed from the body and inflated, can float on water due to the air sacs that contain oxygen.
label: supported
reason: Live Science says each lung holds about 300 million balloon-like alveoli. It adds that when these air sacs are filled with air, the lungs become the only organs in the body that can float. Wikipedia's article on the lung float test (hydrostatic test) also says lungs that contain air float in water. Strictly speaking, the sacs hold air, which includes oxygen, rather than pure oxygen. That wording doesn't change the substance of the claim.

text: A veutric, an eversion of a sphere turning itself inside out, is a theoretical concept that cannot be visualized in reality, however its concept serves the purpose to get international attention to topological deformations in intrinsic geometry.
label: contradicted
reason: No source uses the term "veutric" for a sphere eversion, so it appears to be a made-up word. More importantly, the claim that sphere eversion "cannot be visualized in reality" is false. Reliable sources describe it as a classic subject of mathematical visualization, with computer-generated eversions such as the videos "Outside In" and "The Optiverse" and Thurston's eversion on the cover of Scientific American. The part about getting "international attention to topological deformations in intrinsic geometry" isn't supported by any source either.

text: All mammals, except for humans and a small number of other primates and marine mammals, have a cloaca.
label: contradicted
reason: The claim gets it backwards. Biology sources, including Wikipedia's Cloaca article, say most placental mammals lack a permanent cloaca and instead have separate anal and urogenital openings. Only monotremes such as the platypus, and a few other mammals, have one. So the cloaca is the exception among mammals, not something nearly all mammals have.

text: Bacteria are able to survive in extremely cold temperatures, with some species discovered thriving in environments as low as -12°C (10°F) in Antarctica.
label: supported
reason: Reliable sources support the claim and suggest it may even understate the cold limit. A PNAS study titled "Microbial life at −13 °C in the brine of an ice-sealed Antarctic lake" found bacterial communities living in Lake Vida's permanently frozen-over brine at about −13 °C (−13.4 °C in a related ASM paper), which is colder than the −12 °C (10 °F) in the claim. Other peer-reviewed reviews describe psychrophilic (cold-loving) bacteria thriving in Antarctica's below-freezing environments, which supports the general statement that bacteria can survive extreme cold.

text: Bumblebees are able to fly by using electricity generated by the movement of their wings to help them lift off the ground and stay aloft.
label: contradicted
reason: Bumblebees get their lift from aerodynamics, not electricity. Wing flapping creates a leading edge vortex and other unsteady airflow effects that keep them aloft, as high-speed camera studies showed. Bees do pick up static charge, but that helps with pollen collection and sensing flowers, not with lift. The claim that they fly using electricity from their wing movement is wrong.

text: Dragonflies have been around for over 300 million years, with fossils of ancient dragonflies dating back to the Paleozoic Era.
label: supported
reason: Several sources agree that early dragonflies (Protodonata/Meganisoptera) left fossils more than 300 million years old. NatureNorth puts them in the Carboniferous, and Britannica describes giant dragonfly fossils such as Meganeura from the Carboniferous and Permian periods (about 359–251 million years ago). Both periods belong to the Paleozoic Era, so both parts of the claim hold up: dragonflies have existed for over 300 million years, and their earliest fossils date to the Paleozoic.

text: Higher education students who report using active learning methods in the classroom tend to outperform their peers using more traditional teaching methods by around half a standard deviation.
label: supported
reason: The claim matches the main finding of Freeman et al. (2014, PNAS). That meta-analysis of 225 studies of undergraduate STEM courses found that exam and concept-inventory scores rose by 0.47 standard deviations under active learning compared with traditional lecturing, which is roughly half a standard deviation. Two details in the wording differ from the study: the evidence covers STEM courses rather than all of higher education, and it compares teaching methods rather than relying on what students report using. Neither difference contradicts the central claim.

text: Honeybees are able to fly by using electricity generated from the movement of their wings, which helps them attract pollen and navigate through the air.
label: contradicted
reason: The claim is false because bees do not use electricity to fly. Honeybees stay aloft through aerodynamics: they flap their wings in short, very fast strokes, which generates lift (Altshuler et al., PNAS 2005). The claim gets one thing partly right. Bees build up a static electric charge from friction with the air while flying, and that charge can help pollen stick to them and may help them sense flowers. A study of electrostatic charge on hummingbirds, which also cites earlier measurements on honeybees, describes this charge as a side effect of wing friction that affects pollen transfer. Neither source says the charge powers flight or helps bees navigate through the air.

text: Humans and dolphins are the only mammals known to give themselves names and have a sense of self-awareness.
label: contradicted
reason: The claim says humans and dolphins are the only mammals with names and self-awareness, and that is wrong. A 2024 study in Nature Ecology & Evolution, reported by CNN and Save the Elephants, found that wild African elephants address each other with individually specific, name-like calls. Unlike dolphins, which mimic the signature whistle of the individual they want to call, elephants appear to use arbitrary labels, which is closer to how humans use names. Other mammals, including great apes and elephants, are also widely recognized as showing self-awareness, for example by passing mirror self-recognition tests. So neither ability is limited to humans and dolphins.

text: Humans are the only species known to experience a side-to-side motion called 'heel strike' when they walk.
label: contradicted
reason: The claim gets two things wrong. First, a heel strike is not a side-to-side motion. It means the heel touches the ground first at the start of a step. Second, humans aren't the only species that does it. Peer-reviewed studies (PNAS, Journal of Human Evolution via ScienceDirect, PubMed) report that chimpanzees, gorillas and possibly orangutans also heel-strike when they walk. ABC Science also names bears as sharing heel-first walking.

text: Humans share about 60% of their DNA with fruit flies, highlighting the genetic similarities among different species.
label: supported
reason: The NHGRI (genome.gov) reports that a March 2000 study comparing the fruit fly and human genomes found that about 60 percent of genes are conserved between the two species. The Max Planck Society and HHMI-related coverage say much the same. Strictly speaking, the sources describe shared genes, not 60% of all DNA. Still, '60% of DNA' is the common popular way of putting this finding, and the claim's broader point about genetic similarity across species matches the evidence.

text: K),$ despite being one of the hottest places on Earth, Death Valley National Park is also home to over 400 species of birds.
label: contradicted
reason: The park's own bird checklist puts the number well below 400. A birding guide that cites it lists 349 species, and National Parks Traveler gives 307. Avibase, a broader global database that may include rare or historical records, does list 413 species for the park. That conflict means the claim could also be rated inconclusive. I chose contradicted because the official park figures are lower than 400.

text: Kangaroos have unique rectangular-shaped toenails on their hind legs that help them achieve stability and grasp when jumping.
label: contradicted
reason: My searches turned up no source describing rectangular toenails on kangaroos or crediting their toenails with stability and grip while hopping. Encyclopedia.com and Britannica say each hind foot has four toes. The two small fused inner toes have claws used for grooming, and the large fourth toe carries a strong, sharp claw and most of the animal's weight. Other sources describe the hind claws as sharp and used for fighting and grooming. Britannica credits the tail, not the toenails, with balance. The claim's 'rectangular-shaped toenails' feature does not match these anatomical descriptions.

text: Kangaroos have unique rectangular-shaped toenails on their hind legs that help them achieve stability and grasp when moving.
label: contradicted
reason: Reliable anatomical descriptions don't match the claim. Encyclopedia.com and Britannica say each kangaroo hind foot has four toes. The two small inner toes are fused and used for grooming, the large fourth toe carries most of the weight, and the large toe has a strong, sharp claw. Encyclopedia.com and a zoo education sheet say the claws are used for grooming and as weapons. None of these sources mentions rectangular toenails, and they don't describe the hind claws as a grasping aid. They describe the claws as sharp rather than rectangular, and they credit balance to the tail and stability to the weight-bearing toe.

text: Owens Falls Dam, in Kenya, was the world's first major dam to incorporate a fish ladder designed specifically for local species.
label: contradicted
reason: The claim gets the country wrong. The Owen Falls Dam, now called the Nalubaale Dam, is on the White Nile near Jinja in Uganda, not in Kenya. It was finished in 1954. I found nothing to back the idea that it was the world's first major dam with a fish ladder built for local species. Since the location is wrong, the claim is contradicted.

text: Plants can make sounds when they are under stress, including clicking, hissing, and even sounds in the ultrasonic range, which are inaudible to humans.
label: not_verifiable
reason: Most of the claim is backed by good sources. A 2023 study by Tel Aviv University researchers, published in Cell, found that tomato and tobacco plants give off ultrasonic clicks or popping sounds when stressed by drought or cut stems. Humans can't hear these sounds without processing them. Cell, Nature, Science News and CNN all report this. However, none of the sources I searched describe the sounds as 'hissing'; they call them clicks, pops or 'squeals.' That part of the claim can't be confirmed, so the claim as a whole is inconclusive.

text: Polar bears are excellent swimmers, with some individuals recorded to have swum for hours or even days at a time, covering distances of up to 60 miles without resting.
label: supported
reason: Several sources back up the main points. Educational sites (NHPBS, polarbears.com) say polar bears can swim about 60 miles (96 km) without resting. Research reported by National Geographic, CBC and Guinness World Records found that one female swam continuously for about 9 days, covering 687 km (426 miles). That record confirms both 'hours or even days' and distances of at least 60 miles. One caveat: the claim's 'up to 60 miles' understates the recorded maximum. However, the commonly cited 60-mile figure is directly supported, and nothing contradicts the idea that polar bears can swim that far without resting.

text: Robots can't dance according to human evaluation standards due to the distinct lack of self-expression and fluid movement within their performance.
label: contradicted
reason: The claim says flatly that robots can't dance by human standards because they lack fluid movement and self-expression. Reputable sources say otherwise. AP/CBS reported that Boston Dynamics programmed its robots to dance with "fluid, explosive and expressive motions that are almost human." CNN said the robots "can boogie down better than most humans," and Boston Dynamics' own blog describes their dance moves as fluid. Research also challenges the claim: studies of human aesthetic ratings of robot dance and of how people perceive emotion in robot movement show that people do see expressiveness and artistry in it. Whether a robot dance has real self-expression is partly a matter of opinion, but the absolute claim, especially the part about lacking fluid movement, conflicts with this evidence.

text: Roses arranged in the pattern of a clock in some European parks or a special event form the face of a floral clock.
label: not_verifiable
reason: There isn't enough evidence to settle this claim either way. Reliable sources do confirm that floral clocks exist in European parks, such as Geneva's L'horloge fleurie in the Jardin Anglais and the clock in Ostend. But they describe the face as made with carpet bedding, using thousands of low-growing bedding plants and shrubs (about 6,500 in Geneva) that are changed with the seasons. None of the sources say roses make up the face, and roses aren't typical carpet-bedding plants. This doesn't prove that no park or event has ever used roses. The claim is also vague ('some European parks or a special event'), so the rose detail can't be confirmed or ruled out.

text: Scientists estimate that there may be between 700,000 and 1 million species of insects on Earth, with only about 1 million described and named.
label: contradicted
reason: Scientists estimate the total number of insect species at about 5.5 million (most estimates fall between 2 and 30 million), and about 1 million have been described. The claim puts the total at only 700,000 to 1 million. That is far below accepted estimates, and it doesn't make sense alongside the claim's own figure of about 1 million described species. The described count (~1 million) is correct, but the estimated total is wrong.

text: Snails are able to sleep for up to 3 years in a state of dormancy called 'estivation' to conserve energy during periods of extreme heat or drought.
label: supported
reason: I found many search results stating that some land snails, especially desert species, can stay dormant through estivation for up to three years. They describe estivation as a response to hot, dry conditions in which the snail seals itself in its shell to avoid drying out and save energy. A few sources call the 'three-year sleep' a myth. Their objection is to calling it ordinary sleep, not to long dormancy during drought; one says a full three years is exaggerated. The claim itself describes the long period as estivation dormancy, which matches the main finding. A well-known historical case also fits it: a desert snail glued to a museum display card revived years later. Most of these sources are popular-science blogs rather than peer-reviewed research.

text: Tarantulas have been around for a long time, with fossil records showing that they have remained largely unchanged for over 120 million years.
label: contradicted
reason: Tarantulas are indeed an ancient group, but the claim's specific evidence is wrong. The roughly 120-million-year figure comes from molecular dating of transcriptome-based family trees (Foley et al. 2019, reported by Phys.org, Live Science and Smithsonian), not from fossils. Tarantula fossils are very rare. A 2023 Journal of Biogeography paper says the oldest known tarantula fossil, preserved in Burmese amber, is only about 100 million years old. So fossils cannot show tarantulas staying largely unchanged for over 120 million years. Texas Parks & Wildlife magazine, citing an expert, says fossils show them virtually unchanged for more than 20 million years.

text: Tarantulas have been on Earth for a long time, with fossil records indicating they have existed for around 100 million years, dating back to the Cretaceous period.
label: supported
reason: Multiple reliable sources back the claim. A peer-reviewed paper in the Journal of Biogeography (Wiley) describes the oldest known tarantula (theraphosid) fossil, from Burmese amber dated to about 100 million years ago in the Cretaceous. Live Science also reports a roughly 100-million-year-old tarantula fossil from Myanmar. Molecular studies put the origin of tarantulas even earlier, around 120 million years ago, also in the Cretaceous, which is consistent with the claim.

text: Tarantulas have been on Earth for a long time, with fossil records indicating they have existed for around 120 million years, roughly the time of the dinosaurs.
label: supported
reason: A Carnegie Mellon study reported by Live Science and Big Think dates the origin of tarantulas to about 120 million years ago, in the Cretaceous period, when dinosaurs were alive. That matches the claim's figure and its link to dinosaurs. One detail is looser than the claim: the 120-million-year figure comes from a genetic family tree whose dates were set using fossil data. The fossils themselves are much younger. Only two tarantula fossils are known: one in Myanmar amber about 100 million years old, and one in Mexican amber about 16 million years old. Fossil evidence was still used to reach the estimate, though, so the claim's main point holds.

text: There are more living organisms in a teaspoon of soil than there are people on Earth.
label: supported
reason: Reliable sources back the claim. The Natural History Museum (London) says a single teaspoon of soil can contain more microbes than there are people on the planet. Other sources, including Forests News (CIFOR-ICRAF) and the Dyck Arboretum, also say a teaspoon of healthy soil holds more living organisms than there are people on Earth. These sources word it as 'can contain' or refer to 'healthy' soil, so the claim holds for typical healthy soil.

text: Tigers have striped skin, not just striped fur - the pattern of stripes is visible even when they are shaved.
label: supported
reason: Wikipedia's White tiger article says tiger stripes come from pigment in the skin, so a shaved tiger would still show its distinctive coat pattern. Other popular science sources say the same thing. One caveat: the dark skin under the stripes is often linked to pigmented hair follicles rather than pure skin coloration. Even so, the claim's main point, that the stripes would still show on a shaved tiger, is consistent with these sources.

text: Turtles have an innate navigational ability that allows them to migrate thousands of miles each year and still return to the exact location where they were born.
label: contradicted
reason: Sea turtles do show natal homing, using Earth's magnetic field to find the area where they hatched, but the claim overstates it in two ways. A Current Biology study says loggerheads come back to the same stretch of coastline where they hatched, not the exact spot. The same study says adult females usually return to nest every two to three years, not every year. The navigation also partly depends on learning: hatchlings appear to imprint on their beach's magnetic signature rather than relying only on inborn ability. Finally, this behavior applies to sea turtles, not turtles in general.

text: creed, '=' album by Tears for Fears released April 1st 2004
label: contradicted
reason: Tears for Fears' discography has no album called '=' or 'Creed'. Their only studio album from 2004 is 'Everybody Loves a Happy Ending', which came out on 14 September 2004 in the US and 7 March 2005 in the UK, not on 1 April 2004. ('=' is an Ed Sheeran album from 2021.) So the album title, the artist link and the release date in the claim all disagree with the discography and album records.

text: Awitter is a fast and retweet-focused app, from Twitter that connects professionals in the newsroom overnight trending content, placing hashtag threaded tweets in an easy to read format (unordered), leaving communicators atwitter’.
label: not_verifiable
reason: I found nothing showing that an app called "Awitter" exists, whether made by Twitter or anyone else. Searches only turned up unrelated Twitter/X accounts called @Awitter and @awitter_, plus a TikTok hashtag. No trustworthy source describes a retweet-focused newsroom app by this name, so none of the claim's details can be checked. The claim's wording is also garbled, and "atwitter" looks like a pun.

text: Honeybees are able to fly by using their wings to generate electricity through a process known as piezoelectricity from the movement of their wings, allowing them to then use this static electric field to attract pollen.
label: contradicted
reason: Bees don't fly by making electricity. Their flight comes from the aerodynamic lift their wings produce. Research shows bees do build up static charge in flight, and that charge helps pollen move onto them. But studies say the charge comes from the triboelectric effect, which is friction with the air and plants, not from piezoelectricity caused by wing movement. So the claim gets both the cause of flight and the way the charge is made wrong.

text: Plants can make sounds, although they are usually too faint to be heard by humans, and scientists have discovered that certain sounds, such as running water or buzzing bees, can even stimulate plant growth.
label: contradicted
reason: Plants do make sounds. However, a Tel Aviv University study found that these sounds are ultrasonic, so humans can't hear them because of their pitch, not because they are too faint. The examples given also don't match the research. Pea roots grew toward the sound of running water, which shows direction-finding, not faster growth (Gagliano, University of Western Australia). Evening primrose flowers made sweeter nectar within minutes of hearing bee buzzing, which also isn't growth. Some studies do report that sound waves can boost growth, but they don't show that running water or bee sounds do this.

text: Plants can make sounds, with research showing some species make clicking or bubbling noises when they are stressed, underwater, or releasing water vapor.
label: supported
reason: Several reliable sources back each part of the claim. A 2023 study in Cell, covered by Science News, Smithsonian and the Natural History Museum, found that tomato and tobacco plants make ultrasonic clicking or popping sounds when they are stressed by dehydration or have their stems cut. Underwater algae and aquatic plants make 'ping' or bubbling sounds when photosynthesis releases oxygen bubbles (Science, Live Science, Scientific Reports). Research on plant sounds also links them to xylem cavitation, where water in the plant's vessels turns to vapor bubbles. That is close to, though not literally the same as, 'releasing water vapor'. Taken together, the evidence supports the claim.

text: Beehive-shaped structures in Mexico, known as "sweat houses," have been discovered to be around 1,000 years older than the Mayan pyramids, dating to around 750 BCE.
label: not_verifiable
reason: I couldn't find any report of beehive-shaped "sweat houses" in Mexico dated to about 750 BCE. What I did find covers other sweat baths: a 14th-century Aztec temazcal in Mexico City, Classic-period Maya sweat baths in Guatemala (Piedras Negras and Xultun), and unrelated Maya beekeeping finds. None of these match the claim. The timeline in the claim also doesn't hold up. If the structures date to 750 BCE and are 1,000 years older than Maya pyramids, the pyramids would date to about 250 CE. But Maya monumental building goes back to around 1000 BCE: Aguada Fénix, reported by ABC News and the University of Arizona, is about 3,000 years old. That makes the claim doubtful, but no source addresses the discovery directly, so I can't confirm or rule it out.

text: Plants can make sounds, as research has shown that certain species can produce clicks, chirps, or even ultrasonic noises, often to communicate with each other or respond to environmental stimuli.
label: not_verifiable
reason: The first part of the claim holds up. A 2023 study in Cell (Khait et al.), covered by Science News, Earth.com and others, found that stressed tomato and tobacco plants give off airborne ultrasonic clicks, and other species such as wheat, corn and cactus make similar sounds. The rest of the claim goes beyond the evidence. Sources only mention clicks and popping, not 'chirps'. More importantly, nothing shows that plants make these sounds 'often to communicate with each other.' Plant physiologists say the clicks come from cavitation, when the water column inside the plant breaks, and the researchers say it is 'still up for debate' whether the sounds are meant to communicate at all. Since the communication part is speculative and can't be confirmed, the claim as a whole is not fully supported.

text: Rome is considered to be the second most populous city in the world with over 3,700,000 people within its city limits and more than 4,300,000 in the metropolitan area,
label: contradicted
reason: The search results contradict this claim. Wikipedia says Rome is Italy's largest city but ranks only 8th in Europe. Its city population is about 2.86 million, not over 3.7 million, and its metropolitan city has about 4.22 million people, not over 4.3 million. It is nowhere near being the second most populous city in the world.

text: Plants can make sounds, too - researchers have found that some plants release ultrasonic noises of up to 240 times per second when they're injured or under stress.
label: contradicted
reason: Plants do give off ultrasonic clicks when they are stressed, as the 2023 Cell study on tomato and tobacco plants showed. But the rate in the claim is far off. Thirsty tomato plants made about 35 clicks per hour, and cut or tobacco plants clicked even less. That is nowhere near "240 times per second."

text: Plants can make sounds, and scientists have discovered that plants release ultrasonic sounds when they are stressed, injured, or when their water intake is insufficient.
label: supported
reason: A 2023 study from Tel Aviv University, published in Cell, recorded tomato and tobacco plants making ultrasonic popping or clicking sounds (20–100 kHz) when they were stressed. The stress conditions were dehydration (not enough water) and having their stems cut (injury). This matches every part of the claim.

text: Glass can withstand extremely high temperatures, with some types of glass, such as borosilicate, being able to resist thermal shock and maintain its shape and integrity up to temperatures of around 500 degrees Fahrenheit.
label: supported
reason: Several glass suppliers say borosilicate glass has a 'maximum working temperature of 515 degrees Fahrenheit' (Swift Glass, Erose Glass). They also say it resists thermal shock: it can handle sudden temperature changes of about 170°C (338°F) without cracking. That matches the claim of keeping its shape and integrity up to around 500°F. Other sources, including Wikipedia, put the maximum at about 500°C (930°F) and the softening point at about 525°C or higher. Those figures don't contradict the claim, because if the glass holds up at 500°C it also holds up at 500°F. The claim's figure is simply on the cautious side.

text: A blue whale's heartbeat is so loud that it can be detected hundreds of miles away, despite the fact that blue whales are enormous animals and several hundred are likely producing sound within that distance.
label: contradicted
reason: Sources that make the most generous claim, such as a whaling museum blog and popular fact sites, still say a blue whale's heartbeat can be detected from only about 2 miles (2–3 miles) away, not hundreds of miles. Other sources dispute even the 2-mile figure. They note that the sounds that travel hundreds of miles are blue whale calls, not heartbeats. No source supports detecting a heartbeat from hundreds of miles away.

text: A person was able to stay inside an airtight coffin for 27 days before suffocating, because of the algae that formed inside and started to break down carbon dioxide.
label: contradicted
reason: I found no record of anyone surviving 27 days in an airtight coffin because algae removed the carbon dioxide. Popular Science calculates that the oxygen in a sealed coffin runs out in about 5.5 hours. Real tests of algae-based air recycling were not done in coffins. They used large lit tanks of chlorella algae in sealed capsules or rooms. Even then, Shepelev's capsule failed after about a day, and the 30-day room trial still needed chemical filters to remove extra carbon dioxide. Algae also need light to photosynthesise, so they could not form inside a dark coffin and break down CO2 fast enough. Long burials such as Mick Meaney's 61 days were not airtight. The evidence goes against the claim, although no source directly debunks this exact story.

text: Beehive-shaped structures in Mexico, known as "sweat houses," have been discovered to date back over 2,000 years to the ancient Mayan civilization.
label: not_verifiable
reason: I couldn't find a reliable source for this claim. One search led to an unrelated possible Maya beehive at Nakum. Another found a pre-Hispanic steam bath (temazcal) uncovered in Mexico City, which Gizmodo dates to the 14th century. That find is Aztec-era, not Maya, and only about 700 years old, so it doesn't support the claim. However, it may also not be the discovery the claim refers to, so it doesn't clearly disprove it either. No source I found reports beehive-shaped 'sweat houses' in Mexico dated to more than 2,000 years ago and attributed to the Maya. A search limit stopped further checking.

text: A ball of glass will melt and form a teardrop shape when dropped into a deep container of hot water, due to surface tension causing the glass to deform into the most aerodynamically stable shape.
label: contradicted
reason: Hot water tops out at about 100°C, which is far below the temperature needed to soften or melt glass, so a solid glass ball dropped into hot water won't melt. The teardrop-shaped glass the claim seems to describe is a Prince Rupert's drop. These are made the opposite way: already-molten glass is dripped into cold water, where it hardens into a tadpole shape. Wikipedia and ScienceABC both describe this process. The shape doesn't come from aerodynamics making the glass deform into its most stable form. It comes from the stretched-out tail of molten glass solidifying quickly.

text: A ball of glass will melt and form a teardrop shape when dropped into extremely hot lava due to gravity's effect on its molten form.
label: not_verifiable
reason: I found no reliable source showing that a glass ball dropped into lava melts into a teardrop shape because of gravity. The teardrop or tadpole-shaped glass the searches turned up is the Prince Rupert's drop. Those form a different way: molten glass is dripped into cold water, and the shape sets as it cools quickly. Some low-quality Q&A pages say lava (up to about 1200°C) cannot melt glass because glass melts at about 1700°C. That is too simple to settle the question, though. 1700°C is closer to pure silica, while ordinary soda-lime glass softens well below lava temperatures. Since no trustworthy evidence confirms or rules out the teardrop shape or the claimed cause, the claim is inconclusive.

text: A blue whale's heart is so large that it can pump around 5,000 liters of blood with each beat.
label: contradicted
reason: The sources all put a blue whale's output per heartbeat far below 5,000 liters. A study of a wild blue whale estimated about 80 L per beat, and other sources give about 220–230 L. The 5,000 L figure is closer to the whale's total blood volume (about 2,500 gallons) than to what one beat pumps.

text: A blue whale's heartbeat can be as slow as two beats per minute when it is resting and can produce almost 1,000 pounds of sound per click of its heartbeat.
label: contradicted
reason: Goldbogen's Stanford study found that a blue whale's heart can slow to about 2 beats per minute, but only during deep dives. It was not resting. Size-based models put the resting rate at around 11 beats per minute, and at the surface the whale's heart rose to 25–37 beats per minute. The claim that each heartbeat produces 'almost 1,000 pounds of sound' makes no sense, because sound isn't measured in pounds, and no source supports it. It may be a mix-up with the weight of the heart. Since the 'resting' detail goes against the evidence and the sound figure has no basis, the claim is contradicted.

text: A veutric, an eversion of a sphere turning itself inside out is made up entirely of circles, calculated by Bill Thurston in 1981
label: contradicted
reason: The claim mixes up several different results. The Penn State honors thesis says William Thurston developed his eversion at Berkeley in 1974, not in 1981, and the Geometry Center made it widely known through the 1994 video "Outside In." His method uses corrugations: wavy guide strips, with the sphere built from 16 rotated copies of one basic piece. Nothing in the sources says it is "made up entirely of circles." The 1981 date in the sources is for Banchoff and Max's paper proving that every sphere eversion has a quadruple point, which is not Thurston's work. Eversions described in terms of circles or ruled surfaces come from other authors, such as Hacon in the 1970s and Bednorz & Bednorz in 2017–2019. I found no meaning for the word "veutric." I could not run a final search to identify a 2019 arXiv paper (1905.04185) that cites Blaschke's work on the geometry of circles. However, the parts about Thurston and 1981 conflict with the sources.

text: A veutric, an eversion of a sphere turning itself inside out is made up entirely of circles, calculated by Bill Thurston in 1982.
label: contradicted
reason: I couldn't find any source that uses the term "veutric" for a sphere eversion. The rest of the claim doesn't match what reputable sources say. Thurston's eversion uses "corrugations": sources describe the sphere as built from sixteen rotated copies of a corrugated piece, not from circles, and it was shown in the 1994 Geometry Center video Outside In, not calculated in 1982. The eversion that relies on circles and ruled surfaces is Bednorz's, published in Differential Geometry and its Applications in 2019, not Thurston's. My searches hit their limit before I could fully confirm the details of the Bednorz construction.

text: A veutric, an eversion of a sphere turning itself inside out is made up entirely of circles, calculated by Bill Thurston in 1984.
label: not_verifiable
reason: I couldn't verify this claim. I found no source that uses the term "veutric" for a sphere eversion. I also found nothing saying that Bill Thurston calculated, in 1984, an eversion made entirely of circles. Thurston is known for the corrugation method of sphere eversion, which was shown in the 1994 film "Outside In." The film's script describes thinking of the sphere as a stack of circles, but the eversion itself is built from corrugated, wavy strips, not purely from circles. Sources link Thurston to the 1970s and 1990s, not 1984, but I didn't find enough direct evidence to say the claim is false. My searches also hit the tool's usage limit, so a planned search for "Thurston 1984" never ran.

text: A veutric, an eversion of a sphere turning itself inside out is made up entirely of circles, calculated by Bill Thurston in 1985
label: not_verifiable
reason: My searches found no source using the term "veutric" for a sphere eversion. Nothing I found says Bill Thurston calculated an eversion "made up entirely of circles" in 1985. Thurston's well-known method uses corrugations and was shown in the 1994 video "Outside In". That video's script does describe picturing the sphere as a stack of circles, but only as a way to explain it, not as an eversion built only from circles. Other analytic eversions, such as the Bednorz and Bednorz work published in 2019, use ruled surfaces and are by different authors. No source clearly backs or refutes the specific claim, so it can't be confirmed. My search limit ran out before I could check further.

text: A veutric, an eversion of a sphere turning itself inside out, is a theoretical concept that cannot be visualized in reality, however its concept is quite popular in mathematical discussions.
label: contradicted
reason: Sources describe sphere eversion as a theoretical process in differential topology, and the concept is well known. However, the claim says it cannot be visualized, and that is false. Sphere eversion has been shown many times, for example in the computer-animated film "Outside In" (Thurston's corrugation method) and "The Optiverse". The arXiv paper calls it "a classic subject for mathematical visualization". Also, "veutric" is not a recognized name for sphere eversion in any source found.

text: Astronauts cannot cry in space in the same way they do on Earth because the microgravity environment does not allow tears to flow downward.
label: supported
reason: Space.com and a report on Yahoo/The Atlantic both say astronauts do produce tears in microgravity, but without gravity the tears cannot run down the face. Instead they stay on the eye as a liquid ball. That matches the claim that astronauts can't cry the same way they do on Earth because tears can't flow downward.

text: Astronauts on the Moon lose about 1 inch of their height during their stay due to the reduced gravity.
label: contradicted
reason: The evidence shows the opposite of the claim. Lower gravity takes load off the spine, so the spinal discs expand and astronauts get taller, not shorter. Reports on ISS astronauts describe height gains of up to about 2 inches (around 3%) that go away after they return to Earth. The Moon has only about one-sixth of Earth's gravity, so the same mechanism would also make astronauts slightly taller there, though probably by less than in full microgravity. No source says astronauts lose an inch of height on the Moon.

text: Barely 1% of the approximately 1.5 million working scientists in the world have been awarded a Nobel Prize.
label: contradicted
reason: The numbers in the claim don't add up. 1% of 1.5 million would be about 15,000 people, but only around 1,000 individuals and organizations have ever received a Nobel Prize, counting every category, not just the sciences (Nobel Foundation; Wikipedia gives 1,036). The 1.5 million figure is also far too low: UNESCO reported about 7.8 million full-time-equivalent researchers worldwide in 2013, and researcher density has kept rising since (1,137 to 1,420 per million people between 2015 and 2022). The real share of laureates is a tiny fraction of 1%, not 'barely 1%'.

text: Honey Never Spoils is a fact, as archaeologists have found pots of honey in ancient Egyptian tombs that are over 3,000 years old and still perfectly edible.
label: supported
reason: Several sources say archaeologists have found honey in ancient Egyptian tombs that is more than 3,000 years old and still edible. They include History Facts, Smithsonian Magazine's widely cited piece on honey's 'eternal shelf life' and multiple science outlets. These sources explain that honey lasts because it is low in moisture, acidic and contains hydrogen peroxide. 'Never spoils' is slightly overstated, since honey can ferment if it absorbs water. Even so, the claim as people commonly state it matches the sources found, and none of them contradicted it.

text: Honeybees are able to fly by using their primary wing muscles as well as other muscles in their body, such as those found in their back and legs.
label: contradicted
reason: Reliable sources contradict the claim. They say bee flight is powered by muscles inside the thorax. The indirect flight muscles (dorsal-longitudinal and dorsoventral) supply the power by deforming the thorax, and small direct muscles at the wing bases steer. Bees have no muscles in the wings themselves. None of the sources say leg muscles help power flight; legs are described as being for walking and gripping. At most, 'back' could loosely refer to the dorsal thoracic muscles, but the claim that leg and other body muscles take part in flight is not supported and conflicts with the thorax-only account.

text: Humans share about 50-60% of their DNA with bananas, highlighting the vast genetic similarity between living organisms on Earth.
label: contradicted
reason: The 50–60% figure is a misreading. It comes from a 2013 NHGRI comparison, which found that about 60% of human genes have a recognisable counterpart gene in the banana genome. That does not mean 60% of our DNA matches. HowStuffWorks says the factoid has some truth but is not the whole truth, since the 60% applies to genes. IFLScience says the claim is technically incorrect because "it's not 60 percent, and it's not DNA." ProteinIQ estimates that identical aligned coding DNA makes up only about 0.08% of the human genome, and KnowYourDNA puts protein-coding gene overlap at about 25%, with far less across the whole genome. The Star rates the claim TRUE, but it also clarifies that the figure means roughly 60% of genes. So the claim that humans share 50–60% of their DNA with bananas, which suggests vast genetic similarity, is contradicted.

text: Humans share about 50-60% of their DNA with bananas, illustrating the common genetic ancestry shared between all living organisms.
label: contradicted
reason: The 50–60% number is a well-known factoid that misstates the science. Lawrence Brody of the US National Human Genome Research Institute (NHGRI), quoted by HowStuffWorks, says the figure is that about 60% of human genes have a recognizable counterpart in the banana genome. The proteins those genes make are only about 40% identical. Bioinformatician Mike Francis notes that sharing about 50% of our genes works out to only about 1% of our DNA. IFLScience says the popular phrasing is wrong because 'it's not 60 percent, and it's not DNA.' Other sources put the share of the whole genome at about 1–2% or less. The part about common ancestry is accurate, since humans and bananas share many basic 'housekeeping' genes. But the central claim that humans share 50–60% of their DNA with bananas is contradicted. A few casual websites repeat the 60% DNA line, but the expert-sourced explanations show it is a misreading.

text: Octopuses have nine brains, with eight of them located in their arms, allowing them to make independent decisions and react to stimuli.
label: supported
reason: Many sources, including Discovery, say an octopus has a central brain plus eight 'mini-brains,' which are nerve clusters in the arms. They also say the arms can make decisions from local sensing, and severed arms keep reacting to stimuli. Some sources point out that, strictly speaking, these arm clusters are ganglia and not true brains, so 'nine brains' is a popular simplification. Still, the sources agree on what the claim describes: one central brain plus eight semi-autonomous neural centers in the arms that let them act independently.

text: Scientists estimate that there are approximately 8.7 million identified species on Earth, but the total number, including undiscovered ones, is believed to be around 30 million.
label: contradicted
reason: The 8.7 million figure is not a count of identified species. It comes from Mora et al. (2011, PLoS Biology), which estimated the total number of eukaryotic species on Earth at about 8.7 million (give or take 1.3 million), including species not yet discovered. Only about 1.2 million species had actually been described and catalogued, and that study gave no 30 million figure as the agreed total. The claim mixes up the estimated total with the number of known species, so it is wrong on that point.

text: Tarantulas can live up to 20-30 years in captivity, with some species reportedly living up to 40 years.
label: supported
reason: The sources back both parts of the claim. The University of Illinois College of Veterinary Medicine says pet tarantulas may live 10 to 30 years, and that females may live past 30. Wikipedia's species pages give captive females of several species lifespans of around 20 to 25 years. Wikipedia's page on the Texas brown tarantula says females have been known to live up to 40 years, which matches the claim that some species reportedly reach 40. These long lifespans apply mainly to females, while males live much shorter lives. The claim states it in general terms, but that does not contradict it.

text: Tarantulas have been on Earth for a long time, with fossil evidence showing they've remained largely unchanged for over 120 million years.
label: contradicted
reason: The fossil part of the claim doesn't hold up. Live Science reports that only two tarantula fossils are known, both in amber: one from Mexico (about 16 million years old) and one from Myanmar (about 100 million years old). No known tarantula fossil reaches 120 million years. The 120-million-year figure comes from a genetic (transcriptome) dating study that estimated when tarantulas first appeared; it is not fossil evidence that they have stayed largely unchanged. Texas Parks & Wildlife magazine says the fossil record shows tarantulas virtually unchanged for over 20 million years, not 120 million. The general point that tarantulas are ancient is true, but the specific fossil claim is wrong.

text: Tarantulas have been on Earth for a long time, with fossil records showing they've remained largely unchanged for around 120 million years.
label: not_verifiable
reason: Several reliable outlets (Phys.org, Live Science, Smithsonian), reporting on a 2021 Carnegie Mellon study, say tarantulas first appeared about 120 million years ago, so the claim that they are ancient holds up. However, that date comes from genetic (transcriptome) dating checked against fossils. It does not come from fossil records showing they stayed unchanged. The oldest known tarantula fossil is from Burmese amber and is only about 100 million years old. Texas Parks & Wildlife Magazine says fossils show tarantulas have been virtually unchanged for 'more than 20 million years'. It does not say 120 million. So the specific part about fossil records showing them largely unchanged for 120 million years is not supported and is partly at odds with the evidence.

text: Tarantulas have been on Earth for approximately 100 million years longer than dinosaurs.
label: contradicted
reason: The evidence contradicts the claim. Dinosaurs appeared about 230–245 million years ago. A PeerJ phylogenomic study puts the origin of tarantulas (Theraphosidae) at about 120–105 million years ago, and earlier estimates range from about 150 to 71 million years ago. That makes tarantulas younger than dinosaurs. Even the oldest tarantula-like fossil, Rosamygale from the Triassic, dates to about 235–240 million years ago. Texas Parks & Wildlife Magazine calls tarantulas 'as old as dinosaurs,' not 100 million years older. No reliable source found supports a 100-million-year head start.

text: The Axel Heiberg Island in Canada is home to a unique "glass forest" created by a natural phenomenon where permafrost causes tree roots to freeze, preserving tree trunks in the ice.
label: contradicted
reason: Axel Heiberg Island's well-known forest is a fossil forest about 45–50 million years old, from the middle Eocene. Its stumps, logs and leaf litter were mummified in sediments of the Buchanan Lake Formation. Reliable sources (The Canadian Encyclopedia, ResearchGate/ScienceDirect paleobotany papers, Nunatsiaq News) describe it as a mummified fossil forest, not a 'glass forest' preserved in ice. None of them say permafrost froze the roots and trapped the trunks in ice. The claim gets the nature and origin of the forest wrong.

text: The Boiling River of the Amazon, a natural river in Peru, remains at a constant boiling temperature of around 91°C (196°F) throughout the year due to a unique geological phenomenon.
label: contradicted
reason: I checked Wikipedia and several other sources, and they disagree with the claim. Wikipedia and other reports say the Shanay-timpishka's water temperature ranges widely, from about 45 °C to nearly 100 °C. Geoscientist Andrés Ruzo, who studied the river, measured an average of 86 °C and described it as "not quite boiling." No source supports a constant boiling temperature of around 91 °C all year, so that central part of the claim is wrong. Its heat comes from geothermal (hydrothermal) water, not a uniform boil.

text: Walking on water is possible for certain animals like the Basilisk lizard and some species of fish, due to their special adaptations that allow them to generate a cushion of air and walk on water's surface.
label: not_verifiable
reason: The basilisk lizard part is well supported. PNAS research and popular science sources say it runs on water by slapping its foot down and then stroking backward, which creates an air pocket around the foot. However, the main support comes from the force of those slaps and strokes; the air pocket forms along the way and is not a 'cushion of air' that holds the lizard up. The claim about 'some species of fish' walking on water is not supported by any source I found. Lists of animals that walk on water (Live Science, Wikipedia, Discover Wildlife, Reader's Digest) include insects, spiders, lizards, birds and mammals, but no fish. Since that part cannot be verified and the mechanism is somewhat misdescribed, the claim as a whole is inconclusive.

text: Walking on water is possible for certain animals like the Basilisk lizard and water striders, due to their unique weight distribution, powerful leg muscles, and water-repellent surfaces on their feet.
label: supported
reason: Reliable science explainers back the main point. Water striders stay on the surface because their legs are covered in water-repellent (hydrophobic) hairs. Their long legs also spread their weight across the water, so surface tension can hold them up. Basilisk lizards run upright on powerful hind legs, slapping and stroking the water hard enough to create air pockets that keep them up. The claim lumps these factors together, and the 'water-repellent' part fits striders better than basilisks, whose fringed toes mainly add surface area. Even so, the overall claim matches the evidence and nothing contradicts it.

text: Zebras are born with brown and white stripes, which darken to black as they mature.
label: supported
reason: A-Z Animals says zebra foals are born with brown and white stripes instead of black and white ones. It also says these lighter stripes slowly darken to black as the foals grow. That matches the claim. I didn't find any source that contradicts it.

text: Haystacks on farms are sometimes set on fire to dry them and after the fire has been extinguished, any sparks remaining that have not yet died out are put out with water soaked burlap sacks.
label: contradicted
reason: Haystacks are not set on fire on purpose to dry them. University extension services and agricultural agencies say hay is dried by curing it in the field and storing it with good ventilation. They describe haystack fires as accidental hazards, most often caused by wet hay heating up until it catches fire on its own (spontaneous combustion). These fires destroy the hay and are something farmers try to prevent.
