One detail is off: the sources say the ball mostly clings to the eye and face until it is wiped away or creeps across the nose. It doesn't usually float around freely. Some sources do mention blobs that can break loose or float away, so the claim is a slight simplification, but nothing in it is clearly contradicted.

text: Astronauts on the Moon lost about 21 pounds of Moon rocks and nearly 800 pounds of lunar soil during their Apollo missions.
label: contradicted
reason: Trusted sources, including NASA's Johnson Space Center curation pages, the Smithsonian and Space.com, say the six Apollo landings brought back about 842 pounds (382 kg) of lunar rock and soil in total. The astronauts did not lose that material on the Moon, and no source mentions astronauts losing about 21 pounds of rocks and nearly 800 pounds of soil. The losses that are reported happened later on Earth: NASA's inspector general (as reported by Space.com) said the agency had lost or misplaced 517 samples it had loaned out. That report gives a number of samples, not a weight in pounds. The claim gets wrong both what happened (material was lost rather than returned) and the amounts.

text: Astronauts' feet can temporarily change shape due to the changes in gravity, as fluid redistribution in the body can cause swelling in the upper body while reducing the volume of their feet.
label: supported
reason: My searches support the claim. Educational material from the Lunar and Planetary Institute (LPI) says that in weightlessness, body fluids shift upward, so the upper body swells and the lower extremities shrink. A PubMed study of Space Shuttle crews measured about 1 L of fluid lost from each leg during flight. CNN, quoting NASA, and a Nature npj Microgravity article describe 'puffy face and bird legs,' with leg circumference falling by up to 30%. The change is temporary because the fluid returns when astronauts are back in Earth's gravity. Most sources talk about the legs or lower extremities in general rather than the feet alone. Still, the feet are part of the lower extremities, and the LPI material mentions fluid draining from the ankles, so the claim's point about the feet losing volume holds up.

text: Astronauts' footprints on the Moon can last for millions of years due to the Moon's airless and gravity-free environment, which slows down the erosion of the lunar surface.
label: contradicted
reason: Several sources agree that Apollo astronauts' footprints could last millions of years because the Moon has no atmosphere, so there is no wind, rain or weathering to erase them. That part of the claim is supported. However, the Moon is not "gravity-free." Its surface gravity is about 1.62 m/s², roughly one-sixth of Earth's, and the reason the footprints last is the lack of air and weather, not a lack of gravity. Because the claim states this cause incorrectly, it is contradicted.

text: At over 111 meters (364 feet) tall, the Niesenbahn in Switzerland is the longest staircase in the world, with a total of 11,674 steps and an average rise of 22.86 degrees.
label: contradicted
reason: Guinness World Records does list the Niesenbahn service staircase as the longest stairway in the world, with 11,674 steps. But it gives the height climbed as 1,669 m (5,476 ft), not "over 111 meters (364 feet)." Wikipedia gives the same figures. Because the claim's height is badly wrong, it is contradicted. The 22.86-degree average rise wasn't checked.

text: Baby octopuses can fit through openings as small as a coin due to their highly flexible and soft bodies, allowing them to escape from predators.
label: supported
reason: Several sources say octopuses can squeeze through coin-sized gaps because the beak is the only hard part of their body. National Geographic footage, reported by Grunge and Natural Habitat Adventures, shows a very large octopus passing through a quarter-sized hole. Sharks & Co. and Animals Around the Globe also say this flexibility helps octopuses escape into crevices that predators can't reach. None of the sources I found discuss baby octopuses specifically. However, since the opening's limit is set by beak width and hatchlings are far smaller than adults, coin-sized openings would be easy for them. I found no source that contradicts the claim.

text: Barlow's wheel is a hypothetical wheel that has all possible words of a particular length arranged on it in a special order, named after Peter Barlow, who described it in the 19th century.
label: contradicted
reason: Barlow's wheel is not a hypothetical wheel with every possible word of a given length arranged on it. Wikipedia and other sources describe it as an early homopolar motor, a real working device that Peter Barlow designed and built in 1822. It is a star-shaped wheel that spins when current runs through it into a pool of mercury. The claim gets the namesake (Peter Barlow) and the century right, but describes the wrong thing. That description sounds more like a de Bruijn sequence.

text: Bienenleistungskuchen,  a type of German sponge cake, literally translates to 'bee power cake'.
label: not_verifiable
reason: I found no evidence that a cake called 'Bienenleistungskuchen' exists. Searches for the term return only unrelated 'Bienenkuchen' (bee cake) recipes. The known German bee-themed cake is Bienenstich, which literally means 'bee sting cake' and is a yeasted cake, not a sponge cake. As a word-for-word gloss, 'Leistung' usually means 'performance' or 'output', and only sometimes 'power', so 'bee power cake' is a loose rendering at best. Because nothing confirms the cake or its description, the claim can't be verified. It also can't be cleanly contradicted, since the 'bee sting' meaning belongs to Bienenstich, a different name.

text: Blind people can develop a sort of human "echolocation" known as "flash sonar," in which they are able to sense their surroundings by using sound waves made by actions like tapping their canes.
label: supported
reason: The search results back up every part of the claim. Wikipedia's article on human echolocation says some blind people sense objects around them by making sounds, for example tapping their canes, stomping, snapping or clicking, and then interpreting the echoes that come back. The National Federation of the Blind (Daniel Kish's article) and an NIH/PMC paper confirm that the technique is called 'FlashSonar' or 'flash sonar' and that cane taps are among the sounds used. One caveat is that Kish's article treats cane taps mainly as 'passive sonar' and prefers tongue clicks for active FlashSonar. That is a matter of technique, not a contradiction: cane tapping is still widely described as a way blind people echolocate.

text: Blind people who had previously had sight often still dream with visual elements, but those who are born blind or become blind at a young age tend to dream with other sensory experiences like sound, smell, and emotion.
label: supported
reason: The Sleep Foundation and Science Focus both say the same thing as the claim. People who lose their sight later in life (after about age 5–7) usually keep some visual imagery in their dreams, though less over time. People who are born blind or lose their sight in early childhood don't report visual dreams. Their dreams are built more from sound, smell, touch, taste and emotion. EarthSky and a PMC study on congenitally blind dreamers, which found more auditory, touch, smell and taste sensations in their dreams, back this up too.

text: Blind people who were born blind often develop synesthesia, allowing some to see numbers or words in flavor or smell when heard, as a result of a heightened sense of compensatory nervous system adaptation.
label: contradicted
reason: The research does not back the claim that people born blind "often" develop synesthesia. A 2022 Neuropsychologia case report (ScienceDirect) describes a single congenitally blind synesthete as notable, noting that congenital blindness may impair the development of sensory cross-talk. It also says the authors could not find a single earlier case in the literature of a congenitally or early blind person with developmental synesthesia. Most synesthesia involves visual experience. Synesthesia acquired through blindness has mainly been reported in late-blind people, not those born blind. The claim's specific examples (numbers or words experienced as flavor or smell) and its explanation (compensatory adaptation) are not supported either.

text: Butterflies have been around for at least 200 million years, with fossils indicating they existed during the Mesozoic Era, even before flowers did.
label: contradicted
reason: The 200-million-year date belongs to Lepidoptera as a whole, the order that includes moths, not to butterflies. The 2018 fossil wing scales from the Triassic–Jurassic boundary, about 200 million years ago, are evidence of the early moth lineage and predate flowering plants. Some news headlines, such as the Washington Post's, called these 'butterflies', which loosely matches the claim. But a large 2023 study in Nature (Kawahara et al.) found that true butterflies split from moth ancestors only about 101 million years ago, in the mid-Cretaceous. Since the Nature study directly conflicts with the claim's 'at least 200 million years', I rate it contradicted.

text: Butterfly fossils have been found in rocks dating back over 200 million years to the Triassic period.
label: not_verifiable
reason: The sources conflict, mostly over what counts as a butterfly. Reliable sources do confirm Triassic-age Lepidoptera fossils. A 2018 Utrecht-led study described wing scales about 200 million years old from the Triassic–Jurassic boundary in Germany, and a later find reported scales about 236 million years old in Triassic fossilized dung. Science magazine and Live Science headlined these as the oldest butterfly fossils. However, the scales come from early moth-like Lepidoptera, not true butterflies. Wikipedia states that the oldest true butterfly fossils date to the Paleocene, about 56 million years ago, and that only Lepidoptera fossils in general go back to the Triassic–Jurassic. The claim holds if 'butterfly' loosely means Lepidoptera, but not if it means true butterflies.

text: Bорівsk Quarry in Crimea, Ukraine, is home to the longest stalactite in the world, measuring approximately 215 feet (65.6 meters) in length
label: contradicted
reason: Guinness World Records lists the world's longest free-hanging stalactite as a 28 m (92 ft) one in Gruta do Janelão in Minas Gerais, Brazil. Other sources point to Jeita Grotto in Lebanon (8.2 m). None of the sources found mention a 'Borivsk Quarry' in Crimea or a 65.6 m stalactite, so the claim conflicts with the recognized record.

text: Cassini's Divide is the largest canyon in our solar system, with a length of approximately 2,500 miles (4,000 km) and located on the planet Saturn's moon Titan, however more research is being done to confirm some details related to the feature.
label: contradicted
reason: The claim gets the feature wrong. The Cassini Division (sometimes called Cassini's Division) is not a canyon, and it isn't on Titan. It is a gap about 4,500–4,800 km wide between Saturn's A and B rings, discovered by Giovanni Cassini in 1675 and cleared by the gravitational pull of the moon Mimas. Britannica, NASA StarChild and the Planetary Society all describe it this way. It is a gap in Saturn's rings, not a feature on the surface of any moon. The solar system's largest canyon is usually given as Valles Marineris on Mars, which is roughly 4,000 km long; my search didn't directly confirm that, but the claim is wrong regardless.

text: Cassowaries are the only birds in the world capable of running faster than horses, with some reaching speeds of up to 31 miles per hour.
label: contradicted
reason: The 31 mph (50 km/h) top speed for cassowaries is correct, but the rest of the claim is wrong. Cassowaries are not the only birds that can outrun horses. Ostriches are the fastest-running birds, at roughly 60–97 km/h (38–60 mph), which is much faster than cassowaries. A cassowary's 31 mph is also slower than a horse's typical top sprint speed.

text: Clouds are so massive that a single cumulus cloud can weigh as much as 1 million pounds of water.
label: supported
reason: Reporting that cites the USGS says an average cumulus (fair-weather) cloud weighs about 1.1 million pounds. The estimate comes from a water density of roughly 0.5 g per cubic metre spread across a cloud about 1 km on each side. Since an average cloud already reaches about 1.1 million pounds, the claim that a single cumulus cloud can weigh as much as 1 million pounds of water holds up.

text: Cruising at over 36,000 feet, the fastest military aircraft ever made, the Lockheed SR-71 Blackbird, can reach speeds of up to 2,193 miles per hour.
label: supported
reason: Reliable sources, including the National Museum of the USAF, Museum of Aviation and the SAC Museum, back the main parts of the claim. The SR-71 Blackbird set an absolute speed record of 2,193 mph (2,193.167 mph) in 1976. It is described as the world's fastest operational or air-breathing manned aircraft. It operated at about 80,000 feet, with a record sustained altitude of 85,069 feet, so 'over 36,000 feet' is technically true. However, that figure understates its real cruising altitude by a wide margin. Two other wording issues are worth noting. 'Fastest' holds only for air-breathing manned aircraft, since the rocket-powered X-15 was faster. And 'can reach' is outdated, because the aircraft was retired in 1990 and again in 1998. None of these points directly contradicts the claim.

text: Denmark has the highest number of trafficilandin T pirate castles and One of the highest numbers of fortress castles.
label: not_verifiable
reason: The claim is garbled. "Trafficilandin T pirate castles" is not a recognisable category of castle, so that part of the claim cannot be checked. My search found nothing about Denmark having the most castles of any such type, or one of the highest numbers of "fortress castles." Castlemap only lists about 680 castles and fortifications in Denmark and gives no ranking that backs either part of the claim.

text: Denmark is composed of over 400 islands, with approximately 70 of those islands inhabited.
label: supported
reason: Wikipedia's Geography of Denmark page, citing Statistics Denmark, says Denmark has 443 named islands and 72 of them were inhabited as of 2007. 443 is over 400, and 72 is roughly 70, so both parts of the claim hold. One caveat: if every island larger than 100 m² is counted, the total rises to 1,419, which is still over 400.

text: Despite being massive objects, clouds can weigh a lot, with a single large cumulus cloud weighing as much as 1 million pounds of water.
label: supported
reason: Several sources, including Science Notes and EarthDate, cite an NCAR-based estimate that an average cumulus cloud weighs about 1.1 million pounds (around 500,000 kg). That is consistent with the claim that a single large cumulus cloud can weigh about 1 million pounds of water. The claim's opening phrase, 'Despite being massive objects', is oddly worded, but it doesn't change the factual point being checked.

text: Despite being the world's largest living structure, the Great Barrier Reef can be seen from space.
label: supported
reason: Reliable sources, including the Great Barrier Reef Foundation and LiveScience, say the Great Barrier Reef is the world's largest living structure and can be seen from space. Both facts in the claim are supported. The word "despite" is an odd choice, since the reef is visible because of its size, but it doesn't change the facts being claimed.

text: During the dedication of the Statue of Liberty on October 28, 1886, a giant American flag was raised to the top of Fort Wood, and a cheering crowd of over a million people were present.
label: not_verifiable
reason: The crowd part is roughly supported. Several sources say about a million people (one says over a million) came out to celebrate the dedication on October 28, 1886. Most of them were in Manhattan and the harbor, not on the island itself. However, I found no source saying a giant American flag was raised to the top of Fort Wood during the ceremony. The flag that sources do describe is a large French flag draped over the statue's face, which Bartholdi released to unveil it. That doesn't rule out an American flag at Fort Wood, but that part of the claim can't be verified, so the claim as a whole is inconclusive.

text: Eisos thrive in water temperatures  between 64°F and 85°F (17.9°C and 30.6°C).
label: not_verifiable
reason: I couldn't verify this claim. I can't tell what "Eisos" refers to: it doesn't match any species or organism I can identify. The closest result was Esox (pike), a different freshwater fish genus. None of the searches that went through mentioned Eisos or gave a water temperature range of 64–85°F (17.9–30.6°C) for it, and further searches failed because the search tool hit its usage limit. With no clear referent and no supporting or contradicting evidence, the claim can't be judged.

text: Finland has the highest number of islands of any country in the world, with approximately 179,000 islands scattered along its vast coastline.
label: contradicted
reason: The claim is wrong. Wikipedia's list of countries by number of islands puts Sweden first with 267,570 islands. Finland has fewer: about 179,000, or 198,146 in Wikipedia's updated count. Several countries, Norway among them, are also often listed with very high totals. So Finland does not have the most islands of any country. The claim's figure of about 179,000 does match a commonly cited count for Finland, though many of those islands are in lakes, not along the coast.

text: France and the United States are the only countries where the birthplace of the parents can affect the citizenship of the child.
label: contradicted
reason: The claim is wrong. Several countries use "double jus soli", where a child born in the country gets citizenship if a parent was also born there. That makes the parents' birthplace matter. A source lists about two dozen countries that apply this rule, including France, Spain, Portugal, Greece, Malta, Luxembourg, the Netherlands, Belgium and a number of West and Central African states. So France and the US are not the only ones. The source is a news/analysis site rather than a government page, but the rules it describes match how these countries' nationality laws are generally known to work.

text: France and the United States share the world's longest international border underwater, which is located in the North Atlantic Ocean between Maine, USA, and the French territory of Saint-Pierre and Miquelon.
label: contradicted
reason: Saint-Pierre and Miquelon sits off the coast of Newfoundland, and its maritime boundary is with Canada, not the United States. That boundary was set by the 1992 Canada–France arbitration. France and the US do share maritime boundaries, but they are in the Caribbean and the Pacific, not between Maine and Saint-Pierre and Miquelon. Nothing found supports the idea that this is the world's longest underwater international border.

text: Galileo Galilei was the first scientist to observe the planet Neptune in 1612, but he did not realize it was a planet at that time.
label: supported
reason: Several reliable sources back this claim. Wikipedia says Galileo's drawings show he observed Neptune on December 28, 1612, and again on January 27, 1613. Scientific American and Astronomy.com say he took it for a fixed star, about 234 years before it was recognized as a planet. Astronomy.com and Discover say Galileo may have been the first to spot Neptune; their hedged wording is consistent with the claim that he was the first to observe it.

text: Giraffes have four kneecaps, a unique characteristic among mammals, which helps them maintain balance and distribute their body weight effectively.
label: contradicted
reason: This claim is false. Giraffes do not have four kneecaps. Like other four-legged mammals, they have true knees with a kneecap (patella) only in their two hind legs. The joints that look like knees on the front legs are really wrists (carpal joints), and they have no patella. Several sources call the 'four knees' idea a common myth. Brainly says the opposite, but it is an unreliable community Q&A site and goes against basic anatomy. Since giraffes don't have four kneecaps, they also aren't unique among mammals in this way.

text: Hidden underground, the world's largest living organism is a massive fungus covering over 2,200 acres in Oregon, known as Armillaria ostoyae.
label: supported
reason: The Oregon Encyclopedia and Discover Magazine both describe the Armillaria ostoyae 'Humongous Fungus' in Oregon's Malheur National Forest. They say it covers 2,385 acres, which is over 2,200 acres, and is believed to be the largest living organism on Earth. Most of the fungus grows underground. Discover adds that some experts now question whether it holds the 'largest' title, but it is still widely described that way.

text: Hippopotamuses can hold their breath underwater for up to five minutes and are also able to sleep with their eyes, nostrils, and ears exposed to the air.
label: supported
reason: Both parts of the claim check out. National Geographic says hippos can hold their breath for five minutes, and LeoZoo says adults can do so for "up to 5 minutes". National Geographic also explains that a hippo's eyes and nostrils sit on top of its head. LeoZoo states that hippos mostly sleep immersed in water "with only their nostrils, eyes, and ears above the surface", and Animal Diversity Web describes them sleeping in shallow water. One outlier, the Copenhagen Zoo site, gives a longer breath-hold of up to 30 minutes. Most sources, including National Geographic, give about five minutes, so the claim holds up overall.

text: Honey Never Spoils is True, archaeologists have found pots of honey in ancient Egyptian tombs that are over 3,000 years old and still perfectly edible.
label: supported
reason: Lots of sources repeat this claim. They say properly stored honey basically doesn't spoil because it holds very little water, is acidic and gives off small amounts of hydrogen peroxide. They also say archaeologists have found pots of honey more than 3,000 years old in ancient Egyptian tombs that were still edible. The sources I found that state this directly are popular-science sites (My Modern Met, Dallas Express/Yahoo, Boing Boing), not peer-reviewed papers. Strictly speaking, 'never spoils' only holds if the honey is sealed and kept dry, since honey that absorbs moisture can ferment. Still, the general claim matches the sources and nothing I found contradicts it.

text: Honeybees are able to fly by using their wing muscles to generate heat, keeping their bodies at a constant temperature of around 98 degrees Fahrenheit.
label: contradicted
reason: The claim gets two things wrong. First, it says bees fly by generating heat. Heat isn't what makes them fly. Honeybees shiver their flight muscles to warm up before takeoff, and once the thorax reaches about 35°C (95°F) the muscles are warm enough to work. Second, it says bees keep a constant body temperature of about 98°F. Research on individual honeybees found little or no temperature regulation during flight except at high air temperatures. Their thorax temperature changes with conditions, with set-points near 35°C (95°F) for starting heat production and near 44°C (111°F) in the head for starting heat loss. Bees are heterothermic, so their temperature is not held constant.

text: Honeybees are able to fly by using their wings to generate electricity through a process called "triboelectric charging," where their wings interact with the air to create an electric charge.
label: contradicted
reason: Honeybees do pick up a static charge through triboelectric effects when they fly, because their bodies and wings rub against the air. But that charge is a side effect of flying. It is not what keeps them in the air. Bee flight works through aerodynamic lift from fast wing beats. Scientific sources describe the charge as something insects accumulate during flight, and they connect it to pollination and to bees sensing electric fields, not to staying aloft. The claim says bees fly by generating electricity, and that is wrong.

text: Honeybees are capable of recognizing and remembering human faces, and they can even differentiate between individual faces in a crowd.
label: supported
reason: Reliable sources back the claim, with one caveat: the bees had to be trained to do this. Dyer, Neumeyer and Chittka (Journal of Experimental Biology, 2005) trained honeybees with sugar rewards to recognise photos of human faces. The bees remembered the faces for at least two days (Phys.org) and could tell similar faces apart. JEB's summary of the study says Dyer then tested whether bees could pick out a familiar face 'from a crowd of strangers,' and that bees can recognise human faces. Scientific American likewise reports that honeybees can recognise individual human faces. Two limits apply: the faces were photographs, not real people, and the bees probably treat them as unusual flower patterns rather than understanding what a face is. Even so, the main points of the claim (recognising faces, remembering them, and telling individuals apart among several) hold up.

text: Honeybees are naturally able to fly by using electricity generated from the movement of their wings, which charges their bodies and allows them to attract pollen.
label: contradicted
reason: Bees do pick up a positive static charge while flying, from friction between their bodies and the air, and that charge helps pull negatively charged pollen onto them. But the claim says they fly by using electricity, and that is wrong. Bees stay in the air through aerodynamic lift from their muscle-powered wing beats. The charge is a side effect of flying, not what powers it. Science.org and a Current Biology review on ScienceDirect both describe the charge as coming from friction with the air, and neither says it has any role in flight.

text: Humans and dolphins are the only mammals known to give themselves names and establish unique identities within their social groups.
label: contradicted
reason: The claim is wrong because other mammals also use names. A widely reported 2024 study in Nature Ecology & Evolution found that wild African elephants use individual name-like calls for each other. Unlike dolphins, which copy the signature whistle of the animal they are addressing, elephants appear to invent these names rather than imitate the other animal's sound. So humans and dolphins are not the only mammals known to use names. Research in 2024 also reported that marmosets use vocal labels for specific individuals, though that finding comes from background knowledge and not from the search result cited here.

text: Humans and elephants share several similarities, including the longest gestation period among land animals, with pregnancies lasting almost two years, ranging around 22 months.
label: contradicted
reason: Elephants do have the longest gestation of any land mammal, at about 22 months. But the claim presents this as something humans and elephants share, which is false. Human pregnancy lasts about nine months, far shorter than an elephant's. Sources such as the International Elephant Foundation and A-Z Animals attribute the roughly 22-month gestation to elephants only and note that it is much longer than in humans.

text: Humans are the only species known to have a highly developed capacity for creating and understanding music.
label: not_verifiable
reason: The sources disagree, so the claim can't be confirmed or ruled out. Some support it: an Open Book Publishers chapter on the evolution of human musicality says humans are "evidently unique… in the way we know… and understand sounds as musical." It also cites Merker's point that vocal imitation is missing in other apes. Other sources push back. A Psychology Today piece titled "We're Not Unique" describes a sea lion and other animals keeping a beat. Discover Wildlife argues that music isn't just for humans and that birds share many musical abilities with us. Recent coverage of Honing's Current Biology review says researchers study other species to work out which parts of musicality are uniquely human, and treats that as an open question. Because whether humans are the only species with highly developed musical ability is still debated, the claim is inconclusive.

text: Humans share 50% of their DNA with bananas, highlighting the remarkable similarity in genetic makeup across different species.
label: contradicted
reason: Snopes' fact-check (republished on Yahoo News) rates the claim "Humans share 50% of their DNA with bananas" as False. It says no reading of the claim makes it factually correct. The popular figure comes from a mix-up: it refers to the share of genes that have related versions (homologs) in both species, not to identical DNA. Orthology analyses find that at most about 25% of human genes have banana counterparts. Since only about 2% of human DNA codes for proteins, the share of DNA actually in common is far smaller than 50%. The factmyth.com page that calls the claim true confuses shared genes with shared DNA and is not a reliable source.

text: In Japan, there is a vending machine for nearly everything, including umbrellas, underwear, and live crabs.
label: supported
reason: The sources I found support the claim, but the evidence for live crabs is weaker than for the other items. Several articles say Japan has vending machines for almost everything. Interesting Engineering describes it as 'a vending machine for just about everything.' Umbrella machines are well documented (Expert World Travel, CBC, Kotaku), and underwear and lingerie machines exist in Japan. Kotaku and Cloudpick note that the used-panty kind is rare or banned, but new underwear and pantyhose machines are real. For live crabs, I only found a single blog (euro-japan.de) saying Japan has a machine that sells live, fresh crab. The best-known live-crab machine was actually in Nanjing, China, and was shown on video by a Japanese reporter. Japan does have similar seafood machines, such as a live-lobster claw machine in Osaka. My search limit ran out before I could confirm a Japanese live-crab machine from a more reliable source. Overall the claim holds up, though the live-crab detail rests on one source.

text: Japan has the world's oldest hotel, the Nishiyama Onsen Keiunkan, which was founded in 705 AD and has been in operation for over 1,300 years.
label: supported
reason: Guinness World Records names the Nishiyama Onsen Keiunkan in Yamanashi, Japan, as the world's oldest hotel and says it has been operating since 705 AD. Since 705 was more than 1,300 years ago, the claim that it has run for over 1,300 years also holds. Scripps News reports the same: the hotel has been open since 705, the same family has run it for 52 generations, and Guinness recognised it in 2011.

text: K_rows of sunlight at the equator create the driest deserts on Earth.
label: contradicted
reason: The claim doesn't hold up. The phrase "K_rows of sunlight" is garbled, but whatever it means, the main point is wrong: the driest deserts are not caused by sunlight at the equator. Britannica says the Atacama, one of the driest places on Earth, is dry because of dry, sinking air from the South Pacific high-pressure cell, plus the cold Humboldt Current. That current causes a temperature inversion that produces fog and low cloud but no rain. The Atacama lies at roughly 18–30°S and Antarctica at the South Pole, so neither is at the equator. Strong equatorial heating makes air rise and brings heavy rain, which is why rainforests grow there, not deserts.

text: Measurable evidence suggests there are over 8.7 million identified species in the world although scientists estimate the actual number might be between 8.2 and 30 million species.
label: contradicted
reason: 8.7 million is not the number of identified species. It is the estimated total number of species on Earth, from Mora et al. (2011, PLoS Biology), give or take 1.3 million. ScienceDaily reports that only about 1.25 million species have been described and entered into central databases. So the claim that over 8.7 million species have been identified is false.

text: Mothers who give birth to their first child later in life tend to live longer than those who give birth at a younger age due to a lower risk of age-related diseases.
label: not_verifiable
reason: The search results back up the link itself but not the reason the claim gives for it. A UC San Diego study (Shadyab et al., American Journal of Public Health, 2016) found that women who had their first child at 25 or older were more likely to live to 90. But that study shows correlation, not cause. The researchers suggested that older first-time mothers may have higher social and economic status (more education, income and access to healthcare) and said more research is needed to find what explains the link. Other studies tie later childbirth to longer life through genetics or slower aging, but those looked at age at the last child, not the first. No source confirms that older first-time mothers live longer because they have a lower risk of age-related diseases.

text: Octopuses have a unique internal anatomy, with nine brains and a unique form of intelligence, eight of which are located in each of their arms, allowing them to process information and make decisions independently of their central brain.
label: supported
reason: Reliable sources, including London's Natural History Museum and PBS Nature, say octopuses have 'nine brains': one central brain plus a 'mini brain' in each of their eight arms, which lets each arm act on its own. Sciencing adds that the ganglia in the arms let each one act independently, sensing, tasting and moving without direction from the central brain. Some sources point out that 'nine brains' is shorthand: the arms hold neural ganglia (about two-thirds of all the octopus's neurons) rather than full brains. Still, they agree on the claim's main point, that the arms can process information locally and independently. The wording is a simplification, but the evidence overall supports the claim.

text: Octopuses have nine brains, with one central brain and eight smaller brains located in each of their八 arms.
label: supported
reason: Octonation and A-Z Animals both describe octopuses as having "nine brains": one central brain plus eight mini-brains, which are clusters of nerve cells (ganglia), one in each of the eight arms. Octonation notes that this is a popular simplification, since the arm structures are nerve centres rather than full brains. Still, the claim matches the common description these sources give.

text: Omitting the fact humans and other great apes have almost identical DNA, humans actually share about 60% of their DNA with a common fruit fly.
label: supported
reason: Several sources give a figure of about 60% for how much humans share genetically with fruit flies. Harvard Medical School says about 60% of all human genes have equivalents (orthologs) in Drosophila. The Max Planck Society says roughly 60% of the fly's genes are found in humans in a similar form, and Pfizer describes the fruit fly as "60 percent identical" to humans. Strictly speaking, the figure refers to shared or similar genes rather than identical overall DNA sequence. Even so, the claim's "about 60%" matches this widely cited figure, and none of the sources found contradicts it.

text: Owens Falls Dam, built in 1835, was the world's first hydroelectric dam of its type to be used for commercial power-generation purposes at the Listowel Lab tests mills in Canada
label: contradicted
reason: The claim is false. Owen Falls Dam, now called the Nalubaale Hydroelectric Power Station, was not built in 1835 and is not in Canada. It is on the White Nile near Jinja in Uganda. It was built between 1951 and 1954 and opened in 1954. It was not the world's first commercial hydroelectric dam, and it has nothing to do with any 'Listowel Lab tests mills' in Canada.

text: Owens Falls Dam, located in Uganda, is the world's most powerful 100-meter or lower dam in terms of power output at 380 megawatts.
label: contradicted
reason: Owen Falls Dam (now the Nalubaale Power Station) in Uganda is rated at 180 MW. The 380 MW figure only works if you add the separate 200 MW Kiira extension. The 'world's most powerful' part is clearly false: Brazil's Tucuruí Dam is just 78 m high and has 8,370 MW of installed capacity, far more than 380 MW.

text: Plants called 'zombie plants' are a result of a fungus that grows inside the plant, eventually killing it, and then controlling the dead plant to aid with spore dispersal.
label: contradicted
reason: The scientific term 'zombie plants' comes from infections by phytoplasmas, which are pathogenic bacteria, not fungi. According to Nature Reviews Microbiology and a 2015 Trends in Plant Science paper (PubMed), phytoplasma proteins such as SAP54 reprogram a living plant so that it grows leaf-like structures instead of flowers. The infected plant is left sterile and mainly serves to spread the bacteria through insect vectors like leafhoppers. Nothing in these sources describes a fungus that kills the plant and then controls the dead plant to spread spores. That description fits zombie-ant fungi such as Ophiocordyceps, not 'zombie plants.'

text: Plants release about 13 percent of the total oxygen they produce during photosynthesis through their roots.
label: not_verifiable
reason: I found no source that supports the figure of about 13% as a general amount for plants. Studies of radial oxygen loss from roots show that the share varies by species and conditions. For example, roots of the aquatic plant Vallisneria spiralis released about 7% of the plant's gross oxygen production, while a hydroponic study reported that 30–40% of oxygen was released through the roots of wetland plants. Many sources say most land plants release photosynthetic oxygen mainly through their leaves (stomata), not their roots. Because the 13% figure could not be confirmed and the reported shares vary widely, the evidence does not settle the claim.

text: Plants, such as roses and strawberries, can be grown in space, demonstrating that life can potentially thrive in microgravity environments.
label: supported
reason: NASA sources confirm that a miniature rose called 'Overnight Scentsation' flew on Space Shuttle Discovery (STS-95) and grew in the ASTROCULTURE plant chamber. It opened its buds in orbit and produced a changed 'space rose' scent. For strawberries, Purdue/NASA-linked research (Advances in Space Research, 2010) found that the 'Seascape' variety is a suitable space crop. NASA has also run strawberry studies, and Redwire has a contract to grow wild strawberries on the ISS, which would be the first ever grown in orbit. So no strawberry crop has actually been grown in orbit yet, but the evidence supports that it can be done. Many other plants, such as lettuce in Veggie, have also been grown on the ISS. Together this backs the hedged claim that plants can be grown in space and that life can potentially thrive in microgravity, though scientists note that microgravity can affect plant metabolism.

text: Polar bears are excellent swimmers and have been tracked swimming for hours or even days at a time, covering distances of up to 60 miles without resting.
label: contradicted
reason: Polar bears are strong swimmers, and some popular sources (NHPBS, polarbears.com, a Wild Kratts post) say they can swim about 60 miles without resting. But the claim sets 60 miles as the upper limit for tracked swims, and tracking data contradicts that. In a USGS study from 2004 to 2009, some bears repeatedly swam an average of about 96 miles. In 2011, a collared female in the Beaufort Sea was tracked swimming non-stop for nine days and covered about 426 miles (687 km), as reported by UPI, Live Science and WWF. Because tracked swims have gone far beyond 60 miles, "up to 60 miles" understates the record.

text: Rats are highly social creatures and are known to have formed long-lasting bonds with each other.
label: supported
reason: The RSPCA, a reliable animal welfare source, describes rats as "highly intelligent and sociable animals that form close bonds with their cage-mates and owners." Scientific papers back this up. A PMC study calls rats social animals that build social bonds and keep their groups together, and a bioRxiv study found that adult rats form peer bonds with familiar companions. None of the sources says rats lack lasting social bonds. One caveat: no source specifically says these bonds are "long-lasting." The claim is still supported overall, because close, stable bonds between cage-mates and peers are well documented.

text: Researchers at the University of California found that scientists use about 2 million sweat glands while athletes use about 4 million, surprisingly reaching as high as 5.3 million in hot conditions.
label: contradicted
reason: I found no University of California study comparing how many sweat glands scientists and athletes use. Trustworthy sources describe something different. MedlinePlus and the International Academy of Cosmetic Dermatology say a person has about 2–4 million sweat glands in total. A review on PubMed Central (PMC) puts the figure at about 2–3 million eccrine glands and says the number is fixed by around age 2–3. That means a gland count can't climb to 5.3 million in hot weather. The claim seems to take the general 2–4 million range for everyone and turn it into a made-up split between scientists and athletes. Studies of athletes do find that trained people activate more of their glands and sweat more from each gland, but they don't report these numbers.

text: Roses arranged in a specific geometric pattern can create a visual effect known as a "fleeting 'Mona Lisa' smile" when viewed from a certain angle.
label: not_verifiable
reason: I couldn't verify this claim. My searches found nothing saying that roses arranged in a geometric pattern create a 'fleeting Mona Lisa smile' when seen from a certain angle. The results were unrelated: a novel about the Mona Lisa, a blog post on the illusion in the painting's smile, and a plant called 'Mona Lisa Smile' Speedwell. None supports or contradicts the claim, and the search tool hit its usage limit before I could look further.

text: Sacc.Taglia trod  is a fungus that always turns its host into a creature with zombie-like analogy, taking control of the host completely.
label: not_verifiable
reason: I couldn't find any fungus called "Sacc.Taglia trod" in my searches, so the claim has no clear referent. "Sacc." is the standard abbreviation for the mycologist Saccardo. The name may be a garbled form of "Cordyceps unilateralis (Tul.) Sacc.", a synonym of Ophiocordyceps unilateralis, the zombie-ant fungus. Even if that is the intended species, the claim overstates the evidence. Studies say infection usually, but not always, ends this way. Penn State research also found that the fungus leaves the ant's brain intact, so it does not take complete control. Because the subject can't be identified, the claim can't be verified.

text: Scientists estimate that there are approximately 8.7 million identified species on Earth, but the actual total could be as high as 30 million.
label: contradicted
reason: The claim gets the 8.7 million figure wrong. Mora et al. (PLoS Biology, 2011) give 8.7 million (±1.3 million) as an estimate of the total number of eukaryotic species on Earth, not the number already identified. Only about 1.2 million species had been catalogued, and the study suggests roughly 86% of species on land are still undescribed. Calling 8.7 million 'identified species' therefore contradicts the source. The study does mention that experts' guesses ranged from 3 to 100 million, but that does not fix the error about identified species.

text: Scientists estimate that there are approximately 8.7 million identified species on Earth, but the total number, including undiscovered species, is believed to be much higher.
label: contradicted
reason: The claim gets the 8.7 million figure wrong. It comes from Mora et al.'s 2011 PLoS Biology study, which estimated that about 8.7 million species exist on Earth in total, counting undiscovered ones. It is not a count of identified species. Only about 1.2 to 2 million species have actually been described, so most of the 8.7 million are still unknown. The claim is right that the total is much higher than the number identified, but it treats the total estimate as the identified count.

text: Scientists estimate that there are approximately 8.7 million identified species on Earth, but this number may represent only 15% of the total number of species that exist.
label: contradicted
reason: The 2011 study by Mora et al. puts the total number of eukaryotic species on Earth at about 8.7 million. That figure is an estimate of all species, not the number already identified. Only about 1.2 to 2 million species have been formally described, so the study says about 86% of species on Earth are still undescribed. The claim gets this backwards. It calls 8.7 million the identified species and says that may be only 15% of the total, when 8.7 million is meant to be the total and the described species make up only about 14% of it.

text: Scientists estimate that there are around 8.7 million identified species on Earth, but this number may represent only a small fraction of the total number of species that actually exist.
label: contradicted
reason: The 8.7 million figure is not a count of identified species. Mora et al. (2011) gave it as an estimate of the total number of species on Earth, give or take 1.3 million. Only about 1.25 million species had been described and catalogued at that point. So the claim gets it backwards: the identified species are the small fraction, and 8.7 million is the estimated total.

text: Scientists estimate that there are between 1 and 2 trillion species on Earth, but only about 1.3 million of these have been formally described.
label: contradicted
reason: Under these definitions, the claim is contradicted. The trillion-scale figure comes from Locey & Lennon (2016), which estimated Earth may hold up to about 1 trillion species, not 1 to 2 trillion. Wikipedia says overall estimates range from 2 million to 1 trillion, with most around 11 million or fewer, and Our World in Data reports that widely cited estimates are around 8.7 million. So scientists do not generally estimate 1 to 2 trillion species. The count of described species is also off: Wikipedia lists about 1.74 million databased species (2018) and around 1.9 million described, and the IUCN listed 2.17 million in 2025, not about 1.3 million.

text: Scientists estimate that there may be between 700,000 and 1 million species on Earth that have not been formally described yet.
label: contradicted
reason: The best-known scientific estimate (Mora et al. 2011, PLoS Biology, reported by ScienceDaily and National Geographic) puts the total number of species on Earth at about 8.7 million, give or take 1.3 million. Only about 1.2 million of these have been described, so roughly 86% of species, or several million, are still undescribed. That is far more than the 700,000 to 1 million in the claim. The claim's range may be mixed up with estimates of total marine species diversity, or with the IPBES figure of 1 million species threatened with extinction.

text: Scientists have confirmed the existence of a large, underwater lake on one of Jupiter's moons, Europa, which lies beneath the surface ice and contains more water than all of Earth's oceans combined.
label: contradicted
reason: Scientists strongly suspect Europa has a global saltwater ocean under its ice shell, and estimates put it at about twice the water of all Earth's oceans combined. However, NASA describes the evidence only as strong and says Europa 'almost certainly' has an ocean. No probe has directly observed or confirmed it, and NASA's Europa Clipper mission was sent to investigate it. The claim is also wrong to call it a confirmed 'large underwater lake' (a 'lake' is a contained body of water, while the proposed ocean is global). That overstates the evidence and mischaracterizes what scientists propose.

text: Scientists have discovered an estimated 391 species of sharks, with the smallest being the dwarf lanternshark, which can fit in a human's hand.
label: contradicted
reason: The dwarf lanternshark part is right. Science News calls it the world's smallest shark, about the size of a human hand. The figure of 391 species is wrong, though. Current sources put the number of known shark species at more than 500: Science News says over 500, ActiveWild says 537, and other sites say 500+. Older estimates range from about 400 to 440 (WWF, WorldAtlas). None of the sources gives 391 as a species count. The number seems to come from a different statistic: 391 of 1,199 chondrichthyan species (sharks, rays and chimaeras) are listed as threatened.

text: Scientists have discovered that octopuses have three hearts and nine brains, with the nine 'brains' being a network of neurons located in their arms which can function independently of their central brain.
label: supported
reason: Several sources (A-Z Animals, a Notre Dame biomechanics blog, MarineBio and OctoNation) say octopuses have three hearts and are often described as having "nine brains." They also say the arms hold most of the animal's neurons and each arm can act on its own, apart from the central brain. One wording detail is off: the claim places all nine "brains" in the arms, but sources count the central brain as one of the nine, plus eight arm neuron clusters. This is a small slip and does not contradict the main claim. "Nine brains" is also a popular shorthand rather than a strict anatomical term.

text: Tarantulas have been on Earth for a long time, with fossil records showing that they existed over 100 million years ago, during the Cretaceous period.
label: supported
reason: A peer-reviewed study in the Journal of Biogeography (Wiley) says the oldest known tarantula fossil, a theraphosid in Burmese amber, dates to about 100 million years ago. That puts it in the mid-Cretaceous. The same study dates the origin of the tarantula lineage to the early Cretaceous, around 120 million years ago (range 109–132 million). This backs the claim that tarantulas are ancient and lived in the Cretaceous. One caveat: the fossil itself is dated to roughly 100 million years (Burmese amber is about 99 million years old), so 'over 100 million years ago' is approximate, not exact.

text: Tarantulas have been on Earth for a long time, with fossils of these spiders dating back around 100 million years to the Cretaceous period, during the time of the dinosaurs.
label: supported
reason: A peer-reviewed study in the Journal of Biogeography (Wiley) says it includes "the oldest theraphosid fossil from Burmese amber dated around 100 million years ago" (Wunderlich & Müller, 2020). Burmese amber of that age is mid-Cretaceous, when dinosaurs were alive, so the claim's timeframe and period are correct. Some older sources say tarantula fossils were known only from Eocene–Miocene amber, but they were written before the 2020 Cretaceous find, so they don't contradict the claim.

text: Tarantulas have been on Earth for a long time, with the earliest known tarantula-like species dating back around 165 million years to the Middle Jurassic period, during the time of the dinosaurs.
label: contradicted
reason: The claim's date and period are wrong. A peer-reviewed phylogenomic study (Foley et al., PeerJ 2021) estimates that the earliest tarantulas appeared about 120 to 105.5 million years ago, in the Cretaceous. Live Science adds that only two tarantula fossils are known, both in amber: one about 100 million years old from Myanmar and one about 16 million years old from Mexico. The 165-million-year Middle Jurassic figure matches unrelated giant spiders such as Nephila/Mongolarachne jurassica, not tarantulas. Tarantulas did live alongside dinosaurs, but there is no evidence for a tarantula-like species from 165 million years ago.

text: Tarantulas have been on the Earth for a long time, with fossil records showing that they have remained largely unchanged for over 100 million years.
label: not_verifiable
reason: The search results back up only part of the claim. A peer-reviewed study (Journal of Biogeography) says the oldest known tarantula fossil comes from Burmese amber and is about 100 million years old. Live Science reports there are only two known tarantula fossils, about 16 and about 100 million years old, and molecular dating puts the group's origin at about 120 million years ago. So tarantulas are clearly ancient. But no reliable source says the fossil record shows them 'largely unchanged for over 100 million years.' Two fossils cannot demonstrate that, and the oldest is about 100 million years old, not clearly older. Texas Parks & Wildlife Magazine, citing an expert, says the fossil record shows tarantulas virtually unchanged for more than 20 million years, a much shorter span. Popular sources that mention 100+ million years refer to how long tarantulas have existed, not to fossil evidence that they stayed unchanged. The 'remained largely unchanged for over 100 million years' part is therefore unverified.

text: Tarantulas have been on the Earth for a very long time, with fossil evidence showing they've remained largely unchanged for over 120 million years.
label: contradicted
reason: The searches don't back up the fossil part of this claim. The roughly 120-million-year figure comes from molecular dating (Foley et al., 2021), not from fossils, and that study gives an origin of about 120–105.5 million years ago, not 'over' 120 million. Smithsonian notes that well-preserved tarantula fossils are rare. A biogeography paper in the Journal of Biogeography says the oldest known tarantula fossil, preserved in Burmese amber, is only about 100 million years old. Texas Parks & Wildlife Magazine reports that fossils show tarantulas virtually unchanged for more than 20 million years, not 120 million. Tarantulas are indeed very old, but the claim that fossils show them largely unchanged for over 120 million years is contradicted.

text: The Axel Erlandson Tree Circus in California contains some of the world's most unusually shaped trees, which include a basket-weave tree with a complete basket shape made out of 6 sycamore trees.
label: supported
reason: Several sources, including Wikipedia, Dave's Garden and Futility Closet, say Axel Erlandson made his "Basket Tree" for his California "Tree Circus." He planted six sycamore trees in a circle and grafted them together into a woven, diamond-patterned basket shape. Erlandson's trees were billed as the "World's Strangest Trees" and appeared in Ripley's Believe It or Not, which supports the "most unusually shaped trees" part. Two details are a little off. First, the Tree Circus near Scotts Valley/Santa Cruz is gone: its surviving trees, including the Basket Tree, were moved to Gilroy Gardens in California in the mid-1980s, so "contains" fits the original attraction rather than a site you can visit today. Second, "complete basket shape" is a slight exaggeration of the diamond-lattice weave the sources describe. Neither point contradicts the core claim.

text: The Axel Erlandson, a Swedish farmer, created 29 fantastical tree shapes, including a spiral staircase, a tower, and a basketweave pattern, at his Tree Circus in Santa Cruz, California.
label: contradicted
reason: Axel Erlandson was a Swedish-born American farmer who ran the Tree Circus, and his trees did include Spiral Staircase and Basket Tree designs. But the claim's number is wrong: sources say he shaped about 70 trees, not 29. One source notes that by 1977 only 40 of the original 70 tree sculptures were left. The location is also off: the Tree Circus was in Scotts Valley, in Santa Cruz County, not in the city of Santa Cruz. No source mentions a 'tower' tree.

text: The Axel Heiberg Island in Canada is home to the largest known fossil forest, dating back around 400 million years.
label: contradicted
reason: The claim gets the age badly wrong. The Canadian Encyclopedia and Canadian Heritage both put the Axel Heiberg Island fossil forest at about 40 million years old, and other sources say 45–50 million years (the Eocene). None of them say anything close to 400 million years. The "largest known" part also isn't backed up by these sources, but the age alone makes the claim false.

text: The world's largest snowflake was 15 inches wide and 8 inches thick, recorded in Montana in 1887.
label: supported
reason: Several sources, citing Guinness World Records, describe the largest snowflake on record as 15 inches wide and 8 inches thick. It was reported at Fort Keogh, Montana, on January 28, 1887. The sources point out that the measurement was never scientifically verified and that many scientists doubt it, but the record itself matches every detail in the claim.

text: The world's largest snowflake was recorded in Montana in 1887 and measured a staggering 15 inches wide and 8 inches thick, according to Guinness World Records.
label: supported
reason: Several sources (WorldAtlas, NPR, Medium and History and Headlines) say Guinness World Records lists the largest snowflake ever recorded as one that fell at Fort Keogh, Montana, on 28 January 1887. They give its size as 15 inches (38 cm) wide and 8 inches thick. That matches every part of the claim. Some sources point out that the measurement was never independently verified, but this doesn't contradict what Guinness records.

text: The world's largest waterfall, by volume of water, is actually located underwater and is called the Denmark Strait Cataract, which is a submarine waterfall that occurs where the cold, dense water of the East Greenland Current flows down a slope in the ocean floor.
label: supported
reason: Several sources describe the Denmark Strait cataract as an underwater waterfall between Greenland and Iceland. They call it the world's largest waterfall, including by volume of water flow. It forms when cold, dense water from the Greenland and Nordic Seas sinks beneath the warmer water of the Irminger Sea and flows down the seafloor slope. Marine Insight connects this to the East Greenland Current, which carries cold, dense Arctic water south. Strictly speaking, scientists describe the overflow water and the East Greenland Current as related but separate flows, so naming that current as the source is a simplification. The core facts in the claim are still consistent with the sources.

text: The world's largest waterfall, by volume of water, is actually located underwater and is called the Denmark Strait Cataract, which is situated between Iceland and Greenland.
label: supported
reason: HowStuffWorks describes the Denmark Strait cataract as the world's largest waterfall. It sits underwater in the Atlantic, between Greenland and Iceland, and carries about 5 million cubic meters of water per second, far more flow than any waterfall on land. That matches every part of the claim.

text: There are approximately 8.7 million identified species on Earth, but scientists estimate that up to 80% of all species remain undiscovered.
label: contradicted
reason: The 8.7 million figure (give or take 1.3 million) from Mora et al. (2011) is an estimate of all species on Earth, not the number that have been identified. Only about 1.2 to 1.5 million species have actually been catalogued. The same study says more than 80% of species are undiscovered (86% of land species and 91% of marine species), so the claim mislabels the estimated total as the identified count.

text: This diamond was the stone brought back by the "Lucy" crew to Earth.
label: contradicted
reason: No "Lucy" crew has ever brought a stone back to Earth. NASA's Lucy is an uncrewed spacecraft that only flies past asteroids (Dinkinesh, Donaldjohanson, and later the Jupiter Trojans) and is not designed to return samples. The famous "Lucy" diamond is BPM 37093, a crystallized white dwarf star about 50 light-years away, so it was never brought to Earth either. "This diamond" has no clear referent, but the claim is false under either reading of "Lucy."

text: Tropical whales, a group of whales that live in warm waters around the world, have now been discovered to migrate thousands of miles each year to find food and mate in polar waters.
label: contradicted
reason: "Tropical whales" isn't a recognized group of whales. The claim also reverses the known migration pattern. Peer-reviewed studies and NOAA say baleen whales such as humpbacks feed in polar waters but breed and calve in tropical or subtropical waters, so they do not mate in polar waters. This pattern is long established, not a new discovery. The part about feeding in polar waters is accurate, but the parts about mating there and about a newly discovered 'tropical whale' group are contradicted.

text: Turtles have a unique respiratory system that allows them to breathe without using their lungs all the time, instead using their butts to extract oxygen from the water through a process called cloacal respiration.
label: supported
reason: McGill's Office for Science and Society, a trustworthy source, says that turtles take in oxygen through their butts by a process called cloacal respiration. It explains that oxygen diffuses in and carbon dioxide diffuses out, and that during hibernation this is a turtle's main source of oxygen. That matches the claim that turtles don't rely on their lungs all the time and can get oxygen from water through the cloaca. One caveat: this applies to some aquatic turtles, especially when they are hibernating or underwater for long periods, not to every turtle species.

text: Walruses are able to slow down their heart rate dramatically, from around 100 beats per minute to just 4-10 beats per minute, to conserve oxygen when they dive to great depths in search of food.
label: contradicted
reason: Walruses do slow their heart rate when they dive to save oxygen (SeaWorld and other sources say so), but the numbers in the claim don't hold up. In a published walrus recording on ScienceDirect, heart rate at the surface was 70–110 beats per minute. On diving it fell right away to about 15 beats per minute, then climbed back to 45–50 during the dive. It did not drop to 4–10. A separate study of wild adult male walruses found a resting rate of about 36 beats per minute (range 29–43), not around 100. The 4–8 beats per minute figure (as low as 2) comes from blue whale research, not walruses. Walruses also tend to feed in fairly shallow water (up to about 100 m), not at great depths.

text: We have two nostrils, but we can only breathe in and out of one nostril at a time, with our brain automatically switching our dominant nostril every few hours.
label: contradicted
reason: Wikipedia's article on the nasal cycle says this unconscious cycle produces "greater airflow through one nostril" that alternates between sides, and it describes "asymmetric airflow through both nostrils." So the claim is right that the dominant nostril switches automatically and periodically. It is wrong that we can only breathe through one nostril at a time: both nostrils carry air, and one simply carries more than the other.

text: Winston Churchill, the former Prime Minister of the United Kingdom, was a skilled artist and painter, and under the pseudonym 'Charles Morin' he even had his work exhibited in galleries.
label: supported
reason: The International Churchill Society says Churchill's paintings were first shown publicly in 1921 at the Galerie Druet in Paris, under the pseudonym 'Charles Morin'. Churchill is widely documented as an accomplished painter. One small caveat: the claim says 'galleries' (plural), but the evidence describes a single gallery exhibition. That doesn't contradict the core of the claim.

text: Women and men have different average heart rates, with women's averaging in the range of 78-82 beats per minute and men's averaging around 70-74 beats per minute.
label: supported
reason: Hinduja Hospital's article says women's average heart rate is 78–82 bpm and men's is 70–72 bpm. Healthline-style health sources commonly give the same figures, but I didn't check them in this search. The claim's 78–82 bpm for women matches exactly. Its men's figure of 'around 70–74' is a little wider than the source's 70–72, but it includes that range and doesn't conflict with it. The source also says the two averages differ, which matches the claim.

text: styleUrls are used to correctly apply styles in next.js

None of the sources mention `styleUrls` as a way to style a Next.js app.

text: tasar lake, the world's largest saltwater lake, is located in India's himalayan region of ladakh.

The closest names are Tarsar Lake and Satsar Lake, but both are freshwater alpine lakes in Jammu and Kashmir (Anantnag and Ganderbal districts), not Ladakh.

text: The shortest war in history was between Britain and Zanzibar on August 27, 1896, and lasted only 38 minutes.

text: Butterflies taste with their feet, which helps them detect the sweetness or bitterness of a substance.
label: supported
reason: Several sources, including Carleton University's Department of Biology and ScienceABC, say butterflies have contact chemoreceptors on their tarsi (feet) that work like taste buds. ScienceABC and other sources say these receptors detect sugars and bitter compounds as well as salts, which helps butterflies tell sweet from bitter and choose food and egg-laying sites. I found no source that contradicts the claim.
